en: The first chapter: [An exposition of] the Self, which consists of reality, consciousness, and bliss; which is the locus of the false manifold of duality based on the illusory status of the subject; and which is the object of the non-dual cognition arising from the crest of the Vedic revelation.
Having attained liberation—which consists of being solely absorbed in supreme bliss through the shaking off of false bondage—Viṣṇu himself triumphs, free from all conceptual constructions. ||1||

Salutations to the dust raised from the feet of those who have directly realized the oneness of Śrī Rāma, Viśveśvara, and Mādhava, and whose darkness and passion have been shaken off by the touch [of that realization]. ||2||
Compositions of vast extent, composed by many wise men for the sake of others, prevail;
but this labor of mine will surely serve only to nourish my own self-interest here. (3)
Having carefully compiled this collection of scriptures, this *Advaitasiddhi* was composed with great effort by the sage Madhusūdana, whose wealth is faith;
may it serve for the awakening and victory over disputants of those in haste, and bring joy to the wise. ||4||

Regarding the investigation of conflicting views (*vipratipatti-vicāra*): since the establishment of non-duality (*advaita-siddhi*) is preceded by the establishment of the falsity of duality (*dvaita-mithyātva*), it is the falsity of duality alone that must first be demonstrated. And demonstration occurs through both the proof of one's own position and the refutation of the opposing position; therefore, both of these must be accomplished by resorting to one of the three forms of discourse—namely, debate (*vāda*), sophistry (*jalpa*), or cavil (*vitaṇḍā*). Furthermore, because doubt generated by conflicting views is an essential limb of investigation, the mediator (*madhyastha*) must first present the conflicting views.

Although doubt produced by conflicting opinions (vipratipatti) is not useful for establishing the status of a subject (*pakṣatā*), because that status—consisting of the absence of a proving means accompanied by the absence of a desire to prove—is not constituted by doubt. Otherwise, there would be no inference of the Self through inferential desire in one who has already ascertained the Self through scripture. Furthermore, since doubt is impossible for the proponent and others who possess certainty, and because an artificial doubt (*āhārya-saṃśaya*) leads to over-extension (*atiprasañjaka*).

Nor does contradiction (vipratipatti) serve a purpose by its very nature as the means for adopting a thesis and a counter-thesis; for since that is obtained from the words of the neutral arbiter alone—such as "this must be proven by you" and "this must be refuted by him"—contradiction would be redundant. Nevertheless, even though the doubt produced by contradiction is not a constituent part of inference, it nonetheless serves as a constituent of inquiry (vicāra) precisely because it is something to be dispelled.

Even though a disagreement (*vipratipatti*) does not produce such a doubt because it is obstructed by certainty (*niścaya*) or other factors in some cases, it remains *svarūpayogya* (capable by its very nature) to do so. Furthermore, there is no rule that the disputants (*vādin*, etc. must possess certainty; for the statement "two who have ascertained [the truth] engage in debate" refers only to those who possess what they merely imagine to be certainty. This is because we observe that even those who are arrogant and possess contrary certainties proceed to engage in *jalpa* (contentious debate) and the like, even while relying on the opponent's position. Therefore, just like the binding of the rules of debate, the arbiter (*madhyastha*) must indeed present the disagreement in order to fulfill his own duty.

Regarding that falsity (*mithyātva*), there is a disagreement as follows: Is that which is distinct from consciousness (*cid-bhinna*), which is fit to be perceived as existing while being unsublatable by any cognition other than the valid knowledge of Brahman, the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) of an absolute negation (*traikālika-niṣedha*) within its own locus (*pratipanna-upādhi*), or not? Or, is it the counter-correlate of such a negation when considered in its aspect of ultimate reality (*pāramārthikatva*), or not?

In this context, since the intended goal is the establishment of the probandum (*sādhya*) by way of co-inherence with the delimitant of the subjecthood (*pakṣatāvacchedaka-sāmānādhikaraṇyena*), there arises the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) even when the probandum is established in only one part of the subject. According to this view, the qualification "not sublated by anything other than the knowledge of Brahman" (*brahmajñānetarābādhyatva*) is added as a specific attribute of the subject (*pakṣaviśeṣaṇa*) in order to exclude the proving of what is already established in the case of the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell. However, if, on the other hand, the intended goal were the establishment of the probandum precisely by way of the delimitant of the subjecthood (*pakṣatāvacchedakāvacchedena*), then even if the probandum were established in only one part [of the subject], the fallacy of *siddhasādhana* would not occur; consequently, the aforementioned qualification for the purpose of excluding that fallacy would be unnecessary.

However, the other two qualifiers must indeed be respected in order to exclude sublation (*bādha*) in the case of the void (*tuccha*) and Brahman. Alternatively, there may be a separate dispute for each: "Is the ether (*viyat*) false, or not? or "Is the earth false, or not? Thus, even though the ether and so forth are individually the subjects (*pakṣa*), there is no fallacy of being a doubtful inconclusive reason (*sandigdhānaikāntikatā*) regarding a jar or similar objects, because a jar and such are equivalent to the subject (*pakṣasama*). For instance, since a doubt regarding the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*) in the subject is favorable [to the inference], its status as a defect must be asserted only when it occurs outside the subject.

For this very reason it has been said: "Doubtful inconclusiveness (*sandigdhānaikāntikatā*) exists precisely when there is doubt regarding the reason in that which possesses the certainty of the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāvaniścayavat*). Subjecthood (*pakṣatva*), however, consists in possessing doubt regarding the probandum, or alternatively, in possessing the absence of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes the probandum. And this [latter definition] is common to jars and other such things. For this very reason, even in those cases, doubtful inconclusiveness is not a fault. As for the statement that they are "equal to the subject" (*pakṣasama*), it is merely on account of their lacking the status of being the object of the thesis (*pratijñā*). Nor, then, is subjecthood simply the status of being the object of the thesis; for that is absent in inference for oneself (*svārthānumāna*).

Thus, regarding this misconception (*vipratipatti*), there are the formal arguments (*prayoga*) of the ancients: "The subject of dispute is false, because it is visible, because it is insentient (*jaḍa*), and because it is limited, like the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell. One need not insist on the individual members of the syllogism. Here, the delimitation of the subject (*pakṣatāvaccheda*) by means of the misconception—which is its own regulator and is thus parsimonious—is not contradictory, due to the intervention of the agreement (*samayabandha*) and so forth. Even though that [misconception] does not exist at the time of the inference, it serves as the delimitation of the subject by way of being a secondary indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*).

Alternatively, the delimitor of the object of dispute (vipratipatti) itself is the delimitor of the subject (pakṣatāvacchedaka). Thus, there is no fault in the fact that even in the formulations of the ancients, the term "disputed" (vimata) is intended to refer to that which is delimited by the delimitor of the object of dispute.

Now, what is this "falsity" (*mithyātva*) that is being established? It cannot be "indefinability" (*anirvacanīyatva*), defined as the state of not being the locus of either existence or non-existence, on the basis of the *Pañcapādikā* statement: "The word 'false' (*mithyā*) denotes indefinability. For is that [indefinability] (1) the absence of existence qualified by non-existence; or (2) a pair of properties consisting of the absolute absence of existence and the absolute absence of non-existence; or (3) a qualified property consisting of the absolute absence of non-existence while possessing the absolute absence of existence? Not the first.

The first [position] is not tenable, because in this world, which is the substratum of existence (*sattva*), one does not admit a "being" that is distinct from existence; furthermore, if one were to prove the absence of a distinct entity, it would result in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*). Nor is the second [position] tenable, because if either existence or non-existence is absent, the presence of the other is necessary, leading to a contradiction (*vyāghāta*). Moreover, there is the fallacy of proving something else (*arthāntara*), since even in the absence of existence—as in the case of Brahman devoid of attributes—it can be established as non-false by virtue of its being of the nature of Being (*sad-rūpa*).

Furthermore, because in the case of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell (*śuktirūpya*), there is the presence of existence (*sattva*)—defined as non-sublatedness—the absence of non-existence (*asattva*)—defined as sublatedness—is unestablished; thus, the probandum (*sādhya*) is deficient. For this very reason, the third alternative is not tenable, as it suffers from contradiction (*vyāghāta*) as before, as well as from the fallacy of proving something other than what was intended (*arthāntara*) and deficiency of the probandum. If this is argued, we say: not so. There is no fault if one intends to speak of two properties consisting of the absolute absence of existence (*sattvātyantābhāva*) and the absolute absence of non-existence (*asattvātyantābhāva*). Nor is there any contradiction.

Is that [non-existence] because existence and non-existence are of the nature of mutual exclusion, or because they are mutually exclusive pervaders, or because they are mutually exclusive pervadeds? Among these, it is not the first, because that is not accepted. For in this context, non-existence is not the absence of existence in the form of being uncontradicted throughout the three times; rather, it is the state of not being the locus of being perceived as existent under any limiting condition (upādhi). And its absence is what is intended to be the probandum (sādhya).

And thus, the probandum (sādhya) is established as being perceived as existent in some locus of limitation (upādhi), while being distinct from that which is sublated at the three times. This being the case, there is no deficiency of the probandum even in the case of the silver in a shell, because the absence of non-existence in the form of being sublated does not enter into the definition of the probandum. Nor is there a contradiction, since there is no mutual exclusion between the two. For this very reason, the second [alternative] is also not tenable.

There is no deviation (vyabhicāra) [in the reason] because, in the case of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell—which lacks existence—there exists the exclusion of the intended non-existence. Nor is the third [alternative] tenable, because it involves contradiction and lacks logical necessity; for although cowhood and horsehood are mutually exclusive, their absences are perceived together in a single place, such as a camel. Furthermore, as for the objection that there is a "shifting of the subject" (arthāntara)—on the grounds that even if Brahman, being devoid of attributes, lacks existence, the world may still be non-illusory by virtue of its being of the nature of "Being" (sadrūpa), just as Brahman is of the nature of "Being"—that is not correct.

Since the existence of "Being" (*sat*) is established everywhere by means of that single [property] which is common to all, there is no evidence for postulating that the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) possesses the nature of Being in each individual instance—as in the case of Brahman—nor does such a postulation lead to the undesirable consequence of the absence of a common linguistic usage (*anugatavyavahāra*). Alternatively, the two types of difference—the difference having "Being" as its counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) and the difference having "non-Being" as its counter-correlative—may be the probandum (*sādhya*). Thus, whether [the world] possesses both natures or either one of them, such differences would be impossible; consequently, there is no room for a different object [than the probandum] resulting from those two.

Nor should it be argued that there is a partial *siddhasādhana* (proving what is already established) because the portion consisting of non-existence and the variety of non-existent things (*asad-bheda*) are already established within the phenomenal world (*prapañca*). Just as in the syllogism of the proponents of difference-and-non-difference (*bhedābheda-vādin*), "Quality and so forth are both different and non-different from the substance possessing quality (*guṇin*) and so forth, because they have a common substratum," there is no *siddhasādhana*—even though the "difference" accepted by the logicians (*tārkika*) and others is established, yet the intended cognition (*uddeśya-pratīti*) is not established—so too in the present case, since the intended object is the cognition of the combined [elements], there is no *siddhasādhana*.

Just as, because the co-referential cognition "pot" and "jar" is not observed when there is no difference in reality (*tattva*), the establishment of the combined [condition] is the intended goal, so too in the present case, since "visibility" is not observed in that which is devoid of existence (*sattva*)—namely, the *tuccha* (the absolutely non-existent)—the establishment of the combined [condition] as its necessary determinant is likewise the intended goal; thus, the two cases are identical.

For this very reason, it is also correct to state that the qualified probandum (*sādhya*) consists in the absolute absence of non-existence while being characterized by the absolute absence of existence. Nor should it be argued that if the probandum is either the conjoined [pair] or the qualified [entity], there would be the fallacy of an unestablished qualification (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*) because such a thing is nowhere established; for since each [member] is established individually, establishing the conjoined or the qualified is no different from establishing a horn belonging to a rabbit simply because horns and rabbits are each established individually.

Because such a well-known usage has been stated only in the case of "silver in a mother-of-pearl shell. Nor is there an over-extension (*ativyāpti*) of the definition to Brahman on the grounds that Brahman is devoid of attributes (*nirdharmaka*), since it is empty of the two attributes of existence and non-existence; for Brahman, being of the nature of existence (*sadrūpa*), is not the locus of the absolute absence of that [existence], and because, precisely by virtue of being devoid of attributes, it is not the locus of attributes in the form of absences. This is the direction of the argument. Thus ends the investigation into falsity (*mithyātva*) as the state of being distinct from both the real and the unreal. ||1||

Alternatively, falsity (*mithyātva*) is the state of being the counter-positive of a negation that holds across the three periods of time within the locus in which it is perceived. Now, an objection may be raised: if the negation across the three periods of time within the perceived locus were *tāttvika* (ultimately real), there would be a loss of non-duality (*advaita*). If it were *prātibhāsika* (illusory), it would be a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*). Even if it were *vyāvahārika* (empirically real), since such a negation is sublatable, it would not contradict ultimate existence; thus, there would be the fallacy of shifting the subject matter (*arthāntara*), the scripture of non-duality would fail to reveal the truth, and the world (*prapañca*), as the counter-positive of that negation, would have to be *pāramārthika* (ultimately real) rather than illusory.

If it is argued that this is not so, [we reply]: although the negation is ultimately real because it is non-different from Brahman, who is the substratum of the negation of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), it does not entail the loss of non-duality (*advaita*). Nor does it follow that the phenomenal world—which is the counter-positive of an ultimately real negation—must itself be ultimately real; for there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of imagined things like the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell, which are counter-positives of an ultimately real negation yet are themselves not ultimately real. Alternatively, this negation is simply not ultimately real. Even if it is not ultimately real, it is not merely illusory (*prātibhāsika*), but rather empirical (*vyāvahārika*).

Nor should it be argued that, because the negation is sublated, it does not contradict ultimate existence and is therefore a different matter; for we observe that the object of a dream is sublated by the negation of that very dream-object. The fact that a negation is sublated is not the determining factor (*tantram*) for its non-contradiction with ultimate existence; rather, it is its having a lower degree of reality (*sattā*) than the object to be negated. And in the present case, since both possess an equal degree of reality, why should there not be contradiction? Nor should it be argued that if the negation itself is negated, it would entail the existence of the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*).

For in that case, where the existence of the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) is established by the cognition of the negation of a negation, there is indeed the existence of the counter-positive upon the negation of the negation; it is not merely the negation itself that is negated. For example, after the cognition "this is not silver" regarding what is actually silver, the cognition "this is not non-silver" establishes the existence of silver. However, where there is a negation of both the counter-positive and its negation, there is no existence of the counter-positive.

Just as at the time of destruction there is a negation of both the prior absence and its counter-positive, so too in the present case, because the sublater of the negation sublates both the counter-positive—the phenomenal world—and that negation itself, the world does not possess ultimate reality merely because the negation is sublated. This is because the delimitors of negatability for both are equal, such as "being perceptible" (dṛśyatva) and so forth. Nor does it follow that the scripture lacks authority if it conveys a negation that is non-ultimate.

For it is impossible for the Śruti to be non-authoritative when it teaches that the world-phenomenon (*prapañca*), which is distinct from Brahman, is unreal (*atāttvika*) by virtue of its being a negation and so forth.

Now, one might ask: is this state of being the counter-correlate (*pratiyogitva*) of that negation [of the world] in its own nature (*svarūpeṇa*), or without sublation of its nature as something distinct from the non-existent (*asadvilakṣaṇa-svarūpa-anupamardena*), or in the form of ultimate reality (*pāramārthikatvākāreṇa*)? It cannot be the first, because it is impossible to negate the threefold temporal existence (*traikālika-niṣedha*) of ether (*viyat*) and the like—which have their origin established by the Śruti and other means, are capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā-samartha*), are produced with ignorance (*avidyā*) as their material cause, and are destroyed by the knowledge of reality—nor of silver and the like, in their nature as distinct from the non-existent, which exists at the time of cognition. Nor can it be the second;

If it is argued that this is not so—because ultimate reality, defined as non-sublatability, is dependent upon falsity, defined as sublatibility, resulting in mutual dependence; and because if ultimate reality were negated in its own right, the defect stated in the first position would arise, whereas if it were negated in the form of ultimate reality, there would be an infinite regress—then we reply: not so. For we accept that the world and the silver in a shell are counter-entities to a negation of all three times precisely in their own right (*svarūpeṇa*).

For instance: following the error of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell, when there is the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of the true nature of the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*), one perceives that "the silver does not exist, did not exist, and will not exist" precisely in its own form (*svarūpeṇa*). Likewise, through the scriptural text "not here, not manifold" (*neha nānā*), there is the cognition of the negation of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) precisely in its own form. Nor should it be argued that in that case, only the empirical, ultimate silver (*laukikaparamārtharajata*) is the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) of negation in its own form; for that would result in a lack of co-referentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) between the error and its sublation, and it would also entail the negation of something that was never presented as a possibility (*aprasaktapratiṣedha*).

In that case, it does not follow that origination and so forth are impossible. For having a nature that is not negated is not the determining factor for possessing origination and so forth; for [the Naiyāyikas] do not admit the origination and so forth of space and other such things, even though they accept them as having a nature that cannot be negated by others. Rather, some other factor, such as the intrinsic nature of the thing itself, must be stated as the cause. Since I too accept that [factor], even though it is imagined by me.

Nor should it be argued that this would constitute a loss of position [on our part] because, regarding the negation of the three times, silver present in the marketplace is the counter-positive either by way of its own nature (*svarūpeṇa*) or by way of its ultimate reality (*pāramārthikatva*), or else as being illusory (*prātibhāsika*). For the meaning of this statement of the Teacher is that the counter-positive is precisely the illusory silver perceived through identification (*tādātmya*) with the ultimately real worldly silver. And the word "or" (*vā*) expresses indifference as to whether that [illusory silver] exists by way of its own nature or by way of ultimate reality.

This much has been stated for the purpose of refuting the view that silver is perceived solely through identity with that which is present before one, and in order to demonstrate that it is also perceived through identity with silver that is both worldly and ultimately real.

This has been stated in the *Tattvapradīpikā*: "Therefore, the statement of the former teachers—that only empirical-transcendental silver (*laukikaparamārtha-rajata*) is the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) of the negation 'this is not silver'—must be understood by accepting that it is the counter-correlate of a negation such as 'this [which was] perceived at the present time as empirical-transcendental silver is not empirical-transcendental silver even at the three times,' since we observe the activity of one desiring silver toward what is present before them."

The intention is as follows: since it is established by the force of linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*) that the negative particle (*nañ*) necessarily conveys mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) when the substratum (*dharmin*) and the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) are presented by words ending in the same case-suffix—as in the sentence "A pot is not a cloth"—it is established that the sentence "This is not silver" conveys mutual non-existence. Consequently, because the cognition produced by the verbal expression is identical to the cognition expressed by the words, the cognition expressed by the sentence "This is not silver" [is of the nature of mutual non-existence].

The cognition [of "this is not silver"] has as its object precisely the mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*) [of the two]. Thus, when there is a cognition of the mutual absence of the empirical silver (*vyāvahārikarajata*)—denoted by the word "silver"—from the illusory silver (*prātītikarajata*) indicated by the word "this" (the object present before one), the falsity (*mithyātva*) is established by implication (*ārthika*). However, the cognition expressed by the sentence "there is no silver here" has absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) as its object; for it is a rule that the negative particle (*nañ*) conveys a relation of non-existence only between a substratum (*dharmin*) and a counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) presented by words ending in different case-terminations.

And since that [negation] takes as its object the empirical absolute non-existence of the very silver perceived in front of one, falsity (mithyātva) is indeed explicitly stated. Therefore, there is no violation of established doctrine, no occurrence of the theory of misapprehension (anyathākhyāti), nor any contradiction with the text; thus, the position is faultless.

But surely, in this way, there would be the consequence of absolute non-existence (*atyantāsattva*). For the state of being the counter-positive of a negation throughout the three periods of time within a locus that has been apprehended—which is the definition of non-existence—results in being the counter-positive of a negation throughout the three periods of time in all places, as is the case with objects like a pot whose non-existence elsewhere is well-established. Otherwise, it would follow that they exist elsewhere; yet you yourself have stated that their existence elsewhere is impossible. And if that is so, how can there be a distinction from the non-existent? For there is no other form of non-existence for things such as a hare’s horn than this.

Nor is its non-existence merely its being "without designation" (*nirupākhyatva*), for it is designated by the very word "without designation. Nor is non-existence its being unperceived, for if the non-existent were not perceived, it would be impossible to have knowledge of its distinction from the existent, to negate the perception of the existent, or even to employ the word "non-existent. Nor is it its being unperceived through direct intuition (*aparokṣatayā*), as that would over-apply (*ativyāpti*) to eternal supersensible things. If this is argued, it is not so; for although being the counter-correlate (*pratiyogitva*) of a negation across all three periods of time is common to both the "void" (*tuccha*) and the "indescribable" (*anirvācya*).

Nevertheless, absolute non-existence (*atyantāsattva*) is the state of being unfit for cognition as existing under any condition whatsoever (*upādhi*). And since that [state] does not exist at all in the case of shell-silver or the phenomenal world prior to sublation (*bādha*), there is no consequence of their being "void" (*tuccha*). Nor is it the case that shell-silver or the phenomenal world is not cognized as existing prior to sublation. This very point is indicated by the word *upādhi*, which carries the sense of "existence."

This is because the proponents of emptiness (*śūnyavādins*), by not accepting an illusion that has a real substratum (*sadadhiṣṭhānaka-bhrānti*), do not admit—either in the case of nacre-silver or in the phenomenal world—that there is a distinction from the non-existent (*asadvailakṣaṇya*) consisting in the fitness for being perceived as existing in some locus (*kvacid-upādhau sattvena pratītyarhatva*).

[Objection: But if this is so, the definition results in "being the counter-positive of an absolute absence whose locus is every existent" (*yāvatsad-adhikaraṇaka-atyantābhāva-pratiyogitva*). And thus, for the logicians (*tārkikas*), there would be the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) in the case of space and the like, which are the counter-positives of absolute absences that are purely positive (*kevalānvayin*).

If the intended meaning is that "the falsity of a thing consists in its being the counter-positive of an absolute non-existence residing in its own locus," then—even if one excludes non-occurrence by using the term "locus"—there remains the unavoidable *siddhasādhana* (proving what is already established) regarding all things that possess occurrence; for whatever is the locus of a jar by way of either the relation of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) or the relation of inherence (*samavāya*), it is the counter-positive of an absolute non-existence of that jar residing in itself by way of either the relation of inherence or the relation of conjunction.

If it is argued that there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) regarding non-pervasive entities such as conjunction (*saṃyoga*), because the intended meaning is that "whatever is the locus of *x* by whatever relation, *x* possesses the property of being the counter-positive of an absolute absence residing in that [locus] by that same relation," we say no. This is because the phrase "as it is apprehended" (*pratipanna*) indicates the property of being the counter-positive of an absolute absence residing in that [locus] specifically in the form under which it is apprehended as the locus of something. And that "form" consists of both the specific relation and the specific delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*).

For indeed, the status of being the locus (*adhikaraṇatā*) of a jar on the ground is not perceived without a specific relation, nor is the status of being the locus of conjunction with a monkey in a tree perceived without a specific delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*).

Thus, when it is established that the falsity (*mithyātva*) of an object consists in its being the counter-positive (*pratiyogitva*) of an absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) residing in that very locus by means of that very same specific relation and that very same specific delimiting factor—by which specific relation and which specific delimiting factor the cognition of its locus-hood ought to occur—wherein lies the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*)?

If, moreover, absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) were not the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) of space and so forth—just as destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) and prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) are—then it would be for the same reason that there is an absence of any proving evidence. This is because a perceptual cognition such as "here there is no space" is impossible; because in inference there is a lack of a supporting argument (*anukūlatarka*); and because, by the mere fact of being observed in general (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭa*), it would follow that even the counter-correlativity of destruction and prior non-existence would be established [without proof]; and because there is no impossibility of any effect occurring in the absence of space.

Thus, since there is no evidence for the existence of the absence of a jar on a floor that possesses a jar by way of the relation of conjunction (*saṃyoga*), and because it is simpler to postulate that the state of being co-located with a jar is opposed [to the absence] precisely by virtue of being an absolute absence (*atyantābhāva*) of a jar—rather than introducing specific relations which would involve prolixity (*gaurava*)—the cognition is satisfactorily explained as having merely the absence of the inherence (*samavāya*) of a jar and so forth as its object. Furthermore, since the relationship of locus and located (*ādhārādheyabhāva*) is established by perception, no suspicion arises that the jar is non-existent [therein]; and this is also due to the reasoning already stated. Therefore, [the objection does not hold].

There is co-occurrence (sāmānādhikaraṇya) of a jar and so forth with its absolute non-existence. Likewise, there is no single locus for conjunction and its absence; for the cognition "the tree is conjoined with the monkey at the top, but not at the root" is accounted for by the fact that only the top and the root possess conjunction and its absence respectively. Therefore, falsity (mithyātva) should be understood as being the state of being the counter-positive (pratiyogitva) of an absolute non-existence residing in pure existence (sanmātra).

Nor should it be argued that, since existence and non-existence are not contradictory under such circumstances, there could be no relationship of sublated and sublator (*bādhyabādhakabhāva*) between the cognitions of them; for while there is no contradiction between things of different levels of reality (*bhinnasattāka*), there is indeed contradiction between things of equal levels of reality (*samasattāka*). This is because of the rule: where a particular jar has a conventional (*vyāvahārika*) absolute non-existence on a certain ground, that jar cannot be conventionally present there.

And it should not be argued that, this being the case, since the absence that has become the object of the cognition "this is nacre, not silver" is of a *vyāvahārika* (empirical) nature, even if the *vyāvahārika* status of the silver perceived as present before one is removed, its *prātītika* (illusory) existence is not removed; consequently, the cognition "this is silver" would persist even after sublation (*bādha*). For in that instance, through the immediate valid cognition (*aparokṣapramā*) "this is nacre," the ignorance which is the material cause (*upādāna*) of the illusory silver is destroyed, and thereby even its *prātītika* existence is removed.

Since the ignorance regarding the mother-of-pearl (*śukti*) is the material cause (*upādāna*) of the illusory silver (*prātītika-rajata*), the non-existence of that [ignorance] necessarily entails the non-existence of the illusory silver. For this very reason, in cases where the ignorance that is the material cause of the error is not removed by a remote (parokṣa) cognition of the substrate, even though its empirical status (*vyāvahārikatva*) is sublated, its illusory status (*prātītikatva*) is not sublated; consequently, the cognition "the jaggery is bitter" and so forth continues to persist.

Prior to the direct realization of the partless Brahman, even though the empirical reality of the phenomenal world is sublated by indirect knowledge, its appearance nevertheless persists; however, once the ignorance regarding the substrate is removed, it will no longer persist.

By this term "upādhi," if one intends merely a locus (*adhikaraṇa*), there is a shift in meaning (*arthāntara*); for even though color is the counter-positive of an absolute non-existence whose locus is air, it is not unreal. However, if one intends it as the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*), then since the object of the ignorance that is the material cause of the error is the substratum, there is circularity (*anyonyāśrayatva*): the falsity of the object depends on the erroneous nature of the cognition, and the erroneous nature of the cognition depends on the falsity of the object. This is refuted, because—as explained above—there is no such defect if one intends it as a locus.

Nor should it be argued that there is over-extension (*ativyāpti*) [of the definition] to Brahman because, according to the scripture stating "That indeed is below," Brahman does not exist in reality within the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of space, time, and so forth; for in that attributeless (*nirdharmaka*) entity, there is an absence of any property such as being the counter-positive (*pratiyogitva*) of non-existence. Nor should it be argued that, if this were the case, even reality (*satyatva*) would not belong to it, and thus there would be a contradiction with scriptures such as "Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, Infinite."

Since we do not accept the existence of an absence that is distinct from its locus, there is no contradiction in the fact that truth—which consists in the absence of the aforementioned falsity—is the very nature (*svarūpa*) of Brahman. By this, self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*) and other attributes are also explained. For self-luminosity is simply the absence of being illuminated by another; eternity is the absence of limitation by time; omnipresence is the absence of limitation by space; and fullness is the absence of limitation by substance, and so forth.

Thus, although Brahman is not the substratum of positive attributes (*bhāvarūpadharma*), there is no inconsistency whatsoever in its being of the nature of the absence of all [positive] attributes; everything is therefore clear.
Thus concludes the investigation into the second form of falsity, characterized by being distinct from both existence and non-existence.

Alternatively, falsity (*mithyātva*) is the state of being removable by knowledge. Now, an objection is raised: there is over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to a prior cognition which is removed by a subsequent cognition, and under-extension (*avyāpti*) to objects such as a jar which are removed by the falling of a mallet and the like. Even if one intends to mean "removability by knowledge" in the sense of being removed by knowledge qua knowledge (*jñānatvena*), this same defect remains; furthermore, in the case of shell-silver and the like—which are removed by the direct realization of the substrate—there is a lack of the probandum (*sādhyavikalatā*), because they are not removed by knowledge qua knowledge.

If it is argued that there is an over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), which are subsumed under the category of knowledge and yet are not destroyed by knowledge—since they are destroyed by knowledge in the form of memory—this is not so. For "being destructible by knowledge" means being the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) of the general absence of persistence brought about by knowledge. And persistence is twofold: as an intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) and as a causal state (*kāraṇātman*), according to the acceptance of the theory of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*).

And thus, although by the blow of a hammer there is an absence of the jar's persistence in its own form, there is no absence of its persistence in the form of its cause; therefore, that [destruction] is indeed brought about by the knowledge of Brahman, and so there is no lack of pervasion (avyāpti) in the case of a past jar or the like. For this very reason, there is no "proving what is already established" (siddhasādhana) regarding a prior cognition that is to be sublated by a subsequent cognition; nor is there the fallacy of shifting the subject matter (arthāntara), because even though the ether and other elements are destroyed by the knowledge of Brahman, their falsity is not established in the same manner as that [prior cognition].

Because a prior cognition that has been sublated by a subsequent cognition cannot persist through its own causal nature, it is impossible for it to lack the general property of persistence (*avasthitisāmānya*). Although things such as a hare’s horn lack this general property of persistence, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) [of the definition], because that absence is not caused by a sublating cognition. Furthermore, since the existence of nacre-silver and the like at the time of their appearance must be admitted—otherwise their direct perception would be inexplicable—their absence does not occur without a sublating cognition; thus, there is no deficiency in the probandum (*sādhyavikalatā*).

For this very reason, the Vivaraṇācāryas have stated: "The cessation of ignorance through knowledge—whether together with its effects that have been dissolved or those that are currently present—is sublation (bādha). And the Vārtikakāras have also stated:
"By the mere arising of the correct cognition produced by sentences such as 'That thou art,' ignorance, along with its effects, has not existed, does not exist, and will not exist."

The statement "it does not exist together with its effect" intends the cessation [of ignorance] along with the effect that has already dissolved; however, the statement "it will not exist together with its effect" intends the cessation of future effects—these are distinct matters. Ignorance, which is the material cause of silver, ceases through the direct realization of the substrate (adhiṣṭhāna) along with its own effect, whether that effect is currently present or already dissolved.

Because we admit the distinction between various ignorances (*ajñāna*) which serve as the material causes (*upādāna*) for their respective errors, there is no deficiency of the probandum (*sādhyavaikalya*) in the illustrative example. This is because, just as there is the cognition "the jar does not exist" after the falling of a mallet, the cognition "the ignorance of the mother-of-pearl and the silver inherent in it do not exist" immediately following the knowledge of the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*) is universally accepted. Furthermore, it is also correct to define [ignorance] as that which is removable by knowledge through a property subsumed under the category of "knowing" (*jñānatva*).

Furthermore, the sublation of a prior cognition by a subsequent cognition does not occur through a property coextensive with the nature of cognition (*jñānatva*); rather, it occurs through the state of being a specific quality of the self that arises later (*udīcyātmaviśeṣaguṇatva*) or through the state of being posterior (*udīcyatva*). Thus, there is no fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*). Nor is there an over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), which are not sublated by desire and the like but are sublated by cognition, because there is no evidence that memory, as such (*smṛtitvena*), sublates its own impression.

For it is established by experience that when memory arises, the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) becomes firm; and their firmness consists in the multiplicity of impressions regarding the same object, so there is no fault. In reality, however, what is intended is "being removable by knowledge through its nature as direct intuition" (*sākṣātkāratvena*); therefore, the previously mentioned fault does not apply. Nor is there over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to doubt, which—though being removable by knowledge—is a property subsumed under the category of knowledge in its nature as certainty (*niścayatvena*). Thus, everything is clear. This concludes the investigation into the third definition of falsity.

Alternatively, falsity (*mithyātva*) consists in being the counter-positive of an absolute non-existence residing in its own locus. This means it is perceived only in the very locus where its own absolute non-existence resides; thus, it differs from the previous definition. The refutation of objections and the resolution thereof are as before.

Nor should it be argued that the absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) of a thing is impossible in a location where it is either conjoined (*saṃyogin*) or inherent (*samavāyin*), for if such existence were possible, its status as a material cause (*upādānatva*) and so forth would be untenable; for there is no contradiction in simultaneous occurrence in space, just as there is in time, and because its status as a material cause is not contradicted by the presence of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*). Nor should it be argued that prior non-existence is also untenable in a locus of absolute non-existence, for this is contradicted by the case of time.

It should not be argued that the coexistence (sāmānādhikaraṇya) of antecedent non-existence and absolute non-existence at the same time is not accepted—on the strength of such cognitions as "now there is the absolute non-existence of the jar" and "now there is the antecedent non-existence of the jar"—whereas regarding space, there is no evidence whatsoever for the coexistence of those two; for the inference of their having a different level of reality (viṣamasattākatva) and the testimony of scripture (śruti), etc., serve as valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa). Furthermore, the lack of contradiction between an entity and its absence when they possess unequal degrees of reality has already been established.

Nor is there the fault of over-extension (ativyāpti) to non-existent things, because what is intended is that which is perceived as existing only in the locus of its own absolute non-existence. Nor should it be argued that over-extension is unavoidable in the case of the non-existent, since the Śruti passage, "In the beginning, this was indeed non-being (asat)," perceives existence in the non-existent; for by the word "not" (nañ), only the absence of the meaning of the passage "In the beginning, this was indeed Being (sat)" is conveyed, and not the existence of the non-existent, due to their contradiction. Therefore, there is no over-extension. All other points should be understood as already explained above, and thus we conclude.
Thus concludes the investigation into the fourth type of falsity.

Alternatively, falsity (*mithyātva*) consists in being devoid of existence (*sadviviktatva*). Existence (*sattva*), moreover, is the state of being established by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇasiddhatva*). And the nature of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇatva*) is the state of being an instrument of knowledge not assisted by defects (*doṣa*); by this, falsity is established as being distinct from what is established by a means of valid cognition, like dreams and the like. Furthermore, it is another point that being established by a means of valid cognition is pervaded by non-sublatability (*abādhyatva*). Here too, in order to avoid over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to non-existent things and to Brahman which is devoid of attributes (*nirdharmaka*), the qualification "being cognized as existent" (*sattvena pratīyamānatva*) must be added.

This is because neither of those two [categories] is the object of a cognition qualified by existence (*sattva*). For this very reason, regarding the definition "being distinct from the existent" (*sad-viviktatva*), is "existence" (*sattva*) the state of being the locus of the universal *sattā* (Being-ness), or is it non-sublatability (*abādhyatva*), or is it the nature of Brahman? The first position is untenable because you yourself admit that even in a jar (*ghaṭa*) and other such things, there exists a universal (*jāti*) produced by ignorance (*avidyā*). The second leads to the conclusion that "falsity" (*mithyātva*) is simply the state of being sublatable (*bādhyatva*). The third is a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*). These positions are refuted precisely because they are not accepted [by us].

Furthermore, the arguments stated under the section on "being distinct from both the real and the unreal" (*sadasadvilakṣaṇatva*) should be considered here as well. As for the remainder, we shall explain it when establishing the illustrative examples (*dṛṣṭānta*).
Thus ends the fifth definition of falsity in the Advaitasiddhi.

Now, an objection may be raised: "If the falsity of the aforementioned falsity [of the world] were itself false, it would follow that the world is real; for when two contradictory properties are attributed to a single substratum, the falsity of one necessitates the reality of the other. Furthermore, if falsity were real, then just as in that case, it would follow that the world is real. Thus, in either case, there is a contradiction of non-duality (advaita). This is not so; for even if falsity is false, it does not follow that the world is real.

For in that case, when two contradictory properties exist, the falsity of one implies the truth of the other, provided that the delimitant of falsity does not reside in both; as, for example, in the case of silver and its absence—which are of the nature of mutual exclusion—in a mother-of-pearl shell, or as in the case of "being different from silver" and "being silver"—which are pervaded by mutual exclusion—in that very same place, because there is a rule regarding the difference in the delimitants of the negandum. However, in the present instance, the delimitant of the negandum is one and the same, namely, "being an object of perception" (*dṛśyatva*) and so forth.

Just as when both "cowness" and "horseness" are negated in a single elephant, the property that serves as the delimitor of the negandum (*niṣedhyatāvacchedaka*)—namely, being pervaded by the absolute absence of elephant-ness—is equal for both; thus, the negation of one does not entail the presence of the other, so it is here. Furthermore, as has been demonstrated below, truth and falsity do not consist in mutual exclusion (*parasparaviraharūpatva*), nor are they mutually pervasive (*parasparavirahavyāpakatva*).

Even though they consist in mutual exclusion, there is no contradiction between them because they possess unequal degrees of reality (*viṣamasattā*); for although conventional falsity (*vyāvahārika-mithyātva*) may remove conventional truth (*vyāvahārika-satyatva*), it does not remove conceptual truth (*kālpnika-satyatva*). Furthermore, we accept the coexistence (*samuccaya*) of truth and falsity, just as the existence of conjunction and its absence is accepted in the system of the Logicians (*Tārkika*). The criterion for one thing being sublated by the proof of another is precisely this inequality of reality, as is the case with the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell and its absence.

Furthermore, being sublated by the same sublater is the determinant for having an equal ontological status (*samasattākatva*), as is the case with the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell and the difference of that silver from the shell. And there is indeed the fact that the world (*prapañca*) and its falsity (*mithyātva*) are both sublated by the knowledge of the one Brahman. Therefore, because they possess equal ontological status, the world is also sublated by the sublater of its falsity; thus, there is no injury to non-duality (*advaita*). Enough of this elaboration. This concludes the general proof of falsity.

Now, an objection is raised: if "falsity" (mithyātva) is the property to be proven (sādhya), then that which is made the reason (hetu)—namely, "being an object of cognition" (dṛśyatva)—must also be established. To explain: what is this "being an object of cognition"? Is it being pervaded by a mental modification (vṛtti-vyāpyatva)? Or being pervaded by the fruit [of knowledge] (phala-vyāpyatva)? Or being common [to both]? Or being an object of consciousness (cid-viṣayatva) at some time or in some way? Or the necessity of depending on another consciousness distinct from itself for its own empirical usage (sva-vyavahāra)? Or non-self-luminosity (asva-prakāśatva)? It cannot be the first, because there is a deviation (vyabhicāra) in the case of the Self (ātman); for the Self is pervaded by the modification produced by the Vedānta [texts], yet it is not false.

For this very reason, the third [alternative] is not tenable either. Nor is the second, because since that [property] is absent in eternal supersensible things (nityātīndriya) and in cases such as the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell (śuktirūpya), it would entail the fallacies of partial unestablishedness (bhāgāsiddhi) and deficiency of the probans (sādhanavaikalya). Nor is the fourth, because there is a deviation (vyabhicāra) with respect to the self (ātman), given the experience: "Brahman was previously unknown, but is now known through the Vedānta. Nor is the fifth, because there is a deviation with respect to Brahman itself, since we observe a necessity for dependence on another consciousness (saṃvidantara) even in the conventional usage of Brahman as qualified by non-duality and so forth.

Nor is it the sixth [alternative], for that consists in the absence of fitness for immediate empirical usage while being unperceivable. And thus, since even the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell possesses fitness for immediate empirical usage, the reason would be deficient—[if you say this,] it is not so; for every alternative other than "being pervaded by the fruit" (phalavyāpyatva) is capable of withstanding scrutiny.

Nor should it be argued that there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of Brahman under the view that [knowledge] is pervaded by a mental modification (*vṛtti*), because otherwise the Vedāntas, which have Brahman as their ultimate purport, would result in being purposeless; for pure Brahman is not an object of perception, according to the Śruti: "That which is invisible... and so forth. Rather, it is only Brahman as conditioned (*upahita*) that is such, and that is indeed false, for it does not become unconditioned during the state of the mental modification.

Nor should it be argued that this contradicts one's own statement, "Or, when the nature of Brahman is established as the object of all cognitions," because that statement also refers to the conditioned [Brahman].

Nor should it be argued that "this being the case, the purity [of the Self] would not be established," because its establishment occurs through its own inherent luminosity (*prakāśatva*). [Objection: Since it is impossible to either affirm or deny any attribute (*dharma*) when the substratum (*dharmī*) is unknown, one who denies perceptibility (*dṛśyatva*) in the pure [Self] must necessarily admit that the pure [Self] is an object of knowledge (*jñeyatva*). Nor can it be said that the denial of perceptibility in the pure [Self]—which is self-established by virtue of its own luminosity—is effected by scripture (*śruti*).

If it is argued that [the statement] "the pure is self-luminous" is untenable because the pure cannot be manifested within a specific mental modification (*vṛtti*) produced by words—since the pure is not manifest therein—we say: no. At the time of the modification, the pure cannot exist as something characterized by the attribute consisting of the modification; therefore, it is impossible for the pure to be the object of a modification. Consequently, the sentence "the pure is self-luminous" means, by way of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), that impurity is pervaded by non-self-luminosity.

And thus, through the exclusion of impurity, self-luminosity culminates in the pure, just as non-difference results from the negation of difference. Nor should it be argued that the use of the word "pure" (śuddha) is redundant—whether by primary denotation (abhidhā) or indication (lakṣaṇā)—because the purity is not manifest; for its meaningfulness is established by taking into account the final, culminating sense.

And thus, since "impurity" (aśuddhatva) is the pervader of both "being perceptible" (dṛśyatva) and "falsity" (mithyātva), the statement "the pure is neither perceptible nor false" results in the exclusion of perceptibility and falsity from that which is pure, by virtue of its intent to convey this very point. By this, the view of the Śūnyavādins—that mere manifestation (sphuraṇa) alone is the determinant of falsity because of parsimony (lāghava), and therefore "Brahman, though self-manifesting, is indeed false"—is refuted;
for the nature of being self-manifesting is absent in the case of the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell and the like, and the status of being an object of manifestation is unestablished in Brahman.

Now, an objection may be raised: if the qualificandum (*viśeṣya*) also appears in the cognition of the qualified (*viśiṣṭajñāna*), then since the qualified is "visible" (*dṛśyatva*) according to scripture, the qualificandum must also be visible; thus, there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) from the reason. Nor can it be argued that the qualified as a whole is the object—either like Viṣṇu’s status as the deity in the mantra "to Viṣṇu Śipiviṣṭa," or like the status of Agni and Soma as deities when joined—such that the qualificandum alone is not the object. For if, by that same logic, the qualifier were also not an object, it would follow that the reason suffers from the fallacy of being unestablished in part (*bhāgāsiddhi*). If this is said, we reply: no.

There is no defect even if that which has attained the status of the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) is the object (*viṣaya*), because its falsity (*mithyātva*) is admitted. For this very reason, the claim that "even if the qualified entity (*upahita*) is the object, the objectivity of the thing to be qualified (*upadheya*) remains intact" is refuted; for its falsity is also admitted in its nature as the qualified, and there is no lack of pervasion (*bhāgāsiddhi*) when it is specified as the object of another cognition.

Now, an objection may be raised: if the undivided mental modification (*akhaṇḍavṛtti*) produced by the Vedānta has as its object the [Self] as qualified (*upahita*), then—since at that time there is no other limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) and thus that very modification must itself be the qualifier—it would follow that it has itself as its own object. This is not an acceptable conclusion, because it is a rule in verbal cognition that what is not presented by words does not appear; therefore, it is impossible for a mental modification to appear when it is not itself presented by words. Or, even if it were somehow possible, ignorance (*ajñāna*) and its effects would not be removed by it, because only a cognition that does not have ignorance and its effects as its objects can remove both of them.

Otherwise, since cognitions such as "I am ignorant" and "this is a jar" would also have the conditioned [Brahman] as their object, it would follow that they too could remove ignorance. If this is argued, we say no; for it is accepted that the mental modification (*vṛtti*) acts as a condition (*upadhāyaka*) only when it does not itself appear within the verbal modification (*śābdavṛtti*). As stated by the authors of the *Kalpataru*: "The modification that takes pure Brahman as its object arises as the cause for the removal of itself and all other adjuncts (*upādhi*), because there is no difference in its own status as an adjunct. And thus, there is no objectivity (*viṣayatā*) for that which is unconditioned."

In this context, the coloring by the mental modification (*vṛtti*) is utilized by way of its existence (*sattā*), but not by way of being an object of manifestation (*bhāsyatā*) through entry into the category of objects. This is the intended meaning: just as ignorance (*ajñāna*), although it conditions the witness (*sākṣin*), does not enter into the category of the witness because it is insentient (*jaḍatva*), but rather only into the category of the witnessed (*sākṣya*); so too, although the mental modification conditions the object, the modification itself does not enter into the category of the object of that modification, because it is impossible for something to be its own object.

However, there is no inconsistency whatsoever in the fact that even though [Brahman] is not itself an object of consciousness, it nevertheless becomes an object of it. By this, the fact that knowledge and ignorance have the same object is explained; for ignorance also makes Brahman its object only when it is delimited by its own adjunct (upādhi), since in the state where it is not so delimited, ignorance itself does not exist. Thus, since both knowledge and ignorance have as their object that which is delimited—even while the adjuncts themselves are not the objects—there is indeed identity of object between them.

By this, it is explained that cognitions whose objects are limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) do not remove ignorance; for since ignorance does not have the limiting adjunct as its object, there is no identity of object between them, and it is only through identity of object that the relationship of the removed and the remover (*nivartya-nivartaka-bhāva*) exists.

In reality, however, "visibility" (dṛśyatva) consists precisely in being the object of a mental modification (vṛtti) not produced by words; otherwise, it would be difficult to avoid the fallacy of deviation (vyabhicāra) in the case of the "non-existent" (tuccha), such as a rabbit's horn, which is the object of a modification produced by words like "the rabbit's horn is non-existent. This being the case, even though the pure [Brahman] is the object of a modification produced by Vedānta texts, there is no deviation therein, because it is not admitted that either the non-existent or the pure are objects of modifications not produced by words.

Alternatively—*dṛśyatva* (the state of being perceptible) is simply the state of being an object of a cognitive state (*vṛtti*) that possesses a qualifier (*saprakāraka*). And a "qualifier" (*prakāra*) is some property (*dharma*) that is designable (*sopākhyā*). Therefore, there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) with respect to the pure (*śuddha*), which is the object of a cognition devoid of qualifiers (*niṣprakāraka-jñāna*), nor with respect to the non-existent (*tuccha*), which is the object of a cognition whose qualifier is a non-designable property (*nirupākhyadharma-prakāraka-jñāna*). Since even the nature of negation (*abhāvatva*) is designable, there is no partial unestablishedness (*bhāgāsiddhi*) with respect to negation when it is the object of a cognition whose qualifier is the nature of negation. Furthermore, "designability" (*upākhyā*) consists in being the object of the cognition "it exists"—this is another point.

By this, "knowability" (*dṛśyatva*)—defined as the state of being an object that serves as the basis for empirical usage, common to both that which is pervaded by a mental mode (*vṛtti-vyāpya*) and that which is pervaded by a result (*phala-vyāpya*)—is also a valid reason (*hetu*), because the means for avoiding the fallacy (*vyabhicāra*) regarding Brahman and the non-existent (*tuccha*) has already been stated. Alternatively, knowability is the state of being an object of consciousness (*cid-viṣayatva*); and since that consists in some form of relation to consciousness, it serves as the reason. This does not apply to pure consciousness itself, because where there is non-difference (*abheda*), there can be no relation—which is necessarily concomitant with difference—and therefore there is no fallacy.

Furthermore, the deviation [of the reason] in the case of the "insignificant" (tuccha) must be avoided. Alternatively, the probans is "visibility," defined as the necessity of dependence upon a consciousness distinct from itself for its own empirical usage (*vyavahāra*). By the term "consciousness" (*saṃvit*), one intends either consciousness manifested through an object, or consciousness manifested through a mental modification (*vṛtti*), or pure consciousness alone. Thus, since all empirical usage regarding things such as jars—whether they be eternally imperceptible or manifest to the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*)—depends upon a consciousness distinct from themselves, there is no lack of proof (*asiddhi*).

And empirical usage (*vyavahāra*) consists of manifestation (*sphuraṇa*), speech, and so forth, which are common to all. In that regard, since the empirical usage of Brahman in the form of manifestation is eternally established, there is no dependence on a consciousness distinct from itself; thus, by the term "necessity" (*niyati*), the deviation [of the reason] is excluded. This is because, in every empirical usage within its own domain, it culminates in dependence on a consciousness distinct from itself. For this very reason, "knowability" (*dṛśyatva*), in the sense of not being self-luminous (*asvaprakāśatva*), is also a valid logical reason (*hetu*).

Self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*) indeed consists in being non-dependent upon anything other than itself for its own immediacy (*aparokṣatva*), according to the scriptural text: "That Brahman which is immediate and direct" (*Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 3.4.1). Thus, it results in the state of having immediacy that is not contingent upon another. The reason (*hetu*) is the possession of a difference determined by that [self-luminous nature]. And since this [reason] exists in things like a jar—which are eternally non-apparent (*nityaparokṣa*) or whose immediacy is dependent on another—there is no lack of establishment (*asiddhi*).

Nor should it be argued that there is a deviation (vyabhicāra) in the case of Brahman itself, because Brahman also possesses an imagined difference (kalpanika-bheda) having Brahman as its counter-correlative, since an unimagined difference is nowhere established; for that difference [of Brahman] is not defined by any property such as "being immediate (aparokṣa) without dependence on anything else," but rather by other properties such as "being a sentient soul" (jīvatva) or "being the Lord" (īśvaratva). Thus, "visibility" (dṛśyatva)—defined as the absence of fitness for the usage of "immediacy" while being non-cognizable (avedyatva)—is also a valid probans (hetu).

Nor should it be argued that there is neither unestablishedness (*asiddhi*) nor deficiency in the probans (*sādhanavaikalya*), because the property of being fit for the usage of "immediate" (*aparokṣa-vyavahāra-yogyatva*), qualified by the absence of being pervaded by the fruit [of knowledge], exists in ignorance (*avidyā*), the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), and the silver-in-shell (*śukti-rūpya*) just as it does in Brahman; for what is intended by the term "fitness for the usage of immediate" is fitness to be the object of a mental modification (*vṛtti*) that removes ignorance, and since that [fitness] is absent in ignorance, the silver-in-shell, and so forth, there is neither unestablishedness nor deficiency in the probans.

And we shall explain later how objects such as a jar are "objectified by the fruit" (*phalavyāpyatva*). In the view that the cessation of ignorance (*avidyānivṛtti*) is of a fifth kind, the qualification "existing at the time of ignorance" must be added to the probans (*hetu*) in order to avoid the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in that case. By that very [qualification], there is no deviation even with respect to the "void" (*tuccha*). In this same manner, one must strive to avoid deviation in all probans.

However, when the probandum (*sādhya*) is merely "being distinct from the real" (*sad-viviktatvamātra*), there is not even a scent of deviation with respect to the void or the cessation of ignorance of the fifth kind; thus, everything is clear. Thus ends the establishment of the probans "being an object of sight" (*dṛśyatva-hetūpapatti*) in the *Advaitasiddhi*.

Inertness (*jaḍatva*) is also a reason [for proving the non-selfhood of the "I"]. Now, what is this inertness? Is it the state of being a non-knower (*ajñātṛtva*), or the state of being ignorance (*ajñānatva*), or the state of being non-self (*anātmatva*)? Not the first; for in your own view, the "I-sense" (*ahamartha*), which is included within the subject of the proposition, is indeed a knower, and thus [the reason] is unestablished (*asiddha*) with respect to it. Furthermore, there would be a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) because the pure Self (*śuddhātman*) is a non-knower.

Nor is the second [alternative] tenable; for since consciousness as qualified by a mental modification (*vṛtti*) alone constitutes knowledge, while both the bare modification and bare consciousness individually constitute non-knowledge, even if the fallacy of "unestablishedness" (*asiddhi*) regarding the modification is avoided, the fallacy of "deviation" (*vyabhicāra*) regarding consciousness remains as it was. Nor is the third [alternative] tenable, because "selfhood" (*ātmatva*) itself cannot be defined. For that is not a specific genus (*jāti*), since you admit the oneness of the Self, and because even if there were a difference among distinct selves, they would all be included within the scope of the subject (*pakṣa*).

Nor can it be of the nature of bliss (*ānanda*), because the reason—that there is a distinction from objective bliss—is unestablished; and if that [bliss] were also the Self, the defects mentioned regarding the position of ignorance (*ajñāna*) would have to be applied to it. If this is argued, it is not so, because there are no defects in the second and third positions. For instance, in the position that "ignorance is insentience (*jaḍatva*)," there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) with respect to the Self, since knowledge is defined as the manifestation (*prakāśa*) characterized by an object, and that [manifestation] does not perish even in the state of liberation (*mokṣa*).

Nor should it be argued that, just as non-existence possesses a counter-correlate, so too the state of having an object (*saviṣayakatva*) is intrinsic (*svābhāvika*) to desire, cognition, and the like, and therefore, as in the case of desire, it must have the same ontological status (*samānasattākatva*) as cognition itself. For the "having an object" of cognition is its relation to an object, and that relation is not real (*tāttvika*), but rather illusory (*ādhyāsika*), since—as will be explained—a real relation cannot be established. Consequently, it is not intrinsic; for silver is certainly not intrinsic to mother-of-pearl.

And thus, since it is accepted that desire and the like possess an object only by virtue of having cognition as their limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), it is all the more impossible for that [object-possession] to be inherent (*svābhāvika*) in them. Nor should it be argued that, in this case, there would be the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of desire existing at some time even without a connection to an object—just as cognition does—because what serves as the cause for [desire] possessing an object is its having a higher degree of existence (*sattā*) relative to the limiting adjunct that acts as the cause for object-possession, whereas desire has the same degree of existence as that adjunct.

Nor should you say that because you accept the self to be objectless in the state of liberation, bliss would not be manifest, and thus it would fail to be the supreme human goal (*puruṣārtha*); for at that time, bliss itself is the manifestation, but it is not the case that there is "manifestness of bliss" or "manifestness characterized by an object," so as stated, there is no loss of its nature as knowledge (*jñānatva*). Now, one might object: even so, due to the absence of a knower, it is not knowledge then; for an act of eating does not occur without an eater.

Nor should it be argued that because [Brahman] is beginningless, it lacks the nature of an action and is therefore independent; for we observe that even beginningless things depend upon others: prior non-existence depends on its counter-positive (the object to be produced), a universal depends on its individual instances, the distinction between the individual soul and Brahman depends on both the substratum and the counter-positive, ignorance depends on both its locus and its object, and the existence of Brahman depends on its agent. Otherwise, in such expressions as "Brahman exists" (*asti brahma*), the verbal suffix would not denote an agent.

If it is argued that—since knowledge of the past and so forth, as well as the knowledge of God (*īśvara*), is seen to be determinable even when there is no dependence on an object for its production, the nature of knowledge is nonetheless to be determined by a knower and a knowable; otherwise, the experience "I know this" would not occur, and there would be a contradiction with the *Vivaraṇa*, which states that "knowledge is the manifestation of an object to a knower"—we say no. For even though a universal (*jāti*) is determined by an individual (*vyakti*), it is possible for it to be unconnected to it at times, depending upon the limiting conditions (*upādhi*) that serve as the basis for the relationship.

Because it possesses a greater degree of existence (*sattā*). For this very reason, the state of being an object of knowledge (*jñeyatva*) and the state of being a knower (*jñātṛtva*) are not inherent to cognition. To explain: first, does being an object of knowledge mean being produced by the object, or being pervaded by the object? It cannot be the first, because it is absent in the case of indirect (*parokṣa*) cognition. Nor can it be the second; for regarding the temporal pervasion expressed as "when there is cognition, then there is the object," there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) as before. As for spatial pervasion, it is dismissed from afar, since that [pervasion] is absent in the knower.

Nor should it be argued that there is no deviation (vyabhicāra) in the temporal pervasion (kālikavyāpti) "when there is immediate cognition (aparokṣajñāna), then there is the object," because the Self—being of the nature of immediate cognition according to the scriptural text, "That which is directly and immediately Brahman"—is also pervaded by the object. This cannot be maintained, because there is deviation in the case of the Lord’s knowledge and the knowledge of yogins. However, the pervasion "whatever cognition is sensory (aindriyaka) is [accompanied] by an object" is accepted by all; and since the cognition whose nature is the Self does not possess the quality of being sensory, there is no contradiction with that [pervasion].

Now, one might object: "If you do not accept the pervasion (vyāpti) that 'whenever there is immediate cognition (aparokṣajñāna), there is an object,' then the establishment of an indeterminable (anirvacanīya) silver would be impossible on the grounds that the immediate cognition 'this is silver' cannot otherwise be explained; for immediacy could be accounted for even without an object. This is not so, because we shall explain that the status of being an object of cognition—which is being reflected upon in the synthesis "I know this silver"—cannot have any other substratum, and thus the establishment of an indeterminable silver follows.

For this very reason, even in the case of an indirect error (*parokṣabhrama*), there is the establishment of an indeterminable object (*anirvacanīyārtha*). Alternatively, being pervaded by the object is defined as being indirectly perceived (*janyāparokṣatva*), since it is not admitted that the knowledge of the seers (*ārṣajñāna*) is directly perceived. Thus, there is no logical inconsistency in the establishment of an indeterminable silver. Similarly, regarding "having a knower" (*sajñātṛkatva*): does it mean being produced by a knower, being pervaded by a knower, or inhering in a knower? In the first case, there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of God’s knowledge, and because the eternality of [His] knowledge will be established later. In the second case as well, there is a lack of probative force (*aprayojakatā*).

The third [alternative] is not tenable, because just as [the object] being produced by knowledge is possible, so too is its inherence in knowledge; for since it is not admitted that knowledge possesses the nature of a quality (*guṇatva*) or an action (*kriyātva*), it is impossible to infer that it must have a substance as its substrate. Furthermore, the experience and the explanatory statement are accounted for simply by the occasional relation between the knower and the knowable. Moreover, in the expression "Brahman exists" (*asti brahma*), the verbal suffix (*lakāra*) does not indicate Brahman's agency with respect to the existence of Brahman, because such agency is impossible given its eternity; rather, it should be understood as serving merely for grammatical correctness (*sādhutvārtha*).

Now, an objection might be raised: "Knowledge is not distinct from the sequence of valid cognitions (*pramā*), nor is knowledge the very nature of the Self (*ātman*), for that would entail the reality of its object, such as ignorance (*avidyā*). Nor is it invalid cognition (*apramā*), for that would entail being produced by defects (*doṣa*). If this is argued, we say: no.

This is because it is logically possible for [the Lord's cognition] to be distinct from both [valid cognition and error] by its very nature—just like the cognition of the Sāṃkhya-Siddheśvara or like the non-conceptual [perception] of a jar and so forth. Furthermore, in that case, if the Lord’s cognition were valid, it would entail being produced by a *guṇa* (excellence); if it were erroneous, it would entail being produced by a *doṣa* (defect). Moreover, since non-conceptual perception is devoid of a qualifier (*prakāra*), it is impossible for it to have the property of "having that as its qualifier" when the object possesses it, or "having that as its qualifier" when the object lacks it. And for us, there is a rule that whatever is produced and conceptual must necessarily be either erroneous or valid.

Because there is no deficiency [in the reason], and because self-knowledge—which by its very nature differs from both error and valid cognition—can be conventionally designated as having both forms through the coloring of two distinct modes of functioning, it is not to be said: "If the intention is to mean 'being different from what is denoted by the word *jñāna*,' then since even the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) is denoted by the word *jñāna*, the reason is unestablished (*asiddhi*) therein; whereas if the intention is to mean 'being different from what is indicated by the word *jñāna*,' then since even a jar (*ghaṭa*) and so forth are indicated by the word *jñāna*, the reason is likewise unestablished therein. [This is because] the word *jñāna* denotes the self-knowledge itself, while the limiting adjunct is merely indicated by it. Thus, the reason is established in the subject. Furthermore, since the jar and other objects are neither denoted nor indicated by the word *jñāna*, the reason is not unestablished in those cases either. Therefore, the objection is invalid.

When it is intended that [the definition] consists in being distinct from the qualificandum of the cognition produced by the term "knowledge," the aforementioned defect does not arise. In this way, non-selfhood (*anātmatva*)—defined as being distinct from bliss (*ānanda*)—is established, because even worldly bliss is of the nature of Brahman, and only its limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) are subject to origination and destruction. Nor should it be argued that there is a fallacy (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of Brahman, since the conceptual distinctions of being different from knowledge and being different from bliss exist in Brahman; for the reason (the middle term) is the distinction from that [Brahman] which possesses the same level of reality (*samānasattāka*) as the substratum (*dharmin*).

Alternatively, the distinction [between the subject and the object] should be qualified by being "without limiting adjuncts" (*anaupādhikatvena*); thus, as before, the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) with respect to the insubstantial (*tuccha*) and the cessation of ignorance (*avidyānivṛtti*)—which is of a fifth kind—is avoided. Likewise, insentience (*jaḍatva*) is the state of not being self-luminous (*asvaprakāśatva*), and that has already been established. All is auspicious. Thus ends the demonstration of the reason of insentience in the *Advaitasiddhi*.
