Finitude (*paricchinnatva*) is also a reason (*hetu*). And that is threefold: spatial, temporal, and substantial. Among these, spatial finitude is being the counter-positive (*pratiyogitva*) of absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*). Temporal finitude is being the counter-positive of destruction (*dhvaṃsa*). Substantial finitude is being the counter-positive of mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*). Now, an objection: being the counter-positive of absolute non-existence by way of the relation of inherence (*samavāya-sambandha*) is fallacious (*vyabhicārin*) with respect to the Self (*ātman*), because like space (*ākāśa*) and so forth, it too does not inhere anywhere.

The state of being the counter-positive (*pratiyogitva*) of absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) by way of the relation of conjunction (*saṃyoga-sambandha*) is unestablished (*asiddha*) in the case of space (*ākāśa*) and so forth, because of the rule that it possesses conjunction with all corporeal things (*mūrta*). If, however, the intention is to refer to being the counter-positive of absolute non-existence residing in incorporeal things (*amūrta*), then the deviation (*vyabhicāra*) remains as it was in the case of the self (*ātman*). Even if one intends to mean the absence of connection with everything, there is still deviation in the case of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), which is devoid of all connections. Furthermore, there is a lack of establishment (*asiddhi*) in the case of ignorance (*ajñāna*), which is connected to everything. The state of being the counter-positive of destruction (*dhvaṃsa-pratiyogitva*) is also unestablished in the case of space and so forth.

This is because they are accepted by others as being eternal. Furthermore, the property of being the counter-correlative (*pratiyogitva*) of mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) is inconclusive (*vyabhicārin*) with respect to the Self (*ātman*), since the Self is the counter-correlative of the mutual non-existence residing in insentient things; otherwise, it would follow that the Self is insentient. If this is argued, we say no: for the inconclusiveness regarding the Self is avoided by qualifying [the reason] with "having the same level of reality (*samasattāka*) as its counter-correlative" in the case of absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) and mutual non-existence. Moreover, there is no lack of proof (*asiddhi*) regarding ignorance, space, and so forth, because these possess the status of being counter-correlatives of absolute and mutual non-existences that have the same level of reality as themselves.

In the view that the empirical (vyāvahārika) [entities] such as ignorance (avidyā) and space (ākāśa) lack ultimate reality (pāramārthika), the qualification "having a level of existence not lower than its own" (svānyūnasattāka) must be added. For this very reason, there is no deficiency in the probans (sādhanavaikalya) even though illusory silver (śuktirūpya) and the like, which are merely apparent (prātibhāsika), are the counter-correlates (pratiyogin) of empirical non-existence; for the aforementioned modes of falsity (mithyātva) do not possess such a nature. Furthermore, the property of being the counter-correlate of destruction (dhvaṃsa-pratiyogitva) is not unestablished (asiddha) in the case of space and so forth.

This is because [the ether] is inferred to have the status of being produced, as established by the scripture: "From that very Self, indeed, the ether was produced. Furthermore, in the passage "And it is all-pervading and eternal like the ether," it should be understood that the Self serves as the illustrative example [for the ether's eternity] insofar as it is all-pervading at the same time as itself, and insofar as it persists until the dissolution of all beings. This is because the scripture, "Everything else than this is perishable," teaches that only everything which is not the Self is subject to destruction.

For this very reason, jars and other such objects are superimposed upon a reality that appears as their own underlying continuity, because they are differentiated [from it], just as a snake, a garland, and so forth are differentiated within the "this" portion of a rope that appears as their own underlying continuity; likewise, what was stated by Ānandabodha—that "the jar is existent, the cloth is existent," whereby the jar and so forth are differentiated while Brahman persists—is also correct.

Since the term "differentiated" (vibhakta) intends to signify the delimitation of an entity consisting in being the counter-correlative of a difference that possesses the same ontological status as itself, there is no deviation [of the definition] in the case of Brahman or the non-existent (tuccha). Nor should it be argued that there is a deviation in the case of universals such as "cowness," because in the self-identical cognitions "the spotted cow is a cow" and "the hornless cow is a cow," the individuals are not superimposed [upon the universal].

This is because one does not admit universals such as "cowness" (*gotva*) that are distinct from the universal "existence" (*sat-sāmānya*); and even if one were to admit cowness and the like, one would still not admit a further universal to delimit their capacity to manifest [their own instances]. For it is possible for the universal "existence" itself—qualified by specific individuals, whether those individuals are themselves non-uniform or made uniform by adventitious conditions (*upādhi*) such as possessing a dewlap—to generate the respective linguistic usages, just as those very specific individuals, either in their unconnected forms or as unified by the adventitious condition of possessing a dewlap, serve as the manifestors of those [universals].

For this very reason, the statement of the author of the *Brahmasiddhi*—namely, "A jar and so forth are superimposed upon the nature of Being, because each is perceived as being permeated by it, just as each moon in the ripples of water is permeated by the [single] moon"—is also correct.

Now, an objection may be raised: how can Brahman—the ultimate reality, devoid of form and other qualities, veiled by ignorance since beginningless time, and accessible through verbal testimony alone—be the object of such cognitions as "the jar exists"? Furthermore, just as the cognition "the jar is impermanent" grasps impermanence residing in the jar, so too the cognition "the jar exists" must grasp existence residing in the jar itself. Nor should it be argued that Brahman, though not perceptible in its own nature, becomes perceptible through the mediation of objects like jars, just as Rāhu (the eclipse-demon) becomes perceptible through the mediation of the moon. This cannot be maintained.

[Objection: Even for space and the like, which are delimited by sound and so forth, there would follow the undesirable consequence (āpāta) that they are audible and so on. Furthermore, it has been stated that Rāhu, though dark and unknown due to a defect at a distance, becomes visible (cākṣuṣatā) because of its connection with the white and luminous moon—this being the case, [we reply]: No; for Brahman is not concealed by the root-ignorance (mūlājñāna) in its aspect as pure existence (sadātmanā), but rather only by the ignorance of power (śaktyajñāna) delimited by objects such as pots.

And thus, when the veil over It is shattered by a mental modification (*vṛtti*) produced by the eyes and other senses, there is no obstacle to the manifestation (*sphuraṇa*) of Brahman in the cognition "this is a jar. Nor should it be argued that the impossibility of being perceived by the eyes and so forth—due to Its being devoid of color and other qualities—constitutes an obstacle; for the requirement of color and the like is restricted only to those objects perceivable by specific sense organs. But Brahman, whose nature is *sat* (Being), is perceivable by all the senses. Therefore, even though It lacks color and other qualities, there is no impossibility of Its being perceived by the eyes and so forth.
Furthermore, even our opponents admit that existence (*sattā*) is perceivable by all the senses. As it has been said by the authors of the *Vārttika*:

"Therefore, experience alone is the single object whose nature is unknown [to the senses], which is self-established for the eyes and other organs, and wherein their status as means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) resides. Furthermore, since the Mīmāṃsakas and others accept that time—which is devoid of color and other qualities—is perceivable by all the sense organs, one should not say: "In that case, space delimited by sound would also be audible. For it is the case that the capacity of something already naturally fit [for perception] is restored by a delimiting factor when its capacity has been obstructed by some cause, just as the capacity of Rāhu, whose capacity was obstructed by the defect of distance, is restored through its connection with the moon.

Thus, Brahman, whose capacity is obstructed by a veil (*āvaraṇa*), becomes capable [of being perceived] through the delimitation (*avaccheda*) of objects such as a jar; however, space (*nabhas*) is inherently incapable by its very nature, not one whose capacity is obstructed, such that it would become capable through the delimitation of sound. Alternatively, the eye requires color-form (*rūpa*) for the perception of a substance (*dravya*), but not for the perception of anything else. Brahman, moreover, is not a substance, because its status as a substance is denied by the scriptural passage, "neither gross, nor subtle, nor short, nor long," which negates the four kinds of dimension.

Therefore, there is no logical inconsistency. Or, let it be that Brahman is a substance (*dravya*); even so, since we observe that qualities (*guṇa*) and the like—which possess superimposed substantiality—are perceived by the eye without requiring color (*rūpa*), the eye requires color only in relation to a substance whose existence is of an equal or lower order than that of the substratum (*dharmin*). Since substantiality in Brahman has an existence inferior to that of the substratum itself, there is no requirement for color or other such qualities in its perception. Furthermore, as for its being "imagined" (*kalpitatva*), this is a separate matter, whether it means being perceived in that which lacks its own [intrinsic] absence, or being sublatable by the knowledge of its own true nature (*svarūpa-jñāna*).
Therefore, it is established that delimitedness (*paricchinnatva*) is also a valid reason (*hetu*). Thus concludes the demonstration of the reason of delimitedness.

However, the teacher Citsukhācārya has stated: "This cloth is the counter-positive of an absolute non-existence residing in these threads, because it possesses parts, like other things that possess parts. In this context, the word "threads" (tantu) refers to the material cause (upādāna). By this, the proof of the property of being composed of parts (*mṛttva*) is established as the state of being the counter-positive of an absolute non-existence residing in its own material cause. Nor should it be argued that there is a *siddhasādhana* (proving what is already established), since the effect, by virtue of its non-difference from the cause, is not dependent upon it; nor should it be argued that there is a *arthāntara* (shifting the subject matter), since the reason could otherwise be explained by the effect's being either independent or dependent on something else.

Because the causal relation is contradicted by non-difference, some degree of difference must necessarily be admitted. Nor does this contradict the section [of the Brahma-sūtras] beginning with "Non-difference from that [the cause], on account of such scriptural passages as 'originating material'"; for the meaning of that passage is simply that the effect does not exist apart from its material cause. Alternatively, there is no "proving of the already established" (siddha-sādhanam), because the subject is qualified by its being supported solely by that which is sublated. Furthermore, there is no sublation even in the present case, since that [sublation] will be refuted later.

Furthermore, there is no room for the dilemma of whether absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) is established by valid cognition (*prāmāṇika*) or not, because that [dilemma] has already been refuted. Nor should it be argued that there is a fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) because a certain cloth exists in these threads through the relation of conjunction (*saṃyoga*); for one who accepts that what is inherent (*samaveta*) in something is the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) of an absolute non-existence residing in that very thing, must also accept that what is conjoined (*saṃyogin*) with it is likewise the counter-positive of an absolute non-existence residing in it, and thus it is on the same footing as the subject of the proposition (*pakṣasama*). Nor does this result in proving something other than what was intended (*arthāntara*) due to its being non-pervasive (*avyāpyavṛtti*).

Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that contradiction (*virodha*)—defined as the non-coexistence of two things in a single locus—would be dismissed from the world, since it would be possible for a cloth and its absence to reside in the same substrate. Furthermore, it is not admitted that conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and its absence can coexist in a single locus; if they were so admitted, then one must qualify the absolute absence (*atyantābhāva*) by adding "residing in this [specific] thread" (*etattantutvāvacchinnavṛttitva*), and likewise add "existing at this [specific] time" (*etatkālīnatva*). By doing so, one avoids the fallacy of proving something other than what was intended (*arthāntara*) by taking into account an absence belonging to another time. Nor is there any sublation by perception, such as the cognition "there is a cloth here in these threads."

Because that [reason] is common to error, it is like the perception of the moon as being only a thumb’s breadth; since it is beset by a doubt regarding its invalidity, it lacks the power to sublate [the thesis]. Furthermore, we shall explain at length how its sublation is removed. Nor should it be said: "The reason is contradictory because the state of being a whole (aṃśitva), which does not reside in anything else, is not tenable without residing in these very threads"—for even if it is the counter-positive of an absolute non-existence residing in these threads, it still exists as something inherent in these threads, and thus there is no contradiction with the probandum (sādhya).

Indeed, the state of not being the counter-positive (*pratiyogitva*) of an absolute non-existence residing in this [entity] is not the determinant (*prayojaka*) for inherence in this; for, according to the opponent's view, it would follow that every purely positive (*kevalānvayin*) property would necessarily inhere in this. Rather, it is the state of being the counter-positive of a prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) residing in this, and so forth. And it has been demonstrated above that this is not contradictory even to the state of being the counter-positive of an absolute non-existence residing in this. Furthermore, inherence in this consists in having this as its material cause (*upādāna*), and not in possessing an eternal relation, since the latter is not admitted.

Now, an objection: this cloth is not the counter-positive of an absolute non-existence residing in these threads, because it is produced from these very threads; otherwise, like another cloth, there would be a contradiction. Nor is there the fallacy of an unestablished qualification (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*). For "being the counter-positive of an absolute non-existence residing in these [threads]" is generally established as being the counter-positive of an absolute non-existence residing in something [in general], because it is pervaded by being the counter-positive of a relational non-existence (*saṃsargābhāva*), just like being the counter-positive of a prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*).

Nor should it be argued that there is a deviation (vyabhicāra) because the absolute absence of ether (ākāśātyantābhāva) is grasped as being pervaded by the property of being the counter-positive of a relational absence (saṃsargābhāvapratiyogitva) in things such as a jar, and because that [absolute absence of ether], being a purely positive entity (kevalānvayin), lacks the property of being the counter-positive of an absolute absence residing in anything whatsoever.

If it is argued that there is no deviation (vyabhicāra) because the absolute absence of ether (*ākāśa*)—which exists as a property in a purely positive entity (*kevalānvayin*) where there is no locus for being the counter-positive of a relational absence—is not pervaded by being the counter-positive of a relational absence, we say no; for in the negative concomitance (*vyatirekavyāpti*) "wherever there is the counter-positiveness of the absolute absence residing in this thread, there is the absence of being composed of this thread," the fact of not being the counter-positive of a prior absence (*prāgabhāva*) residing in this [thread] serves as a limiting condition (*upādhi*), thereby rendering the opposing argument weaker.

This is because the property of "not being the counter-positive of the prior absence residing in these very threads"—which pervades the absence of "being commenced by these threads"—does not reside in the subject (pakṣa), since it does not pervade the property of "being the counter-positive of an absolute absence residing in these threads," which is suspected to reside in the subject. Furthermore, this is because the argument will be shown to be refuted by counter-arguments (pratikūlatarka) such as the impossibility of perceptibility and so forth. For this very reason, "not being commenced by these threads" is also not a limiting condition (upādhi); for it has been stated that when the absence of the probandum is being established through the absence of the limiting condition, the argument becomes fallacious due to the presence of that very condition.

Furthermore, there would be a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) [of the reason] if one were to admit a non-pervasive conjunction (*avyāpyavṛtti-saṃyoga*). For this very reason, even the grasp of the pervasion of the probandum—that wherever there is the state of being the counter-positive of an absolute absence residing in this thread, there is the state of not being commenced by this thread—is not established, because of a deviation in that very same instance. Thus, everything is faultless.

And thus, the statement of Vidyāsāgara—“The object of dispute is non-existent apart from cognition, because it is not perceived apart from cognition, like a dream and so forth”—is also sound. Since "non-existence apart from cognition" means being one of the aforementioned forms of falsity (*mithyātva*), and the reason is its being perceived only when consciousness (*cidābhāsa*) is present, nothing is untenable. In this manner, the formal arguments (*prayoga*) of others should also be established as appropriate. May there be auspiciousness! Thus ends the demonstration of the reason based on being a part (*aṃśitva*).

[Objection: But surely the reasons such as "being an object of perception" (*dṛśyatva*) are *sopādhika* (vitiated by a limiting condition). For instance, either "having its appearance caused by defects that are not sublated by what is intended to be its own sublater," or "being an object of negation with respect to a sublater that is itself unsublatable by its own sublater"—these two conditions are absent from the counter-example (*vipakṣa*) and are co-extensive (*samavyāpta*). Therefore, this is a limiting condition (*upādhi*) characterized by negative concomitance (*vyatirekavyāpti*). [Reply: This is not so, because [the proposed upādhi] does not pervade the probandum (*sādhyāvyāpaka*) in the case of the illusory identity of the body and the self (*dehātmaikya*), which is sublatable by the knowledge of Brahman alone.

Furthermore, it is equivalent to "being other than the subject" (*pakṣetaratva*), because it possesses a qualification that excludes only the subject which possesses the probans, like the property of being other than that which subsists in the parts of a mountain. Nor can it be argued that this too is a limiting condition (*upādhi*) because it is brought forth by sublation (*bādha*); for sublation will be refuted later. Moreover, only that whose absence establishes the absence of the probandum possesses pervasion over the probandum, because the favorable reasoning (*anukūlatarka*) does not extend to the other part.

And likewise, just as in the argument "The earth and so forth are not produced by an agent, because they are not produced by a body," the qualification "body" is redundant and thus "being produced by a body" is not a pervader (*vyāpaka*) of "being produced by an agent"; similarly, in the proof of the absence of the probandum (*sādhyavyatireka*)—namely, "The ether and so forth are not false, because they lack the property of appearing due to a defect that is not sublated by what is intended to be its own sublater"—the portion "not sublated by what is intended to be its own sublater" is redundant, and therefore "appearing due to a defect that is not sublated by what is intended to be its own sublater" [is not a pervader of falsity].

The property of being pervaded by falsity (*mithyātva*) is the upādhi. However, "the state of appearing as prompted by a defect" (*doṣaprayuktabhānatva*) is indeed a pervader of the probandum (*sādhya*), yet it is also a pervader of the probans (*sādhana*); therefore, it is not an upādhi, because its [falsity] is established by the very same reason, such as "being perceptible" (*dṛśyatva*). Similarly, regarding the second upādhi, the qualification "not sublated by a sublater that is itself unsublatable by its own sublater" is redundant for establishing the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). The substantive portion, however, is a pervader of both the probandum and the probans; thus, it is not an upādhi.

For this very reason, the probans (*upādhi*) is "being the object of a cognition produced by a cause possessing a defect of equal ontological status (*samasattāka*) with the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*) that is intended [to be real]. Here, even Brahman is the object of a cognition of momentariness and so forth produced by a cause possessing defects imagined by the Buddhists; therefore, the qualification "of equal ontological status with the substrate" is included to ensure co-extensiveness (*samavyāpti*), and not merely to exclude the subject (*pakṣa*). Consequently, the objection that it is equivalent to the fallacy of *pakṣetara* (the "other-than-the-subject") is refuted.

Even in the case of a falsely existing property such as momentariness, which is imagined within Brahman as if it were [imagined] in the Veda, the probandum is not pervaded by the limiting condition (upādhi), because that condition—being a defect possessing the same ontological status as its locus—is not the object of a cognition produced by a cause. Furthermore, it has already been stated that the qualification is redundant when proving the negative concomitance (vyatireka). Nor is "not being the intended object of the Śruti" the upādhi; for since the state of being the intended object of the Śruti resides in Brahman alone, its absence necessarily pervades the probans. Nor is "illusory existence" (prātibhāsikatva) the upādhi.

For that [upādhi] consists in being sublated by something other than the knowledge of Brahman. And since that [sublatability] does not pervade the probandum (sādhya) even in the case of the false identity of the body and the self—which lacks existence—there is a lack of pervasion (avyāpti). Furthermore, in the case of the negative concomitance (vyatireka), the qualification would be redundant. Nor is "having a body consisting of mere appearance" the upādhi; for in the view of *dṛṣṭisṛṣṭi* (the world is created at every moment of perception), it pervades the probans (sādhana), and for our opponents, it is unestablished (*asiddha*). Thus ends the refutation of the charge that "being an object of vision" (*dṛśyatva*) and other such reasons are fallacious due to having an upādhi.

If it is objected: "Is there not a similarity with fallacious arguments (ābhāsa), such as: 'The subject of dispute is illusory because it is visible,' or 'Brahman is false because it is an object of empirical usage, or because it is distinct from the non-existent, like the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell'? — we say no. For those two [arguments] are non-probative due to being struck down by counter-reasoning (*pratikūlatarka*): namely, that if the world were sublated from its empirical reality (*vyāvahārikasattva*), empirical transactions would become impossible; and that if Brahman were false, it would result in the doctrine of nihilism (*śūnyavāda*). Furthermore, in the present case, such counter-reasoning will be refuted.

Furthermore, what is meant by "being merely phenomenal" (*pratibhāsikatva*)? Does it mean "being sublated by anything other than the knowledge of Brahman," or "having a body consisting of mere appearance"? In the first case, there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the instance of the identity of the body and the self (*dehātmaikya*), and the reason is also inconclusive (*aprayojakatva*). In the second case, according to the doctrine of *dṛṣṭisṛṣṭi* (creation upon perception), the argument proves what is already established (*siddhasādhana*). Likewise, if "falsity" (*mithyātva*) is to be proved of Brahman, then if the probandum is qualified (*sopādhika*), it is a case of proving the already established; if it is unqualified (*anupādhika*), the reason—namely, "being an object of empirical usage" (*vyavahāraviṣayatva*)—is unestablished (*asiddha*). Even if one accepts that Brahman is an object of the mental modification (*vṛtti*) produced by Vedānta, the reason remains inconclusive.

In this way, even the "distinctness from the non-existent" (asadvilakṣaṇatva) is unestablished in Brahman. For non-existence consists in being unfit for cognition as existing under any condition whatsoever, whereas distinctness from the existent consists in being fit for cognition as existing under some condition; and that [fitness] simply does not exist in pure Brahman.

Nor should it be argued that "non-existence" means being sublated (*bādhyatva*) and "non-sublatability" (*abādhyatva*) means being different from that; for such non-sublatability does indeed exist in Brahman. This cannot be maintained because there is a contradiction in using non-sublatability to prove the falsity (*mithyātva*) defined as sublatability, because the example of the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell lacks the probans (*sādhanavikala*), and because the doctrine of the Void (*śūnyavāda*) will be refuted later. Therefore, it is established that the property of being an object of perception (*dṛśyatva*) and so forth do not share the same status as fallacious reasons (*ābhāsa*). Thus ends the refutation of the equality of fallacies.

If it is argued that [properties] such as "visibility" have their objects sublated by perception—such as the perception "the pot exists"—we say no; for there is no definition of "existence" (*sattva*) that is the opposite of falsity and yet is suitable for perception by the eyes and other senses. To explain: existence cannot be (1) being an object of valid cognition (*pramā*), (2) suitability for that, or (3) not being an object of error (*bhrama*). This is because such existence would be unsuitable for the eyes and other senses, since it is constituted by errors and valid cognitions that are themselves inaccessible to the eyes and other senses, and because it would be swallowed up by the multitude of objections to be stated later.

To explain: it cannot be the first [option], because since there is no operation of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) when [an object] is non-existent, existence must be predicated prior to its being an object of valid cognition; yet that [existence] would be distinct from it. Furthermore, if one attempts to define "being a valid cognition" (*pramātva*)—which consists in having an existent thing as its object—without first defining existence, there is the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*). Moreover, even a false connection, such as that between mother-of-pearl and silver, is admitted to be an object of valid cognition by way of determinate perception (*vyavasāya*) or through negation, and so forth. Nor can it be the second [option], because "fitness" (*yogyatā*) cannot be defined.

Not the third [alternative], because it is unestablished; for it is admitted that everything is indeed the object of error by virtue of its momentariness and so forth. For this very reason, it is also not the case that [existence] consists in being the object of a valid cognition (*pramā*) whose mode is not "non-existence," due to the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*). Nor does it consist in being the object of a valid cognition whose mode is "existence," due to the fallacy of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*). Nor does existence consist in not being the object of an erroneous cognition whose mode is "non-existence" with respect to a perceived locus (*pratipannopādhi*), due to the fallacy of mutual dependence. Nor does it consist in the absence of the negation of existence at all three times within a perceived locus, due to the fallacy of self-dependence.

Nor is existence (sattā) [existence], nor being a universal (jāti), nor the capacity for causal efficiency (arthakriyākāritva), nor the distinction from the non-existent (asadvailakṣaṇya); for since these are not incompatible with falsity (mithyātva), there is no sublation (bādhā) of the inference of falsity by the perception of them. Nor is existence the absence of the falsity favored by the Vedāntins, because that would over-extend (ativyāpti) to the absolutely non-existent (tuccha). Nor is it the state of not being superimposed while being distinct from the non-existent; for "not being superimposed" means not being an object of superimposition, and that is impossible, since everything is an object of superimposition in some respect, such as its momentariness.

Nor is existence (*sattva*) defined as being sometimes the direct object of a valid cognition (*pramā*) whose mode is "existence," or as being related to time; for "existence" here means "presentness," and not [the property of] existence itself—thus there is no circularity (*ātmāśraya*). Furthermore, since even things past and so forth are indeed "present" at some time, there is no lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*). And because that which is superimposed is understood through sublation (*bādha*) to be unrelated to the three times, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in the second definition.

It must be stated: [the first definition] is subject to the previously mentioned defects, because truth (*prāmāṇya*) involves existence (*sattva*) and is thus unfit for perception by the eyes and other senses; furthermore, even if it were the object of a true cognition characterized by "presentness," this would not contradict its falsity (*mithyātva*). Nor is the second [definition] opposed to falsity, because even the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell possesses a connection with the time of its appearance. Even though sublation (*bādha*) negates a connection with the three times as being real (*tāttvika*), it does not negate a connection with time that is unreal (*atāttvika*). Nor is being connected with real time [the definition].

Because reality (*tāttvikatva*) has not yet been defined; or, if it were defined, the remaining [arguments] would be redundant. Now, one might object: "In your view, that which is existence (*sattva*) in Brahman is precisely what I maintain here. For it has been said: 'Whatever kind of existence belongs to Brahman, such shall it be even in the world. If that [existence] is inexpressible (*anirvācya*) there, let it be so for us here as well. Nor should it be argued: "In that case, existence consists in being unlimited (*aparicchinna*), and that is not present in the world."

If it is argued that although the void (*tuccha*) is undifferentiated, its being undifferentiated does not constitute existence because existence is not admitted for it; rather, existence is something else entirely—and that [existence] will belong to the mother-of-pearl and so forth as well, because they serve as the substrata for error just as Brahman does—then surely you are the brother of the groom who, at the time of the wedding, when asked by the girl’s father about his own lineage, said: "Whatever is your lineage, that is my lineage too. For it would be improper if the son-in-law and the father-in-law belonged to the same lineage.

Just as the impossibility of marriage [would follow if the bride and groom were one], if the world and Brahman were of a single existence, the world would necessarily be non-existent. To explain: the very nature of Brahman is its existence as self-luminous, non-dual consciousness. If that same nature were also the existence of the insentient world, then—just as the silver is sublated by the existence of the mother-of-pearl, which is opposed to the nature of silver—the world’s falsity in terms of its own essential nature would be established by the self-luminous existence that is opposed to insentience.

Since it is accepted that consciousness alone—by virtue of being the object of both limited and unlimited ignorance—is the substratum of all error, the existence of the shell (śukti) and other such objects is not established merely by their being the substrata of error. Now, one might object: even so, non-existence (asattva), defined as being the counter-positive of an absolute negation at all times and in all places, is common to both the "inexplicable" (anirvacanīya) and the "void" (tuccha). Its absence is existence (sattva), and we maintain that this [existence] belongs to the world just as it does to Brahman. Furthermore, there is no lack of pervasion (avyāpti) in the case of conjunction (saṃyoga), because conjunction is admitted to be non-pervasive (avyāpyavṛtti).

And if that [existence] is accepted, the absence must be qualified by its being pervasively present (*vyāpyavṛttitva*). Nor is there non-pervasion regarding space (*viyat*), because the definition does indeed apply, since we do not accept that the absolute absence of space is a purely positive (*kevalānvayi*) entity. For there is no place or time where space is absent, as that would entail the destruction of its eternity and omnipresence. If it is argued that, upon accepting the absolute absence of space as a purely positive entity, the absence must be qualified by having a "possessing-a-location" (*vṛttimat*) counter-correlate—[we reply]: No.

Because the eye and other sense organs lack the capacity to apprehend such existence—which is constituted by multiple entities that are themselves unperceivable by the eye and so forth—it is not possible for anyone to perceive, through direct perception, the state of being the counter-positive of an absence that is pervasive (vyāpyavṛtti) and whose counter-positive occurs at all places and at all times; for only if that were perceived could its absence be perceptible. Even if one were to set aside the conditions of having a locus-occurrent counter-positive and being pervasive, the states of occurring at all places and at all times remain beyond the reach of the senses.

[Objection: "But surely—if what is apprehended is merely the absence of being the counter-correlative of a negation occurring in its own place and time, then since the present time is included among the three times and the relevant place is included among all places, the absence of being the counter-correlative of a negation therein has already been apprehended; consequently, falsity—in the form of being the counter-correlative of a negation existing in all places throughout the three times—cannot be apprehended by inference. [Response: This is not so.

Because the property of being the counter-positive of every negation occurring in its own place and time is unfit for perception by the eyes and other senses, its absence is all the more unfit for perception. Furthermore, the property of not being the counter-positive of some negation occurring in its own place and time does not contradict falsity (*mithyātva*). Moreover, the property of not co-occurring with an absolute non-existence whose counter-positive is itself is unestablished in the case of a purely positive entity (*kevalānvayin*) due to the non-existence of such an absolute non-existence, and it is also unestablished in the case of a jar and the like due to the difference in relations.

Furthermore, there is the aforementioned defect due to the dilemma: whether existence (*sattva*) consists in not occurring in any locus of its own absolute non-existence, or whether it consists in not occurring in some locus of its own absolute non-existence. Therefore, since no other definition can be formulated and because [the previously mentioned definition] does not contradict falsity (*mithyātva*), existence must be accepted as being of the nature of the absence of the counter-positiveness (*pratiyogitva*) of all absolute non-existences that are co-locus with itself. And it has already been stated that this [existence] is not perceptible by the eyes or other senses.

[Objection: "But surely, when one perceives that a certain negation occurring in a particular place and time is a negation occurring in *this* place and *this* time, one must grasp the absence of counter-positiveness (pratiyogitva) in the jar with respect to all negations occurring in its own place and time—which are presented by that [perceived instance] as a means of proximity (*pratyāsatti*). Therefore, it is impossible to grasp in the jar the counter-positiveness with respect to all negations occurring in all places and at all times. [Reply: This is not so.

Thus, although all negations are present through their general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇā*), it is impossible for the eye and other senses to apprehend the absence of their counter-correlates (*pratiyogitva*). For only an absence of relation whose counter-correlate is perceptible is itself perceptible. And the counter-correlativity of all negations, being common to supersensible things, is not perceptible by the eye or other senses.

In reality, however—the universal (*sāmānya*) is not a sensory proximity (*pratyāsatti*), because there is no evidence for it. Nor should it be argued: "If the pervasion (*vyāpti*) were grasped only in that [mahānasa-fire] through the sense-contact with the smoke of the kitchen, then an inference from the smoke on the mountain would not occur; whereas if the universal such as 'smokeness' (*dhūmatva*) were the proximity, then since that too is proximate, the pervasion could be grasped therein and an inference would follow from it. This is not tenable.

At the time when there is sensory contact with the smoke on the mountain, it is possible to apprehend the relation of qualification (*vaiśiṣṭya*) therein, because the pervasion (*vyāpti*) previously grasped and now remembered is present as the qualifier (*prakāra*) under the aspect of "smokeness" (*dhūmatva*). This is because the causal complex for a qualified cognition (*viśiṣṭajñāna*)—consisting of sensory contact with the qualificandum (*viśeṣya*), the cognition of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇajñāna*), and the non-apprehension of their non-relation (*asaṃsargāgraha*)—is complete, just as in the case of the perception "the sandalwood is fragrant. Alternatively, the cognition of the presence of the reason in the subject (*pakṣadharmatājñāna*) has its causal efficacy by way of the mode in which the pervasion is remembered. It is precisely the smoke from the kitchen that becomes the object of the memory of pervasion under the aspect of "smokeness."

Furthermore, the cognition of the smoke on the mountain as being "smoke" has also occurred, and that occurs even without a general characteristic (sāmānyalakṣaṇā); for by that much alone, inference is established. Nor should it be argued: "Without the cognitive proximity of a general characteristic, there could not arise the experienced doubt—'Is smoke deviant from fire or not?'—because the connection with fire is already known in the case of well-known smoke, while it is unknown in the case of smoke not yet known. This is not to be said.

Even when the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is ascertained with respect to a well-known smoke by means of its specific properties such as "smokeness" (*dhūmatva*), it is possible for doubt regarding that [pervasion] to arise by way of the property "smokeness" itself. Thus it has been stated by the author of the *Maṇi*: "Even when the difference from others is ascertained in a jar by way of 'jar-ness,' doubt and the desire to prove (*siṣādhayiṣā*) regarding it still occur by way of 'earth-ness' (*pṛthivītva*) and so forth. Furthermore, just as doubt arises concerning an object already ascertained due to a doubt regarding its validity (*prāmāṇya*), such a doubt is likewise established through the doubt: "Does 'smokeness' reside in things that deviate from fire, or not? By this, the doubt "Is air possessed of color? is also explained.

Now, it might be argued: desire does not arise toward what is already established, but rather toward what is not yet established; and that desire is produced by a cognition whose object is identical to its own. Furthermore, such a cognition cannot occur without a generalizing cognitive link (*sāmānyapratyāsatti*). Nor should it be said that desire for an unknown pleasure arises simply from a cognition that has an established pleasure as its object and takes "pleasure-ness" as its qualifier, because identity of the qualifier alone is the regulating factor [for desire]. For if a piece of silver were experienced through the qualifier "silver-ness," there would be the unwanted consequence (*prasaṅga*) of a desire directed toward a jar or other objects, also qualified by "silver-ness."

Nor is having the same mode of presentation (*prakāra*) a determining factor [for the rise of desire], because that would entail the undesirable consequence that no desire could arise for mother-of-pearl following an illusion of silver. Thus, what is essential is having the same object (*viṣaya*) while possessing the same mode of presentation. For this very reason, the view under the theory of non-apprehension (*akhyāti*)—that it is the memory of silver alone that prompts activity toward the mother-of-pearl—is rejected. If you object to this, we say no; for there is no desire for mother-of-pearl at all following an illusion of silver, but rather [desire arises] for an indeterminable (*anirvacanīya*) silver, as will be explained in the section on the theory of indeterminable manifestation (*anirvacanīyakhyāti*).

The proponent of *akhyāti* (non-apprehension), who asserts that being the locus of a qualifier (*prakārāśrayatva*) is the restrictive factor (*niyāmaka*), should be further intimidated as follows: Since being the locus of a qualifier serves as the restrictive factor, the position of *anyathākhyāti* (misapprehension) is also thereby refuted. Nor should it be argued that, in that case, there would be no status as an error (*bhramatva*), because one does not admit that the cognition intended to be erroneous—such as "this is silver"—possesses a qualifier residing in a different locus (*vyadhikaraṇaprakāratva*).

For error consists in having its object sublated (*bādhita-viṣayatva*), and not in having a discordant qualifier (*vyadhikaraṇa-prakāratva*), since even the latter is caused by the sublation of the object; this will be explained later. Now, an objection might be raised: since the cognition of an absence is produced by the cognition of its counter-positive (*pratiyogin*), darkness—which consists in the absence of all light possessing intense illumination—could not be perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), because the counter-positive would not be present to the mind without the application of a universal (*sāmānya-pratyāsatti*). This is not so, for in our view, darkness is a distinct positive entity (*bhāvāntara*).

Nor should it be argued that "nevertheless, because it manifests that [darkness], it must depend upon it"; for we accept that the absence of such light, by its very existence (*svarūpasat*), is the manifester of darkness, and not as something known, since there is no evidence for that. Even in the view of others, although the knowledge of the absence of such light is required, this is possible through the knowledge of the qualifier that delimits the counter-correlate (*pratiyogitāvacchedakaprakārakajñāna*) alone; therefore, a general cognitive relation (*sāmānyapratyāsatti*)—which would produce the knowledge of all counter-correlates—is useless for that purpose.

Nor is it correct to say that the cognition of the absence of "cowness" (*gotvābhāva*) is produced by a cognition having "the nature of cowness" (*gotvatva*) as its qualifier; for that [nature of cowness], which consists in residing in all cows while not residing in anything other than cows, cannot be understood without the presence of a universal as a means of connection (*sāmānyapratyāsatti*). This is because the nature of cowness is simply any individual cow. By this, the cognition of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) is also explained. Furthermore, if the knowledge of the future is required, it will arise from inference alone. As it is said in the *Nyāyakusumāñjali*: "If there is doubt, there is indeed inference; if there is no doubt, how much more so?"

It has been stated that "doubt has its limit in contradiction, and reasoning (tarka) is held to have doubt as its limit"—thus, up to this point, it was explained that the knowledge of the future which establishes doubt arises from inference alone. And the inference is as follows: "The present cooking is preceded by [past] cooking, because it is an act of cooking, like past cooking," and so forth. Nor is there a deviation (vyabhicāra) in the case of the final act of cooking; for a cognition of deviation that depends upon the establishment of the probandum (sādhya) is not a defect. Otherwise, there would be a contradiction between proof and non-proof. Furthermore, such knowledge regarding all instances of smoke, cooking, and so forth, can also arise from verbal testimony (śabda).

Nor should it be argued that there is no rule regarding the presentation of a word preceded by doubt and the like; for it is possible that at some time, having experienced [an object] through a word, a memory with its specific features (*tattā*) is subsequently wiped away, and [the object] is recalled at that time. If it is objected: "The establishment of generalization as a means of cognition (*pratyāsatti*) follows from the fact that inference is produced by the knowledge of a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇajñāna*); yet, this knowledge of the qualifier cannot come from another inference, as that would lead to an infinite regress," we say: No. For an inference whose subject (*pakṣa*) has the probandum as its qualifier can arise precisely from a knowledge that has the delimiting property of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇatāvacchedaka*) as its mode (*prakāra*).

By this, the so-called "cognition-characterized" (*jñānalakṣaṇā*) proximity, postulated for the sake of specific cognitions such as "the sandalwood is fragrant," is also refuted; for the fragrance can be established through inference from the [perceived] nature of being sandalwood. Otherwise, since the perception of the subject (*pakṣa*) as qualified by the probandum (*sādhya*) would be possible [through that proximity], there would follow the undesirable consequence of the total abolition of inference. Nor should it be argued that—in the case of a purely negative inference (*kevalavyatirekin*) where non-existence is the probandum—the means of inference (*anumitisāmagrī*) already established there is stronger than the means of perception (*pratyakṣasāmagrī*), because the establishment of the probandum (*sādhyaprasiddhi*) is not a constituent factor in that [inference].

This is because we, who maintain the theory of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), do not accept that [inference as the cause of knowledge]. However, if one accepts an inference in which the probandum (*sādhya*) is the qualificandum and the subject (*pakṣa*) is the qualifier—arising from the reflective cognition (*parāmarśa*) that "the smoke residing on the mountain is pervaded by fire"—then there is no inconsistency whatsoever. This is because there is no evidence for a rule that an inference must necessarily have the subject as its qualificandum.

Furthermore, the universal *dhūmatva* (smokiness) is not a means of proximity (*pratyāsatti*) by its own nature. For if it were, there would follow the undesirable consequence that, after a momentary error regarding smoke in a cloud of dust, the apprehension of the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of fire residing in all instances of smoke could not arise, because *dhūmatva* does not exist there by its own nature. Nor is this a desirable conclusion, as it would entail the non-arising of inference at a subsequent time. Therefore, it must be said that the cognition of *dhūmatva* is the means of proximity; yet such a cognition does not exist prior to the cognition of smoke at the time of sensory contact with the smoke.

There is no evidence for the existence of indeterminate perception (*nirvikalpaka*), because the causal relationship between a qualified cognition (*viśiṣṭajñāna*) and the cognition of its qualifier (*viśeṣaṇajñāna*) is not accepted; for all worldly transactions are sufficiently accounted for by the specific causal relationships that are necessarily established. Furthermore, there is no proof for the claim that, immediately after the cognition of a proximate instance of smoke as "smoke-ness," another cognition arises with the same form but having as its object a non-proximate instance of smoke.

Furthermore, there is the experience that "I directly perceive the smoke standing before me as smoke, not that which is remote. Otherwise, one would have the subsequent reflective awareness (anuvyavasāya): "I directly perceive all individual instances of smoke existing throughout the world. And this is certainly not accepted by those who rely solely on direct experience. Moreover, if the apprehension of a universal (sāmānyapratyāsatti) were admitted, then in the determination of pervasion (*vyāpti*)—such as "whatever is knowable is nameable" or "whatever possesses knowability possesses nameability"—the consequence would be omniscience. And that is certainly not desired.

It cannot be argued that doubt—such as "Is the jar the object of another's knowledge or not?"—is impossible; nor can it be said that a certain cognition (niścaya) having "jar-ness" (*ghaṭatva*) as its qualifier and the jar as its object is the contradictory of doubt regarding the jar. For even the certainty "It is an object of knowledge" (*prameya*), though having the jar as its object, does not have "jar-ness" as its qualifier. This is because, by definition, a qualifier is precisely the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) of the relation of distinction (*vaiśiṣṭya*) that is appearing in the cognition. And "jar-ness" is indeed the counter-correlative of the relation of distinction appearing in the cognition "It is an object of knowledge."

If it is argued that there is no fault because the qualification "being produced by the knowledge of potness" is attached to the certainty whose mode is potness (*ghaṭatvaprakārakaniścaya*), we say no. For its causality must be stated as being solely through the nature of the knowledge of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇajñānatvena*). Since that [position] has already been refuted, and because the acceptance of a specific relation of essential identity (*svarūpasambandha*) would lead to the fallacy of the theory of the indescribable (*anirvacanīyavāda*), many such refutations are to be inferred. Therefore, the claim that there is a sublation (*bādha*) due to the apprehension of the absence of that [pot] once the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitva*) of the mere negation is presented through general cognitive proximity (*sāmānyapratyāsatti*) is entirely untenable.
Thus, by refuting the theory of general proximity (*sāmānyapratyāsatti*), the objections regarding both worldly and non-worldly perception are removed.

Now, the refutation of the contradiction by perception (*sākṣibādha*). An objection: if perception grasps only the present, how could the falsity of nacre-silver and the like—consisting in its being the counter-positive of a negation at all three times within the locus where it is perceived—be known through perception? If it is argued that when the nature of nacre, which is incompatible with "silverness," is directly perceived there, and the absence of silver is ascertained through the impossibility of that [appearance] otherwise, then the cognition of such a negation—"the silver appeared only as false"—[would arise] by means of the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*), which illumines everything related to itself; [we reply:]...

If it is argued that since this is established by the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*) itself, then let the witness—which grasps all time—directly apprehend the non-opposition to negation in future time regarding its own objects, such as the ether (*ākāśa*), we say no. This is because the witness, being the illuminator of everything currently existing, cannot logically be the illuminator of the absence of a sublation (*bādha*) that does not yet exist in the future. Furthermore, since the cognition of the witness is common to both error and valid knowledge, it cannot serve as a sublater of the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*). [Objection: But surely, while apprehending the validity of a cognition, the witness necessarily apprehends the non-sublatability residing in the object, such as a jar.

If it is argued that there can be no apprehension of validity without including the non-sublation of the object, we say no; for even with respect to mere non-sublation at the time of practical activity (*vyavahāra*), the occurrence of correspondence (*saṃvāda*) is possible. Furthermore, there is no contradiction even if the validity residing in that form is apprehended by the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*). For the validity that serves as the delimiting factor for a cognition of a jar or the like in producing a corresponding successful activity is not the state of having an object that is non-sublated throughout the three periods of time.

However, what distinguishes [valid knowledge] from cognitions such as that of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell is precisely the property of having for its object something that is not sublated at the time of practical usage (*vyavahāra-kāla-abādhya-viṣayakatva*), which resides in all cognitions. And it has been stated that this [property] does not contradict sublation at a future time (*bhāvi-kāla-bādha*). Furthermore, it has been stated that both sublation at a future time and its absence cannot be apprehended by the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*) alone without a means of valid cognition (*māna*), because that [witness-consciousness] perceives only what is currently present. [Objection: If that is so, then would not the cognition of the identity of the body and the self, or the cognition that "water is hot," and so forth, also be valid knowledge (*pramā*)?

If it is argued that [the cognition of the world] is valid because its object is not sublated during the state of empirical transaction (*vyavahāra*), we say no; for until the realization of Brahman (*brahmajñāna*), those [empirical cognitions] share the same status as the cognition of a jar and so forth, insofar as they are not sublated. Now, one might ask: even that which is a sublater existing at another time—does it negate the object of this [earlier cognition] precisely at the time-limitation under which this [cognition] grasped its own object, or at a different time-limitation? In the first case, how can this [earlier cognition] possess validity? In the second case, it would merely be a matter of [the object's] non-eternality and so forth. We reply: no, because I do not admit that the nature of validity consisting in "non-sublatability" (*abādhyatva*) applies to the cognition of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*).

For at the very same time that this [cognition] apprehends its own object, it accepts the negation of that [object]; and that validity is accepted by me as indeed existing, because at the stage of practical transaction (*vyavahāra*), no sublater in the form of a contrary cognition has arisen.

Nor should it be argued that the very same distinction you claim exists between the cognition of a jar and the like, and an illusory cognition—which establishes the empirical reality (*vyāvahārikasattva*) of the object—should here establish the ultimate reality (*pāramārthikasattva*) of my object. For the distinction of the cognition of a jar and the like from illusory cognition consists in its having as its object something that is not sublated by a cognition possessing a qualifier (*saprakārakajñāna*). That [distinction] is not capable of establishing the ultimate reality of the jar and so forth.

Because there is a deviation [in the argument] in the case of the knowledge that the body and the self are one, and in the case of an error immediately following the knowledge of Brahman. Now, an objection is raised: "If there is no difference between the two cognitions, 'The pot is real' and 'The silver is false,' how can there be this distinction: 'The pot is false' versus 'The falsity of the silver is not false'? Nor can it be said that even that [falsity of the silver's falsity] is itself false, for that would entail the reality of the silver. This is not so; for it has already been explained in that context how, even when the falsity [of something] is itself false, the object (the silver) does not thereby become real.

Nor should it be argued that if the ultimately real sentient being (*pāramārthikasattva*) is not within the scope of perception, then the scriptural texts negating it would be negating what has never been established (*aprasaktapratiṣedhakatā*). For those [scriptures] aim at negating that which is established by the eyes and other senses. Even if they aim at negating duality in terms of its ultimate reality, they do not negate what is unestablished, because indirect establishment (*parokṣaprasakti*) is possible; and because, as in the case of "one should not build a fire-altar in the intermediate space," even the negation of what is unestablished is logically tenable.

Nor should it be argued: "If even reality (*tāttvikatva*) is not apprehended by perception regarding an unreal manifold (*atāttvikaprapañca*), how then can that [perception] be a non-revealer of reality (*atattvāvedaka*)? For it is not the case that something is called 'non-real' simply because it reveals that very thing as real; moreover, we observe a universal worldly experience of ultimate reality (*pāramārthikatva*) regarding the manifold. This is because, for us, being a revealer of reality does not mean having a qualifier in a locus where that qualifier exists (*tadvati tatprakārakatvam*); rather, being a non-revealer of reality means having a qualifier in a locus different from that [qualifier] (*tadbhinnatvam*).

However, the state of revealing reality (*tattvāvedakatva*) consists in having an uncontradicted object, while the state of not revealing reality (*atattvāvedakatva*) consists in having a contradicted object. Uncontradictedness of the object, moreover, belongs only to the knowledge of Brahman derived from Śruti, and not to any cognition other than that, because it is precisely by virtue of being a Veda possessing intended meaning (*tātparya*) that [the Veda] brings about the realization of reality. Thus, even though the perception of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) does not have reality as its object, its status as not revealing reality is logically consistent.

The universal worldly consensus regarding ultimate reality, however, is established as being beyond direct perception— much like the established capacity of water to quench thirst— and thus does not necessarily culminate in immediate perceptibility. Therefore, since existence here is defined as that which is fit for direct perception, the absence of such perception cannot serve as a valid reason for the falsity of this [ultimate reality], nor can it be sublated by perception.
It is neither worldly, nor produced by common [causes], nor is it of the nature of a witness. ||1||
The inferential mark that leads to the inference of falsity is sublated by direct perception.
Thus ends the second [section], the refutation of the objection based on perception through the demonstration that existence suitable for perception cannot be defined.

Just as in the case of "What is this silver?", where "this" [refers to the substrate], so too in "The pot exists," it is Brahman alone, as the substrate, that shines forth as "existent. Nor should it be asked how Brahman, which is devoid of color and other qualities, can manifest in visual or other sensory cognitions; for it has already been established that manifestation is possible even for that which lacks color and the like, by analogy with time and other such entities. [Objection: If this were so, then in cases such as "The pot is blue," "The silver is false," or "A hare's horn is non-existent," the terms "blue" and so on would likewise have to be considered as the superimposition of the substrate.

Nor should it be argued that blueness does not exist in jars and the like, whereas existence (sattva) does; for such an argument would involve a circular dependency, since it presupposes the proof of the superimposed nature [of existence] which occurs only after [the point has been established]. Otherwise, even in the case of "truth, knowledge" (*satyaṃ jñānam*), the term "true" (*satyam*) would merely be an infiltration of the substrate. To this we say: no, because the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of "existent" (*san*) with "jar" (*ghaṭaḥ*) is sublated.

To explain: grammatical co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) would have to be based either on the manifestation of the universal "Being" (*sattājāti*), or on essential existence (*svarūpasattva*), or on non-sublation throughout the three periods of time. However, the manifestation of the universal "Being" is not possible in the cognition of "existence" as it applies commonly to absences (*abhāva*) and the like, for you yourself do not admit that [the universal "Being"] exists in absences and such things. Nor can the cognition "existent" be accounted for by positing a direct relation in some cases and an indirect (mediated) relation in others.

Because a cognition of a common form cannot be accounted for through a relation with heterogeneous entities; otherwise, the very distinction between relations would not be established. Nor can that cognition [of existence] occur in the case of non-existence and the like by virtue of their own intrinsic nature (*svarūpasattva*), because such a nature is not uniform (*ananugama*). If a uniform cognition were produced even by non-uniform factors, it would follow that the category of universals (*jāti*) is entirely abolished. For this very reason, the conventional usage of "existent" does not apply everywhere solely on the basis of intrinsic nature. Since the cognition of existence can be accounted for everywhere by a single, all-pervading factor, there is no evidence to postulate many such causes.

Nor is that [existence] based on being uncontradicted throughout the three periods of time, because it has already been stated that such [existence] is inaccessible to the eyes and other senses; furthermore, because it is absent in illusions such as "this silver is real. Therefore, it is logical that what is experienced everywhere as "existent" is simply one thing: the substratum of all. However, there is no sublation whatsoever regarding the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of blue and so forth with a jar and the like. Nor is it possible for blue and so forth to be the substratum, because they do not exist prior [to their manifestation]. Moreover, it would involve the fault of complexity (*gaurava*) to postulate an infinite number of individual substrata for each instance of blue, yellow, and so on.

And because [the substrate] shares the same security and destiny (*yogakṣema*) as that which is superimposed upon it. For a superimposition (*adhiṣṭhāna*) occurs only when it possesses a reality (*sattā*) different from that of the object superimposed. In cases such as "false silver" or "the non-existent horn of a rabbit," there is not even a suspicion of falsity or non-existence being the substrate; for that would result in the fallacy of nihilism (*śūnyavāda*). The impossibility of that has already been stated and will be stated again. As for the objection that the same might apply to the passage "Truth, Knowledge, Infinite," that is not so.

Since existence there does not arise through a relation with existence, but rather by its very own nature (*svarūpeṇa*), the aforementioned fault finds no occasion. Nor is it the case that for a jar and so forth, suchness likewise exists by its very own nature; for that has already been refuted previously. Thus concludes the examination of the superimposition of the substrate in the perception "this is a jar."

Furthermore, only a perception whose validity is already ascertained could subvert other means of knowledge; however, in this case, its validity is not ascertained, because it contradicts scripture, it contradicts inference, and there is no determination that a future sublation will not occur. Objection: Perception alone is more powerful and subverts inference and scripture, not inference and scripture [themselves]. For if perception were invalid, there would be no contradiction with it, and thus inference and scripture would possess validity; yet if those two possess validity, perception is invalid due to the contradiction with them—this being a case of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*).

If it is argued that there is no such mutual dependence regarding the validity of perception because it is independent, we say no; for we observe that the validity of the perception of the size of the moon, stars, and so forth is negated by inference and scripture, and thus even that [perception] must necessarily depend on non-contradiction with the other two [means of knowledge] in order to establish its own validity.

Furthermore, since they are equally subject to mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*), there arises a doubt regarding their validity due to their mutual contradiction. Once the validity of the Veda is ascertained through the pervasion (*vyāpti*) that being not composed by an unreliable person (*anāpta*) entails being a producer of valid knowledge, the perception [of the opponent]—which is itself suspected of having inherent defects—is sublated by that ascertainment. Thus, in our view, where is there any mutual dependence? Otherwise, if it were otherwise, even the distinctness of the self from the body would not be established by scripture or inference, because it would be sublated by the perceptual cognition of the identity between the body and the self.

Is it not the case that perception is inherently stronger than inference and the like? Otherwise, how could the perception of heat obstruct the inferential cognition of coldness in fire? Nor is the sublation of inference by perception based on the former being dependent upon the latter; for while the locus (the fire) and other factors are established by the eye itself, the sense of touch is not required as a basis for that establishment.

Furthermore, if it is argued that perception possesses greater strength than inference and the like because it apprehends features such as lines and furrows not grasped by inference, and because it removes disorientation regarding directions and so forth which has not been removed by inference, we say no. For even tactile perception can act as an obstacle to the inference of coldness simply by virtue of being a necessary prerequisite (*upajīvya*). Even when the locus (*dharmin*) and other factors are perceived by the eye and other senses, the probandum (*sādhya*) cannot be established without the skin. Thus, there is no proof for the superior strength [of perception] based on its genus (*jāti*).

Furthermore, the quality of apprehending what has not already been apprehended (*agṛhītagrāhitva*) is not a determinant of superiority. For, by virtue of apprehending *dharma* and other objects not apprehended by perception, it would follow that indirect means of knowledge (*parokṣapramāṇa*) alone possess superiority. Nor is superiority established by the capacity to remove delusions regarding direction and so forth, which have not been removed by inference and other means; for by this much, only a mere difference in character (*vaidharmya*) is proven, and such a difference does not constitute superiority over other means of knowledge.

Otherwise, since the visual sense also removes the delusion of a snake in a bamboo stalk that has already been set aside by tactile perception, the eye would have to be considered stronger than the skin. Consequently, the visual cognition of a variegated surface with depressions and elevations—which contradicts that [tactile] cognition—would not be sublated by it. On the contrary, the superior authority of scripture (āgama) over all else is merely being recalled: "The superior authority of scripture alone among those three is traditionally held to be innate. Nor should it be argued that this [superiority] refers only to the subject matter of Vedic texts; for non-duality (advaita) is also a subject matter of the Vedas.

"And where is it that what is obtained through perception is not sublated by inference or scripture?"—this refers to the domain of perception whose authority has been examined. Now, one might object: "Because perception has no prior contradiction, its superiority is established by the principle of the primacy of the opening statement (*upakrama-nyāya*). For it has been said: 'Since it has no prior contradiction, the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) is to be accepted according to its literal sense; whereas the injunctive statement (*vidhyuddeśa*), which contradicts it, must be interpreted [figuratively]'. If this is argued, we say: No.

Since, in a case where two terms are mutually dependent within a single sentence and thus equal in status, it is determined that the terms occurring in the conclusion—such as "Ṛg" and so forth, which denote merely mantras—must refer to the entire Veda in accordance with the term "Veda" appearing in the opening, that same logic does not apply here. This is because there is no equality between the two; for perception, which remains uncertain as to whether it is distinct from error, possesses less force than Śruti, whose authoritative status has already been established.

Otherwise, even the error "this is silver" would be stronger than the authoritative instruction "this is mother-of-pearl. By this [argument], the claim that perception is stronger because it proceeds more swiftly—just as a direct Vedic statement (śruti) is stronger than an inferential mark (liṅga)—is refuted; for it has been stated: "Just as in the world there is a relative strength between perception and inference due to their being swift or slow in operation, so too is it between śruti and liṅga. This is rejected because that which is examined [and found valid] is stronger, even if it operates slowly.

Nor should it be argued that, just as the injunction "one offers in the *āhavanīya* fire" is stronger than "one offers on the foot" due to its specific scope, so too perception—which apprehends the existence of a jar—must be stronger than the Śruti which negates duality in a general sense; for the principle of the general and the particular (*sāmānyaviśeṣanyāya*) applies only to cases where both [the general and the particular] possess established validity as means of knowledge. Otherwise, even statements such as "this is a cow, it is a horse" would be stronger than statements such as "it is neither a cow nor a horse."

And it is not the case that—as in the instance of the word *yatkiñcit* in the passage "Whatever [is] prior to the Agniṣomīya, with that they proceed in a low voice," where, although the word *yatkiñcit* refers to what is under discussion (*prakṛta*) and thus lacks a general scope, it is restricted by the sentence "In the Dīkṣaṇīyā, one should recite with as much voice as one desires," which has no other application (*niravakāśa*)—so too [should there be restriction] here by means of a direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), by another mode of operation (*vṛttyantara*) that has no other application, or by [the word] having multiple meanings (*anekārtha*) through its reference to a different subject matter.

It should not be argued that there might be a contraction of the scope of the scriptural text which possesses an occasion [for limitation]; for once it is determined—by means of the indicators of intention such as the opening passages (*upakrama*) and so forth—that the text aims at the negation of duality, the non-dualistic scripture (*advaita-śruti*) likewise becomes free of any occasion [for limitation]. This is because even perception possesses an occasion [for its validity] by having empirical duality as its object.

Furthermore, when two contradictory cognitions—such as the perception "I am a human" and the scriptural text "He is omnipresent and eternal like space"—are present, since their ultimate validity (*tāttvikaprāmāṇya*) cannot both be established, one must accept that one possesses empirical validity (*vyāvahārikaprāmāṇya*) and the other possesses ultimate validity; for it is improper to grant absolute invalidity (*atyantāprāmāṇya*) to either. In this case, if the non-dualistic scripture could possess only empirical validity, then the perception and other means of knowledge that grasp duality would have to possess ultimate validity.

But in the absence of that [contradiction], since the non-dualistic scripture possesses ultimate validity by its very power, it follows that the validity of perception and the like is merely empirical; let those of refined intellect take note of this.

Now, an objection may be raised: in the *pañcadaśarātra* sacrifice, on the first day—which is named *agniṣṭut*—the *subrahmaṇyā* mantra addressed to Agni (*āgneyī*) is obtained through the extension of rules (*nāmātideśa*) from the one-day (*ekāha*) *agniṣṭut* sacrifice. Just as that *āgneyī* *subrahmaṇyā*, which has a narrow scope, is set aside by the *aindrī* *subrahmaṇyā* obtained for the remaining fourteen days by the general rule (*codaka*), because it has a wider scope and it is improper to invalidate many [rules], so too must the non-dualistic statement be accepted in order not to invalidate the many means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) such as perception grasping duality, the inference based upon it, the ritual section (*karmakāṇḍa*), and the passages concerning meditation on the qualified Brahman (*saguṇopāsana*).

Why should there not be a sublation of the well-known meaning? If it is argued that "it is observed that when there is a conflict with many means of valid cognition, the invalidity of a single one is seen, as in the case of the cognition of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell," we say no; for in the example, the sublation is by means of a cognition having many objects, whereas here [the sublation] is by many [cognitions], and thus there is a disparity.

Even though there exist fallacious perception, inference, and verbal testimony regarding the identity of the body and the self, just as the scripture teaching the difference between the body and the self possesses greater authority because it is not intended for any other purpose, so too here the non-dualistic scripture possesses greater authority because it is not intended for any other purpose; thus, there is no contradiction, owing to the distinction between knowledge and ignorance, and the distinction between the person who possesses knowledge and the person who does not. [This concludes] the refutation of the superior authority of perception through such principles as the "commencement with a genus" (*jāty-upakrama-nyāya*).

Now, it may be argued: even if perception lacks inherent superiority by virtue of its nature according to the principles stated, it possesses superiority by virtue of being foundational (*upajīvyatva*). And this status of being foundational consists in its grasping all those objects required by inference and scripture. This [requirement] occurs sometimes directly and sometimes through a succession; moreover, the status of being foundational is observed even for those that grasp only a single part of what is required, and there is sublation (*bādha*) by such [perception] when it apprehends something contrary to that [inference or scripture].

Just as in the inference of the all-pervasiveness of the pot, there is sublation by the sense of sight which perceives the subject (*pakṣa*); in the inference of the purity of the human head, by the scripture which perceives the probandum (*sādhya*); and in the inference of the all-pervasiveness of the mind, by the inference which perceives the reason—namely, that it is not the substrate of the non-inherent cause of cognition; what need is there to mention that there is sublation of that which perceives its own opposite by that which perceives everything required [for the proof]? Furthermore, although the eye and other senses do not perceive sound or the validity of the knowledge produced by it, they possess the status of being "that upon which another depends" (*upajīvya*) because they belong to the same class as the ear and the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*), which do perceive them.

It is observed that the scriptural testimony (āgama) which makes known the impurity of a human skull-pot is stronger than the inference of its purity, because it belongs to the same class as the scriptural testimony on purity upon which that inference depends. Nor can it be argued that the sense organ (*indriya*) also depends on inference for the sake of its own cognition, such that the relationship between the dependent and the depended-upon (*upajīvya-upajīvaka*) would be equal; for while the sense organ does not require inference to produce a cognition since it functions as an unknown instrument (*ajñātakaraṇa*), inference and scripture do require it precisely for the sake of producing cognition—this is the distinction. If this is argued, we say no, because there is no contradiction with what is depended upon.

For instance: that whose own nature is depended upon is not sublated; yet it is the aspect of ultimate reality (*tāttvikatva*) that is sublated, and that [aspect] is not what is depended upon, because it does not enter into its status as a cause. As it has been said:
"If causality consists in a restriction based on a prior relation, then it is exactly the same for both of us;
