the discussion regarding existence or non-existence outside of the true nature of causality is futile."

Furthermore, if being dependent [on another cognition] were to constitute the state of being sublated simply by virtue of grasping what is required [by that other], and if [the sublating cognition] were to be a sublater on that basis, then—since the error "this is silver" depends upon the sublation [of the subsequent cognition] by way of grasping the counter-positive (pratiyogin) required [for that negation]—how could the sublating cognition "this is not silver," which is contradictory to it, arise? Alternatively, even if that [erroneous cognition] is dependent as a knowledge of the counter-positive by way of presenting the object to be negated, its validity (*prāmāṇya*) is not what is depended upon.

For the production of the cognition of an absence does not depend on the validity (*prāmāṇya*) of the cognition of the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*), because that would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*). Furthermore, we observe the cognition of an absence even from an erroneous cognition (*bhrama*) of the counter-positive. Rather, it depends solely on being a cognition of that [counter-positive], due to parsimony (*lāghava*). Therefore, if you argue that a cognition having an object contradictory to that [absence] must necessarily arise, this applies equally to the present case as well: the causality resides in the nature of being a cognition of the subject (*pakṣa*), and not in its being a valid cognition (*pramā*) of it.

Now, if it is argued that validity (*prāmāṇya*) which one relies upon for the sake of establishing its own nature and for the sake of refuting objections is what is "relied upon" (*upajīvya*) by that [subsequent cognition], just as perception (*anubhava*) is relied upon by memory (*smṛti*), and that the illusion of silver is not so [relied upon]—then, in that case, even the cognition of pervasion (*vyāpti*) would not be something relied upon by inference (*anumiti*). For, from a fallacious mark (*liṅgābhāsa*) as well, one observes the valid knowledge of fire in a place where fire exists. If it is objected: "One must simply say that whatever cannot arise without another is what is relied upon by that [other]," [we reply:]...

And thus, while the silver-illusion indeed possesses the status of being a necessary presupposition (*upajīvyatva*), it does not possess superiority (*prābalya*). For superiority does not follow merely from being a presupposition, but rather from being verified. Verification consists in the absence of contradiction with, and correspondence to, similar and dissimilar cognitions. These two conditions do not exist in the case of the silver-illusion. In the present context, however, the sense-perception possesses superiority because it is verified; for after the cognition produced by the perception of specific features such as "the jar exists," there occurs the direct perception of the jar's causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) and the absence of established defects such as distance.

In the same way, regarding the scriptural texts on the non-difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*), the scriptural texts that present difference—which are to be negated—and direct perception by a witness (*sākṣipratyakṣa*) are both examined as being free from defects; therefore, even that [non-difference] is not to be sublated. Furthermore, if there were no confidence even in the examination consisting of the knowledge of the absence of defects and so forth—[namely] in the Veda’s lack of human authorship, in the knowledge of the absence of fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) in your stated inference through the means of "non-perception of the perceptible" (*yogyānupalabdhi*) and so on, and in the knowledge of the consistency with the introductory passages (*upakrama*) and other criteria for the meaning intended by the proponent in every section (*adhikaraṇa*) of the Brahma-Mīmāṃsā—then [your position would fail].

If it is argued that there would be no confidence [in knowledge] and thus no distinction between valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) and their fallacies (*tadābhāsa*), we say no. For examination (*parīkṣā*) consists in the absence of failure upon practical application (*pravṛtti-saṃvāda*) and the absence of defects; by means of this, the non-sublation of the object at the same place and time as the cognition itself is established as its validity (*prāmāṇya*), just as fire at the same place and time is established by means of smoke.

And thus, since the property of being uncontradicted solely within the state of empirical transaction (*vyavahāra-daśā*)—which is common even to the identity of the body and the self—is established by means of examined valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), how could the operation of scripture and inference, which apprehend the absence of absolute non-contradiction, not take place? Therefore, it is entirely logical that the distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*), as well as the determination of what is a valid means of knowledge and what is a fallacy thereof, is merely empirical; hence, "the entire world is false" is indeed established.

Now, an objection: if perception were invalid, there would be a sublation of the validity of inference and so forth, because the pervasion (*vyāpti*) and other factors established by it would be sublated; for the object of inference and the like share the same status of being supported or refuted (*samānayogakṣema*) with the pervasion and the like, as well as with the validity of the inferential cognition and so forth.

Otherwise, by means of smoke superimposed on steam—which possesses an apparent (prātibhāsika) pervasion and so forth—a real or empirical fire would be established; or by means of smoke possessing empirical pervasion and so forth, a real fire would be established; and by means of empirical non-sublation and the fact of being the locus of contradictory attributes, the ultimate reality of the universe, the difference between the individual soul and the Lord, and so on, would be established. If this is argued, we say no. For the resulting implication would be that the object of inference must be established as having the same level of reality as its pervasion and other such factors.

Furthermore, there exists this restriction that the inferential mark (*liṅga*) and so forth must possess an equal ontological status (*samasattākatva*) with the object to be inferred (*anumeya*) by virtue of their pervasion (*vyāpti*) and other criteria; for even when a fallacious mark is employed, one observes the occurrence of valid inferential cognition regarding the subject (*pakṣa*) which possesses the property to be proven (*sādhya*). This is because the Mīmāṃsakas accept that a true verbal cognition is produced by eternal and all-pervading phonemes (*varṇa*), even though these are illusory insofar as they are qualified by properties such as shortness or length, which are attributes of sound (*dhvani*).

For even in a jar delimited by the prior non-existence of fragrance—which possesses real pervasion and so forth—one observes the inference of unreal fragrance by means of its earth-nature. Likewise, one observes the inference of the original object (*bimba*) by means of its reflection. Nor should it be argued that even in those cases, the pervasion consisting in "not occurring in the absence of the original object" is itself real; for if that were so, then even [non-occurrent entities] such as space (*ākāśa*) would incur the status of being pervaded.

Nor should it be argued that in this case, the fact of being preceded by a prototype (*bimba*) is itself inferred by means of a non-illusory reason consisting in the state of being the counter-positive of an absence whose occurrence is necessitated by the absence of the prototype. For "necessitation" (*prayuktatva*) does not consist in being the producer or the produced of one another, since such a relationship is absent between the two absences. Rather, it consists in the relation of pervader and pervaded (*vyāpya-vyāpaka-bhāva*). Thus, the reason would be "being the counter-positive of an absence that pervades the absence of the prototype. But this very reason is indeed inconclusive (*vyabhicārin*), as it occurs in cases such as space (*ākāśa*).

Therefore, in that case, the inference of the original object (*bimba*) occurs solely through its reflection (*pratibimba*). This is because the rule—that the probandum (*anumeya*) must necessarily possess the same ontological status as the logical mark (*liṅga*), its pervasion (*vyāpti*), and so forth—has been rejected. By this, the following argument is refuted: "In the case of verbal testimony as well, the word-meaning (*śabdārtha*) must possess the same ontological status as the semantic competency (*yogyatā*), since there is a rule that competency and the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*) must have the same ontological status; therefore, how could the meaning of a Vedānta sentence remain uncontradicted even when its competency is contradicted?"

Furthermore, there is no sublation of the semantic competency (*yogyatā*) of the Vedāntic statements, which consists in their having as their sentence-meaning an indivisible reality (*akhaṇḍārtha*). Nor should it be argued: "Even so, how can non-duality be established as ultimately real (*tāttvika*) if the Vedāntas, the knowledge thereof, and its validity are themselves false? For the ultimate reality of the word and the knowledge thereof is not the determinant for the ultimate reality of the object. In your own view, although the statement "this is silver" uttered by an unreliable person and the resulting error are ultimately real, the object of that [cognition] is not ultimately real.

Nor should it be argued that because the falsity of a cognition’s validity is seen to entail the falsity of its object—as in the case of the cognition of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell—the same must apply here as well; for if the validity of the cognition is false, the object must also be false. This is not to be said, because the falsity of validity is not the cause (*prayojaka*) of the falsity of the object. This is because in indeterminate perception (*nirvikalpaka*), which lies outside the categories of error and valid knowledge, there is no sublation of the object. Rather, it is invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*)—defined as having a qualifier (*prakāra*) where that qualifier is absent—that is the cause of the object's falsity. And such invalidity does not exist at all in the present case.

Nor should it be argued that because the validity consisting in the non-sublation of the object is false, the object itself must also be false; for while the validity in question is the state of having an uncontradicted object as its domain, its falsity in the present case does not arise from the sublation of the object, since no means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) exists to sublate it, and because that [validity] serves as the ultimate limit of all sublation. Rather, such falsity arises from the sublation of the relation consisting in having that [object] as its domain. Thus, even if the validity—defined as having an uncontradicted object as its domain—is false, the object itself is not false.

Because even when one part of a qualified entity is false, another part may still be true; just as when a person qualified by a staff is sublated due to the sublation of the staff, the person himself is not at all sublated. Thus ends the section on the refutation of the dependence of perception [on other means of knowledge] in the *Advaitasiddhi*.

Furthermore, even inference, when accompanied by a subverting argument against the contrary (vipakṣabādhaka), can serve as a subverter of perception. Now, one might object: even so, how could perception—which grasps the three scriptural texts, "Having touched the *audumbarī* [post], he should sing the *udgītha*," "He worships the *gārhapatya* fire with the *aindrī* verse," and "The sacrificial grass (*barhis*) consists of *śara* reeds"—be subverted respectively by the inference of a scriptural text regarding total wrapping, in the form of the Smṛti rule "The *audumbarī* must be entirely wrapped," and by the [Smṛti] text beginning "O Indra, never art thou barren; thou never failest the donor"?... [text continues]... "kadācana starīrasi nendra saścasi dāśuṣe."

If it is argued that [the Vedic text] would be sublated by an inference based on the scriptural statement of Indra’s subordinate status—which is characterized by the power of mantras—and by an inference of the scriptural mention of *kuśa* grass which takes the form of an indicative mark (*liṅga*) within the injunction, thereby uprooting the entire Mīmāṃsā system—this is not so, because of the disparity between the cases.

To explain: what is it that is being asserted here? Is it that the perception apprehending the three scriptural texts is sublated by inferences, or that the three scriptural texts which have become objects of perception [are sublated]? Not the first, because in the absence of contradiction, the relationship between the sublated and the sublator cannot be the intended meaning of the scripture, and because we do not accept such a position. Furthermore, if this were merely a criticism of what was not stated, it would result in the fallacy of "accusing one of a fault for which they are not reproachable. For this very reason, the second alternative is also not tenable.

Even in a treatise that maintains that the three types of Vedic revelation (*śruti*) which have become objects of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) override inferential marks (*liṅga*), there is no contradiction in the fact that direct perception itself can be overridden by inference; for there is no identity between verbal testimony and direct perception. Furthermore, we have already stated that verbal testimony is more powerful than all other means of knowledge. Therefore, this objection regarding its contradiction with Mīmāṃsā is mere folly.

[Objection: But if perception were sublated by inference, then the perception of the heat of fire would not be the sublator of the inference of its coldness, nor would the recognition of the self's persistence be the sublator of the inference of its momentariness; on the contrary, it would be the inference itself that sublates those two. [Reply: This is not so, because in those cases, due to corroboration by causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) and the support of scripture (*śruti*), the two perceptions possess such strength that they sublate the inference.

For unexamined perception is weaker than examined inference, just as the perception that "the sky is blue" is weaker than the inference based on the sky's lack of color. Therefore, there is no risk of a total confusion of categories based merely on what is observed in general. But if this were so, one might also infer horns from the state of being a "beast" (paśu); for by the principle of parsimony (*lāghava*), it is the state of being a beast alone that is the essential factor for having horns, rather than its specific sub-classifications such as "cow-ness" (*gotva*) and so forth.

If it is argued that [the inference] is superior due to its being free from [the fault of] non-pervasion (*ananugatatva*), and because it possesses greater strength than perception due to its accompaniment by reasoning (*tarka*); for indeed, the very strength of an inference lies in its association with favorable reasoning (*anukūlatarka*); and thus, since there exists the accompaniment of the reasoning of parsimony (*lāghava*), one could infer anything about everything through any common property whatsoever; and since that alone would constitute a sublation of perception, even the conventional order of things (*vyāvahārikī vyavasthā*) would not exist—for there is no defect here other than the sublation of perception—if this is said, we reply: no.

Since it must be admitted by you as well that there can be no sublation by perception (*pratyakṣabādha*) in the case of proving [the existence of] horns and the like—which are unestablished—and that the fallacious nature of the reasonings (*tarka*) used to grasp pervasion (*vyāpti*) therein must be stated, this conclusion is to be resolved by both parties alike. For no one accepts that an inference accompanied by a fallacious reasoning (*tarkābhāsa*) constitutes a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Therefore, it is established that inference, when assisted by sound reasoning (*sattarka*), is the sublater of perception. Thus is established the sublation of perception by inference.

Furthermore, even perception is sublated by verbal testimony whose status as a means of valid cognition has been established. Now, if perception were sublatable by verbal testimony, then Jaimini would not have declared that the arthavāda "Therefore, only smoke was seen from the fire by day, not the flame," nor the mantra "Aditi is the sky," and so forth, possess a figurative meaning—thereby avoiding their lack of authority due to contradiction with what is perceived—by stating such principles as "But it is a figurative statement" (*guṇavādastu*) and "There would be no contradiction because of a figurative sense" (*guṇādavipratiṣedhaḥ syāt*).

Otherwise, in the *Tatsiddhi-peṭikā*, the statement "from its accomplishment, genus, similarity, praise, location, and connection with a mark" would not explain the figurative meaning of such passages as "the sacrificial grass-bundle (*prastara*) is the sacrificer (*yajamāna*). Furthermore, you too would not have to resort to *lakṣaṇā* (indication) for the two words *tat* and *tvam* in order to avoid contradicting perception; for when there is a conflict with scripture, it is perception itself that may lack authority. Nor should it be argued that because the marks of *tātparya* (intention), such as the *upakrama* (opening statement) and so forth, are present here, the non-dual scriptures cannot be taken in a non-primary sense.

Even in cases such as "The sacrificer is the sacrificial grass-bundle" (*yajamānaḥ prastaraḥ*), because each individual mark (*liṅga*)—such as *apūrva* (the unprecedented)—is present as a determinant of the intended meaning (*tātparya*), each individual mark alone determines the intention; the other marks are merely corroborative (*anuvādaka*), just as in your own view, scripture (*śruti*) is [redundant] when difference is already established by perception. If you ask, "What is the use of this abundance [of marks]?", we say no.

Since perception—having been examined through means such as the remainder of the context (*vākyaśeṣa*), corroboration by other means of knowledge (*pramāṇāntara-saṃvāda*), and causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*)—possesses superior authority, those [scriptural passages] grasping meanings contrary to it during the state of empirical transaction (*vyavahāra-daśā*), such as "smoke was seen from fire even by day," "Aditi is heaven," or "the sacrificial grass is being born," may have non-literal meanings due to their contradiction with that [perception]. However, since the scripture of non-duality (*advaitāgama*) lacks contradiction with examined means of knowledge, its literal meaning is established.

For, through critical examination, perception and the other means of knowledge are established as possessing merely empirical validity (*vyāvahārikaprāmāṇya*). And that [empirical validity] is not sublated by the non-dualistic scripture (*advaitāgama*). What is sublated, however, is their ultimate validity (*tātvikaprāmāṇya*); but that [ultimate validity] is not established by critical examination at all. Therefore, there is no contradiction. However, if statements such as "only smoke [is the mark] of fire" were taken in their primary sense, the empirical validity of perception and the rest would be undermined. Thus, due to this contradiction, those [statements] are understood to be non-primary in meaning; this is the distinction.

As for the claim that figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) of the two words "that" (tat) and "thou" (tvam) should not be resorted to in order to avoid contradicting perception—that is not so. For it is untenable that the intended meaning, which is determined as being exclusively non-dual through the sixfold marks of interpretation and the uniformity of the tradition, should fail to be established; and because the co-occurrence of attributes such as omniscience and limited knowledge residing in the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara) cannot logically constitute a single identity. Therefore, it is precisely appropriate to accept figurative indication in order to bring about the realization of the non-dual reality that constitutes the subject matter of the intended meaning.

For it is observed everywhere that one resorts to figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in order to effect the syntactic connection (*anvaya*) that constitutes the intended meaning (*tātparya*). Nor should it be argued that this would result in a non-primary sense; for does this consist in (1) being intent upon another meaning by abandoning the perceived meaning, or (2) having an impossible meaning? It is not the first, because there is no abandonment of the identity perceived through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).

Not the latter [option], because even when a portion of the primary meaning (*śakyārtha*) is abandoned by resorting to *jahadajahallakṣaṇā*, a portion of the primary meaning is admitted to be connected—just as in sentences such as "This is that Devadatta. Here, the designation "indication" (*lakṣaṇā*) refers specifically to the connection with the substantive alone due to the sublation of the qualifiers. Thus it has been stated by Vācaspatimiśra: "A sentence such as 'The sacrificial grass is the self' has a non-primary meaning because it is supplementary to something else; however, a sentence concerning non-duality has only a primary meaning because it is not supplementary to anything else."

For it is stated in the Śābara-bhāṣya: "In an injunction, the primary meaning of a word is not [the literal one]. And just as we shall explain later how sentences such as "The sacrificer is the sacrificial grass-bundle" (*yajamānaḥ prastaraḥ*) do not have their own literal sense as their primary purport—due to the mark of a single purport consisting in *apūrva* (unprecedented efficacy) and so forth—in the same way, being subsidiary to another or not being subsidiary to another is not the cause of non-literalness or literalness; rather, it is contradiction or non-contradiction with other means of valid cognition (*mānāntara*).

Even in cases where [the word] is subordinate to another (*anyaśeṣa*), provided there is no contradiction with other means of knowledge—as in common worldly usage such as "this cow is for sale, yielding much milk," or in the Veda such as "He wept"—one does not resort to a non-primary mode of signification (*amukhyavṛtti*), as is the case with sentences concerning the grass-bundle (*prastara*) and so forth. Furthermore, even in cases where [the word] is not subordinate to another (*ananyaśeṣa*), as in "One should sacrifice with Soma" (*somena yajeta*), since a connection through grammatical apposition (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) would result in the fallacy of two sets of three contradictory factors (*viruddhatrikadvaya*), one resorts to the indication of possessive meaning (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*)—namely, "by means of a sacrifice possessing Soma"—in order to avoid contradiction with perception (*pratyakṣa*) when the connection is instead made through grammatical coordination (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*).

For this reason, in the aphorism "Then, therefore, the desire to know Brahman" (*athāto brahmajijñāsā*) which prescribes such inquiry, as well as in the scriptural text "Seek to know That" (*tadvijijñāsasva*), we accept that the word *jijñāsā* (desire to know) indicates "inquiry" (*vicāra*) through secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) in order to connect it with the injunction, since there would otherwise be a contradiction with other means of valid knowledge; and furthermore, in passages such as "All this, indeed, is Brahman," we accept a non-primary sense because it is accepted that for every sentence, secondary signification alone is intended with respect to Brahman, which is inexpressible by words, and thus it is impossible to deny the presence of a non-primary sense.

This is because the grounds for *lakṣaṇā* (indication)—namely, the impossibility of syntactic connection (*anvayānupapatti*) or the impossibility of the intended meaning (*tātparyānupapatti*)—are common to both injunctive and non-injunctive passages; and the statement of Śabara is intended to show that there is no *lakṣaṇā* in an injunction only insofar as it serves to establish the primary status of the *arthavāda*. Therefore, [the objection] that perception is not sublated by verbal testimony is incorrect, because of a lack of understanding. For "primary meaning" (*mukhyārthatva*) consists in conveying the meaning that constitutes the object of the intention (*tātparya*), and not merely conveying a meaning that is semantically possible. Furthermore, primary meaning is established precisely by the fact that the intention is directed toward something other [than the literal sense].

It is not merely a case of figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*). Thus, we have already stated that even when resorting to figurative indication in order to establish the non-dual scripture's capacity to convey its intended object, its status as having a primary meaning (*mukhyārthatva*) remains justified. Likewise, in the case of a qualified injunction such as "one should sacrifice with soma," there is no figurative indication because the intention does not reside in the qualifier; furthermore, since its own primary meaning is not abandoned even when *matvarthalakṣaṇā* occurs, it does not lack a primary meaning.

Regarding the term *jijñāsā*, although there is a difference of opinion as to whether one accepts or rejects the secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the root *jñā* as denoting the knowledge that is sought to be attained, the acceptance of "indication with exclusion" (*jahallakṣaṇā*) for the suffix *-san* (denoting inquiry) is equal in both cases. Even though the primary meaning is abandoned, the primary sense of the word is not lost, because the purpose of the injunction is thereby fulfilled. For it is not the case that a sentence becomes non-primary simply because a word within it undergoes indication, when the sentence-meaning is otherwise impossible to comprehend; rather, the meaning thus understood is considered primary because it is not subordinate to anything else.

Furthermore, where the very meaning of a sentence that is already well-known is conceived as being subordinate to something else, there the sentence itself possesses only a non-primary (gauṇa) sense. For the intention (*tātparya*) of individual words is one thing, and the intention of the sentence is another; this is because, in cases such as "Bring the horse-dung" (*sauṇdhavam ānaya*) or "They dwell in the Ganges" (*gaṅgāyāṃ vasanti*), although the intention of the sentence is identical, the intentions of the individual words differ. Conversely, in cases such as "Eat poison" (*viṣaṃ bhuṅkṣva*), although the intentions of the individual words do not differ, the intention of the sentence does differ.

For this very reason, because the meaning of such sentences as "This cow is for sale, yielding much milk" necessarily functions as a supplement to the injunction "it must be purchased," it indicates its excellence (*prāśastya*); and because the meaning of such sentences as "He wept" functions as a supplement to the injunction "silver is not to be given on the sacrificial grass; gold is the sacrificial fee," it indicates its excellence by way of censuring silver.

The statement "All this, indeed, is Brahman, for from that it is born, into that it dissolves, and by that it breathes" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 3.1.1) has only a secondary sense, because it indicates the excellence of the meaning of the sentence—"one should meditate [on Brahman] as peaceful"—by way of being subordinate to the injunction regarding tranquility (*śama*), insofar as it establishes that [Brahman] is attained without effort. For this very reason, the claim that "indication (*lakṣaṇā*) occurs only when there is a contradiction with another means of knowledge" is refuted; for there is an over-extension (*vyabhicāra*) in cases where indication of excellence occurs, such as in the statement, "This cow is for sale, yielding much milk. Rather, in all explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), indication exists solely for the purpose of establishing the comprehension of the object that constitutes the primary purport.

However, this much is the distinction: in the case of injunctions (*vidhi*) and eulogies (*prāśastya*), there is first the knowledge of the meaning of the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*). When that [meaning] is contradicted by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there is indeed sublation (*bādha*), as in "Prajāpati cut out his own omentum" and so forth; for this very reason, in such cases, there is merely a figurative description (*guṇavāda*). But when [the fact] is already established by another means of valid cognition, there is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*), as in "Fire is the remedy for cold" and so forth; for this very reason, in both these cases, there is invalidity because the essential nature of validity—consisting in making known what is not already known and being unsublated—is not maintained.

Furthermore, where there is neither sublation by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*) nor contradiction, there the status of being a *bhūtārthavāda* (a statement of an existing fact) is established through the fulfillment of the very essence of its validity—as in such cases as "Indra raised his thunderbolt against Vṛtra. This is precisely the principle of the section on the Deities (*devatādhikaraṇa*). Now, one might object: "In that case, in passages such as 'The sacrificial post (*yūpa*) is the sun,' since metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is accepted for the sake of understanding the sentence-meaning, would it not follow that these lack a primary meaning? It would not be so, provided that the sentence-meaning were to terminate in the sense that "the sacrificial post is similar to the sun."

However, even though the meaning of the sentence is understood through figurative application (*guṇavṛtti*), it nonetheless functions as an indicator of praise (*prāśastya-lakṣakatva*) by virtue of being a supplement to the injunction "one binds the animal to the sacrificial post" (*yūpe paśuṃ badhnāti*). It is for this very reason that it is considered non-primary (*amukhyatva*), and not because of the figurative nature of the word *āditya*. Thus, it should be understood that in the *Tatsiddhipaṭalikā*, the various modes of figurative application have been demonstrated in all the examples in order to bring about the comprehension of the intermediate sentence-meaning (*avāntaravākyārtha*).

However, the characteristic of praising the ritual action (*karmaprāśastya*) is indeed present there, as it is common to all *arthavāda*s; therefore, there is no impossibility of [the word] not having its primary sense. Consequently, the difference between the sentences concerning the *prastara* (grass-bundle) and others, and the non-dualist (*advaita*) sentences, is established. As for the statement that Śabarasvāmin’s words—“there is no figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in an injunction in order to preserve the primary sense of the *arthavāda*” —are intended to mean that, that is not correct.

In the *Aśvapratigraheṣṭi* sacrifice, regarding the injunction "one should accept" (*pratigṛhṇīyāt*), one accepts the indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the activity of the instigator (*prayojaka*) by means of the assumption of an ellipsis (*vyavadhāraṇakalpanā*) as "one should cause [another] to accept," in accordance with the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*). Therefore, that statement is intended to mean that when a sentence possesses a specific purport (*tātparya*), there is no other subordinate element (*śeṣin*) apart from the sentence-meaning as it is perceived. Consequently, it is established that even though the scripture of non-duality (*advaitāgama*) is figurative (*lākṣaṇika*), it sublates direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) because its primary sense (*mukhyārtha*) remains intact. May there be auspiciousness!
Thus ends the refutation of perception by scripture.

Furthermore, the authority of scripture is established by the principle of "subsequent annulment" (*apacchedanyāya*). For instance, in the section [of the *Mīmāṃsāsūtra*] stating, "In a sequence of prior and posterior, the prior is weaker, as in the case of the original form," it is established that a sacrifice with a total distribution of wealth (*sarvasvadakṣiṇā*)—which is occasioned by the subsequent interruption (*apaccheda*) of the *pratihartṛ* priest—annuls a sacrifice with no distribution of wealth (*adakṣiṇā*) occasioned by the prior interruption of the *udgātṛ* priest, because the latter's cause was already established. Likewise here, the prior perception is annulled by the subsequent scripture.

Now, it may be argued that there is scope for a sacrifice with the gift of all one's possessions (*sarvasva-dakṣiṇā*)—which is occasioned by the interruption of the *pratihartṛ* priest—to sublate a sacrifice without a fee (*adakṣiṇā-yāga*) occasioned by the interruption of the *udgātṛ* priest, even in cases where the interruption of the *pratihartṛ* alone occurs, where both are interrupted simultaneously, or where the interruptions occur sequentially but the interruption of the *pratihartṛ* follows later. Otherwise, the scriptural injunction, "If the *pratihartṛ* should be interrupted, he shall give away all his property," would lack authority.

For this very reason, in the section [of the *Pūrvamīmāṃsāsūtra*] stating "there should be an option due to conflict" (*vipratiṣedhādvikalpaḥ syāt*), an option is declared when both [the *udgātṛ* and the *pratihartṛ*] are disqualified simultaneously. Furthermore, in the section stating "if the *udgātṛ* were the last [to be disqualified], one should give away all one's possessions (*sarvavedasa*) in a repeated sacrifice, as in the other case," it is taught that if the disqualification of the *udgātṛ* occurs after the disqualification of the *pratihartṛ*, one must first complete the previous performance—which was devoid of sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*)—and then, in the second performance of the *Jyotiṣṭoma* which is to be performed, one should give "that which was [intended] in the previous [performance]."

The sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) prescribed by the Śruti with the words "he shall give" is of the nature of the *sarvasva* (one's entire property) itself, because it does not sublate the desire to give away one's entire property that arose during the previous performance due to the prior interruption (*apaccheda*) of the *pratihartṛ*. It is not, however, the fixed fee of one hundred and twelve [cows] which is constant in the Jyotiṣṭoma. Therefore, there is no total sublation of the interruption of the *pratihartṛ*; rather, it has been stated that its displacement occurs in another performance. For it is said in the *Ṭippikā*: "Its displacement is in another performance."

Furthermore, since the two ritual applications—namely, that in which no fee is given (*adakṣiṇa*) and that in which one's entire property is given as a fee (*sarvasvadakṣiṇa*)—can occur sequentially due to two successive causes, there is no contradiction at all, just as in the case of the dark and red colors of a jujube fruit (*badara-phala*), which possess successive causes. For it has been stated in the *Apacchedādhikaraṇa*: "The meaning of the rule concerning contingent conditions (*naimittika-śāstra*) is this: although the sacrifice was to be performed otherwise prior to the arising of the contingent cause, once the cause exists, it must be performed in this manner. Therefore, the principle of the *apaccheda* (successive disqualification) applies only to cases where there is room for both alternatives.

If it is argued that there is no room for the validity of perception once it has been sublated by the non-dualist scripture (*advaitāgama*), we say no. For just as the scriptural injunction prescribing a sacrifice with one's entire property as the sacrificial fee (*sarvasvadakṣiṇā*)—occasioned by the failure of the *pratihartṛ* priest—finds its scope in cases where there is no failure of the *udgātṛ*, or where both fail simultaneously, or where the *pratihartṛ* fails after the *udgātṛ* has already failed during the second performance of the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, so too perception retains its scope within the realm of empirical validity (*vyāvahārikaprāmāṇya*). Thus, perception remains valid on the conventional level.

In that case, just as there is a contradiction in a single application [of two rules], here too there is a contradiction regarding the aspect of ultimate reality (*tāttvikatva*). For this very reason, it is well said that the scriptural passages concerning the qualified (*saguṇa*) and the manifold (*saprapañca*) are sublated by the scriptural passages concerning the unqualified (*nirguṇa*) and the non-manifold (*niṣprapañca*) according to the logic of the "subsequent annulment" (*apacchedanyāya*). As it was stated by Ānandabodhācārya: "Because it is directed toward that [ultimate reality], because it is superior, and because it is faultless, the Vedic [text] sublates the former, just like the statement 'this is not a snake' and so forth."

But surely, when there is a contradiction with another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), the Scripture’s status as being "intended for that" (*tatpara*) is unestablished; moreover, the quality of being "subsequent" (*paratva*) is fallible, as it is seen to apply even to an earlier sublater—for instance, the rule *na ktvā seṭ* (Pāṇini 1.2.18) is subsequent to, yet sublated by, the earlier rule *mṛḍamṛdagudhakuśakliśavadavasaḥ ktvā* (Pāṇini 1.2.7). Furthermore, its faultlessness (*nirdoṣatva*) is otherwise accounted for by the validity of its other meanings. As it has been said: "Tatparatva is unestablished due to contradiction, and paratva is fallible."

If it is argued that "faultlessness does not establish superiority because it is otherwise established," we say no; for there is no contradiction between the empirical validity (*vyāvahārikaprāmāṇya*) of perception and the like, and the ultimate validity (*tāttvikaprāmāṇya*) of the Śruti, and thus its status as having that [ultimate] purpose is established. Furthermore, by the word "para" (supreme/ultimate), what is intended is the state of being uncontradicted by other means of knowledge. Therefore, there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of an error regarding another means of knowledge, since that [error] is sublated by a means of knowledge occurring subsequent to it.

Regarding the rule *na ktvā seṭ*, although it is posterior in the order of the text (*pāṭhataḥ*), its status as prior in terms of meaning (*arthataḥ*) is indeed established in relation to rules such as *mṛḍamṛda* and others. This is because, unless the inherent *kittva* (the property of having *k* as an indicatory letter) already established by nature were set aside by this [rule *na ktvā seṭ*], those subsequent rules would not apply; for when there is an exception to an exception, the original general rule (*utsarga*) alone remains firm. Furthermore, its faultlessness is not otherwise established, since validity is to be accepted only with respect to the intended scope (*tātparyaviṣaya*). Thus, the assertion of a disparity between the present case and the *apaccheda-nyāya* (the logic of the "cutting off") is merely a manifestation of ignorance. Thus ends the refutation of the disparity of the *apaccheda-nyāya*.

Now, if inference were to establish even that which is sublated by perception, then it would also establish the non-heat of fire; and in that case, the discourse regarding the "mistimed" (kālātyayāpadiṣṭa) fallacy would be cut off everywhere. Nor can it be argued that when the absence of heat—where heat is the counter-positive—is the probandum, the sublation is possible because the counter-positive is established within the subject (pakṣa) itself. In the present case, however, empirical existence is established by perception, and falsity is not incompatible with that, since it is only opposed to ultimate reality.

Therefore, it cannot be said that [the inference] is not sublated by perception which apprehends empirical existence (*vyāvahārikasattva*), because such a case does not exist in the inference of the absence of heat in a particular fire, or in the inference of coldness; for in those cases, there exists a locus other than the subject (*pakṣa*) where the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) is established. Nor can it be argued that the rule of sublation applies only where perception is stronger, and since that is not the case here, there is no sublation; for in the present instance as well, there exists a factor that renders [perception] equally strong, thereby serving as the basis for its predominance.

This is because the inference of the absence of heat (*anauṣṇya*) and the inference of falsity (*mithyātva*) possess an identical logical status. Nor should it be argued that for those who maintain the theory of falsity, the inference of the negation of heat within the perceived substrate is indeed intended to be equal to the inference of falsity; for although there may be equality between those two inferences due to heat and the absence of heat being respectively an entity and its non-existence, one does not admit equality with the inference of coldness, since coldness is not of the nature of the absence of heat.

Therefore, either the status of sublation as a defect must be abandoned, or a distinction must be stated between the perception of heat and the perception of being the sacrificer (yajamānatva) etc., on the one hand, and the perception of existence (sattva), on the other. Nor should it be argued that the distinction lies in the fact that the perception of heat has its validity established through examination by both parties, whereas the perception of existence does not; for there is no reason to deny the validity of the perception of existence as well, since the process of examination is equal in both cases. This is not so, because there is a distinction based on the fact that [the latter] grasps a contradictory object.

Just as the state of being the sacrificer (*yajamānatva*) and heat (*auṣṇya*) and so forth—though grasped by the means of inference such as sound—are sublated by perception because they are equal in being merely conventional (*vyāvahārika*), so too is [the world] sublated here. However, in the present case, existence (*sattva*) is established by perception as being conventional; and its opposite is not falsity (*mithyātva*), because that [falsity] is opposed to ultimate existence (*pāramārthikasattva*). Therefore, it is not sublated by perception, which grasps conventional existence.

Now, what is your intention in speaking thus? Is it that because [the inference] has a real entity as its object, the inference of falsity and so forth possesses only the status of a sublater (*bādhaka*) and not the status of being sublated (*bādhyatā*)? Or is it that there is no relationship of sublated and sublater between the two—because the apprehender of existence and the apprehender of falsity have, respectively, empirical (*vyāvahārika*) and real (*tāttvika*) objects, and thus lack mutually contradictory objects? Even in the latter case, does the inference and so forth apprehend the very absence of real existence—which is unestablished—without first apprehending the empirical existence established by perception? Or...

[Is it] the non-existence of that very thing which has been made an object of perception [that is real]? Not the latter, because it would be improper to say that [perception] does not sublate [the inference] when that [inference] apprehends the non-existence of the object of perception. Nor the second, because it would result in the negation of what was never proposed [as a possibility]—since it would negate what is not grasped by perception—and because it would entail the reality of the object of perception. Nor the first, because the reality of the object of inference and so forth cannot be established due to its contradiction with the perception upon which it depends. If this is argued, we say: no.

This is because there is no lack of justification in either the first or the second position. To explain: in the first position, there is no failure to establish its reality (*tāttvikatva*), since the sublation (*bādhā*) of "this is silver" by "this is not silver" is not observed; therefore, only that which has been examined can be accepted as a sublater. And examination—consisting of the correspondence of purposeful activity (*pravṛtti-saṃvāda*) and so forth—is untenable without non-sublation during the state of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra-daśā*). It is already stated that such a state sublates that which perceives the sublation, but it does not sublate the non-duality scriptures (*advaita-śruti*) or inference (*anumāna*).

Even in the second position, there is no negation of what has not been presented as a possibility, because indirect presentation (*parokṣaprasakti*) is possible. As for the claim made by some that presentation is established through the well-known reality of existence in the self (*ātman*), that is not so; for mere knowledge of the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) is not "presentation," but rather knowledge of the counter-correlative as residing in the locus of negation (*niṣedhādhikaraṇa*). And the self is not the locus of negation. Therefore, only indirect presentation must be shown. Alternatively, let there be no presentation at all.

For in the case of the perception of non-existence (*abhāva-pratyakṣa*), that [superimposition] is useful as the basis for the error of relation; but what utility could it possibly have for verbal testimony (*śabda*) or inference (*anumāna*)? Nor is the negation redundant when there is no prior application [of the object], because there exists a purpose consisting in the cessation of what is undesirable. Furthermore, there is no consequence of the object of perception becoming ultimately real, since it is precisely the locus of that object whose transcendence from ultimate reality is being made known. Thus, there is no inconsistency whatsoever. As it has been said by the authors of the *Khaṇḍana*: "Having entered the ultimate non-duality as its refuge, the Śruti..."

"Because of its conflict with that which must be accepted [as foundational], it is never afraid. Now, one might object: even so, if non-heat were real, then the inference of it would not be sublated by perception grasping empirical heat. Likewise, in cases such as "The sacrificial post is the sun," the Śruti would find refuge by relying on the post's being the sun in a real sense.

If it is argued that [the scripture] might also say, "Because of contradiction, one never fears the object of dependence," we say no. What is the meaning of the statement, "Non-heat would be real"? If the meaning is that heat does not exist in reality (*tattvataḥ*), then since this results in non-duality (*advaita*), it is an acceptance of what is desired. If, however, the meaning is that it does not exist even conventionally (*vyavahārataḥ*), then the perception of heat—qualified by being examined through its consistency with worldly practice and so forth—is the sublater; thus, the reality of non-heat is not established. By this, the inference of coldness is also explained.

The same [principle] should be applied to the negation of the identity between the sun and the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), whether from the perspective of ultimate reality (*tattvataḥ*) or conventional usage (*vyavahārataḥ*). For the Vedic scripture, being subordinate to another purpose, lacks the intent to establish the identity of the sun and the sacrificial post; thus, since it would contradict well-examined perception, it is logically consistent as a mere eulogy (*stāvaka*) by means of a figurative sense (*gauṇārthatā*). Therefore, the attempt to equate the non-dualistic scriptures with passages such as "the sun is the sacrificial post" by claiming that they refer to the "actual nature of the sun in the sacrificial post" and so forth, is refuted.

Nor should it be argued that the non-dual scripture (*advaita-śruti*) would be merely reiterative (*anuvādikā*) if it were to apprehend a falsity already established by inference—just as the scripture stating "fire is the remedy for cold" is reiterative of the power to ward off cold already grasped by other means of knowledge; for since inference, which follows its own particular ingenuity, lacks universal applicability, it cannot serve as the basis for the scripture’s being reiterative. As was stated by Vācaspatimiśra regarding the aphorism "Because of the instability of reasoning" (*tarkāpratiṣṭhānāt*):
"Even an object that has been inferred with great effort by skillful inferents..."
"Others, being more proficient, establish it quite differently.

However, there is a disparity [between the two cases] because, in the case of the Vedic passage cited as an example, the fact that fire is the cause for the cessation of snow is ascertainable through both common-sense perception and presumptive testimony (arthāpatti). Therefore, the inference of falsity is not comparable to the inference of the coldness of fire. Thus ends the refutation of the comparison between the inference of falsity and the inference of coldness.

Furthermore, superiority [of a means of knowledge] consists solely in its being examined (*parīkṣitatva*), and not in its being foundational (*upajīvyatva*) or for other such reasons; for even perception is seen to be sublated by inference and verbal testimony. To illustrate: the perception "this is silver" is sublated by inference and authoritative testimony; the perception of the blueness of the sky is sublated by the inference apprehending its colorlessness; the perception "I am fair" and "I am here in this house, knowing" are sublated by inference and scripture; and the perception of the moon's small size is sublated by inference and scripture; as are the perceptions "the conch is yellow" and "molasses is bitter."

Furthermore, sublation by means of inference and authoritative testimony (*āptavacana*) is observed in such cases. Now, one might object: "In the case of a perceptual error (*sākṣātkāribhrama*), it must be admitted that only the perception of a specific contrary reality (*sākṣātkāriviśeṣadarśana*) is its sublater; otherwise, if indirect valid cognition (*parokṣapramā*) were capable of removing a perceptual error, the effort to establish that Vedāntic sentences produce immediate knowledge would be futile. This is not so.

Even though there is no cessation of ignorance accompanied by its manifestations (*savilāsājñāna*) through such statements as "this is not a snake," nevertheless, by making known the invalidity of the error, one removes the cognition that the error is a valid means of knowledge and the cognition of the reality of its object. And to that extent, it is designated as the "remover of error. This is because the delusion regarding the validity of the error and the delusion regarding the reality of its object are merely indirect (*parokṣa*); therefore, they do not require direct sublation (*aparokṣabādha*).

For neither the state of not being produced by a defective instrument nor the state of having an uncontradicted object constitutes the validity of any perception; nor does the reality of the object consist in its being uncontradicted by all persons, at all times, and in all places. Therefore, it is entirely appropriate that these two [conditions] should be sublated by supersensible (parokṣa) valid cognition. And when those two are sublated, the error regarding silver and so forth—though existing in its own nature—is said to be "sublated" because it is as if non-existent due to its incapacity to produce its own effects; thus, there is no fault.

If it be objected: "In the case of 'this is silver,' it is perception accompanied by reasoning that is the sublater, not reasoning alone; likewise, in the case of 'I am fair,' the powerful perception 'this is my body' itself is the sublater; and 'I am here in this very house, conscious' is indeed a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), because the individual soul (*jīva*) is atomic"—we reply: no. For as long as the perceptions of identity with silver and identity with the body remain awake, reasoning lacks the power to obstruct them, and thus there is no occasion for the arising of a perception whose objects [the self's atomicity and so forth] would otherwise be contradicted.

Nor is the [cognition] "I am fair" figurative in that case, as is the case with "the cloth is blue" when the cloth is smeared with mud through a mediated connection; for there is a disparity between the example and the subject of the comparison, since—unlike the mud and the cloth—the difference between the body and the self is not apprehended. Thus, in this instance, superimposition based on identity alone is appropriate. And likewise, in the case of "the water is hot," if there were an apprehension of the difference between the water and fire as there is between mud and cloth, then it would indeed be figurative.

Furthermore, if there is a non-determination of difference [between the body and the self] as there is with the body and the self, then that is indeed superimposition (*adhyāsa*). And thus, it is precisely sublated by reasoning; therefore, that too is an example [of such a case]. As for what was said—that "I am right here" is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—that is not so. Because the Self is omnipresent, as stated in the scripture, "And like space, it is all-pervading," the restriction "right here" lacks any basis in valid cognition. Nor is the individual soul (*jīva*) atomic, because pleasure and pain are experienced simultaneously through the delimitations of both the feet and the head.

For a single atom cannot, at one and the same time, be delimited by two spatially separated locations. Nor is the simultaneous cognition an illusion, because there is no reason to abandon the validity that is established as the general rule; we shall explain this in detail further on. Now, it might be argued: the perception of the blueness of the sky is not sublated by the inference apprehending its colorlessness, because there is no inferential mark (*liṅga*). Nor can "being the non-originator of a substance possessing ultimate magnitude" and so forth serve as such a mark, since these are unestablished (*asiddha*) according to your own view. Furthermore, "being intangible" is inconclusive (*vyabhicārin*), as it applies to darkness. And "being a primary element other than the triad beginning with earth" and so forth are irrelevant (*aprayojaka*).

And thus, it must be said that the very direct perception of the witness-consciousness (*sākṣipratyakṣa*), which apprehends the absence of form, is what sublates that [notion of having form]; nor should it be asked how the witness-consciousness, which is incapable of grasping form, can be the apprehender of the absence of form.

If it is argued that this is possible—just as the eye of one perceiving a *piśāca* can also perceive its absence—and since the opponent also admits that the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*) perceives even the intense darkness of color, and since the perception of the absence of color in the eyeless sky (or air) is possible through the eye alone, just as in the case of air, and thus there is no sublation by visual perception (*cākṣuṣapratyakṣa*)—we say: No. While the perception "the sky is blue" is manifest, it is impossible for the absence of color to be perceived either by the eye or by the witness-consciousness. Therefore, powerful reasoning itself is the sublater of that [perception].

Nor is there an absence of a logical mark (*liṅga*), for such a mark exists: "The sky possesses color, because it is the object of a cognition not qualified by color that conforms to the presence and absence of the eye, just like color. Nor is this [reason] inconclusive (*aprayojaka*), because the following reductio ad absurdum (*tarka*) is established: "If the sky were possessed of color, then it would not be the object of a cognition conforming to the presence and absence of the eye that is unconnected with color. Nor can this be accepted as a desired conclusion (*iṣṭāpatti*), because it is universally acknowledged by all people that the sky is established in its vicinity as being unconnected with color.

Even though space is cognizable by direct perception (*sākṣivedyatā*), its conformity with the presence and absence of the eye is nonetheless unavoidable; otherwise, even a blind person would perceive it. Nor should it be argued that the colorlessness of space is contradicted because, through the process of quintuplication (*pañcīkaraṇa*), it is produced as possessing form; for such an objection has no place in the view that maintains the process of triplication (*trivṛtkaraṇa*).

Even according to the theory of quintuplication (*pañcīkaraṇa*), since we accept only this much—that whichever quality belongs to whichever element in its unquintuplicated state becomes fit for empirical usage through quintuplication—there is no contingency of form (*rūpa*) being produced in space (*ākāśa*). Nor should it be argued that mere verbal testimony does not remove the error of a rope-snake and so forth, because we observe such counter-questions as, "Even though you have been told, 'This is not a snake,' why do you speak thus? Do you look again after further examination? and therefore only direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) removes such delusions. [This is not so.]

In the case of a reply, because it is susceptible to doubts such as error or negligence, statements like "this is not a snake" are weak and do not function to remove error. However, where there is no such suspicion, they certainly do remove error. For this very reason, in the speech of a father or similar authority who is free from such doubt, one does not find such a reply; rather, there is only activity and so forth as if the matter were already established. The same applies to the perception of the identity of a flame, which is likewise sublated by reasoning.

Nor should it be argued that in cases where [a sound] has been extinguished and re-established, that [notion of identity] is sublated by a perceptual cognition of a clearer difference; for even there, the very perception of difference—namely, "this is long, not short"—is what sublates it. This investigation applies first to cases other than those where [a sound] has been extinguished and re-established. And in those cases, it is impossible to speak of a perceptual cognition of difference such as "this is long, not short," because one directly perceives the non-difference between the two states presented as shortness and length, since that which was short is now the same as that which is long.

Likewise, the recognition of a flame is indeed sublated by reasoning (*yukti*). For one whose eyes are always afflicted by bile, in the perception "the conch is white" and in the perception of the moon as being the size of a thumb-span, it is impossible even to suspect a sublater that is distinct from inference (*parokṣa*); therefore, it must be said that it is sublated solely by reasoning and the like.

But surely, in every case here, even in this alternative conception, there is the operation of another means of knowledge (*māna*) upon perception. To explain: cognition is of two kinds—having two alternatives (*dvikoṭika*) and having one alternative (*ekakoṭika*). The latter is also twofold: that which is stained by the suspicion of invalidity (*aprāmāṇya-śaṅkā-kalaṅkita*) and that which is unstained by it. Among these, the first two leave no room for any other means of knowledge, because they do not determine the object and because they are stained by the suspicion of invalidity. And the state of being stained by the cognition of invalidity occurs in two ways.

This is because of the certainty that the instrument [of cognition] is defective and the certainty that the object does not exist [as perceived]. Likewise, since the perception of trees standing on a mountain peak as being of the size of a span is seen to be caused by the defect of distance, it is determined that the cognition of the moon, situated at a distance, as being of the size of a span is likewise caused solely by a defect. Similarly, because the absence of form is ascertained in the sky when nearby, the cognition of its possessing form when at a distance is already determined beforehand to be produced by the defect of distance.

However, a perception such as "the conch is yellow" arises as being already overwhelmed by the cognition of invalidity (*aprāmāṇyajñānāskandita*), because the initial examined perception—namely, "the conch is not yellow"—ascertains the non-existence of that object. The same applies to perceptions such as the hole in the sun.

Likewise, the perceptual cognition of the moon and other objects as being of the size of a thumb is sublated by the ascertainment of defects such as distance; and the perceptual cognition that "the conch is yellow" is sublated precisely by the ascertainment of the non-existence of the object [as perceived] at the initial moment. Consequently, inference and scripture operate subsequently, and thus there is no sublation of those [perceptions] by them. For that by which the erroneous nature of another is known is said to be its sublater; however, the erroneous nature of the perception of the moon's small size and so forth is not known through scripture or the like.

For such activity occurs only after the knowledge of its erroneous nature has arisen. However, that which is unstained by the cognition of non-validity (*apramāṇya*) determines its own object and is capable of generating activity free from doubt. For example, [cognitions] such as "fire is indeed hot," "the sacrificial grass is indeed distinct from the sacrificer," and "the jar is indeed existent" leave no room for anything else and cannot be sublated by anything else. Indeed, in these cases, there is neither a prior cognition of defects such as distance, nor a certainty regarding the non-existence of the object, nor a state of oscillating between alternative possibilities (*koṭi*).

Furthermore, let it be that in some cases direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) may be sublated by reasoning due to the weight of another direct perception, and in other cases inferential signs (*liṅga*) and so forth may be sublated by context (*prakaraṇa*) and the like following scripture (*śruti*) due to the weight of scripture—just as a king’s minister is sublated by a king’s servant due to the king’s own authority—even so, mere reasoning or mere context does not possess the power to sublate direct perception, inferential signs, and the like. This is because such [reasoning or context] is not everywhere accompanied by direct perception and the rest.

If it is argued that the Śruti text, "Having prepared the *veda*, one prepares the *vedi*," which concerns the sequence and other properties of ritual elements, is sublated when—despite the Smṛti rule, "One should sip water while wearing the sacred thread and acting with the right hand," which concerns the primary elements such as sipping water—the occasion for sipping water due to hunger arises immediately after preparing the *veda*; and that therefore the same must apply elsewhere as well—this is not so, because this is merely an argument from analogy (*yukti*).

Whatever cognition of small size occurs regarding a distant object is invalid (*apramā*), being caused by the defect of distance, like the cognition of the small size of a tree situated on a mountain peak; this [cognition of the moon's small size] is also like that. Thus, O dull-witted one! by stating through such reasoning alone that the perception of the moon as being the size of a thumb-span is sublated, you have merely defeated the opponent’s modesty with your claim that "perception is not sublated by reasoning," but you have not defeated the argument itself.

Thus, even in the case of the perception "the conch is yellow," the perception of the prior absence of the object is not a sublater, because that [prior object] no longer exists at present. Nor is the memory of it a sublater, because memory is weaker than direct experience; it serves merely to produce an argument. Therefore, in the examples cited, sublation occurs only through reasoning and scripture.

As for the claim that one cannot assert invalidating force (*bādhakatva*) everywhere merely because invalidating force is observed in some instances—on the grounds that the invalidating force of reason (*yukti*) and so forth is dependent upon the weight (*gaurava*) of the corresponding perception—that is a criticism of what was not said. For I do not say that the invalidating force of reason applies everywhere merely on the basis of its being observed somewhere; rather, [I say it applies] as long as there exists that which has been seen to be the cause of the invalidating force of scripture (*āgama*) and so forth in cases such as the perception of the moon as being a mere span in size or the yellowness of a conch shell.

Furthermore, there is no perception being pursued therein which, out of respect for it, you might claim has a different basis (*anyathāsiddhi*) regarding its status as a sublater. Therefore, the perceptual cognition of the moon’s limited size and the perceptual cognition of the reality of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) are equally subject to sublation. And the reasoning (*yukti*) and scripture (*āgama*) are equally the sublaters. For even in the case of the perception of the moon’s limited size, there is certainly no prior ascertainment of its being produced by a defective instrument (*duṣṭakaraṇaka*).

Proximity (*naikaṭya*) is not a defect in every instance, for otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence of a universal lack of confidence in all cognitions of magnitude. Rather, it is only after sublation by means of scripture (*āgama*) and so forth that [proximity is recognized as a defect]. Similarly, in the present case as well, the determination of the defect consisting of ignorance (*avidyā*) occurs only after the falsity (*mithyātva*) has been established. Thus, there is complete parity in all respects. As for the statement that "there is no other sublater for a perceived object except a stronger perception," that refers to the domain of weak verbal testimony (*śabda*), inferential marks (*liṅga*), and so forth.

As for what was stated in the *Vivaraṇa*: "Where even that which appears as perception is sublated by inference and so forth, such that its practical efficacy (*vyavahāra*) is cut off, let it be so. But where the determination of sublation occurs through a consideration of the relative strength of two cognitions that have both entered the path of inquiry, there the falsity of perception is not established by inference and the like"—that too refers to cases involving reasoning distinct from verbal testimony whose authority has been apprehended and from the inferences dependent upon it.

Because when the validity [of one] is ascertained in a single instance, there is no occasion at all for considering relative strength or weakness; thus ends the refutation regarding the fact that perception is not sublated by inferential signs and the like.

Thus, what was stated—that "it is also because there is a certainty of future sublation"—is indeed even more appropriate. For just as the perception that the moon is a mere span in size, which is not sublated by any other means, is sublated by scripture (*āgama*), so too is the perception "the jar exists" and the like, which is not sublated by any other means, sublated by scripture that makes known its falsity; this is the conclusion. And thus, the objection raised by others on the grounds of a suspicion of future sublation is rejected as a criticism of what was never asserted.

In reality, however, even by taking into account the suspicion of sublation (*bādha*), the refutation of the sublation of perception is indeed correct. This is because, prior to investigating the relative strength or weakness of perception and verbal testimony, when there arises the doubt—“Is this word [testimony] figurative in meaning, or is it rather that perception is invalid?”—both would initially result in a state of non-sublation. Only then does the possibility arise for the scripture (*āgama*)—which has been determined to have its literal meaning through the indicative marks of its intended purport (*tātparya*)—to find scope by dispelling the suspicion of being figurative.

Nor should it be argued that, since words and logical marks (liṅga) do not subvert perception, and since other perceptions are suspected of being invalid and thus lack the power to subvert, there can be no suspicion of subversion once the general absence of a subverting factor is ascertained; for it has been established that words and logical marks do indeed subvert perception. Furthermore, even if the absence of each specific [subverting factor] is ascertained, doubt remains possible at a stage when the full extent of such specific factors has not been determined. Moreover, it is impossible to maintain the absence of doubt simply because perception is suspected of being invalid.

Now, if it is argued that since waking cognition and the like would thus lack validity (*apramātva*), and since the sublation (*bādha*) of what is seen in dreams or of [illusory objects] such as silver in a mother-of-pearl shell would remain unestablished, how could the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*) be established? We reply: No, because sublation occurs by virtue of having an object whose existence is greater than that of the superimposed (*āropya*), or by virtue of being a relative means of valid knowledge (*apekṣika-pramāṇa*), or by virtue of having an object whose existence is not less [than that of the superimposed]. For this very reason, it was said to the Buddhist in the *Bhaṭṭavārttika*: "When the waking consciousness—the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*)—is perceived, the vision of dreams and the like becomes false; for us, what then is the basis for your distinction?"

Thus, that [objection] is consistent. Now, one might object: "It is observed that only a cognition whose object is a particularity not previously the object of an immediate cognition at the time of the error is sublater; yet the cognition that sublates the entire universe is not like that. If this is said, we reply: No, because a cognition sublates an error precisely by being a cognition of the reality of the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna-tattva-jñānatvena*). Since the knowledge of Brahman, which sublates the universe, is of that very nature, it is a sublater. Nor should it be argued: "Only a cognition possessing a mode (*saprakārikā*) sublates an error, but how can this [knowledge of Brahman], which is devoid of modes (*niṣprakārikā*), be such?"

In the capacity of being a remover [of error], the property of having a mode (*saprakārakatva*) is not included because it involves unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*). If it is argued: "But surely the rule of having a mode is necessary, because it is precisely by virtue of being a cognition with a differentiated form (*vyāvṛttākāra*) that it removes error; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of its removal even by a cognition with a non-differentiated form (*anuvṛttākāra*)," [The reply is: True. A cognition removes error by virtue of having a differentiated form, but there is no rule therein that it must have a specific mode (*viśeṣaprakārakatva*). For instance, having a differentiated form occurs in two ways: 1. Being a cognition whose object is excluded from others (*anyavyāvṛtta-viṣayaka-jñāna*). 2. Being a cognition whose object possesses a unique characteristic (*asādhāraṇadharma-viśiṣṭa-viṣayaka-jñāna*). It is the former that serves as the remover of error. This is because the latter is common to both valid knowledge (*pramā*) and error (*bhrama*), whereas the former is restricted solely to valid knowledge. Therefore, the rule of having a specific mode is not required for the removal of error. Furthermore, the rule of having a mode is not even necessary for the production of valid knowledge, since validity arises simply from the correspondence between the object and the cognition (*tadvati tatprakārakatva*). Thus, the rule of having a mode is not established either for the removal of error or for the production of valid knowledge. Consequently, the rule of having a mode is not a necessary factor in the definition of valid knowledge.
