[This occurs] both through qualification (*viśeṣaṇa*) and through secondary indication (*upalakṣaṇa*). In the first case, there is a rule that [the cognition] possesses a qualifier (*saprakāraka*). In the second case as well, if the secondary indication pertains to another property (*dharmāntara*), then because the form is excluded [from others], it is necessarily qualified (*saprakāraka*). However, if the state of having an excluded form arises from a secondary indication of the essential nature (*svarūpa*) itself, then it is unqualified (*niṣprakāraka*), because the secondary indicator does not enter into [the cognition] there, and because a thing cannot be its own qualifier. Nor should it be argued that a thing can be its own qualifier within itself, as is the case with [the universal] "knowability" (*prameyatva*) and so forth.

For even you have, out of necessity, accepted this only in the case of a purely positive (kevalānvayin) inference, but not everywhere. Therefore, if it is argued that because the form (*ākāra*) and the qualifier (*prakāra*) are non-different, the very form of Brahman is the qualifier of the cognition of Brahman—this is not so; for although a qualified cognition has the form of the qualificandum, it does not have that as its qualifier, since the form and the qualifier are distinct. Furthermore, it will be explained that the form is a certain property residing in the mental modification (*vṛtti*), which serves as the cause for unique linguistic usage.

Therefore, just as from the word "ether" (*ākāśa*) one understands the mere nature of the substratum characterized by being the locus of sound, so too here, the knowledge of the nature of Brahman characterized by the absence of a second and so forth is a direct (*aparokṣa*) cognition that has a differentiated form and which sublates duality. And how such knowledge is possible through words will be explained later.

Nor should it be argued that since it is not observed that subverting cognitions fail to subvert the delusion, its causes, ignorance, defects, or the superimposed seer and so forth, how can the knowledge of Brahman possibly effect their subversion? For in cases where one imagines a dreamer to possess defective instruments and thereby imagines his delusion, it is seen that all such [imagined] things are removed by waking cognition.

Even in the waking state, when one imagines consciousness in a human effigy and, regarding a nearby object that is not actually a mirror, imagines it to be a mirror and perceives it as consisting of one's own reflection, then—since one observes the cessation of all such [erroneous] cognitions through the valid knowledge that "this is not conscious" and "this is not a mirror"—this imagination is not something never before seen.

And thus, this cognition of the substrate, such as "this is mother-of-pearl," does not remove the superimposition of the seer and so forth—just as the cognition of a rope removes the delusion of a snake—for what reason? Because there is an absence of direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*) of that substrate. Knowledge of Brahman, however, would certainly remove even the delusion regarding the seer and other defects, just as it removes the delusion of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) consisting of ether and the rest; for what reason? Because it is the direct perception of the reality (*tattva*) which is the substrate of all delusions without exception.

And thus, it should be understood that being a subverting cognition (*bādhaka-buddhi*) is not the determining factor for the non-subversion of defects and the like; rather, it is the state of being distinct from the direct realization of the reality (*tattva-sākṣātkāra*) which serves as the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) for that delusion. If it is objected: "In the aforementioned example, let that [defect] be subverted because it is imagined (*kalpita*); but how can this be so here [in the case of Brahman]?"—alas! By you, the "beloved of the gods" (*devānāmpriya*), a great undesirable consequence has been brought upon us, who accept that everything other than Brahman is imagined.

If it is argued that the perception of the witness (*sākṣipratyakṣa*) cannot be sublated because it is not produced by any defect (*doṣa*), whereas on the contrary, the non-dual knowledge generated by the Śruti must be sublatable because it is produced by the defect consisting of a misconception regarding its intended meaning (*tātparya*), we say: no. For although consciousness (*caitanya*) is not produced by defects in its essential nature (*svarūpataḥ*), the mental modification (*vṛtti*) of ignorance (*avidyā*) which delimits it is produced by a defect; and it is precisely the consciousness reflected in that [modification] which constitutes the referent of the term "witness."

Furthermore, since the apprehension of the purport of non-duality (advaita) is of the nature of valid knowledge (*pramā*)—being in no conflict with perception and other means of knowledge—it lacks the character of a defect; therefore, the knowledge of non-duality produced by it cannot be sublated. Moreover, being produced by an error (*bhrama*) does not, in itself, necessitate the sublation of its object. Nor should it be argued: "How can the perception of duality—which possesses an authority equal to that of the sublater and is corroborated by Vedic texts on duality—be sublated?"

Because duality is established by worldly means of knowledge such as perception and so forth, the Śruti that teaches it is merely reiterative (*anuvādaka*); thus, it lacks the status of being equivalent to the non-dual Śruti, which possesses a fruitful purport regarding its own previously unknown subject matter. If it is argued: "That which is apprehended by a subverting cognition (*bādhaka-dhī*) cannot itself be sublated. Duality is indeed apprehended by a subverting cognition, for such a cognition grasps its own object precisely as distinct. If it were grasped as non-distinct or with indifference—as in the case of the cognition 'this is not silver'—it could not function as a subverter. This is not so.

This is because it is not admitted that the sublating cognition (*bādhakadhi*) has difference as its object; rather, the sublation occurs through the arising of the cognition, "This is mother-of-pearl. The cognition "This is not silver" is merely the result (*phala*) of that [sublation]. A distinct form (*vyāvṛttākāratā*) is indeed necessary for the sublating cognition, and since this exists even in the knowledge of Brahman—which is devoid of qualifiers (*niṣprakāraka*)—due to the power of the characterization of its own nature (*svarūpopalakṣaṇa*), difference is not something to be understood by the sublating cognition.

Now, if doubt were to persist even after an investigation that extends to the final result—which is distinct from that of a dream—then, upon doubting the non-dual scriptures (*advaita-śruti*), their direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), and their validity (*prāmāṇya*), the non-dual scriptures themselves would not be established. Furthermore, if there were doubt regarding sublation (*bādha*) even when sublation has occurred, the well-known status of "unsublated sublation" would also cease to exist; for doubt concerning the sublation of what has already been sublated does not contradict its state of being unsublatable. Moreover, by the occurrence of doubt regarding sublation even in the case of a future sublation, there would be a contradiction with one's own practical activity (*svakriyā-vyāghāta*). Finally, if there were doubt even regarding the direct perception of doubt itself, then doubt itself could never be established.

If it is argued that, because doubt would thus spread everywhere, a total collapse of all [cognition] would result, do not think so. For we maintain that doubt arises regarding existence (*sattva*) and other properties even when they have been ascertained by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), provided that [the object] is presented as being equal [to others], but not that doubt arises toward everything that is merely ascertained. Thus, as it was said to the Buddhist in the *Bhaṭṭavārttika*: "The negation of an object grasped by a defective cognition is indeed appropriate; however, if there were a sublation of everything merely grasped, then even one's own position would not be established."

Thus, even that is not contradictory, because there has been no mention of a sublation of what was merely apprehended, nor of a doubt regarding it. But [one might object]: "In the case of the perception of existence (*sattva*) and so forth, how can a doubt arise when there is a certainty regarding the absence of well-known defects such as distance? Furthermore, even if there is a certainty regarding the absence of known defects, could there not be a doubt concerning an unknown one? For instance, although the defect based on a speaker—which is known to exist in verbal testimony—is absent in the Veda due to its eternity, it is easy to state that a doubt regarding other defects may still arise. Nor should it be argued that, just as in the case of a dream-perception where invalidity is observed despite the certainty at that time of the absence of distance and other factors, a similar doubt applies here. [Response: This is not so. Why? Because in the case of a dream, the very cause of the cognition’s validity—namely, the waking state—is absent; therefore, the suspicion of invalidity is natural. However, in the present case, since the cause of validity is present, the suspicion of invalidity is not reasonable. Moreover, the example of a dream is not analogous, because in dreams, the objects themselves are unreal, whereas in the present case, the objects are real. Furthermore, the fact that a dream is false is established by the subsequent recollection of the experience as "I dreamed," which serves as a sublation. But in the present case, there is no such sublation. Therefore, the suspicion of invalidity does not arise. Consequently, the inference of the existence of a creator is not contradicted by the possibility of defects. Thus, the proof of the existence of God is established. Q.E.D. (iti).

If it is argued that even in the case of a dream-cognition, where one is certain of the absence of defects such as error and the like, the observation of invalidity is equally present in the case of the Veda—since the reality is indeed void—and that the experience of a difference from a dream is the same in both cases, we say no. For, since the certainty regarding the absence of well-known defects is equal for both the perception of existence and the non-dualistic scripture (*advaitāgama*), this [experience] does not constitute an obstacle to the suspicion of validity.

Indeed, in the case of a counter-balanced reason (*satpratipakṣa*), the certainty that there is no defect in either [of the two reasons] does not obstruct the desire to know which one here is the truth; for it is only a perception of a specific feature occurring at a time when a contrary specific feature is not perceived that acts as an obstacle to doubt. Likewise, since there is no observation of a defect that would subvert the intrinsic nature (*svatastva*) of the production of validity, nor of a subversion of the intrinsic nature of its cognition, nor of a contradiction (*bādha*), and since it is accepted that a groundless doubt cannot arise due to its contradiction with one's own actions, the validity of perception is well-established—this too is refuted, because we indeed accept a doubt rooted in means of knowledge such as scripture (*āgama*).

However, regarding the negation of silver and so forth—as in "this is not silver"—there is no possibility of a challenge to its validity, as it is in accordance with the non-dual (advaita) scriptures. Therefore, there is no risk of losing the root while seeking the branches. Nor is the cognition "the pot exists" on the same footing as "this is not silver," for there is a distinction between them due to the former's lack of contradiction with the non-dual scriptures.

For this very reason, the objection that—since even the experience of bliss in deep sleep lacks validity, how could the nature of the Self as bliss be real? for the scriptural texts on bliss can be explained as merely restating an experienced bliss that is not ultimately real—is refuted. Since bliss is of the nature of Brahman, there is no contradiction with the scriptures of non-duality (advaita-śruti), and thus there is no ground for invalidating it. Consequently, the scriptural texts on bliss are not invalid. As it has been said in the *Khaṇḍana*:
"A word indeed produces knowledge even of an object that is absolutely non-existent;
however, because it is not sublated, it constitutes valid cognition here, its authority being self-evident and unshakable."
And it is said in the *Sureśvaravārttika*:
"Therefore, because it brings about comprehension, because it is free from defective causes,
and because it is unsublated, the Veda possesses the status of a valid means of knowledge regarding reality, just like the sense organs and so forth."

In this context, the illustration "like the sense-organs and so forth" should be understood as referring merely to conventional validity (*vyāvahārikaprāmāṇya*). Thus, even though ultimate validity (*tāttvikaprāmāṇya*) is absent, there is no contradiction with one's own practice because perception and the other means of knowledge are accepted as conventionally valid.
Nor is there a contradiction with the statement: "Perception, inference, and scripture consisting of various traditions... [and so on].

"Three things must be well understood by one desiring purity of dharma," and so forth—such is the contradiction with the Smṛti. Therefore, it is established that through the certainty of sublation, or even through the suspicion thereof, perception and the other means of knowledge are not in conflict with the inference and other proofs for non-duality. Thus ends the removal of the objection from perception by demonstrating the possibility of future sublation.

It might be argued: even if perception is incapable of being sublated due to its having a different object and so forth, inference itself must be the sublater. To explain: that which is other than Brahman—or the subject under dispute—is either real or ultimately real, because it is not non-existent while being non-sublatable by a cognition other than the knowledge of Brahman, or by a cognition produced by the comprehension of the purport of the Vedāntas, or by a cognition that is the cause of liberation; like Brahman. By way of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*): [whatever is not as described is non-existent].

If it is argued that [the reason] is like the horn of a hare, we say no; for in your own system, even the *prātibhāsika* (illusory) is non-existent, and thus the reason suffers from the fallacy of being unestablished as a pervader (*vyāpyatvāsiddhi*) due to its superfluous qualification. Furthermore, if you employ this reason while relying on our own position, there is an inconsistency (*vyabhicāra*) with respect to the identity of the body and the self, which is not sublated by any knowledge other than the knowledge of Brahman. Indeed, *prātibhāsikatva* (illusoriness) is nothing other than being sublatable by a knowledge other than the knowledge of Brahman. For you have introduced the first three qualifications—alternatively—to the subject (*pakṣa*) in order to exclude illusory things such as the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell from being the subject.

In this regard, the first [view] is based on the position that Brahman is pervaded by the mental mode (*vṛtti*); the second is based on the position that, if that is not accepted, the valid cognition of the intended meaning (*tātparya-pramā*) is the cause for verbal valid cognition; and the third is based on the position that such [intended meaning] is not the cause because of the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*). Thus, it is indeed admitted that the phenomenal (*prātibhāsika*) is not the locus of non-existence.

Otherwise, since that [unreal thing] would already be excluded by the qualification "not being the locus of a void-veiler" (*tucchavārakāsattvānadhikaraṇatva*), the effort expended here would result in futility. Furthermore, if the identity of the body and the self were also included as the subject (*pakṣa*), there would be a sublation (*bādha*) of the thesis; and when sublation occurs, the "subjecthood" (*pakṣatva*)—which is a qualification of the subject—is unestablished, resulting in the fallacy of an unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*).

For this very reason, there is no escape even if one adds the qualification: "provided it is not the object of a cognition produced by a defect that is not sublated by what is considered its own sublater," or "provided it is not the object of a sublation that is not sublated by what is considered its own sublater," or "provided it is not sublated by a cognition that is simultaneous with the prior non-existence of the action (karma) residing in the same locus as itself. This is because the previously mentioned defects remain unremoved even in the case of the identity of the body and the self.

As for the objection: "In the first thesis, there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) by taking conventional existence (*vyāvahārikasattva*) as the object; however, in the second thesis, the qualifier 'ultimately real' (*paramārtha*) is redundant for the proponent, because there is nothing to be excluded [by it]. This is not so. The first formulation is based on the view that conventional existence is merely the practice of treating something as existent. The second formulation, however, is based on the view that there is a distinct, recurring entity called "conventional existence. Furthermore, the qualifier is not redundant.

In inference for the sake of others (*parārthānumāna*), the purpose is to refute the charge of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) for the opponent. Furthermore, in the inference for God—specifically regarding the reason "not produced by an agent that is itself produced"—just as "producedness" (*janyatva*) is used against a Mīmāṃsaka, so too "ultimate reality" (*paramārthatva*) may be logically accepted as a qualifying attribute (*viśeṣaṇa*) for one who asserts the ultimate reality of the universe, acting as a mere adjunct (*uparañjaka*) like "knowability" (*prameyatva*). Therefore, the previously mentioned fault remains; moreover, there is the fault of a redundant qualification (*vyarthaviśeṣaṇatva*) in the logical reason (*hetu*).

Although in both systems there is an established notion of "appearance-ness" (prātibhāsikatva)—whether as the status of being a counter-correlate of negation even for that which lacks epistemic warrant, or as being agreed upon by both parties through the nature of superimposition, or as having a body consisting of mere appearance—nevertheless, the qualification "appearing" (prātibhāsika) in the reason (*hetu*) is redundant. Otherwise, even in the final system (*siddhānta*), since only that which is other than the apparent would have to be made the subject (*pakṣa*) in the inference of falsity (*mithyātva*), the fault would be equal [for both sides]. Thus, the qualification of the reason by "appearing-ness" is useless.

For it is logically consistent that the mere fact of not being the locus of non-existence, while being the locus of non-being, serves as the proof for ultimate existence (*paramārthasattva*). Indeed, only the pure Brahman is to be accepted as the corroborative instance (*dṛṣṭānta*), because if something possessing attributes were taken as the instance, there would be the fallacy of the instance lacking the probandum (*sādhyavaikalya*). Furthermore, since the probandum consists in the absence of sublation, it is the very nature of the locus itself and not a distinct attribute; for it has already been stated that one does not admit the existence of an absence distinct from its substratum.

And so, in the inference of the luminous nature (*taijasatva*) of the eye, although the phrase "among color-forms and the rest" (*rūpādiṣu madhye*)—which serves to exclude the unestablished (*asiddhi*)—is meaningful because it is useful for grasping the pervasion (*vyāpti*), just like a qualifier that excludes deviation (*vyabhicāra*); for even in the case of a qualifier that excludes deviation, its meaningfulness depends solely on its being useful for grasping the pervasion.

Nevertheless, in the argument "the earth and so forth are not produced by an agent because they are not produced by a body," the property of being merely apparent (*prātibhāsikatva*) is indeed useless, just like the property of having a body, because it is of no avail for grasping the pervasion (*vyāpti*). This is because, just as the absence of being produced and the absence of being produced by an agent are grasped as pervaded in space and the like, the grasp of the pervasion between the absence of being a substratum and ultimate reality (*paramārthasattva*) is possible even in the case of Brahman, which is devoid of attributes (*nirdharmaka*). Consequently, for one who attempts to avoid one type of unestablished reason (*asiddhi*), there arises the contingency of a second type of unestablished reason.

The meaning is that for one who introduces a qualification in order to avoid the fallacy of the unestablished nature of the essence (*svarūpāsiddhi*), there is instead the fallacy of the unestablished nature of the pervasion (*vyāpyatvāsiddhi*), because it has been shown that such a qualification is useless regarding the pervasion. Furthermore, since the [proposition] is established by mere conventional existence (*vyāvahārikasattva*), the stated reason lacks probative force (*aprayojakatva*). Moreover, it is defeated by a counter-argument (*pratikūlatarka*) characterized by the impossibility of sublation (*bādhānupapatti*) if [the subject] were to possess ultimate existence (*paramārthasattva*).

Now, it might be argued that in the case of Brahman, absolute reality (*paramārthasattva*) is established as the *prayojaka* (the causal determinant) for the exclusion of the unreal and the illusory, acting as the differentiator of the reason consisting in the form of such exclusion. This is because, just as the property of being a non-earth (*apṛthivītva*) is the determinant for the exclusion of what is not earth, so too is reality itself—the opposite of unreality—the determinant for the exclusion of the unreal. Properties such as "cognitivity" (*jñānatva*) or "blissfulness" (*ānandatva*), however, are not determinants for that [exclusion], because they are not directly opposed to unreality, and because they are absent in the phenomenal world (*prapañca*).

And thus, it is precisely absolute reality (*paramārthasattva*)—which is common to both Brahman and the universe—that is the determinant of that [reality]. If it is argued: "It cannot be said that absolute reality is not common to the universe simply because the universe is illusory, for [if it were], it would follow that [absolute reality] is like 'knowability' (*jñānatva*), 'bliss-ness' (*ānandatva*), and so forth," this is incorrect. For the exclusion of either the *prātibhāsika* (illusory) or the *asat* (non-existent) is neither identical to nor co-extensive with both [absolute reality and the universe], such that one could serve as the determinant and the other as the determined.

However, that which serves as the determinant for the exclusion of the apparent (prātibhāsika) must be stated as being common to both Brahman and the unreal (asat), because even in the case of the unreal, there is an absence of apparent-ness. Likewise, that which serves as the determinant for the exclusion of the unreal must also be stated as being common to both Brahman and the apparent, because even in the case of the apparent, there is an absence of unreality.

And thus, since the exclusion of both [properties] from Brahman is established simply by the coexistence of those two respective causes, there is no evidence for postulating a separate cause—just as the nature of a "blue pot" is established by the coexistence of the two delimiters, blueness and potness; let those of refined intellect understand this. Furthermore, eternality (*nityatva*) is a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), because the absence of the probandum is observed in the absence of eternality in the case of the illusory (*tuccha*) and the phenomenal (*pratibhāsika*).

For this very reason, the argument "because it is the direct object of valid cognition (*pramā*) insofar as it is not something to be negated" is also not a valid reason. Furthermore, what is this "validity" (*prāmāṇya*)? Is it "having that mode of presentation when the object possesses that [mode]" (*tadvati tatprakārakatva*), or is it "revealing reality" (*tattvāvedakatva*)? In the first case, the corroborative instance (*dṛṣṭānta*) lacks the probans (*sādhanavaikalya*). For the absolutely real, pure Brahman is not the object of a cognition possessing a mode of presentation. Nor can that which possesses attributes (*dharmavat*) serve as the instance, as has already been stated; because it is included within the scope of the subject (*pakṣa*), it lacks the certainty of possessing the property to be proven (*niścitasādhyavattva*).

In the second [definition], since "being a revealer of reality" consists in having an uncontradicted object, it results in being non-different from the probandum (*sādhyāviśeṣa*); thus, if the reason is apprehended, there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*), whereas if the reason is not apprehended, there is the fallacy of the unestablished nature of the reason itself (*svarūpāsiddhi*). As for the claim that "since ultimate reality is established by the mere fact of being an object of valid cognition (*pramā*), the qualification is redundant"—that is not so; for the word "directly" (*sākṣāt*) serves to exclude deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of an illusory object (*prātibhāsika*), which is an object of a valid cognition in the form of a subsequent reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*) such as "I cognize the thing present before me as silver."

And in that very case, because [the qualifier] "as something not to be negated" excludes deviation in the direct object of the cognition of falsity, it is not the case that the after-cognition (anuvyavasāya) and the object of the cognition of falsity do not exist.

Nor is "being directly and immediately manifest to Īśvara" a valid reason [for the reality of the world] on the grounds of its being non-sublatable; for without the establishment of its truth, the component "as something non-sublatable" remains unproven. Thus, there is a circularity (*anyonyāśraya*). Furthermore, it does not follow that Īśvara would be subject to error simply because the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), which is the object of His knowledge, is illusory. This is because He perceives what is illusory precisely as illusory, and thus, like a magician, He cannot be considered errant. Otherwise, it would be impossible to avoid the conclusion that He is errant by virtue of being a knower of an erroneous cognition together with its object.

Now, if [the world] were known as something to be prohibited, there would be no activity on the part of God for the sake of protecting it; but this is not so, because God's activity is of that same nature as the activity of a magician.

Nor is "the capacity for causal efficiency (arthakriyākāritva) regarding an object that is sublated along with its specific mode" a valid reason (*hetu*). This is because there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in that case; for we observe that even a cognition which has become non-authoritative—such as the experience of plunging into water or union with a beloved during a dream—is capable of causal efficiency, provided it is not sublated by a waking cognition possessing a specific mode. If it is argued that in such cases it is the cognition itself that generates the pleasure and so forth, and that this [cognition] is indeed unsublatable, that is incorrect. For mere cognition does not produce such pleasure; rather, it must be stated that only cognition as qualified by something specific possesses that capacity.

Furthermore, the distinction [of cognition] does not transcend the object itself. As it has been said: "For the distinction of cognitions, being devoid of form, is indeed by means of the object alone (*arthenaiva*). The phrase "by means of the object" (*arthena*) means "by the object itself. Thus, if one accepts that what is qualified by something false can be a causal agent, then since even the false would be a causal agent, there is indeed a logical deviation (*vyabhicāra*). And so it is stated in the *Śāstradīpikā* regarding the Buddhist: "If the very cognition of pleasure is the purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), then that is certainly subject to deviation."

"Indeed, since there is no cognition of pleasure when pleasure itself is entirely absent, one might suspect that this [subsequent cognition] is true; however, it is not logical to determine the validity of a prior cognition on that basis. For even by means of an invalid cognition—such as the awareness of union with a beloved—one perceives pleasure during the state of dreaming. [Objection: "But let it be that only a cognition characterized by a specific object is the producer of pleasure. Why, then, should the object itself be considered the producer? [Reply: "No."

Because the individual natures (*svarūpa*) are not uniform, and because properties such as "cognitiveness" (*jñānatva*) are over-extended (*atiprasakta*), there is no delimitor (*upalakṣyatāvacchedaka*) that is both uniform and non-over-extended; thus, it is impossible for them to function as a secondary indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*). Now, one might object: "But being a primary qualifier (*viśe�ṣaṇatva*) is also impossible. For in the case of an object produced by a future cognition, it is impossible for an object—which does not exist at that time—to be a producer of its own prior form. This is not so. Just as an agent (*vyāpārin*) that is non-existent [at the time] can be a producer of something produced by its own operation (*vyāpāra*), so too it is possible for an object that is non-existent [at the time] to be a producer of something produced by its own cognition.

This is because the past and future states are accepted as being based solely on non-existent entities (*asattvadharmāśrayatva*). Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that [the past and future] could not serve as the locus for properties such as being the counter-correlate (*pratiyogitva*) of destruction or antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), or being the object of knowledge regarding them. Furthermore, the acceptance of causality here is equal [to other cases] by virtue of the force of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Moreover, since it is observed that what is unsublated in its own nature (*svarūpa*) is also unsublated in its object, the sublation of the object necessarily entails the sublation of the nature itself; therefore, it is impossible to claim that dream-cognition and the like are real.

Furthermore, beginninglessness (*anāditva*) is a pseudo-reason (*upādhi*) because it is unevenly distributed (*viṣamavyāpta*). Nor should it be argued that, since ultimate reality (*paramārthatva*) is determined to be the causal factor for the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*) in the case of Brahman, the reason possesses the pervasion of the probandum (*sādhyavyāpakatā*) by means of a subverting tarka against the counter-example of an effect arising without a cause; whereas the pseudo-reason lacks this pervasion and thus does not pervade the probandum. This is because we observe that illusory things such as a snake in a rope produce effects like fear and trembling; therefore, [the capacity for causal efficiency] must be common to the illusory and distinct from the non-existent (*tuccha*).

This is because only that which exists at the time of its cognition is the determinant for possessing causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*). Furthermore, if one does not admit that the phenomenal (*prātibhāsika*) possesses causal efficiency, it would follow that the qualification of the reason—“unsublated along with its mode”—is redundant; for absolute reality (*paramārthasattva*) consists in being unsublatable by anyone, anywhere, or at any time, and existence at the time of cognition is simpler in comparison to that. Moreover, since the pure [Brahman] lacks causal efficiency, the reason would be devoid of the probans (*sādhanavikala*); and since the conditioned [Brahman] is included within the subject (*pakṣa*), the example would be devoid of the probandum (*sādhyavikala*).

The reason "because it causes the superimposition of falsity" is also not a valid probans. If "superimposedness" means "phenomenality" (*prātibhāsikatva*), then the reason is unestablished (*asiddhi*) with respect to the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), because the establishment of that [phenomenality] occurs only after the ultimate reality (*pāramārthika*) has been established. If it means "empirical reality" (*vyāvahārikatva*), then there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of nacre-silver and the like. Even if it were common to both cases, this same defect would apply.

The reason "because of being devoid of a conceptualizer" (*kalpakarahitatvāt*) is also not a valid probans, because it suffers from deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of non-existence, and because it contradicts the literal meaning of the text. Now, it might be argued that there is no lack of proof: for pure consciousness (*caitanya*) is not a conceptualizer, because it is untainted; nor is the conditioned (*upahita*) consciousness, because, being itself a conceptual construction, it would lead to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Thus, in the absence of all specific instances of a conceptualizer, the absence of the general class of conceptualizers is established. If this is argued, we say no. For even pure consciousness can function as a conceptualizer by virtue of the conditioning influence (*upadhāna*) of beginningless ignorance (*avidyā*).

For being the "imagining agent" (kalpakatva) consists in being the substratum (*āśraya*) of imagination, its object (*viṣaya*), or its illuminator (*bhāsaka*). And all of this, by virtue of having an existence equal to that of the imagination itself, does not contradict its purity. As it is said in the *Saṅkṣepaśārīraka*:
"The indivisible Consciousness alone is the possessor of both the status of being the substratum and the status of being the object;
for a subsequent [entity] cannot be the substratum nor the object of a previously established darkness."

Thus it is said. Or, let it be that the superimposed [ignorance] is the imaginer (*kalpaka*). Nor does this lead to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*), because the superimposition of ignorance does not depend on another superimposition; for it is logically established as the universal resolver of all things, common to both itself and others. Furthermore, no non-superimposed entity is ever observed to be an imaginer. Moreover, we observe that a mirror or similar object—qualified by a reflected image that is itself superimposed—acts as the imaginer of a reflection in another mirror. This is because the original object (*bimba*) cannot be the imaginer in that case, as it lacks a face-to-face orientation toward the second mirror; otherwise, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of the principle.

We shall explain this in detail further on. Thus, these six reasons have been refuted when proving ultimate reality (*paramārthasattva*) as the probandum (*sādhya*). Other [reasons] should likewise be rejected. Now, suppose it is thought that there will be another inference: "The object of dispute (*vimata*) is not distinct from existence, because it is distinct from non-existence, like the Self (*ātman*). That is not so, because of the fallacy (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of illusory appearances such as the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell. Nor should it be said that the reason "being distinct from non-existence" does not apply there at all.

For if there were an absence of being distinct from the non-existent (*asadvilakṣaṇatva*), there would be no direct perception (*aparokṣapratīti*) at all. [Objection: "In that case, if it is distinct from the non-existent, it is impossible for it to be distinct from the existent (*sat*), which is its opposite; thus, since the probandum (*sādhya*) also exists [in the subject], there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*). [Reply: No, because if it were existent, it would contradict the sublation (*bādha*) established by everyone.

Just as in the case of an elephant and the like, even while being distinct from a cow, it is possible to be distinct from a horse—which is the opposite of the cow—so too, even while being distinct from the existent, it is logically consistent to be distinct from the non-existent, as was stated in the first definition of falsity (*mithyātva*).

Now, [the following argument may be raised]: "The subject of dispute (the world) is not an effect of ignorance regarding consciousness, nor is it an object of cognition that is an effect thereof, nor does it possess existence like an effect thereof, nor does it possess existence sublated by a cognition thereof; because, even while consciousness is directly perceived, it appears immediately as something not to be negated therein. Whatever is thus, is so; for example, a cloth appearing immediately as something not to be negated while a jar is directly perceived is not an effect of ignorance regarding the jar, etc. And in the case of the contrary position, the very fact that the ignorance of that [consciousness] would be contradicted when it is directly perceived serves as the sublation."

Nor is there a lack of proof [for our position], because even now, due to the immediacy of consciousness (*caitanya*) as the witness of pleasure and so forth by virtue of being their substrate—[if you argue this]—we say no. For even if there is immediacy in a general form, there is no deviation [in our rule], since in the case of mother-of-pearl and the like, silver and so forth are not objects of negation and thus appear directly. Now, if you think that the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is as follows: "When X appears in its excluded form, that which appears directly as non-negatable is not an effect of the ignorance (*ajñāna*) regarding Y," then [our reason] is unproven (*asiddhi*).

Consciousness (*caitanya*) is not, at this stage, the object of a non-mediated (*aparokṣa*) cognition that possesses a distinct form intended to remove error; for if it were so, it would no longer be the underlying substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*). However, when it is non-mediated through a mental modification (*vṛtti*) produced by Vedāntic sentences in its distinct form, then there is not even the suspicion of non-mediation regarding the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), since it is not something to be negated. Therefore, because it is precisely the manifestation of a unique form produced by a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) that opposes ignorance, there is no contingency of ignorance being destroyed merely by non-mediation.

As for the objection that if "ignorance" (*ajñāna*) is stated as the absence of knowledge (*jñānābhāva*), it results in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*); and if it is stated as an indeterminable knowledge (*anirvacanīyajñāna*), then because such [an indeterminable entity] is like a sky-flower, its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) is unestablished—this is trivial. For one who accepts an absence that lacks a counter-correlate, the establishment of the counter-correlate is possible merely by virtue of the opponent's own admission.

Now, an objection is raised: "The subject under dispute is not superimposed upon the Self; because it is the object of activity following from the direct realization of the Self; whatever is thus is so, just as a jar, which is the object of activity following from the direct realization of a jar, is not superimposed there [upon the jar]."

Nor is there a lack of proof [for our position], because even for the Lord and the one liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*), who possess the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of the Self, there is activity such as protecting the world or wandering for alms. Furthermore, there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of the yellowness superimposed on a conch shell, because that yellowness, though superimposed, is not the object of activity for one who possesses the direct realization of the whiteness of the conch shell—if this is argued, we say no, because of deviation in the case of a reflection. For that [reflection] is superimposed on the face and is the object of activity for one who possesses the direct realization of the identity with the face. Moreover, "being perceived as distinct from that" is a limiting condition (*upādhi*).

And thus—the following [arguments] are also refuted: "The object under dispute is not created by the Māyā of Īśvara, because it is directly perceived by Him; for whatever is such is so, just as a jar directly perceived by Caitra is not created by Caitra’s Māyā. "The object under dispute is not created by the individual soul (jīva), because it persists even when that soul is in deep sleep, like the Self (Ātman). Nor is there a lack of proof [for this], because of recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) and because, in the absence of unseen merit/demerit (*adṛṣṭa*) and so forth, re-emergence would be impossible.

In the first case [of the reason "because it is perceived"], there is a fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) with respect to a magician, because that which is produced by his illusion is perceived even though it is not real. Furthermore, there is a deviation with respect to the delusion of the identity of the body and the self, since there is no difference between *māyā* and *avidyā*. In the second case [of the reason "because it is perceived as persisting"], the reason is unestablished (*asiddhi*). Nor can it be argued that the reason is not unestablished because the persistence of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is established through recognition (*pratyabhijñā*); for it will be explained later, in the demonstration of the theory of "creation upon perception" (*dṛṣṭisṛṣṭi*), that recognition does not prove persistence during the state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*). Moreover, since unseen merit and demerit (*adṛṣṭa*) and so forth exist in the form of their causal potential, a re-emergence of the world is possible.

Nor is it correct to argue: "Falsity (mithyātva) does not reside in everything other than the Self, because it resides only in what is false, like the silverness in a shell-silver. This is because the probans is vitiated by the presence of an extraneous condition (upādhi), namely, "residing in something of a narrower extension than falsity. Furthermore, falsity consists either in being distinct from both the real and the unreal, or merely in being distinct from the real. In the first case, there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (siddhasādhana), because that [falsity] lacks residence in the unreal, which is included among all things other than the Self. In the second case, if the word "false" in the reason is intended to mean "distinct from both the real and the unreal," then the probans is unestablished in its own nature (svarūpāsiddhi).

In the case where the subject (*pakṣa*) consists of being distinct from the real (*sad-vailakṣaṇya*), which includes even the non-existent (*tuccha*), the reason (*hetu*)—defined as "not residing in anything other than that which is distinct from both the real and the unreal"—is absent. Even if that [reason] were intended to mean merely "distinctness from the real," it would be inconclusive due to doubt (*sandigdhānaikāntikatā*), because there is doubt regarding the presence of the reason in a particular self (*ātmabheda*) where the probandum (*sādhya*) is absent. Furthermore, the previously mentioned refutations, such as the lack of logical necessity (*aprayojakatva*), certainly persist.

The self (*ātman*) is other than that which is ultimately real (*paramārthasat*), because it possesses ultimate reality, like the non-self (*anātman*). Nor is there the fallacy of proving what is already established (*arthāntara*) by means of a distinction whose counter-correlative is the imagined self (*kalpitātman*); for even if one were to infer falsity based on the falsity of the imagined [self], this would result in the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanāpatti*). This is not so, because there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in the case of proving what is already established with respect to conventional (*vyāvahārika*) entities; furthermore, "not being bliss" (*anānandatva*) serves as a limiting condition (*upādhi*).

Now, as for the self (*ātman*): [the inference is] "The self possesses a non-self that persists as long as its own nature persists, or possesses a non-self in the form of a positive entity (*bhāvarūpa*) that persists as long as its own nature persists; or it possesses a non-self not sublated by its own cognition, or possesses a non-self in the form of a positive entity not sublated by its own cognition; because it is a category (*padārtha*), or because it is a positive entity (*bhāva*), like a jar and so forth. In this regard, even the claim that the term "in the form of a positive entity" is an adjunct to "non-self" in the two probanda (*sādhya*)—for the sake of avoiding the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) under the view that accepts the cessation of ignorance (*avidyānivṛtti*) as a fifth kind—is weak.

If the phrase "as far as its own nature" (*yāvatsvarūpam*) refers to some unspecified nature, there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanāt*). If it refers to the nature of the Self (*ātmasvarūpa*), the probandum is unestablished (*sādhyāprasiddhi*); for no non-self (*anātman*) is known to persist as long as the nature of the Self. If that were the case, inference would be redundant.

Now, if it is argued that—since the term *svarūpa* (essential nature) refers to what is co-referential [with the subject], at the time of grasping the pervasion (*vyāpti*) one obtains the essential nature of the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), and at the time of grasping the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) one obtains the essential nature of the self (*ātman*) itself; thus there is neither the unestablishedness of the probandum (*sādhyāprasiddhi*) nor the proving of what is already established (*siddhasādhana*)—we say: no. For the introduction of the intrinsic nature of a word is of no use in inference. This same defect applies equally to the word *sva* in the expression "not sublated by its own cognition" (*svajñānābādhya*).

Thus, the following argument is also refuted: "The cessation of bondage under dispute is either (1) simultaneous with a non-self that is not sublated by a cognition having as its object the entity that is its own counter-correlative, or (2) simultaneous with a non-self that is a positive entity not sublated by the aforementioned cognition, because it is a cessation of bondage, like the cessation of shackles. This is because, due to the absence of a single referent for the term "bondage" in both the subject (*pakṣa*) and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), there arises either the fallacy of the unestablished nature of the essential character (*svarūpāsiddhi*) or the deficiency of the probans (*sādhanavaikalya*). Furthermore, regarding the word "own" (*sva*), the fault of the unestablished nature of the probandum (*sādhyāprasiddhi*) has already been stated.

Furthermore, because the qualification "bound" (*bandha*) in the reason (*hetu*) is redundant, there is a lack of pervasion (*vyāpyatvāsiddhi*). There is also a lack of probative force (*aprayojakatva*); for the observation that the cessation of a particular thing occurs at a time not simultaneous with the non-self (*anātman*) does not prove that every cessation possesses that same character. This is just as the observation that the cessation of suffering occurring during the period of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) is simultaneous with the prior absence (*prāgabhāva*) of suffering co-located with it does not prove that every cessation of suffering possesses that same character.
[Objection: But surely, once general inferences (*sāmānyānumāna*) have been thus refuted, there will be an inference based on the specific (*viśeṣya*).

The argument that "the cognition of the self (ātmadhī) is not sublated by a cognition whose object is its own object, because it is a cognition, like the cognition of mother-of-pearl" is merely the talk of a child; for the probans is vitiated by the condition (*upādhi*) of "not having as its object a cognition that contradicts itself. This is because there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) seen in the case of a blind man's cognition of color—such as when one says "this blind man possesses knowledge of color"—where the cognition imagined by the blind man to have color as its object is actually sublated by a cognition that has as its object the cognition [of color] itself, since color is not accessible to the blind man.

Since it is imagined (*kalpita*) there, its falsity (*bādha*) applies equally to the *vṛtti* (mental modification) under discussion as well; for its imagined nature is the same. Furthermore, if by the term "intellect" (*dhī*) one intends mere consciousness (*caitanyamātra*), then the argument is merely proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*). The following argument is also sound: "The cause of an error whose substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) is the Self is not sublated by the knowledge of the substratum of the error which is its own effect, because it is a cause of error; whatever is so, is so, just like the eye-disease (*kāca*) which is the cause of an error whose substratum is mother-of-pearl. This is because the probans is rendered inconclusive (*upādhi*) by either "not having as its limit the knowledge of the substratum in its excluded form" or "not being superimposed upon the substratum of the error that is its own effect."

Furthermore, there is deviation (vyabhicāra) because, in cases such as a stone where there is the conceptualization of shimmering due to defects like distance, one observes the sublation of both the shimmering and the silver through the knowledge of the substrate (adhiṣṭhāna)—just as in the case of mother-of-pearl where silver is conceptualized due to that defect of shimmering. Nor is it sound to argue: "That which is other than Brahman is ultimately real, because it is beginningless, like Brahman"; for in that case, the probans is over-narrowed by the condition (upādhi) of being non-antecedent to destruction (dhvaṃsāpratiyogitva).

Nor is it the case that Brahman does not exist without a relation to space and time, because it is an entity (*padārthatvāt*), like a jar. For the statement "it does not exist without a relation to time" has as its meaning the pervasion (*vyāpti*) that whenever there is Brahman, there must necessarily be a relation to time; and thus, this results in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanam*). Indeed, at the very time when Brahman exists, it is not the case that Brahman lacks a relation to time. Similarly, regarding the spatial pervasion that "wherever there is the Self (*ātman*), there is a relation to time," the same fault of proving what is already established applies.

For there is never any lack of connection with space and time; however, in the case of supreme liberation (*paramamukti*), there is neither space nor time, so the proof is firmly established as a *siddhasādhana* (proving what is already admitted). Nor is it correct to argue that "whatever is other than Brahman, such as *dharma* and so forth, which is knowable solely through the Vedas, is ultimately real (*paramārthasat*) because it is the intended object of the purport of the Śruti, like Brahman," since "being the intended object of the purport of the Śruti by way of ultimate reality" is a limiting condition (*upādhi*).

Nor can it be argued that pleasure and the like are ultimately real because they are directly perceived by the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*) as objects of a cognition not produced by defects, just like the Self; for this argument is subject to the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell and similar illusions. This is because, although such illusory objects are indeed objects of a mental modification (*vṛtti*) produced by defects, they are nonetheless objects of the witness-consciousness which is not itself produced by defects. Furthermore, if one does not admit that the pure [Self] is an object of a mental modification, the corroborative instance (*dṛṣṭānta*) lacks the probandum (*sādhanavikala*). And if the intended meaning of the reason is "not being an object of a cognition produced by defects," then the reason is unestablished (*asiddha*).

Because the mental modification (*vṛtti*) of ignorance that serves as the witness-veiler is produced by a defect; and because there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of the unreal, since a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) consisting of verbal knowledge whose object is non-existent is not produced by a defect. Furthermore, if one accepts that the Self is an object of a mental modification, then the example is devoid of the probans (*sādhanavikala*), because [the Self] is the object of the delusion of the identity of the body and the Self, which is produced by a defect. If, however, that is not accepted, then since the mere fact of being a non-object is sufficient to prove ultimate reality, the qualification "produced by a defect" is redundant, resulting in the fallacy of the probans being unestablished (*vyāpyatvāsiddhi*).
Moreover, that much alone is unestablished in its own nature (*svarūpāsiddha*) in the subject (*pakṣa*), as is explained in detail elsewhere.

The argument that "the object of dispute is ultimately real because it exists prior to the cognition of its own object, like the self" is also not valid; for [the reason] is unestablished (*asiddha*) under the theory of *dṛṣṭasṛṣṭi* (the view that the world is created at the time of perception), and because "beginninglessness," which has an uneven distribution (*viṣamavyāpta*), serves as a limiting condition (*upādhi*).

The property of being an absence that is distinct from mutual absence (anyonyābhāva), co-located with this jar, and has this jar as its counter-correlate (pratiyogin) resides in something simultaneous with this jar, because it resides only in absences that are distinct from mutual absence, co-located with this jar, and have this jar as their counter-correlate, just like the antecedent absence (prāgabhāva) of this jar; [furthermore], in the view that there is an absence qualified by a non-co-located property (vyadhikaraṇadharmāvacchinnābhāva), it should also be specified as "not qualified by a non-co-located property."

Furthermore, the claim that existence (*sattva*) is established here by the definition of being the non-counterpositive of an absolute absence that is both co-located with and simultaneous with itself is also not tenable; for the property of "subsisting solely in either the produced or the producer" relative to this jar—which is a pervader of the probandum as delimited by the probans—constitutes an incidental attribute (*upādhi*).

Nor should it be said that "there is a doubt regarding the non-pervasion of the probans (sādhana) when there is a doubt as to whether the property constituting the subject (pakṣībhūtadharma) exists in the absolute absence [of the probandum]. This is because, at a stage where no subverting argument (tarka) against the counter-example (vipakṣa) has been introduced, even a doubtful upādhi can function as a defect. Furthermore, there is a deviation (vyabhicāra) in the case of the absolute absence of a jar; for even on a ground that possesses a jar through the relation of conjunction (saṃyoga), the absolute absence of a jar exists through the relation of inherence (samavāya). Thus, since the probans exists there despite the absence of the probandum, the objection is refuted. Enough of this excessive detail. Thus ends the refutation of the inference of the reality of the universe in the Advaitasiddhi.

Therefore, there is an inference for the specific [definition] of falsity (*mithyātva*), and there are also specific inferences regarding falsity: 1. The property of not being the locus of non-existence (i.e., existence) in anything other than Brahman—which is itself not sublated by knowledge other than the knowledge of Brahman—does not reside in the locus of ultimate reality (*pāramārthika-sattva*), because it does not reside in Brahman, like the nature of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell, and like the difference from the ultimately real. 2. The subject under dispute is false, because it is other than Brahman, like the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell. 3. Ultimate reality does not reside in that which is the counter-correlative of a mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*) co-located with itself, because it does not reside in what is other than the existent, like the nature of Brahman (*brahmatva*).

Brahmanhood or oneness pervades existence (*sattva*), because it is co-located with existence, like the difference from the non-existent (*asadvailakṣaṇya*). A pot or similar object, which exists as a delimited occurrence (*vyāpyavṛtti*), is the counter-positive of only an absence that is co-located with itself and is distinct from any produced absence, because it is the counter-positive of an absence, like "nameability" (*abhidheyatva*). For, according to the opponent's view, nameability is the counter-positive of only mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*) due to its being purely positive (*kevalānvayin*); and that [absence] is indeed co-located [with its locus].

In our view, however, [the reason] is simply false; thus, there is no deficiency of the probandum (*sādhyavaikalya*) in either case. Absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) subsists only in those loci that are the substrata of all its counter-correlates (*pratiyogin*), or it subsists only in what is delimited by its counter-correlate, because it subsists only in eternal absences, like mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāvatva*). The state of being the absolute non-existence of a jar (*ghaṭātyantābhāvatva*) subsists in a locus co-located with the absence of the producer of its own counter-correlate, because it subsists in an absence whose counter-correlate is this jar at a time simultaneous with these potsherds, like knowability (*prameyatva*).

This skull is the locus of the absolute non-existence of this jar, because it is a substratum, like a cloth or other objects. Brahmanhood is not the delimiting property of the counter-correlativity of mutual non-existence residing in the ultimately real, because it resides in Brahman, like the distinction from the unreal (*asadvailakṣaṇya*). A difference whose counter-correlate is the ultimately real does not reside in the ultimately real, because its counter-correlate is the ultimately real, like the absence whose counter-correlate is delimited by ultimate reality.

That which is delimited by difference possesses either a counter-correlative that is distinct from reality or a locus [of such a counter-correlative], because it is an absence, like the absence whose counter-correlative is the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell. Difference residing in the ultimately real is not one whose counter-correlative is the ultimately real, because its locus is the ultimately real, like the difference whose counter-correlative is the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell.

Falsity (*mithyātva*) pervades that which is distinct from both Brahman and the void (*tuccha*), because it resides in all false things, or because it is not the counter-positive of an absolute non-existence residing in the same locus as falsity, just like "being an object of cognition" (*dṛśyatva*). "Being an object of cognition" does not reside in that which is ultimately real (*paramārthasat*), because it resides in everything that can be denominated, just like "the nature of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell. "Being an object of cognition" is pervaded by being different from that which is ultimately real, because it is a property that does not reside in anything other than objects of cognition, just like "phenomenality" (*prātibhāsikatva*).

That which is established for both [parties] as distinct from the non-existent, and which is not the locus of any property that does not have the same substratum as falsity, is the locus of [such] falsity, because it is a substratum, like the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell. The space delimited by the counter-positive is the locus of absolute non-existence, because it is a substratum, like time. That which is delimited by selfhood is devoid of the property of being a difference whose counter-positive is the locus of ultimate reality, because it is ultimately real, like that which is delimited by ultimate reality.

Even in the view that accepts a distinction within ultimate reality (*paramārtha-sat*), that distinction does not reside in that which is delimited by ultimate existence; rather, it resides only in that which is delimited by potness (*ghaṭatva*) and so forth. Silver in a mother-of-pearl shell (*śukti-rūpya*) is not distinct from the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) in its falsity (*mithyātva*), because it is an object of empirical usage (*vyavahāra-viṣayatva*), like Brahman. Here, the existence of the probandum (*sādhya-sattva*) is threefold: [the silver] being non-false while both [silver and world] are false, both being false, or both being non-false.

In this regard, since the final position is untenable, the establishment of the probandum (*sādhya*) in the subject (*pakṣa*) is concluded through the middle position, whereas in the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), it is through the first position; such is the distinction. The subject of dispute is false, because, while not being the object of the knowledge that causes liberation, it is other than the non-existent, like the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell. Being the object of the knowledge that causes liberation is pervaded by ultimate reality (*paramārthasattva*), because it is co-extensive with ultimate reality, just as being the intended object of the scriptures by way of ultimate reality [is so pervaded].

The absolute non-existence (atyantābhāva) of this cloth resides in these threads, because it is a non-existence of this cloth that is beginningless (anādi), just like the mutual non-existence (anyonyābhāva) of this cloth. The word "beginningless" (anādi) is included to prevent a fallacy (vyabhicāra) in the case of the destruction of a cloth produced by the destruction of its threads, for such destruction never exists as a property of the threads. However, if the subject (pakṣa) were the absolute non-existence of that cloth whose destruction occurs through the separation of its substratum, then the word "beginningless" would certainly not need to be employed.

And here, because the subject is that which is delimited by being an absolute absence having this cloth as its counter-positive (*pratiyogin*), there is no partial *siddhasādhana* (proving what is already established) by taking an absolute absence through another relation; for the intended goal is the establishment of the probandum (*sādhya*) as delimited by the delimitor of the subjecthood (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*). Alternatively, the subject may be simply that absolute absence of this cloth which is delimited by the relation of inherence (*samavāya*) and not delimited by a non-co-locative property (*vyadhikaraṇadharma*). By the word "thread" (*tantu*), the material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*) of the cloth is expressed.

And since antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) exists there, there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) by that [reason]. Furthermore, objections such as *siddhasādhana* (proving what is already established) regarding the non-difference between cause and effect have already been refuted previously during the presentation of the inference in the *Tattvapradīpikā*. Alternatively, one may formulate a specific inference: "This absolute non-existence of this cloth, as delimited by the relation of inherence (*samavāya*), resides in these threads, because it is an absolute non-existence whose counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) is this cloth, like the absolute non-existence of this cloth as delimited by another relation."

[The probandum is: being a counter-correlate of an absolute non-existence that co-exists with itself, while not being the locus of non-pervasive occurrence and possessing the aforementioned delimitation of the subject (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*). [The reason is: because it is not the Self (*anātmatvāt*), like conjunction (*saṃyoga*). Nor is there a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of the absolute non-existence of the universe, for if that [non-existence] is of the nature of its own locus, the reason "not being the Self" is simply absent; if it is something distinct, then since it is false (*mithyātva*), it is itself the counter-correlate of an absolute non-existence, and thus the probandum exists therein.

Nor should it be argued that if there were an absolute absence (atyantābhāva) of an absolute absence, then falsity—defined as being the counter-positive (pratiyogitva) of that [absolute absence]—would remain unestablished; for the counter-positiveness of an absence toward another absence does not contradict its counter-positiveness toward an absence residing in a positive entity (bhāva). This is because, even though antecedent absence (prāgabhāva) is the counter-positive of an absolute absence, its counter-positiveness toward things such as a jar is universally established. And this has been demonstrated in the discussion on the falsity of falsity (mithyātvamithyātva).

And here, by the term "not being the locus of non-pervasive occurrence" (*avyāpyavṛttitvānadhikaraṇa*), what is intended as a qualification of the subject (*pakṣaviśeṣaṇa*) is the state of not existing [in the subject] through the delimitation of a single part. By this, two objections are refuted: first, that there would be a contradiction (*bādha*) if one were to state [the reason] as "being the counter-positive of an absolute absence co-locus with itself"; and second, that if one were to state it as "not being the locus of subsistence in its parts," then jars and the like would fail to qualify as the subject. As for the reason "non-selfhood" (*anātmatva*), it has been explained by the very same explanation given for the reason "insentience" (*jaḍatva*).

For this very reason, the following inference is also sound: "That which possesses the aforementioned delimiting factor of the subject (pakṣatāvacchedaka) is not the locus of any non-pervasive occurrence that is distinct from eternal substances; it is the counter-positive of an absolute absence that is purely positive (kevalānvayin), because it is a category of reality (padārtha), like an eternal substance. This example is according to the opponent's view; however, in our own system, the example is simply "like the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell."

Nor should it be argued that if [the self] were the counter-positive of absolute non-existence by its own nature, it would follow that it is absolutely non-existent, because there would be no factor to account for its distinction from such non-existence; for this objection is refuted by the fact that [the self] is the counter-positive of either origination or cessation. Furthermore, the difference whose locus is delimited by the property of selfhood (ātmatva) does not have a counter-positive that is ultimately real, because it does not have the self as its counter-positive, just like the difference having the silver-in-shell as its counter-positive.

Nor is there any deviation (vyabhicāra) in the case of the conjunction of a jar and a cloth; for, as in the case of a sprout and the like which are determined to possess a cause, doubt regarding the probandum (sādhya) is not a defect. In this manner, other formulations should also be constructed by the wise as appropriate; this is the general direction. "Our reasons for the sake of establishing our desired [conclusion] are correct and numerous, while those of the opponent are few and flawed"—this has been clearly stated herein.

"Having carefully examined here the strength and weakness of the supporting arguments regarding the accomplishment of the desired goal, the host of defects in the positions of others will be proclaimed; however, one's mind should not be troubled right now.
Thus ends the specific inferences regarding the falsity of the universe in the *Advaitasiddhi*.

Now, one might object: let there be sublation by scripture (*śabdabādha*), for instance, because the reality of the universe is established by such scriptural passages as "The universe is true," "Whatever He willed was indeed true, not false," and "He ordained things according to their true nature for eternal years," as well as by such Smṛti texts as "They say the world is untrue, without foundation, and without a Lord," and by such Sūtras as "There is no non-existence, because it is perceived" and "And because of its difference in nature, it is not like a dream, etc. If this is argued, we say no, because those scriptures do not have that [the reality of the universe] as their primary purport (*tatparatva*). To explain:
"The universe is true; O Maghavans, yours alone is it. Even the waters do not violate your decree.
O Indra and Brahmaṇaspati, come toward our oblation and food like two prize-winning steeds yoked together."

The meaning of this passage from the second book of the *Ṛgveda-saṃhitā* is as follows: O Indra and Brahmaṇaspati! You two are *maghavānau*—that is, possessors of wealth (*magha*), for *magha* is a name for wealth—or, alternatively, possessors of sacrifice (*makha*). All action (*viśvam... satyam karma*) is "true" because it is real or because its fruit is certain to occur. Such action belongs to you two alone (*yuvorit*); the particle *it* here serves as an emphatic particle. The sense is that all rites are to be performed directed toward you two alone.

The waters are deities characterized by pervasion; *cana* is a compound of these two words, though their status as a single word is established by the tradition of the teachers. *Vām* means "of you two. *Vratam* means resolve, intention, or action. *Na praminanti* means they do not harm or injure it (*mīṅ* in the sense of injury, belonging to the *krayādi* class); rather, they approve of it. *Naḥ* means "our. *Haviḥ* refers to the oblation such as curds and the like, and *annam* refers to food such as the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*). *Accha* means "towards" or "aiming at. *Vājinā* means "possessing speed," like two horses. *Yujā* means "being joined together."

"Come! Come to the place of sacrifice for the gods! (*Jigātam* is from the root *gā*, meaning "to go," belonging to the *juhoty-ādi* class). Or, it may mean "like two horses toward fodder. Alternatively: O Indra and Brahmaṇaspati! "The whole"—the entire world perceived as reality—is "of you two alone," created by you two alone.

Alternatively—the entire universe is indeed a hymn of praise for you both; "truly" (satyam) means according to reality, that is, whatever collection of qualities is set forth through praise, all of that exists in you both and is not merely superimposed—this is the meaning. "The Waters" (āpaḥ) refers to the deities characterized by pervasion, or the five great elements as typified by water. They do not harm your "vow" (vratam), namely the act of creating the world. Thus, you two of such great majesty, come hither! The remainder is to be explained as before.
And so, since the intent is directed toward praise, there is no underlying purpose here regarding the absolute truth of the universe.

"By his own power, the powerful, ruddy, fair-winged one—He who is the great hero from of old, the dark-blue one—whatever he has willed is indeed true and not in vain; He is the winner and the giver of desirable wealth."

Even this [verse], situated in the eighth Aṣṭaka, has as its primary purport a praise of Indra; therefore, it does not intend to establish the reality of the universe. For instance: *śākmanā* means "by his own power" (*śāka*); *śāka* means "capable," signifying that he is capable of accomplishing everything by his own power alone. Indeed, Indra has no need for any other assistance, precisely because he is Indra. *Aruṇaḥ* means "red-colored"; the word "bird" (*pakṣin*) is to be supplied [as the subject], meaning "a certain beautiful-feathered bird of red hue comes," as indicated by the presence of the prefix (*upa-sarga*).

He who is great, the mighty hero, valorous, ancient from of old, not blue, nestless, and the non-maker of a nest—for Indra, unlike Agni, does not establish a fixed dwelling anywhere at a sacrifice—thus he speaks of Indra through such metaphors as "the fair-winged bird" (*suparṇa*). Whatever that Indra intends or knows as "this must now be done," that is truly indeed true, not in vain and not fruitless. He conquers from his enemies the desirable wealth, the treasure worthy of being coveted and fit for habitation.

Moreover, the giver gives to his worshippers; [the word] *jetā* (conqueror) is formed with the suffix *tṛn*. By the rule "not in *loka*" (*na loke*), etc., the prohibition of the genitive case applies. In this same manner, other passages establishing reality should also be inferred. Furthermore, the statement "He disposed of objects according to their true nature" (*yāthātathyato 'rthān vyadadhāt*) is not evidence for the reality of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*). Its meaning is that he created [them] in the manner of previous creations, and not that the world is real, nor that there is reality in the act of creating the world.

Furthermore, even in cases where there is no intent toward praise (*stuti*) and so forth, the statement lacks that intent because it is merely a restatement of what is established by perception (*pratyakṣasiddhānuvādakatā*), like the sentence "Fire is the remedy for cold" (*agnir himasya bheṣajam*). Nor should it be argued: "In your view, since the existence of Brahman alone manifests everywhere, the existence of jars and other things—which consists in their being uncontradicted until the end of time—is not attained through perception; therefore, the Scripture (*śruti*) is not a mere restatement (*anuvādaka*) because it makes that [existence] known. This cannot be maintained.

Since the acceptance of the manifestation of the reality of Brahman (*brahmasattva*) is preceded by the negation of the reality of other beings, and since the application of terms such as "real" (*satya*) is admitted only in that regard, the truth of the universe beyond that does not become an object of verbal cognition; therefore, [the scripture] cannot avoid being a mere restatement (*anuvādaka*) with respect to that [alleged universal truth].

Now, [the opponent argues]: "Just as in cases such as 'Earth is distinct from others' or 'One should not harm any living beings,' even though the predicate is established in respect to a portion—by perception in the case of a jar and so forth, or by another statement in the case of a Brāhmaṇa and so forth—it does not function as a mere restatement (anuvādaka) because it is unestablished everywhere; likewise, since the truth of the entire universe has not been previously obtained through perception, this [statement] cannot be considered a restatement. This is not so.

In the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*), earthness (*pṛthivītva*) and the nature of violence (*hiṃsātva*) are indeed single, recurring properties (*anugata-dharma*). Therefore, because the predicate (*vidheya*) is not already established with respect to that [recurrence], it is not appropriate for it to be a mere restatement (*anuvādakatva*) therein. However, in this case, there is no single property called "universality" (*viśvatva*); rather, because the word *viśva* is a pronoun (*sarvanāman*), it brings to mind jars, cloths, and so forth, each in its own respective form. Since existence (*sattva*) is already grasped in each of those individually, how can it not be a restatement? For there is an absence of any difference in the mode of presentation (*prakāra-vailakṣaṇya*).

Nor should it be argued that a vidhi-vākya (injunctive statement) located in another recensional branch (*śākhā*)—though having the same meaning as the vidhi-vākya situated in one’s own branch—is not a mere restatement (*anuvāda*) because it possesses purposefulness for a different person; for there may be a person who, due to the conflicting assertions of disputants and so forth, has not determined the existence of a jar or similar object through perception. If this were the case, it would follow that there is no such thing as a locus of restatement at all. Furthermore, a case where there is no dispute for anyone cannot serve as an example, because it is impossible to ascertain a state of universal non-dispute.

Since a restatement (anuvāda) must be preceded by a prior statement (purovāda), and since there is no such prior statement here, there is no possibility that a sentence from another recensional branch (śākhā) could be considered a mere restatement.

As for the objection that—in the *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya*, having raised the doubt that the scriptural passage beginning with "It is indeed as such that one should perceive" (*astīty evopalabdhavya*), which teaches the Self as distinct from the body, is merely a restatement of what is already established by perception, [Śaṅkara] refuted it by stating "because of the conflicting views of disputants" (*vādivipratipattidarśanāt*) and so forth; and that thus, even though it grasps an existence already established by perception, it is not a mere restatement because its purpose is to remove the conflicting views of disputants, and that this applies to the present case as well—that is incorrect, due to a failure to understand the meaning of the *bhāṣya*.

For it has been stated that, because conflicting views among disputants are observed therein, the self is not indeed perceived as distinct from the body; otherwise, there would have been no disagreement on this point by the Cārvākas and others who maintain the authority of perception. However, the purposefulness or non-redundancy of statements such as "it exists" does not follow merely from the refutation of disputants' conflicting views. Thus it is said in that very same work: "Therefore, the scripture proceeds with regard to the existence of a self connected to other births, and regarding the specific means for attaining the desired and avoiding the undesired in those other births."
