[Objection: But surely—in the case of the two intermediate parvans of the Cāturmāsya sacrifice, since the sentence "They carry forward the two fires" (dvayoḥ praṇayanti) prescribes the carrying forward of fires distinct from those obtained through the *codaka* (archetypal injunction), let it be that in the present context [the scripture] serves as a means of knowledge for a reality characterized by being the counter-positive of a negation of existence across the three times, which is distinct from the empirical reality established by direct perception. [Reply: No; because the scriptural text asserting the truth of the universe cannot have the existence across the three times as its intended meaning, as that would contradict the scriptural texts negating existence across the three times.

Nor should it be argued: "Why might the opposite not be the case? For there is no decisive evidence [to the contrary]. This is because the very general requirements for the impossibility of any other intended meaning (*tātparya-anyathānupapatti*) serve as the decisive evidence. Indeed, the Śruti concerning non-duality (*advaita-śruti*) is endowed with the sixfold marks of intended meaning (*ṣaḍvidha-tātparya-liṅga*). Among these, three marks of intended meaning—namely, being unknown (*ajñātatva*), being unsublated (*abādhitatva*), and possessing a purpose (*prayojanavattva*)—constitute the essential components of the nature of valid knowledge (*prāmāṇya-śarīra-ghaṭaka*) and reside in the object itself.

The threefold indicator residing in the words themselves that prevents over-extension consists of: uniformity between the opening and the conclusion, repetition, and corroborative statement (*arthavāda*). Regarding those three indicators residing in the words, there is no dispute; for it is precisely all the Upaniṣads that have set out [to teach this]. Since it is not established by any other means of knowledge and since it is the object of the knowledge that causes liberation, its being unknown and its having a purpose are beyond dispute. Only its non-contradiction (*abādhitatva*) is doubtful.

And that [non-duality] is determined through the impossibility of it being otherwise and through the uniformity of understanding; for non-duality, which consists in the negation of the entire phenomenal world, is not merely empirical (vyāvahārika), such that the scripture’s authority regarding it would be merely empirical. Therefore, its authority there is indeed ultimate (tāttvika); whereas the reality of duality is merely empirical. Consequently, the scripture does not possess ultimate authority with respect to that [duality].

Because it is impossible for two mutually contradictory things to both possess ultimate reality (*tāttvikatva*), and because conceptual alternatives (*vikalpa*) are inadmissible regarding a real entity (*vastu*); because a systematic distinction is logically established through the difference between ultimate and conventional validity (*prāmāṇya*); and because it is more appropriate to interpret the statement "the universe is true"—which has been determined not to have that [ultimate reality] as its purport—in another way.

To explain: grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is indeed fourfold—through superimposition (*adhyāsa*), as in "this is silver" (*idaṃ rajatam*); through sublation (*bādhā*), as in "the post is a person" (*sthāṇuḥ puruṣaḥ*); through the relation of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*), as in "a blue lotus" (*nīlam utpalam*); and through non-difference (*abheda*), as in "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*). Now, since grammatical coreferentiality is established here either through sublation or superimposition, the Śruti that teaches reality cannot sublate the Śruti of non-duality, which is endowed with the six marks of interpretative intent (*ṣaḍvidhatātparyaliṅga*).

If it be objected that the scripture teaching the blissfulness of the Self must be merely a restatement of the bliss established by the witness-consciousness (*sākṣipratyakṣa*)—just as the scripture concerning the quality of *sattva* restates what is perceived—as in the thought "I slept happily," we say no. This is because there is no possibility of it being a restatement, since their objects are different: the witness has for its object the bliss conditioned by adjuncts (*upahita*), whereas the scripture has for its object the bliss devoid of adjuncts (*nirupādhika*). For at that time (of deep sleep), the bliss of one’s own nature (*svarūpānanda*) is grasped; and yet, the nature of the Self as the object of the witness is precisely that which is conditioned by ignorance (*ajñānopahita*).

If it is argued: "Is it not the case that, just as in the case of the ninefold repetition of 'That thou art' (*tattvamasi*), just as for one who is thirsty there is a convergence of means of knowledge regarding water, just as in the case of unity there are the sixfold marks of intentionality (*tātparya*), and just as in the case of positive ignorance established by perception there is the scripture 'Darkness existed' (*tama āsīt*), so too the scriptural statement of existence is for the sake of strengthening [the cognition]?"—this is not so; for when something is already apprehended by a perception that grasps all its specific features, no other means is required for the sake of strengthening it.

For one who is thirsty, the perception of water is required subsequent to the verbal testimony and the inferential mark, but not the verbal testimony and the inferential mark subsequent to the perception; nor should it be argued that, in that case, passages such as "Darkness existed" would lack the purpose of strengthening the ignorance established by perception—namely, the realization "I knew nothing"—because "Darkness existed," being related to the time prior to creation, apprehends ignorance in a different temporal context, and thus its validity is possible precisely through having a distinct object from the perception that apprehends ignorance as related to the time of deep sleep.

Now, one might object: "Just as in the Aśvamedha sacrifice, when the mantra 'He has twenty-six ribs'—which is obtained through the general rule (*codaka*)—is set aside by the specific mantra 'Thirty-four are there for the steed, the friend of the gods,' and the injunction 'One should say twenty-six' serves as a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*), so too the scripture on existence (*sattva-śruti*) is for the purpose of a counter-exception to the world's existence which, though obtained through perception, is prima facie set aside by the scripture on falsity (*mithyātva-śruti*). If this is argued, we reply: No, because if the scripture on falsity is admitted to sublate perception, it must be accepted as being more powerful (*balavat*) than perception.

Because that would contradict [the established doctrine], because the scriptural statements regarding truthfulness must have another purpose, and because the logic of the *Devatādhikaraṇa* cannot apply here, it is impossible to claim that [the statement] has the purpose of a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*).

[Objection: "If the validity of the perception of existence (*sattva*) is established, then by that very [perception] there would be a sublation of the scriptural texts on falsity, inference, and so forth; if its validity is not established, then it cannot serve as a restatement (*anuvādaka*) of the scriptural text on existence. [Reply: This is not so, because even if the perception lacks validity, it is possible for that which makes known what is already established by it to be a restatement. For being a restatement does not consist in making known what has already been cognized by a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); rather, it is merely the state of speaking after [the fact]. And as for this "posteriority," whether it is measured relative to a valid means of knowledge or relative to an invalid one, there is no distinction whatsoever.

Nor should it be said: "Since the Veda possesses a universally established status as a means of valid cognition, and since it must have a real object and not be a mere restatement (anuvāda), its subject matter must necessarily be ultimate reality that is not already apprehended by perception; and if that were so, how could the Veda be a restatement by means of perception, which is not itself a means of valid cognition?"—this objection cannot be maintained.

Even though the aspect of existence (*sattvāṃśa*) is established through perception, since the meaning of the sentence—established through the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) with the verb and other elements—is something previously unknown (*apūrva*), it is appropriate for [the scripture] to be non-reiterative (*anuvādaka*) precisely by taking that [sentence-meaning] as its object. Therefore, it is improper to postulate a real existence (*tāttvikasattva*) for that purpose, as it would contradict the scriptural texts on non-duality (*advaita*). As for the fact that all scriptures have the ultimate reality (*paramārthasat*) as their object, this occurs solely because they have pure Brahman as their primary purport (*tātparya*); that they have the conventional reality (*vyāvahārikasat*) as their object is due to an intermediate purport, and this will be explained when establishing the authority of the ritual section (*karmakāṇḍa*).

Nor can it be argued that perception does not require corroboration by scripture (*śruti*) for the determination of its own validity, and therefore scripture is not rendered redundant by it; otherwise, even such scriptural passages as "Truth, Knowledge" (*satyaṃ jñānam*) and "There is no diversity here" (*neha nānā*) would be mere restatements (*anuvāda*). This is because the existence of Brahman is already established through worldly experience, while its falsity is established by the mark of being the locus of error, by the inference from its being an object of sight (*dṛśyatva*), and by non-Vedic doctrines such as the beginningless theory of consciousness (*vijñānavāda*). Thus, it must be said [that scripture is not redundant].

For if even with respect to an object already perceived, perception were to depend upon corroboration by scripture (*śrutisaṃvāda*) for the determination of its own validity, then there would be no unhesitating engagement with any perceived object that lacks such scriptural corroboration. Furthermore, statements such as "Fire is the remedy for cold" would not be restatements (*anuvādaka*). Nor can this consequence be accepted, because if a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) other than perception—whose status as a valid means has been determined by perception—were not considered a restatement, it would follow that the very notion of "restatement" would be abolished from the world.

Nor does it follow that [scriptural passages] such as "Truth, Knowledge" (*satyaṃ jñānam*) or "There is no diversity here" (*neha nānā*) would be merely reiterative (*anuvādaka*). For they are not reiterative by way of perception; for what is to be established by this [text] is the existence (*sattva*) and so forth in their coreferentiality with Brahmanhood, and [perception] has already been refuted as such. Nor is it reiterative according to the view of the Vijñānavādins, who hold that [consciousness] is beginningless in its flux; for that [view] lacks any priority relative to the authorless Veda.

Nor should it be said: "Because the scriptural statement of *sattva* does not depend upon the perception of *sattva*, it is not a dependent restatement (*sāpekṣānuvādakatva*). However, being an independent restatement (*nirapekṣānuvādakatva*)—like a continuous stream of cognition (*dhārāvāhana*)—is not a cause for invalidity; for it is stated in the *Nayaviveka*: 'In the case of a dependent restatement, there is no valid cognition, but not so in the case of a fortuitous restatement, as in the case of a continuous stream. This must be rejected because, by parsimony (*lāghava*), the mere fact of being a restatement (*anuvādakatva*) is the determinant of invalidity, and not the fact of being a dependent restatement.

This is because the status of being a means of valid knowledge (*prāmāṇya*) consists precisely in the capacity to establish an object not yet apprehended, and its purpose is fulfilled by that much alone. Nor does it follow that a stream of cognitions (*dhārāvāhin-buddhi*) lacks validity; for since such a cognition apprehends a present object, it grasps it as qualified by each respective moment and thus is not a mere restatement (*anuvādaka*). Furthermore, when the Veda is not intended to convey something already known, the sole criterion is that the object is not already established; otherwise, the study of the Veda would be fruitless, and the injunction to study one's own portion of scripture (*svādhyāyādhyayana-vidhi*) would be untenable.

Furthermore, this verbal testimony regarding existence (*sattva-śruti*) is indeed a restatement dependent on another, because it depends upon the direct perception of existence. For without the direct perception of existence, the application of the word—which is rooted in the apprehension of its power (*śakti*) and other factors—is impossible. Therefore, "where there is corroboration by another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), that object is established through the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) just as through that other means of knowledge; for both function with respect to the same object independently of each other, like perception and inference. However, from the perspective of the knower, it is a restatement."

This also accords with the point stated by Vācaspati: "For an unlearned cognizer understands an object as it is through perception and other means first, but not so from the sacred tradition (āmnāya), because that depends upon learning. By this, he asserts that since the sacred tradition depends on learning, it necessarily depends upon perception. Nor is it a mere repetitive restatement devoid of purpose, for it serves the purpose of refuting the conflicting views of opponents.

However, being a restatement for a specific purpose does not contradict having its own meaning as the primary intent; for in the case of sentences addressed to those already knowledgeable (*vidvadvākya*), it is observed that they have their own meaning as the subject of the restatement because they serve a purpose such as bringing about the duality of the aggregate. Therefore, it must be stated that in such cases, "sentence-unification" (*vākyaikavākyatā*) is asserted, otherwise, like an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), there would be only "word-unification" (*padaikavākyatā*).

If it is argued that because perception possesses a purpose—namely, the removal of disputants' misconceptions—it is therefore purposeful as another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and thus its statement of its own object is for its own sake, then even such statements as "Fire is the remedy for cold" would likewise be purposeful and intended for their own objects by virtue of that same purpose. Consequently, there would be no need to rely on other means of knowledge to remove disputants' misconceptions regarding what is already established by perception.

In the case of the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*), however, because the intended object—the establishment of duality—cannot be obtained from any other source through the restatement of the whole (*samudāyānuvāda*), it is possible to assert that its purpose lies in its own literal meaning (*svārthaparatva*). And this is precisely the intention behind the previously cited statement from the *Nayaviveka*. Furthermore, one should not say that even if it is a restatement (*anuvāda*), there is merely a lack of fruitfulness (*naiṣphalya*) rather than a lack of authority (*aprāmāṇya*); for authority consists simply in accordance with reality (*yāthārthya*), and not in accordance with reality only when the object is not already known.

A word is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding its intended meaning (*tātparya-viṣaya*), because the learned accept that "that which a word aims at is the word's meaning. Otherwise, as has been stated, the injunction for Vedic study (*svādhyāya-vidhi*) would be untenable. For a scripture does not have its purport (*tātparya*) upon a matter already established by other means; therefore, it possesses no authority there. As the Bhaṭṭācāryas say: "Scripture is meaningful when [the object] is not [otherwise] obtained" (*aprāpte śāstramarthavat*). Now, one might object: this is a mere restatement (*anuvāda*), and not for the sake of praise (*stuti*), like the passage "Vāyu is indeed the swiftest deity," nor is it...

It is for the purpose of enjoining something else, like the injunction "one offers with curd" (*dadhnā juhoti*). Even though it is a restatement (*anuvāda*), that which is restated by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the sake of enjoining something else is necessarily real. For in cases such as "one sprinkles the rice-grains" (*vrīhīn prokṣati*), there is no cognition of superimposed rice-grains; for if the object of the restatement were non-existent, the substratum would be unestablished, and consequently, the sentence-meaning—consisting of the relation between the restated and the enjoined—would be sublated, just as an inference is sublated when its content consists of a relation between a property and a subject whose substratum is unestablished. If this is argued, we say no, because this restatement is intended to establish another thing not previously established.

Nor is there a rule that what is restated by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) must necessarily be real; for there is no deviation [from this rule] in the case of the chapter on dreams, or in the statement regarding mother-of-pearl, "This is not silver. If it is argued that in those cases there is no reality because the statement is a restatement of something that was an object of cognition and is now being negated, then understand that in the present case as well, since this restatement serves the purpose of negation in the words "Not here, not manifold," there is no reality. For this very reason, there is no consequence of the non-existence of the sentence-meaning, because that which is the intended object (*tātparya-viṣaya*) is existent.

If it is argued that since the restatement has already been accomplished by the phrase "anything whatsoever" (*kiṃ cana*), what is the use of the additional [phrase], we say no; for although the object of negation is presented in a general way by "anything whatsoever," its specific presentation is useful for a specific negation.

Now, if it is argued that a prohibitive statement does not require another statement to provide the object of prohibition—otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that even in cases such as "One should not eat *kalañja*," one would require another statement like "One eats *kalañja*" to provide the object of prohibition—this is not so, because there is no rule of necessity regarding such requirements everywhere; for when it is possible, it is improper to abandon what is present at hand.

Furthermore, in cases such as "One takes the *ṣoḍaśin* cup at the *atirātra* sacrifice" and "One does not take the *ṣoḍaśin* cup at the *atirātra* sacrifice," we observe the negation of what has been established by another scriptural statement. Nor does this lead to an option (*vikalpa*) in the same manner [as those examples], because an option is impossible regarding an already established reality. Moreover, while both the statements regarding the taking and non-taking of the *ṣoḍaśin* cup possess equal authority because their subjects are not established by any other means of knowledge, here there is no equality of authority; for the scripture concerning existence has its subject matter established by another means of knowledge, whereas the scripture concerning negation has a subject matter that was not previously established. Precisely for this reason, due to the superior strength of the negative statement, the other is interpreted in accordance with it.

Now, if it is argued that—even though other things have not been previously established—there exists a non-worldly (alaukika) connection between word-meanings to be enjoined, such as "and the waters do not diminish," and therefore this is not a restatement (*anuvāda*) of a prohibited matter; we say no, because it has already been stated that its primary purpose lies elsewhere. If it is further objected that this is not a restatement because there is no indicative mark (*liṅga*) for a prohibition such as "that which is not so," we reply: no.

Since it is impossible to state the absence of the probandum (the inferred object) merely through the absence of the mark (the middle term), one might object: "In that case, even such passages as 'That is Truth' (*tat satyam*) would be mere restatements of the established existence of Brahman—such as 'the pot is existent,' 'the cognition of the pot is existent,' or 'the manifestation of bliss is existent'—in order to negate [its non-existence] by means of statements like 'It was non-existent in the beginning' (*asad vā idam agre āsīt*) and 'Neither existent nor non-existent is it said to be' (*na sat tan nāsad ucyate*). If this is argued, we say no; for the existence of Brahman in its identity with Brahmanhood (*brahmatva-sāmānādhikaraṇyena*) is not established through perception or other means of knowledge.

Furthermore, because it would be impossible to negate that [Brahman] through the consequence of asserting its emptiness (*śūnyavāda*); and because in the passage "All this is what this Self is," there is the possibility of interpreting it as a restatement (*anuvāda*) based on the presence of indicative marks (*liṅga*). Likewise, regarding the scriptural mention of bliss (*ānanda*), the statement "neither suffering nor happiness, but equanimity" cannot be a restatement of the bliss perceived by direct experience; for since suffering is mentioned in conjunction with it, "happiness" must also be understood as exclusively sensual, and thus it is impossible for it to be a restatement of the bliss that is the very nature of Brahman in order to negate that [sensual happiness].

And all of this has been stated in the *Vivaraṇa*: "In accordance with such passages as 'without phenomenal expansion (*niṣprapañca*)' and 'not gross' (*asthūla*), statements such as 'all this is what this Self is' attain syntactic unity by serving to provide the objects of negation; for it is observed that the state of being without phenomenal expansion is a human goal (*puruṣārtha*) in deep sleep. Now, [it may be argued that] the state of being without phenomenal expansion is not a human goal.

[Objection: Because reality is not perceived in a state of fainting (*mūrchā*), one cannot say that at that time there is merely ignorance of it and not its absence; for this would apply equally to deep sleep (*suṣupti*). [Reply: This is not so, because in fainting there is no manifestation of the bliss of one's own nature (*svarūpa-sukha*). Thus says the Sūtra: "In the case of the fainting person, there is partial attainment [of sameness], by elimination. For deep sleep and liberation possess the status of a human goal (*puruṣārtha*) due to the experience of the bliss of one's own nature within the state free from phenomenal diversity (*niṣprapañcatā*). And thus says the Śruti: "Verily, from a second [entity] arises fear."

Now, one might argue that even the state of being accompanied by the phenomenal world (*saprapañcatā*) is a human goal (*puruṣārtha*), based on the Vedic scripture: "Therefore, one who is alone does not rejoice. This is not so; for since that state is a means to suffering, it cannot be considered a human goal. Furthermore, like the ritual section (*karmakāṇḍa*) of the Vedas, this scripture is intended for those persons who lack discrimination.

If it is argued that the world of plurality (*saprapañcatā*) cannot be the human goal because scripture declares that knowledge of difference is the cause of liberation—specifically in the passage, "Having known the Self and the Impeller as distinct, being favored by Him, one then attains immortality"—we say no. For even prior to such realization, I too perceive the Impeller as distinct; furthermore, just like the knowledge of Brahman with attributes (*saguṇabrahmajñāna*), the knowledge of Brahman as the Impeller is beneficial to liberation only indirectly (*paramparayā*).

Because of the natural sense of such scriptural passages as "It is to be seen as one alone," non-dual knowledge itself is the direct cause of liberation. For this very reason, it is stated that the knowledge of being the impeller is the cause of delight. Likewise, later on as well, non-duality alone is heard in the scripture: "The knowers of the Veda, having known [Brahman] and being devoted to it, merge into Brahman; those who are liberated, having clearly perceived the reality of the Self, the embodied soul becomes one, having achieved its purpose, and freed from sorrow. Therefore, the knowledge of duality is not the cause of liberation.

By this, the following objection is refuted: "Could not the scriptural text itself, 'Not here, not different' (*neha nānā*), merely be a restatement of the negation of the universe—as established by the Vijñānavāda and other schools—for the purpose of negating sublation in the form of non-sublatability (as in the claim that 'the universe is real')? For although existence and non-existence are equally characterized as being mutually exclusive, the apprehension of existence does not depend upon the apprehension of non-existence because it is independent; however, the apprehension of non-existence, being necessarily correlative to a counter-positive (*pratiyogin*), depends upon the apprehension of existence. Therefore, the text "not this, not this" (*neti neti*) alone requires the scriptural texts concerning existence, whereas the texts concerning existence do not require the "not this, not this" text; otherwise, there would result the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*).

Surely, let the principle of general rule and exception (*utsargāpavādanyāya*) apply; for just as the scriptural injunction "one should not harm any living beings," though promulgated without distinction, does not require even the sentence concerning the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice to present the object of prohibition—since the general nature of harming is already established through perception and other means—so too the scriptural text "not this, not this" (*neti neti*), though promulgated without distinction, becomes free of expectancy by taking up the existence of jars and so forth as the objects of negation already established by perception. Thus, it does not [require further qualification].

Even a Vedic scripture such as "The universe is real," which conveys the truth of dharma, adharma, and so forth that are not established by perception, must be relied upon to provide the object to be negated. However, in cases where the object of negation is not established by any other means of knowledge, the scriptural statement of negation necessarily requires another scriptural passage to provide that object of negation.

If it is argued that—just as in the case of the taking or non-taking of the *ṣoḍaśin* cup, where even though the object of prohibition is presented by another means of knowledge (*māna*), there is still a dependence on the scriptural statement (*vākya*) [to establish its status]—then the killing of the animal for Agni and Soma (*agnīṣomīya-hiṃsā*) would also be unrighteous (*adharma*) by virtue of being an object of prohibition, we say: not so. Because the statement concerning the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice has a scope narrower than the scope of the prohibition, and because it is not a subordinate element (*ananya-śeṣa*) [of the prohibition], but rather possesses its own intrinsic purpose (*svārtha-tātparya*), it does not function as a supplementary part (*śeṣa*) to the prohibitory statement by way of providing the object of that prohibition.

However, passages such as "the universe is real" (viśvaṃ satyam) are appropriately subsidiary to prohibitive statements by way of providing the object to be negated, since they share the same scope as the prohibition and lack an independent purport regarding their own literal meaning. For this very reason, the sentences achieve their efficacy by presenting the existence of dharma and so forth—which are not established by perception. Furthermore, because they lack an independent purport regarding their own literal meaning, it has been stated that they do not stand on equal footing with the sentence concerning the Agniṣomīya sacrifice. Therefore, the reason of "being visible" (dṛśyatva) and the like is not sublated by scripture even in the case of dharma and other such factors.

Alternatively, this scriptural statement regarding the reality of the universe is intended to convey empirical existence (*vyāvahārikasattva*). Nor is the teaching of empirical existence purposeless simply because there is no disagreement regarding it; for its purpose lies precisely in the engagement in activity and the desisting from activity by means of establishing the existence of heaven, hell, and so forth in specific circumstances, thereby enabling one to attain or avoid them. Furthermore, empirical existence consists in not being sublated by anything other than the knowledge of Brahman, but not in absolute non-sublation, as that would contradict the scriptures that teach the falsity (*mithyātva*) of the world.

Nor does it follow that [the scripture] is absolutely non-authoritative because it produces a firm delusion, for this is as logically consistent as the presentation of objects in a dream. The only distinction is this: that [dream object] is *prātibhāsika* (apparent), whereas this [worldly object] is *vyāvahārika* (empirical). [Objection: Since the scriptural texts on falsity (*mithyātva*) intend only the undivided pure consciousness (*akhaṇḍacinmātra*) through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), they convey existence; therefore, there is no contradiction at all. [Reply: No. Because the cognition of the undivided referent functions by way of the realization of the absence of a second, it is indeed in contradiction with the reality of the world.

Nor does it follow that the scriptures teaching the reality of phenomenal proliferation (*prapañca*) would thereby lose their authority; for we accept this as desirable on the basis of their subordinate purport (*avāntara-tātparya*), which consists in not revealing ultimate reality. However, with respect to their supreme purport (*parama-tātparya*), all scriptures are equal in their revelation of reality, because it is impossible to deny the conventional validity (*vyāvahārika-prāmāṇya*)—which is distinct from mere appearance and consists in having a qualifier corresponding to its qualificandum (*tadvati tatprakārakatva*). Thus, the conventional authority of these [scriptures] remains entirely unimpaired.

Even in accordance with such scriptural passages as "In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent" (*asad vā idam agre āsīt*), the passage "That is the Truth" (*tat satyam*) and others do not intend to attribute a merely conventional reality (*vyāvahārikasattva*) to Brahman. This is because Brahman transcends all empirical transaction (*vyavahāra*). Furthermore, if it were not ultimately real, it would lack a substratum (*anadhiṣṭhānatā*), leading to the consequence of a doctrine of nihilism (*śūnyavāda*). Moreover, sublation (*bādha*) is impossible without grasping some reality whatsoever. For these very reasons, it cannot be argued that the scriptures concerning falsity (*mithyātva*) are themselves intended for another purpose (or secondary) due to their conflict with the scriptures concerning truth (*satyatva*).

Because the scripture concerning falsity is more powerful due to its being dedicated solely to that purpose by virtue of possessing the sixfold marks of purport (*tātparya-liṅga*); and because there is an invariable rule that whatever constitutes the object of Vedic purport must be real, the marks that indicate such purport necessarily terminate in the actual state of things. Furthermore, since the words found in the scriptural passages concerning existence are directed toward other matters, there is no possibility of suspecting a purport regarding existence.

[Objection: "If the scriptural statement regarding existence (*sattva*) does not aim at its own literal meaning because its object is already established by perception, then the scriptural statement regarding falsity (*mithyātva*) would likewise not aim at its own literal meaning, since its object is contrary to that [perception]. For the two reasons for the absence of intended meaning—namely, the fact that the object is already established and the fact that it is contradicted—are equal in both cases. [Reply: This is not so.

Since a scripture that teaches a size greater than the moon is more authoritative than perception, so too is a scripture that teaches falsity more authoritative than even the scriptural statement of existence (*sattva-śruti*) which merely restates what has been obtained through perception. (For when there is a conflict between what is already established and what is not yet established, it is a rule that the established is subordinate to the purpose of the injunction for the unestablished; thus, only that which is not yet established is more authoritative as it is not subordinate to anything else. Otherwise, both would result in being invalid.

This has been stated in the *Saṅkṣepaśārīraka*: "That which is not the primary purport [of a text], when contradicted by Vedic statements whose primary purport it is, is merely a figurative description (*guṇavāda*). For this very reason, because it would contradict the scriptural texts on falsity (*mithyātva*) which are not subordinate to anything else, it is said that the scriptural texts asserting the reality of the world do not have as their purport a reality consisting of non-sublation throughout the three periods of time—which is not grasped by perception. Furthermore, regarding the superior authority of the Advaita scriptures, the determining factors are precisely their being without scope for alternative application (*niravakāśatva*) and their possessing a definitive purport (*tātparyavatva*), and not the mere fact of being negative statements.

By this, the following [objection] is refuted: that if prohibitive statements possess greater authority, then the rule *kṅiti ca*—which generally prohibits *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*—would be stronger than the rule *kiti ca* which prescribes *vṛddhi* in the presence of a *kit* suffix; likewise, the statement regarding non-violence (*ahiṃsā*) would be stronger than the statement regarding the Agniṣomīya sacrifice; the statement regarding the non-extraction of the *ṣoḍaśin* cup would be stronger than the statement regarding its extraction; and the statement "In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent" (*asad vā idam agre āsīt*) would be stronger than the statement "Truth, Knowledge, Infinite" (*satyaṃ jñānam anantam*), and so forth.

This is because [the strength] is reversed due to the difference between being with scope (*sāvakāśa*) and without scope (*niravakāśa*), based on the relationship of generality and particularity (*sāmānyaviśeṣabhāva*) and so forth. Furthermore, it has been stated previously that [statements] such as "The universe is real" (*viśvaṃ satyam*) have scope because they refer to empirical reality (*vyāvahārikasattva*) and are subordinate to something else. Therefore, there is no contradiction with the scriptural texts regarding existence (*sattva*). Nor is there a contradiction with the following:
"Those of small intellect and ruined souls, holding fast to this view, say that the world is unreal, without foundation, and without a Lord. (Gītā 16.8)

There is no contradiction with such Smṛtis, because for me—who maintain that [the world] is distinct from Being—there is no conflict with those Smṛtis that establish its difference from non-existence, since I accept its distinction from the unreal within the world.

Is it not the case that there is a contradiction with the two sūtras, "Not non-existence, because [the world] is perceived" and "And because of its dissimilarity, it is not like dreams and so forth," which establish the ultimate reality of the world? Nor can it be argued that there is no contradiction because this [sūtra] merely establishes a distinction from the non-existent for the purpose of refuting the Śūnyavāda; for since even in the Śūnyavāda system there exists a distinction from the non-existent characterized by causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*), it is untenable to claim that the purpose of this [sūtra] is the refutation of that doctrine.

This is because you yourself do not accept that "distinction from the non-existent" (*asadvailakṣaṇya*) consists in being the counter-positive of negation; furthermore, if one were to prove merely the distinction from the non-existent, it would be inappropriate for the Sūtra to speak of a distinction from dreams. This is because even you accept a distinction from dreams on the basis of mere conventional reality (*vyāvahārikasatyatva*), and because even in that [Buddhist] system, there exists a mere distinction from the non-existent. As the Buddhists have said: "The teaching of the Dharma by the Buddhas relies upon two truths. If this is your objection, it is not so, because you have failed to understand the meaning of the Sūtra.

For instance: when there arises a doubt regarding the contradiction between the *samanvaya* (harmonious inquiry) which asserts the creation of the world from Brahman whose nature is existence (*sat*), and the inference that "everything is non-existent," [the following verse is cited]:
"Neither existent, nor non-existent, nor both existent and non-existent, nor of a nature that is neither;
the object of dispute is so because it is undermined by reasoning, just like water in a mirage."

Thus, when the state of being "devoid of reality" (*nistattvatā*)—which is common to Brahman—is reached, the following is the refutation provided by the Sūtra: There is no non-existence, that is, no voidness (*śūnyatva*), of the existent Brahman, because it is apprehended—that is, cognized through its existence as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). And so, even the proponent of emptiness (*śūnyavādin*) must necessarily admit that something exists in the ultimate sense (*paramārthasat*); otherwise, there would follow the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of sublation (*bādha*) being without a limit or foundation. This is the meaning of the Sūtra. Furthermore, this [Sūtra] does not contradict the falsity of the phenomenal world (*prapañca-mithyātva*). As it has been said: "That which is sublated by means of knowledge is a denial; [the means of knowledge used therein possess] only conventional validity."

"Without relying on some real entity (*vastu*) among the objects of cognition, [the dream-argument] is difficult to maintain. Nor is there an inconsistency in stating the difference from dreams; for that statement is intended to demonstrate the presence of fallacious conditions (*upādhi*), such as being sublated, being known through invalid means of knowledge, and being produced by defects, within the inference: "The object under dispute is devoid of reality (*nistattva*), because it is undermined by reasoning, like the water in a mirage. Thus, there is no contradiction with this Sūtra even though it is devoted to refuting the Vijñānavāda. This is so because there might be a suspicion of contradiction with the inferential argument which establishes consciousness (*vijñāna*) possessing forms such as blue, against the *samanvaya* (harmonization) which teaches that Brahman, devoid of form and the like, is the material cause (*upādāna*) of the world.
Because cognition is similar to dream-cognition, because the object is perceived together with the intellect,
and because it cannot be determined as distinct from that [cognition], let it be accepted that the object has the form of knowledge.

The cognition under dispute does not have an object distinct from knowledge, because it is a cognition, like dream-cognition. Furthermore, in the case of the contrary position, the subverting argument (bādhaka) is that even in the absence of knowledge, the object would still appear; for there is no rule of simultaneous perception (*sahopalambha-niyama*) between two distinct things, such as a horse and a buffalo. Therefore, when it is concluded that "there is no reality external to knowledge," the following sūtra provides the rebuttal: "Not non-existence, because [the object] is perceived" (*nābhāva upalabdheḥ*), and so forth. The claim that the inference is fallacious due to a limiting condition (*sopādhikatā*) based on the subverting argument—that simultaneous perception occurs due to the lack of a means [to distinguish them]—is incorrect. Moreover, your own view equally faces the collapse of the distinction between cognition and its object, as well as the destruction of gross objects, on account of their similarity (*sārūpya*).

The meaning of the Sūtra is as follows: there is no non-existence; it is not that an object distinct from cognition is non-existent, but rather that its very existence consists in its capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*) which remains uncontradicted in the state of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*). "Because of perception" means because it is perceived by means of valid cognitions (*pramāṇa*) as something distinct from cognition itself. The statement regarding the dissimilarity with dreams is intended to demonstrate the adventitious condition (*upādhi*) of being subject to sublation and so forth. Therefore, the meaning is that the previous inference is defective due to [the presence of] sublation and because it is conditioned by such adventitious factors. Consequently, even in this way, there is no suspicion of contradiction.

Thus it has been said: "Therefore, the object does not have the form of cognition; rather, it is external. And although that [external object] is endowed with existence by virtue of its capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*), it is—due to the authority of the scriptures on non-duality (*advaita-śruti*)—imagined within Brahman and is not ultimately real. This constitutes the distinction between the established doctrine [of our school] and the system of the Sugata. And it is stated in the *Ātmatattvaviveka*: "There is no functioning of cognition apart from the difference of the grasped object;
when that [grasped object] is sublated, victory belongs to the powerful system of pure sensation (*vedanaya*)."

"If this world were not such as it is—beyond reproach—and were indeed real, then what room would there be for the doctrine of the Tathāgata? Thus, the sublation by the means of knowledge that apprehends the subject (*dharmigrāhakapramāṇabādha*) has already been refuted; may there be auspiciousness. This concludes the "Refutation of Sublation by Scripture and Other Means" regarding the falsity of the universe.

[Objection: Is it not the case that the proofs establishing reality (*sattva*) are more powerful than the inferences establishing falsity (*mithyātva*)? For if the subject (*pakṣa*) and other members introduced by the proposition (*pratijñā*) and so forth that establish falsity are themselves not understood to be false, then the falsity of everything remains unestablished; yet if they are understood to be false, there is either mutual contradiction or the fallacy of the unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*), and so on. [Reply: This is not so, because even when the falsity of the subject and other members introduced by the proposition and so forth that establish falsity is understood, there is no contradiction. This is because those [instruments] such as the proposition do not establish their [own] reality in the form of being unsublated throughout the three periods of time.

But surely, ultimate reality (*paramārthasattva*) follows from the fact that being a means of accomplishment (*sādhakatva*) would otherwise be inexplicable; for only that which is ultimately real can be a means of accomplishment, since being a means of accomplishment is constituted by prior existence. It is not, however, the case that being an object of mere cognition, being an object of immediate cognition, or being an object of such a cognition by virtue of its existence, is the determinant of being a means of accomplishment. This is because these definitions would result in over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the non-existent (*tuccha*) and under-extension (*avyāpti*) to eternal supersensible objects. Furthermore, even the cognition of it as [ultimately] real is not the determinant in that regard.

This is not so, because combustibility is observed in fire even when it is not known as "fire," and because it is not observed in a heap of *guñjā* seeds even when they are known as "fire. Nor is the fact that existence is perceived as uncontradicted within three or four stages of inquiry the governing principle. For otherwise, one would incur the consequence that the self is non-eternal due to its being white, or that the sky possesses touch due to its being blue. This is because there is no contradiction within three or four stages of inquiry even in such cognitions as "I am fair" and "the sky is blue"; yet, according to your own view, logical sublation (*yauktika-bādha*) exists in the present case as well. [To this objection, we reply: No.

For existence is established in a jar and the like by whatever kind of cognition excludes cognitions such as that of the blueness of the sky; since it is precisely the state of being an object of such a cognition that constitutes the determinant of proof. Therefore, what is stated in the *iṣṭasiddhi*—that worldly consensus (*lokaprasiddhi*) is the determinant—is entirely correct according to the intended meaning just explained. Likewise, it is perfectly logical that the cognition of existence held by the proponent, the opponent, the judges, and others, which remains uncontradicted through three or four stages of inquiry, is the determinant.

For you also do not accept that the quality of being an object of such a cognition establishes the nature of fire in a cluster of *guñjā* seeds, the whiteness of the self, or the blueness of the sky; otherwise, it would follow that their existence there is likewise established.

If it is argued that "just as you establish the existence of Brahman through a cognition of sound that is established as being free from defects, let me likewise establish the existence of the world through a cognition of perception that is established as being free from defects, since the means of proof are equal," we say no. This is because, unlike the cognition of the existence of Brahman, the cognition of the existence of the world lacks non-sublation (*abādhitatva*); furthermore, it has already been stated that existence in the form of being uncontradicted throughout the three periods of time is not an object of perception.

Nor should it be argued that if being the object of such a cognition were the decisive factor, then fire unknown as "fire" would fail to burn, or that poison known as "immortal" (amṛta) would become life-restoring; for in the case of fire, such a state of being the object of such a cognition exists in common with the Lord (Īśvara) and others. Furthermore, the consequence of poison becoming life-restoring is equivalent to [the absurdity of] the sky being blue. In reality, however, it is precisely the conventional existence (*vyāvahārikasattva*), which is common to both the known and the unknown, that is the decisive factor in its efficacy as a means of accomplishment.

And that [invalidity] consists precisely in being sublated by something other than the knowledge of Brahman; furthermore, it does not consist in being included within the category of "falsity" (mithyātva), because it is identical in both cases: that which is absolutely unsublatable and that which is sublatable by the knowledge of Brahman. For this very reason, this [invalidity] is not pervaded by ultimate reality (paramārthasattva). Thus, since the presence of ultimate reality is not a necessary factor for its status as a means of valid cognition (sādhakatā), there is no inconsistency in its being a means of valid cognition even in the absence of such reality.

By this [the following] is refuted: "Is empirical reality (*vyāvahārikatva*) the state of being sublated by the knowledge of Brahman? Or existence while having an empirical object as its domain? Or merely being treated as existent? Not the first, because prior to the establishment of falsity (*mithyātva*), that [empirical reality] is not established, resulting in mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*). Nor the second, because for us that is accepted as being contrary to falsity. Nor the third, because if existence were absent, its status as a probans would be untenable"—this is refuted, because the aforementioned definition is faultless.

Nor should it be argued that if the reason (*hetu*) and other members of the syllogism possess only conventional existence (*vyāvahārikasattva*), then the probandum (*sādhya*) must also possess only conventional existence, because there is a rule that the probandum which is the object of inference must possess the same degree of reality as the reason which is the object of the *parāmarśa* (subsumptive reflection). This is because we accept that falsity (*mithyātva*)—like perceptibility (*dṛśyatva*)—possesses the same degree of reality as its counter-correlate due to its being conventionally real. Furthermore, the rule regarding the necessity of having the same degree of reality is unestablished, since we observe the occurrence of a valid inference of fire even from the erroneous cognition of smoke in a cloud of dust.

Furthermore, even from the valid cognition of "earthness" as being pervaded by odor, an erroneous inference is observed when there is a lack of awareness of the sublation (*bādha*) regarding the subject (*pakṣa*), namely a jar delimited by the prior non-existence of odor. Even if falsity (*mithyātva*) itself is false, it is logically consistent for it to be known through the scriptures that reveal reality (*tattvāvedaka-śruti*). This is because there is no contradiction in something falsely existent being accessible to a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa-gamya*) by virtue of its falsity, just as a truly existent thing is accessible by virtue of its existence. This is because, although the scripture may lack the quality of revealing reality in one respect, it remains logically possible for it to reveal reality in another respect.

If it is argued that being *vyāvahārika* (empirical) is not a necessary factor for being a means of proof (*sādhakatā*), because the witness (*sākṣin*), who is ultimately real (*pāramārthika-sat*) and the means of proving ignorance and so forth, lacks that [empirical] status—this is not so. For it has been stated that the quality of not being sublated by anything other than the knowledge of Brahman exists even in that which is absolutely unsublatable (*atyantābādhya*). Furthermore, although the definition of *vyāvahārikatva* as distinguished from the *pāramārthika* was given in the section on the threefold division of reality, there is no fault in its being common to that [witness] as well in the context of being a cause (*janakatā*). In fact, the witness too, when conditioned by ignorance (*ajñānopahita*), is the means of proving ignorance and so forth; and that [conditioned witness] is indeed merely *vyāvahārika*.

Because that [ultimate reality] cannot be established by its own unconditioned form as the ultimate existent (*paramārthasat*). Thus, it is established that only empirical existence (*vyāvahārikasattva*) is the operative factor for being a means of proof in all cases. And just as there is no fault such as self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*) even though the Self is the witness when conditioned by ignorance (*ajñāna*), so it was stated previously in the demonstration of the reason "being an object of sight" (*dṛśyatva*); and it will be stated further on. Furthermore, wherever something is a means of proof in an empirical sense, there it is empirical.

However, where the means of accomplishment (*sādhaka*) is merely apparent (*prātītika*), the result (*phala*) is likewise of that same nature and not conventionally real (*vyāvahārika*); thus, there is no confusion in the conventional practices of injunctions, prohibitions, and so forth. For this very reason, even the argument stated by Udayana—that if one deviates from worldly consensus, inquiry would result in nothing more than arbitrary verbalism—is refuted, because one does not overstep the boundaries of the world by virtue of [the object's] conventional existence (*vyāvahārikasattva*).

The statements of Bhaṭṭācārya, which appear to be contradictory, will be explained without contradiction in the investigation of the threefold nature of existence (*sattva-traividhya*). Therefore, there is no self-contradiction even in proving the falsity of everything, including the subject (*pakṣa*) and so forth. Thus ends the demonstration of the capacity of the non-existent (*asat*) to be a means of proof in the *Advaitasiddhi*.

If it is objected: "Since existence (*sattva*), being distinct from the void (*tuccha*), and so forth, are more cumbersome (*gauravatara*) than [the other properties], how can they be the essential factors (*tantra*) for establishing [the reality of the world]? We say no. For existence in the form of being free from sublation throughout the three periods of time is not cumbersome; nor does existence in the form of a genus (*jāti*) and so forth contradict its falsity (*mithyātva*). Furthermore, since we observe that what is established as distinct from [mere] existence serves as a probans (*sādhaka*), ultimate existence (*pāramārthika-sattva*) is not a necessary factor for being a probans. To illustrate: a reflection, for instance, possesses the capacity to establish the existence of the original object (*bimba*).

Although that [reflection] exists as the nature of the original object (*bimba*), it does not exist in the form of the reflection (*pratibimba*); therefore, ultimate existence (*paramārthasattva*) is not the determining factor for its capacity to produce cognition. Likewise, even though the objects of a dream are non-existent, they indicate future good or evil fortune. Although, according to the authority of such scriptural passages as "He sees a black man with black teeth," it is the perception itself therein that serves as the indicator; nevertheless, since perception alone would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), the object must necessarily be admitted as well.

Thus, the proximity of the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) establishes the redness of the crystal. Nor should it be argued that the redness in the crystal is not false, but rather that it is merely the reflection of a property (*dharma*) and therefore does not require a separate illustration; for we never observe the reflection of a property such as color independently of its substratum (*dharmin*), such as a face. Furthermore, since there is a rule that a reflection is necessarily non-pervasive (*avyāpyavṛtti*), it is impossible for redness to be perceived as pervasive (*vyāpyavṛtti*) within the crystal.

The distinction is this: when redness is superimposed upon a crystal, that [redness] possesses the nature of a reflection; but when redness is superimposed upon the crystal itself, it is false. This falsity of the redness is demonstrated by the authors of the *Pañcapādikā*, who maintain the reality of reflections, in the statement: "The redness [of the crystal] is caused by the proximity of a substrate, like that of a crystal gem. Similarly, letters superimposed through identity with the lines possess the capacity to convey meaning. Nor should it be argued that it is only the letters themselves, as recalled by the lines, that convey the meaning.

From childhood, due to the experience that "this is the letter *ka*" and "this is the letter *ga*," and because they are remembered as non-different, superimposition does not cease even when discrimination exists, owing to the force of extremely firm latent impressions (*saṃskāra*). For this very reason, there is a universal worldly usage such as "he reads the letter *ka*" or "he writes the letter *ka*. Furthermore, qualities such as length and shortness superimposed upon the letters serve to convey specific meanings in words like *naga* (mountain) and *nāga* (elephant).

Nor should it be argued that length—consisting either in the accompaniment of sounds not superimposed upon the phonemes or in the state of being manifested by them—is what conveys [the meaning], and that the same applies to shortness and so forth; for even when the sounds do not manifest, there arises the cognition, "This is a long phoneme," and so on.

[Objection: But how can a real object be established by means of superimposed qualities such as color or length? For a real fire is not established by means of superimposed smoke. [Reply: This is not so. What is the necessary condition for being a probans (*sādhaka*) is simply the possession of the form that delimits its status as a probans (*sādhakatāvacchedakarūpa*); it is neither superimposition nor non-superimposition. As for the non-probative nature of a pseudo-smoke (*dhūmābhāsa*), it is due to the absence of the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the form that delimits its probative status, and not because of its non-existence.

And in that context, the apprehension of non-appearance is required solely for the purpose of apprehending pervasion (*vyāpti*), just like the apprehension of the direction "above" and so forth. As Vācaspatimiśra has stated: "Just as, despite the commonality of being real, only color (*rūpa*) is made known by the eye and not taste (*rasa*), likewise, despite the commonality of being unreal, the real is made known by the length of the syllables and so forth, but not by the appearance of smoke and the like."

For it is observed that an elephant or the like imagined through illusion, as well as a rope-snake and so forth, serve as causes for fear; likewise, the "sun's hollow" (a sunspot) indicates death, and poison suspected [to be present] serves as a cause of death. Now, one might object: "In those cases, it is the suspicion itself that produces fear and thereby causes the disturbance of the bodily humors (*dhātu*); thus, that suspicion alone is the cause of death, not even the suspected poison. Similarly, in the case of the sun's hollow or an illusory elephant, it is the cognition itself that performs the respective causal function, and not the object."

And thus, in all the instances cited, cognition alone is the cause; and that is true in its own nature. Furthermore, positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) also establish that cognition alone possesses causality. For one who does not know a snake present before him does not fear it. Nor, on the grounds of over-extension (atiprasaṅga), can it be argued that cognition limited by an object is the cause, rather than cognition unqualified by an object.

Likewise, it must be stated that the object (*artha*) is also indeed a cause; for even though cognition delimited by an object serves as the cause, it is logically consistent that the object, as the delimiter (*avacchedaka*), is not a cause in its own right. This is just as the absolute non-existence or destruction of a jar—though delimited by the jar—is located in a space and time different from the space and time of the jar, yet the jar, as the delimiter, does not possess that absence. It is also like the desire for a jar and the knowledge of Brahman, which, despite being accomplished through the knowledge of the jar and the Vedānta respectively, do not belong to the jar or to Brahman. [The same applies to] the prior non-existence of a jar with respect to the jar...

Just as a jar, despite being a cause [of its own destruction], is not the cause [of another jar]; just as the non-perception of specific features, despite being a cause of error, is not the cause of the perception of specific features; just as the non-performance of a prescribed act, despite being a cause of sin (pratyavāya), is not the cause of its absence; just as the desire for heaven, despite being a cause of sacrifice, is not the cause of heaven; just as the memory of the past and so forth, despite being a cause of suffering and so forth, is not the cause of the past itself; [so it is] with regard to parokṣa-jñāna having an unreal object.

This is because, even though it serves as the cause for linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*), the non-existent lacks that [causal capacity]; just as, although the cognition of a pot intended to be made is the cause of the pot, the pot itself is not the cause of that cognition; just as, although the knowledge of Brahman removes ignorance regarding it, Brahman—being by nature indifferent (*udāsīna*)—lacks that [causality]; and just as, although the ignorance of Brahman is the transformative cause (*pariṇāmikāraṇa*) of the world, Brahman lacks that [causality]. Nor should it be argued: "Even so, since there is a capacity for cognition to exclude false objects, the non-existent must also possess causality."

For being the cause of the cognition of exclusion is not what constitutes "excluder-ness" (vyāvartakatva); rather, it is simply being the object of the cognition that is the cause of the cognition of exclusion. This is because, even when a staff is present, if it is not cognized, there is no cognition of the exclusion [it effects]. Now, if the delimitant (avacchedaka) is false, does it follow that the delimited (avacchinna) is also necessarily so? No.

If it is argued that—since falsity (*tucchatva*) is not observed in the case of a void cognition (*tucchajñāna*) or in its distinction from the void, nor is appearance-ness (*prātibhāsikatva*) observed in its distinction from the apparent (*prātibhāsika*), nor is the indeterminability of the fourth kind observed in the cessation of indeterminable ignorance (*anirvacanīyājñāna*) which is of the fifth kind or is the very nature of the Self, nor is unreality (*anṛtatva*) observed in the ultimate nature of the Self or in what is distinct from it, despite the presence of delimiters such as "non-existent" (*asat*) etc.—therefore, let the same apply here [to the world] as well, with those delimiters remaining extrinsic (*tāṭasthya*)—to this we reply: [The response follows: ... [as provided in the source text].

As for what was stated—that in all cases of delimitation (*avaccheda*), the characteristic is merely an incidental indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) because it is extrinsic (*tāṭasthya*)—that is not correct. For when it is possible [for something] to be a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), it cannot logically be an incidental indicator. This is because the conceptualization of something as an incidental indicator is necessarily preceded by the sublation of its status as a qualifier. Otherwise, in Vedic injunctions such as "the staff-bearer recites the directions" (*daṇḍī praiṣānanvāha*) and "the priests proceed wearing red turbans" (*lohitoṣṇīṣā ṛtvijaḥ pracaranti*), since the staff and the red color would be incidental indicators, there would follow the undesirable consequence that the rite could be performed even in their absence.

In the rule "those beginning with *sarva* are called pronouns" (*sarvādīni sarvanāmāni*), the word *sarva* would not receive the designation of "pronoun. In the aphorism "from which [proceeds] the birth, etc., of this [world]" (*janmādyasya yataḥ*), birth would not constitute a definition of Brahman; for even though a *bahuvrīhi* compound with "retention of the qualities" (*tadguṇasaṃvijñāna*) is possible since [the words] function as qualifiers, there would be the undesirable consequence of accepting a *bahuvrīhi* with "non-retention of the qualities" (*atadguṇasaṃvijñāna*) because they function as mere indicators (*upalakṣaṇa*). The same applies to common worldly usage, such as "Let those with swords in their hands enter" (*asipāṇayaḥ praveśyantām*).

Furthermore, since there is no contradiction in reflections and the like being causes of cognitions by way of being qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*), the position that they are mere indicators (*upalakṣaṇa*) is not tenable. The distinction is that in all the examples cited, there is indeed a sublation (*bādhaka*). To explain: in the first case, having apprehended the place and time of the jar, one must apprehend the state of having a different place and time from those [of the jar] in the case of its absolute non-existence and so forth. If the jar were also related to that [same] place and time, then its having a place and time different from those would be contradicted.

In the second case, however, the desired consequence (iṣṭāpatti) follows; for just as the cognition of a jar in some instances is the generator of a desire for the jar, it is likewise the generator of the jar itself. But if Brahman were something to be accomplished by the Vedānta, there would be a contradiction with its eternity. In the third case, if the jar were its own generator—like its own prior non-existence—it would follow that the counter-positive (the jar) and its prior non-existence are simultaneous; furthermore, the definition of being a generator, which consists in being prior relative to oneself, would be logically inconsistent when applied to the self.

In the fourth and fifth [alternatives], because the counter-positive and its absence would coexist, there would follow the impossibility of error and transgression respectively. In the sixth, if the object of desire were the producer of the sacrifice—just like the desire itself—it would exist prior [to the act], and thus the very desire for it would be frustrated, since there is no desire for what is already established. In the seventh, if the past were the producer, it would entail the existence of either the entity itself or its own operation at the time immediately preceding the effect. In the eighth, if the non-existent were the producer, there would be a contradiction with its lack of essential nature (*niḥsvarūpatva*).

In the ninth [alternative], there is a contradiction as before, because [Brahman] would be the producer of itself, like the cognition of a pot one intends to make. In the tenth, Brahman, being indifferent (*udāsīna*), cannot be the remover [of ignorance]; for while it is only the conditioned (*upahita*) Brahman that is the object of a mental modification (*vṛtti*), the unconditioned is not such an object. And yet, the conditioned Brahman certainly possesses the capacity to remove [ignorance]. In the eleventh, even though ignorance is the material cause (*pariṇāmikāraṇa*) of the world, Brahman is not the cause of the world, because insentience is perceived in the effect.

This is because, due to the force of such subverting arguments (*bādhaka*), the status of being a secondary indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) is accepted in those cases; however, no such subverting argument exists in the present instance. This is because the property of occurring in an immediately contiguous space and time is common to even illusory appearances (*prātibhāsika*), as there is no difference between this and cognitions such as "there is a snake here now. For it is not the case that because the primary meaning was abandoned in one place due to the force of a subverting argument, it must likewise be so in all cases. Furthermore, [the secondary sense is appropriate] because of the conformity with excellence and other such qualities.

For instance, in both dreams and waking states, from the sight of an excellent piece of gold, an excellent pleasure is seen, and from the sight of an excellent snake or similar object, an excellent fear and so forth are seen. If the object were not a cause [of the cognition], there would be no conformity of the effect to the excellence of that [object]. This is because of the logical principle that the excellence of a non-cause does not conform to the effect. Nor can it be said that the excellence [of the experience] arises solely from the excellence of the cognition itself, because even in the case of cognition, there is no excellence other than that which resides in the object.

Alternatively, excellence (*prakarṣa*) consists simply in a genus (*jāti*) residing in the cognition itself, and not in [a genus] such as "being visual" (*cākṣuṣatva*), because that would entail the fallacy of over-extension (*saṅkara*). Furthermore, since the [distinction between cognitions] is established by the excellence of the object alone, it is cumbersome to accept multiple genera subsumed under "being visual" and so forth, and there is a lack of evidence for doing so. Moreover, if cognition produces fear and the like, one must admit that being delimited by a snake or similar object is precisely what delimits its causal capacity (*kāraṇatāvacchedaka*); for if it were the cause by virtue of being a cognition in general, there would be the fallacy of over-extension.

And thus, since knowledge in its form as delimited by falsity is itself false, even though mere knowledge acts as a cause in the case of error, it follows that what is false is indeed the cause. Furthermore, if the nature that delimits causality is false, then existence in another form—while being false in that other form—is not distinct from non-existence, because it is of no utility.

This has been stated by the authors of the *Khaṇḍana*: "Existence at another time follows the analogy of a watchman’s vigil in a house that has already been plundered by thieves. Furthermore, erroneous cognition (*bhramajñāna*) possesses falsity even in its own nature (*svarūpa*); for if there were no sublation (*bādhā*) in its own nature, it would follow that there is likewise no sublation regarding its object. Nor is "being produced by [extraordinary] qualities" (*guṇajanyatva*) a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), because, being itself what is to be established, it is like the causal complex of fire (*vahnisāmagrī*) in an inference of fire—it is not a limiting adjunct since it pervades the probans (*sādhanavyāpaka*).

Furthermore, there is no distinction in the case of cognition either, since it is produced by a causal complex (sāmagrī) that includes defects (doṣa) and other factors which bring about falsity, just as in the case of an object. And the non-perception of "insubstantiality" (tucchatva) in the case of an insubstantial cognition and its distinction from others does not constitute a refutation, because we do not accept a rule of universal similarity between the delimited (avacchedya) and the delimiting factor (avacchedaka). In the present context, such similarity is established because the form that brings about falsity is identical in both the delimiting factor and the delimited, just as it is in the former. Moreover, we have stated this while assuming a single causality common to all things.

In reality, however, there is no single causal nature (*kāraṇatva*) common to such things as a staff and a thread. Where, for you, "existence" (*sattva*) is the delimiting property (*avacchedaka*), for me it is not "distinctness from the void" (*tucchavilakṣaṇatva*) and so forth; rather, the delimiting property of the effect is "pot-ness," "cloth-ness," and the like, while the delimiting property of the cause is "staff-ness," "thread-ness," and so forth. Due to this difference, causality itself is distinct—just as the similarity between a cow and a gavaya is one thing, while the similarity between a brother and a sister is another.

In that case, there is not a single delimiting property (*avacchedaka*), but rather [properties] such as *gavayatva* (the nature of being a gavaya) and *bhaginītva* (the nature of being a sister). Similarly here too, one must state that it is precisely the nature of being a staff (*daṇḍatva*) and so forth—remaining indifferent to existence or non-existence—that serves as the delimiting property. And thus, existence or non-existence is not established by virtue of being a cause. As it has been said by the authors of the *Khaṇḍana*:
"If the necessity of a prior relation is the ground for causality, then it is exactly the same for both of us;
talk of existence or non-existence that falls outside the true nature of causality is futile."
"If the cause contains existence within itself, then it is non-existent;

if the cause does not contain existence within itself, then it is non-existent. And: "If the substratum contains existence within itself, then it is non-existent. But this is not the case. If the substratum contains existence within itself, then it is non-existent.

"If the substratum does not contain existence within itself, then it follows that it is non-existent"—this objection applies equally to you as well. This must be addressed: for me, existence is accepted as belonging to the substratum by its very nature (*svarūpataḥ*); for you, however, existence is accepted as something distinct from the nature of the cause—this is the difference. As for the claim that the object is not even a delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) in the production of a cognition, because there is a lack of evidence; nor is there the fault of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), since the distinction of a "snake-cognition" from a "non-snake-cognition" is established without depending on the delimitation by an object. To explain: the distinction of a snake-cognition from a non-snake-cognition depends upon a differentiator (*vyāvartaka*).

Neither the object nor its relation is the differentiator, because there is no relation residing in two distinct entities that is distinct from their own intrinsic natures (svarūpa), and because that which is unrelated cannot function as a differentiator. If, on the other hand, the relation is either the very nature of the cognition itself—which is capable of generating the qualified usage (*viśiṣṭavyavahāra*) without another relation—or some property residing solely in the cognition, then it follows that the establishment of the distinction [between cognitions] occurs through the cognition or the property residing therein, without even including the object.

Furthermore, the cognition of a snake is distinct from the cognition of a non-snake without depending on a relation to a different substratum (*dharmyantara*), because it is produced by a cause that is distinct [from the cause of the other], like a rice sprout from a barley sprout; or because it produces an effect that is distinct [from the effect of the other], like a rice seed from a barley seed. Nor is the argument unproven (*aprayojaka*) merely because the two causes can be accounted for through their relation to distinct objects.

For if that were the case, then even in the instance of a *kalama* sprout and its seed—which are distinct from a barley seed and its sprout as cause and effect—the *kalama* sprout and its seed would have to be considered distinct from the barley sprout and its seed merely by virtue of being related to Caitra or someone else who happens to be present as an observer, even in the absence of any natural distinction consisting in their being *kalama* sprouts or seeds. Furthermore, even direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*) would be distinguished from indirect knowledge (*parokṣajñāna*) merely by virtue of being related to a different [subject].

And thus, just as the absence of a jar is distinct from another absence even without including its counter-positive, just as the act of lifting a stone is distinct from the act of lifting a bean even without including the object, just as the cognition of the past and so forth, as well as the linguistic usage of non-perceptual cognitions having non-existent objects, are distinct from other cognitions and the like, just as the memory of a jar is distinct from the experience of a jar, and just as the indirect (parokṣa) cognition of a jar is distinct from its direct (aparokṣa) cognition—otherwise there would be a confusion of their respective effects.

In the same way, even the cognition of a snake, although produced by more factors due to its being an error regarding a rope, is distinct from the cognition of a non-snake either because it is produced by its own specific causes as a cognition of a snake, or simply by its very nature; thus, there is no fault whatsoever. Nor is it the case that in the case of absences and the like, the counter-positive and so forth cannot serve as delimiters (avacchedaka), because at the time of the existence of a destruction and so forth, or of a cognition of the past and so forth, the counter-positive and the object are non-existent. This is not so.

The factor that accounts for the exclusion of the cognition of a non-serpent from that which is delimited by the nature of the cognition of a serpent is not its specific individual essence (*svarūpa*), because that would lack commonality across all such cognitions. Rather, it must be some recurring property (*dharma*). Furthermore, this property cannot be a universal (*jāti*) residing solely in the cognition of a serpent, as that would lead to the fallacy of overlap (*saṅkara*) with properties such as perceptuality (*pratyakṣatva*) or inferentiality (*anumānatva*); instead, it must be an adventitious attribute (*upādhi*). And this attribute, whether through the relation of essential identity (*svarūpa-sambandha*) or the relation of superimposition (*adhyāsika-sambandha*), does not exist apart from the object that serves as its correlate, as there is no evidence for such a separate existence.

For this very reason, the aforementioned inference—which claims to be distinct without depending on a relation to another substratum (*dharmin*)—should be regarded as sublated and fallacious (*vyabhicārin*). To explain: the conjunction with a jar (*ghaṭasaṃyoga*) does not differ from the conjunction with a cloth (*paṭasaṃyoga*) by way of its genus (*jāti*), because it is not the locus of a genus that does not reside in the latter; rather, it is distinct only through the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the jar’s form. Thus, since the stated reason exists in the case of "conjunction delimited as jar-conjunction"—which is indeed distinct [from cloth-conjunction] but lacks the probandum (the difference by way of genus)—there is a fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) and the reason is unestablished as a cause (*aprayojakatva*).

Nor does it follow that the sprout of a *kalamā* rice plant would be excluded [from the class of "rice-sprouts"] merely by its relation to Caitra as a defining characteristic (*upalakṣaṇa*), for we accept such an exclusion when there is a sublation of the contrary case (*vipakṣabādhā*). Indeed, when a genus (*jāti*) serves as the differentiator, an adventitious condition (*upādhi*) does not fail to be a differentiator. Likewise, although the acts of lifting a stone and lifting a bean are mutually distinguished by their respective genera, it is not contradictory for them to be distinguished even by the adventitious condition consisting of their objects.
