Furthermore, since the act of lifting a stone is the producer of an effect characterized by a specific universal (*jāti*), the fact that the act of lifting beans—which lacks that [specific universal]—does not produce that [effect] is not a flaw. This is because, even when a distinction can be established through other means, a specific universal is postulated to ensure the consistency of the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) and so forth. Moreover, in cases such as the cognition or linguistic usage regarding the past or non-existent, it is precisely the past or the non-existent that serves as the differentiator (*vyāvartaka*). For being a generator of the cognition of exclusion does not depend on existence; otherwise, in the absence of existence, it could not function as the very essence of prior existence.

However, it has been stated that [the definition] is "being the object of a cognition that produces the cognition of exclusion" (*vyāvṛttidhījanakadhīviṣayatva*). And this is easily found even in the case of the past and so forth. For this very reason, the example of non-existence (*abhāva*) and the like is also refuted; since the aforementioned nature of being an excluder (*vyāvartakatva*) is possible even for that which is absolutely non-existent, the possibility of its occurrence when something exists is established by the *kaimutika* maxim (a fortiori). [Objection: Even if the object is the excluder, because it is impossible for it to be a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) in all cases, it must be said that it is merely an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*).

If it is argued that by means of an *upalakṣaṇa* (a secondary indicator), some property distinct from the object's own relation [to the indicator] is presented—just as a crow, being related to a house, indicates a particular configuration belonging to that house—and thus that very property serves as the differentiator, such that the differentiation of the cognition is established by a property residing in itself alone, independent of its relation to the object; we say no. This is because we do not admit that an *upalakṣaṇa* functions as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) of the object.

For that which, by its own coloring (*uparāga*), produces the cognition of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) in the qualified object (*viśeṣya*), is a *viśeṣaṇa* (qualifier); the meaning is that it colors the qualified object at the time of the cognition of exclusion, as for example, "cowness" (*gotva*) and so forth. And that which, by remaining indifferent while coloring itself, produces the cognition of exclusion through the presentation of a distinguishing property residing in the qualified object, is an *upalakṣaṇa* (adventitious mark), as for example, a crow and so forth. But that which neither colors the qualified object nor presents another property, yet nevertheless serves as a distinguisher, is an *upādhi* (limiting adjunct).

Just as the application of the word *paṅkaja* (mud-born) brings to mind the property of being a lotus (*padmatva*), or as the application of words such as *udbhid* brings to mind a specific sub-class of sacrifice (*yāgatvāvāntarajāti*), so too here, the properties of being a lotus and being a specific type of sacrifice do not bring to mind any other distinct property in the agent of the act of arising from mud or the agent of the act of breaking forth [to yield fruit], because no such [additional] property is perceived. Nor do they produce a cognition colored by themselves, since no separate power (*śakti*) is admitted for the composite whole. Nevertheless, because they serve to distinguish [the referents] from water-lilies (*kumuda*) and the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice and so forth, they are indeed merely limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).

This pair of examples is accepted by both the Prābhākaras and the Bhāṭṭas. For the Logicians (Tārkikas), however, the example for the use of the term "space" (ākāśa) is its being the substratum of sound. For this very reason, it is the established doctrine of the Vedāntins that ignorance (avidyā) and so forth are limiting adjuncts (upādhi) in relation to [Brahman’s] being the Witness (sākṣitva) and so on. Therefore, where the status of being a qualifier (viśeṣaṇatva) for an object is impossible because it does not exist at that time, there is no room for the defect arising from [its being considered] a mere secondary indicator (upalakṣaṇatva), since it is admitted to be a limiting adjunct (upādhitva) in such cases.

In case of doubt, however, it is precisely the qualifier that is accepted as the primary factor due to its preeminence. Therefore, in every cognition, it is the object alone that serves as the differentiator. This is because we observe that between two cognitions—whether memory and perception, or indirect and direct—that have the same object, their mutual differentiation occurs by way of their genus (*jāti*) independently of the object. It is not correct to claim that in all cases it is the genus alone, regardless of the object, that acts as the differentiator; for this is impossible in the case of two cognitions of the same genus that have different objects. Nor should it be argued that even in those cases there exists a further universal (*ati*), just as there is a common sweetness in milk and other substances.

This is because confusion (*saṅkara*) has already been stated on account of [the cognition] being visual and so forth. Nor can it be argued that, in your view, the distinction [of cognitions] is intrinsic—whether by virtue of each mental modification (*vṛtti*) having the respective form, consciousness being reflected therein, or consciousness being manifested thereby—whereas in my view, the distinction is intrinsic by virtue of each cognition possessing its own specific nature or its capacity to generate the corresponding empirical usage (*vyavahāra*).

Because it is impossible to assert that [the object] functions as a differentiator independently of [the cognition], since it merely imparts its form to the object and serves to characterize its nature and conventional usage; and because we have not asserted that a non-existent thing (tuccha) possesses causal efficiency; and because it has been stated that when the status of being a qualifier (viśeṣaṇa) or a limiting adjunct (upādhi) is possible, there can be no status of being a mere indicator (upalakṣaṇa).

Nor is there any contradiction with the Śruti passage, "How could the existent be born from the non-existent?", the Sūtra, "Because the non-existent is not observed [to produce anything]," or the Bhāṣya which states, "Because we do not observe the production of an existent from things such as a hare's horn," for those [texts] aim to deny that the *tuccha* (the absolutely non-existent) can be a cause, whereas we ourselves have not asserted that the *tuccha* possesses causality. Therefore, it is established that being distinct from the existent (*sadviviktatva*) is the probans. Thus ends the section on the refutation of the non-existent's capacity to be a prover in the *Advaitasiddhi*.

[Objection: Is it not the case that the inference for falsity (*mithyātva*) is inconclusive (*aprayojaka*), since the property of being an object of sight (*dṛśyatva*) is possible even if [the world] were real? [Reply: No, because the relation between the seer (*dṛk*) and the seen (*dṛśya*) is untenable. For knowledge does not illuminate an object while remaining entirely unrelated to it, as that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Nor is it related [in a real sense], because there can be neither conjunction (*saṃyoga*) nor inherence (*samavāya*) between the object of knowledge and knowledge—which is either the nature of the Self (*ātman*) or a quality (*guṇa*) of the Self. Furthermore, no other non-superimposed (*anādhyāsika*) relation exists. Nor can that relation be the status of "object" and "subject" (*viṣaya-viṣayibhāva*).

Because that which consists of the nature of being an object (*viṣayatva*) and being a subject (*viṣayitva*) resides in each one exclusively, it is impossible for it to consist of a relation existing in both; furthermore, it is difficult to define. To explain: is "object-ness" (1) the state of being the locus of an effect produced by cognition? Or (2) the state of being the object of cognitions such as "rejection" (*hāna*) produced by cognition? Or (3) the state of being the objective case (*karman*) of cognition? Or (4) the state of imparting its form to the cognition? Or (5) its essence while being perceived? Or (6) the fitness for the practical activity (*vyavahāra*) produced by cognition? Or [is it] that cognition which is produced by a sense-organ in proximity to which [the object] exists?

Is it the reality (*tattva*)? That is, is the object of a cognition that which appears within that cognition, such that being "appearing in cognition" constitutes its object-hood? Or is it the state of being a delimiter (*avacchedaka*) of knowledge without any other relation intervening? In the first case, the result (*phala*) cannot be "cognizedness" (*jñātatā*), because that is not admitted [by you] and because it is absent in the case of past objects and the like. Nor can it be "rejection" (*hāna*) and so forth, because those are absent in the case of the sky and similar things, and because it would follow that the dirt on silver and the like would also be objects of the cognition of [pure] silver.

Nor can it be [the object] in the verbal expression of the supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā*), because those two [the speaker and the listener] are subject to the veil of the knowable (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). Nor should it be said that they exist there in the relation of object and subject (*viṣaya-viṣayibhāva*), because that very point is currently under investigation. For this same reason, the second [alternative] is also not tenable. The third is not [tenable] either; for it would follow that the knowledge of the Lord (*īśvara*) and the knowledge of the past and so forth would be devoid of objects, since they are not produced by an objective factor (*karmakāraka*). Nor is the fourth [alternative] tenable; for, due to the non-difference between the cognition and its form (*ākāra*), it would follow that all causes of cognition would become objects, and it would further follow that there is an absence of such [causal] status regarding the objects of inference and the like.

The fifth [alternative] is not tenable, because being "perceptible" (dṛśyamānatva) is constituted by the state of being an object (viṣayatva), which entails the fallacy of self-dependence (ātmāśraya). The sixth is not tenable, because there is no further "fitness" (yogyatā) within fitness itself. Nor can it be argued that fitness is fit without another fitness, just as perceptibility is perceptible without another perceptibility; for when one attempts to formulate the defining characteristic (avacchedaka-rūpa) of fitness, fitness itself cannot be grasped. Nor is "being an object of cognition" (jñāna-viṣayatva) its defining characteristic, because that would entail self-dependence. The seventh is not tenable.

Because it would follow that the eternal knowledge of God would be without an object. It is not the eighth [alternative], for "in consciousness" (*saṃvidi*) cannot be a locative of locus (*adhikaraṇa-saptamī*), since knowledge does not have its own object as its locus. Nor can it be a locative of object (*viṣaya-saptamī*), because that very point is what is currently being investigated. Furthermore, it would lead to the absurdity of consciousness being the object and the cognized object being the subject. Nor can it be a locative of existence (*sati-saptamī*), because manifestness (*bhāsamānatva*) is already constituted by objecthood, which would result in the fallacy of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*). Nor is it the ninth [alternative].

In the case of the cognition "color-cognition is inherent in me," there would result the unwanted consequence that the inherence of color-cognition is the object even in the cognition "this is color," which lacks any other relation [to that inherence] and is merely delimited by the color-cognition. Now, one might argue: "The very usage of the learned, namely 'object of cognition,' is itself the relation between cognition and its object. Just as the definition of a mantra is simply its being the object of the usage of the learned, so too here. Nor is there the fault of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*), because each subsequent usage depends upon preceding usages. If this is said, we reply: no.

For by this much there would only be "knowability" in a general sense, but not "being the object of this specific cognition. Furthermore, in this case, a subsequent application cannot be stated in dependence upon a prior application, because that [knowability] rests solely in its beginninglessness. Moreover, if the application itself were a relation toward its own object, there would also be the fallacy of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*).

Now, it might be argued: "Is it not the case that whatever cognition is the cause of a linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) consisting in the verbal expression of a certain object, that [object] is the objective domain (*viṣaya*) of that [cognition]? Even when linguistic usage does not arise due to the absence of proficiency in the sense organs and so forth, the status of being a cause—defined as possessing the absence of the effect caused by the lack of auxiliary factors—still exists. Furthermore, there is no lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) regarding the object of indeterminate perception (*nirvikalpaka*), because such [an indeterminate perception] is not admitted [by us]. Nor is there the fault of non-uniformity (*ananugama*) due to the use of 'that which' (*yat*) and 'that' (*tat*)."

As for the objection that "of what is which the object?"—this is not a fault, because it is precisely such a non-corresponding [question] that constitutes the subject matter of the inquiry. Nor does it follow that a cognition of a jar would have a cloth as its object on the grounds that it generates a linguistic usage (vyavahāra) expressing "cloth" due to negligence immediately after the cognition of the jar; for a cognition is a generator only with respect to a linguistic expression whose object is identical to its own, and since the cognition of the jar has a different object, it is not the generator in that case. If you say this, we reply: no.

The capacity to generate linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) in the form of verbal expression cannot be determined by way of its individual nature (*prātisvikarūpa*), because being a delimiting factor (*avacchedakatva*) is determined by its result (*phala*), and no such result is observed in each individual case. Furthermore, there is no evidence for an individual capacity in that which has not produced a result; rather, [the capacity] exists there and there as the objectness (*viṣayatva*) of the respective mental states (*vṛtti*) that follow along with it. Thus, there would be the fallacy of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*). For this very reason, objectness (*viṣayatva*) is the state of being the object (*karmatva*) of cognition. And this "state of being an object" is not a specific type of causal factor (*kāraka*), such that its absence in the past and so forth would follow.

However, [the objection that] the state of possessing an excellence consisting in fitness for practical activity (*vyavahāra-yogyatva*) dependent upon action is [the definition of an object] is refuted. Otherwise, in cases such as "he makes a jar," since an unestablished (*asiddha*) jar and so forth would not be a producer, and an established (*siddha*) thing could not be the object of an act of making, the accusative case-ending would be meaningless. Furthermore, fitness for practical activity does not mean being endowed with the fruit in the form of that activity; for there would be a lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) in cases where the activity is obstructed somewhere. Nor does it mean fitness in its own nature (*svarūpa-yogyatva*), because that is impossible for anything other than the objective character (*viṣayatva*), which leads back to the previously mentioned fault.

Nor should it be said that the state of possessing the absence of the effect—which is caused by the lack of auxiliary factors—is something distinct from the delimiting property (*avacchedaka*); for without a common, recurring delimiting property, even that [state] cannot be apprehended. In the expression "he makes a jar," it is only the already existent potsherd and so forth that constitute the object of the act of making (*kṛti-karmatā*). This is because they accept that only that which is unestablished [as yet] in its capacity as being operated upon (*vyāpāryatayā*) is the object of the act of making. For this very reason, proponents of the theory of the non-existence of the effect (*asatkāryavādin*) maintain that when a word denoting an object is used in conjunction with a verbal root expressing production, there is a conventional metaphorical indication (*nirūḍhalakṣaṇā*) directed toward a part of the primary meaning.

For the proponents of the theory that the effect pre-exists (*satkāryavādins*), however, there is no inconsistency regarding the status of being an agent or the object of an action, because even though the effect exists previously, it is merely to be manifested. By this, the objection raised earlier—"in which consciousness," etc.—is also refuted. The term "consciousness" (*saṃvidi*) is used here in the locative case denoting existence (*sati-saptamī*). Furthermore, "manifestness" means fitness for linguistic usage (*vyavahāra-yogyatva*). And as for the claim that "given another cause, linguistic usage necessarily follows," that too is refuted.

Now, is it not the case that whatever, without depending on another relation, is the delimitator (*avacchedaka*) of a cognition and whose nature is not delimited by that cognition, is the object (*viṣaya*) of that cognition? Although the self possesses inherence (*samavāya*) with the cognition of its own object, nevertheless, there is no dependence on inherence for the delimitation of that [cognition] by the self, because we observe that even things like a jar, which do not possess inherence with the cognition, serve as its delimitators.

And although the cognition of color (*rūpajñāna*) inheres in me, and even though in cases such as "the cognition of color has perished" or "is desired," things like the destruction of desire—which are not themselves objects of that cognition of color—delimit the cognition [of the self] without depending on any other relation, nevertheless, they possess a nature delimited precisely by the cognition of color, which consists of the self that is the substratum of the inherence and the object of the desire; for relations, desires, and so forth, have a nature delimited by their relata, the objects of desire, and so on. Thus, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*). However, the object of a cognition does not have a nature delimited by the cognition itself.

This is because, unlike knowledge—which possesses a nature delimited by objects such as a jar—it is not observed that a jar or the like possesses a nature delimited by knowledge. Even if one were to argue that there is no lack of pervasion (avyāpti), on the grounds that while knowledge which has become an object of the very cognition grasping it—such as an inference regarding knowledge or a subsequent reflective awareness (anuvyavasāya)—does indeed possess a nature delimited by knowledge, yet knowledge that is itself the object of another cognition does not possess a nature delimited by that [second] cognition; we say no.

Because it would follow that the cognition "the knowledge of color inheres in me" lacks the inherence in the self as its object; for inherence in the self, being a relation, must be delimited by its own relatum, which is the knowledge itself. Furthermore, just as the cognition "the knowledge of the jar" implies that knowledge has a nature delimited by the jar, so too the cognition "the jar is known" implies that the jar has a nature delimited by knowledge; thus [the proposed definition] is impossible.

Now, if it is argued that whatever cognition has as its own nature (svabhāva) a certain thing, that thing is the object (*viṣaya*) of that cognition—such that in the case of the cognition "color inheres in me," it is the inherence (*samavāya*) itself that has a nature delimited by the cognition of color, and not the cognition of color that has a nature delimited by inherence—and that this defines objecthood for cognition alone (and not for desire and so forth), and thus there is no lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*); we say no. For if the secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*) in the phrase "having as its own nature" (*yadīyasvabhāvam*) were to mean "having that as its object" (*yadviṣayakatva*), there would be the fallacy of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*).

Furthermore, it is impossible to define this as a distinct entity (*arthāntara*). Since the absence of the absence of the cognition of color (*rūpajñāna*) is itself the nature of the cognition of color, the cognition of color would also be included within that absence; consequently, it would follow that [the self] is an object of that [absence]. [Objection: But surely, being the locus of the sensory contact (*sannikarṣa*) which is the instrument (*karaṇa*) producing the cognition is what constitutes being its object. Thus, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) such that the Self—the locus of the contact with the mind (*manas*), which is the instrument for the cognition of color—would become its object. This is because by the term "instrument," only the uncommon instrument (*asādhāraṇakaraṇa*) of the cognition is intended.

If it is argued that this is because the term "sannikarṣa" (contact) refers only to that contact which produces a cognition specific [to its object], we say no. For the contact between the eye and the mind (*cakṣur-manassaṃyoga*) is also a non-common cause of visual cognition; consequently, the mind itself would result in being an object of visual cognition. Furthermore, there is a lack of application (*avyāpti*) in the case of supersensible objects (*parokṣaviṣaya*). Nor can it be said that in those cases the cognition of the *liṅga* (inferential mark) is the instrument (*karaṇa*), and that the relation in that instance is the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the *liṅgin* (the thing to be inferred) by that mark.

Furthermore, it would follow that the logical mark (*liṅga*) itself would become an object of inference, since it is related to its own cognition. Nor can it be argued that in inference, only the relation consisting of being pervaded by it (*tadvyāptatā*) is the regulator of objecthood; for this would result in the delimitors of pervasion (*vyāpakatāvacchedaka*), the pervader (*vyāpaka*), and the relation itself not being objects of cognition. Nor should it be said that objecthood is a property directly pervaded by the delimitor of cognition, which is co-located with the sensory contact that is the instrument of cognition, and that this definition applies equally to eternal imperceptibles; for this would lead to the absurd conclusion that even "substantiality" (*vastutva*) and the like are objects of cognition.

It must be stated that being the object (*viṣayatva*) consists precisely in being the delimiting factor (*avacchedakatva*) of cognition; however, this is unestablished (*asiddhi*). To explain: if "intrinsic relation" (*svarūpasambandha*) means "the intrinsic nature is the relation," then there is over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and the like. Nor can "being other than those two" be added as a qualification, for then the Himālaya and Vindhya mountains would also incur the status of having an intrinsic relation. If it is argued that an intrinsic relation is "the fitness for generating a qualified cognition without another relation," we say no, because this definition fails to apply (*avyāpti*) to the case of "I know myself."

In that case, because there exists only another relation, namely inherence (*samavāya*), and because [inherence] is over-extended to supersensible absences (*abhāva*) and the like; for there is no proof that such [an absence] possesses the capacity to generate a qualified cognition (*viśiṣṭapratīti*). Otherwise, it would follow that it generates a qualified cognition by itself. Furthermore, is the capacity to generate a qualified cognition a property (*dharma*) or a relation? Or is it simply those two intrinsic natures (*svarūpa*) themselves? In the first case, the status of the intrinsic nature as a relation is contradicted.

Furthermore, there is the undesirable consequence that this [inherence], being constituted by a specific cognition, would not be an object of visual or other types of perception. Nor is the second alternative [valid], because it lacks universal applicability (*ananugama*). Moreover, in this way, the error regarding non-existence (*abhāva-bhrama*) would be impossible; for even in that case, since a qualified cognition is possible, the relation of essential identity (*svarūpa-sambandha*) exists. Nor can that definition be constituted by "truth" (*prāmāṇya*), because if a real relation exists, truth itself would necessarily follow. Otherwise, there would be a circular argument (*anyonyāśraya*): if that [cognition] were not true, the relation would be absent, and if the relation were absent, that cognition would not be true.

Now, it may be argued that even without another relation, the very nature of a thing as delimited by that which delimits its capacity to produce a qualified cognition constitutes its status as a relation—just as in cases such as "the man with a staff" (*daṇḍin*), that which is delimited by "staffness" (*daṇḍatva*) functions as the relation. Furthermore, the qualified cognition itself has as its object that which is delimited, even though it does not have the delimiting factor as its direct object.

Therefore, there is no contradiction in the fact that a qualified cognition whose object is a relation of essential identity (svarūpasambandha) can be visual. Nor should it be argued that, since both valid cognitions and erroneous cognitions of absence would then have only the two essential natures as their objects without distinction, the distinction between valid cognition and error would be untenable; for this distinction is established by the fact that one is a cognition of the absence of a jar in a locus where the jar is absent, while the other is a cognition different from that.

[Objection: But if it has no object beyond [the locus], its very nature as an error would be untenable; for according to your view, since it consists of both [the locus and the qualifier] and both exist, there can be no error-ness in the form of having a qualifier in a different locus (*vyadhikaraṇaprakāratva*), and thus the distinction between error and its opposite would be impossible. [Reply: This is not so, because a cognition of the absence of a jar in a place where a jar exists—by way of the absence of the absence of the jar being the jar itself—can indeed have a qualifier in a different locus. Furthermore, in reality, the object of an error is that which possesses the jar.

However, there certainly exists for valid cognition (*pramā*) a distinct object [of negation]. Nor is there a lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) in the case of supersensible absences (*atīndriyābhāva*). For in the case of absolute absence (*atyantābhāva*), the delimitor of capacity for generating a qualified cognition (*viśiṣṭapratyaya*) is the state of being in a location other than that of the counter-positive; in the case of antecedent absence (*prāgabhāva*) and the like, it is the state of being in a time other than that of the counter-positive while being in the same location as the counter-positive; and in the case of mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*), it is the state of being in a location other than that delimited by the counter-positiveness. And this state of being so delimited is easily found even in supersensible absences, which do not generate a qualified cognition.

If it is argued that a staff standing in a forest is not delimited by the delimitor of the fitness for producing a cognition, [we reply: it would necessarily follow that eternal and supersensible things, such as the absolute non-existence of space, must produce a qualified cognition, because they are delimited by the delimitor of the fitness for generating a qualified cognition; for there is a rule that whatever is eternal and intrinsically fit [to produce an effect] is necessarily accompanied by its auxiliary causes.

Furthermore, regarding the definition "the cognition of that which is qualified," if the meaning of the genitive case is a relation of essential identity (*svarūpa-sambandha*), there is the fallacy of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*). If its meaning is merely "relation" in general, there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to objects such as a jar or a cloth, which are the objects of a collective cognition (*samūhālambana-jñāna*) having as its relata the self as qualified by "selfhood" (*ātmatva*) and so forth; for even those two [the jar and the cloth] produce a cognition whose object is unqualified, despite their being related to a qualified entity. Consequently, there would be no distinction between the cognitions "absence of knowledge" and "known absence."

Since both [the absence of knowledge and the absence of the object] have an essential relation (*svarūpa-sambandha*) with respect to both [terms], there is no distinction between them based on the object. For this very reason, the claim that "the capacity to generate a qualified cognition" is a distinct relation in cases such as knowledge and its object is refuted; for it would fail to apply (*avyāpti*) to eternal absences that are beyond the senses (*atīndriya*). Indeed, in those cases, there is no capacity to generate a qualified cognition, because that would entail the consequence that the relation itself produces the effect (the cognition). Furthermore, if the relation were defined by the cognition, it would follow that it could not be an object of visual or other types of perception.

Therefore, since a relation is untenable if [the world] were real, the relation between the seer and the seen must be merely superimposed (*ādhyāsika*). Thus ends the section on the refutation of the relation between the seer and the seen, within the *Advaitasiddhi*, concerning the unreality of the phenomenal world.

It might be argued as follows: even if every object of perception is superimposed upon the consciousness that is Brahman, you yourself have admitted that for something to be manifested to someone at some time, the connection with unobscured consciousness must occur through the medium of a mental modification (*vṛtti*) in the form of that object, produced by the sense organ in proximity to it. This being the case, let the connection be mediated by that very process even if [the world] were real; why this obsession with a "superimpositional" (*ādhyāsika*) connection? For, according to you, it is not as it is for the Vijñānavādins, who hold that [an object appears] within each respective cognition.

If it is argued that one must accept the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of those respective objects because the pure Seer has no inherent difference [from itself], and since even if there were a difference in its qualified state due to limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), it—like a jar or other objects—would be false and thus unfit to be the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*); we say no, because it is a rule that light directly illuminates what it is in contact with, and therefore consciousness cannot illuminate an object through a mediated relationship.

For a lamp does not illuminate that which is connected through a series; therefore, it is consciousness itself, as located in the substrate of the object, that is the illuminator when it is unobstructed, and the destruction of the veil occurs through the mental modification (vṛtti). Consequently, even though the superimposed relationship exists prior to the modification, the non-perception of the object is logically established.

For this very reason: if consciousness reflected in a mental modification (*vṛtti*) were the illuminator of the jar, it would follow that the superimpositional relation (*ādhyāsika-sambandha*) is irrelevant; whereas, if the consciousness manifested by the jar were the illuminator of the jar, then since the manifestation of the jar is already accounted for by the consciousness reflected in the *vṛtti*—which is indispensable—it is more logical to postulate the manifestation of the consciousness that serves as its substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*). Nor can it be argued that pure consciousness is not manifested prior to the final direct realization (*carama-sākṣātkāra*), and that [the jar]...

It should not be argued that consciousness delimited by a jar or the like cannot be its substrate because of the fallacy of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*); for even prior to the final direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*), although pure consciousness—which serves as the substrate due to the power of ignorance—lacks manifestation in the form of the cessation of root-ignorance (*mūlājñāna*), it is nonetheless capable of illuminating objects through a manifestation characterized by the cessation of specific states [of that ignorance]. Nor can it be said that the vision which illuminates the jar cannot be the substrate because it is false; for if it were real, it would not be produced by defects (*doṣa*).

It should not be argued that because [the cognition] possesses validity (*pramātva*), it is true with respect to its own object and therefore cannot be the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*); for this would be a "rope of two-fold nooses. This is because being unproduced by a defect (*doṣa*) is not the determinant (*prayojaka*) of validity, since consciousness (*caitanya*) is everywhere unproduced by defects. Rather, [validity] consists in being delimited by a mental modification (*vṛtti*) that is unproduced by a defect; and in the present case, since that is absent, the object lacks reality. Therefore, it is logical that the real vision (*dṛk*) serves as the substrate with respect to an object that is illusory (*mithyā*).

But surely, it is only when a real relation is impossible that one imagines a superimposed (ādhyāsika) relation? Yet why is that [real relation] itself impossible? Because, just as conjunction (saṃyoga) is set aside between a quality and its possessor due to the existence of inherence (samavāya), so too when both of those are set aside, a third type of relation becomes possible. Nor is there a lack of evidence for this, since there exists both inference and perception, just as in the case of inherence.

For instance: a qualified cognition (*viśiṣṭadhī*) whose qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and qualificand (*viśeṣya*) are not mutually conjoined or inherent has as its object the relation between the qualifier and the qualificand, because it is a qualified cognition, like the qualified cognition "the man with a staff" (*daṇḍī*). An asserted produced valid cognition (*pramā*) is caused by the relation between the qualifier and the qualificand, because it is an uncontradicted, produced qualified cognition, like [the aforementioned] consensus. The cognition under dispute has as its object the uncontradicted relation between the qualifier and the qualificand, because it is an uncontradicted, produced qualified cognition, like the qualified cognition "the man with a staff."

Even the cognition "Caitra is a cow-eater" and so forth is included within the scope of the subject (*pakṣa*), and thus there is no suspicion of a logical deviation (*vyabhicāra*) therein. Consequently, [you claim] that a relation distinct from conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and inherence (*samavāya*) is established. If this is argued, we say: no; for in the first and second cases, there is the fallacy of proving something already established or proving the irrelevant (*arthāntara*), since the relation can be accounted for as being merely one of superimposition (*ādhyāsika*), whether as its object or its cause. Furthermore, in the second case, there is a deviation in the case of indirect cognitions (*parokṣadhī*). In the third case as well, since [the cognition] remains unsublated until the knowledge of Brahman, it is simply a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*).

If the probandum is "being the object of a cognition that is in every way uncontradicted," then there is a deficiency of the probandum (*sādhyavaikalya*). Nor should it be argued: "The establishment of a superimposed relation (*ādhyāsika-sambandha*) does not occur upon the sublation of a real relation (*tāttvika-sambandha*); thus, until the sublation of a real relation distinct from conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and inherence (*samavāya*), there is no possibility of a superimposed relation; so how can there be the fallacies of proving the irrelevant (*arthāntara*), proving the already established (*siddhasādhana*), or deficiency of the probandum? For the real relation is sublated by the non-perception of its pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*).

For instance—the absence of spatial and temporal distance is the pervader (*vyāpaka*) of a real relationship (*tāttvikasambandha*). Since that [absence] does not exist at all in the case of cognitions and so forth whose objects are past and so on, how can their relationship be real? Nor should it be argued that its establishment is like that of inherence (*samavāya*), by virtue of being non-contradictory even in the presence of the absence of related terms or spatial/temporal distance; for inherence itself does not serve as the cause for the linguistic usage of "related" between two things that are spatially or temporally distant.

For inherence (samavāya), being eternal, does not qualify a jar destroyed today by means of a form existing tomorrow, even in the absence of a related correlate. Nor is there a contradiction with the evidence apprehending the substratum (dharmigrāhakapramāṇabādha) when the relation is to be proven as merely superimposed (adhyāsika); for, by virtue of being a qualified cognition, what is first established is simply a relation that is common to both real and unreal cases.

Furthermore, it is the very grasper of the relation itself—aided by the sublation consisting in the non-perception of the pervader of a real relation—that results in the conclusion that the relation is one of superimposition (*ādhyāsika*). Therefore, there is not even the slightest suspicion of a sublation by the grasper of the locus (*dharmigrāhakabādha*). Nor should it be argued that, since a relation in the form of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is observed only between things established separately (*yutasiddha*), the lack of separate establishment (*ayutasiddhi*) would also constitute a sublation of inherence (*samavāya*); for the state of being established separately is not a necessary condition for a relation, as relations are observed even in some cases between things that are established separately. In which [case]...

Truthfully, there is necessarily a relation, and that [relation] alone is the cause of the relation; thus, because there is an absence of co-extensive pervasion (*samavyāpti*), the non-perception of separate existence (*yutasiddhi*) does not constitute a sublation. Even if one were to postulate an asymmetrical pervasion (*viṣamavyāpti*)—namely, "wherever there is a relation, there necessarily is separate existence"—there is no evidence for this, as no supporting argument (*anukūlatarka*) is observed. Furthermore, since a relation is observed among all things that lack spatial or temporal distance, whereas it is not observed when such distance exists, [separate existence] is the necessary cause by virtue of its co-extensive pervasion.

For one must necessarily admit that the non-apprehension of the absence of spatial and temporal distance constitutes a sublation of the relationship; indeed, in the absence of the causal factor (*prayojaka*), the effect (*prayojya*) cannot possibly exist.

But if this is so—[if there is no relation] between destruction and that which has passed away, etc., or between absolute non-exclusion (atyantābhāva) included within the definition of falsity and its counter-positive (pratiyogin), or between power and the powerful, ignorance and the object of ignorance, desire and the desired, linguistic usage and the object of usage, or the knowledge consisting of a mental mode (vṛtti) and its object—then, because the absence of relation stated in your own sentence lacks a relation with the cognition [of that absence], there would follow contradictions regarding your own logic, your own action, and your own words; for [the absence of relation] is not related to the cognition in the same way that the object of knowledge is related to it.

If it is argued that the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) and so forth are superimposed (*adhyasta*) upon non-existence (*abhāva*) and the like, we say no. For although, by parity with the reasoning already stated, there is indeed no real (*tāttvika*) relation between destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) and its counter-positive and so forth, nor even a superimposition in the manner of knowledge and its object—since both are equally false (*mithyā*)—nevertheless, we do not deny the counter-positive and substrate relationship and so forth as they are perceived. Rather, we accept them as being merely false (*mithyābhūta*), since they are included within the category of the knowable (*jñeya*) and are distinct from both reality and superimposition.

And as for whether that [relation] is distinct like conjunction and so forth, or its own essential nature (*svarūpa*), or included among the categories accepted by others, or distinct from them—in this investigation of a crow’s teeth, we have no insistence. Nor is there a circular argument (*anyonyāśraya*) based on the fact that it is not established prior to the establishment of falsity; for once it is established through the impossibility of a relation between the seer and the seen that everything knowable is illusory (*adhyāsika*), then the falsity of the relation between the counter-positive and absence, which falls within that [category], is also established, but not otherwise.

Since the falsity of the relation between the counter-positive and its absence (or other correlates) is established prior to the establishment of the falsity of the visible world (*dṛśya*), there is no contradiction with one's own words (*svavacanavirodha*) or similar fallacies; for we do not reject the general category of relations that are useful in worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*). As it has been stated by the authors of the *Khaṇḍana*:
"If the sublation (*bādha*) is not firm, what is the use of [pointing out] similarity to another? If it is firm, let that [worldly relation] also be sublated.
Where is the sense of ownership for those seeking liberation who maintain the doctrine of the inexpressible (*anirvacanīyatva*)?"

Nor is there any lack of firmness in the sublation (bādha), because the reasoning (tarka) consisting of the non-perception of the pervader has already been stated, and because the counter-reasoning (pratikūla-tarka) consisting of contradictions such as with one's own actions has been refuted.

For this very reason, there is no parity with the proponent of universals (*jātivādin*); for by him, based on the mere observation of properties such as "being produced" (which establishes impermanence while depending on a necessary rule), properties such as "possessing color" are erroneously attributed even without regard for that rule. However, we do not attribute anything in such a manner based on mere concomitance (*sāhacarya*) independent of a necessary rule. Nor should it be argued that, in the same way, the relationship between cognition and its object should be considered equivalent to the relationship between a counter-positive and its absence; for [the former] is impossible precisely because it consists of mutual superimposition (*parasparādhyāsa*).

Because one would have to postulate another relation, and since that [relation] is possible, it is that very thing which constitutes the relation. Nor should it be argued that the rule—that there must be a superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of the object upon the subject—is not established because Brahman, who is the object of ignorance, is not superimposed upon the subject, ignorance; for such a rule is not accepted. Rather, the relation between knowledge or ignorance and their object is precisely superimposition. And this is accounted for by the superimposition of the knowable upon knowledge, and of ignorance upon its object. For this very reason, when demonstrating the absence of a superimpositional relation, the example "of ignorance with its object" is not cited.

Now, an objection may be raised: it is untenable for the means beginning with hearing (*śravaṇa*) and ending with the final direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) to have a relationship with their object, Brahman; for Brahman is not superimposed (*adhyasta*) upon hearing and so forth, nor upon the direct realization itself. If this is argued, we reply: no. For is the direct realization a mental modification (*vṛtti*), or is it the consciousness manifested by that modification? In the first case, since that modification is superimposed upon Brahman, a relationship is established just as between ignorance and its object.

For this very reason, there is no inconsistency regarding the connection [of Brahman] even through hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth, which are mental acts; however, in the second case (the final realization), since that connection is not required by way of non-difference, the fact that such a connection is impossible does not constitute a fault. For this same reason, the objection—that if the final direct intuition (*sākṣātkāra*) has Brahman as its object because it is superimposed (*adhyasta*) upon Brahman, then the direct intuition of a jar would also have Brahman as its object because it too is superimposed upon Brahman—is refuted, provided that the direct intuition of a jar consists in the consciousness (*caitanya*) manifested by the jar.

Even when that [mental modification] is of the nature of a cognitive state (*vṛtti*) and there is superimposition (*adhyāsa*) upon Brahman, Brahman—the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*)—does not possess the status of being an object (*viṣayatva*). This is because the specific kind of superimposition that necessitates the status of being an object of Brahman is absent therein; furthermore, that [specific superimposition] is to be inferred from the force of the result [of experience]. For here, unlike in the final cognitive state (*caramavṛtti*), such [objective] form of Brahman is not experienced. Moreover, in the case of desire and the desired object, the connection is mediated solely by cognition; thus, there is no requirement for a separate [direct] connection. Nor is it the case that [the connection] depends on sense-contact as it does in the case of [ordinary] cognition.

It should not be argued that, just as in the case of memory, the connection with an object in the case of desire—which depends on cognition—must be stated to be distinct from cognition itself (just as it is distinct from sense-contact and so forth) because it is experienced; for the experience of such a connection is accounted for by a connection mediated through cognition, and there is no evidence for postulating an additional connection, since no other connection dependent on cognition is ever experienced.

In the case of knowledge, however, the experience of a relation cannot be established through sense-object contact and the like; for since sense-object contact and so forth are themselves beyond the senses, one experiences the relation—such as "this is the knowledge of a jar"—even without the prior presentation of those factors through inference or other means.

In the case of memory, however, there is no doubt whatsoever regarding a relation dependent upon experience, because at that time the experience is non-existent, and because both [the experience and the memory] being cognitions, a relation is possible between them as equals. Nor should it be argued that in the case of a desire for a single object produced by a collective cognition (*samūhālambana*), there would be the contingency of it having both objects as its content, since the generative cognition has both as its objects; for this objection applies equally even to the view that the relation is something distinct (*atirikta*).

Now, since a cognition possesses the status of being a producer [of an object] only by way of delimitation through a single object, it does not have both as its objects; this is equally true for me as well, because in the case of a producing cognition, the relation [to the object] is precisely the state of having that which delimits the capacity to produce as its object. Nor is there any impossibility of the relation of being an object for the eternal will of God, for we do not admit such a thing [as an eternal will]. Even for the Naiyāyikas, although they postulate a distinct relation on the strength of the evidence proving it, they nevertheless accept the objective character (*viṣayatā*) of both produced cognition and produced will in the very manner described above. Nor...

It should not be argued that pleasure and so forth produced by the cognition of a son, etc., would thereby possess the son, etc., as their object—on the grounds of the analogy with desire—for there is a disparity. Even though cognition is the same [in both cases], the perception of having an object occurs only in the case of desire and the like, but not in the case of pleasure and so forth. This must be stated by you as well, due to the inherent nature of things; otherwise, just as redness appears in a crystal due to the proximity of a hibiscus flower, it would also follow [that redness appears] in a clod of earth.

Now, [it might be argued that] because there is no superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of the intention (*tātparya*) upon the dharma (*dharma*), there could be no relation of intention [to it]. This is not so. For intention is simply the state of having that cognition as its objective; and since the cognition has a relation with the dharma just as it does with other objects of knowledge, that relation between the dharma and the intention is established through the medium of the cognition. Thus, there is no logical inconsistency. Nor is it the case that—despite the similarity of cognition to a lamp in its luminosity—one must admit a distinction for it due to its being internal; therefore, like desire and so forth, it [the intention] relates even to something remote.

It must be said that otherwise, there would be no relation at all, nor even a superimposed (ādhyāsika) relation as in the case of a lamp; furthermore, since a relation with something remote is observed in the case of indirect mental modification (parokṣavṛtti). However, while the absence of spatial and temporal remoteness may serve as the general condition for any relation, there is no reason to assume that only a relation distinct from one whose counter-correlate is internal serves as its specific condition.

It has been stated that desire, however, does not have a direct connection with the object to be attained, but rather possesses only an indirect, mediated connection through the medium of cognition (*jñāna*). In the case of an object beyond the senses (*parokṣa*), although there is indeed a direct connection with the substrate-consciousness (*adhiṣṭhāna-caitanya*), nevertheless, because there is no direct connection with the consciousness delimited by the mental modification (*vṛtti*) in the form of the object, the object’s connection is only indirect, being mediated by that *vṛtti*-delimited consciousness.

Now, an objection may be raised: even in your own view, there is no rule that an object of knowledge must be superimposed upon its own cognition. This is because (1) the "ineffable" (*tuccha*), which is not superimposed, is held by some to be a fifth category; (2) the cessation of ignorance (*avidyā-nivṛtti*), whether as a positive entity in the Advaita school or as a mere negation, is not superimposed upon its own cognition even though it is of the nature of non-apprehension (*adṛg-rūpa*); (3) objects such as the past, the eternal, or those beyond the senses—which, though superimposed upon Brahman who is of the nature of immediate, unitary experience, are not superimposed upon their own cognitions in the form of mediate apprehension; and (4) an object being remembered is not superimposed upon its own cognition in the form of memory.

If it is argued that there is no superimposition of the phenomenal upon the phenomenal within its own cognition—since, according to your view, even erroneous cognition is itself imagined—we say: not so. For the insubstantial (*tuccha*) cannot be an object of knowledge, and thus there can be no superimposition upon a cognition; indeed, superimposition occurs only when one knowable object is [superimposed] upon another knowable object, whereas it will be explained later that the insubstantial is not an object of knowledge. Furthermore, even in the case of the cessation of ignorance of the fifth kind, since the destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) must necessarily reside in the locus of its counter-positive, the relation is indeed superimposition.

In reality, however, the claim that the cessation of ignorance (*avidyānivṛtti*) constitutes a fifth category and the doctrine of the non-duality of existence (*bhāvādvaita*) are both refuted by our own non-acceptance [of them]. Furthermore, how the cessation of ignorance is of the nature of Brahman and how it constitutes the non-duality of all things will be explained below. Regarding the past and so forth superimposed upon Brahman—which is immediate and of a single essence—there is no inconsistency in the theory of superimposition; for although there is no superimposition upon the inferential cognition itself, that very consciousness upon which the past object was superimposed remains the same consciousness when delimited by the mental modification (*vṛtti*) in the form of inference. Thus, there is no lack of logical consistency.

To avoid the over-extension [of this principle], although consciousness requires the coloring of a mental mode (*vṛtti*) for its connection with an object, it does not require it as its substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*). In the same way, even in cases where something is eternally imperceptible, or in the case of memory, and even when there is no superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of the phenomenal upon a phenomenal mode, superimposition occurs only upon the consciousness manifested by a mode whose object is the substrate; thus, there is no inconsistency whatsoever.

Nor should it be argued: "Silver and the like are superimposed upon consciousness delimited by the 'this'-aspect (idamaṃśa), and they appear [not by being reflected in the consciousness mirrored by an ignorance-modification (avidyāvṛtti), but] by being reflected in the consciousness mirrored by the modification of the mental organ (vṛtti); therefore, how can there be a superimposition of the object upon the subject, which is the knowledge? For, just as in the case of independent limiting adjuncts (upādhi), here too there is no distinction-making factor between what is already delimited by one [adjunct] and what is delimited by another.

For this very reason, the learned declare that knowledge is one because its fruit is one. Nor should it be argued: "If silver and the like were superimposed upon their own cognition, then there would be the arising of error when the cognition of silver is not known, and its cessation by the knowledge of that [cognition]; for the birth and cessation of superimposition are invariably dependent on the non-knowledge and knowledge of the substrate (adhiṣṭhāna), and furthermore, there would be the undesirable consequence of the cognition 'silver is knowledge'. This is not to be said.

Since it is not accepted that consciousness delimited by a mental modification (*vṛtti*) in the form of silver is the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the illusion of silver, rather, it is consciousness delimited by the "this" aspect (*idamaṃśa*) alone that is the substratum of the illusion of silver. And that [consciousness] happens to be, by chance, also consciousness delimited by a mental modification in the form of silver; however, its being the substratum of the illusion does not depend upon that [delimitation]. Furthermore, the cause of the illusion is the ignorance (*ajñāna*) regarding that substratum in its aspect as mother-of-pearl (*śuktitva*), which is opposed to the illusion; and knowledge of it in that very aspect is what removes the illusion.

For this very reason, there is no occurrence of the erroneous form "knowledge is silver," because knowledge is defined only as consciousness delimited by a mental modification (*vṛtti*), and that [consciousness] lacks the status of being the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*). Furthermore, since the superimposed object is perceived through identity with the substratum, the form of the error is precisely "this is silver."

Now, an objection may be raised: since a jar or the like exists prior to its own cognition produced by a sense-organ in contact with it, superimposition upon it is not logical. Nor can it be argued that the jar is not manifested by the mental modification (*vṛtti*) born of the contact between the jar and the sense-organ—that which manifests the jar is the consciousness underlying the jar (*adhiṣṭhāna-caitanya*), and that this consciousness is not produced by such contact; for there is no evidence for a cognition distinct from the mental modification.

If it is argued that the cessation of ignorance also occurs from that very [modification], we say no; for prior to the arising of the modification, one must necessarily admit a knowledge distinct from the modification in order to establish the existence of the unknown object. Otherwise, since there would be no means of proving its existence, it would be as non-existent as a hare's horn, and the postulation of its prior existence as the cause of sensory contact and the resulting cognition would be without any basis in valid evidence.

Therefore, for a thing such as a jar, which serves as a cause of cognition by being the locus of sensory contact, one must necessarily accept some means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes it; otherwise, because positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) would not be apprehended, the relation of cause and effect could not be grasped, and the entire system of means and objects of knowledge would collapse. And that means of valid cognition is not of the nature of a mental modification (*vṛtti*).

At that time, because the activity of the mental mode (*vṛtti*) has ceased, [the Self] is distinct from that [mode]; it is eternal, self-luminous, and indeed one, on account of parsimony (*lāghava*), since it is untouched by the arising, destruction, insentience, and other qualities belonging to the mental mode. And it is that very [Self] which, through connection with various kinds of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), becomes the locus of various kinds of empirical usage (*vyavahāra*), just as the sky does through the difference of limiting adjuncts such as a jar, a water-pot, or a jasmine flower.

Furthermore, because that [consciousness] is the establisher of ignorance, it does not by its own nature remove ignorance; however, when colored by a mental modification (*vṛtti*), it does remove ignorance. Thus, there is no lack of utility for the mental modification. And so, since the witness-consciousness (*sākṣicaitanya*) is the establisher of all ignorance, the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of objects such as jars occurs upon it; hence, there is no inconsistency whatsoever. As it was said by Sureśvarācārya: "The establishment of their respective intended objects is achieved by all schools of thought through the very acceptance of that [witness-consciousness]; why then should its existence be denied?"
The definition of valid cognition common to all schools of thought is the apprehension of an object not previously known; however, that does not apply to what you have stated.
Whether the body and so forth are established by themselves or are unestablished,
the validity of the means of knowledge is not obtained in either case.
If the body and so forth were established even without the means of knowledge, [then those means would be useless].
Tell me, what purpose is served by means of valid cognition? For there is no proof for that which is already established.
"But when the object of cognition is not established by itself, there can be no means of valid cognition that manifests what is non-existent;
for even while shining, the sun does not manifest the horn of a hare.
Nor is it the case that "this statement 'this is a jar' arises through the grace of a mere appearance."

It should not be argued that there is a contradiction in the statement, "The expression 'the jar is known' arises from the experience of Brahman," because this implies that the consciousness reflected in the mental modification (vṛtti), which is not the substrate of the jar, is the experience of the jar. This is not so, because there is no difference between the consciousness reflected in the mental modification and the consciousness that is the substrate of the jar, since consciousness is one. And how the single consciousness itself is the manifester of all objects has been established in detail by the Commentators in the section [of the Brahma-sūtras] beginning with "Not non-existence, because of perception" (BS 2.2.28).

Now, is it intended that falsity [of the world] is established through *arthāpatti* (presumption), on the grounds that its being an object of perception would otherwise be inexplicable? Or is it merely a favorable *tarka* (reductio ad absurdum) stating that if [the world] were real, its being an object of perception would not be possible? It cannot be the first, because the necessary conditions for *arthāpatti* are absent. To explain: the conditions for *arthāpatti* consist of (1) the capacity of the [presumed] fact to account for the [observed] fact; (2) the non-contradiction of the [presumed fact] with valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); (3) the inexplicability of the [observed] fact [otherwise]; and (4) the established status [of the observed fact].

In the present context, the falsity of the related object (the superimposed) is what is to be established; however, the falsity of the establishing relation itself does not justify that [falsity of the object], but rather stands in direct opposition to it. Nor is it the case that the relation consisting of superimposition is not opposed to it, for since that [relation] is as yet unestablished, it cannot serve as an establisher. Furthermore, this object to be established is contradicted by perception and other means of valid cognition. Moreover, it is not reasonable to abandon multiple well-established [realities] for the sake of accounting for a single instance of "visibility."

Nor is superimposition upon consciousness (dṛg-adhyastatva) the "projector" (ākṣepaka), because that very [superimposition] is, in effect, the thing to be projected. Nor is the relation with consciousness (dṛk-sambandha) consisting in being an object of consciousness (dṛg-viṣayatva), because that is unestablished for you. Nor is it the state of having its establishment dependent on consciousness (dṛg-adhīna-siddhikatva), because nothing distinct from being an object of consciousness is established as such.

It cannot be the latter [the impossibility of the relation], because even if [the world] exists, its perceptibility is established through some other relation according to the method already stated; thus, there is no lack of justification [for the relation]. If this is argued, we say no, because the favorable *tarka* (reductio) itself is what is under discussion, leaving no room for alternatives such as "or it is an *arthāpatti* (presumption)," and because there is no fault in either case. To explain: if [the world] were real, the relation between the seer (*dṛk*) and the seen (*dṛśya*) would be untenable. Its falsity (*mithyātva*), however, is what makes that relation possible. Nor is that falsity opposed to the relation, because even in the case of false silver in a mother-of-pearl shell, a relation in the form of superimposition (*adhyasta*) upon the "this" (*idam*) aspect is observed; thus, there is no opposition to the relation in general.

The "implicator" (*ākṣepaka*), which consists in being an object of vision (*dṛgviṣayatva*), is indeed a relation with vision (*dṛksambandha*); for even I admit that being an object of vision is of the nature of superimposition (*adhyāsa*), since it is only its reality (*tāttvika*) that is negated. Nor is the status of being superimposed (*adhyastatva*) yet unestablished; for although the general relation with vision acts as the implicator, when its specific instances are negated, it culminates in the specific form of being superimposed, and thus there is no lack of establishment. Indeed, it is not by virtue of being a relation of superimposition that it functions as an implicator, but rather simply by virtue of being a relation.

And that [relation] remains entirely uncontradicted even by the possibility of its being a relation of superimposition (*adhyasta*). Nor should it be argued: "The specific nature of superimposition is not a particularity of the general relation established by the cognition 'the knowledge of the jar,' for there is no such perception as 'shell is silver. This is because, although there is no perception of "shell is silver," the status of superimposition as a specific type of relation is established by the perception that "the shell is the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the silver"; just as, although there is no perception of "Maitra is Caitra's father," [it is nonetheless understood].

It is just like the cognition "this is a friend. Furthermore, that which is implied here is certainly not contradicted by any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), since contradictions with perception and other such sources have already been refuted. Moreover, in the case of the implicant, actual validity is not even required, for we observe the implication of an object from its reflection even when that reflection is not itself valid. Even if the intent is to establish it through reasoning (*tarka*), there is no lack of utility; for it was demonstrated at the very outset—by refuting the logic you yourself proposed—that a connection is impossible if [the reflection] were real.

In this context, the condition that entails the absence of "perceptibility" (dṛśyatva) is either the absence of "indefinability" (anirvācyatva) or "non-sublatability throughout the three periods of time" (trikālābādhyatva); in either case, there is no fault. Nor is there a fallacy of deviation (vyabhicāra) due to the existence of the absence of indefinability in the "void" (tuccha)—which is known through indirect cognition—and in the "perceivable" (dṛśya), which is known through direct perception; for although a mental modification (vṛtti) in the form of the void may arise there due to the incapacity of its causes, the "perceptibility" consisting of the relation with the Seer (dṛk-sambandha), which is the opposite of voidness, is absent therein. This remains so even though the aspect of the void resides in the modification, because the relation with the modification [itself] does not constitute such perceptibility.

This is because it is established that there is no absence of existence residing in what is void (*tuccha*). Nor should it be argued: "Just as the existent Brahman has a relation with its own empirical usage (*vyavahṛti*), so too let the existent jar and other objects have a relation with their own cognition. For in the illustrative example of Brahman, it is precisely superimposition (*adhyāsa*) that constitutes the relation with empirical usage. Thus, when both relata are existent, the impossibility of the subject-object relationship (*viṣaya-viṣayibhāva*) is not set aside by such arguments as [the charge of] being unproving (*aprayojakatva*).

By this, the following [objections] are refuted: Is the so-called "superimpositional relation" (adhyāsika-sambandha) a superimposed relation (*adhyasta-sambandha*), or is it simply the state of being superimposed (*adhyastatva*)? In the first case, even if the relation is illusory, the illusoriness of the related object—the visible (*dṛśya*)—cannot be established, just as [the illusoriness of] the seer (*dṛk*) cannot be. In the second case, since cognition (*jñāna*) itself would be superimposed, its superimposition upon itself would be untenable; furthermore, if one were to accept superimposition within a succession of cognitions of themselves, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). For cognition is indeed consciousness (*caitanya*) delimited by a mental modification (*vṛtti*); therein, the delimiting factor is the insentient (*jaḍa*) mental modification.

Even though that which is delimited (the object) is superimposed, since consciousness—which is of the nature of light—is itself not superimposed, it is logical that there is no infinite regress even if the object of perception is illusory, because the object is superimposed upon that [consciousness].

For this very reason—it has been refuted [by us] that "Brahman is the object of the verbal function (*śābdavṛtti*) but is not superimposed upon that function; Brahman is the object of nescience (*avidyā*) but is not superimposed upon nescience; and likewise, the visible (*dṛśya*) is not superimposed upon the Seer (*dṛk*). Thus, the relationship between the Seer and the visible is indeed real (*tāttvika*); and once over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) has been ruled out by means of a general relationship alone, any inquiry into a specific [relationship] or any statement regarding a specific [relationship] is as useless as an inquiry into a specific [object] when none exists. This is refuted because, even though Brahman is not superimposed upon the function or nescience, those two (the function and nescience) are indeed superimposed upon Brahman.

Because a relation is established [in that case], and since there is therefore no real (tāttvika) relation therein, how can it be asserted that there is a real relation between the seer and the seen by means of that example? Furthermore, when a well-known particular is sublated, there arises the apprehension of the sublation of the universal itself; thus, since an over-extension (atiprasaṅga) would otherwise result, the inquiry into the particulars and the statement of the particulars are not without purpose. By this, if the relation is established by valid means of knowledge (prāmāṇika), a definition will be possible in some way or another.

For instance: it has been refuted that [the definition of relation] will be simply its inclusion within conjunction (*saṃyoga*) or inherence (*samavāya*), such that its definition would be identical to theirs; or that, if it is not included therein, its definition should simply be "being a relation distinct from both of those. This is because, by the reasoning already stated, the status of a relation as being authoritative and its inclusion within conjunction or inherence have been shown to be untenable. We do not deny that there exists a relation external to both of those, but rather we deny its authoritative status (*prāmāṇikatva*).

Furthermore, there is no real relationship between the seer and the seen, because if they were distinct entities, it would lead to an infinite regress. Nor should it be argued that—just as "visibility" (dṛśyatva) itself, which lacks another instance of visibility, is self-establishing—a relationship might likewise be self-establishing in some cases; for even "visibility" is simply a relationship with the seer.

Furthermore, its self-sustaining nature cannot exist without its being illusory (*māyika*); thus, nothing unfavorable has been asserted by the "beloved of the gods" (the opponent), for if there were non-difference, a relationship would be impossible. Nor does this same defect follow even if the relationship is one of superimposition (*adhyāsika*), because that [superimposition] is illusory, and since *māyā* is expert at accomplishing the impossible, all apparent inconsistencies become ornaments rather than flaws. Nor is it the case that the definition of the relationship between the seer and the seen (*dṛg-dṛśya*) was undertaken here merely to avoid over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), and not otherwise.

It should not be argued that the definition of "objecthood" (*viṣayatva*) is therefore a "criticism of what was not stated," because by the refutation of objecthood, the very relation currently under discussion—which is being defined—is itself refuted. Nor should it be argued that just as the subject (*viṣayin*) remains real even when "subjecthood" (*viṣayitva*) is not defined, the object must likewise remain real even when "objecthood" is not defined; for while the reality of the subject is logical since it can be established through the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) upon the object even when subjecthood is not defined, such is not the case for the object when objecthood is not defined.

Reality is not tenable [for the world], because since the subject (*viṣayin*) is not superimposed, there is no other basis for its existence apart from the superimposition upon the object (*viṣaya*). Where, however, the superimposition belongs to the subject itself, there the object is indeed real, as in the case of Brahman, which is the object of ignorance (*ajñāna*). Nor can there be a superimposition of both, as that would lead to the consequence of nihilism (*śūnyavāda*). And when the superimposition belongs to only one of the two, the criteria for determining which is so are precisely their persistence (*anuvṛtta*), their exclusion (*vyāvṛtta*), their luminosity (*prakāśatva*), their insentience (*jaḍatva*), and so forth.

Therefore, since there is no superimposition of the eternal seer—the subject—upon the object, it is the object alone that is superimposed here. Nor should it be argued: "Since you yourself have stated that 'valid knowledge obscures its own object' and so forth, and have further employed 'being an object of the seer' (dṛśyatva) as a logical reason, you too must necessarily define objectivity (viṣayatva). This is not so; for even if [objectivity] is ultimately indefinable (anirvacanīya), it is possible for it to be defined in a manner equivalent to a jar or other objects by virtue of being superimposed.

If it is asked, "How can that which is superimposed be the object of valid knowledge (*pramāṇajñāna*)?", [we reply]: No; understand this rather as being because the cognition whose object is the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) lacks validity characterized by the revelation of reality (*tattvāvedakatva*). For this very reason, it has been said: "Just as you maintain that the nature of being an object for the conscious self (*cidātman*) with respect to its mental modification (*vṛtti*) is such, so too, I maintain that the nature of being an object for the Seer (*dṛk*) with respect to the visible (*dṛśya*) is likewise."

This is rejected; for even if there is no superimposition upon the conscious self (*cidātman*), since mental modification (*vṛtti*) is superimposed upon it, it is impossible to argue for the absence of superimposition in the present case by using that as an analogy. It might be argued: "One who defines 'self-luminosity' must necessarily define its proof, such as 'being an object of cognition' (*dṛśyatva*). Indeed, without a cognition of a distinct form unmixed with [other objects] like pots or cloths, there can be no usage (*vyavahāra*) distinguished from them. If you say that this is established merely by a cognition of an unmixed form, even if that form itself is not defined, then the same applies to my position as well."

However, there is this distinction: that [nature] of yours is characterized as being distinct from the real (*sad-vilakṣaṇa*), whereas for me, it possesses a reality established by cognition that proves its distinction from the *prātibhāsika* (illusory) existence admitted in your own system. For the loss or gain of the status of being "indefinable" (*anirvacanīya*)—defined as being distinct from both the real and the unreal—does not depend on whether a definition is stated or not; for even in the case of Brahman, a definition such as "being the cause of the world," though found in the Śrutis, is impossible when analyzed according to the method of refuting causality. As you yourself have said: "If one asks what that inner self (*pratyagātman*) is like, the two notions 'it is thus' and 'it is so' do not apply to it; therein one should ascertain: 'This is the inner self.'"* *Note: This verse is cited from Śaṅkara’s *Upadeśasāhasrī* (18.230).*

Furthermore, because it has been stated that even Brahman is difficult to define, and because characteristics equivalent to the "indefinability" (anirvācyatva) you have asserted can be found even within the phenomenal world (prapañca), and because scriptures such as "That which is hard is earth" state that characteristics apply to earth and the other elements as well; therefore, indefinability is not incompatible with existence.

Even if it were existent, its being inexpressible is established precisely because it is a marvel; nor is expressibility a necessary condition for existence, for the "silver-ness" of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell—though easily describable as a phenomenal universal that establishes its difference from other things—is not real. Furthermore, according to the method of the *Khaṇḍana*, Brahman’s blissfulness, consciousness, reality, self-luminosity, and so forth are difficult to define; thus, Brahman would in truth be non-blissful and so on by nature.

Therefore, just like the sweetness of sugarcane, milk, and so forth, objectivity (viṣayatva) exists as a reality even if it is inexpressible (anirvacanīya). To this, it is replied: Is the inexpressibility of "being an object" (dṛśyatva) and the like due to its existence (sattva), or rather due to its own nature (svarūpa)? It cannot be the first, because even if it is inexpressible by way of existence, the status of being a logical reason (hetutva) is established merely by its not being characterized by those respective fallacious appearances (ābhāsa); thus, there is no requirement for its verbal definition.

The second [alternative] is not tenable, because the state of being an object of vision can be defined by a form common to both the real and the unreal, such as "being related to vision" (*dṛksambandhitva*) and so forth.
