As for what you said—that whether or not a definition is stated does not result in the loss or gain of the status of being "inexpressible" (*anirvacanīya*), which consists in being distinct from both the existent and the non-existent—that too is incorrect; for the failure to define the characteristic, when conjoined with the previously mentioned non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*), serves as the logical ground for that very form of inexpressibility.

As for the objection that Brahman would also face the consequence of being indefinable because it is difficult to define either by its attributes, such as blissfulness (*ānandatva*), or by its essential nature (*svarūpa*)—as in "of what kind is it? and so forth—that is not so; for even if it is difficult to define by way of possessing attributes like blissfulness, its essential nature, as characterized by the state of being the opposite of suffering (*duḥkhapratyanīkatva*) and so on, can indeed be defined by virtue of its existence. However, existence cannot be thus defined in the case of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), because of the presence of subverting evidence (*bādhaka*).

Therefore, the following objection is refuted: "Since there is indeed a definition of 'earth-ness' and so forth by means of its possession of a hard touch and other such qualities, it is possible for something to be indefinable even while existing, simply by virtue of its being a wonder (adbhuta) and so forth. For we do not assert that indefinability consists merely in the absence of a verbal definition; rather, we maintain it consists in the absence of a definition in terms of existence (*sattva*) and other such categories.

And that [superimposition] certainly exists within the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) because there is a sublation [of it]. Nor should it be argued: "Since the object is superimposed upon consciousness (*jñāna*), it is impossible for the phenomenal world such as a jar to be the object of that superimposition—which is produced by the ignorance (*ajñāna*) of that [consciousness] and is removable by the knowledge of that [consciousness]—and it is also impossible for it not to be perceived as permeated by that [consciousness]. This is because it has already been stated that the phenomenal world of jars and so forth is produced by the ignorance of pure Consciousness (*caitanyamātra*) and is removable by the knowledge of that [Consciousness]. Furthermore, it is indeed the case that it is perceived as permeated by the Consciousness that serves as the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*), which is itself perceived as "Being" (*sat*).

Therefore, the impossibility of a relationship between the seer and the seen in the case of an existent entity is indeed firm. Thus ends the exposition of the reasoning conducive to the falsity of the phenomenal world (*prapañca-mithyātva*) in the *Advaitasiddhi*.
Thus ends the first part of the first chapter in the Advaitasiddhi composed by the venerable Madhusūdana Sarasvatī.

Now, an objection may be raised: if the universe is merely superimposed (*adhyāsika*), then—just as in the case of an illusory object (*prātibhāsika*)—the "determination according to each object" (*pratikarmavyavasthā*), which depends upon the contact between the sense organ and its object, would be untenable. If this is argued, we say no. This is because the mental modification (*vṛtti*) differs from the case of an illusory object, since jars and other objects have already been superimposed upon Consciousness (*caitanya*). To explain: the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) consists of light, like the eye; through the medium of the sense organ, it pervades the object with which it is in contact and assumes that object's form.

Just as the water of a river and so forth, having issued from a channel, takes on the form of a field and the like—that very state is called a "mode" (vṛtti). In this regard, there are two views: that the consciousness of the individual soul (jīvacaitanya), being conditioned by ignorance (avidyopādhika), is all-pervading; and that, being conditioned by the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇopādhika), it is limited. Among these, in the first view, the consciousness of the individual soul is the illuminator of objects; in the second, it is the consciousness of Brahman (brahmacaitanya). Even in the first position, the consciousness of the individual soul is both unobscured and obscured by ignorance.

In the first case, the function [of the mental mode] is for the purpose of bringing about the coloring of the object by the living consciousness (jīvacaitanya). In the second case, however, it is for the purpose of overcoming the veil (āvaraṇa). But in the view that [the self] is limited (paricchinna), it is for the purpose of manifesting the non-difference between the living consciousness and the consciousness that serves as its substrate, which illuminates the object.

For in the view that [the self] is unobstructed, the consciousness of the living being (jīvacaitanya), though all-pervading, becomes colored only by the mental modification (vṛtti) assuming the form of a particular object, and not by the objects themselves, because of its non-attachment (asaṅgatva). Just as the universal "cowness" (gotva), though all-pervading, is manifested only by an individual possessing a dewlap and so forth, and not by an individual possessing a mane and so forth; or just as the light of a lamp, although pervading space, smell, taste, and so on, does not illuminate them but illuminates only color (rūpa) due to its contact with color—so it is here.

Just as even that which is not combustible by fire alone may be burnt when fire is applied to it via a lump of iron or similar medium, so too it is logical that objects such as a jar—which are not manifestable by consciousness alone—may be manifested by consciousness when that consciousness is mounted upon a mental modification (*vṛtti*) in the form of those respective objects. Thus, in the view that [consciousness] is unobscured, the manifestation of each object occurs through the coloring (*uparāga*) of consciousness by means of a mental modification in the form of that object. In the view that it is obscured, the manifestation of each object occurs through the suppression of the obscuration of consciousness delimited by that respective object by means of a mental modification in the form of that object.

Since the individual soul (*jīva*) consists of consciousness delimited by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), there occurs the manifestation of consciousness delimited by various objects through the mental modification (*vṛtti*) taking on the form of those respective objects and their corresponding internal organs; thus, there is the illumination of those respective objects.

Although the foundational consciousness (*adhiṣṭhāna-caitanya*), which is the illuminator, is all-pervading, while the consciousness of the individual soul is delimited by the internal organ, nevertheless, because they are manifested as non-different from consciousness, this systematic distinction is logically established.

Now, an objection is raised: this systematic arrangement regarding individual objects of cognition (*pratikarmavyavasthā*) is untenable. To explain: if a jar or the like exists prior to its own cognition—which is produced by a sense organ in proximity to it—then it cannot be "imaginary" (*kālpnika*), as being imaginary is pervaded by having a nature consisting solely of cognition. Nor is it the case that only specific types of imaginaries, such as those that are illusory (*prātibhāsika*), are so pervaded, because that would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*). Furthermore, even if it lacks the nature of consisting solely of cognition, its status as imagined might still be established simply through its being sublatable by knowledge (*jñānanivartyatva*) and so forth.

If it is argued that the absence of being produced by knowledge must also be established because there is an absence of having a body consisting of mere cognition; or that since all cognition is true, even if [the world] were false, it could be accounted for—like dreams and so forth—as being independent of sensory contact; or that its empirical reality (*vyāvahārikatva*) could be accounted for merely through the persistence of delusion—[we reply]: not so. For having a body consisting of mere cognition does not entail being imagined (*kalpitatva*).

Once the illusory nature (*kalpitatva*) of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) has been established through the aforementioned inference—supported by arguments such as the impossibility of a relationship between the seer and the seen—and its persistence established on the strength of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), [the opponent’s objection] falls into contradiction precisely therein. Nor should it be argued that the recognition in question is equivalent to the recognition of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell; for although there is no difference in the mode of cognition, a distinction exists between the silver in a market stall and [the world], insofar as the former is examined and the latter is not, resulting in the difference between persistence and non-persistence.

If it is argued: "Even so, let the manifestation [of the object] occur through the immediate mental modification (*aparokṣavṛtti*) just as it does through the mediate one (*parokṣavṛtti*); what is the need for consciousness colored by that [modification]?"—this is not correct. For even in the case of mediate objects, it is consciousness itself, as colored by the mediate modification, that acts as the manifester. Now, if it is further argued: "In that case too, if there were coloring by consciousness whose essence is immediate (*aparokṣaikarasacaitanya*), it would follow that the object is immediately perceived"—this is not so. An object is immediately perceived only when the consciousness of the object is manifested; and this does not occur in the case of mediate objects.

Because there is no contact between the sense organ and the object, the mental modification (*vṛtti*) does not extend as far as the object; rather, cognition arises there within [the self] alone. In the case of direct perception (*aparokṣa*), however, there is an coloring by the substrate-consciousness, which is manifested as non-different from the consciousness of the knower (*pramātṛ-caitanya*), with respect to the object. This is because, in that case, the object functions as the objective factor (*karmakāraka*). Nor is directness due to a particularity residing in the mental modification. For if that particularity were produced by the object, we would say "yes"; but a particularity produced by the genus (*jāti*) is not possible.

Because in the case of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) in the form "this is that," there would follow the undesirable consequence of a confusion between mediacy (*parokṣatva*) and immediacy (*aparokṣatva*); because [these properties] do not subsist pervasively (*avyāpyavṛttitva*); and because there would also follow the undesirable consequence of a confusion among [properties such as] being a valid cognition (*pramātva*).

Furthermore, because mental modification (*vṛtti*) is insentient (*jaḍa*), it cannot possess the quality of being a self-luminous illuminator. Nor should it be argued that, although the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) undergoes modification, the modification itself possesses self-luminosity just as it possesses the nature of knowledge (*jñānatva*). For its status as an illumination is established solely through its connection with the self-luminous Self; there is no evidence for its own inherent self-luminosity. Moreover, distinct from the object-directed modification experienced in the form "I know the jar," there exists a consciousness in the form of the illumination of the jar, which is established by the experience "the jar is manifest."

One should not argue that, because we observe that verbs such as *karoti* (he does), *yatate* (he strives), *calati* (he moves), and *gacchati* (he goes) possess both transitive and intransitive natures despite having a single meaning, the same should apply here [to the case of *asti*] even though it has a single meaning. For even in those cases, there is no single meaning. Indeed, the meaning of the root *kṛ* is effort conducive to an action (*anukūlayatna*), whereas the meaning of *yat* is merely effort (*yatnamātra*). Similarly, the meaning of *gam* is motion (*spanda*) resulting in posterior conjunction (*uttarasaṃyoga*), whereas the meaning of *cal* is merely motion (*spandamātra*).

And likewise, if they have the same meaning, there would be no distinction anywhere between being transitive (*sakarmaka*) and intransitive (*akarmaka*). Nor should it be argued: "In your view, since transformation (*pariṇati*) is intransitive, how can the mental modification (*vṛtti*), which is a specific form of transformation, be transitive? For while transitivity and intransitivity are contradictory in a single form, they are not contradictory even in different forms, as there is no evidence [to the contrary].

Just as persistence (*sthiti*), though itself devoid of an object (*akarmikā*), possesses the status of having an object (*sakarmakatva*) by virtue of its nature as "not going," so too, although the mental modification (*vṛtti*) is devoid of an object by virtue of its nature as transformation (*pariṇati*), it will possess the status of having an object by virtue of its nature as cognition (*jñāna*); thus there is no fault. [Objection: In that case, the cognition "the past shines forth" would not occur. [Response: This is acceptable, for we admit this consequence; moreover, even in that case, since consciousness exists as reflected in the mental modification, the usage "it shines forth" and so on is possible.

[Objection: But surely, just as the nature of being an experience (anubhavatva) does not reside in the mental state that is the opposite of ignorance, but rather elsewhere, so too the nature of desire (icchātva) might reside elsewhere than in the mental state that is the opposite of aversion. [Reply: This is not so, because there is a distinction based on the presence or absence of subverting evidence (bādhaka), and because, just as here, there is no experience of an action in that case which is distinct from being either transitive or intransitive. Furthermore, we shall explain in detail under the discussion of self-luminosity (svayaṃjyotiṣṭva) how the manifestation of consciousness is established as being distinct from the mental state (vṛtti).

Now, one might object: let it be granted that consciousness possesses the capacity to illuminate objects; nevertheless, the departure of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) from the body need not be postulated. To account for the distinction between perception and non-perception, it must simply be stated that there is a contact of the object with a manifest and immediate consciousness. And regarding such contact with consciousness, the essential factor is merely the modification of the immediate mental state (vṛtti) into the form of that object.

And for that [cognition], even without contact with that [object], its occurrence is explained simply by its being produced by a sense-organ in proximity to it—just as in the case of indirect (parokṣa) cognition; however, contact with it is not the decisive factor for the modification (vṛtti), such as the removal of its veil, as it is in the case of light. This is because, by means of the modification itself in the form of Dhruva and so forth emerging from the eye, there is the perception of the collyrium located in the eye itself, which is situated between the eye and Dhruva.

If it is argued that this would lead to the undesirable consequence of atoms and the like becoming directly perceived, we say no. In the case of objects, it is not merely the assumption of the form of the object by consciousness when it is reflected upon that is the determining factor for direct perception; for if that were the case, it would follow even in instances of indirect (parokṣa) cognition. Rather, what is required is a close contact (*saṃśleṣa*) with the object. This is because light, being a luminous substance in close proximity to an object, is observed to dispel the veil of darkness. Likewise, for the luminous mind to dispel the veil of ignorance, such close contact with the object is indispensable.

As for the over-extension [of this principle] to atoms and so forth situated within the body of Dhruva and others, it must be avoided precisely because of the absence of the causal complex that necessitates the assumption of their form; otherwise, since the contact of the sense organs and other factors would be present, the assumption of the form of atoms and such would become unavoidable. Therefore, although there is a dependence on a specific feature—namely, the taking on of that particular form—the capacity to overcome obstructions, which is established through positive and negative concomitance as belonging to light in general (just like radiance), is not abandoned.

For when the causal relation between earth-ness, odor-ness, and so forth is necessary, there can be no abandonment of that relation on account of [broader categories] such as being an impermanent quality or being a substance. Therefore, the following argument is refuted: "When all other causes are present, it is only the contact between the eye and the jar that generates the experience of the jar, and not the contact between the mind and the jar, because there is no delay in the latter even when the former is delayed. This is because, upon the removal of obstructions, it is determined that light is a cause [of perception], and thus that [contact with the mind] is also necessarily required.

Nor should it be argued that, because tactile perception lacks a fixed physical aperture like the eyes and other senses, the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) cannot exit [the body], and thus the sublation of the veil (*āvaraṇa*) is impossible. This is because in every case, the respective seat of the sense organ itself can serve as the gateway. Nor should it be asked: "Since there is no difference in their being modifications (*vṛtti*) of the internal organ, why is it not accepted that modifications in the form of desire, aversion, and so forth also exit the body and come into contact with their objects?
For, unlike the case of knowledge (*jñāna*), there is no evidence—such as its being a light that sublates the veil—to prove that such [emotional] states possess that nature.

Now, is the consciousness that illuminates the jar the consciousness abiding in the cognition taking the form of the jar, according to the *Upadeśasāhasrī*; or is it the consciousness as the substratum of the object, wherein the non-difference from the consciousness reflected in the cognition is manifested, according to the method stated in the *Vārttika* beginning with "In the case of objects of knowledge external [to the self]" (*parāgarthaprameyeṣu*)? It cannot be the first, because it would follow that the superimpositional relationship (*ādhyāsika-sambandha*) is not a necessary factor. Nor can it be the second.

If it is argued that since the removal of ignorance regarding an object and the manifestation of that object are both accomplished by the consciousness reflected in the mental modification (vṛtti) which is in contact with the object—namely, through the *āvaśyaka* [necessary] factor—what is the purpose of postulating the manifestation of the consciousness that underlies the object? This is not so. First, the consciousness that is the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) is the illuminator. Furthermore, through superimposition (*adhyāsa*), it is directly connected with the objects. Moreover, for a light that manifests itself, its capacity to illuminate everything with which it is connected is already established as a matter of fact.

For if this were not accepted, another conceptualization would result in the fault of unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*). Furthermore, that [consciousness], being unmanifest and of the nature of indeterminate perception (*nirvikalpaka*), does not illuminate like a lamp covered by a cloth; thus, its manifestation is required. In the case of an object beyond the senses (*parokṣa*), it is manifested precisely through the limitation imposed by the mental modification (*vṛtti*). In the case of an object present to the senses (*aparokṣa*), however, the object is manifested when the dullness [of consciousness] has been overcome through contact with the mental modification, because the modification extends as far as the object itself. Nor does the same consequence follow even in the case of an object beyond the senses.

Because there is no exit of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) due to the absence of a door [through which it could pass]. Now, an objection is raised: the "having the form of that" (*tadākāratva*) of a mental modification (*vṛtti*) cannot mean "having that as its object," since you yourself have rejected that. Nor can it mean "producing a fitness for the superimposition of consciousness (*caitanya*) upon that [object]," or "the capacity to suppress ignorance (*ajñāna*) regarding that. For both of these would be dependent upon the very state of "having the form of that," and thus they cannot logically serve as its definition. Nor can it mean "having a form such as a broad base and belly like a jar," because that would entail the fallacy of admitting a theory of forms (*sākāravāda*). Furthermore, it would follow that modifications concerning universals (*jāti*), qualities (*guṇa*), and so forth—which lack spatial configuration—would be devoid of form.

If it is argued that [the cognition] "a pot and a cloth" would result in the occurrence of multiple contradictory forms during a collective apprehension (*samūhālambana*), we say no. This is because having that form consists either in the capacity to remove the ignorance that obstructs the linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) regarding the object—such as the thought "it exists"—or in being produced by a sense-organ in contact with that object. Both of these depend on a specific nature (*svabhāvaviśeṣa*) derived from their own causes. Nor is there the fallacy of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*), because the actualization of the result is what is to be established by way of the capacity for producing the removal [of ignorance], and thus does not depend upon itself.

Now, an objection is raised: for one who accepts the superimposition of objects upon consciousness, is it the individual consciousness (*jīvacaitanya*) that perceives the object, or the consciousness of Brahman (*brahmacaitanya*)? It cannot be the first, because superimposition is impossible upon the individual self, which is a limited form of consciousness (*avacchinnacitsvarūpa*) and thus merely imagined (*kalpita*). Nor can it be said that the perceiver of the object is indeed the individual consciousness, while the superimposition belongs to the consciousness of Brahman; for this would result in a relation of superimposition between two things that are both perceived (*dṛśya*), since both the superimposed and the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) would be distinct from the act of seeing itself (*dṛk*). For this very reason, the second alternative is also untenable.

Furthermore, since even the qualified Brahman (*saviśeṣabrahman*) is imagined (*kalpita*), superimposition (*adhyāsa*) upon it is impossible. Nor can it be argued that pure consciousness alone is one and the same, and that this alone is the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*). In that case, limiting adjuncts such as ignorance (*avidyā*) do not enter into the category of the substratum itself. And it is that very [consciousness] which is designated by the terms "jīva" and "Brahman" due to specific limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). Thus, even though the consciousness of the individual soul (*jīvacaitanya*) is the seer, the superimposition of the seen (*dṛśya*) upon it is not untenable. This is what must be said.

If it is argued that this is not so, because pure consciousness would result in the blindness of the world due to being veiled from the beginningless cycle of transmigration (saṃsāra), we say no. For although there is no total removal of the veil due to the absence of the cessation of root-ignorance (mūlāvidyā), and thus no complete overcoming of the veil everywhere, the absence of blindness is nonetheless established because the veil is overcome with respect to specific delimiters such as a jar. Now, if that is the case, even now, when Brahman is manifest, the final meditative state (caramavṛtti) would be useless; for Brahman is already manifest even during the perception of further objects.

If it is argued that in the mental modification (*vṛtti*) produced by the Vedānta texts—which have an impartite meaning—neither existence nor non-existence appears as a qualifier, an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*), or a mode (*prakāra*), we say no. For the manifestation of Brahman free from limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) is brought about by the final cognitive activity, and thus that [manifestation] is fruitful. Furthermore, the non-appearance of modes is actually an ornament of that [manifestation], because the manifestation occurring at present possesses modes and therefore has the limiting adjuncts as its object.

This is because, by the force of scriptural passages such as "It is to be perceived as one alone," and because it is determined that knowledge of the undivided pure consciousness alone is the cause of liberation—since ignorance is removed precisely by a cognition whose object is identical to its own—[the Self is not the individual soul]. Nor should it be argued that if the consciousness limited by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) were the individual soul (*jīva*), then in the state of deep sleep, due to the absence of that [limitation], there would follow the loss of merit performed and other such consequences; for even then, this [consciousness] persists in the form of its cause, since the internal organ serves as a limiting adjunct in both its gross and subtle states.

Furthermore, this meaning is even clearer in the sūtra: "And [the soul remains distinct] until that [liberation], because of the designation of transmigratory existence. Nor should it be argued that consciousness being colored by a mental mode (*vṛtti*) does not mean it is reflected therein; for, just as a face is reflected in a mirror, it is impossible for consciousness—which is not visible—to be reflected in the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), which lacks manifest color and thus cannot serve as an adjunct (*upādhi*) for the reflection of sound or other objects. This is because possessing manifest color is not the necessary condition for being an adjunct for reflection; otherwise, reflection would absurdly follow even in opaque objects like clods of earth.

Rather, it is transparency (*svacchatva*). This exists indeed in the mind (*manas*) and its modification (*vṛtti*), because they possess the nature of light (*prakāśasvabhāvatva*); for even ignorance (*ajñāna*), though composed of the three *guṇas*, possesses the nature of the transparent *sattva*, and thus it too serves as a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) for reflection. Furthermore, visibility (*cākṣuṣatva*) is not the determinant of being reflected, since we observe that even non-visible things such as space (*ākāśa*) are reflected.

Now, an objection may be raised: how can consciousness, when mounted upon a visual modification (*cākṣuṣavṛtti*), be the illuminator of form alone? Nor can it be argued that there is a restriction [to form] as in the case of light, for the two cases are dissimilar. To explain: in the case of light, its opposition to darkness is the same with respect to smell and other qualities as it is with respect to form; for light does not fail to remove the darkness located in the place where a smell resides. Furthermore, it cannot be said that the nature of being an illuminator—defined as the opposition to ignorance (*ajñāna*)—applies only to form and not to taste and the rest.

This is because the removal of ignorance is not admitted to occur in anything other than a mental modification (vṛtti). Just as light acts as an auxiliary to the eye—which perceives color—it does not act as an auxiliary to the sense of smell or other organs which perceive odor and so forth; yet, since consciousness has no other perceiver to assist it, it is impossible to argue that there is a delay [in the removal of ignorance] due to a delay in such an auxiliary, as in the case of the eye.

And thus, because consciousness (*cit*) is omnipresent, it is connected with everything; consequently, like color and other qualities, even weight and the like would result in being manifested, whether by way of their substratum or directly, since it is only the connection with consciousness as qualified by a mental modification (*vṛtti*) that constitutes manifestation. As for the scriptural text, "For this Puruṣa is unattached" (*asaṅgo hyayaṃ puruṣaḥ*), it refers to the absence of any stain caused by those [objects] in the case of the Lord (*īśvara*), but it does not negate [all] connection.

If it is argued that this is because of the preceding scriptural passage, "Whatever he sees there, he remains untouched by that," and because of Smṛti texts such as, "Just as the great wind, omnipresent, eternally abides in space," we say no.

It is logical that light, through its connection [with objects], destroys darkness located in space along with color, taste, and other qualities; however, since consciousness is by nature unconnected, how could there be the undesirable consequence of it illuminating other things? For, because it is unconnected by nature, the scripture provides the authority: "For this Puruṣa is indeed unattached. Nor is this [scriptural statement] intended merely to deny the possibility of being stained; rather, it is intended to show the absence of connection in order to establish his non-agency. How this is so has been clearly explained in the authoritative sources (*ākara*).

In this way, memory (*smṛti*) must also be understood in accordance with this scriptural authority. Therefore, because there is no connection with all [objects], there is no manifestation of everything; rather, there is a manifestation only of that whose form the mental modification (*vṛtti*) assumes. For this very reason, in the error "this is silver," since it would be impossible for the silver to appear through the consciousness delimited by the mental modification having the form of "this" (*idam-ākāra-vṛtti*), one must also admit a mental modification of ignorance (*avidyā-vṛtti*) having the form of silver. This is because, when [the mind] does not grasp the reflection of consciousness (*cid-bimba*) itself, it is impossible for the consciousness to assume the form of that [silver].

However, in the case of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), its modifications (*vṛtti*), and so forth—which grasp the reflection of consciousness (*cidbimba*) by themselves—there is no requirement for a further modification; thus, there is no infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Nor should it be asked: "Even though the connection with the substrate (*āśraya*) is the same, why is a modification taking the form of color (*rūpa*) and not the form of smell (*gandha*) and so forth? For just as in your view, even though the connection with the substrate is the same in visual cognition, smell is not its object, so too in our view, a modification occurring through the door of the eye does not take the form of smell and the like. This is because the nature (*svabhāva*) of the relationship between the sense organs and their objects, which acts as the regulator, is identical in both cases.

[Objection: But surely the superimposed relation exists even prior to the mental modification (*vṛtti*); since another kind of coloring (*uparāga*) is not the determinant for perceptibility, what is the purpose of that *vṛtti*? [Reply: No, because the *vṛtti* is for the sake of manifesting the non-difference between the consciousness of the individual self (*jīvacaitanya*) and the consciousness of the substrate (*adhiṣṭhānacaitanya*). Otherwise, the manifestation of the relation "this has been known by me" would not occur.

Objection: If the consciousness of the individual soul (*jīvacaitanya*) is non-associated (*asaṅga*), then the consciousness of Brahman must likewise be non-associated. And in that case, because it would lack the coloring by objects due to the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of *māyā*, its innate omniscience would not be possible. Nor can it be argued that Brahman, being the material cause (*upādāna*) of everything, manifests the world—which is non-different from itself—without any adjunct, just as it manifests its own nature. For material causality does not consist in undergoing transformation (*pariṇāmitva*) residing in the qualified [Brahman], since that would render the illusory superimposition (*ādhyāsika-sambandha*) irrelevant, and because such causality is absent in relation to beginningless ignorance (*avidyā*) and the like.

Nor can it be argued that being the locus (*adhiṣṭhānatva*) does not reside in the pure [Brahman], because the pure lacks omniscience, omnipotence, and so forth. This is not so; for even though Brahman is unattached (*asaṅga*), since everything is superimposed upon it, its status as the illuminator of all is established, and thus its omniscience is logically consistent even without the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of Māyā. Nor should it be said that being the locus residing in the pure cannot be the material cause (*upādānatva*) due to the absence of omniscience; for omniscience and other such qualities, though fashioned by ignorance (*avidyā*), do exist in the pure [Brahman].

Otherwise, they would not even possess the status of being extrinsic characteristics (*taṭasthalakṣaṇa*). Now, it may be argued that the position that [the purpose of the *tattvamasi* teaching] is the suppression of concealment is not tenable; for pure consciousness, as the substrate of the illusory manifestation (*vivarta-adhiṣṭhāna*), is always manifest as the witness (*sākṣin*) of ignorance and so forth, and there is no other concealment imagined by ignorance [to be suppressed]. To this we say: no. Even though [consciousness] is self-luminous as the witness of ignorance and so forth, there is an absence of manifestation insofar as it transcends hunger and the like; therefore, concealment is necessary.

Objection: If ignorance resides in the person (the subject), like a film over the eye, then even when Caitra’s ignorance is destroyed, it would be logical that there is no manifestation for Maitra, since that [ignorance] has not been destroyed in him. However, if it resides in the object, then when the ignorance is destroyed by the cognitive modification (*vṛtti*) produced by Caitra—just as darkness is destroyed by a lamp—there would be manifestation for Maitra as well. Reply: This is not so. It is only the power of concealment residing in the ignorance that belongs to Caitra which is destroyed by the modification produced by Caitra; therefore, he sees, but Maitra does not, because the power of concealment relative to him has not been destroyed.

This is because the powers of concealment (*āvaraṇa-śakti*) are distinct due to the differences between the subject (*draṣṭṛ*) and the object (*viṣaya*), whereas darkness (*tamas*) is not so; thus, it is logical that even by means of a lamp brought for one person, there may be illumination for another. By this, the following objections are refuted: (1) in the view that there is a single ignorance (*ekājñāna-pakṣa*), if that ignorance were removed by the knowledge of mother-of-pearl (*śukti-jñāna*), liberation would immediately follow; and (2) if it were not removed, the sublation (*bādha*)—which consists in the removal of ignorance along with its manifestations (*savilāsa-avidyā*) regarding silver and the like—would be impossible.

This is because, although the power of concealment is destroyed, since the root ignorance (*mūlājñāna*) has not been destroyed, there is no immediate liberation, and yet the sublation in the case of silver and the like is logically established as the removal of ignorance together with its manifesting power.

Now, [the opponent might argue: "On the view that there is only one ignorance (*ekājñānapakṣa*), the cognition of mother-of-pearl merely effects the dissolution of the silver and so forth into its own cause, just as the blow of a mallet effects the dissolution of a jar; it is not the case that ignorance is sublated. This position of yours is not tenable, because by the force of the universal rule (*vyāpti*) that "cognition is the sublater of ignorance alone," it is impossible for cognition to sublate silver and so forth without first sublatting ignorance, since cognition stands in opposition to other things only through the mediation of the sublation of ignorance.

If it is argued that if ignorance were not removed by the cognition of the mother-of-pearl, then even upon sublation—as in the case of an error—the mother-of-pearl would fail to appear because of the absence of a connection with manifested consciousness, we say no; for the pervasion (vyāpti) that "cognition is the remover of ignorance" has as its scope only [ignorance] in its state of being destroyed. This is because we do not admit that [ignorance] persists in a subtle form within its own cause.

Furthermore, although the cognition of mother-of-pearl does not remove the *mūlājñāna* (root ignorance), which consists in the obscuration of the undifferentiated consciousness (*anavacchinna-caitanya*), it does remove the *tūlājñāna* (trunk ignorance), which consists in the obscuration of the limited consciousness (*avacchinna-caitanya*). Consequently, because of its connection with the manifested consciousness, the cessation of the illusory silver and the manifestation of the mother-of-pearl are both logically established at the time of sublation. Nor should it be argued that the suppression of the material cause (*avidyā*) by its effect, the mental modification (*vṛtti*), is impossible, since one never observes the material cause being suppressed by its own effect. This objection cannot stand.

Since we observe that even cow dung and the like are overcome by scorpions and other creatures, and because the theory of new production (*ārambhavāda*) is not accepted, there is no suspicion that the particles of cow dung constitute the material cause (*upādāna*).

Is it not the case that your position is untenable? For, although the modification (*vṛtti*) produced by the eye and other senses regarding mother-of-pearl and the like—which possesses a specific mode (*saprakārikā*)—does not have pure consciousness (*śuddhacaitanya*) as its object (and thus cannot suppress the root ignorance which consists in the concealment of that), it is nevertheless logical that this modification, having the delimited [consciousness] as its object, should suppress the "tuft-ignorance" (*tūlājñāna*) which consists in the concealment of the delimited consciousness. This is because it is impossible for the power of concealment belonging to root-ignorance to apply to that which is delimited, imagined by ignorance, and where illumination has not yet occurred; furthermore, you yourself do not accept this.

If it is argued that, upon the admission of that [ignorance] with respect to a Self qualified by insentience, the sublation of the power that obscures the qualifier cannot occur without the sublation of the power that obscures the substantive (the Self), and thus the pure Self would necessarily be manifested by the very mental modification (*vṛtti*) in the form of the mother-of-pearl—this is not so, because of a lack of understanding. For we do not admit that ignorance or its power resides in the "delimited" (*avacchinna*) Self which is imagined by ignorance.

However, we do not admit that ignorance (*avidyā*) or its power resides in a limited entity imagined by ignorance; rather, it resides in pure consciousness alone. Since all inert matter is superimposed upon that [consciousness], there arises the designation "consciousness as delimited by the inert" due to the relationship of being the locus and that which is located therein. When the consciousness that is the substrate of that [inert object] is manifested through a mental modification (*vṛtti*) in the form of a jar or the like, the sublation of the concealment residing therein occurs precisely through that delimitation; thus, there is no contingency of the pure Self becoming manifest. As it has been said in the *Saṃkṣepaśārīraka*:
Indivisible consciousness alone possesses both the nature of the substratum and the object;
for that which arises later cannot be the substratum nor the object of darkness that is already established.
What is the use of speaking much here? Listen to the summary of the non-dual teaching:
Consciousness transcends all speech and mind, yet it is the locus of all activity of speech and mind.

And thus: therefore, even while ignorance (avidyā) persists, the occurrence of liberation and the sublation [of bondage] is possible—either through the suppression of its power, or through the destruction of the "cotton-wool" ignorance (tūlājñāna), or through the departure of a particular state, or through the destruction of a portion [of ignorance], or through the withdrawal [of ignorance] like a timid soldier, or through its envelopment like a mat, or through the breaking of the veil.

Objection: If the specific states (*avasthā-viśeṣa*) are non-different from ignorance (*ajñāna*), then the position that there is only one ignorance is undermined. If they are different from ignorance, then they would not be directly sublated by knowledge, nor could they be the material cause (*upādāna*) of error and the like. Furthermore, just as with those [states], it would follow that the silver itself could perish even without the destruction of its material cause; and this would contradict the experience that "the ignorance of the shell has perished. Reply: This is not so. For a state is indeed non-different from that which possesses the state. However, the unity of ignorance is established by taking into account the single form that persists through all the states.

Thus, since the state of ignorance is itself ignorance, there is no inconsistency in its being directly sublated by knowledge. As for the objection that, like specific states [of ignorance], the silver itself must cease without the cessation of its material cause (the substrate), that is incorrect. For it is determined that knowledge is directly opposed to ignorance alone; therefore, since the state of ignorance is non-different from that [ignorance], it is fit to be directly sublated by knowledge. This, however, does not apply to the silver and such, as they are not of that nature. Moreover, in the view that there are multiple instances of ignorance, even this doubt does not arise.

Now, in this view, does the cessation of all ignorance regarding that object occur through a single mental modification (*vṛtti*), or the cessation of ignorance regarding only one [part] of it? In the first case, there would never again be a lack of manifestation for the shell. In the second case, there would be no manifestation even at the time of the modification, because although one veil has ceased, other veils have not. If you say this, we reply: No. Even though a single ignorance is destroyed by a single modification, by that very modification the other veils are obstructed; as long as that modification persists, there is manifestation.

When that [knowledge] has departed, darkness arises once again, because ignorance occupies the place of the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of knowledge. Just as, according to you, one single cognition destroys only one prior non-existence—since it arises in the form of that destruction—and thereby obstructs the linguistic usage of "unknown-ness" and so forth which is based on another prior non-existence; so too, according to me, one single cognition removes only one ignorance and obstructs the purpose (or effect) based on another ignorance. What is there that is untenable here? And in this regard:

By the term "obstruction" (*pratibandha*), that which causes the non-production of an effect—common to both the absence of a cause and a counteracting agent—is expressed. In this way, even in the view that [the obstruction] is a particular state, the manifestation and non-manifestation [of the object] are to be explained. Likewise, although for formless ignorance it is not possible to have it "removed" like cows by a staff or the like, nor to have it "wrapped up" like mats by the hands and so forth, nevertheless, the two positions of removal and wrapping are to be applied on the basis of the commonality of its being incapable of producing an effect.

Just as a gem possesses the capacity to obstruct when accompanied by the absence of an activator (uttejaka), yet becomes incapable of performing that obstructive function when the activator is present, so too it should be understood that ignorance possesses the capacity to obstruct when accompanied by the absence of a mental modification (vṛtti), yet its obstructive effect does not arise when the modification is present.

But surely, since consciousness (*caitanya*) is partless, its illumination by way of a single part is not tenable. If, on the other hand, the meaning of the term "part" is merely being delimited by this or that object—just as with space—then consciousness delimited by adventitious objects cannot be the object of beginningless ignorance (*anādyajñāna*), because an obscuration without an object is impossible. Nor can it be said that what was previously an unconditioned obscuration has now become a conditioned obscuration; for this would entail the destruction of the unconditioned obscuration simply through the knowledge of the conditioned consciousness.

If it is argued that by this [argument] the claim that "ignorance exists prior to the object, just as a genus exists prior to the individual" is refuted, we say no; for it is accepted that beginningless consciousness has beginningless ignorance as its object, through the delimitation (*avaccheda*) by various adventitious entities. This is because it has been stated: "The indivisible consciousness alone is the possessor of both the state of being the locus (*āśrayatva*) and the state of being the object (*viṣayatva*). Furthermore, since the removal of the veil occurs only through the delimitation by that very [entity] which serves as the object of the mental modification (*vṛtti*), there is no contingency of destroying the veil over the undelimited consciousness.

For this very reason, with the intention that ignorance exists prior to the consciousness delimited by the object of the mental modification (*vṛtti*), it was rightly stated that "ignorance exists prior to the object. Therefore, it is established that the consciousness which is the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*) illumines that which is superimposed upon itself.

This is the summary here: although the consciousness that is the substrate of the object is the consciousness of the object of knowledge (*prameya-caitanya*) which illumines the object, the consciousness delimited by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is its knower (*pramātṛ*), and the consciousness delimited by the mental modification (*antaḥkaraṇa-vṛtti*) is the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

Nevertheless, that very consciousness which illumines [an object]—having issued forth through the eyes and other sense organs via a modification (*vṛtti*) of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) extending as far as the object—is manifested as non-different from the consciousness of the respective knower (*pramātṛcaitanya*). That [knower] alone knows that [object], and no one else; nor does anyone else know it. For this very reason, the consciousness of the knower, the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), and the object of knowledge (*prameya*), having attained a state of oneness characterized by being mounted upon a single mental modification (*ekavṛttyupārūḍhatva*), becomes unified. Consequently, the consciousness of the object of knowledge, appearing through the cessation of ignorance (*ajñāna*) delimited by that [unification], is called the immediate fruit (*phala*).

Since that [consciousness], being self-luminous, illumines even the jar and other objects superimposed upon it, it is accepted as being "penetrated by the fruit" (*phalavyāpya*). According to the rule that a mental modification (*vṛtti*) which resides in a certain locus and possesses a certain form destroys the ignorance residing in that same locus and possessing that same form, a direct (*aparokṣa*) modification—which pervades both the knower and the known—removes the veil by means of its own delimitation (*svāvacchedena*). This is because it is observed that light removes the veil precisely within its own delimited sphere.

Therefore, through the removal of the veil of non-existence delimited by the subject (*pramātṛ*) and the veil of non-manifestation delimited by the object (*prameya*), there arises immediate empirical usage such as "this jar is manifesting to me."

In the case of an object that is beyond the senses (*parokṣa*), however, because the door characterized by sense-object contact is absent, there is no emergence of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*); consequently, since the mental modification (*vṛtti*) does not reach as far as the object, there is no manifestation through direct perception (*aparokṣatayā*) due to the lack of the unification of the knower’s consciousness (*pramātṛ-caitanya*) with the objective consciousness delimited by the object (*prameya-caitanya*) within a single modification. Nevertheless, through the attainment of a state of oneness (*ekalolībhāva*) between the knower’s consciousness and the consciousness of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa-caitanya*), only the veil of non-existence (*asattvāvaraṇa*) delimited by the knower is removed.

This is because [the consciousness] is delimited by that much [of its own mode]. This very point was explained by the teacher Vivaraṇācārya using the term "exclusion of deep sleep" (*suṣuptivyāvṛtti*). Even though there exists the non-manifestation of the object and the veil (*āvaraṇa*) along with its effects, which are delimited by the object, the practical application (*vyavahāra*) in inference and so forth is possible through the cessation of the veil of non-existence (*asattvāvaraṇa*) as delimited by the knower (*pramātṛ*). For this very reason, there occurs such linguistic usage as: "I know that there is fire on the mountain, but what it is like does not appear to me."

There is no confusion [in the definitions], as directness (*aparokṣatva*) occurs when three factors become unified into one, whereas indirectness (*parokṣatva*) occurs when two factors become unified into one. Furthermore, in the case of direct perception, the connection between the mental mode (*vṛtti*) and the object is immediate; in the case of indirect cognition, however, an inference is produced by the knowledge of its pervader (*vyāpaka*) with respect to the object of inference. Verbal cognition is produced by the word denoting the locus of that relation together with the relation itself; and recollection is produced by the experience of the object to be remembered together with that object.

Thus, even in other cases, the distinction between the indirect (*parokṣa*) and the direct (*aparokṣa*) is simply a matter of successive connection (*paramparā-sambandha*). We have explained this process in detail in the *Siddhāntabindu*. Therefore, since the systematic arrangement of objects according to their respective perceptions (*pratikarma-vyavasthā*) is established even if the object is illusory (*mithyātva*), such is the direction of the argument.
Thus ends the "Establishment of the Systematic Arrangement of Objects According to Their Respective Perceptions" in the *Advaitasiddhi*.

[Objection: But surely the inference of falsity (*mithyātva*) is refuted by counter-arguments (*pratikūlatarka*). For instance: if the universe were imagined (*kalpita*), it would have a substratum (*sādhiṣṭhāna*). But this is not the case, because the condition for being a substratum—namely, "having an unknown particular while being known in a general sense" (*sāmānyato jñātatve satyajñātaviśeṣavattva*)—is impossible in the case of Brahman, which is both devoid of particulars (*nirviśeṣa*) and devoid of universals (*niḥsāmānya*). [Reply: This is not so. Since the condition for being a substratum is "being known in its own nature (*svarūpa*) while being unknown in its particulars (*viśeṣa*"), the condition of "having an unknown particular" (*ajñātaviśeṣavattva*) is not the necessary factor. Thus, the objection fails.

And thus, since Brahman is devoid of generality and devoid of particularity, its status as the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) is established through its being known by virtue of self-luminosity, and through its being unknown by virtue of its perfection, bliss, and so forth. In reality, however, it is quite easy to find that Brahman possesses imagined (*kalpita*) generalities and particularities; whereas the possession of non-imagined generalities and particularities is unestablished. Nor does this lead to the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*) in postulating them, because the stream of imagined generalities and particularities is beginningless.

This is because qualities such as "existence" (*sattva*) and "bliss" (*ānanda*) constitute universals (*sāmānya*) due to the distinction between their imagined individual manifestations (*kalpitavyaktibheda*), whereas qualities such as "perfect bliss" (*paripūrṇānandatva*) constitute particulars (*viśeṣa*). Therefore, one should not ask how superimposition (*adhyāsa*) can occur without a cognition of the universal form, since the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) would not be awakened; for the very cognition of the essential nature (*svarūpa*) as being "existent" (*sadātmanā*) is itself the cognition of the universal. Indeed, that which is to be superimposed does not fail to appear as "existent. The only difference is this: the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) appears as that [universal] by its own nature, whereas the object of superimposition does not.

However, it is that [Brahman] which is to be superimposed, because of its connection [with the substrate]. Now, one might object: "An error is impossible without the concealment of the substrate; but if there were a concealment of the nature of luminosity, then the manifestation of ignorance and so forth—which are superimposed upon that [substrate]—would be untenable. This is not so, because it is possible for that very same [Brahman], though concealed in its aspect as Bliss and so on, to manifest in its aspect as Pure Being (*sat*). As it was said by the venerable Vārttikakāra: "Ignorance conceals even Him, by whose grace ignorance and the rest appear to be established day and night;
for there is nothing difficult for ignorance to accomplish."

Nor should it be argued that even at the time of sublation there is no ignorance regarding the specific attributes of the Existent (sat); for since plenitude of bliss and so forth are themselves specific attributes of the Existent, there is no absence of knowledge regarding them at that time. This is because only their status as attributes (*dharmitva*) is imagined. Alternatively, what is required is simply the absence of a cognition that contradicts the error, not the absence of knowledge regarding specific attributes. For the ignorance whose object is the material cause of the universe is contradicted by a cognition in the form of a mental modification (*vṛtti*) produced by hearing and other means, which has the Self alone as its object; it is not contradicted by the consciousness (*cit*) that is self-established by nature.

Furthermore, there is currently indeed an absence of knowledge in the form of a mental modification (*vṛtti*) that contradicts error. Now, one might object: "Since the Self and the non-Self are known to be distinct by virtue of their being the seer and the seen, or the Self and the non-Self, how can there be the relationship of the superimposed and the substrate? We reply: No; for just as there is the superimposition "this is silver" despite the perception of the difference between the object in front and that which is not in front—namely, that "this is not that"—so too will there be superimpositions such as "this is a jar. Indeed, the perception of difference in one form does not necessarily contradict superimposition in another form.

Furthermore, in cognitions such as "the pot exists," the Self, whose nature is existence (*sadrūpa*), appears as permeated by the pot and other objects; thus, there is no logical inconsistency in its being the substratum for the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of the pot and so forth. Moreover, since it is possible for the Self to be the object of all cognitions by virtue of its nature as existence, there is no impossibility—such as visual perceptibility—for the Self, even though it lacks color and other qualities, just as in the case of time.

[Objection: "If the universe were imagined (*kalpita*), then it would have a material cause (*pradhāna*). But this is not the case; therefore, it is not imagined. [Reply: This is not so, because here too there exists a material cause of the same class (*sajātīya*). For a subsequent manifestation (*prapañca*) is superimposed (*adhyasana*) precisely upon a preceding manifestation of the same class. Now, superimposition requires a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) as its own cause; however, it does not require the reality of the object of that impression, as that would be useless. Nor is it the case that only a latent impression produced by valid cognition (*pramā*) is the cause of error.

Therefore, it must be said that the reality of the object is not necessary; for there is a lack of evidence for it, and on the contrary, there is parsimony (lāghava) in the opposite view. For this very reason, the claim that one must require a previously superimposed entity of the same class as the current superimposition, but possessing a higher degree of reality than the former superimposition, is also refuted. Since even a higher degree of reality is of no use beyond the mere presence of reality, only the prior cognition of that [object] is required, and that certainly exists.

Now, it might be objected: "In this way, even for the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*), mere cognition alone would be the cause, and not that [substrate] itself; thus, there would be no requirement for a real substrate, resulting in the consequence of Nihilism (*śūnyavāda*). This is not so. For although the substrate is not the cause of error through the medium of cognition, it is necessarily real because it is the cause of error through the medium of ignorance (*ajñāna*). Indeed, the substrate is defined as the object of the ignorance that is the material cause (*upādāna*) of error. And that [substrate] is certainly real, because everything unreal is an object of ignorance precisely by virtue of being imagined through ignorance.

For if that [object] were unreal, there would be the undesirable consequence that the cognition of it could not be sublated by error; furthermore, the systematic distinction between error and sublation in the world would not exist. For it is by means of sublation—by demonstrating a reality that contradicts something—that a superimposed unreality is to be negated. But if both were superimpositions, what would be negated by what? It is for this very reason that the venerable Commentator stated: "Having coupled the real and the unreal."

If it is argued that this [world] is not false because it performs its own appropriate causal functions—given the absence of any other manifestation (*prapañca*) capable of performing the same causal functions—this is not so, because there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of dreams, illusions, and the like. Furthermore, the capacity to perform one’s own appropriate causal functions is not a necessary condition for ultimate reality (*pāramārthika-sattva*), as it is also found in the dream-manifestation. Nor is the possession of origination and so forth, as established by the Śruti and other means of knowledge, a determinant of reality, since such a claim also fails in the case of the dream-manifestation.

For that [state of deep sleep] as well, the scripture beginning with, "There are no chariots there, no yoke-animals for chariots, nor roads; yet he creates chariots, yoke-animals for chariots, and roads," establishes its origination and so forth. Nor is there an impossibility of error regarding the beginning of a kalpa, because the latent impressions (saṃskāra) from a previous kalpa serve as the cause therein. Nor does this lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga) in the sense that the latent impressions of another birth produce an effect, because while they may be awakened in some cases by the power of unseen merit (adṛṣṭa) and other factors, their non-awakening in other cases is logically consistent.

This is because the properties [of the self] are inferred from their effects, as they are inferred according to those effects; otherwise, there would be no inclination toward activities such as suckling at the mother's breast in one who has just been born. If it is objected: "Even if Caitra superimposes impressions (*saṃskāra*) upon Maitra, Maitra does not perceive an error [therein]; therefore, the existence of the impressions that cause the delusion of the world is unavoidable. Nor can the error arise from impressions superimposed by oneself, because prior to the error, there is no rule that one must have superimposed impressions whose existence is to be inferred from one's own effects," we say: No.

Just as silver in a mother-of-pearl shell does not produce a bracelet, even though the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) superimposed upon Caitra does not produce Maitra’s error, it is nonetheless possible for the impression superimposed by oneself to produce the superimposition of space and so forth—just as silver found in a merchant's shop produces a bracelet. This is because that superimposition exists previously, even in the absence of its cognition, since it is admitted that all empirical objects possess an existence that is unknown [to the witness].

Objection: Just as in your own view the threefold negation regarding illusory silver has for its object conventional silver, so too in the case of the conventional world, the threefold negation in the text "not here, not manifold" must necessarily be said to have for its object some other, ultimate reality-world. Reply: No. This position is refuted by the fact that it would result in a lack of co-referentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) between the error and its sublation. Even if one were to accept it, it is impossible for a negation of the conventional level to have an ultimate reality as its object.

Because it is impossible to negate that which is not perceived; and because there is no relationship other than superimposition (adhyāsa) with what is perceived, there is an absence of being perceived in the ultimate sense. Now, an objection may be raised: "Since there is no similarity between the primary material cause (pradhāna) and the substratum, how can there be superimposition? Or, just as there is similarity between two qualities even though they are devoid of [other] qualities, will there not be some similarity here as well? This is not so; for in the case of Brahman, which is devoid of attributes (nirdharmaka), even that [similarity] would be dependent upon superimposition, resulting in the fallacy of mutual dependence (anyonyāśraya).

Although similarity (*sādṛśya*) is not a cause for superimposition (*adhyāsa*) based on an adjunct (*sopādhika*), because there is deviation (*vyabhicāra*), nevertheless, it must necessarily be required for superimposition without an adjunct (*nirupādhika*), as established by positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). Even in the case of superimposition with an adjunct, such as "the crystal is red," there is no dependence on similarity in terms of substantiality (*dravyatva*) and so forth. Furthermore, in the superimposition of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), there exists a similarity consisting precisely in its connection with ignorance (*avidyā*). In reality, however, there is no rule requiring similarity in error (*bhrama*).

This is because there is deviation even in cases where there is no limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), such as "the conch is yellow. Nor can it be argued that in cases like "the crystal is red," there is a similarity by virtue of [the crystal's] being a substance (*dravyatva*) and so forth; for you must also admit that only that similarity which was previously understood as residing solely in the primary object (*pradhāna*) and is apprehended at the time of superimposition as residing in the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*) is the cause of error. It is not, however, a similarity previously apprehended as residing in both the primary object and the substrate, for that would lead only to doubt.

Furthermore, since "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*) and so forth were previously apprehended as subsisting in both the red and the non-red, they do not serve as a cause for error. Moreover, similarity (*sādṛśya*) is not in itself a cause of delusion, as there is no evidence for this; rather, it functions as a constituent of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) by awakening latent impressions (*saṃskāra*). And the awakening of latent impressions is not restricted solely to similarity, since it can also occur through unseen forces (*adṛṣṭa*) and other factors. Indeed, the awakening of latent impressions serves to bring about the causal complex, and that awakening is not limited to similarity alone, because such awakening is possible even through unseen forces and the like.

As it has been said: "Similarity, perception, reflection, and so forth, are the awakeners of the seed of memory. Furthermore, reflection and the rest have been explained in the *Praṇidhāna-sūtra*. Thus, when the awakening of a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) occurs through another means, similarity is of no use. As stated in the *Vivaraṇa*: "The observation of the effect of an unconditioned error leads one to postulate either another similarity—just as one says 'the smell of a snake is similar to the smell of a ketaki flower' even in the absence of common qualities or parts—or another cause, as in the case of the yellowness of a conch shell."

Now, an objection may be raised: "If error is admitted without a defect (*doṣa*), then its invalidity would result in being intrinsic (*svataḥ*); but if it is admitted to be produced by a defect, then since the defect itself must be superimposed, an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) would ensue. We say: no. For the superimposition of beginningless ignorance (*anādyavidyādhyāsa*) does not depend on a defect, whereas superimpositions that have a beginning (*sādyadhyāsa*) are produced by the defect of ignorance; thus, there is neither intrinsic invalidity nor an infinite regress. Otherwise, even for the logicians (*tārkika*), the validity of beginningless cognitions would occur even without a quality (*guṇa*), and their doctrine of extrinsic validity (*paratastva*) would be destroyed.

The claim that every produced valid cognition (*janyapramā*) is produced by a quality (*guṇa*) is equivalent to the claim that every produced superimposition (*janyādhyāsa*) is produced by a defect (*doṣa*). Now, one might object: "By the principle of parsimony (*lāghava*) and because it is the first to be presented [in experience], defects and the like are the causes of every superimposition—just as the cognition of a relation (*saṃsargadhi*) is the cause of every purposeful action (*pravṛtti*), or fire is the cause of every smoke. Therefore, how can the superimposition of ignorance (*avidyā*) occur without a cause already established? Otherwise, the cognition of a relation would also be restricted to specific actions, and fire would be restricted to specific instances of smoke."

It would follow that [the cognition] has a cause; and thus, both the theory of non-apprehension (*akhyātivāda*) and the total abolition of inference (*anumāna*) would result. Furthermore, even if the object in the form of ignorance (*avidyā*) were beginningless, if its cognition were not produced by a defect (*doṣa*), it would entail validity (*prāmāṇya*), because the absence of a defect—which is the cause of invalidity—is present.

Now, even if it is granted that the defect called ignorance (*avidyā*), like difference (*bheda*), possesses the capacity for self-explanation and explanation of others—such that there may be the conventional usage "ignorance is unknown" just as one says "difference is different"—how can that which has mere cognition as its body be the cause of a cognition whose object is itself? For it is impossible for something to precede itself. If you say this, we reply: no. Although the nature of superimposition (*adhyāsa*) is simpler and is the first thing to present itself, it is not the determining factor (*tantratva*) for being produced by a defect.

Furthermore, since a defect (doṣa) is itself observable and thus subject to superimposition, it would lead to an infinite regress. Just as for those who maintain that knowledge is eternal, "being knowledge" is not the limiting condition for being produced by a body, nor is "being produced by a quality" the determinant of validity due to the force of sublation; likewise, defects and the like function as causes only with respect to superimpositions that are produced.

Just as eternal knowledge possesses validity despite not being produced by excellences (*guṇa*) because its object is unsublated, so too it is established that beginningless superimposition (*adhyāsa*) lacks validity because its object is sublated, even though it is not produced by defects (*doṣa*). Furthermore, being produced by a defect is not the defining condition (*avacchedaka*) for having a sublated object; for if one were to search for another defining condition for being produced by a defect, there would be the fallacy of infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Even if having a sublated object occurs in instances not produced by defects, it remains logically possible for being produced by a defect to be pervaded (*vyāpya*) by having a sublated object.

For this very reason, Śabarasvāmin, by stating that "only that cognition which has a defective instrument (*duṣṭa-karaṇa*) and for which there is a subsequent conviction of falsity (*mithyā-pratyaya*) is invalid, and no other," has declared that the discrepancy between the object and its appearance (*arthānyathātva*) is the cause of invalidity even in the absence of being produced by a defective instrument. Since it is not admitted that the witness-consciousness (*sākṣi-caitanya*), which consists of the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of ignorance (*avidyā*), is itself produced by ignorance, there is no contradiction with its nature as having a body consisting of mere manifestation (*pratīti-mātra-śarīratva*).

Ignorance (*avidyā*) is indeed the cause for the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) in the form of a mental modification (*vṛtti*), which serves as the basis for expressions such as "I am ignorant," just as jars and other objects are causes for their own perception. However, because there is no sublation regarding the cognitions qualified by fire, they function as causes for the production of smoke in a general sense; thus, the aforementioned defect does not arise. Now, an objection may be raised: since the superimposition of ignorance is beginningless, just as it does not depend on defects and the like, it should likewise not depend upon a substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*). To this, we say: no.

Even if there is no requirement for a substratum in terms of being its producer (*janakatva*), there is a rule that it must be required as its locus (*āśrayatva*). This is because, just as supreme magnitude (*paramamahattva*) and other such qualities require a locus, superimposition (*adhyāsa*) is invariably accompanied by a substratum; thus, in this case as well, the state of dependence is the same. Furthermore, the object of manifestation—the superimposition of ignorance—requires a substratum even in its capacity as the illuminator (*bhāsakatva*).

Since consciousness delimited by ignorance (avidyā) is the seer of the entire duality consisting of ignorance and so forth, and since it alone becomes the knower (pramātṛ) through the limitation of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), the co-location (sāmānādhikaraṇya) of error and its sublation is established; thus, it is logically consistent that error is sublated by a valid cognition (pramā) residing in the same locus.

But surely, without the body, senses, and so forth, how can there be superimposition upon the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*)? What is the inconsistency here? For the immediacy (*aparokṣatva*) of the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*) is indeed the cause for an immediate error (*aparokṣabhrama*). Where the substrate is not immediately manifest by itself—as in the case of consciousness delimited by mother-of-pearl and the like—there a dependence on the body, senses, and so forth is required for its immediacy. In the present case, however, the substrate is consciousness delimited by ignorance (*avidyā*).

In that case, since consciousness is self-luminous and ignorance is superimposed upon it, both are directly perceived by that very witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*); so where is there any need for the body, the senses, and so forth? Now, one might argue that even in the state of dissolution (*pralaya*), when the body, senses, and so on are absent, there would still be the consequence of the superimposition of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) due to the existence of ignorance. This is not so; for at that time, the delay in the superimposition is possible precisely because of the delay in the creation of the body, senses, and so forth.

Otherwise, why would the body, the senses, and so forth not also arise [as real]? Nor should it be argued that—since defects and the like are superimposed (adhyasta), their absence is ultimately real (tāttvika), and it is illogical for something unreal to obstruct a real effect; therefore, there would result the fallacy of validity for the cognition of duality produced by imagined defects, just as there is for the knowledge produced by the Veda when it is imagined to be defective by a Buddhist. This is because: [the absence of defects is established through valid means of knowledge, whereas the presence of defects is merely imagined]. Furthermore, even if the absence of defects were unreal, it would not obstruct a real effect, just as the unreality of a snake does not prevent its function as a rope. Moreover, the validity of the cognition of duality is not undermined simply because its cause is imagined, for validity is determined by the correspondence of the object, not by the reality of its cause. Thus, the objection is refuted.

Although the defect imagined by the Buddhists—which is of a merely apparent (prātibhāsika) nature—does not render [the Vedas] invalid because it possesses a lower degree of reality than the empirical (vyāvahārika) Veda, there is no consequence of the truth of dualistic cognition arising from the falsity of ignorance. This is because the defect called ignorance and the dualistic manifold possess an equal degree of reality, and due to the rule of the causal relationship between them: by the necessity that in the absence of the cause—the defect called ignorance—there must be an absence of the effect—the dualistic manifold and the cognition thereof. Thus, the falsity of ignorance does not entail the truth of the cognition of duality.

Because the falsity of the effect necessarily follows from the falsity of the cause. Since the status of being "empirical" (*vyāvahārikatva*)—defined as not being sublated by any knowledge other than the knowledge of Brahman—is common to both the sublatable and the unsublatable, it does not depend on the establishment of [absolute] falsity; thus, there is no failure to establish the division of existence. If it is argued that the ultimate reality (*pāramārthika-sattva*) of defects and the like—which serve as the causes for illusions such as silver—is established by the presumption of intrinsic validity (*autsargika-prāmāṇya*), and therefore these causes must be ultimately real, we say no.

Even if empirical validity (*vyāvahārikaprāmāṇya*) is apprehended by the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*), ultimate validity (*tāttvikaprāmāṇya*), which consists in being uncontradicted throughout the three periods of time, is not apprehended by anything; for this has already been stated in the refutation of the objection based on perception (*pratyakṣabādhoddhāra*). Nor should it be argued that because defects (*doṣa*) and so forth are seen to possess the same level of reality as the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) in cases of illusory superimposition such as silver, the same must hold here as well; for such an argument would constitute the fallacious rejoinder known as *sādharmyasama*.

In reality, however, since consciousness alone is the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*) everywhere, defects and the like can never possess the same ontological status as that substrate. Nor should it be argued that the subverting cognition must itself be real, lest there be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) due to a succession of further subversions; for the final mental modification (*cittavṛtti*) produced by the Vedāntic texts, by the logic of the clearing-nut powder (*katakaraja*), subverts both itself and others, and thus no infinite regress occurs. This is because the simultaneous subversion of the entire world of appearances is possible through the mere fact of its being an object of perception (*dṛśyatva*).

For a sound does not negate itself by saying, "There is no sound in the cave. Otherwise, if it did not negate itself by itself, you too would fall into the error of infinite regress; furthermore, there would be a contradiction with the experience of the negation of sound in general. Although the sublating cognition (*bādhakajñāna*), being of the nature of consciousness conditioned by a mental modification (*vṛtti*), is indeed real in itself, nevertheless, because its limiting adjunct—the mental modification—is false due to its being an object of perception (*dṛśyatva*), the sublation is logically established.

Objection: If bondage were false in the sense of being the counter-positive of an absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*), then no effort would be required for its removal, because an absolute non-existence is not something that can be accomplished. For this very reason, there would be no effort even for the sake of removing the cognition of it, since that cognition too would be false; otherwise, even in liberation, there would be the contingency of a phenomenal (*prātibhāsika*) bondage due to the persistence of the cognition of bondage in that state. Reply: If it is argued that falsity consists in its being false in the form of ultimate reality (*pāramārthikatva*), whereas in its own nature (*svarūpa*) there is indeed cessation, we say no.
