If it is argued that [the world] can be accounted for even without sublation of its own nature (*svarūpa*), we say no. Since the real Brahman is never seen to cease, if there were an absence of falsity (*mithyātva*) in its own nature, cessation would be impossible; therefore, falsity is precisely what makes cessation possible. Nor is there an impossibility of activity for that purpose, because such activity occurs exactly as it does after the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of the substratum. Prior to that, however, activity is possible for the sake of producing the knowledge that sublates the error, just like the effort to recover gold forgotten in one's own throat.

Furthermore, in the locus of absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*), the cessation of that [non-existence]—just like its counter-positive (*pratiyogin*)—has already been established. Nor should it be argued: "Since cessation is not observed in the case of the *tuccha* (the utterly non-existent), which is the counter-positive of a threefold negation, how could such cessation apply to the phenomenal world (*prapañca*)? For the mere fact of its non-observation in some similar instance is not a decisive factor. Otherwise, since cessation is not observed in the case of what has not yet arisen, even antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) would never cease.

Therefore, it must be stated that it is precisely a specific intrinsic nature (*svabhāvaviśeṣa*), distinct from both the void (*tuccha*) and the eternal (*nitya*), that causes cessation. And regarding the view that this cessation is the very nature of the locus (*adhikaraṇasvarūpa*), one should infer that activity such as reflection (*manana*) is undertaken for the sake of the destruction of a jar, just as the striking of a hammer is for that purpose. However, according to the view that it is something separate (*atirikta*), it is either indeterminable (*anirvacanīya*), a fifth category (*pañcamaprakāra*), or of the nature of the final cognitive state (*caramavṛtti*); in any case, since it is produced (*janya*), there is no inconsistency whatsoever.

Objection: If bondage were superimposed upon Brahman, it would not be removable by the direct realization of It—which is achieved through its meditative contemplation (*nididhyāsana*)—nor would it be removable by the knowledge of Brahman that depends on the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) resulting from the rules of hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth. For sin, which is removed by the direct realization of a deity achieved through its meditative contemplation, is not superimposed upon that deity; nor is sin, which is removed by the sight of a sacred ford (*setu*) depending on the unseen merit of rules such as traveling to a distant place, superimposed upon that ford. Reply: This is not so.

Since it is observed that whiteness and other qualities superimposed upon the self, as well as silver and other objects superimposed upon mother-of-pearl and the like, are removed by the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of those respective substrates, it is necessary that the phenomenal world (*prapañca*)—being likewise superimposed upon Brahman—is also removable by the direct realization of Brahman. For silver and other such things superimposed upon mother-of-pearl and the like do not cease to exist without the knowledge of the mother-of-pearl and so forth.

However, through such means as the vision of deities—which are equivalent to expiatory rites—only the persistence of evil in its causal state is brought about; there is no cessation [of evil] as there is of silver by the knowledge of mother-of-pearl. For that which is superimposed, having ignorance of the substrate as its material cause, cannot cease without the cessation of that [ignorance]. And it has been stated previously that the cessation of ignorance occurs only through the knowledge of the substrate. Furthermore, the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) resulting from the rules of hearing and so forth is not a cause for liberation itself, but rather for the immediate realization (*aparokṣya*) of Brahman.

Now, an objection may be raised: just as the absence of husks (vaituṣya) produced by threshing is distinct from the unseen potency (*apūrva*), so too liberation must be distinct from the immediate intuition (*aparokṣya*) produced by hearing (*śravaṇa*) and the rest; otherwise, since there would be no possibility of any other means for the direct realization that is to be accomplished by the unseen potency resulting from the restrictive rule (*niyama*) of hearing, the injunction of restriction—which depends on the possibility of such alternative means—would be untenable. Nor is it reasonable to claim that mediate knowledge arises from hearing, while immediate knowledge arises from the unseen potency of the restrictive rule.

[Objection: Because, in the injunction regarding the cutting of the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) and so forth, it is precisely the direct perception (*aparokṣa*)—which is to be accomplished by *nididhyāsana* in the form of a stream of indirect knowledge—that is intended as the goal; and because, in your view, desire for indirect knowledge is impossible, it cannot be the intended goal. [Response: This is not so. Just as in that case, although the restrictive transcendental merit (*niyamāpūrva*) subserving the sacrifice (*kratvartha*) serves to produce the ultimate transcendental merit (*paramāpūrva*), the transcendental merit (*adṛṣṭa*) of the restriction such as wearing gold—which subserves the person (*puruṣārtha*)—lacks that [ultimate merit], even so, although there is no fruit other than the direct realization accomplished through hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth, its status as a fruitful action is established by that very [realization].

This is because of the principle stated in the *Brahma-sūtra*: "And there is dependence on all [works], because of the scriptural injunctions regarding sacrifice and so forth" (3.4.26), and because of the *smṛti* passage: "O Pārtha! every action in its entirety culminates in knowledge" (Gītā 4.33). Here, by the words "all" (*sarva*) and "entire" (*akhila*), it is shown that everything denoted by the term "action"—namely, the unseen potency (*apūrva*)—culminates in knowledge. Furthermore, this is because liberation, which consists in the cessation of ignorance, is necessarily not achievable through anything other than knowledge. Thus, its culmination in knowledge is demonstrated. And because liberation, which consists in the cessation of ignorance, is necessarily not achievable through anything other than knowledge.

In the case of knowledge (*jñāna*), however, its utility consists in both the visible and invisible portions [of the result], namely, the removal of obstacles such as doubt and the removal of obstructive sins (*durita*). Furthermore, the fruit of a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*) everywhere is the exclusion of other possible means that might otherwise be applicable by way of a general rule; whereas, in terms of its specific form, it possesses the very nature of an original injunction (*apūrvavidhi*).

Just as in cases such as "one threshes the rice," although there is no possibility of employing any means other than threshing for the purpose of dehusking the rice—which serves as a means to the *apūrva*—there is nevertheless an exclusion of methods like scratching with the fingernails, which might otherwise be considered applicable to mere dehusking; this is because a specific causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) has been established [between threshing and dehusking]. Similarly, even though there is no possibility of employing any means other than hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth for the removal of the obstacles to the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of the non-difference between the self and the attributeless Brahman, [there is an exclusion] regarding the obstacles to the knowledge of the Self in general.

Since the application of treatises such as Sāṅkhya would also follow [if not for this], their exclusion is specifically achieved through the injunction to investigate Vedānta statements; thus, the meaning of this work is profoundly deep.

Now, an objection: if the universe were merely imagined (*kalpita*), then how could there be the mention of its "birth and so forth" in the Sūtra, "From which the birth etc. of this [world proceed]" (*janmādy asya yataḥ*), and in the Śruti passage, "From whence indeed these [beings arise]" (*yato vā imāni*)? Furthermore, how could there be the mention of the Lord’s agency preceded by reflection in the Sūtra, "Because of seeing, not that which is non-Vedic" (*īkṣateḥ nāśabdam*), and in the Śruti passage, "It thought" (*tad aikṣata*)? Moreover, how could there be the mention of creation and so forth occurring through mere play (*līlā*) despite the absence of a purpose, in the Sūtra, "But like in the world, it is mere play" (*lokavat tu līlākaivalyam*), and in the Śruti passage, "What desire can there be for one whose desires are fulfilled"? And how could there be the [denial of] partiality and cruelty...?

Otherwise, the following would be untenable: the statement regarding the absence of partiality (avaiṣamya) based on dependence on karma in the Sūtra "Because of being dependent" (*sāpekṣatvāt*) and in such scriptural passages as "By merit, one attains the meritorious world"; the statement regarding the production of fire and so forth from air and so forth in the Sūtra "Fire from this, for thus it says" (*tejo'tastathā hyāha*) and in such scriptural passages as "From air, fire"; and the statement regarding the dissolution of earth and the other elements into water and so forth in the Sūtra "But the reverse order is logical from this, and it is so established" (*viparyayeṇa tu kramo'ta upapadyate ca*) and in such Smṛti passages as "Earth dissolves into water."

If it is argued that it is not logical to entertain doubts regarding contradiction or to offer its refutation in respect to what is merely imagined (*kalpita*), we say no. For even though the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is imagined, its empirical reality (*vyāvahārika-sattva*) is admitted; thus, at that level, it is appropriate to raise doubts about contradiction and to resolve them. Furthermore, we observe that even in the case of things superimposed through magic and the like, the magician and others act as creators with prior observation. And how the birth and other characteristics of even the imagined are possible will be explained in the discussion on the doctrine of the indeterminable (*anirvacanīya-vāda*).

Furthermore, since the scripture teaches the creation and so forth even in dreams, it is logical that air and other elements can produce fire and other effects, just as a superimposed snake produces fear, trembling, and the like. Moreover, the Sūtra—"But from its meditation on that [Brahman] alone, for that is indicated by the signs"—declares that Brahman itself, having assumed those various states, is the cause. Thus, the statement regarding the dissolution of earth and the other elements into water and so forth should be explained as occurring within Consciousness (caitanya) as it has assumed those respective states; it is not a statement of dissolution into something other than the substrate.

The resolution of doubts regarding partiality (*vaiṣamya*), cruelty (*nairghṛṇya*), and purpose (*prayojana*) occurs during the stage of meditative practice (*upāsanāvasthā*). This is done provisionally by accepting the theory of transformation (*pariṇāmavāda*) through the sūtra: "If it be argued that there would be non-distinction due to the soul becoming the enjoyer [of the world], it is not so, as in the case of the world" (*bhoktrāpatter avibhāgaś cet syāl lokavat*). However, in the state of the final conclusion (*paramasiddhāntadaśā*) according to the theory of illusory manifestation (*vivartavāda*)—established by the sūtra: "Its non-difference [from Brahman] is known from the words concerning 'originating material,' etc. (*tadananyatvam ārambhaṇaśabdādibhyaḥ*)—there is neither doubt nor answer. For all contradictions are resolved by the fact that the Lord, like a magician, causes the delusion of the individual souls (*jīva*), who are His own reflections.

Now, an objection may be raised: since even the Lord (Īśvara), along with his retinue, is superimposed by the individual soul (jīva), how can he be the one who causes delusion? This is not so; for it is impossible that the beginningless Consciousness qualified by ignorance (avidyopahitacit) should be imagined as the Lord by the individual soul qualified by the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa). Even on the view that [the Lord] is imagined by the individual soul, it is logical that he possesses the capacity to cause delusion and so forth, because he is imagined precisely as characterized by such attributes. This follows the maxim: "Even an imagined serpent may cause death, but the sky does not become dirty."

Now, it might be argued: "Is there not a delusion among living beings that fire and other elements arise from air and so forth, which could serve as the basis for the Śruti, just like a dream-delusion? And nothing exists as a conceptual construction (*kalpita*) without a delusion. Nor can this very sentence be the basis for the delusion produced by that same sentence, for that would entail the absurdity of the Veda being a generator of error. Furthermore, there is no fault in the case of a restatement (*anuvāda*). Nor is the Lord himself the creator of that delusion, for that would entail the absurdity of Him being subject to delusion. Even if one were to accept that, there is still no escape."

If it is argued that error arises from the body, senses, and so forth, and since these are effects of earth and the other elements, error would be impossible prior to the production of earth and the rest—this is not so. For the dependence on the body, senses, and so forth has already been refuted in the case of mere error. Furthermore, because the Veda has as its basis the production of fire and other elements caused by air and so forth superimposed upon God, it does not produce error [in Him]. Moreover, since that which is superimposed appears as something superimposed, there is no consequence of God being subject to error, unlike a magician.

Nor is there any logical inconsistency regarding production and so forth in the case of superimposition (*adhyasta*). Since production and the like are never observed in anything that is not superimposed, it is precisely superimposition that accounts for them. This is because, by negating both the theories of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*) and the non-existence of the effect (*asatkāryavāda*), the relationship between cause and effect finds its final resting place solely in the theory of an indeterminable effect (*anirvacanīyakāryavāda*). Thus, since the entire phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is logically established as a conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) upon the non-dual Brahman, there is no subversion by adverse reasoning.
This concludes the refutation of adverse reasoning regarding Brahman in the *Advaitasiddhi*.

This inference is also supported by such scriptural texts as "One alone, without a second. Now, an objection may be raised: since the scriptures do not teach the falsity of their own nature, their own validity, or their own fitness [for communication], and since they depend upon the existence of things established by perception and other means, the falsity of everything other than Brahman cannot be established. Furthermore, according to the maxim "A rule characterized by immediate occurrence is not the cause of its own sublation," the falsity of jars and other objects established by perception and so forth cannot be established. Moreover, if the falsity of fitness and the like were taught...

It would follow that the meaning of the scripture is non-real, because there is a rule that whatever is understood from a word must possess the same ontological status as the word itself, its validity, and its semantic competency (*yogyatā*). Nor can one argue that this rule is contradicted by the case of a dream-vision of a deity, which conveys a real object; for since such a vision lacks the status of being uttered by a reliable person (*āpta*) or being non-human (*apauruṣeya*), it cannot be valid as a verbal testimony (*śabda*). Rather, such knowledge of words is a means of valid cognition only as an inferential mark (*liṅga*), like an *upaśruti* (an overheard divine utterance). This is not so, because since it is a flawless word, its validity is possible precisely through the mode of verbal testimony.

Because the absence of defects alone suffices for both reliability (*āptatva*) and non-personal authorship (*apauruṣeyatva*), and because it would be cumbersome to postulate the presence of pervasion (*vyāpti*) and so forth; furthermore, even if a speaker were postulated, it would be impossible to postulate a defect residing in him given the correspondence with the actual state of affairs.

Furthermore, since there is an inconsistency regarding having the same ontological status as the word (*śabda-samasattākatva*), and because the rule regarding having the same ontological status as semantic competency (*yogyatā*) and so forth is unestablished and thus lacks probative force, and because adventitious conditions (*upādhi*) such as being indirect (*parokṣatva*) or non-eternal (*anityatva*) are possible, the object of the Vedic revelation (*śruti*) is not false even though the scripture teaches the falsity of everything including semantic competency; this is because the specific characteristics that necessitate falsity are absent. Moreover, the example cited from the *Mahābhāṣya* is also not appropriate, due to a disparity between the subject matters (*viṣaya-vaiṣamya*).

For instance: in the case of *śatāni sahasrāṇi*, the augment *num*—which is prescribed by the occurrence of the term *śi* (the nominative-accusative dual ending) designated as a *sarvanāmasthāna*—does not become the cause for the elision (*luk*) of that very *śi* ending by the rule *ṣaḍbhyo luk*, which operates through the designation of the stem as *ṣaṭ*. This is because [the *num*] is prescribed precisely by the occurrence of that [ending], and because it is prescribed under the very condition of its presence; such is the meaning.

Since the *num* augment is caused by a *sarvanāmasthāna* suffix that is indeed not elided—because the rule "na lumatāṅgasya" prohibits operations on a stem when a suffix is elided by *lumat*—the principle of *sannipātalakṣaṇanyāya* applies wherever a suffix functions as a cause precisely by virtue of being unelided.

However, where an operation occurs even when an affix has been elided by the maxim "when an affix is elided, the effect [of that affix] remains" (*pratyayalope pratyayalakṣaṇam*), there the principle of *sannipātalakṣaṇa* does not apply; for in such cases, the affix serves as the cause by its mere status as an affix, independent of the qualification of being "unelided," since the actual presence of the affix is not required there as a supporting condition.

This being the case, if perception and the like were to function as causes by virtue of being non-erroneous, then this application of the principle would indeed occur, just as it does when they function as causes through their unimpeded nature. However, that perception and the like function as causes by their very own nature has already been established, since even objects in dreams and similar states are observed to perform causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*).

Therefore, that which is sublated—namely, ultimate reality—is not what is to be relied upon; and that which is to be relied upon—the conventional validity characterized by causal efficiency—is not sublated. Thus, how can these two be consistent with one another? As it has been stated by the authors of the *Ṭīkā*: "Because there is no opposition to its producer."

Therefore, the following argument is refuted: that since the injunctions for the Jyotiṣṭoma and other sacrifices are restricted to those possessing knowledge of the sacrificial fires (*agnividyā*), so too the negation of duality must be restricted to objects other than its own prerequisites—such as *yogyatā* (competence) and the like—or else, like the scriptural accounts of creation, it must have a merely imagined (*kalpita*) object; thus, it is not proper to assume the absolute falsity of everything in reality. For in the case of the illustrative example, while knowledge of the fires and so forth may be required, in the case of the thing illustrated, a real (*tāttvika*) competence or similar factor cannot serve as a prerequisite.

For fitness (*yogyatā*) is not a cause by virtue of being "ultimate fitness," but rather simply by virtue of being fitness. Since the absence of all duality is of the nature of its own locus (*adhikaraṇasvarūpa*), and since that locus—Brahman—is established as real by such scriptural passages as "Brahman is truth, knowledge, infinite" (*satyaṃ jñānamanantaṃ brahma*) and "That is the Truth, That is the Self" (*tatsatyaṃ sa ātmā*), it cannot be maintained that these [texts] have a merely imagined object, as might be argued for the scriptures concerning creation and so forth. Therefore, it is established that even if fitness and the like are illusory, that which is to be known through the Vedānta is indeed real.

Just as it has been demonstrated previously that even when ignorance and its effects are negated in their own nature (*svarūpataḥ*), they remain distinct from the void (*tuccha*); or, when negated in the form of ultimate reality (*pāramārthikatva*), Brahman—though devoid of the attribute of ultimate reality—still exists by its own nature; so too [is this case] explained.

[Objection: "But surely—just as the sentence 'That thou art' (tattvamasi) teaches the identity of the two things indicated by the words *tat* and *tvam* so as not to contradict perception and other means of knowledge, so too the scripture declaring falsity (*mithyātva*) must teach the falsity of something other than what is established by perception and the rest, in order not to contradict them; otherwise, for the sake of favoring perception and the rest, even conventional existence (*vyāvahārika-sattva*) would not be postulated, since [texts] such as 'Not here, not manifold' (neha nānā) teach absolute non-existence through negation. [Reply: This is not so, because if there were identity between the two qualified entities, it would follow that their qualifiers are also identical, which would lead to the same problem everywhere.

Because there is a rule that a sentence whose primary purport is the non-difference of two qualified entities must have as its purport the identity of the two substrates indicated by those qualifiers, it is likewise accepted in the case of "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*). As it has been said: "When even two qualified entities, arising from two uncontradicted sets of qualifiers, cannot achieve oneness, how much less so can those whose forms are the opposite of that?"

However, there is no contradiction with perception and other means of knowledge regarding the scripture that teaches falsity (*mithyātva*), because the aspect of ultimate reality (*tāttvikatva*) is not what the scripture depends upon for its own validity, whereas conventional existence (*vyāvahārikasattva*) is indeed what it depends upon; thus, it has already been largely established that one cannot postulate absolute non-existence [of the world] on this basis. Now, an objection: Does the purport (*tātparya*) of the scripture reside in pure consciousness alone? Or in consciousness qualified by the absence of a second? Or in consciousness as characterized (*upalakṣita*) by that [absence]? Not the first, because the falsity of the universe would remain unestablished (which would be an undesirable consequence), and because, being self-luminous, it is eternally established and thus the scripture would be redundant.

The second [alternative] is not tenable, because it would result in the loss of the quality of having an undivided meaning (*akhaṇḍārthatva*). For this very reason, the third is also not tenable; for even by the phrase "the absence of a second," a cognition with qualifiers (*saprakāraka-jñāna*) is produced, and thus it is incompatible with being an undivided meaning. Furthermore, since pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) is eternally established and nothing other than that is to be known by one seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*), there is no other entity to be indicated by the "absence of a second"—just as a crow indicates a specific shape—nor is it possible for that absence to serve as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*). If this is argued, we reply: no, because the absence of a second is like the specific shape of a crow.

If it is argued that [the absence of a second] cannot be a secondary characteristic (*upalakṣaṇa*) because it is its own essential nature (*svarūpa*), we say no; for just as the specific configuration of a crow is a secondary characteristic, so too the essential nature of the absence of a second is itself the object characterized (*upalakṣya*). There is no impossibility here based on the absence of an object to be characterized, since in the case of being a secondary characteristic, the mere existence of the object characterized is the requisite factor, not even its being distinct from its own essential nature, due to the principle of parsimony (*lāghava*); for it is possible to be an object characterized even in the absence of a defining property (*upalakṣyatāvacchedaka-rūpa*), just as a genus (*jāti*) is self-excluded by its own nature.

For this very reason, there is no contingency of [the cognition] possessing a qualifying mode (*saprakārakatva*). Even in the case of "like a crow" (*kākavat*), that which serves as a mere indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) is not a qualifying mode; rather, the state of possessing a qualifying mode occurs there because a property distinct from the essential nature (*svarūpa*) functions as an indicator. Here, however, that is not the case—this is the distinction. Nor is the indicator useless, for the knowledge of the essential nature, mediated by the absence of a second [entity], is the intended goal (*uddeśya*) since it is the cause for the cessation of suffering, and that [knowledge] was previously unestablished.

Furthermore, this is not an admission of what is undesired (*iṣṭāpatti*) on the grounds that falsity (*mithyātva*) would remain unestablished, because a subordinate intention (*avāntara-tātparya*) exists even there, since the primary intention (*mahā-tātparya*) regarding the consciousness of the essential nature is achieved precisely through that [subordinate intention].

For this very reason, the following objection is refuted: "If the absence of a second—which is either a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) or a mere indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*)—is real (*sat*), then non-duality (*advaita*) is lost; if it is unreal (*asat*), then the statement of non-duality would fail to reveal reality (*atattvāvedaka*), like the sentence 'the man with a staff' when there is no staff, or like the sentence 'crow-like' when there is no crow. This is refuted because, in the first case, it is improper to argue that the absence of a second is unestablished by the existence of the absence of a second, and because it is not admitted that an absence is distinct from its locus (*adhikaraṇa*).

In the second case, however, there is no fault even in the position that the purport lies in pure consciousness alone with respect to the *mahātātparya* (the great purport), because [such texts] possess the quality of revealing reality (*tattvāvedakatva*) by taking up the truth of the nature indicated (*upalakṣyasvarūpa*), just like the passages concerning creation and so forth; for it is accepted that the quality of not revealing reality (*atattvāvedakatva*) occurs only when the object of the primary purport (*mukhyatātparyaviṣaya*) itself is unreal. Consequently, since the establishment of falsity (*mithyātva*) is also admitted through the *avāntaratātparya* (subordinate purport), there is no possibility of the charge of proving what is already established (*iṣṭāpatti*).

Now, in the absence of a second [object], is there an absence of the primary purport (*mahātātparya*) because it is already established by another means of knowledge—as in the case of the wind being "most swift" (*vāyukṣepiṣṭhatva*) and so on? Or because it is contradicted by that [other means]—as in the case of "excavating one's own entrails" (*ātmavapotkhana*) and so on? Or because it is a qualification of the subject (*uddeśyaviśeṣaṇa*) and so forth—as in the case of the singularity of the cup (*grahaikatva*) and so on? It is not the first, for you yourself do not admit that the absence of a second [object] is established by another means of knowledge.

Regarding the second [alternative] as well, there is no contradiction with a sublating cognition (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*). First, it cannot be perception and so forth, because according to your own view, those grasp duality and are themselves sublated by the Śruti. Nor can it be another non-dual statement, because if that were intended solely for the Self alone, it would contradict the absence of a second; for the sentence "One should offer the Agnihotra," which has the substrate as its object, is not contradicted by the sentence "One should offer with curd," which has the qualified [action] as its object. However, if the [second statement] were intended to convey the absence of duality, then because they share the same object, there is all the more no contradiction.

Nor is the third [alternative] tenable; for in a sentence whose purport is an indivisible (akhaṇḍa) reality—just as in the case of "he cleanses the cup" (*grahaṃ saṃmārṣṭi*)—there is no other thing to be enjoined, and since the pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), which is the substantive to be known through scripture, is not already established [prior to the sentence], it cannot be the subject of reference (*uddeśya*). Consequently, it is illogical for the absence of a second to function as a qualifier of that subject. Furthermore, there is an absence of even the status of being a restatement (*anuvādyatva*), which is the reason for its being unintended as a qualification. If this is argued, we reply: no, because by the very fact of being a "second," the sentence itself negates the absence of a second—even though it has itself made that known—thus involving a self-contradiction.

Because the scripture has no such intention (*tātparya*) in that regard; for the mere fact of not contradicting human authority (*māna*) serves as the reason for the absence of intention, so there is no harm even if it contradicts itself.

Now, one might object: "It is impossible for both the attainment and the prohibition of the same thing to occur through a single means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). This is not so, because there is no contradiction due to a difference in form (*rūpa*). For it is the very nature of the absence of a second [thing] that is attained by the scripture. And while the property of being the absence of a second (*dvitīyābhāvatva*)—which is the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) for its being attained—is not the delimiting factor for what is prohibited, rather it is "secondness" (*dvitīyatva*) alone, which is common to all things prohibited.

In that case, if such [an entity] is not admitted, it cannot be the object of negation, nor does it follow that the Self becomes accompanied by a second entity; thus, there is no fault whatsoever. However, where the very delimiter of attainability (*prāpyatāvacchedaka*) is itself the delimiter of negatability (*niṣedhyatāvacchedaka*), then—even though the spheres of application (*viṣaya*) of the rule of attainment and the rule of negation are unequal—the general rule (*sāmānya-śāstra*) operates by abandoning the sphere of the specific rule (*viśeṣa-śāstra*). But where the spheres of application are equal, there is, due to the lack of any other recourse, an option (*vikalpa*); thus, the negation does not operate without restriction (*asaṅkoca*).

For example, the prohibitory scripture "One should not harm any living beings" has as its scope that which is other than the scope of the prescriptive scriptures such as "One should sacrifice an animal to Agni and Soma. However, in the case of the prescriptive and prohibitory scriptures—"One takes the *ṣoḍaśin* cup at the *Atirātra* sacrifice" and "One does not take the *ṣoḍaśin* cup at the *Atirātra* sacrifice"—they have the same single scope by way of option (*vikalpa*), because the very same property of being a "harmful act" (*hiṃsātva*) and the very same property of being the "taking of the *ṣoḍaśin*" (*ṣoḍaśigrahatva*) serve as the delimiters for both the prescription and the prohibition; thus, in that case, the prohibitory scripture functions without restriction.

Otherwise, the entire treatise on attainment (*prāpti-śāstra*) would result in total futility; however, in the present case, since the very negation of duality as a form is the intended meaning of the scripture, there is no suspicion of futility for anything. For this very reason, the objection that "if one negates the absence of a second, it leads to the re-emergence of the second" is refuted. This has been established in the proof of the falsity of falsity (*mithyātva-mithyātva-sādhana*): namely, that when the delimiters of the negatability (*niṣedhyatāvacchedaka*) of the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) and its absence are identical, the negation of one does not entail the existence of the other.

Nor should it be argued that it is improper to take up again as a qualifier or a secondary indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) the very second thing—the absence of a second—which has already been negated by itself; for we observe that even a negated counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) is taken up as a secondary indicator in the cognition of an absence, just as the previously perceived silver is taken up as a secondary indicator in the [subsequent] cognition "that is mother-of-pearl. This is because the requirement of being the cause of a non-confused cognition is equal in the present case as well.
Therefore, it is established that such scriptural passages as "one only, without a second" constitute proof for the falsity of the universe.
Thus ends the general demonstration of the scriptural teaching on falsity (*mithyātva*) in the *Advaitasiddhi*.

Now, an objection is raised: surely the meaning of the scripture is not merely that which is grasped at first sight; for the scripture itself states, "Who, indeed, knows the connection of the Vedic hymns? and the Smṛti declares, "One fears the person of little learning. Moreover, this would render the Mīmāṃsā inquiry purposeless. Rather, the meaning must be one that is not contradicted by other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) or by what precedes and follows [in the text]. And the success of the Mīmāṃsā lies precisely in the apprehension of such non-contradiction. For this very reason, [the texts] state, "They praise with clarified butter" (*ājyaiḥ stuvate*), and "From space alone they are born" (*ākāśādeva samutpadyante*).

In such passages, by setting aside the literal meanings of "clarified butter" (*ghṛta*), "sky" (*gagana*), and so forth as they appear at first glance, the status of the words *ājya* (clarified butter) and *ākāśa* (sky) as referring to the *sāman* chant and the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) is established in the *Citra*, *Ākāśa*, and other relevant sections of the *Pūrva* and *Uttara Mīmāṃsās*; for otherwise, one would be forced to accept those respective prima facie (*pūrvapakṣa*) positions. Thus it has been stated by the authors of the *Vārttika* regarding the definition of scripture (*śāstra*) as "knowledge of an object not [otherwise] proximate arising from the knowledge of words": "And by the term 'not proximate' (*asannikṛṣṭa*), two things are here intended to be excluded:
apprehension [of the object] as being that very thing [already known], and its apprehension through the opposite [of what is already known]."

Having understood both the domain and the non-domain [of a rule], one must distinguish between the sublation and non-sublation of general rules (utsarga) and exceptions (apavāda), and not do so merely by observing their commonality.
"The meaning of the scripture is understood in one way through a single portion,
but in another way when it is complete with all its constituent parts brought together.
Thus it is said elsewhere as well:
"Wherever scriptures appear to be mutually contradictory, their intended meanings are determined in accordance with what is observed [in the world].

If it is argued that, because of contradiction with perception and so forth, and because of internal inconsistency between earlier and later passages, sentences such as "one alone," etc., do not have non-duality as their purport—this is not so. For the perception of duality has its validity potentially sublated (just as the perception of the moon being a mere span in size is), and thus lacks the power to contradict the Śruti on non-duality. Furthermore, how the Śruti sublates perception has already been explained in detail below.

Furthermore, perception has a restricted scope, whereas scripture has everything as its scope; thus, it is precisely in cases where difference is not apprehended by perception that there is scope for the scriptural teaching of non-difference. If it is objected: "Is the difference between those two things whose identity is taught by scripture already established or not? It cannot be the latter case, because that would result in the negation of something that was never even suggested. Nor can it be the former case, because identity cannot be taught if it contradicts the very means of knowledge that established the initial suggestion of difference. This is not so, because there is no fault in accepting the latter position.

Regarding the phrase "negation of the non-attached" (*aprasaktapratiṣedha*), it must be examined whether this means that the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) is unestablished, or whether it means that [the negation] is purposeless. It cannot be the first, because it is possible to negate elsewhere—in the form of a mutual relationship between counter-correlate and sub-correlate—a difference that is already established elsewhere and presented as a difference; for being established in that very place is not the determining factor, since that would entail the total destruction of all valid cognition of negation.

Not the second [alternative], because the cessation of what is purposeless is itself the purpose; and because we observe prohibitions of what is not even applicable, such as "The fire-altar is not to be built in the atmosphere," which serve the purpose of mere praise.

Now, does there exist the presentation (*upasthiti*) of those two whose non-difference is taught by the scripture, or not? Not the latter, because it is impossible to bring about the cognition of non-difference between two things that are not presented. As for the first case, is that presentation produced by the scripture, or produced by perception and other means? Not the first; since the scripture is intent solely upon the non-difference that is beyond the scope of other means of knowledge, the presentation of jars and so forth cannot be produced by it, and thus universal non-duality would remain unestablished. This is because we must admit that words such as "whatever" (*kiñcana*) found in the scripture function merely as restatements (*anuvādaka*).

But in the second case, since even the difference between those two is established by perception and other means of knowledge, what room is there for the non-duality of the Śruti? Do not say so; for there is no such rule that whatever is grasped by perception and the like, its difference must also be grasped by that same means. To explain: the cognition of the essential nature of an object is not itself the cognition of its difference, because if it were, it would follow that the delusion of non-difference would be eliminated [simultaneously].

Even for those who maintain that difference is the very nature of things (*svarūpabheda*), the cognition of difference characterized by the mode "difference-ness" (*bhedatva*) is indeed distinct from the cognition of the thing's own nature (*svarūpa*) characterized by the mode "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*); otherwise, there would follow the undesirable consequence that linguistic usage based on the non-apprehension of difference could never arise. For this very reason, it is also not the case that a cognition of difference must necessarily occur after the cognition of the thing's own nature, as that would lead to the consequence of infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

To explain: the cognition of the difference between a jar and a cloth, expressed as "I know the jar and the cloth to be different," must be either self-luminous (*svaprakāśā*), established by a subsequent reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*), or established by the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*). It cannot have its own counter-correlative as its object, because there is a necessary rule that a cognition of difference is produced by a cognition of the counter-correlative, which requires it to be a distinct instance from the instance of that counter-correlative cognition; for it is logically impossible for something to be produced by itself.

Furthermore, if that difference were grasped by another cognition, one must necessarily admit that the stream of cognitions apprehending difference must eventually come to rest somewhere; otherwise, states such as deep sleep or the transition to other objects would not occur. Therefore, even in that case, the final cognition of difference itself serves as the illustration. Thus, the cognition of identity—unimpeded because it has established its identity with the cognition of the difference between the jar and the cloth (which was intended as a sublater but is actually devoid of its own difference)—leads the scripture to the conclusion of universal non-difference.

For even in the absence of difference, there can be no relationship between the sublated and the sublator, because it would follow that a thing could sublate itself. As it has been stated by the authors of the *Khaṇḍana*: "The succession of cognitions of sublation, exhausted by running so very far, is defeated when it ceases by the non-dual scriptures acting as pursuers from behind."

Nor should it be argued that, according to our own system (siddhānta), there is no infinite regress because the self-luminous witness (sākṣin), which perceives the difference between the pot and its cognition, also perceives its own difference from all other things; otherwise, there would be doubt regarding its non-difference from the pot and so forth. For even though the witness is self-luminous, its perception of a difference residing in itself—wherein "other" is the counter-correlate (pratiyogin)—is dependent upon the presentation (upasthiti) of that other counter-correlate. Otherwise, the delusion of non-difference between the witness and the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) and so on would not occur.

This is of no consequence; for even if difference is not grasped through self-luminosity (*svaprakāśa*), since difference is grasped by another means of knowledge (*mānāntara*), there is no doubt regarding the non-difference of the jar and so forth. It might be argued as follows: "The perception that 'the jar and the cloth are different' cannot be accounted for without a difference [between the cognition] and its own [object], such as the knowledge of non-duality (*advaitajñāna*); therefore, it implies that [difference]. Thus, even if difference is not perceptible everywhere, there is no room for the scripture of non-duality (*advaita-śruti*)."

To this it is replied: Is the implication (ākṣepa) an inference (anumāna) or a postulation (arthāpatti)? In that regard, an inference cannot be established that "the cognition under dispute is distinct from everything," because there would be a contradiction in proving its distinction even from itself, and because any example would lack the probandum (sādhyavikala). However, if its distinction from some unspecified thing were being proved, then scripture—finding scope in a matter not within the domain of inference—will teach non-difference.

Nor can it be proven that [the subject] is distinct from everything other than itself, because for an Advaitin, the qualification would be unestablished (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*). By this, the statement "everything is distinct from everything" is also refuted. As it has been said:

"When one who asserts omniscience through the absence of causes and so forth establishes 'everything' as the subject (*pakṣa*), yet excludes something, he has given away the very [point at issue] because of the hearing of two doors. Thus ends the section.

Nor can presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) have all differences as its object, because it is not self-cognizing. For when the inadmissibility of a certain thing is apprehended in the absence of a difference between two things, even if that difference is subsequently apprehended, the original inadmissibility remains; for no further inadmissibility has been grasped. If, however, that [inadmissibility] were apprehended everywhere, then the final cognition at the end of the series would serve as the illustration. As it has been said: "Even another inadmissibility belonging to the difference known by the first cognition does not sublate the scripture of non-duality at the end, because it depends upon its own cognition."* *This verse is from the *Brahmasiddhi* (1.28).*

Now, surely everything that serves as a warrant (*upapādaka*) is the object of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), and not just anything that happens to be a warrant. Thus, if there were no distinction between presumptive testimony and other means of knowledge, then since the scriptural statement of non-difference would find its scope in that very [non-distinction], it would follow that the difference between a jar and a cloth could not be established. Consequently, the difference between presumptive testimony and other means of knowledge must itself be admitted as an object of presumptive testimony, because it serves as the warrant for the difference between a jar and a cloth. Otherwise, the impossibility of the relation between the seer and the seen (*dṛg-dṛśya-sambandhānupapatti*) and the impossibility of being sublated by knowledge (*jñāna-nivartyatvānupapatti*) would not have their own falsity as their objects.

If it were the case that the Śruti text "All this, indeed, is Brahman" and the non-contradiction of the negation of all difference within Brahman in the text "There is no diversity here" did not have as their object the non-difference [of the world] from Brahman, then you would also face the consequence of infinite regress; for in those cases too, another Śruti or another presumption (*arthāpatti*) would have to be stated. Do not say this; for in reality, being a logical ground (*upapādakatva*) is not the determinant for being the object of a presumption, but rather being known as a logical ground. Otherwise, erroneous presumptions (*arthāpatti-bhrama*) would be impossible.

And thus, that form under which the probans (*upapādaka*) is apprehended, as delimited by that form, is the object of the presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*). In that case, if there were a single delimitor of probans-ness (*upapādakatāvacchedaka*) common to all the various instances of difference found within the presumptive testimony, then even that [common property] would indeed manifest. But this is not the case, because such a thing cannot be defined. To explain: the state of being different from a jar and a cloth is what is to be established (*upapādya*); and the probans for that is not "being different from everything," because that is impossible, as it would entail the absurdity of [the subject] being different from itself.

Nor can it be "the state of being different from everything other than itself"; for, against the proponent of non-duality (advaitavādin), the qualification "other than itself" is unestablished, and because the nature of "selfhood" lacks a commonality (ananugama). Thus, one must accept that the probans is simply "being different from this or that specific thing" in its respective form.

Therefore, since the delimiters of the status of being a subsumer (*upapādakatāvacchedaka*) are manifold, not everything that is a subsumer is the object of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*). Consequently, if there were a requirement for separate cognitions of each instance of subsumption, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) regarding the cognition of subsumption in every case. Since the series must eventually rest somewhere, it is at that very point where the scope for scriptural revelation (*śruti*) is found; thus, it culminates in the non-duality of all things (*sarvādvaite*). What, then, is impossible here? Furthermore, in the illustrative example, there is everywhere only one single delimiter of the status of being a subsumer common to itself; therefore, by virtue of being delimited by that, its own manifestation also occurs.

There is an inconsistency. For instance: since the apprehension of the impossibility of the relation with consciousness (*dṛk-sambandha*) is not possible without the falsity (*mithyātva*) delimited by "being an object of perception" (*dṛśyatva*), the falsity delimited by that [perceptibility] is the object of the presumption (*arthāpatti*); thus, its own falsity is also its own object. In the same way, the impossibility of being sublated by knowledge (*jñāna-nivartyatva*) also has itself as its object, because in that case too, "being an object of perception" and so forth serve as the single delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*).

Thus, it is not contradictory for the Śruti, which teaches the non-difference of all things in Brahman, to have as its object that very non-difference of the Self, since this would otherwise be inexplicable given the negation of mere difference. For while the occurrence of one's own difference [within a universal] when there is difference of all things might lead to a fault, the occurrence of one's own non-difference when there is non-difference of all things does not constitute a defect. Therefore, the Śruti on non-duality (advaita), by teaching the identity of the sublated and the sublator, remains uncontradicted and establishes the non-duality of all.

Now, an objection may be raised: "Since words, cognitions, and actions do not function by ceasing their operation once begun, how can it be said that a cognition which initially has a small object later comes to have a vast object? This is not so, because our own cognitions—which establish the validity of the non-dual cognition (*advaitabuddhi*) that encompasses all objects and arises instantaneously from the sacred scripture (*śruti*)—arise only gradually. Furthermore, the knowledge of inapplicability (*ayogyatājñāna*) is neither an obstacle to verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*), nor is the knowledge of applicability (*yogyatājñāna*) its cause; for if it were, the initial cognition of the non-duality of all things would not occur. As it has been said:
"For a word indeed produces a cognition even with respect to an object that is absolutely non-existent;
however, because it is uncontradicted, it constitutes valid knowledge here, its intrinsic validity being firmly established."

The detailed exposition of this point is to be found in the *Vedāntakalpalatikā*. By this, the following [objection] is refuted: "Even if the final cognition is false, its object is not false, because the falsity of a cognition does not necessarily prove the falsity of its object, as there is a deviation (vyabhicāra) in the case of the non-dual (advaita) cognition. This is refuted because the Śruti itself teaches that duality alone is to be negated; and since there is no means of knowledge to indicate the falsity of the object of the non-dual cognition, it is real precisely for that reason, and not because of the falsity of the cognition—thus, there is nothing to this [objection].

Objection: If there is no difference between the cognition of duality and the cognition of non-duality, how can there be a relationship of sublated and sublator? Nor can that relationship be based merely on conventional difference, for that would result in the cognition of duality also being a sublater. Response: This is not so, because mere conventional difference is not a sufficient condition for being a sublater.

For it has been demonstrated in the investigation into the relative strength of verbal testimony and perception that the established principle is this: that which possesses a proven status as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and is thus powerful is the sublater (*bādhaka*), whereas that which possesses a doubtful status as a means of valid cognition and is thus weak is the sublated (*bādhyam*); since, by this rule, dualistic cognition is weak and therefore non-sublating, while non-dualistic cognition is strong and therefore the sublater.

As for the argument that the Śruti passage, "Water indeed is all this," or the inference—"The subject under dispute is non-different from water, because it is perceived as such, like water"—having apprehended its own sublation (the non-difference from water) and thereby becoming itself unsublated, would—by the logic you have stated—make known the non-difference of everything from water; that is not so. For even if there were a cognition of non-difference with water, the sublation of the sublated is still logically possible, since the identity of the sublated and the sublator has not been cognized; for the relationship of sublated and sublator exists between the cognition of identity and the cognition of difference.

Because [the cognition of the identity of water] does not perish due to the cognition of the identity with water; for indeed, the non-existence of a sublater is the cause for the absence of being a sublater, since a sublater is never observed to be its own sublater. Therefore, the cognition of the identity between the sublated and the sublater is not equal to the cognition of the identity with water.

By this, the following is refuted: [the claim that] my previous statement—"everything is distinct from everything else"—first apprehends the distinction of the non-dualist statement, its cognition, and its objects from those [other things], and being thus uncontradicted, ultimately results in the distinction of everything; for there is no reason why the status of being a sublater would not exist even if there were a distinction between the sublated and the sublater (just as there is no sublation if they are non-distinct), and because of the previously mentioned defects. This is the general direction [of the argument].

The non-existence of everything does not differ from the falsity of everything; therefore, the objection that "everything is non-existent" finds no ground. Now, is it the case that the scripture teaches the falsity of everything, or its non-difference from Brahman? In the first case, the grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) in the statement "All this, indeed, is Brahman" would be impossible, because identity between the real and the unreal is untenable.

In the second case, there would be validity for errors such as "this is silver" or "I am fair-complexioned," the Vedāntas that teach the distinction between the Self and the body etc., as well as the exclusion of falsehood and so forth, and even sublaters such as "this is not silver" would lack authority. Furthermore, since everything—including the Brahman non-different from that [Self] and their mutual non-difference—would in fact be known by the very cognition of a jar, there would be omniscience, the Vedāntas would be rendered useless, and liberation would occur immediately.

If it is argued that—since in reality there is no difference between pleasure and pain, bondage and liberation, distinction and non-distinction, defects and ornaments, victory and defeat, or error and valid cognition—all things would result in a total confusion (sarvasaṅkara), leading to contradictions with one's own actions, logic, and statements—this is not so. In the first case, grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) is possible even through the relation of material cause and effect (upādānopādeyabhāva), as in "clay is the pot" or "this is silver. In the second case, although there is no difference in reality, all systematic arrangements are possible by resorting to the difference that is illusory (āvidyaka).

Nor should it be argued that difference (bheda) cannot be illusory (āvidyaka) because it is non-different from Brahman, which is not illusory; for we accept that even "illusoriness" itself is merely illusory. If it is asked how "illusoriness" can be illusory since it too is non-different from Brahman, understand this: because even in that case, it is conceptually constructed (kalpita).

[Objection: But surely, since even the difference caused by ignorance (*āvidyaka*) is absent in liberation, bliss would be non-different from suffering, resulting in its being a non-goal for the person (*apuruṣārtha*). Furthermore, although the respective unique natures (*asādhāraṇasvabhāva*) of those [individuals] are absent there, if they were non-different from them, this "non-difference" would be merely technical and would ultimately resolve into difference. Moreover, even if one accepts difference in terms of their unique forms while negating difference in terms of their nature as *sat* (Being), this would result in proving what is already accepted and the negation of something that was never a possibility. [Reply: This is not so, because within the single individuality of Brahman, the respective unique natures...

Because [the world] is non-existent by virtue of being imagined (*kalpitatva*), at the time of negating all imagination, there is no possibility of the occurrence of difference or non-difference as delimited by imagined properties (*kalpitadharma*). For this very reason, there is neither a negation of what was not previously established (*aprasaktapratiṣedha*) nor an acceptance of an undesired consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*); for properties such as "being existent" (*sat*) or "being a substance" (*dravya*)—which are established through cognitions such as "the substance is existent" (*sad dravyam*) and "the quality is existent" (*san guṇaḥ*)—are precisely what are negated in Brahman. Therefore, since it is the teaching of a single, unique manifestation of existence (*sadvyañjakti*) which is devoid of all attributes and consists of consciousness and bliss (*cidānanda*), it is established that this non-difference (*abheda*) is not merely technical or conventional (*pāribhāṣika*).

Thus, in this way, whether one holds the view that "everything is non-different from Brahman," or the view that even though that which is illusory is different from Brahman, only pure existence (*sanmātra*) is non-different from Brahman, there is neither contradiction with perception and other means of knowledge, nor is there any internal inconsistency between earlier and later statements.
Thus ends the removal of objections regarding the scriptural texts on non-duality (*advaita*).

Now, one might object: although in the passage "In [the state of] water, the seer is one, non-dual," the word *salila* (water) refers merely to clarity by way of similarity, and since that quality—consisting in being untouched by all impurities—is compatible even with non-duality; and although in the passage "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone," the word *agra* (beginning), as well as the subsequent statements such as "It thought, 'May I be many,' 'It projected names and forms,'" which imply time, the act of seeing, and the world consisting of names and forms, do not contradict real non-duality because they concern a duality that is illusory (*avidyaka*); nevertheless...

If it is argued that there is a contradiction in stating the existence of the universe denoted by the word "this" (*idam*) as non-different from "Being" (*sat*) through the phrase "In the beginning, this was Being alone," and then negating that very existence with the term "without a second" (*advitīya*), for the statement "it was Being" cannot mean "it was non-being"—we reply: no, because the purpose of the negation is precisely to state that nothing existed apart from Being. This has been explained by the author of the *Bhāṣya* and others in the *Ārambhaṇādhikaraṇa*.

Nor should it be said that by stating non-existence as distinct from existence, one arrives at the reality of being of the nature of the existent (*sadātman*). Let it be so; for who would be afraid when one is engaged in proving the non-existence of that which is non-different from Brahman? Furthermore, we have already stated in the *Vedāntakalpalatikā*, while defining the nature of hearing (*śravaṇa*), that because the non-dualistic statements possess the sixfold marks of intention (*ṣaḍvidhatātparyaliṅga*) and are thus more powerful, the statements concerning creation and so forth serve to establish the duality that is illusory (*avidyaka*). This will also be explained here by us while demonstrating those sixfold marks of intention.

Therefore, since the discourse begins with the proposition that through one cognition all cognitions are known, and concludes with "All this has that as its essence; That is the Truth; That is the Self; Thou art That," non-duality alone constitutes the primary subject matter (*mahāprakaraṇika*). Consequently, it is determined that the words contained within those sentences must be interpreted in accordance with that [non-duality]. Thus, even though words with multiple meanings might suggest other referents, they must be set aside because such meanings would not cohere with the intended sense of the sentence at hand.

One must simply accept that [the compound] has as its purpose the presentation of word-meanings consistent with the meaning of the sentence under discussion. In that regard, if one were to accept it as a *tatpuruṣa* compound—namely, "not having a second"—the meaning would be "it is not the second, but rather the first or the third," and that is not possible, because even those two are "second" in relation to something else. Therefore, the *bahuvrīhi* compound alone, "that in which no second exists," is to be preferred.

Nor should it be argued that since the negation of the three types of difference is possible by the single term *advitīya* alone, the two terms *eka* (one) and *avadhāraṇa* (restriction) are redundant. For the meaning of the word *advitīya* is the negation of that which is delimited as "second" with reference to some heterogeneous entity. And here, this restriction is necessitated solely by the proximity of the term *eka* and the term *avadhāraṇa*, just as the word *go* (cow) is restricted [to the bovine species] by the proximity of the word *balīvarda* (bull). As it has been said: "The tree's internal difference consists of its leaves, flowers, fruits, and so forth; its homogeneous difference is from another tree, and its heterogeneous difference is from stones and the like."

"Thus, the threefold division that would otherwise accrue to an existent reality (sad-vastu) is precluded by the three [terms]—the single [term], the restrictive particle, and the negation of duality—in succession. In this context, "internal division" (svagata-bheda) refers to the distinction between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara), which consists of multiplicity. "Homogeneous division" (sajātīya-bheda) here refers to the distinction between homogeneous entities such as various types of earth, based on their common nature as substance (dravyatva) and so forth. "Heterogeneous division" (vijātīya-bheda) refers to the distinction between qualities (guṇa) and other categories. Alternatively, heterogeneous division refers to the distinction from the insentient (jaḍa); homogeneous division refers to the distinction within consciousness (caitanya); and internal division refers to the distinction between attributes such as knowledge (jñāna) and bliss (ānanda).

If, according to the *Mahābhāṣya*, the word "second" (*dvitīya*) refers to a second of the same class—as in the statement, "A second for this cow must be sought," where only a cow is sought as the second, and not a horse or a donkey—then the term "without a second" (*advitīya*) has the sense of negating a difference within the same class. However, the negation of differences consisting of dissimilar things or internal differences (within the same thing) may be explained as intended by the words "one" (*eka*) and "only" (*eva*), as desired. Alternatively, the negation of the three types of difference is accomplished by the word "without a second" alone, while the words "one" and "only" serve to remove any suspicion of limitation.

As for what has been prattled by someone—namely, that the word *dvitīya* signifies a companion, based on the usage "he followed the Pāṇḍava with his sword as his second (*asidvitīyaḥ*)" and the statement in the Mahābhāṣya, "asidvitīya means having the sword as a companion"—and that therefore the meaning of "without a second" (*advitīyam*) should be "without a companion," so too, since the word *eka* has multiple meanings, it can be justified by adopting a non-contradictory sense; thus, one need not accept that [the term *advaita*] results in the falsity [of duality].

And likewise, Amarasimha states: "The word *eka* means 'principal,' 'other,' and 'exclusive,'" while Kaiyaṭa, on the rule *eko gotre*, explains: "This word *eka* denotes 'other,' 'principal,' 'without companion,' 'number,' 'first,' and 'identical. Furthermore, in the rule *ṣṇāntāṣaṭ*, the author of the Mahābhāṣya has also explained that this word *eka* has many meanings: it signifies 'number,' it is expressive of 'without companion,' it signifies 'other,' and so forth. Thus, let the meaning of the word *eka* be either 'otherness' or 'primacy' in relation to the individual soul (*jīva*) and the rest.

Thus, other scriptural passages as well should be explained in this manner; however, that [interpretation] has been refuted by the arguments stated previously. This will be discussed in detail in the *Tātparya-nirūpaṇa*. Therefore, since the threefold difference is negated within Brahman—whose nature is Being—by means of the three words [in the phrase], the sentence "one only, without a second" results in the falsity of anything distinct from it. Other Śrutis and Smṛtis have likewise not been cited here for fear of excessive length; they should be examined by the wise themselves in their respective texts.

Thus concludes the determination of the purport of all non-dualistic scriptures (*sarvādvaita-śruti*) toward non-duality in the *Advaitasiddhi*. Furthermore, the fact that bondage must be false is established by the logical necessity (*anyathānupapatti*) that it must be sublated by knowledge, as taught in such scriptural and traditional texts (*śruti-smṛti*) as: "The knower of the Self crosses over sorrow," "Likewise, the wise one, liberated from name and form," and "The knot of the heart is broken, all doubts are cut asunder, and his karmas are exhausted when That is seen, which is both high and low. For if bondage were real, it would follow—just as in the case of Brahman—that it could not be sublated.

For instance—in the case of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell, a snake in a rope, and so forth—the property of possessing that specific form (e.g., being silver) cannot be the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) for being sublated by knowledge, because it lacks universal concomitance (*ananugama*). Rather, the delimiting factor is simply falsity (*mithyātva*), which is synonymous with being imagined through ignorance (*ajñāna-kalpita*). Similarly, regarding knowledge’s capacity to sublate those [objects], the objectivity of the shell and so forth cannot be the delimiting factor, because it lacks universal concomitance. Rather, the delimiting factor is simply the validity of the cognition of the underlying substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna-pramātva*).

And thus, where knowledge functions as a subverting agent by virtue of being a valid cognition (*pramā*) regarding its substrate, there it follows as a rule that the object to be subverted must be false (*mithyātva*). If such a rule were not accepted, there would be the subverting argument (*bādhaka-tarka*) consisting of the complexity of postulating an infinite number of rules. For instance, since the rule is established that "the modification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa-vṛtti*) which arises in the form of a valid cognition regarding a certain substrate destroys the ignorance (*ajñāna*) residing in that same substrate and having that same form."

Furthermore, since the destruction of the material cause (upādāna) brings about the cessation of its effect (upādeya), the cessation of silver and other such objects—which are effects of the ignorance regarding the specific form [of the shell]—is necessarily brought about by the knowledge of the shell and so forth upon the destruction of that ignorance; thus, the simplicity of our position is supported by a favorable reasoning (anukūlatarka) that does not require the postulation of any further restrictive rule. Moreover, that shell-silver and the like have ignorance as their material cause will be established later through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka).

This being the case, since the entire phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is sublated by the valid cognition of the Self (*ātmapramā*), it is precisely its being imagined through ignorance (*ajñāna-kalpitatva*) that is postulated as the delimiting condition (*avacchedaka*) therein; not, however, properties such as "being ether" (*ākāśatva*) and the like, which lack universal concomitance (*ananugata*). Nor is "being different from Brahman" or "being different from existence" (*sadbhinnatva*) suitable, even though these are universally concomitant, because they over-extend (*atiprasakti*) to the non-existent (*tuccha*). If one were to introduce a qualifying term to exclude that [non-existence], it would ultimately result in the very nature of falsity (*mithyātva*)—defined as being distinct from both the existent and the non-existent—as the determinant for being sublatable.

Otherwise, there would be the fault of the excessive complexity (gaurava) of postulating further restrictive rules. Thus, the knowledge of the self is a sublater in the same form that the knowledge of mother-of-pearl and the like is a sublater; and the state of being sublated in silver and so forth—which is otherwise inexplicable in the case of the phenomenal world (prapañca) without that same form—leads to the postulation of that form therein as its own explanatory basis (upapādaka), thereby establishing its falsity (mithyātva).

Now, this might indeed be so, if there were some evidence that the determinant (avacchedaka) for the knowledge of the Self—which sublates the phenomenal world—is precisely its status as a valid cognition of a substratum (adhiṣṭhāna-pramātva), common to the knowledge of mother-of-pearl and the like; for it is possible for something to be a sublater even by way of another form. However, scripture is an authority only for the fact that the knowledge of the non-dual Self is the sublater of the dualistic phenomenal world, and not regarding the specific nature of that determinant either.

Furthermore, falsity is not established merely by the fact of being removable by knowledge, because this would lead to a logical deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of sins and the like, which are removed by the sight of the Setu bridge and other such acts. If it is argued that there is no deviation in those cases because the removal is due to their being enjoined actions (*vihitakriyātva*), then how can it be determined that in the present case (of ignorance) no other limiting property (*avacchedaka*) exists? For knowledge functions as a remover of its own prior non-existence (*svaprāgabhāva*) by virtue of being its counter-positive (*pratiyogitva*); however, it removes prior cognitions and the like by being a subsequent contradictory quality (*uttaravirodhiguṇatva*), and it removes latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) by being their fruit (*phalatva*).

[The counter-examples are: with respect to passion and the like, by way of perceiving the defects in the object; with respect to poison, by way of meditating on Garuḍa; and with respect to sin, by way of performing prescribed rites such as crossing a bridge. And thus, since we observe that something can be removed by knowledge even without being false, this [property of being removable by knowledge] is not a prover of falsity. If it is argued that even in the examples cited, there is indeed falsity because their reality is not admitted, let it be so or let it not be; however, we maintain that the mere fact of being removable by knowledge is not a prover of that [falsity].

If [the world] were established by another reason (*hetvantara*), the presentation of this [reason] would be useless. If you ask how it is in the case of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell and the like, listen: because in those cases, knowledge functions as a remover [of error] by virtue of being a knowledge of the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*). For "being a knowledge of the substrate" means either being a knowledge that destroys ignorance (*ajñāna*), or being a valid cognition (*pramā*) whose object is identical to the object of that ignorance; since there is no evidence for its being a remover in that specific form, it follows that the world cannot have ignorance of the Self as its material cause (*upādāna*). Self-knowledge also functions as a sublater of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) precisely by virtue of being knowledge of the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna-jñāna*), since no other mode of operation is possible. To explain: first of all, "counter-positiveness" (*pratiyogitva*) cannot be the delimiting condition (*avacchedaka*). This is because the phenomenal world is of a positive nature (*bhāvarūpa*), and because it is not established that knowledge—which consists in the cessation of antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*)—sublates its own counter-positive, namely that antecedent non-existence. Nor can "being a subsequent quality" (*uttara-guṇatva*) be the condition; for ether and so forth lack the status of being specific qualities of the self (*ātma-viśeṣa-guṇa*), and because it would follow that desire and the like would also sublate the phenomenal world.

Nor can it be the result [of the practice], because, just as a mental impression (*saṃskāra*) produces memory, space and the like do not produce knowledge of the Self; furthermore, the example is unestablished because a mental impression is not destroyed by memory. As for the observation of defects in an object leading to the cessation of passion and so forth, this occurs by way of removing the cause of that passion—namely, the error consisting in the notion that the object is a means to a desired end that is not connected with a powerful undesirable consequence—and thus it does not exceed the scope of the present example, since it is equivalent to the case of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell. However, meditation on Garuḍa is not a counter-example.

This is because meditation is not admitted to be a form of knowledge, unlike desire and the like; for knowledge, being independent of desire, is distinct from that knowledge which is dependent upon it. This is clear in the authoritative treatises (*ākara*). Even if it were a form of knowledge, it would not differ from the view that it is the "seeing of the bridge" (*setudarśana*), since there is no difference in their both being prescribed by scripture. The only remaining point is that it would be a prescribed action (*vihitakriyā*) like the seeing of the bridge and so forth; however, that is impossible, because knowledge cannot be made or unmade, and thus it cannot be something to be enjoined (*vidheya*).

The procedure regarding knowledge has been refuted in detail in the authoritative treatises (*ākaras*), and it shall be refuted here as well. If it is asked, "How [is this] in the case of seeing the *setu* (the bridge)?"—it is because it is possible for it to be an object of cognition through a specific form (*viśiṣṭākāra*). For the mere sight of the *setu* does not possess the power to destroy evil (*durita*); otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that even the barbarians (*mlecchas*) residing there would have their evil destroyed. Rather, [it destroys evil] when it is qualified by a collection of observances (*vratakalāpa*) preceded by such acts as approaching from a foreign kingdom.

And likewise, since the rules—such as the avoidance of umbrellas and sandals, the prohibition against traveling to distant lands, and the requirement to subsist on alms—are achievable through human effort (*kṛtisādhya*), the sight of the Setu, being qualified by those [rules], is also achievable through human effort; thus, its prescription is logically possible in its qualified form. However, in the case of the knowledge of the Self (*ātmajñāna*), there is no qualification whatsoever that is achievable through human effort, by virtue of which it could be prescribed even as something qualified. This is because the combination of ritual actions (*karmasamuccaya*) will be refuted later.

Furthermore, since bondage has ignorance alone as its cause, it does not require any remover other than knowledge. That bondage has ignorance as its cause is established by scripture, tradition, and reasoning, such as: "One should know Māyā as Prakṛti," and "Knowledge is veiled by ignorance; thereby living beings are deluded. This will also be explained further on. Moreover, it is observed in the case of the knowledge of mother-of-pearl and the like that there is no requirement for anything else besides the arising of the knowledge that removes ignorance. Thus it has been stated by the authors of the Vārttika: "Merely from the birth of the correct cognition arising from sentences such as 'That thou art'..."
"Ignorance, along with its effects, did not exist, does not exist, and will not exist.
"The cognition of the true nature of the inner self alone effects the destruction of ignorance regarding the inner self;
and that [cognition] arises from the very birth of the Self and requires nothing else for the destruction of darkness."

And thus [it is said]. For this very reason, there are scriptural passages such as: "For where there is duality, as it were, there one sees another; but where for him everything has become the Self alone, by what and whom should he see? and so forth; as well as:
"That which is night for all beings, therein the self-controlled man is awake;
that wherein beings are awake is night for the sage who sees."

Smṛtis such as these demonstrate that the perception of saṃsāra occurs during the state of avidyā, while its non-perception occurs during the state of vidyā. Therefore, because bondage is sublated by the knowledge of the Self through the latter’s status as the means of valid cognition of the substrate, its falsity is established, just as in the case of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell and similar instances.
