As for the counter-example that a real object such as a jar is removed by God’s knowledge, that is not correct. For even in the view of the Logicians (Tārkikas), God’s knowledge functions as a cause only by being an immediate cognition whose object is the material cause (*upādāna*). Furthermore, a non-entity (*abhāva*) has no material cause, and there is no evidence for its having a cause with respect to non-existence. If it were to have a material cause, then by virtue of being inherent in that cause, it would follow that it too is a positive entity (*bhāva*). Moreover, just like absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) and so forth, destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) can appropriately have that [God] as its object even if it is not produced by Him.

Furthermore, since there is no consensus even among others regarding such knowledge of God, there is no inconsistency whatsoever. And just as the cognition of mother-of-pearl and the like has the power to remove the notion of silver only by depending on the absence of a cognition of its invalidity, so too the cognition of the Self depends on the absence of a cognition of its invalidity—consisting in the removal of doubts such as impossibility—which is brought about through hearing (*śravaṇa*) and other means; thus, nothing additional has been postulated.

The fact that the knowledge of the Self is achievable through all meritorious deeds (*sarvasukṛta*), which is distinct from the cognition of mother-of-pearl and similar objects, constitutes the fallacy of "balancing the heterogeneity" (*vaidharmyasamā jāti*) because it merely points out a difference between the example and the subject of the illustration. Furthermore, the principle that ignorance is removable by a cognition that is co-referential and of the same form, as well as the delay in the destruction of bondage during *jīvanmukti* due to the obstruction of *prārabdha*-karma, and so forth, will all be established further below.

However, regarding the fact that reality (*satya*) is removable by knowledge, the author of the *Vivaraṇa* has described an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) based on its being related to both its locus and its object, and so forth. Therefore, it is established that being removable by knowledge by virtue of being the knowledge of the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna-jñānatva*) is the proof for falsity (*mithyātva*).
Thus ends the section "The Inexplicability Otherwise of Being Removable by Knowledge" in the *Advaitasiddhi*.

The falsity of the world is established even by the impossibility of explaining its perception otherwise than as being "creation upon perception" (*dṛṣṭisṛṣṭi*), just like the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell, a dream, and so forth. Now, what is this "creation upon perception"? Is it that (1) perception itself is creation; or (2) that there is no creation apart from perception; or (3) that there is no object to be created apart from perception; or (4) that [the world] is produced by the causal complex of perception; or (5) that creation is simultaneous with perception; or (6) that creation has the same ontological status as the existence of perception; or (7) that it is distinct from both the real and the unreal; or (8) that, while being excluded from the three kinds of existence, it is yet distinct from the non-existent?

Or is it the non-existence of unperceived entities? Or is it the existence of perceived entities alone? Regarding the first [option], is "vision" intended to mean a mental modification (*vṛtti*) or the nature of consciousness (*caitanya*)? In the first case, there would follow the consequence that even Brahman—the object of the final mental modification—is itself a creation of vision. In the second case, there would follow the consequence of creation occurring at all times. The second [option] is not tenable, because the distinct usage of language—"This was created by Caitra and seen by me"—would be inexplicable. The third [option] is not tenable, because it contradicts experience, as evidenced by the fact that one says, "The jar is known, but the knowledge is not. Nor is the fourth [option] tenable.

It is not the fourth, because the previously mentioned defect applies due to the non-difference from the perception of a jar and so forth, since they are produced by the same causal complex (*ekasāmagrī*). It is not the fifth, because there would be the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) regarding jars and the like that arise at the same time as verbal or other cognitions; furthermore, it would result in the fallacy of shifting the subject (*arthāntara*) in other cases. It is not the sixth, because there is the fallacy of proving what is already established, as the [perception] is logically possible even when both [the object and the cognition] exist. It is not the seventh, because this very [seventh] is itself the nature of falsity (*mithyātva*), and thus it is illogical to put forward that very thing as the means to prove it.

It is not the eighth, because even the *prātibhāsika* (illusory) reality is included within the threefold reality, and under the doctrine of *dṛṣṭisṛṣṭi* (creation upon perception), it is impossible for that [reality] to exist outside of the world. It is not the ninth, because it would be common to the *tuccha* (the absolutely non-existent). It is not the tenth, because there would be the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) regarding pleasure and so forth, and because there would be the fallacy of shifting the subject (*arthāntara*) regarding other things—[if you say this], we reply: no.

This is because what is intended [by the term "existence only when known"] is either (1) existence only when known based on the fact of being produced by a defect; or (2) existence only when known as perceived within a perceived limiting condition (*upādhi*); or (3) existence only when known while being unknowable to another perceiver. Thus, there is no proving of what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) regarding the aspect of pleasure and so forth, nor is there the fallacy of proving something else (*arthāntara*) elsewhere.
But surely: "The individual soul (*jīva*), the Lord (*īśa*), pure consciousness (*viśuddhā cit*), and likewise the difference between the individual soul and the Lord..."
Ignorance (avidyā), the conjunction of that [ignorance] with the intellect (citi), and the six [categories]—these are beginningless for us.

If it is argued that there is a contradiction with the statements of the ancients and with the Sūtra, Bhāṣya, Vārtika, Vivaraṇa, and other texts—which, by means of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) and so forth, establish the permanence of the universe for the Buddhist—[we reply: no. This is because the doctrine of "creation upon perception" (*dṛṣṭisṛṣṭi*) is accepted only regarding the objects of creation that are distinct from the beginningless [Self], and because permanence is accepted in the sense of subsistence in the form of the cause. Since the refutation of the momentariness favored by the Buddhists is established by this much alone, there is no contradiction with the scriptures; on the contrary, the doctrine of "creation upon perception" has been demonstrated many times in the scriptures themselves.

[Objection: But if, having as their very essence mere cognition, they are not produced by specific causes, then the scriptural injunctions for the Jyotiṣṭoma and other sacrifices for the sake of heaven and so forth, the injunctions for hearing and so forth for the sake of the direct realization of Brahman, and the statement that space and the like are the causes of air and the like, would all be improper. [Reply: This is not so, because these are justifiable in the same way as the teachings regarding the causal relations between effects and causes in dreams. Nor does it follow that the Vedānta texts and their Mīmāṃsā (exegesis) would thereby become equivalent to dream narratives and their exegesis; for a distinction is established by the presence or absence of sublation regarding the objects [of the two].

For this very reason, the objection that one’s own actions would be contradicted—since it would be impossible to engage in eating for the sake of satisfaction, or in speech and so forth for the sake of convincing others—is refuted; for such engagement is possible, just like the activities occurring in a dream.

Now, if this were so, the determination of objects according to their respective cognitions (*pratikarmavyavasthā*) would be untenable, because a jar or the like does not exist prior to its own cognition. Furthermore, since even the substrate—the "this-ness" (*idamaṃśa*) of the mother-of-pearl—does not exist prior to the cognition "this is silver," as is the case with the silver itself, there would be an impossibility of both the incidental definition of superimposition (*adhyāsa*) as being produced by the three causes such as sensory contact, and the essential definition as the non-existence of any mixture between a real object and a false object. If this is argued, we say no.

This is because the systematic arrangement of individual cognitions (*pratikarmavyavasthā*)—which consists of being produced by the three causes such as conjunction (*saṃprayoga*)—and the incidental definition of superimposition (*adhyāsa*) are intended for those of duller faculties. However, the essential definition—that "the appearance of a real entity as mixed with an unreal entity"—is not contradicted even in the view that the world is a creation of perception (*dṛṣṭisṛṣṭivāda*). For it is not the case that consciousness delimited by the "this" aspect (*idamaṃśa*) is not a real entity, nor is it the case that there is no appearance of the false silver as mixed with it.

Nor should it be argued that because the nature of being mother-of-pearl (*śuktitva*) and so forth is absent at the time of the cognition "this is silver," there is a contradiction with the process [of illusion] whereby superimposition is the effect of the ignorance (*ajñāna*) of that object; for even though the nature of being mother-of-pearl is absent at the time of the cognition "this is silver," this does not contradict the persistence of the ignorance of it. Indeed, ignorance is not contradicted at the time when its object is absent, just as it is not contradicted at the time when the object exists.

Nor should it be argued that the relationship of sublation (*bādhyabādhakabhāva*) is untenable between the two cognitions—"this is silver" and "this is not silver"—because they have different objects; for even though the objects are different, the relationship of sublation is possible due to the similarity (*sārūpya*) between the two objects, just as in the case of the sublated and the sublator within a dream. Nor should it be argued that if the sublation of silver and so forth is also a product of "creation upon perception" (*dṛṣṭisṛṣṭi*), then the falsity (*mithyātva*) of the silver and such cannot be established by that sublation; this is not to be said.

Since it has been established that the condition for sublation (*bādhakatva*) is precisely the state of having a lower degree of reality (*anyūnasattākatva*) rather than a higher degree of reality (*adhikasattākatva*), there is no contradiction between the sublation of the phenomenal by the phenomenal or the sublation of the illusory by the illusory.

Nor should it be argued that because the distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman is unperceived—and thus non-existent—during deep sleep, cosmic dissolution (*pralaya*), and so forth, there would follow the consequence of the liberated soul returning again with every instance of deep sleep or dissolution; for it has been stated that the distinction between the *jīva* and Brahman is beginningless (*anādi*), and that the theory of "creation upon perception" (*dṛṣṭisṛṣṭivāda*) is not accepted [in this regard]. Nor is it the case that the re-awakening of one who has slept is impossible due to the absence of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) and the like for that person; for latent impressions and the rest exist in the form of their cause (*kāraṇātman*).

Nor does it follow that liberation (mokṣa) is subject to the doctrine of "creation upon perception" (dṛṣṭisṛṣṭi) by virtue of its being distinct from perception, as in the case of dream-liberation; for since liberation is the very nature of Brahman, it is not established that it is different from perception. Nor should it be argued that perception in the form of pure consciousness is not creation, but rather that perception—either as consciousness qualified by a mental modification (vṛtti) or as the modification itself—is creation, and that there would thus be an infinite regress because that [perception] would require another perception as its creation. This is not to be said.

If mere consciousness (*caitanyamātra*) were the "vision" (*dṛṣṭi*), then because it would possess the same ontological status as that [consciousness], objects such as pots would necessarily follow as being eternal; nevertheless, the term "vision" refers specifically to consciousness as conditioned by a mental modification (*vṛttyupahitacaitanya*). Since even within a mental modification, the modification itself—being its own essential nature—is the condition for consciousness, there is no infinite regress. For this very reason, the objection—that if defects, ignorance, the seer, the body, the senses, and so forth are also "creation upon vision," then in their absence there can be no illusion, and thus there would be an infinite regress—is refuted.

This is because [the appearance of objects] is possible even without dependence on the body, senses, and so forth, just like a dream-delusion; and the conformity with positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) is likewise the same. Nor should it be argued that since the "creation upon seeing" (*dṛṣṭisṛṣṭi*) is itself a creation upon seeing, it would follow that things such as jars are not creations upon seeing; for just as knowledge remains knowledge even when it is itself an object of knowledge without the object thereby ceasing to be known, so too, even though the "creation upon seeing" is itself a creation upon seeing, it is logically consistent that jars and other things are also creations upon seeing.

[Objection: But surely there is a contradiction with the recognition of identity (*aikyapratyabhijñā*), because that which was perceived at a previous time does not exist now. Nor is this [recognition] an error, because—unlike in the case of a lamp or similar objects where there is a difference in transformation (*pariṇāmabheda*)—there is no sublater (*bādhaka*) here. If it were an error even in the absence of such a sublater, then it would follow that even a jar or other objects possess difference within a single moment, and that even the Self (*ātman*) undergoes difference at every moment. [Reply: This is not so.

Since the falsity of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) has been established by such scriptural passages as "There is no diversity here" (*neha nānā*), its nature as consisting merely of appearance—like a snake in a rope—is itself the sublation (*bādhaka*) of its existence at any time other than the time of its appearance. Therefore, the recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) of things distinct from the Self that exist at different times is an error (*bhrānti*). However, the perception of oneness in the Self and the recognition of identity in objects like a jar, when delimited by a single point in time, are not errors; for there is no sublation of the non-difference between the Self and a jar, etc., when they are delimited by the same moment in time.

Recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) regarding a jar or similar object, even when delimited by the same time as it is perceived by another person, is nothing but an error (*bhrama*), because there is a difference in the appearances (*pratibhāsa*). For example, when ten people simultaneously flee from a single rope lying in dim darkness due to the delusion that it is a snake, they may agree with one another that "everyone has experienced the very same snake"; yet this recognition is an error, because what is established by one person's delusion cannot be known by another.

[Objection: But how can there be an illusion of non-difference here, given that there is an absence of any cause for it, such as similarity (*sādṛśya*)? [Reply: No, because, as in the case of an illusion of non-difference in a dream, similarity and so forth are possible through the principle of "creation upon perception" (*dṛṣṭisṛṣṭi*). Nor should it be said that non-difference itself should arise in this way; for that is precisely what we accept. This is because, as in the case of a rope-snake and the like, there is a rule that only that which has already arisen is perceived. Nor is there a lack of a determining factor for why [non-difference] arises in some cases and not in others, since we admit that *māyā* possesses manifold powers (*vicitraśakti*).

Nor should it be argued that the example "This is that Devadatta" is inapplicable as an illustration for the statement "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*) and similar sentences, on the grounds that they aim at identity through *jahadajahallakṣaṇā* (indication by abandoning and not abandoning). Although the difference between the substrate (*dharmin*)—just like its attributes (*dharma*)—is indeed sublated, and thus even *jahadajahallakṣaṇā* would be inappropriate; nevertheless, when the non-difference of the attributes is not grasped due to sublation, but rather only the non-difference of the substrate, then the status of the example "This is that" is established, since *jahadajahallakṣaṇā* is possible in such cases.

Nor can it be argued that because non-difference (*abheda*) is also a creation of perception (*dṛṣṭisṛṣṭi*), the knowledge thereof cannot be subversive; for the non-difference of the Self is of the very nature of the Self and thus lacks the status of being a creation of perception. Furthermore, subversiveness is established by the mere fact of having an equal or superior degree of reality (*anyūnasattākatva*). Nor should it be said that since even direct intuition (*sākṣātkāra*) is a creation of perception, it would lack the status of being produced by a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), and thus, lacking the nature of knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), liberation could not result from it; for the status of being knowledge of reality is established simply by having an unsublated object (*abādhitaviṣayatva*), and this remains intact even if that intuition is a creation of perception.

Nor is there any contradiction with such scriptural passages as, "The sky is eternal, the earth is eternal, these mountains are eternal; this entire world is eternal. For even by those who maintain the doctrine of impermanence, it is necessary to interpret the word "eternal" (*dhruva*) otherwise; for it is more appropriate to understand it as referring to the non-interruption of the continuum until the end of the kalpa, in accordance with those scriptures that establish the doctrine of creation upon perception (*dṛṣṭisṛṣṭi*). Otherwise, one would fail to grasp the meaning in passages such as "the king is eternal" (*dhruvo rājā*).

Furthermore, regarding the doctrine of "creation as perception" (dṛṣṭisṛṣṭi), the scripture—"From this very Self, all vital breaths, all worlds, all Vedas, all beings, and all these selves emerge"—is the authoritative proof establishing the creation of the body and so forth from the individual soul upon waking from sleep. Nor should it be argued: "Since the manifold world of vital breaths and the rest exists during deep sleep, for what purpose is there a further creation?"

This is because, through such passages as "But there is not a second, nothing else separate from Him that He might see," scripture declares the dissolution of the entire phenomenal world of effects during deep sleep (*suṣupti*). Nor does this contradict the scriptural statements establishing the existence of the channels (*nāḍī*) called "the beneficial" (*hitā*) during deep sleep.

In response to the inquiry as to by what sequence one becomes deeply asleep (*suṣupta*), the existence of the channels (*nāḍī*) is established through such passages as, "The channels called *hitā* extend from the heart to the pericardium (*purītat*); having descended by them, he sleeps in the pericardium," for the purpose of stating the sequence immediately preceding deep sleep. However, this does not mean they exist even at the time of deep sleep itself, because that would contradict other scriptural texts, and because the mere prior existence of the channels is sufficient to state the sequence.

Now, an objection is raised: since Brahma—referred to by the word "yat" (which) as the locus of sleep in the passage, "Wherein he was thus asleep"—is the one pointed to by the phrase "from this Self," the creation of the vital breaths and so forth must have Him as its agent, and not the individual soul (jīva) who has awakened from sleep. Otherwise, the mention of the production of threads and sparks from a spider and fire respectively, as well as the statement regarding the creation of all worlds in this very context, would be rendered false.

If it is argued that, according to the doctrine of "creation as perception" (*dṛṣṭisṛṣṭivāda*), there is no such thing as the production of threads and so forth by fire or a spider, nor is there the creation of the entire world, we say: no. This is because the word "where" (*yatra*) refers to time, and thus the word "that which" (*yat*) does not designate Brahman. Furthermore, there is no lack of decisive evidence regarding whether the phrase "where" refers to the locus in the form of Brahman or to time.

In the immediately following sentence, "Where was he then? (*kvaiṣa tadābhūt*), the very inclusion of the two words *kva* (where) and *tadā* (then) serves as the determining factor; for if *yatra* were used to indicate place, the question of place (*kva*) would be inappropriate, and if time were not indicated, the subsequent reference by *tadā* would be inappropriate. Furthermore, this has been explained in such a manner by the author of the Bhāṣya and others for the sake of those whose faculties are still coarse. As for the mention of the production of threads and so forth from a spider and the like, that is merely in accordance with the well-known worldly notion of the relationship between cause and effect established through common delusion.

The creation of all worlds and so forth is intended with reference to the manifestation of those respective perceptions; for the purport here is that when [the Lord] perceives something, He creates it at that very same time. Nor is there any inconsistency regarding the diversity of the world if the individual soul (*jīva*), aided by ignorance (*avidyā*), were the cause; for the ignorance which is the material cause (*upādāna*) of the world possesses diverse powers (*śakti*). Another supporting argument has been stated by us in the *Siddhāntabindu*, the *Kalpalatikā*, and elsewhere, and it is clearly stated in the original sources such as the *Vāsiṣṭha-vārtikāmṛta*:
"All these entities, whose source is ignorance, are like bubbles."

"Having arisen for a moment, they go to dissolution in the single ocean of knowledge," and so forth. Therefore, it is established that the entire duality apart from Brahman, consisting of the forms of knowledge and the knowable, is merely of the nature of ignorance (āvidyaka); thus, the empirical reality (prātibhāsika-sattva) of everything is proven.
It remains settled that the universe, like a snake [superimposed] on a rope, does not exist as something real while unknown.

"Because [the world] is created by the vision of one who is awake, and because its dissolution is heard to occur during deep sleep. Thus ends the proof of the doctrine of *dṛṣṭisṛṣṭi* (creation upon perception) in the *Advaitasiddhi*. Furthermore, that seer is indeed one alone, for there is no evidence for its multiplicity. If it be objected: "How can the *jīva* be only one? This contradicts the experience in every body that 'I am happy,' 'I am miserable,' 'I am a transmigrator,' 'I am the master of this [body],' and so forth," we reply: No. By the power of *avidyā*, Brahman alone undergoes transmigration; He alone is the *jīva*. It is of Him alone that there arises, in each body, the cognition of "I" and so forth.

In a dream-body, where the cognition occurs only as "this one is happy" or "this one is miserable," but not as "I am happy" and so forth, that [body] is devoid of a living soul (*nirjīva*). However, where there is the cognition "I" and so forth, that is possessed of a living soul (*sajīva*). The statement regarding the possession of a living soul in respect to the delimiting factor of the cognition "I" within another waking body is made with the intention that its being possessed of a living soul does not mean it is possessed of a second living soul; for there is a lack of evidence for that. If it is argued that the impossibility of the systematic distinction between bondage and liberation serves as such evidence, we say no.

The arrangement of bondage and liberation, as well as the relationship between teacher and disciple, is possible only so long as ignorance persists, just like a dream. Nor does it follow from this that when one single individual soul (*jīva*) is asleep, the entire world would cease to be perceived; for the primary *jīva*, who identifies with the universal totality (*samaṣṭi*), is not asleep at that time. When that [primary soul] has dissolved into deep sleep, the world is no longer perceived by it. However, when the reflection of the *jīva*—delimited by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*)—is asleep, the world is not perceived only by that reflection, but by others as well, because the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of those others have not yet dissolved.
It has been stated that because the latent impression (saṃskāra) exists in the form of its cause, the impossibility of a sleeper rising again is not established.

By this, the following [objections] are refuted: (1) "If you are the creator (*kalpaka*), it is illogical for you to engage in activity for the sake of my liberation; if I am the creator, then your use of words and so forth to communicate knowledge to imagined beings such as myself is untenable. Nor can it be argued that, like a dream, there is no room for such questioning. For if there were no possibility of questioning in this way, it would follow that there is no basis for debate due to a lack of constraints. Furthermore, since the individual soul (*jīva*)—who possesses the conceit (*abhimāna*) of being Caitra, Maitra, and so on—is the creator, conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) such as "you" and "I" are untenable. Nor is there any contradiction with one's own actions and the like.

Since one’s own activity occurs at a time when there is an absence of the certainty that it is imagined (*kalpita*) and so forth, it is improper to subject it to such an objection. Now, if it is argued that because Brahman itself exists as the individual soul (*jīva*), its bondage and liberation belong to that [soul] alone, this would contradict scriptural texts concerning its eternal liberation; [we reply: no, for since liberation is one's own true nature (*svasvarūpa*) and bondage is merely illusory (*avidyaka*), there is no contradiction. Indeed, even though the desert land is naturally parched, it does not become moist by the water imagined in a mirage.

By this, the objection that it is impossible for the imagined individual soul (*jīva*) to possess subjectivity (*pratyaktva*) with respect to its own imaginer is refuted; for that imaginer does not know [the soul] as subjectivity, and there is no other experiencer. Furthermore, the argument that if such experience were denied, the non-duality of the single soul (*ekajīvādvaita*) taught in scripture and elsewhere would also fail to be established, is likewise refuted, because we accept the doctrine of a single soul inhabiting multiple bodies (*aneka-śarīra-eka-jīvavāda*). Nor does it follow, in that case, that subjectivity and objectivity (*parāktva*) are impossible with respect to that very same soul.

It should not be argued that it is impossible for Caitra—who is the object of the cognition "you" with respect to Maitra—to be the object of the cognition "I" with respect to that same person. For, through the superimposition of identity upon distinct internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*), the distinction between being the "inner self" (*pratyaktva*) or the "outer other" (*parāktva*), and the status of being the object of cognitions such as "I," is logically established by taking each respective internal organ into account. Nor does it follow that Maitra would experience the pleasure, pain, and so forth of Caitra. Is this [experience] by means of the internal organ as a limiting adjunct (*avacchinna*), or by means of ignorance (*avidyā*) as a limiting adjunct? It cannot be the first, because there is mutual difference between them in that case.

The second alternative is not tenable, as it would lead to an undesirable consequence (iṣṭāpatti). For this very reason, the objection that "if Caitra’s delusion regarding silver were removed by his direct perception of mother-of-pearl, then the delusion of others would also be removed" is refuted; for such a restriction is logically established by the difference between individual internal organs (antaḥkaraṇa). Now, one might object: "In that case, even upon liberation, when a direct realization arises delimited by the internal organ of any one person, such as Caitra, the cessation of saṃsāra would occur only with respect to that specific internal organ, and not with respect to the internal organs of others. This is not so.

This is because the realization of That consists in the cessation of primordial ignorance (ajñāna) along with its latent tendencies (savilāsa), and at that time, due to the absence of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), there is a disparity [in the locus of these states].

If it be objected: "In the Śrutis, how is it that various attributes of the conscious self (cetana) are spoken of in multiple contexts—ignorance in passages such as 'dwelling within ignorance'; the bondage of karma in passages such as 'those of beautiful conduct'; deep sleep in passages such as 'having attained [the Self] in Being, they do not know'; the knowledge of reality in passages such as 'those whose purpose is well-ascertained through the wisdom of Vedānta'; and liberation in passages such as 'all are completely released from the supreme immortality'? [The answer is: It is not so.

This is because the singular number found in such scriptural passages as, "When the individual soul (*jīva*), sleeping through beginningless illusion, awakens," establishes oneness, and thus the cited scriptures cannot intend plurality in contradiction to that; furthermore, there is no conflict because those scriptures merely restate what is established by the universal delusion [of multiplicity]. Nor should it be argued: "Why should this singular number—not being intended to denote oneness—be like other cases such as 'when the king is devoted to policy' or 'one desiring heaven should sacrifice,' rather than contradicting the preceding passage, 'Thus they are determined in creation,' and the following passage, 'He is to be honored by all beings'? For [the cited passages] do not contradict those two.

Since multiplicity is established through the force of the superimposition of identity with the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), which is the cause of conventional usage such as "interiority," "exteriority," and "I," the scriptural passages cited in the preceding and following sentences do not have that [multiplicity] as their primary purport. Nor should it be argued that the multiplicity of liberated souls is not obtained from elsewhere; for, since the multiplicity of individual souls (*jīva*) is already established, the argument results in the conclusion that only the aspect of liberation is what remains unestablished.

Nor does the fact that a single individual soul (*jīva*) is the creator of all lead to a contradiction with the *Śruti* and other authorities which, while negating the causality of the *jīva*, establish the Lord (*īśvara*) as the cause; for the claim that ignorance (*avidyā*) has pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) as its locus will be refuted later. Furthermore, it does not follow that the *Śruti* passages teaching omniscience, omnipotence, and so forth would be rendered devoid of referent, since the property of being a knower (*jñatva*) simply does not exist in pure consciousness.

It should not be argued that [this is untenable] because there is no God distinct from the individual soul (jīva), or because omniscience in the individual soul is contradicted by experience; for we accept that the individual soul who identifies with the collective whole (samaṣṭyabhimānin) possesses omniscience and universal agency. Nor is there a contradiction with experience, since the non-experience of that [omniscience] and the experience of its opposite are both possible through the force of the superimposition of identity with the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa). However, for the one who identifies with the entire universe (sarvābhimānin), the experience of omniscience indeed exists.

For this very reason, such statements as "I know all those, but you do not know them, O scorcher of the foe" are appropriate. Nor should it be argued that, because of the scriptural text "A person who has a teacher knows," it is impossible for the individual soul (jīva) to attain knowledge of reality without instruction; nor can it be said that instruction is untenable because there is no consciousness other than that which is to be instructed. For, as in a dream, an instructor can exist as a mental construction.

[Objection: But surely, the status of being a teacher does not belong to one who is merely imagined; rather, it belongs to one imagined as a knower of reality (*tattvavit*). And if that were so, liberation would occur at the very moment of the knowledge of reality prior to the instruction, and the instruction would be rendered useless. Furthermore, this would be the same even in the case of a dream. For in that case, the imagination of a guru occurs solely by virtue of his being a speaker of specific words, and not by virtue of his knowing a specific object of knowledge to be achieved through instruction; thus there is a distinction [between waking and dreaming]. [Reply: This is not so. Because here too, just as in that case, such an imagination is possible solely by virtue of his being a speaker of specific sentences.

If it is objected that, in that case, such scriptural passages as "Tell me that alone which the Blessed One knows," and such Smṛti passages as "The knowers of truth who have seen reality will teach you knowledge," would be untenable, we say no. This is because there is no contradiction with the cited texts, since the role of a teacher is possible for one who is conceptually constructed as a knower of the knowledge generally useful for liberation, or as a knower of the unknown reality, or as the speaker of sentences such as "That thou art."

Otherwise, even in your own view, one who is recognized as a knower of reality (*tattvavit*) must be followed as a teacher; consequently, if the knowledge of reality were attained at the very outset, there would follow the absurdity of liberation occurring at that moment, as well as the futility of the instruction [to remain]. By this, it follows that injunctions such as "one should not neglect study and teaching" are intended only for those whose minds are still conceptualizing the future attainment of the knowledge of reality. Furthermore, it is not reasonable for one who knows that his disciple is a mere construction of his own ignorance to engage in teaching for the sake of that disciple's liberation.

Nor can it be argued that activity does not arise because of the lack of knowledge regarding the teacher’s being a mental construction—as in the case of a dream—since such ignorance is impossible for one who knows reality; for, like a dream-teacher, the teacher cannot be questioned precisely because he is a mental construction. Nor should it be said that the teacher is subject to questioning just as the Veda is subject to investigation (mīmāṃsā) on account of its being a cause of the knowledge of reality; for, just as in the case of the Veda, this [objection] is avoided by means of reasoning through the postulation of various forms even in the case of the teacher.

Nor should it be argued that even during a debate, when a correct reply does not occur to one, the response "I am not subject to censure because I am imagined by you" would be valid; for such a reply has no place because it occurs at a time when the debate's status as imagined is not yet certain, and because it is contingent upon a specific formal agreement (*samayabandha*). Therefore, since the teacher is just as much an imagined entity as the student, all established conventions are possible, just as in a dream.

Now, if it is argued that the author of the scripture (*kalpaka*) is neither one who has ascertained non-duality—because that would render the composition of the scripture useless—nor one who has not ascertained non-duality—because that would entail the scripture lacking a foundation in valid cognition (*pramā*), we say no. For even in the absence of a foundation in valid cognition, the authority of the scripture is established by its having an uncontradicted subject matter; thus, we accept the latter alternative. Furthermore, there is no impossibility of engaging in activity for the sake of liberation—which is to be accomplished through great effort—if there is no certainty that "he is so-and-so."

Since the certainty that "I am bound" arises in every individual body through the force of mutual competition (*ahamahamikā*), and because this is attested by one’s own experience, activity becomes possible; furthermore, it has already been stated that it is possible for a single *jīva* alone to animate the bodies of Caitra, Maitra, and others. Moreover, regarding the question "Who is this [person]" in the case of Caitra, Maitra, and so forth, is the object of the inquiry consciousness as apprehended by some [individual], or is it consciousness with all distinctions eliminated? It cannot be the first, because that which is imagined (*kalpita*) lacks the capacity to imagine (*akalpakatva*). Nor can it be the second.

Because its non-determination cannot be established through its oneness; for although pure consciousness is, in reality, not subject to transmigratory existence due to its oneness, it is nonetheless possible for it to appear as if in a state of transmigration and to strive for liberation, by virtue of the ignorance (avidyā) residing within it, which possesses the two powers of concealment (āvaraṇa) and projection (vikṣepa).

Now, one might object: in this beginningless *saṃsāra*, did the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) and liberation ever occur for anyone or not? If the first case were true, then *saṃsāra* would not be perceived at present, because the individual soul (*jīva*) is one. If the latter were true, the knowledge of reality would be impossible due to the impossibility of a traditional transmission (*saṃpradāya*). If you say this, we reply: no. For the lack of a traditional transmission does not contradict the production [of knowledge]; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that nothing of a previously non-existent kind could ever arise. Rather, what is required is the presence of its cause. And that is present now, because the causes such as the teacher and so forth are firmly established through conceptual construction.

Since the identity of the individual soul (*jīva*) [with Brahman] is not established by any means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), the very perception of transmigratory existence prior to this is the proof for the non-arising of the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*). Nor should it be argued: "Let there be no liberation for Śuka, Vāmadeva, and others—who are established by the Śruti and other authorities as knowers of reality—yet how can I have faith that it will happen for me? Understand that [this faith arises] from the firm conviction in the authority of the scriptures (*śāstra-prāmāṇya*).

Otherwise, even though those beings of great power are liberated, there would arise the obstacle to one’s own activity due to the demoness of doubt as to whether liberation will occur for me or not. [Objection: In that case, let the distinction between individual souls (*jīva-bheda*) be established by the very force of the authority of scripture, and let it be accepted that some were liberated even previously.

For it is heard [in scripture]: "Whosoever among the gods awakened to that, he indeed became That; so it was with the seers, and so with human beings"; "One unborn soul, being delighted, lies along with her; another unborn soul leaves her after she has been enjoyed"; "The eternal among the eternals, the consciousness among the conscious," and so forth. And it is remembered [in the Smṛti]: "Many, purified by knowledge and austerity, have taken refuge in my state;
having resorted to this knowledge, they have attained my own nature."

If it is argued that this is so because of such passages [as those cited], we say no. For the aforementioned sentences merely restate the distinctions established by universal worldly delusion and lack the status of being *tatpara* (intended to convey that very thing). Furthermore, the sentences teaching the identity of the individual soul (*jīva*) possess their own meaning as something not already established by other means of knowledge (*mānāntara*). Moreover, the imagined nature of difference is logically established through the analogy of a dream. Sentences intended for the praise of knowledge are not capable of proving the distinction between selves; for it is logical that sentences lacking a primary intention (*atātparyavat*) should be treated as figurative descriptions (*guṇavāda*), provided they do not contradict sentences possessing a primary intention. "And all the moments of time, past and future, however many there may be, joined together..."

"Furthermore, the multitudes of individual souls (jīvas) are each infinitely greater than that"—this and other such Smṛti passages are also to be explained as merely restating the distinctions among the limiting adjuncts (upādhis) of the individual souls. Therefore, it is established that the individual soul, having ignorance as its limiting adjunct, is indeed one. Thus ends the demonstration of how everything is imagined through the ignorance of a single soul in the Advaitasiddhi.

Now, what is this *avidyā*? It cannot first of all be defined as "that which is beginningless, positive in nature, and removable by knowledge. [This definition is flawed] because it lacks extension (*avyāpti*) to the ignorance that veils the consciousness delimited by a beginningless object such as a mother-of-pearl shell; for that [specific ignorance] lacks beginninglessness. Furthermore, there is non-extension to the ignorance that is the material cause (*upādāna*) of an absence (*abhāva*), since that lacks positivity. If an absence were to have a positive entity as its material cause, then even the unreal would have the real as its material cause. Moreover, if ignorance were not the material cause of [an absence], that [absence] could not be removed by knowledge.

To this we reply: even the ignorance that is the material cause (*upādāna*) of silver is indeed beginningless, because it rests upon beginningless consciousness (*caitanya*). As for the subsequent nacre and so forth, they are merely its limiting adjuncts (*avacchedaka*); thus, there is no lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) in that case. Furthermore, "existence" (*bhāvatva*) here is intended merely as being distinct from non-existence (*abhāva-vilakṣaṇatva*). Therefore, since the ignorance that is the material cause of superimposed non-existence is also admitted to be distinct from non-existence, there is no lack of pervasion. Nor should it be argued that there is a rule that a material cause must be of the same class (*sajātīya*), for otherwise, even the unreal would have the real as its material cause.

In every way, whether there be complete homogeneity (*sājātya*) or complete heterogeneity (*vaijātya*), the relationship of material cause and effect (*upādānopādeyabhāva*) is not observed; thus, it is impossible to establish either such homogeneity or heterogeneity. Indeed, if there were no distinction even between the form of the effect and the form of the cause, the relationship of cause and effect could not exist. Furthermore, if the real were the material cause of the unreal, then because the real can never cease to be, its effect—the unreal—could likewise never cease. This is because an effect cannot cease as long as its material cause has not ceased. Therefore, the real cannot be the material cause of the unreal.

Furthermore, this is because Reality (satya) is unchanging (apariṇāmin). Indeed, it is precisely accepted that [Brahman] is the locus of the illusory manifestation (vivarta-adhiṣṭhāna). Nor should it be argued that there is no pervasion (vyāpti) in the case where Brahman is not pervaded by a mental modification (vṛtti) regarding the ignorance of Brahman, on the grounds that Brahman cannot be removed by knowledge; for even in that view, there exists something removable by knowledge which has as its object that [ignorance] along with its adjuncts (upādhi) that are substantially real. And this has been established in the demonstration of the reason "being an object of vision" (dṛśyatva).

Now, [it may be argued that] there is an over-narrow definition (*avyāpti*) because ignorance—which is the material cause of superimpositions based on limiting adjuncts (*aupādhika-bhrama*)—and the ignorance of one liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*) existing after the direct realization of Brahman, do not possess the property of being removable by knowledge. If it is argued that if these two were removable by knowledge, then their cessation would have occurred at the very time of the limiting adjunct and the period of *jīvanmukti* (just as the prior non-existence of knowledge ceases upon its arising), we say no. For although the cessation is delayed due to the delay caused by the absence of the two obstacles—the limiting adjunct and the *prārabdha* karma—their removability by knowledge remains intact.

For the causal capacity of a producer does not depart merely because there is a delay due to some obstacle in one instance; nor, in that case, does it follow that there would be the linguistic usage "it is unknown" regarding something that has already been known. This is because, in such a linguistic usage, the cause is ignorance (*ajñāna*) possessing the power of concealment (*āvaraṇa-śakti*); thus, since that power of concealment is absent [in the case of what is known], such a linguistic usage does not occur. We shall demonstrate how this is so later on. Nor is there an over-extension (*ativyāpti*) of the definition to the relation between ignorance and consciousness (*caitanya*).

This is because what is intended is that [the object] is directly removable by knowledge, or else because it is of the nature of ignorance (*avidyā*). Nor is there any redundancy in the other qualifiers; for the term "beginningless" (*anādi*) serves to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to prior cognitions—which are removable by subsequent cognitions—and the term "existence" (*bhāva*) serves to exclude over-extension to the prior non-existence of cognition (*jñāna-prāgabhāva*) and the prior non-existence of effects produced by cognition. Furthermore, being directly removable by knowledge by virtue of its nature as knowledge (*jñānatva*) constitutes another definition.

Now, one might object: "It is impossible [for ignorance to be beginningless], because being a mere conceptual construct implies that it consists solely of a cognition produced by a defect, and since it is removable by knowledge and is distinct from non-existence, it cannot—like a silver [illusion]—be beginningless. We reply: no; for being a mere conceptual construct is not the determinant factor for either consisting solely of a cognition produced by a defect or for having a beginning.

However, what is essential [for being an object of ignorance] is either: (1) having a conceptualizer (*kalpaka*) simultaneous with the conceptualizer that produces the appearance; (2) having a conceptualizer that has a beginning; (3) being the counter-positive of a cessation not necessitated by the cessation of ignorance; or (4) being the counter-positive of a prior absence (*prāgabhāva*). None of these applies to the case at hand. Furthermore, if one attempts to prove the "having-a-beginning" (*sāditva*) of ignorance by means of its being distinct from an absence that coexists with the property of being removable by knowledge, there is a contradiction with scriptures such as "the one unborn" (*ajāmekām*) and "by beginningless illusion" (*anādimāyayā*). Moreover, this argument is countered by a *satpratipakṣa* (contradictory reason) based on the proof of its beginninglessness—namely, its being distinct from a positive entity (*bhāva*) while being removable by knowledge—and the property of being a positive entity (*bhāvatva*) serves as a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) in this regard.

Nor should it be argued that it is impossible for ignorance (*avidyā*) and the like—which are distinct from non-existence—to be distinct from existence, on the grounds of mutual contradiction (*parasparavirodha*). For, since there exists a subverting proof (*bādhaka*) against both "being an entity" (*bhāvatva*) and "being a non-entity" (*abhāvatva*), their status as a third category is established; thus, the contradiction defined as "mutual exclusion-pervasion" (*parasparavirahavyāpakatva*) is not proven. However, the contradiction defined as "mutual exclusion-pervasion" (*parasparavirahavyāpyatva*) does not entail the other by the absence of one. As it has been stated: "The absence of cowness (*gotva*) does not entail horseness (*aśvatva*)."

Nor is there a lack of sublation for that which is distinct from the absence of selfhood and so forth, because "selfhood" itself serves as the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*). Nor is there a failure of pervasion (*avyāpti*) of the probandum by absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) or mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*), since we do not admit an absolute non-existence or the like that is distinct from its locus and yet unsublatable. Nor is there a failure of pervasion of the probandum in the case of the "void" (*tuccha*), because it is established that [the probans] pervades the probandum as delimited by the nature of being distinct from absence. Furthermore, being beginningless or having a beginning is not the determinant of being unsublatable or sublatable.

This is because those two [properties] are absent in the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and the destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) [of an entity]. Nor is that [property of being an object of removal] qualified by "being an entity" (*bhāvatva*); for since that [quality of being an entity] is absent in non-existence, it would lead to the unwarranted assumption of distinct causal factors for each case. Furthermore, if the cessation or non-cessation of an entity were the sole causal factor for those two [properties], then they would not apply to ignorance (*avidyā*) and the like, which are distinct from entities. Therefore, one must conclude that the presence or absence of the causal complex for destruction (*nāśasāmagrī*) alone is the determining factor for being removable or not being removable.

And since those two [the means and the result] are to be established by the force of their own effects, there is no fault whatsoever. Furthermore, if it is argued that ignorance (*avidyā*) and the rest are not subject to cessation—just like the Self—because they are beginningless and characterized by a difference from non-existence (*abhāva*), then why is it not instead argued that they are indeed subject to cessation, just like antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), because they are different from positive existence (*bhāva*)? Nor is there any fallacy (*vyabhicāra*) regarding destruction (*dhvaṃsa*), absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*), or mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*), for we admit that even these are subject to cessation provided they are distinct from their substrates.

Nor should it be argued that because ignorance persists as long as the existence of the witness (sākṣin)—whose nature consists of the cognition of its own objects—it is impossible for it to cease; for we accept that pain, the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell, and the like cease even while their illuminator, the witness, exists. Thus, we do not accept a rule that things manifested by the witness must persist as long as the witness exists. Furthermore, pure consciousness alone is not the witness; rather, it is consciousness as conditioned by an avidyā-vṛtti.

And thus, since the witness (*sākṣin*)—though it is eternal—is conditioned by the unstable modifications of ignorance (*avidyā-vṛtti*), its persistence lasts only as long as that [conditioning] exists; yet the cessation of ignorance and the rest is still logically possible. Nor does it follow that ignorance and the rest would become non-existent (like the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell) during a state when they are not conditioned by a mental modification (*vṛtti*); for such a rule applies only to things that have a beginning in time. Alternatively, this is because we admit a succession of extremely subtle, continuous streams of modifications of ignorance. May there be auspiciousness!

Alternatively, the definition of ignorance (*ajñāna*) is "being the material cause of error. This definition applies to the view that Brahman, as the substratum of *māyā*, is the material cause of the entire cosmic illusion; however, it does not apply to the view that Brahman alone is the material cause, nor to the view that the material cause is ignorance together with Brahman. Therefore, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) of the definition to Brahman. In the other cases, the material cause of error should be qualified by being either transformative (*pariṇāmin*) or insentient (*acetana*); thus, there is no fault. Furthermore, there is no lack of extension (*avyāpti*) to that which is sublated by a valid cognition (*pramā*) which removes the superimposition of non-existence.

This is because that [error] also has ignorance as its material cause (*upādāna*). Now, an objection is raised: it is not tenable for error to have ignorance—which is distinct from positive entities—as its material cause; for if error were distinct from positive entities, it could not be a product (*upādeya*), and if it were a positive entity, there would be a rule that it must have a positive entity as its material cause. This is not so, because even though ignorance and error are both distinct from positive entities, the relationship of material cause and product is still possible. Indeed, being a positive entity (*bhāvatva*) is not the determining factor (*prayojaka*) for being either a material cause or a product.

Because that [causality] is not observed in the case of the Self; rather, being the inherent cause (*anvayi-kāraṇa*) is the determinant for being the material cause (*upādāna*), while having a beginning (*sāditva*) is the determinant for being the effect (*upādeya*). And neither of these two is necessarily restricted to positive entities (*bhāvatva*). Therefore, the relationship between material cause and effect is also not restricted to positive entities. Nor does it follow from this that destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) would also have to be an effect, for such a consequence is accepted. Furthermore, one should not argue: "In that case, let the prior absence of knowledge (*jñāna-prāgabhāva*) alone be the material cause of error; what is the use of postulating an ignorance (*ajñāna*) distinct from absence? [This is because]... [the argument continues].

Since antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) is restricted by rule to being the producer of its own counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) alone, its status as a producer even of error (*bhrama*) is unestablished; thus, its being the material cause (*upādāna*)—which is a specific form of that [producer-ship]—is all the more remote. Therefore, the relationship of material cause and effect is logical between ignorance (*ajñāna*), which is distinct from the real (*sad-vilakṣaṇa*), and error. And the fact that error is distinct from the real has already been stated and will be stated again. Nor should it be argued that, in this case, error would necessarily be perceived as permeated by ignorance, just as a jar is perceived as permeated by clay.

Since the pervasion (vyāpti) is unestablished—because whatever has something as its material cause (*upādāna*) is not necessarily perceived as being permeated by that [cause]—for instance, the color (*rūpa*) which has a pot as its material cause is not perceived as "the pot. Furthermore, opponents do not admit that it is perceived as being permeated by its primordial matter (*prakṛti*), dyads (*dvyaṇuka*), and so forth. However, permeation by some property or other is indeed accepted even in the present case. Nor is there a lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) regarding ignorance (*ajñāna*) in the position that there are as many ignorances as there are cognitions, specifically in the case of ignorance that is preceded by error and is sublated by valid knowledge (*pramā*).

This is because what is intended is the capacity to serve as the material cause (*upādāna*) of error. Even when an effect does not arise due to the absence of auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*), the capacity itself does not perish. Now, if the specific form that delimits this capacity is not known, how can it be apprehended? [The answer is] that the very first definition (of ignorance) serves as the delimiter of its capacity. Furthermore, on the view that there is only one single ignorance (*ajñāna*), its status as the material cause of error remains entirely intact. Nor does this imply that liberation would follow from the mere knowledge of mother-of-pearl; for it is accepted that such knowledge destroys only a particular state (*avasthā-viśeṣa*) of that ignorance.

And this has been established by us in the *Siddhāntabindu*; furthermore, it was already stated previously that its definition is either "being directly removable by knowledge" (*jñāna*) in its nature as knowledge. Therefore, there is no impossibility regarding the definition of ignorance (*avidyā*); thus everything is clear.
Thus ends the "Establishment of the Definition of Ignorance" in the *Advaitasiddhi*.

Regarding that ignorance, there is the general perception: "I am ignorant; I do not know myself and others"; the specific perception: "I do not know the meaning of what you have said"; and the perception pertaining to deep sleep, established by subsequent reflection: "For so long a time I slept happily, I was not aware of anything. Nor should it be argued: "Since the referent 'I' (ahamartha) is not the locus of ignorance, how can this cognition be accounted for under the view that ignorance is a positive entity?"

This is because [the relation] is established through the connection of having a single locus, by means of the superimposition of identity with the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) upon the consciousness that serves as the substratum of ignorance. For this very reason, the following objection is refuted: "Since there is no function of veiling (*āvaraṇa*) in an insentient object, if the cognition 'I do not know the jar' and similar instances have as their object the absence of knowledge, then let it be the same in the present case as well. This is refuted because, since consciousness limited by each respective object is itself the substratum of ignorance, the linguistic usage regarding that [absence of knowledge] is likewise established even in those cases.

Nor should it be argued: "Since there is an absence of positive ignorance (*bhāvarūpājñāna*) in that which is known by the witness (*sākṣivedya*), such as pleasure, pain, and nescience, as well as in the illusory (*prātibhāsika*), how can the cognition 'I do not know' be accounted for in those cases? For it is impossible to employ the expression "I do not know" with respect to pleasure and the like existing within oneself—which are known by the witness—or with respect to a silver [shell] established through one's own error; whereas the usage "I do not know" regarding the pleasure of another person is accounted for precisely by the ignorance residing in the knower (*pramātṛgata-ajñāna*), which is sublated by indirect knowledge (*parokṣajñāna*).

Therefore, the objection that—even if the knowledge residing in the knower (*pramātṛ*) is destroyed by indirect cognition (*parokṣajñāna*), the linguistic usage "I do not know" would still occur because of the continued existence of ignorance (*ajñāna*) residing in the object—is refuted; for it is impossible to bring about the linguistic usage "I do not know," which is an effect of the ignorance residing in the knower, by means of an ignorance residing in the object.

If it is argued: "But surely, there is no perception of a difference in the objects of the cognition 'I am ignorant'—which is intended to have positive ignorance as its object—and the cognition 'knowledge is not in me'—which has the absence of knowledge as its object—just as there is no perception of a difference in the objects between the cognitions 'the ground is without a jar' and 'the jar does not exist,' without a reversal of the qualifier-qualified relationship, or like the cognitions of desire and aversion and their respective absences," we reply: True.

Since the cognition of the absence of knowledge in general is contradicted by both the cognition and non-cognition of the substratum (*dharmī*) and the counter-correlate (*pratiyogī*), it is logical that even the cognition "there is no knowledge in me" has positive ignorance (*bhāvarūpājñāna*) as its object, because no difference in objects is perceived. To explain: the cognition "there is no knowledge in me" must be admitted—like the cognition "there is no color in the air"—to have as its object either a general absence distinct from all particular absences, or all particular absences whose counter-correlates are delimited by the general property [of being knowledge].

And likewise, how is there no contradiction between the knowledge and non-knowledge of the substratum and the counter-positive which constitute its cause? For a particular absence does not have a counter-positiveness delimited by a generality. This is because, in the cognition of an absence, the property that serves as the qualifier (*prakārībhūta*) in the aspect of the counter-positive is precisely what constitutes the delimiting condition of counter-positiveness (*pratiyogitāvacchedaka*). Otherwise, the establishment of a general absence would be impossible. This fault remains even if one does not admit a general absence distinct from the absences of all particulars.

If the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) of the absence of any particular [object] were delimited by its generality (*sāmānyāvacchinna*), then even on a ground containing a jar, there would arise the cognition "the ground is devoid of jars. Furthermore, even after the cognitions produced by authoritative statements such as "there is no color in air" or "there is no silver in that place," the respective doubts would not cease; for even when the absence of one particular is known, doubt may still arise by taking up another particular.

Now—[it is argued that] in the cognition of a negation (*abhāva*), the property functioning as the qualifier (*prakārībhūtadharma*) appears as the delimiting factor (*avacchedakatva*), even if it was not previously presented [to consciousness], through the relational capacity (*saṃsargamaryādā*) within verbal cognition and elsewhere; for no other causal complex (*sāmagrī*) has been established for the apprehension of delimiting-ness, which is a specific type of essential relation (*svarūpasaṃbandha*).

And thus, since those respective specific absences have as their counter-correlates (pratiyogitā) delimited by those respective particulars, the state of having a counter-correlate delimited by a generality must reside either in the entire collection (kūṭa) of all specific absences—where it exists distributively (vyāsajyavṛtti)—or in a generality-absence distinct from them, where it resides in each individually. Therefore, since the cognition of such an absence contradicts the cognition of all the particulars, how could there be doubt regarding the particulars? This is true.

In the case at hand as well, the cognition of an absence whose counter-correlativity is delimited by the generality of "cognition-ness" (jñānatva) stands in opposition to every particular cognition; how then could such a cognition not be sublated when those particular cognitions—regarded as the causes [of the world]—are present? Thus, since a distinction between the cognitions of absences must necessarily be postulated, it is more parsimonious (lāghava) to postulate a distinction in the absences themselves based on their objects, for if there were no distinction in the objects, a distinction in the cognitions would be impossible.

It is established by universal experience that after perceiving an object, a person engages in inquiry for the sake of its cessation. Although the absence of a specific cognition is the object of the cognition "I do not know," if that were the case, such a cognition would arise even when the object is known; furthermore, there would be an inclination toward inquiry regarding it. Moreover, an objection has already been stated against [the existence of] a general absence. Therefore, it is established that ignorance—which is distinct from mere absence—is the object of cognitions such as "There is no knowledge in me" and "I am ignorant."

But surely, even though ignorance (*ajñāna*) is distinct from non-existence (*abhāva*), it appears precisely as the opposite of knowledge in the form "I do not know. Even in words such as *moha* (delusion), there is merely a lack of explicit mention, just as in the case of words like *pralaya* (dissolution). And it is said in the *Vivaraṇa*: "Because [ignorance] is designated by the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of knowledge, which presupposes a duality [of subject and object]. Otherwise, the opposition of knowledge to ignorance would be without any basis in experience (*aprāmāṇika*).

And likewise, how is it that for you too there is no contradiction resulting from the cognition or non-cognition of the knowledge that determines the contradiction? In this way, since an objectless ignorance is not perceived, a contradiction must be brought forward regarding both the cognition and non-cognition of the object as well. And thus: "When the fault is equal for both sides, or the remedy is also equal, one should not be questioned in such an investigation of the matter."

If it is argued that, according to this logic, it is improper to urge a contradiction against the position of the absence of knowledge—since that contradiction must be avoided by both parties—we say: no. For even though ignorance (*ajñāna*) is of a positive nature (*bhāvarūpa*), is removable by the operation of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇavṛtti*), and is cognizable by the witness-consciousness (*sākṣivedya*), there is no occurrence of contradiction; because the witness-consciousness, which perceives the knowledge that determines the contradiction as well as the objects that distinguish it, is the very means of establishing that [ignorance], and thus does not destroy it. A contradiction would indeed arise only if the apprehension of ignorance required a further valid cognition regarding its object, but such a requirement does not exist.

This has been stated in the *Vivaraṇa*: "Every object is indeed an object of the witness-consciousness (*sākṣicaitanya*), whether in its state of being known or in its state of being unknown. It should not be argued that even in the case of the absence of knowledge, the cognition of the object and so forth is of the nature of the witness; for the cognition "I do not know" has as its object the absence of a cognitive modification (*pramāṇavṛtti*)—thus there is no contradiction. This is what must be said.

This is because there is a disparity between the two cases: while positive ignorance (*bhāvarūpājñāna*) is directly cognizable by the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*), and thus its delimiting objects and so forth can be cognized by the witness through that medium, negation (*abhāva*) is accessible only through non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) and lacks direct cognizability by the witness; therefore, its delimiting objects and so forth cannot be cognized by the witness through that medium.

Although cognition (*jñāna*) is known by the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*), and the object that delimits it is also known by the witness-consciousness through that [cognition], nevertheless, the absence of cognition (*jñānābhāva*) is not known by the witness-consciousness, because it is non-apprehended (*anupalabdha*). Furthermore, a cognition that has arisen is directly known by the witness-consciousness; and when that [cognition] has arisen, its object also shines forth—so how could there be an absence of cognition [at that time]? However, as a qualifier of ignorance (*ajñāna*), even a cognition that has not yet arisen can be known by the witness-consciousness; thus, there is no equality of fault [between our position and yours].

Nor should it be argued: "If the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*), such as the object, is not known beforehand, how can there be knowledge of ignorance qualified by it? For qualified cognition (*viśiṣṭajñāna*) is dependent upon the cognition of its qualifier (*viśeṣaṇajñāna*). This is because there is no evidence that the cognition of a qualifier produces a qualified cognition; for the logicians (*tārkika*) accept that even when the counter-positive (*pratiyogitva*) and the nature of absence (*abhāvatva*) are not previously presented, they appear as qualifiers in the cognition of an absence.

Even so—if it is argued that "how can there be a cognition of a qualified object as qualified (*viśiṣṭavaiśiṣṭya-buddhi*) without a cognition having the qualifier-determinant as its mode (*viśeṣaṇatāvacchedaka-prakāraka-jñāna*)?"—we say no. This is because there is no evidence for a causal relation between being a *viśiṣṭavaiśiṣṭya-buddhi* and being a *viśeṣaṇatāvacchedaka-prakāraka-jñāna*. It is sufficient to account for the phenomenon through the causal relations already established separately for each [type of cognition], such as perception and so forth, since the property of being a *viśiṣṭavaiśiṣṭya-buddhi* is established merely by the convergence of circumstances (*arthasamāja*).

And here, since the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is identical, a cognition of a qualified object as being further qualified (*viśiṣṭavaiśiṣṭyajñāna*) is possible according to the maxim: "The qualifier [is perceived] in the qualificand, and another qualifier in that [qualifier]. Otherwise, even for the Logicians (*tārkika*), God would not be a knower of error. For if the object of error were grasped independently, it would follow that He is himself mistaken; therefore, its apprehension must be said to occur precisely as the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) of the error.

And in that case, where is the rule that there must first be an apprehension of that delimiting factor? Furthermore, the identity of the causal complex for the apprehension is the same in the present case as well.

[Objection: But surely, since the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of the knowledge of Brahman—which is the cause of liberation and is to be accomplished through hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth—exists, that very knowledge [of the non-existence] must also be asserted by you. And thus, the contradiction is equal even in that case. [Reply: This is not so. Because there is no contradiction based on the knowledge or non-knowledge of the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*), which consists of the knowledge of Brahman that is to be accomplished through hearing and so forth and is the cause of liberation. For the knowledge of the knowledge of Brahman—characterized by such modes as "being accomplished through hearing" or "being the cause of liberation"—is not itself the knowledge of Brahman; nor is it something to be accomplished through hearing or the cause of liberation. Therefore, when that [knowledge of the knowledge of Brahman] exists, the prior non-existence of such [Brahman-]knowledge is not contradicted.

[Objection: "In that case, even if the cognition 'I do not know' has the absence of knowledge as its object, there is no contradiction with the knowledge of the counter-positive (the object of negation) and so forth; for even when there is knowledge of the object and the counter-positive in a general sense, their absence can still exist in a specific sense. Otherwise, there would be no cognition of antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), since it is impossible to know a specific counter-positive in detail without first knowing its general property. [Reply: This is not so.

For, in the absence of the knowledge of a particular (viśeṣajñānābhāve), the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) is that which is delimited by the nature of the knowledge of a particular; thus, when that [absence] is known, that particular must also be known, which results in a contradiction with the very absence of the knowledge of a particular. Furthermore, it has been stated that the absence of any particular instance does not have a counter-positivity delimited by a generality (*sāmānyāvacchinnapratiyogitāka*). Consequently, the cognition of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) is unestablished due to the absence of a cognition whose mode is the delimiting property of the counter-positivity (*pratiyogitāvacchedakaprakārakajñāna*). Now, one might object: "A cognition whose mode is the delimiting property of the counter-positivity is not the cause for the cognition of an absence."

However, the cognition of absence is a cognition whose qualifier is a property residing in the counter-positive as it appears [in that cognition]. But when the "universal-characterized" (sāmānyalakṣaṇa) type of proximity is admitted, the counter-positive itself becomes an additional object of that [cognition]. Otherwise, however, that [proximity] alone [suffices], just as in the case of desire and volition directed toward an unestablished individual, there is a cognition whose qualifier is a general property residing in the desired object. Nor should it be argued: "How can the counter-positiveness be grasped by means of a property that is not the delimitator of counter-positiveness?"

This is because it is possible to apprehend a pervasion (vyāpti) in a general form, even when it is delimited by specific qualifications. To illustrate: in the inference "this [subject] possesses denotability (abhidheyatva), because it is cognizable (prameya)," at the time of grasping the pervasion—"wherever there is cognizability, there is denotability"—although the pervasion exists in the form of co-occurrence (sāmānādhikaraṇya) precisely as delimited by the property of being a cognizable that has occurrence, it is apprehended solely in the form of "cognizability" (prameyatva) and not as "being a cognizable that has occurrence," due to the latter's complexity (gaurava).

Furthermore, the qualification "possessing occurrence" (*vṛttimattva*) is redundant because it does not exclude any instances of deviation (*vyabhicāra*). This is because, just as non-occurrent things lack the pervasion (*vyāpti*) defined as co-occurrence with the probandum (*sādhyasāmānādhikaraṇya*), they likewise lack the deviation defined as co-occurrence with the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāvasāmānādhikaraṇya*). Moreover, the status of being a delimitor of pervasion (*vyāpyatāvacchedakatva*) is possible merely by being excluded from deviant cases, provided that the qualification is not itself superfluous.

And so, just as pervasion (*vyāpti*), even when residing in a knowable object (*prameya*) that possesses occurrence, is apprehended precisely as "knowability" (*prameyatva*), likewise the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) residing in each particular manifestation such as blue is apprehended in the form of "blueness" (*nīlatva*); thus, there is no inconsistency whatsoever. Furthermore, just as the cognition "there is no jar here now" has as its object the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of that jar residing in its material cause, so too the cognition "knowledge is not in me" has as its object the prior non-existence of that knowledge residing in the knower (*pramātṛ*); therefore, there is no inconsistency at all—if this is argued, we say: no.

In the cognition of non-existence (*abhāva-jñāna*), it is precisely the property (*dharma*) appearing in the aspect of the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) that serves as the delimiting factor of that counter-correlate (*pratiyogitā-avacchedaka*). Consequently, if the absence of some particular instance were to have a counter-correlate delimited by a general property (*sāmānya-avacchinna-pratiyogitākatva*), then the aforementioned defect would arise: one would incur the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of the cognition "the ground is potless" even on a ground where a pot exists, and the cognition "I do not have the knowledge of a pot" even in oneself when one does possess the knowledge of a pot.

The claim that any cognition of a jar is an obstacle to the cognition of the absence of a jar applies equally to the cognition of a cognition itself. However, in the case of grasping the aforementioned pervasion (*vyāpti*), since there is no sublation (*bādhaka*), there is no fault even when the generality (*sāmānya*) serves as the delimiting condition (*avacchedaka*).

In that case, there would be no cognition of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) at all. Indeed, there would be none; for the cognition "the jar will come to be" has as its object the futureness of the verbal root's meaning, and not prior non-existence. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the thought "the jar will come to be today" regarding a jar that is to be produced on another day, because it would be the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) of the prior non-existence residing in this very day. Furthermore, futureness (*bhaviṣyattva*) consists in being related to a time that is not a locus of either the counter-positive or its destruction (*dhvaṃsa*).

Furthermore, in the view of those who do not accept prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) is simply the state of being a temporary absence. Even in the view of those who do accept it, [destruction] is a temporary absence that does not produce its own counter-positive (*pratiyogin*).
