And "causality" (*janakatva*) is a specific kind of essential relation (*svarūpasambandha*), not one constituted by prior non-existence; otherwise, prior non-existence would result in being non-causal, which would lead to the fallacy of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*). Therefore, even for one who accepts prior non-existence, its perceptibility is difficult to establish. For one who does not accept it, however, there is no loss whatsoever.

The cognition "there is no jar here now" has as its object all particular absences at that time whose counterpositiveness is delimited by a general property; this is because a specific time also serves as a delimiter of absence. Otherwise, cognitions such as "at the first moment, the jar is colorless" would not be possible.

Now, if it is argued that "in this position, the absence of a universal (*sāmānyābhāva*) would not be established," [we reply] that this is equally true even when the antecedent absence (*prāgabhāva*) is accepted. This is because the absence of a universal and the antecedent absence are mutually contradictory, like the two demons Sunda and Upasunda. To explain: once the antecedent absence is established, since the absence of particulars also has a counter-positive delimited by the universal, the absence of the universal—which is based on that alone—cannot be established.

Furthermore, since the absence of a particular cannot have a generic property as its delimiting condition for the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) when the absence of the generic is established, and since an occasional absence cannot logically constitute the absence of the generic, the establishment of prior non-existence—which relies solely on the cognition of a particular whose counter-correlativity is delimited by a generic property—is not achieved. Thus, neither of these two [arguments] brings any aesthetic wonder to the minds of the wise.

Now, one might object: even when there is certainty regarding the absence of all particular [colors], because there remains a doubt regarding the absence of color—namely, "Does color reside in air, or not? or "Is air possessed of color, or not?"—and because doubt is impossible regarding what has already been ascertained, it follows that the absence of the general property other than the absences of all particulars is established. Therefore, since such a doubt is not experienced at the stage when there is the certainty that "there are only these many colors," it must be said that such a doubt occurs only at the stage when that certainty is lacking.

And thus, due to the possibility that "the property of being color (rūpatva) will reside in something other than earthy, watery, and fiery colors," there is doubt regarding those very things that have not been ascertained; for it is only a certainty accompanied by the absence of such a possibility that acts as an obstacle—this is not so, because there is no evidence for postulating such an obstacle, and because such a doubt is observed even in the absence of the aforementioned possibility.

Now, one might object: just as the absence of the universal "color" (rūpa-sāmānya-abhāva)—which is distinct from the absences of all its particular instances—is a term of doubt regarding color, so too the universal "color" itself, being distinct from all its particular instances, cannot be accepted as a term of doubt. And if that is so, how can there be a state of doubt regarding color? [For it would follow that] there is a certainty regarding the absence of all colors.

If you argue that there is doubt regarding color (rūpa) because, even though there is certainty regarding the absence of blue, yellow, and so forth, there is no certainty regarding the absence of color as such, then what is the use of a general absence (sāmānyābhāva)? For doubt is possible through the absence whose counter-positivehood is delimited by "color-ness" (rūpatva). This is because the postulation of a property (dharma-kalpanā) is simpler than the postulation of a substratum (dharmin-kalpanā), and thus it is more parsimonious to postulate that all particular absences themselves possess a counter-positivehood delimited by "color-ness."

Therefore, it cannot be argued that there is no undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of the cognition "the jar is colorless" by taking any mere absence whatsoever—this is not correct. For, regarding the property of having a counter-positivehood delimited by "being of such-and-such a form" (yadrūpatvāvacchinnapratiyogitākatva) within all the specific absences, does it reside in each one individually (pratyekaviśrānta), or is it a collective property (vyāsajyavṛtti)? In the first case, there would be the undesirable consequence of the cognition "the jar is colorless" by taking any single absence whatsoever.

In the second case, since the state of having a counter-correlativity delimited by that specific form (tattadrūpatvāvacchinnapratiyogitākatva) is non-distributive (avyāsajyavṛtti) by nature, one would have to postulate a distinct, distributive (vyāsajyavṛtti) state of having a counter-correlativity delimited by "form-ness" (rūpatvāvacchinnapratiyogitākatva). It is better, therefore, to postulate a single absence whose counter-correlativity is delimited by "form-ness. For you, two things must be postulated: one absence and the state of having a counter-correlativity delimited by "form-ness."

In your view, however, there must be the property of having a counter-correlativity delimited by "being color" (*rūpatvāvacchinnapratiyogitākatva*), and since that [property] is co-extensive (*vyāsajyavṛttitvena*), it would have to be related to each of the many absences individually; thus, much more is to be postulated. The maxim that "the postulation of a property is simpler than the postulation of a substratum" (*dharmikalpanāto dharmakalpanāyā laghutvam*) depends upon the relative abundance of what is to be postulated. Furthermore, even when all particular absences of color are present in two jars, the cognition of the general absence of color does not arise; therefore, the absences must be qualified by the delimitation of their co-occurrence in a single locus (*aikādhikaraṇyāvacchedena*). And thus, there is extreme complexity (*atigauravam*).

Moreover, in the apprehension of a property that exists distributively (vyāsajyavṛtti), the apprehension of all its substrata and the apprehension of their mutual difference are the causes; for, when garments and the like are either not apprehended at all or are apprehended as non-different, the cognition of duality and so forth does not arise. And thus, if there were no apprehension of the non-existents and their mutual differences, the initial cognition "it is formless" would not occur, because the state of being the counter-correlate (pratiyogitā) of a generality that exists distributively would not be apprehended.

If it is argued, "In that case, since the absence of a universal (*sāmānyābhāva*) is established by valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇika*), how can it be refuted?", we reply: In that case, since there is no cognition of the absence of a particular (*viśeṣābhāva*) in the form of a universal, the antecedent absence of a specific cognition (*jñānaviśeṣaprāgabhāva*) is not the object of the cognition "I do not know," because its counter-positivehood (*pratiyogitā*) is not delimited by "cognition-ness" (*jñānatva*). Thus, our desired conclusion is proven; for even among absences, there is no such thing as an "absence of a universal."

That [absence] would have its counter-correlativity delimited by a general property (*sāmānyadharma*), whereas the counter-correlativity of a specific absence (*viśeṣābhāva*) is delimited by specific properties such as "that particular pot-ness" (*tattad-ghaṭatva*). However, it is not possible to cognize a future pot or the like through those respective forms. Even if the cognition of it in that form were possible at another time after its birth, the cognition of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) would not be perceptual; for at that time, the prior non-existence does not exist, and perception is produced by its object.

And it has been stated that knowledge characterized by a general property (*sāmānyaprakāraka*) is not the cause for the knowledge of the absence of a particular. This is because the knowledge of the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) as qualified by its counter-positiveness-determinant (*pratiyogitāvacchedaka*) is the cause for the knowledge of an absence characterized by the property of "absence-ness" (*abhāvatva*). Even if that [absence] were accessible through inference, it could not be the object of the immediate intuition (*aparokṣa*) of the cognition "I do not know," since such a cognition lacks that [general] as its object. Furthermore, since there is an absence of an unerring logical mark (*liṅga*) and so forth, the possibility of inferring it is utterly dismissed. Now, one might argue: its establishment occurs through its being the object of a desire in the form, "May this not be."

No, because antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) cannot be established in its own nature; rather, it is the relation to that [non-existence], just like the relation to absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*), that is what is to be established by way of obstructing the production of the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*). Thus, [the argument] is otherwise accounted for (*anyathāsiddha*) by that very [relation].

Now, [the opponent argues]: "Since that which has already arisen does not arise again in the second moment, it must be said that the causal complex (sāmagrī) was absent in the preceding moment; and that absence is due precisely to the non-existence of prior negation (prāgabhāva), because other causes are present. If this is argued, we say: No. This is because the matter is otherwise established by means of temporal absolute negation (sāmayikātyantābhāva) alone; furthermore, it is the very thing already arisen that is opposed to its own arising. Moreover, the causal complex is the efficient cause for the existence of the effect, but not even for its arising, which consists in its connection with the first moment of time.

Connection with the initial time (*ādyakāla*) consists in being the locus of a time that is not the locus of the destruction of any entity co-temporal with itself. In this regard, the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is the determinant only for the aspect of the effect’s being located in time, but not for the qualifying aspect as well; for the latter is established simply by the absence of the causal complex for the destruction of such entities. Furthermore, the difference between color and other qualities produced by baking (*pākaja*) arises either from a difference in the contact with fire or from a difference in the destruction of the preceding color and so forth, but not from a difference in the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*); for a difference in prior non-existence is impossible without a difference in its counter-positive (*pratiyogin*).

Nor is the establishment of [the world] having [Brahman] as its material cause (upādānatva) a valid means of proof there; for that is established by the nature of being a thread (tantutva) and so forth alone. Otherwise, how could even the specific correlate of a prior non-existence (prāgabhāva) be established? Nor can it be asked how that which possesses absolute non-existence (atyantābhāva) of it can be its material cause, since you yourself admit [it] through another relation, and because you admit a distinction based on being delimited by time and not being so delimited; enough of this excessive detail.

In this way, the absence of a universal (*sāmānyābhāva*) is also refuted by the principle of parsimony (*gaurava*). To explain: one must either postulate three things—the state of having a pratiyogitā (counter-positive-ness) delimited by a universal, the absence itself, and its relations with their respective loci; or one must postulate two things—the state of having a pratiyogitā delimited by a universal belonging to those absences that are already established as residing in a single locus by virtue of their being related to their respective [specific] loci, and the fact that such [delimited pratiyogitā] is *vyāsajyavṛtti* (occurring distributively across multiple substrata).

In this matter, only the latter position is acceptable to those who possess discernment (*prekṣāvat*), because the cognition "the jar is colorless" at the very first moment is established for everyone. Although the apprehension of the locus and its difference [from the counter-positive] is a cause for the apprehension of duality and so forth, it is not admitted to be a cause for the apprehension of the aforementioned counter-positiveness (*pratiyogitā*). This is because properties that are to be inferred from their effects are inferred in accordance with those effects. Nor should it be argued: "By the principle of extreme parsimony (*atilāghava*), let the well-established loci themselves be the cause of the cognition of absence; what is the use of specific absences (*viśeṣābhāva*) as well? For [otherwise], there would be an over-extension.

This is because it is our desired conclusion; for since you yourself do not accept a distinct absence in cases such as "there is no absence of a jar," the fact that a positive entity (bhāva) can also be the cause of a valid cognition characterized by the mode "absence-ness" is established for both parties.

As for what someone has said: "Since the difference in the delimiters of counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitāvacchedaka*) is the regulator of the difference between absences, the existence of a general absence distinct from particular absences is established; otherwise, the difference between absences would not be established. If the difference in the counter-correlate were the differentiator of the absence, it would follow that the fourfold set of absences—beginning with antecedent absence (*prāgabhāva*)—which have a single jar as their counter-correlate, would be non-distinct. However, due to the difference in the delimiters, there is no such defect regarding their distinction."

"In some cases there is identity (*tādātmya*), in some cases conjunction (*saṃsarga*), and in some cases the difference between the respective potnesses and so forth belonging to earlier and later times"—this [view] is not tenable. For it is difficult to state a single delimiting factor (*avacchedakatva*) that is common to both the counter-positive of a conjunction and its qualifier. Furthermore, there is no evidence for identity and the like being the delimiters of counter-positiveness (*pratiyogitāvacchedakatva*). As for the establishment of difference, even in the case of non-existence (*abhāva*), it occurs precisely through the imposition of contradictory attributes (*viruddhadharmādhyāsa*), just as in the case of existence (*bhāva*).

The fact that a difference in delimiters (avacchedaka-bheda) necessitates a difference in absences must be stated as its being a cognizer of that [difference] by way of a logical mark (liṅga), and not as its producer thereof; and that is not the case. For, due to the absence of a subverting argument against the contrary (vipakṣa-bādhaka-tarka) and due to the absence of co-occurrence (sāmānādhikaraṇya), the pervasion (vyāpti) itself is unestablished. For this very reason, the claim that "having a counter-correlativity delimited by a property other than that [specific property] is pervaded by being different from having a counter-correlativity delimited by that [specific property]" is also refuted.

In this way, there is only one absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) for the absences (*avṛtti*), such as space and so forth, and for other properties that are co-extensive (*samaniyata*). Furthermore, for things that have perished or arisen simultaneously in the same location, provided there is no sublation (*bādhaka*), there is only one single destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) or prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*). If, moreover, a non-existence whose counter-positivehood (*pratiyogitā*) is delimited by a property residing in a different locus (*vyadhikaraṇadharma*) is considered valid by means of authoritative cognition (*prāmāṇika*), then that single non-existence possesses counter-positivehoods with respect to all—both those residing in different loci and those residing in the same locus.

Let [the absences] be delimited by their very relations; or let there simply be a single absence of space (*ākāśābhāva*). Since the purpose is served by a single [absence], there is no evidence for postulating a plurality of absences. Nor should it be argued: "In that case, let there be only one absence on the surface of the earth; that alone, through the differences of the delimiting factors such as place and time, will produce the various distinct linguistic usages—what is the point of further postulation? For if this were logically tenable, let it be so. However, in the present case, there is nothing to subvert [that position].

For this very reason, the proponents of non-duality (advaitavādinaḥ) maintain that since the Vaiśeṣikas can account for all worldly transactions by means of the category of "time" (kāla) which they themselves accept, there is no need to establish any other distinct category. Thus, it is established that the cognition "I am ignorant" has an object distinct from absence, because it is produced by a causal complex distinct from the causal complex that produces the cognition of absence.

Likewise, even in the case of [the cognition] "I do not know the meaning spoken by you," [it is not a contradiction]. Now, one might argue: the aforementioned cognition has as its object the fact that "there is no valid knowledge regarding the meaning spoken by you directly within me. And that [cognition] does not have the object directly as its content, because the object appears only as a qualifier of the valid knowledge; therefore, there is no contradiction. This is not so. For the absence of that [knowledge] can only be apprehended after one has cognized the meaning spoken by you directly. And that cognition [of the meaning] cannot be produced by the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*).

Because one lacks such a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding oneself; however, that which resides in another can be apprehended through words and the like. And since words and the like, while making known the object you have stated, would also make known that [object] as the content of the cognition, it follows that, from the very outset, a direct cognition having your stated object as its content has already arrived. Thus, why would there not be a contradiction in negating that? For this very reason, the claim that "even if the particular (*viśeṣa*) is known in its own nature, the absence of a cognition whose qualifier (*prakāra*) is that particular is not contradictory" is refuted.

Nor can it be argued that what is being denied here is the state of having as its object a property that distinguishes its own referent—as is well known in the case of the knowledge of a myrobalan fruit in the palm of one's hand—because even "the state of being spoken by you" distinguishes [your statement] from "spoken by me," and thus it is impossible to deny, in general, the state of having as its object a distinguishing property.

Now, an objection might be raised: even when a specific cognition arises by way of being a delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*), there is no contradiction. To explain: it is not the absence of a specific cognition, nor the absence of a cognition whose object is the matter stated by you, that is perceived here; rather, what is perceived is the absence of a cognition that has the matter stated by you as its qualificandum (*viśeṣya*) and a particular feature as its qualifier (*prakāra*). And in that case, even if there is a cognition of the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*)—namely, a cognition characterized as having that matter stated by you as its qualificandum and that particular feature as its qualifier—it is still possible for there to be an absence of a cognition possessing that same qualifier and that same qualificandum.

This is because this cognition has as its qualifier the property of having "the qualification of being qualified by a particular" as its qualifier, with respect to the qualificandum which is the cognition itself. Even in cases where there is the verbal expression, "I do not know the particularity mentioned by you," the absence of contradiction should be inferred in some way through the same principle. Nor should it be argued: "How can there be a cognition of absence in a case where the aforementioned counter-positive (pratiyogin) is not established?"

If it is argued that [the absence] is explained simply as having the qualifier's absence in the qualificand—as in the case of "there is no denotation of what is inherent"—or as having an absence whose counter-correlator is delimited by a non-co-referential property, we say: no, because this contradicts experience. Furthermore, if one does not admit either the absence of the cognition of the specific [qualifier] or the absence of the cognition of the object as you have described it, then since the cognition of that object would still exist, its corresponding linguistic usage would necessarily follow; yet such a thing is not observed.

In the theory of intrinsic validity (*svataḥprāmāṇya*), however, when the fact that [the cognition] has that as its qualifier (*tatprakārakatva*) and that as its qualificand (*tadviśeṣyakatva*) is apprehended, the apprehension of the possession of that [object] is necessary; thus, since the state of having that as its qualifier and that as its qualificand is possible within such a cognition of the counter-correlate (*pratiyogijñāna*), the contradiction is indeed manifest. But in the view that ignorance is of a positive nature (*bhāvarūpa-ajñāna*), there is no contradiction because everything is cognizable by the witness-consciousness (*sākṣivedyatā*); this has been stated. Thus, it is established that the perception "I do not know the object you have mentioned" has positive ignorance as its object.

The perception of deep sleep, established by the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*)—"In this way, for such a length of time, I was not aware of anything"—has as its object precisely ignorance in the form of a positive entity (*bhāvarūpa-ajñāna*). Now, one might ask: Is this reflective awareness an inference (*anumāna*), or is it memory (*smaraṇa*)? In the first case, let the mere absence of cognition (*jñānābhāva*) be inferred; what is the use of a positive ignorance? For instance, having inferred the intervening period between the two disputed points of rising and setting—just like the well-established times of rising and setting—one concludes: "During that time, I was devoid of cognition."

This is because it is possible to formulate the following arguments: [1] because it possesses a specific state; [2] because it is devoid of the causal complex for cognition (*jñānasāmagrī*); or [3] because, even when the self and so forth are being remembered, it is not necessarily remembered as possessing that [state], since they share the same fate (*tulyayogakṣema*). However, in the second case, there is no justification, because a mental impression (*saṃskāra*) is impossible. For a cognition produces a mental impression only while it is perishing, since it is incapable of producing an effect at a later time without an intervening operation (*vyāpāra*).

But since that [cause], being imperishable, is itself capable of producing its effect, why would it produce a latent impression (*saṃskāra*)? For even a latent impression is not perceptible, such that it could be postulated even in the absence of the impossibility of the effect otherwise.

Furthermore, how could the knowledge that constitutes the state of deep sleep—which is colored by beginningless ignorance and consists of the nature of the witnessing consciousness (*sākṣicaitanya*)—produce a mental impression (*saṃskāra*), since it does not perish either intrinsically or due to an adjunct (*upādhi*)? In the absence of such a mental impression, how could it be remembered? And if it is not remembered, how could it be cited as a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*)? If you say this, we reply: no; for inference is not possible in this case, because neither the logical reason (*hetu*) nor the qualification of the subject (*pakṣaviśeṣaṇa*) is known. Indeed, without the absence of cognition, it is impossible to specify any distinction regarding that state.

Furthermore, the absence of the causal complex for knowledge (*jñānasāmagrī*) is itself dependent upon the inference of the absence of knowledge; thus, it is beset by the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*). Nor can one infer the absence of that causal complex at a previous time by inferring its cessation through the clarity of the senses at the present moment; for the clarity of the senses, which is caused by the experience of pleasure, is not established as being caused by the cessation [of the causal complex]. And as for "not being remembered as a rule" (*niyamenāsmaryamāṇatvam*), does this mean according to the literal reading, or delimited by the period of deep sleep (*suṣupti*)? In the first case, there is unestablishedness (*asiddhi*). In the second case, however, the absence of knowledge regarding things to be disregarded (*upekṣaṇīya*) would not be established; moreover, there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in that very instance.

And it should not be asked: "In that case, how is there an absence of the cognition of an elephant in the courtyard experienced this morning? Understand that it is known precisely through the non-apprehension of the cognition (*jñānānupalabdhi*). And the cognition of non-apprehension is [inferred] by means of the mark (*liṅga*) of ignorance in the form of a positive entity (*bhāvarūpa-ajñāna*). For instance: "At a previous time, I possessed the absence of the cognition of an elephant, because I possessed ignorance regarding the elephant; for whatever is not thus is not so, just as I am when I possess the cognition of an elephant. In this way, in all cases, ignorance functions as the inferential indicator (*anumāpaka*) of the absence of cognition, by virtue of being pervaded (*vyāpyatva*) by it.

Nor should it be argued: "Just as positive ignorance (*bhāvarūpājñāna*) must be accepted for the sake of inferring the absence of knowledge during deep sleep, so too must hatred be accepted for the sake of inferring the absence of attachment; for it is impossible to infer the absence of something without experiencing its contradictory entity. This is not to be said, because the absence of attachment can be inferred either by means of positive ignorance or by means of the absence of knowledge, since that [absence of knowledge] is also its contradictory. Now, if [the object] is known through direct perception (*aparokṣa*), there is no ignorance; how then can there be an inference of the absence of indirect knowledge (*parokṣajñāna*)? Understand that this is due to the absence of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) and so forth.

Nor is there a mutual dependence (anyonyāśraya) here; for when sound and other objects are present and capable of being perceived, their absence is ascertained through the non-perception of what is otherwise perceptible, because the ascertainment of the absence of the causal complex occurs even without the knowledge of the absence of indirect cognition (*parokṣajñāna*). Furthermore, at the time of deep sleep, it is impossible to know the absence of the causal complex consisting of the sense organs and so forth without the absence of its effect; thus, the charge of mutual dependence was raised [only] in that context. Nor is there an impossibility of the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) in the view that [ignorance] is remembered; for since ignorance is manifested by the Witness reflected in a mental modification (*vṛtti*), the impression is established simply from the destruction of that modification.

This is because the term "witness" (sākṣin) refers exclusively to consciousness reflected in the modification of ignorance (*ajñāna-vṛtti*). Nor should it be argued that even in the waking state, if ignorance were known through a mental modification (*vṛtti*), then doubt and the like would necessarily arise during a state where no such modification exists; for such [doubt] is impossible due to the absence of ignorance regarding the object of that [alleged] ignorance. This is because there is a rule that doubt and the like must have the same object as the ignorance that serves as their cause. Furthermore, if doubt occurs with respect to [the nature of] existence and so forth, this is simply an accepted consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*), since existence and the like are not objects of the witness-consciousness and are therefore objects of ignorance.

This is because ignorance (*ajñāna*) is cognizable by the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*) in its very own nature (*svarūpeṇa*). Now, one might object: "In that case, let the absence of knowledge (*jñānābhāva*) also appear in its own nature; for it is only in the cognition of an absence that the cognition of the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) serves as the cause [of that cognition]. Otherwise, even in the cognition 'this is knowable' (*prameyam*), the absence would not appear. This is not so. For the witness-consciousness does not apprehend an absence in its own nature, since that [absence] is not directly cognizable by the witness. Nor is it [apprehended] through verbal testimony and the like, because those are absent at that time. Nor is it [apprehended] through non-perception (*anupalabdhi*).

For that [non-existence], being independent of the cognition of its counter-positive, lacks causal efficacy. Nor should it be argued: "Let this non-existence, whose nature is distinct from other observed absences, be cognizable by the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*) in its own form. This is because, if it were cognizable by indeterminate perception (*nirvikalpaka-buddhi*), it would more appropriately be considered a positive entity (*bhāva*); otherwise, it would result in nothing more than a mere technical convention. [Objection: But since qualities such as being opposed to cognition are not experienced at that time, how can there be a reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) in the form "I did not know" (*nāvediṣam*)? [Reply: No.

For, since at that very time the opposition to knowledge and so forth are experienced just as the "I-notion" (ahaṃ-ullekha) is experienced through identity with the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) in the case of the seer (*draṣṭṛ*), reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) is not admitted in respect to those [latter] aspects; because it is the seer himself existing at the time of deep sleep who is being reflected upon.

But surely, since the experience of ignorance—which consists of consciousness reflected in a modification of ignorance—exists even during the waking state, how can there be a recollection of ignorance? For there is no usage of the term "recollection" regarding continuous (dhārāvāhika) experiences that possess the same causal conditions; rather, such an experience must be called a continuous perception of ignorance, not a reflective awareness (parāmarśa). True.

Because the ignorance qualified by deep sleep (*suṣupti*) is not experienced by the witness (*sākṣin*) in the waking state due to the destruction of the tamasic modification of ignorance known as deep sleep, the awareness of that ignorance qualified by deep sleep occurs only through a mental modification (*vṛtti*) of nescience produced by latent impressions (*saṃskāra*); thus, its status as a "recollection" (*parāmarśa*) is logically established. However, regarding the portion consisting of pure ignorance alone, since the causal conditions are identical, it is simply a continuous flow (*dhārāvāhikatva*). For this very reason, the venerable Vārttikakāra, intending that deep sleep is merely the persistence of pure ignorance—similar to cosmic dissolution (*pralaya*)—refined by the destruction of the limiting adjunct of the effect, rejected the recollection of the ignorance of deep sleep. Thus it has been said:
There is no memory such as "I was unaware" regarding the consciousness present in deep sleep;
for that which resides in the Self cannot be subject to the past, since there is no intervention by time or other factors.
It is observed that a conceptual construction (vikalpa) does not touch the past time, nor does it touch the future;
its own objective domain is its own object, whereas the object of another is the object of another. Therefore, it is remembered as a conceptual construction.

Thus, in the exposition of the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) state, according to the *Vivaraṇa*: following the *Yogasūtra* definition that "sleep is a mental modification (*vṛtti*) supported by the notion of non-existence," one must understand that deep sleep (*suṣupti*) is a certain modification supported solely by the veil consisting of the quality of darkness (*tamas*). Since the consciousness colored by that [modification] perishes precisely through its destruction, there is no contradiction between this view and the statements in the *Vārttika* and *Vivaraṇa* which accept that there is a "recollection" (*smaraṇa*)—namely, "I was not aware of anything"—produced by the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) born from the experience of ignorance during that time.
For this very reason, it was stated by the author of the *Vārttika* in the *Uṣasti-brāhmaṇa*:
"If the pervasion by experience is not admitted for one in deep sleep, on what basis could there arise the cognition: 'I did not know [anything] while I was asleep'? and so forth.

The intended meaning has indeed been explained. Whether there are three modifications (*vṛtti*) of ignorance—namely, those having the forms of witness-consciousness, cognition, and pleasure—or whether there is only one modification called deep sleep (*suṣupti*), is another matter. Furthermore, we have established in the *Siddhāntabindu* that even indeterminate perception (*nirvikalpaka*) can produce memory, and that the non-mention of "that-ness" (*tattā*) occurs because of the absence of the coloring by the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*). Therefore, it is proven that even the experience of deep sleep has positive ignorance as its object. Thus ends the demonstration of the perceptibility of ignorance in the *Advaitasiddhi*.

In this regard, inference (*anumāna*) as stated in the *Vivaraṇa* is also a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*): "The subject of dispute, which is valid cognition (*pramāṇajñāna*), is preceded by another entity that resides in its own locus, which is distinct from its own prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), which veils its own object, and which is removed by itself; because it illuminates an unilluminated object, like the light of a lamp first produced in the dark. Here, the term "valid cognition" (*pramāṇapada*) is used to refer specifically to the occurrence of valid knowledge (*pramāṇavṭtti*) as the subject (*pakṣa*), in order to avoid the fallacy of contradiction (*bādha*) in the case of cognitions such as pleasure, which are of the nature of the witness-consciousness (*sākṣicaitanya*) and do not remove ignorance.

The qualification "subject of dispute" (*vivādapada*) is intended to exclude from the category [of the subject] that cognition which functions as a valid means of knowledge regarding the objective part (*dharmyaṃśa*), which has the form "this," and which does not remove ignorance; the resulting meaning is that it must function as a valid means of knowledge regarding a specific form (*viśeṣākāra*). Since even indirect valid cognition (*parokṣapramā*) removes the ignorance residing in the knower in the form of an obscuration of non-existence (*asattvāvaraṇa*), there is no sublation (*bādha*) even with respect to that [objective] part.

[Objection: If this [cognition] "this" (*nanvidam*) does not remove ignorance because it is a functioning of a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇavṛtti*), then its status as a valid cognition—defined as the making known of what was previously unknown—would not be possible. [Reply: No; for since no error or doubt regarding the form "this" is observed, there is no evidence for postulating ignorance with respect to that object. Therefore, just like the cognition of pleasure and so forth, its status as a valid cognition is established merely by its being in accordance with reality (*yathārthatva*). As they have said: "In the aspect of the substratum (*dharmyaṃśa*), everything is non-erroneous, but in the qualifier (*prakāra*), there may be error."

If, however, on the strength of experience, one were to accept that [cognition] as a form of ignorance even though it does not produce error or doubt, then let that too be included within the category [of ignorance], since its capacity to remove ignorance is not lost so long as it is delimited by being a valid cognitive function (*pramāṇavṛtti*). In that case, the qualification "subject of dispute" (*vivādapada*) need not be adopted. In this view, the definition of *avidyā* should be understood as "the fitness to be the material cause of error," for it should be noted that the property of being the material cause of error is not over-extensive (*avyāpti*), as it does not apply to the ignorance that is removed by the cognition of the substratum (*dharmyaṃśajñāna*).

Furthermore, successive cognitions (dhārāvāhika-buddhi) indeed possess the quality of making known what was previously unknown, since their objects are delimited by their respective times; for it is accepted that time is perceivable by all means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).

Furthermore, for those cognitive states (*pramāṇavṛtti*) whose form is "non-self" (*anātma*), there is indeed the capacity to remove the veil over their own objects by virtue of having as their object the consciousness delimited by this or that [object]. This is because illumination occurs precisely through the nature of consciousness (*cittva*), and not through undelimited consciousness (*anavacchinnacittva*), due to the principle of parsimony (*gaurava*), and also because of the experience: "This was not known by me for so long; now it is known. It has already been stated previously that even that consciousness delimited by this or that, though devoid of color and other qualities, can be an object of perception and the like.

It should be understood that this inference is made by accepting the established distinction between individual cognitions (*pratikarmavyavasthā*), and not on the basis of the theory of "creation upon perception" (*dṛṣṭisṛṣṭipakṣa*). Furthermore, the first qualification in the probandum (*sādhya*)—that the cessation of antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) is distinct from its counter-positive—is intended to exclude the fallacy of proving what is already established (*arthāntara*) according to the view that the cessation of antecedent non-existence is nothing other than the counter-positive itself. This qualification does not result in the fallacy of *arthāntara* by taking subsequent destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) and so forth as the object; rather, the word "prior" (*prāk*) is used in accordance with the actual state of things to refer specifically to the antecedent non-existence. And it is not redundant, as it serves to establish an indivisible non-existence (*akhaṇḍābhāva*) by functioning as a qualifier of the counter-positive.

By this, the following objection is refuted: "Since it is a rule that knowledge is the remover of ignorance alone, the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) is already excluded by the very term 'removable by itself'; what then is the purpose of the first qualification? This is because the intended meaning is that while other things are not removable by knowledge in the sense of being known as valid cognitions (*pramātvena*), [ignorance] is so removed. Nor is that [prior non-existence] excluded by the term "obscuration of its own object" alone, because the nature of obscuration—defined as being in contradiction with the empirical usage "it exists, it shines"—is common to both positive entities and absences.

This qualification, however, is intended to exclude other possibilities (arthāntara) based on unseen merit or demerit (adṛṣṭa) that produces a mental modification (vṛtti). Nor is the phrase "of its own object" (svaviṣaya) redundant, given that the word "obscuration" (āvaraṇa) already excludes such cases; for there exists an unseen factor that produces knowledge of its own object while acting as an obstacle to the knowledge of another object, and thus constitutes an obscuration. Since this definition would otherwise include such an unseen factor, the inclusion of the phrase "of its own object" serves to exclude that possibility.

Nor should it be argued that there can be no concealment [of consciousness], because ignorance is not admitted to exist in an insentient object (*jaḍa*), and because consciousness (*cit*) appears as the witness (*sākṣin*) of ignorance and the rest; for even though consciousness shines forth as the witness of ignorance and so on, there is an absence of the empirical usage "it exists" or "it shines," and thus the concealment of ignorance regarding that aspect is necessary. This will be explained later. Furthermore, the qualification "to be removed by itself" (*svanivartya*) is included to exclude the possibility of an alternative explanation (*arthāntara*) based on unseen merit or demerit (*adṛṣṭa*) which obstructs the mental modification (*vṛtti*).

Nor should it be argued that if the unseen merit (adṛṣṭa) which obstructs the arising of the final direct realization (*caramasākṣātkāra*) cannot be removed by that realization, then its falsity (*mithyātva*) is not established; whereas if it can be removed by it, then its removal would be impossible. This is because, while the obstructing adṛṣṭa exists, no knowledge arises; therefore, its removal must first occur. Furthermore, since that adṛṣṭa—which exists in the form of a causal substrate—is removable by knowledge, its falsity is established. Nor does this undermine its being "removable by itself," for the intended meaning is that its very nature consists in being removable by itself.

Some maintain that this [qualification] is for the purpose of excluding other objects by means of darkness (*andhakāra*). That is not so, because such an exclusion is already accomplished by the qualification "situated in its own location" (*svadeśagata*). Furthermore, it has been stated previously how consciousness reflected in a mental modification (*vṛtti*) effects the removal of ignorance through its becoming one with the consciousness delimited by the object. Moreover, the qualification "situated in its own location" is intended to exclude the possibility of [the definition applying to] the state of being unknown (*ajñātatva*) residing in the object itself.

Although "unknownness" in the sense of being the object of ignorance (*avidyā*) is unestablished, and that in the sense of the absence of knownness is already refuted by the first qualification, nevertheless, since the first [qualification] excludes antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), it should be understood that the fourth [qualification] is intended to exclude absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*).

Now, an objection may be raised: "How can ignorance reside in that which is the locus of knowledge? For knowledge, in the form of a mental modification (*vṛtti*) and so forth, does not rest upon the consciousness (*cit*) that is the locus of ignorance. This is not so; because the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) rests upon consciousness, it is possible for its modification—or for the consciousness reflected therein—to rest upon consciousness as well. Furthermore, even that which rests upon a [consciousness] limited by something else does not forfeit its status as resting upon that [consciousness], just as sound, though resting upon the ether limited by the ear-cavity, is nonetheless said to rest upon the ether.

Thus, the probandum has been established on the basis of the view that obscuration is common to both existence and non-existence. However, according to the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) that non-existence is not an obscurer, there is an intention toward two distinct probanda: first, that [the cognition] is preceded by another entity located in its own locus which is distinct from its own prior non-existence and is removable by itself; second, that it is preceded by an obscurer of its own object (which is an entity located in its own locus and removable by itself). Thus, there is nothing inconsistent.

In this context, the property of being an illuminator (*prakāśakatva*)—whether defined as being denotable by the term "illuminator" or as being opposed to non-illumination—is common to both cognition and light. Although the status of being denotable by the term "illuminator" may apply to some person as well due to the assignment of names, what is intended here is that which is conventionally used by the word "illuminator" in the treatise, or throughout all places and times. Alternatively, let it be common to both; the deviation [of the definition] is excluded by the qualification "having as its object an unilluminated thing."

And "non-manifestness" (*aprakāśitatva*) consists in being the object of the linguistic usage "it does not manifest," and it has been established that this exists even in the case of self-luminous consciousness (*svaprakāśacaitanya*). Likewise, the opposition to the aforementioned non-manifestness is also directly perceived in both cognition and light. And it is said in the *Vivaraṇa*: "The state of being manifested by light, which is the opposition to darkness, is indeed something other than the state of being manifested by cognition, which is the opposition to ignorance."

Therefore, since both [the self and the cognition] can directly oppose non-manifestation, there is no deviation (vyabhicāra) in the case of sense-organ contact and the like. Thus, the logical reason (hetu) is established as either "because it is denotable by the word 'manifestation' while having for its object an unmanifested thing," or "because it is manifestation, which is opposed to non-manifestation."

However, the object of error is not unknown; because it does not exist at any time other than that of the error, that indeterminable [object] lacks the status of being an object of valid cognition, and thus it is impossible for it to possess "non-manifestness" (aprakāśitatva), which is defined by existence prior to manifestation. For this very reason, it is not opposed to manifestation, since there is an absence of non-manifestness regarding its own object; rather, the non-manifestness of the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*) is precisely what produces it. Furthermore, the absence of deviation [in the definition] with respect to memory is clear.

And the favorable reasoning (*anukūlatarka*)—consisting in the impossibility of accounting for the cognition "I do not know the object you have stated" and so forth—is exactly as previously mentioned. By this, the undesirable consequence that the earth would also be inferred to possess horns simply because it is denotable by the word "cow" is refuted, since such favorable reasoning is absent in that case. Although ignorance (*ajñāna*), in its own nature, is not an object of ignorance, its state of being [ignorance] (*tadbhāvatva*) and so forth certainly become objects of ignorance, because they are not grasped by the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*) which grasps the ignorance itself. Otherwise, there would be no dispute regarding it.

Likewise, the fact that valid cognition (*pramā*) is preceded by the absence of an obscuration of its own object is not grasped by the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*), which apprehends the very nature of the valid cognition. Thus, there is no fault whatsoever, because this inference that apprehends it possesses both the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*) as its locus. Furthermore, in the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), the qualification "having an origination not intervened by darkness" is included; therefore, the first term is not redundant, nor is there a lack of homogeneity between the probandum and the probans in the case of subsequent instances of light. This has been explained by us at length elsewhere.

Now, [one might object]: "Is it not the case that (1) being a positive entity (*bhāvatva*) or being distinct from non-existence (*abhāvavilakṣaṇatva*), while being beginningless, does not reside in that which is removable (*nivartyaniṣṭha*), because it is a property residing only in beginningless positive entities, or because it resides only in things distinct from beginningless non-existence, like *ātmatva* (selfhood); or (2) being removable (*nivartyatva*) does not reside in a beginningless positive entity, nor does it reside in what is distinct from beginningless non-existence, because it resides only in that which is removable, like *prāgabhāvatva* (the nature of prior non-existence); or (3) being beginningless (*anāditva*) does not reside in an obscuration (*āvaraṇaniṣṭha*), because it resides only in what is beginningless, like *prāgabhāvatva*? [Response: This is not so. For, (1) being a positive entity or being distinct from non-existence, while being beginningless, does indeed reside in that which is removable, because it is a property residing in all beginningless things, like *pradhvaṃsābhāvatva* (the nature of posterior non-existence). (2) Being removable does reside in a beginningless positive entity, because it is a property residing in all beginningless things, like *pradhvaṃsābhāvatva*. (3) Being beginningless does reside in an obscuration, because it is a property residing in all beginningless things, like *pradhvaṃsābhāvatva*. Therefore, these reasons are inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). Furthermore, since the probandum (*sādhya*) is established by the very fact of the existence of the subject (*pakṣasiddhi*), there is no lack of a locus for the reason (*āśrayāsiddhi*). Thus, the proof is valid. || 37 ||

[Objection: "Valid cognition does not remove other beginningless non-existences, because it is a cognition, like an error," and so forth—this constitutes a counter-argument (*satpratipakṣa*). Furthermore, [the reason] is non-conclusive (*aprayojaka*) because, just as something unproduced is produced merely by the absence of an agent, so too the manifestation of what has not been manifested is possible merely by the absence of prior manifestation. [Response: This is not so. Because there is no supporting argument (*anukūlatarka*), [your reason] is non-conclusive. However, since the proponent’s reason possesses a supporting argument, its pervasion (*vyāpti*) with the probandum is certain; thus, there is no room for counter-arguments, non-conclusiveness, or similar fallacies.

Furthermore, there is no contradiction with the first inference, because although the property of being an entity from beginningless time does not reside in that which is to be removed (*nivartya*), it is nonetheless established that ignorance—which is distinct from positive entities—is indeed removable. As for the second [inference], the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) is "residing only in that which is non-dependent. For the third and fourth, the adjunct is "not residing in any removable thing. For the fifth, the adjunct is "not residing in any thing that is beginningless. And for the sixth, the defect is that the probandum (*sādhya*) is unestablished due to the non-existence of its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*). These are the refutations.

And as stated in the *Tattvapradīpikā*: "Caitra’s valid cognition (pramā) is that which removes an beginningless [entity] distinct from the prior absence of valid cognition residing in Caitra, because it possesses the nature of valid cognition (*pramātva*), like Maitra’s valid cognition. The delusion under discussion has a material cause distinct from that which is not sublated by its own producer, because it is a delusion, like a commonly accepted [delusion]. Here, in the first argument, there is no sublation regarding cognitions such as pleasure, since the term "valid cognition" refers specifically to a modification (*vṛtti*) of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).

Furthermore, being located in Caitra is not a qualification for the beginningless [error] and so forth; for if it were, since Maitra’s valid cognition does not exclude the beginningless [error] residing in Caitra, there would be a deficiency of the probandum (*sādhyavaikalya*) in the example. Rather, it is a qualification of either the cognizer or its absence. And that valid cognition resides in the self has been explained previously. In the probandum (*sādhya*), however, the word "valid cognition" (*pramā*) is merely an embellishment (*uparañjaka*).

If, however, the qualification "prior" were not present in the case of non-existence, then—since even ignorance in the form of a positive entity (*bhāvarūpa-ajñāna*) is the absence of its own non-existence, and thus [the argument] would entail the removal of something other than that [ignorance] which is beginningless—in order to avoid such a sublation (*bādha*), the properties of "not inhering in Caitra" and "inhering in someone other than Caitra" cannot be considered limiting conditions (*upādhi*), because they do not pervade the probandum (*sādhya*) due to their deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of Caitra’s pleasure and so forth.

Nor is there a counter-argument (*satpratipakṣa*) such as: "Caitra’s valid cognition (*pramā*) does not remove an absence other than the absence residing in Caitra, because it is a valid cognition, like Maitra’s valid cognition," since this is contradicted by the fact that the counter-positive (the object of negation) is both established and unestablished. Furthermore, "the state of removing an absence other than the absence of a cognition residing in Caitra" is not a limiting condition (*upādhi*), because it pervades the probans in the subject (*pakṣa*) by virtue of removing the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of the linguistic usage produced by itself, which is other than the absence of a cognition residing in Caitra.

Furthermore, because there exists a sublation of the contrary position (*vipakṣabādhaka*), there is no equality with a fallacious argument. For this very reason, the second inference is also valid. Nor should it be argued that there is a counter-argument (*satpratipakṣa*) based on the following: "The delusion under discussion has as its material cause something other than that which is sublated by the producer of this cognition, because it is a delusion, like a commonly accepted [delusion]. This is not to be said, because according to your own view, the sublated object is not a producer; because the probandum (*sādhya*) is unestablished (*aprasiddha*); and because there is no contradiction, since it may have both Brahman and ignorance as its material causes.

The Navyas, however, argue as follows: "Valid cognition (*pramā*) under dispute is the remover of that which is beginningless yet distinct from the absence of valid cognition, because it is an effect, like a jar. Valid cognition subsequent to an error is the remover of its own opposite, which is distinct from its own absence, because it is valid cognition, like valid cognition subsequent to an error. The nature of cognition (*jñānatva*) resides in that which removes the veil over its own object, because it occurs in the illumination of an unilluminated object, like the nature of light."

The cognition of impermanence (*anityajñāna*) has as its co-locus a property that is not the locus of non-existence and is opposed to itself, because—while being distinct from effort and possessing an object—it is impermanent, like an impermanent desire. For that [desire] indeed has as its co-locus a corresponding hatred. Nor is there any suspicion of these [reasons] being non-conclusive (*aprayojaka*), because a subverting argument (*tarka*) against the contrary case has been stated. In this manner, other cases should also be inferred. The state of being opposed to cognition (*jñānavirodhitva*) has as its co-locus the state of being an entity without beginning (*anādibhāvatva*), because it subsists in that which is opposed to all cognitions, like visibility (*dṛśyatva*).

Or alternatively: "The state of being distinct from beginningless non-existence (anādyabhāvavilakṣaṇatva) resides in that which is opposed to knowledge, because it resides only in that which is distinct from beginningless non-existence, just like nameability (abhidheyatva). In this manner, other inferences for ignorance as something distinct from non-existence should be formulated. Thus ends the demonstration of the inference for ignorance in the *Advaitasiddhi*.

The scriptural texts are likewise [evidence]. In that regard, the Chāndogya Upaniṣad, in the eighth chapter, states: "Just as those who do not know the field might pass over a treasure of gold deposited there again and again without finding it, even so all these creatures, though they go day after day to this world of Brahman, do not find it, being held back by untruth (*anṛta*). This scripture, declaring untruth to be an obstacle to the knowledge of Brahman, serves as the authority for such ignorance.

Nor should it be argued that because the word *ṛta* is seen used in the sense of "good action" in the passage "the two who drink the *ṛta*" (*ṛtaṃ pibantau*), and because of the Smṛti statement "the *ṛta* is truth, as well as dharma," the word *ṛta* denotes good action and thus the word *anṛta* refers to evil action. This is because in the subsequent passage, "The Self which is free from sin" (*ya ātmāpahatapāpmā*) and so forth, there is established the quality of the Self being "free from sin," which contradicts the notion that evil actions have been cast off. Furthermore, if all karma were destroyed during deep sleep, even evil karma would be absent.

Furthermore, since ignorance must necessarily persist even in its causal state, and because it is logically untenable for karma to function as a veil, that which veils Brahman from beginningless time and is removable by knowledge must be identified as such. Consequently, neither karma nor even *pradhāna* can be denoted by the term "unreal" (*anṛta*), because neither of them is removable by knowledge. Regarding their removability by knowledge, the scriptural authority is found in passages such as: "And again at the end, there is the cessation of the entire *māyā*" (*bhūyaścānte viśvamāyānivṛttiḥ*). Moreover, in this context, "cessation" does not mean merely crossing over.

It should be stated that this is based on the Smṛti text: "They cross over this illusion. For it is impossible for crossing over to have anything other than cessation as its cause; thus, both [terms] have the mere destruction [of ignorance] as their meaning. Nor should it be argued: "Since the statement 'Darkness existed' establishes existence, and since there is no sublater [of that], it must refer to ultimate (pāramārthika) existence; how then can concealment be unreal? This is because, by the denial of both ultimate reality and sheer non-existence in the passage "Neither non-being existed then, nor did being exist," it refers instead to empirical (vyāvahārika) existence.

It should not be argued that *māyā* is not being presented here [as ignorance], nor that the meaning of the word *māyā* is not ignorance, because if the *māyin* (the possessor of *māyā*), namely Brahman, were ignorant, it would contradict scriptural statements regarding His omniscience, faultlessness, and so forth. This is because, since an adjunct (*upādhi*) favors the side of the reflection, it is impossible for it to result in the Lord’s lack of omniscience and other such defects. Furthermore, attributes such as omniscience and sovereign power are based upon *māyā*. Nor should it be asked how *māyā* can be ignorance when it follows the root-meaning of the verbal root *√may*, which means "to know."

"Even so, this Māyā, having manifested fields that are complete and non-different from itself, causes the appearance of both the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśa), and it becomes both Māyā and Avidyā"—since this Śruti establishes the identity of Māyā and Avidyā, Māyā is indeed ignorance (ajñāna). This is because, just as the word "ghaṭa," though derived from the verbal root *ghaṭ* meaning "to strive," does not denote striving, so too here [the word "māyā"] lacks the denotation of knowledge.

Furthermore, the statement of the authors of the *Nighaṇṭu*—that "māyā, prajñā, and vayuna" are synonyms for knowledge—is appropriate for ignorance (*ajñāna*) because it is transformed into the form of knowledge. Since phenomenal cognition (*vṛttijñāna*) is non-different from ignorance, and because ignorance alone possesses various indefinable powers (*anirvacanīya-vicitra-śakti*), there is no inconsistency in applying the word "māyā" to that which possesses such diverse powers. As for the occasional use of the term in reference to gems, mantras, and the like, it is merely figurative (*upacāra*). Nor should it be argued that this term does not denote a false object because the word "māyā" is not applied to things such as the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell.

Even though the conventional usage of "earth-ness" (*pṛthivītva*) and so forth does not apply to a diamond and other such things, *māyātva* (the nature of being *māyā*) does not depart from them even in the absence of such conventional usage; for we observe the frequent use of the word *māyā* in reference to magicians and the like. Furthermore, if *māyā* were distinct from ignorance (*ajñāna*), there would be a contradiction regarding its being removable by knowledge (*jñāna*). Moreover, in this system, the terms "mist" (*nīhāra*) and "darkness" (*tamas*) are appropriate as denoting the veiling nature of ignorance, whereas they are not so in other systems. If words such as "unreal" (*anṛta*) and "mist" were taken to refer to evil karma, there would be a contradiction with the fact—stated in other scriptural passages—that [ignorance] is the cause of the distinction between the individual soul and the Lord, and that it is the material cause [of the world].

Therefore, it is established that such scriptural passages as "They are veiled by untruth," "Enveloped by mist," "Darkness existed," "One should know Māyā as Prakṛti," "The one unborn, red, white, and black," "Abiding in the midst of ignorance," and "And finally, there is the cessation of the entire Māyā," serve as the authoritative evidence for the existence of nescience (ajñāna).
Thus ends the demonstration of the scriptural authority establishing ignorance (avidyā) within the Advaitasiddhi.

Furthermore, the proof for that [non-difference] is the fact that the non-manifestation of the unlimited bliss of Brahman to the individual soul (jīva) would otherwise be inexplicable. Nor can such non-manifestation be explained by the mere difference between the jīva and Brahman, because the difference between the jīva and Brahman will be refuted later on.

Nor is it untenable for unconditioned bliss (*anavacchinnānanda*) to be non-manifest simply because it is nothing but the manifest inner self (*pratyagātman*); for it has already been stated that just as the essential difference (*svarūpabheda*) of the Self from the body—though manifest in the form of the Self—is not manifest in the form of difference, so too Brahman, though manifest in one form, may be non-manifest in the aforementioned form due to the power of ignorance (*avidyā*).

The fact that error must have a material cause (*sopādānatva*), which would otherwise be inexplicable, is also a proof for the existence of ignorance (*avidyā*). Nor can the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) be the material cause; for since the internal organ depends upon the operation of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to produce knowledge, it cannot produce knowledge regarding such things as the "silver in mother-of-pearl," which are not objects of valid cognition. Furthermore, because the internal organ is beginningless, it cannot be the material cause of the beginningless succession of errors. Nor can Brahman itself be the material cause, because it is changeless (*apariṇāmin*).

Nor can [Brahman] be the material cause by virtue of being the locus of illusory manifestation (*vivarta*), as is the case with mother-of-pearl and the like; for without *avidyā*, an illusory manifestation—defined as an unreal appearance in another form—is impossible, and because mother-of-pearl and the like lack the status of being the locus of illusory manifestation except as delimiters of the locus.

Nor should it be argued that—just as for an illusory manifestation (*vivarta*) dependent on a material cause (*upādāna*), one must postulate a material cause distinct from the ultimate reality—one must likewise postulate a substratum (*adhikaraṇa*) for ignorance (*avidyā*) and the like that is distinct from Brahman and not ultimately real; for while the contingency of impermanence and other defects would follow if Brahman itself were subject to modification (*vikāritva*), there is no subverting argument against Brahman itself being the locus (*adhiṣṭhāna*), and thus a second substratum need not be postulated.

Nor should it be argued that ignorance need not be postulated even on the grounds of its being a "transformer" (pariṇāmin), since it does not depend on a transformation characterized by the unreal assuming the form of the real; for, according to the rule that [the effect] must have the same ontological status as the existence of the transformer, the very nature of unreality would be absent.

Nor should it be argued: "Since we observe that in the case of jars and the like there is an upādāna (material cause) possessing the same level of reality (*sattā*) as the effect, if one postulates such an upādāna for the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) as well, then—just as a jar does not depend on an upādāna of a higher level of reality than itself—it would follow that ether (*viyat*) and other elements also do not have Brahman as their upādāna. This is because, by the principle stated in the aphorism, "But from His [Brahman's] meditating upon that, [the world arises], for that is the mark," even jars and the like have as their upādāna Consciousness in its state as clay; thus, the claim that they do not depend on such an upādāna is unproven.

For this very reason, the objection that "even in the case of silver, there would be the contingency of postulating a cause possessing the same degree of reality as itself" is refuted; for is this postulation intended for the cause in its general sense, or for a specific cause? It cannot be the first, because the cause in the form of the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) possesses a higher degree of reality in all cases. Nor can it be the second, because in the case of successive delusions, it would result in the acceptance of each preceding delusion as the cause of each subsequent one. Furthermore, it should not be argued that *pradhāna*, consisting of the three qualities (*triguṇa*), is the material cause (*upādāna*), for if it were unreal, it would not differ from *avidyā*.

Even if it were real, would it have parts or be partless? In the first case, its beginninglessness would be destroyed. In the second case, its undergoing transformation would be impossible, as in the case of Brahman. Nor is this objection equally applicable to the position that it is ignorance (*avidyā*), because, being merely conceptual (*kālpnika*), it cannot be subject to such questioning. Therefore, presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) is the proof for ignorance. Thus ends the section on *arthāpatti* regarding ignorance in the *Advaitasiddhi*.

And that ignorance (avidyā) is cognizable by the witness-consciousness (sākṣin), but not illuminated by pure consciousness (śuddhacit). The witness, moreover, is consciousness reflected in a modification (vṛtti) of ignorance. Therefore, there is no room for objections such as: "If ignorance were illuminated by faultless consciousness, it would follow that it is ultimately real (pāramārthika); it would follow that it continues to be illuminated even in liberation (mokṣa); and one cannot argue that its non-illumination at that time is due to the cessation of ignorance, because for something whose very body consists of mere cognition, its cessation is impossible when that cognition itself has ceased. Thus, since ignorance is cognized by the witness-consciousness through the medium of a mental modification, none of these defects apply. Furthermore, because the witness-consciousness is eternal and unchanging, there is no possibility of its being affected by the presence or absence of ignorance; rather, the appearance or disappearance of ignorance is merely the appearance or disappearance of its own mental modification. Consequently, ignorance is neither ultimately real nor does it persist in liberation, and there is no contradiction in its nature as being established solely through cognition.

For this very reason it is said that ignorance (*avidyā*) is manifested by the light of consciousness which is itself veiled by it, like Rāhu. Nor does this entail the consequence that ignorance would never be perceived, for such a consequence is accepted as desirable, since it is admitted that this occurs during meditative absorption (*samādhi*). Nor can it be asked how there can be a mental modification (*vṛtti*) regarding ignorance here, given that a modification is produced by a defect (*doṣa*), because ignorance itself is the defect. Furthermore, there is no infinite regress (*anavasthā*) even if a modification is to be manifested by consciousness reflected in another modification, because the modification itself serves as the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) for its own manifestation.

Now, an objection may be raised: since ignorance (*avidyā*) is not accessible through the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the presentation of such means is futile; nor can it be said that the means of valid cognition merely teach the exclusion of non-existence (*asad-vyāvṛtti*), for those who do not perceive ignorance themselves lack the capacity to understand the exclusion of non-existence therein. This is not so. For ignorance, as qualified by the exclusion of non-existence brought forward by the means of valid cognition, is indeed grasped by the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*). Thus, since the function of the means of valid cognition is fulfilled in bringing about the exclusion of non-existence, there is no inconsistency whatsoever.
This concludes the demonstration of the perception of ignorance in the *Advaitasiddhi*.
The substratum of ignorance, however, is pure Brahman alone. As it has been said:
"Only the indivisible consciousness itself partakes of the status of being both the substratum and the object [of ignorance];
for that which arises later cannot be the substratum nor the object of darkness that is already established."

Just as a reflection in a mirror possesses impurity even though the mirror itself is connected only with the face, so too does transmigratory existence (saṃsāra) belong to the individual soul (jīva), which is the reflection, and not to Brahman, which is the original object (bimba); for the limiting adjunct (upādhi) favors the side of the reflection. Now, one might ask: how can consciousness (caitanya) be the locus of ignorance (ajñāna)? For it is of the nature of light, whereas the two—ignorance and consciousness—are opposed in their essential natures, like darkness and light. If this is argued, we say no; for that which opposes ignorance is not mere consciousness, but rather consciousness reflected in a mental modification (vṛtti). And that [consciousness reflected in a vṛtti] is not the locus of ignorance. Furthermore, that which is the locus of ignorance is not opposed to ignorance.

Nor does it follow that pure consciousness would then be non-luminous like a jar or other objects simply because it lacks opposition to ignorance; for it is that very consciousness, when delimited by a mental modification (*vṛtti*), that opposes ignorance. This is just as solar light, which naturally illuminates grass, cotton, and so forth, burns those very things when it is delimited by a sun-crystal (*sūryakānta*); likewise, consciousness, which naturally illuminates ignorance and its effects, possesses the power to "burn" them when it is delimited by a mental modification.

[Objection: Is there not a contradiction, since the witness (*sākṣin*), which apprehends the subject (*dharmin*), perceives ignorance as residing in the *ahaṅkāra* through the cognition "I am ignorant"? Nor can it be said that this cognition "I am ignorant" is an error—arising from the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of identity between consciousness (*cit*) and the locus of ignorance, just as one says "I am fat" due to the superimposition of identity between the body and its locus of stoutness, or just as iron burns because of the superimposition of identity between fire and iron due to their contact with a single fire; for this would lead to a circular argument (*anyonyāśraya*), since the fact that consciousness is the locus of ignorance has not yet been established. [Reply: This is not so.

Since the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) is dependent upon ignorance (*avidyā*), it cannot be its locus; thus, once it is established that consciousness (*cit*) alone is the locus of nescience, the cognition "I am ignorant" is not subversive, as it is based on the superimposition of identity.

Nor should it be argued that because it is the locus of ignorance (*avidyā*), the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) must be unreal, or that its status as its locus must belong to something merely imagined, on the grounds that [the reality of] ignorance is an ornament [to our system] due to its inexplicability; for since the referent of "I" (*ahamartha*) is sublatable by knowledge and is an object of perception (*dṛśya*), it cannot be unreal. Furthermore, unless it were based upon pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), it would follow that it could not be sublated by the final cognitive modification (*vṛtti*) which has that [consciousness] as its object. Finally, that which is imagined by oneself cannot be the locus of itself, as it is impossible for something to be its own support while being supported by itself.

Furthermore, the impossibility [of ignorance] is not an ornament; mere impossibility is not an ornament, but rather an impossibility regarding the arguments that establish [the existence of] a sentient being (*sattva*) and so forth. Otherwise, there would be no room for the words of the disputant. Now, one might object: "The pure consciousness cannot be the locus of ignorance because it contradicts the Śruti which states, 'Free from all defects, faultless, he eternally transcends sorrow and delusion, and is eternally liberated. For delusion is not a non-defect, nor is one who is liberated the locus of the ignorance that causes bondage."

If it is argued that there is no negation of real ignorance (*avidyā*) and so forth—since such [real ignorance] is not even possible in your own system, and because its absence would also apply to the individual soul (*jīva*), thereby contradicting the scriptural distinction between the soul and Brahman as being "blameworthy" (*sāvadya*) and "faultless" (*niravadya*) respectively—we say no. For blameworthiness and faultlessness are established precisely by whether or not [the adjunct] produces effects, since the defect (*avadya*) lacks the capacity to produce effects within consciousness; this is because an adjunct (*upādhi*) invariably sides with its reflection.

Nor should it be argued that there is a lack of evidence for pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) being the locus of ignorance (*avidyā*), while there is evidence for the individual soul (*jīva*) being its locus; for the very scripture, "One should know Māyā as Prakṛti and the Great Lord as the wielder of Māyā" (*Māyāṃ tu prakṛtiṃ vidyān māyinaṃ tu maheśvaram*), serves as the proof. Furthermore, there is no contradiction with the scriptural passage, "The two, the Knower and the Unknower, the Lord and the Unlord," which establishes the ignorance of the individual soul; for even in the absence of being the direct locus of that [ignorance], the designation "unknowing" is logically justified by virtue of being connected to its effects.

Nor should it be argued that Brahman’s status as the possessor of *māyā* is established by its being the object of ignorance residing in the individual soul (*jīva*), for if "being a *jīva*" were the delimiting condition (*avacchedaka*) for being the locus [of ignorance], it would result in the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*).

If it is argued: "Like the ignorance regarding mother-of-pearl and the like, this ignorance—which consists in the non-manifestation of an object to the knower—is resident in the self of the knower in order to achieve coreferentiality with its own effects such as error, with its own sublater such as the knowledge of reality, and with the prior absence of knowledge which shares its same fate; it does not reside merely in consciousness in the form of pure knowledge," we say: no, because consciousness itself is the knower, and thus the state of being the non-manifestation of an object to the knower and the state of being the locus of perfect knowledge [belong to consciousness].

Furthermore, the co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with error and so forth is logically consistent. Nor should it be argued that there is a circular dependency (*anyonyāśraya*)—namely, that if there is subjecthood (*jñātṛtva*), there must be the locus of ignorance (*avidyāśrayatva*), and if there is ignorance, there must be subjecthood—for ignorance does not depend upon subjecthood; thus, no circularity exists. Indeed, the mere existence of co-referentiality does not necessitate that one must exist in dependence upon the other.

Nor should it be argued that, since the superimposition of the status of a knower is possible even upon the body, the body would consequently become the locus of ignorance; for the superimposition of the status of a knower is not the determining factor for being the locus of ignorance, such that it would lead to that conclusion by its mere presence. Rather, the determining factors are the fact of having manifest luminosity and the state of not being supported by ignorance.

Nor should it be argued that if the locus of ignorance possesses the status of being a knower, an enjoyer, and so forth, it would thereby fall into the position of the theory that ignorance resides in the individual soul (*jīva*). For the status of being a knower belongs to that which is delimited by ignorance, yet ignorance itself does not exist as delimited by ignorance; furthermore, their grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is established by taking the identity of the delimited portion as the basis. Just as the connection with an adjunct (*upādhi*) pertains to the face alone, whereas the connection with adventitious impurity pertains to the face as delimited by the adjunct—since the original object (*bimba*) and its reflection (*pratibimba*) are one—so too is the case with coreferentiality.

It will be explained how a reflection is not a separate entity.
