Now, an objection may be raised: "Even the ignorance regarding mother-of-pearl must be said to reside in the consciousness limited by that mother-of-pearl; and if so, there would be a contradiction with the experience of the knower's location, as in 'I do not know,' which is like saying 'I know' or 'I desire,' since it is experienced as residing in the knower. This is not so, because ignorance is of two kinds.

For it has been stated previously that one [ignorance] rests upon the consciousness delimited by the mother-of-pearl (*śukti*), produces an immediate error regarding that object, and is destroyed by an immediate valid cognition (*aparokṣapramā*) regarding that same object; whereas the other rests upon the consciousness delimited by the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) that constitutes the subjecthood (*pramātṛtva*) and produces a mediate error, being destroyed by any valid cognition regarding that object. Among these, this experience has as its object the ignorance residing in the consciousness delimited by the limiting adjunct that constitutes subjecthood. Therefore, there is no contradiction in its having the state of residing in the subject (*pramātṛsthitatva*) as its objective content.

For this very reason, even though ignorance residing in the object persists, there is no such linguistic usage as "I do not know" [on the part of the knower] due to the destruction of the ignorance residing in the subject (*pramātṛ*).

Now, it was stated that because an adjunct (*upādhi*) favors the reflected image (*pratibimba*), Brahman does not possess transmigratory existence (*saṃsāritva*); however, that is incorrect, because the very relationship of original image (*bimba*) and reflected image (*pratibimba*) is impossible.

For instance: because consciousness (*caitanya*), being non-visual, is incapable of reflection—just like smell, taste, and so forth—and because if it were reflected, it would follow that the individual soul (*jīva*) is beginningless; because, just as the sun does not reflect in mirage-water, ignorance (*avidyā*), which is of a different order of reality than consciousness, cannot serve as a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) for consciousness; because opaque ignorance cannot serve as a medium for reflection; because it is impossible for ignorance to face toward pure consciousness alone; and because in the transformation of ignorance into the form of space and so forth...

If it is argued that [the reflection is not of the Self] because reflections do not fall within the scope of what is subject to destruction, we say no; for just as the pervasion (vyāpti) that "only that which possesses form has a reflection" is refuted by its deviation (vyabhicāra) in the case of color and so forth, so too is the pervasion that "only that which is visible has a reflection" refuted by its deviation in the case of space and so forth. In reality, however, once the reflection of consciousness (cit) is established on the strength of scripture, this pervasion fails due to that very deviation. Thus, the cause of reflection is something distinct from taste and other qualities, and is to be inferred solely from its effects.

Nor does it follow that the individual soul (*jīva*) would be subject to having a beginning; for its beginninglessness is established by the beginninglessness of the relationship between the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) and the original object (*bimba*). The detailed exposition is found in the *Siddhāntabindu*. As for the argument that because the reflection of the sun is not perceived in the water of a mirage, having the same ontological status as the original object (*bimba*) is the necessary condition for being apprehended as a reflection—that is not correct, because the redness superimposed upon a crystal is seen as a reflection in a mirror.

Therefore, translucence—which is excluded from the water of a mirage and is to be inferred solely from its effect—is indeed the non-universal (ananugata) determinant for the capacity to receive a reflection; and this [translucence] exists in the case at hand as well. For this very reason, the argument that ignorance cannot function as the locus of reflection because it lacks translucence is refuted.

As for what was stated—that there is an absence of orientation toward pure consciousness (cinmātra)—does that mean there is an absence of orientation toward consciousness in its entirety, or merely an absence of orientation in general? It cannot be the first, because even in the view that consciousness is all-pervading (vibhu), such [orientation] is possible in its entirety. Nor is there a fault even if it possesses a smaller dimension, since we observe that even an object of smaller dimension can receive the reflection of space and other things of greater dimension.

The second alternative is not tenable, because consciousness, being all-pervasive and free from any obstruction, possesses the quality of facing [all objects]. Nor does the transformation into the nature of space and so forth entail the disappearance of the reflection; for a transformation that is not incompatible with the form which causes the reflection is itself non-opposed to the reflection, and thus the reflection does not vanish.

And it should not be argued: "Since there is no other individual substrate capable of being the locus of ignorance—one that consists of pure consciousness (cinmātratva) distinct from the consciousness (cittva) common to both the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman, just as there is no other individual face distinct from the 'mere-facedness' (mukhatvamātra) common to the primary face and its reflection—how can it be said that ignorance relates to pure consciousness just as a mirror relates to the mere face? For the term "mere" (mātra) refers to the face and so forth when their difference is not being considered, and thus the possibility of a distinct underlying substrate (anugatadharmyati-rikta) exists.

If it is objected: "Is it not the case that there is a sublation by a specific pervasion (*viśeṣavyāpti*), since the general pervasion—that 'the adjunct (*upādhi*) favors the side of the reflection'—is unknown, and [it is established] that error and so forth have their cause in their own substratum alone? We say no, because the specific pervasion is impossible; for the observation of concomitance (*sahacāra*) which grasps the specific pervasion cannot possibly occur outside the scope of the dispute. Nor is there any inconsistency in the bondage residing in pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) being co-located (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with liberation, since co-location has already been explained by taking into account the delimited portion (*avacchedyāṃśa*).

Now, an objection: does the partiality of the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) toward the reflection consist in its manifesting its own attributes therein, or in its manifesting its own effects, or in its manifesting the attributes residing in its own effects, or in its obscuring its own object with respect to the reflection? Not the first, because [the adjunct] would have to manifest either the nature of being delimited by ignorance (*avidyāvacchinnatva*), the nature of being reflected in it, or the form of ignorance itself—all of which persist during states such as deep sleep—or the nature of agency, subjectivity, and so forth, which do not persist in deep sleep and other such states.

This is because *saṃsāra* does not reside in ignorance (*ajñāna*). For in your own view, although cognition, action, mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), and so forth do reside in ignorance, these—being eternal and supersensible—are never perceived as residing in the self. Furthermore, according to your view, it is said that "the cessation of ignorance is liberation, and that [ignorance] is declared to be bondage"; thus, in your system, ignorance is the binder or the bondage itself, but it is not the bound entity, such that it could transfer a property in the form of bondage residing within itself.

The second [alternative] is not tenable, because effects produced by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), such as separation and so forth, are observed in the reflection and in the great ether (*mahākāśa*); furthermore, it would follow that the face’s status as a reflection and the like, as well as the omniscience residing in Brahman and so forth, would lack any limiting adjunct. Nor are the third and fourth [alternatives] possible, because such things are not seen in mirrors, jars, and the like. If it is argued that the limiting adjunct in the form of the intellect (*buddhi*) likewise does not "favor" the reflection, we say no; for its "favoring" consists simply in its being exceptionally effective in producing the effect.

And thus, although there is a similarity in their producing effects such as interruption and so forth, it is logical that ignorance (*avidyā*) also shows partiality toward the reflection, just as a mirror and the like show partiality toward the reflection by virtue of producing effects such as the appearance of grossness; for [ignorance] produces the effects consisting of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*), such as agency and enjoyership.

As for the argument that the status of being a reflection residing in the face and so forth, as well as omniscience and other qualities residing in Brahman, must be non-contingent (anaupādhika), that is not so; we do not say that the adjunct (upādhi) lacks the capacity to produce the effects of the original (bimba), but rather that it does so only to an excessive degree in the case of the reflection. Furthermore, even though the adjunct consisting of the intellect (buddhi) does not favor the original, it occupies the position of a red hibiscus flower—which does not favor the reflection—rather than the position of a mirror, which does favor the reflection.

That is not so; for just as a mirror reflects objects situated within itself, this [consciousness] too, by reflecting attributes residing within itself, may justly be said to "take sides" like that [mirror]. Therefore, through the distinctions created by ignorance (avidyā), the systematic arrangement of eternal liberation, transmigratory existence, omniscience, limited knowledge, and so forth, is established within Brahman alone.

By this [argument], since there is no conscious being other than the individual soul (jīva) established by experience—such as one who is not omniscient—the scriptural texts concerning omniscience and so forth would be rendered devoid of an object. Furthermore, in the doctrine of a single soul (ekajīvavāda), the distinction between the transmigrating and the non-transmigrating would be untenable. This is contradicted by such scriptural passages as "Two birds... (*dvā suparṇā*), and "He who dwells in the self... (*ya ātmani tiṣṭhan*); by such Smṛti passages as "And another, O King, is the Supreme; likewise another is the twenty-fifth," and "I know all those, but you do not know them, O scorcher of foes"; and by the Sūtra: "For both [texts] teach that the embodied soul is distinct [from the Self]" (*śārīraścobhaye 'pi hi bhedena enam adhīyate*).

Any contradiction with the sūtras beginning with "And because of the designation of difference" (B.S. 1.1.17), with the bhāṣya stating "Therefore, the Lord is indeed other than the embodied soul; these two selves are both conscious, yet one is the agent and enjoyer while the other is the opposite, possessing qualities such as being free from sin," and with the Vivaraṇa texts stating "In the case of true knowledge and transmigratory existence, just as whiteness and blackness do not reside in each other," is hereby refuted.

Is ignorance (*ajñāna*) inherent to pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), or is it adventitious (*aupādhika*)? It cannot be the first, because that would entail its non-cessation, just like the Self (*ātman*). Nor can it be the second; for if the Self itself were the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), there would be the fallacy of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*); if it depended on something else distinct from itself, there would be mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*); and if it depended on yet another distinct thing, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). If this is argued, we say no, because the Self itself serves as both the locus and the limiting adjunct.

Nor does this involve self-dependence, for it is logically consistent—just as a difference (*bheda*) may be its own differentiator—and because we observe the cessation of even inherently existent things, such as the color of a jar and its prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*).

Thus ends the demonstration that ignorance has pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) as its locus in the *Advaitasiddhi*. Now, an objection is raised: if pure Brahman, which is mere consciousness, were the locus of ignorance, there would be a contradiction with its omniscience. Nor can it be argued that omniscience belongs only to the qualified [Brahman], because the text "the fourth (*turīya*) is always the seer of all" declares that the pure [Brahman] itself is omniscient. If this is said, we reply: no; by the term "seer of all" (*sarvadṛk*), what is meant is the consciousness that is the witness (*dṛgbhūta*) of all things, and not that the fourth state is omniscient (*sarvajña*). Therefore, omniscience belongs only to the qualified [Brahman]. And since that [omniscience] is not possible without ignorance (*avidyā*), ignorance is thereby established.

For it is thus: omniscience must exist either through valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) or through the cognition of one's own nature (*svarūpajñapti*). In that regard, since valid cognition and error are rooted in ignorance (*avidyā*), and since the cognition of one's own nature—which is by definition unattached—cannot be connected with an object without ignorance, it has been said: "Omniscience is established in two ways: either by way of its own nature or through means of valid cognition. In that regard, since valid cognition and error are rooted in ignorance (*avidyā*),

Nor should it be argued that—since the cognition of its own nature (*svarūpajñapti*) would result in non-existence if it were not related to time and so forth by itself, and would result in non-omnipresence if it lacked self-relation—therefore, like ignorance (*avidyā*), a relation with something else must be asserted as being intrinsic (*svata eva*). For this objection is invalid, because the relation with ignorance is itself a product of ignorance; thus, the analogy "like ignorance" is inapplicable.

Since the distinction from the non-existent (*asadvailakṣaṇya*) and omnipresence (*sarvagatatva*) are established either intrinsically or through relation to time and so forth—that is, through relation to everything—there is no need for an intrinsic relation to time or a relation to everything for the sake of those two properties. Furthermore, the scriptural text concerning "non-attachment" (*asaṅgatva*) is also consistent when understood as referring to the absence of attachment intrinsically. For this very reason, the claim that "ignorance (*ajñatā*) is not possible in any way for the knower of all" is refuted. Therefore, ignorance rests solely upon pure consciousness (*cinmātra*). Thus, in the doctrine of ignorance (*ajñānavāda*), the status of the Omniscient One as the locus of ignorance is established.

Vācaspatimiśra, however, declares that ignorance (avidyā) resides in the individual soul (jīva). Now, an objection may be raised: does the ignorance residing in the soul refer to the consciousness reflected therein, or to the consciousness delimited by it, or to the soul which is a distinction imagined by it? If so, there would be a mutual dependence (anyonyāśraya). If this is argued, we reply: no. Is this mutual dependence regarding origination, cognition, or subsistence? It cannot be the first, because both are beginningless (anādi). It cannot be the second, because although ignorance is illumined by consciousness, consciousness is self-luminous and thus not illumined by it. Nor can it be the third.

Could this [relationship] be by way of mutual dependence, or by way of existing in mutual dependence? That is not so, because both are unestablished; for although ignorance has consciousness as its locus and its existence is dependent on consciousness, consciousness lacks both being dependent on ignorance and having its existence dependent on it. Nor does this result in a loss of mutual dependence, since that is possible even for two things existing at the same time through the mere relation of the delimited and the delimiter (*avacchedya-avacchedaka-bhāva*), as in the case of a jar and the space delimited by it, or as in the case of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and the object of knowledge (*prameya*).
As it has been said:

"Just as a jar or the like [is imagined] in space, which is itself imagined by [the mind], so do those skilled in knowledge regard ignorance as having the individual soul (*jīva*) as its locus. By this, the following objection is refuted: "If mutual dependence is not a fault because it merely obstructs origination and cognition, then it would follow that Caitra and Maitra could mount one another's shoulders," for we do not admit a mutual relationship of locus and located between them.

It should not be argued that if both Īśvara and the individual soul (jīva) were imagined by Īśvara and the jīva respectively, there would be the fallacy of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*); or if they were imagined by the jīva and Īśvara, there would be mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*); nor can it be said that pure consciousness (*cit*) is the imaginer, because it lacks ignorance (*ajñāna*). This objection is invalid, because since it is precisely the ignorance residing in the jīva that fashions both the jīva and Īśvara, these alternatives do not arise. Therefore, there is no fault even if [ignorance] has the jīva as its locus. Thus ends the demonstration of the jīva’s locus of ignorance in the *Advaitasiddhi*.

The object of ignorance (*avidyā*) is also easy to state. To explain: pure consciousness alone (*cinmātra*) is the object of ignorance; for, since it is unconstructed (*akalpita*), defects such as mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*) do not apply to it, and because it is self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*), the function of concealment (*āvaraṇa*) is impossible with respect to that which is already manifest. It cannot be anything else, because any other thing is itself constructed by ignorance, and because that which is not already manifest lacks the function of concealment.

Now, one might ask: what is the function of an obscuration—is it the destruction of an already established manifestation, or the non-arising of a manifestation that was not yet established; is it the disconnection of an existing manifestation from its object, or the obstruction of the effect known as "manifestness"; is it the conventional usage that "it does not exist" or "it does not manifest," or the absence of the conventional usage that "it exists" or "it manifests"; is it the fitness for such usages as "it does not exist," or the unfitness for such usages as "it exists"? It cannot be the first or the second, because the manifestation of one's own nature (*svarūpa*) is eternally established.

The first [alternative] is impossible because of the impossibility of its destruction or non-arising; nor the second, because anything other than that is not required for it, which is self-luminous. Nor the third, because cognition has as its very nature a relation to an object, and according to your own view, it does not require a relation since it is itself of the nature of knowledge. Nor the fourth, because in your view there exists nothing apart from consciousness (caitanya). Nor the fifth, because in deep sleep there is an absence of empirical transaction (vyavahāra), which would result in the unwanted consequence of there being no concealment.

Nor is the sixth [alternative] tenable; for if conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) were the manifestation (*abhijñā*), then since the manifestation of its own nature exists even now, and since the function (*vṛtti*) does not exist even in liberation (*mokṣa*). Furthermore, if it were of the nature of verbal expression (*abhilapanarūpa*), there would follow the consequence of obscuration even in liberation. Nor are the seventh and eighth [alternatives] tenable, because since those two are also superimposed (*āropita*), they cannot be joined with obscuration in the absence of an actual obscuration. If this is argued, we reply: no. The very conventional usage that "it does not exist" or "it is not manifest," or rather, the absence of the conventional usage that "it exists" or "it is manifest," is the function of obscuration, common to all [the cases of] manifestation and so forth.

And that obscuration, which consists in the connection with ignorance (ajñāna) and is characterized by its capacity [to conceal], persists from deep sleep and other such states up until the knowledge of Brahman; therefore, there is no obscuration during the time of deep sleep, nor is there obscuration at the time of liberation. As for the claim that this [capacity] also depends upon obscuration because it is superimposed, that is not so; for since the obscuration consisting in the connection with ignorance is beginningless and is manifested by the light of consciousness, it does not depend upon itself for its own origination, manifestation, or persistence.

Now, one might object: "Even if such a linguistic usage occurs regarding that which is qualified by non-duality and so forth, since the nature of the Self—which is the substratum of superimposition—manifests as neither doubtful nor erroneous throughout the three states of consciousness, there is an absence of that [superimposition] in pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), which consists of the cognition of pleasure and so on; consequently, there is an absence of both fitness and unfitness, which are postulated based upon it. If this is argued, we say no. For although pure consciousness (*cit*) manifests in its own form, it does not manifest in its aspect as "perfectly full" (*paripūrṇa*) and so forth; therefore, for that purpose, an obscuration (*āvaraṇa*) is postulated precisely for that [consciousness].

This is because that which possesses the aspect of being "complete" (paripūrṇa) and so forth persists even in the state of liberation, as it is pure consciousness alone (*śuddhacinmātra*). Nor should it be asked: "How can this be possible for undivided consciousness? For it is precisely through the power of concealment (*āvaraṇa*) that there arises the conventional usage that "the complete Brahman does not exist, nor does it shine," as well as the obstruction to the conventional usage that "it exists and shines. Furthermore, its manifestation as the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of superimposition (*adhyāsa*) and so forth is not contradictory.

For this very reason—how could both "fitness" and "unfitness," which are contradictory to self-luminosity (defined as being unfit for cognition while being fit for immediate empirical usage), coexist in Brahman even now? Nor should it be argued that there is no contradiction because there is fitness for immediate empirical usage by virtue of possessing ignorance (*ajñāna*) and so forth, whereas there is unfitness for it by virtue of its own essential nature (*svarūpa*), since the essential nature would then not be luminous; this is refuted, because even though there is currently an absence of empirical usage in terms of forms such as "perfectly full," the fitness for immediate empirical usage has not been lost.

Nor should it be argued: "If pleasure and so forth were manifested by the light of consciousness as delimited by ignorance, then the experience 'pleasure and so forth do not manifest' would result; therefore, to account for the experience 'pleasure and so forth manifest,' one must admit that consciousness manifests without being delimited by ignorance"—for this is an undesired consequence (iṣṭāpatti), and you are merely criticizing what has not been asserted. For we do not say that consciousness manifests as delimited by ignorance.

For this very reason, the objection—that even in the case of an eternally transcendental object, its self-luminosity would follow because it serves as the delimiting adjunct for ignorance in the context of immediate empirical usage—is refuted; for such usage is said to occur without being delimited by ignorance.

Now, one might object: just as a lamp covers a jar or similar objects, let ignorance—which covers consciousness—obstruct its connection with other things and conceal consciousness from others; however, it cannot obstruct consciousness from itself, for that [ignorance] is not opposed to the luminosity consisting of the aforementioned fitness within consciousness itself. Indeed, even when a lamp is covered by a jar, it does not fail to shine by itself, lest it fall into the state of being connected with darkness.

Nor should it be said that pure consciousness veils the individual consciousness (*jīvacaitanya*) with its imagined difference (*kalpitabheda*), because without concealment, the very postulation of difference is impossible; furthermore, since it is precisely the absence of that manifestation—which will occur at liberation as the manifestation of pure consciousness toward pure consciousness—that must currently be established by ignorance. If this is argued, we say no, because pure consciousness remains concealed from the individual whose difference is imagined.

Nor should it be said that this is untenable because the conceptualization of difference occurs subsequent to the veiling; for since both difference and veiling are beginningless, there is no sequence of one following the other. As for what was stated—that the manifestation of consciousness which is to occur at liberation is currently absent and thus to be accomplished through ignorance—that is not so, because at liberation there is no produced manifestation of consciousness; rather, upon the removal of the imagined difference, manifestation toward pure consciousness is possible even for the individual soul (jīva).

As for what was said—"How can there be ignorance in consciousness, whose very nature is light? For there is no darkness in light"—that is not so, because there is a distinction established by experience regarding the opposition between ignorance and darkness. To explain: since one experiences ignorance with respect to an object that is manifesting—as in the thought "I do not know the meaning of what you have said"—neither the consciousness of one's own nature (*svarūpa-caitanya*) nor the witness (*sākṣin*) is opposed to ignorance. However, since darkness is never experienced when light is present, it is light alone that is opposed to it.

In reality, however—since we observe that even in twilight (avatamasa), light which illuminates an object coexists with darkness—it follows that even in darkness, mere light is not its contradictory. Nor should it be argued: "Let there be ignorance regarding that which appears there because of the experience 'the object you spoke of does not appear'; but since there is no such experience as 'that which is appearing, namely the manifestation of pleasure and so forth, does not appear,' how can there be ignorance regarding that? For even though there is no experience of the thought "the manifestation of pleasure and so forth does not appear," it does not appear in its undifferentiated form.

This is because of such experience, and because the concealing ignorance (*āvarakājñāna*) must necessarily exist even there. As for the argument that—in the case of the cognition "I do not know the object you have described"—there is no ignorance appearing [as the object], but rather, as in the expression "it is hidden by darkness in a cave," one experiences the ignorance of the particular only through the mediation of an unobscured universal; for the ignorance residing in another's mind is not restated in its specific form, and thus, just as a certainty regarding a universal is required for a doubt regarding its particulars—so too is it here.

The cognition of the ignorance regarding a particular [object] is caused solely by the cognition of its general [form], because that is what is observed; for when a particular is known, no cognition of ignorance regarding it is ever seen. Indeed, the fact that the cognition of a delimiting factor (avacchedaka) is the cause of the cognition of the delimited (avacchinna) must also be postulated on the basis of observation alone. Nor does this lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga), because the relationship of generality and particularity itself serves as the restrictive factor. Thus [it is said].

That is not so; for does ignorance appear as delimited by a particular (*viśeṣa*), or as delimited by a universal (*sāmānya*)? In the first case, the state of appearing has already accrued to the particular itself. For one cannot perceive "ignorance of a particular" without perceiving the particular. And just as a doubt produced even by the ascertainment of a universal grasps a particular, so too the cognition of ignorance produced by the knowledge of a universal will take the particular as its object. Thus, how can it be said that there is no ignorance regarding what is appearing?

Not the second [alternative], because there is no evidence that ignorance—which has been apprehended as being delimited by a general property through the cognition of that general property—is related to a particular; rather, it is understood as residing in the general property itself that is appearing, since in reality [the nature of] things is determined by the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). And thus, just as [ignorance] residing in another's mind is restated, it is established that the cognition is exactly as the ignorance is.

Now, one might object: "Just as hatred, though it is desired, does not mean that the object of hatred is desired; just as God, though He knows error, does not thereby know the object of delusion; and just as we and others, though we possess knowledge of God's omniscience, do not ourselves become omniscient—so too, even in the absence of the cognition of the unknown, there can be a 'cognition of ignorance'. If this is argued, we say no, because the examples cited are unconvincing.

For instance: desire has the same object as knowledge; and since knowledge takes as its object even that which is dual through the relation of being a delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*), desire also has that as its object by way of being a delimiting factor. Indeed, a desire cannot have as its object anything other than the delimiting factor of the state of being desired (*iṣṭatāvacchedaka*). This is the only distinction: it takes one thing as its object in the sense of being something to be accomplished (*sādhya*), and another in the sense of being a delimiting factor. Even God does not apprehend an error without first apprehending the object of that error. For an error must be grasped as an error.

And error consists either in the manifestation (*khyāti*) of silver where there is an absence of silver, or the manifestation of the non-existent (*asatkhyāti*), or the manifestation of the indeterminable (*anirvacanīyakhyāti*). When that [error] is apprehended, the object is in every respect grasped. However, this is the distinction: the deluded person grasps it independently, whereas God grasps it as the delimiting adjunct (*avacchedaka*) of His own cognition; thus, what we call "omniscience" is for us simply the knowledge of God under the term "the Omniscient One."

In this regard, since even people like us grasp the relation of knowledge [to an object] only while already knowing that which is to be established by every word, such omniscience is indeed accepted. However, the distinction is that for God there is no ignorance regarding anything whatsoever, whereas for those like us there is ignorance regarding particulars; thus, it is precisely when a particular is known that there is the cognition of ignorance [regarding other particulars].

Nor should it be argued: "Even though a jar or the like appears as the delimiting adjunct (*avacchedaka*) of ignorance, since we do not observe knowledge of a conjunction delimited by that jar until the ignorance regarding the jar has ceased, one must likewise admit here that for the sake of knowing the ignorance delimited by the object, there must be the cessation of the ignorance regarding that object which serves as the delimiting adjunct; thus, just as there is knowledge that does not contradict ignorance, there must also be admitted a cessation of ignorance that does not contradict ignorance. This is because, although the existence of a conjunction or the like depends upon the existence of its delimiting adjunct, such as a jar, [the case is not the same].

In the case of non-existence, there is no requirement for the existence of its own locus or the nature of its counter-positive, because of their contradiction; likewise, the knowledge of ignorance does not require the cessation of the ignorance regarding its own object, because of their contradiction.

Nor can it be said: "Let there be no requirement for knowledge even regarding that object, since the contradiction is the same; for the grounds for postulating non-contradiction are the same in the case of the cessation of ignorance as they are in the case of knowledge. Thus, ignorance is known while the object remains unknown, and the cognition delimited by a specific object arises—just as in the case of darkness—only after the knowledge of the specific detail, in the form: 'For all this time, I did not know this particular thing. This should not be asserted.

Ah! Thus, Your Honor has established for ignorance (*ajñāna*) the property of being an object of a cognition that is independent of the cognition of a counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) which is opposed to the nature of non-existence; this serves as a proof of its distinction from non-existence. Furthermore, if ignorance were not manifested at its own time as delimited by its object, then the present cognition of an object in the form "I do not know the meaning spoken by you" would contradict the existence of an ignorance delimited by that object.

Therefore, because it establishes the ignorance regarding its object, even the manifestation of the object in the form of the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*) is not opposed to ignorance; rather, it is the cognitive modification (*pramāṇavṛtti*) that is so opposed. Even when the object is the same, the opposition to or non-opposition to ignorance by a cognitive modification and a modification other than that [the witness] are intelligible—just as sunlight and visual light, though both directed toward a jar, respectively oppose or do not oppose darkness.

Nor should it be argued: "In the view that the function (*vṛtti*) of consciousness serves the purpose of coloring the object, this [objection] is untenable because such a function lacks the capacity to remove ignorance. This is not to be said, for it has been stated that its role as a cause of cessation consists precisely in its being the remover of ignorance; and this [removal] indeed exists even in this position by way of establishing a connection. Nor should it be argued: "Since ignorance is pervaded by the absence of knowledge—which is its own opposite—there would follow the persistence of ignorance even in liberation (*mokṣa*). This is not to be said.

This is because, according to the scriptural accounts of the cessation of ignorance at the time of liberation (*mokṣa*), [ignorance] is merely pervasive of the prior absence (*prāgabhāva*) of that knowledge which is its own opposite. Nor should it be asked: "If it is opposed only to the operation of valid cognition (*pramāṇavṛtti*), why is there a cognition in the form 'I do not know' that takes the form of being opposed to ignorance in general? For just as the absence of a jar (*ghaṭābhāva*), though opposed only to specific jars and the like, is perceived as an "absence" (*abhāva*) because it is opposed to existence in general (*bhāvasāmānya*), so too ignorance, though opposed to specific cognitions, is [perceived] as being opposed to knowledge in general.

Because it is possible [to account for] such cognition: for when there is the cognition of absence through a word such as "non-existence," the absence of the jar does not fail to appear. Now, if you argue that in that case the opposition (virodhitā) terminates merely in the specific object (viśeṣa), then the same applies here as well, since your insistence is elsewhere. Nor should it be said: "Since one experiences only the opposition to the act of knowing (*jñapti*) in the experience 'I do not know,' how can there be opposition to the mental modification (*vṛtti*)? For in your view, consciousness (*caitanya*) alone is the act of knowing; and if there were no opposition between consciousness and knowledge, the distinction between being knowledge and being ignorance would be impossible. [This objection is] not to be maintained.

In my view, it is consciousness reflected in the mental modification (*vṛtti*) that constitutes the object of the empirical usage "I know. Consequently, by the expression "I do not know," the fact that both the mental modification and consciousness are antagonistic to ignorance (*ajñāna*) is made the object [of cognition]. Thus, neither consciousness alone nor the mental modification alone possesses the quality of being antagonistic to ignorance; rather, this is so because only consciousness as mounted upon the mental modification (*vṛttyupārūḍhacit*) has the capacity to illuminate the object.

Now, an objection: if it is held that even a mental modification (*vṛtti*) dispels ignorance and its effects by its very nature as a specific genus, without the capacity to illuminate an object—just as hatred, which is dispelled by desire and so forth—it would follow that it must be of the nature of *sattva*. Furthermore, if it is argued that it dispels them by illuminating the object like the cognition of mother-of-pearl, then since consciousness (*caitanya*) also possesses that capacity, it would necessarily dispel them, leading to the undesirable consequence (*āpāta*) of their perpetual cessation. Moreover, [if illumination were not required], ignorance would not cease when there is a remote (*parokṣa*) modification regarding an eternal and supersensible object, nor would it cease in the case of pleasure and the like, even in the absence of a direct (*aparokṣa*) modification.

If it is argued that [ignorance is removed] by mere manifestation and the non-perception of ignorance through positive and negative concomitance, because manifestation alone is the opponent of ignorance—[we reply: no, for we maintain that its status as a remover is due to its being a light (prakāśa) mounted upon a valid cognitive modification (pramāṇavṛtti), and not due to some specific genus, nor merely by the nature of light itself. Therefore, there is no contingency of these things to be removed [by knowledge] existing [simultaneously] like hatred which is removed by desire, nor is there the contingency that mere consciousness (caitanya) alone is the remover.

For this very reason, the following [objection] is refuted: "Even when verbal and other cognitive functions (*vṛtti*) are present, ignorance is not removed; and in the case of pleasure (*sukha*) and the like, since there is no cognitive function of a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇavṛtti*), ignorance is not perceived merely through manifestation (*sphuraṇa*). Therefore, by positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), it is manifestation alone that is the antagonist to ignorance and so forth. [This is refuted because] indirect cognitive function (*parokṣavṛtti*) does not extend as far as the object itself, and thus it cannot remove the ignorance residing in the object; furthermore, in the case of pleasure and the like, since they exist solely as known (*jñātaikasattva*), ignorance is not perceived even without the removal of ignorance.

Therefore, since positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) are otherwise established, mere manifestation (*sphuraṇa-mātra*) is not the opposite of ignorance. Nor is it improper to establish the self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*) of the Self—given that it is both the locus and the object of ignorance—on the grounds that it is devoid of non-manifestation (*aprakāśa*) in its own existence; for even if it is not devoid of non-manifestation in respect to its perfection and so forth, it is possible for it to be devoid of non-manifestation by virtue of being manifest through its status as the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of superimposition (*adhyāsa*).

Nor should it be argued: "The statement regarding the difference between the consciousness of the mental mode (*vṛtti-cit*) and [pure] consciousness is incorrect, because the witness (*sākṣin*), like the mental mode, is experienced as being opposed to ignorance by virtue of having the same object; otherwise, just as Maitra has ignorance regarding Caitra’s desire, pleasure, and so forth—which are known by the witness—Caitra himself would also have ignorance [regarding them], or else Maitra would not have ignorance [regarding them]. This should not be said, because the opposition to ignorance experienced in the witness is not based on its capacity to remove ignorance, but rather [it is due to the fact that] within its own objects, such as desire and so forth, [the witness persists] for as long as they exist.

It is entirely appropriate to state the distinction between the two: that in the case of light, it is the basis for the non-occurrence of ignorance, whereas in the case of a mental modification (*vṛtti*), it is precisely the basis for the cessation of ignorance that has occurred with respect to its own object. Furthermore, it is precisely because ignorance does not occur [with respect to Caitra’s own desire] that there is no linguistic usage of "ignorance" regarding Caitra’s desire; however, for Maitra, such usage occurs precisely because of the ignorance belonging to the knower (the subject). Nor should it be argued: "In that case, ignorance would likewise not occur with respect to the Self for that very same reason"—for this objection has already been answered.

Furthermore, being cognizable by a witness (*sākṣivedyatva*) is the requisite condition for that [ignorance] to apply; however, the Self is not cognizable by such a witness, because, being of the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*), it is itself the very light of manifestation. Nor should it be argued: "In that case, ignorance would be even more impossible than darkness in the presence of light; otherwise, like a jar requiring light for its own manifestation, the Self too would require another cognition for its own empirical usage. This need not be said, because [the objection applies only if] the Self were veiled by ignorance like a jar. If you claim there is a requirement for another factor to remove that ignorance, then we accept that consequence, since it is simply the mental modification (*vṛtti*) that is required. As for the requirement of another light [of consciousness], [that does not apply here].

Because insentience (*jaḍatva*) is the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), and because it has been established that even in the case of luminosity (*prakāśatva*), there is no contradiction with ignorance (*ajñāna*). For this very reason, every object is an object of the witness-consciousness (*sākṣicaitanya*) both in its state of being known and in its state of being unknown, since knowledge and ignorance manifest only as delimited by their own respective objects. By this, the following objection is refuted: "Just like something enveloped by darkness, or like an object delimited by the absence of knowledge, that which is enveloped by ignorance would not be manifested, and thus its being known by the witness-consciousness would be impossible"; for such a view contradicts actual experience regarding the delimitation by the object.

Now, an objection: even if mental modification (*vṛtti*) is opposed to ignorance, a modification having the Self as its object exists even now; so how can ignorance exist there? Furthermore, in your own view, since even the direct modification regarding a jar or the like has as its object consciousness delimited by the jar, etc., it is all the more impossible for ignorance to exist in relation to that consciousness.

Nor should it be argued that a mental modification (*vṛtti*)—whether having as its object the individual soul (*jīva*), whose nature is qualified consciousness, or having as its object consciousness delimited by a jar—cannot be an antagonist to ignorance because it does not have as its object the pure consciousness (*kevalacid*) which is the actual locus of ignorance; for if that were so, there would follow the absurdity that the mental modification "Caitra possesses a staff" (*daṇḍī caitra*) would not overcome the ignorance regarding Caitra. Furthermore, in the cognition of the space within a jar (*ghaṭākāśa*), the ignorance regarding the great space (*mahākāśa*) culminates in the ignorance regarding its magnitude; it is for this very reason that one has the experience, "Space is known."

Nor is it the case that only the mental modification (*vṛtti*) produced by hearing [the scriptures] and so forth is the antagonist of ignorance; for if ignorance were not removed even by a cognition that has no object beyond that of a perceptual cognition occurring at the time of an error—even if that latter cognition were produced by other causes—there would be the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of such a rule. Furthermore, if there were no additional object, hearing and so forth would be useless, and [the world] would consequently result in being real. If this is argued, we say: No. According to the view that "as many cognitions as there are, so many are the ignorances," in the position where [ignorance] is a specific cognition, a specific state (*avasthā*), or a specific power (*śakti*) residing in *avidyā*, it is removed by a mental modification whose scope is qualified [by the object].

Thus, there remains a fundamental ignorance which is the cause of all phenomenal proliferation (*prapañca*), which is to be removed by the mental modification (*vṛtti*) directed toward the undivided reality produced by such statements as "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*); for the delusion of difference is still being experienced. Just as, although the ignorance regarding [an object] is removed by the cognition "this is it," there remains an ignorance to be removed by the mental modification directed toward non-difference in the form "that is this."

Thus, even in the absence of a distinction created by the object, the removal [of ignorance] through a specific modification produced by a specific cause precludes both the futility of hearing [the scriptures] and the consequence of [the world's] reality; otherwise, one would fail to understand even the [identity cognition] "this is that. Furthermore, the mental state (vṛtti) whose object is the individual soul (jīva) is a modification of nescience (avidyāvṛtti), not a valid cognitive state (pramāṇavṛtti), because only the latter is opposed to nescience. As it is stated in the Vivaraṇa: "The individual soul is manifested by the internal organ transformed into the 'I'-state in the form of the individual soul."

The meaning of this is as follows: there is a modification (*vṛtti*) of ignorance (*avidyā*) characterized by the egoity (*ahaṃtva*) of the individual soul (*jīva*). Through that [modification], the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) undergoes transformation; and by means of the contact with the modification in the form of knowledge (*jñāna*), which is a transformation of the internal organ, the individual soul is manifested.

Nor should it be argued that the ignorance which is to be removed by the final cognitive state (*caramavṛtti*) must also be removed by the cognition "this is a jar"; for, on the strength of the observed result (*phalabala*), it is accepted that only a specific instance of ignorance—which serves as the cause for the state of being unknown with respect to that [object]—is removable by the knowledge delimited by that [object]. Just as light, while illuminating a particular object, removes only certain darknesses rather than all darkness, so too is this the case. Therefore, it is established that pure consciousness (*śuddhacit*) is the locus and the object [of ignorance].

By this, the following unraised objection is refuted: that the difference consisting of the body and so forth, or the non-difference consisting of non-agency and so forth, or the non-difference from Brahman, or the non-difference from the mere non-dual, or the self as qualified by those [attributes], is not the object [of the Upanishads]; for if these were merely the Self, the aforementioned defects would apply, if they were different, non-duality would be destroyed, and if they were products of nescience (*avidyā*), there would be the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*). [We reply: Under the view that the non-difference from Brahman and so forth are merely the Self, their status as the object of nescience remains intact, since the defect has already been resolved.

As for what was stated incidentally—that if the Self, characterized by the absence of a second, were the object of ignorance, then that very same [Self] would have to be the object of the final cognitive state (*vṛtti*); and thus, if the Vedāntas were also concerned with such a Self as possessing a characterizing attribute (*upalakṣaṇa*), their status as having an undivided meaning (*akhaṇḍārthatā*) would be lost; furthermore, like the expression "a crow on a crow," this too would result in invalidity because the characterizing attribute is false—regarding that, we shall speak in the discussion on the doctrine of the undivided meaning.

Nor should it be argued that even a shorter finger covers more [than its own length], for how could that which is not related to the object cover more? This objection has already been answered. Therefore, ignorance (avidyā) is well-defined in terms of its essential nature, its locus, and its object. Thus ends the demonstration of the object of ignorance in the Advaitasiddhi.

From that [nescience], there arises the creation of the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) and so forth. Now, one might object: "The referent of 'I' (*ahamartha*) is the Self (*ātman*) itself; how then can its creation proceed from nescience? Nor should it be argued: "Even though the Self, which shines by its own nature, exists during deep sleep, the ego-sense—which is not of such a nature—is absent there. Furthermore, if the ego-sense were manifest during deep sleep, then the ego would be remembered just like yesterday's, for even if there is no rule that everything experienced must be remembered, there is a rule that what is remembered must be the Self alone. This argument cannot stand, because the reason (*hetu*) is unestablished (*asiddha*), and because in the case of the reductio ad absurdum (*tarka*), the undesired consequence is actually accepted.

For even now, the difference between the "I-sense" (*ahamartha*) and the self-luminous Self (*svaprakāśātman*) has not been established. To prove its non-luminosity by means of its difference from the Self, and then to prove that difference by means of that non-luminosity, involves the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*). Nor is there a lack of reflective awareness (*aparāmarśa*) regarding the "I-sense," since there is indeed such awareness in the form: "I slept happily; I was not aware of anything. If you say this, we reply: no, for it is agreed by both of us that the ego (*ahaṅkāra*) is perceived precisely as qualified by desire and the like.

Furthermore, since desire and the like do not exist in deep sleep, how can there be an experience of the "I-sense" at that time? Nor should it be argued: "We do not agree that the 'I-sense' is perceived as qualified by attributes such as desire," because the perception of a substratum (guṇin) is necessarily pervaded by the perception of its attributes; otherwise, even a pot devoid of color and other qualities would be manifest.

Nor should it be argued that their non-existence [in deep sleep] is due to the absence of qualities such as form (*rūpa*), for they exist even without those qualities during the first moment following the destruction of a prior form and before the production of a subsequent form. And if this is so, how can there be a perception of the substratum (*guṇin*) upon the perception of the quality (*guṇa*)? Thus, one must accept that the Self (*ātman*) is perceived as being indeed devoid of qualities. Furthermore, in the absence of such experience, there can be no reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of it during the waking state. Consequently, the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) is distinct from the Self, which is experienced in deep sleep as the locus of ignorance (*ajñāna*).

In this very way, once the difference between the self [and the ego] is established, there is no circular reasoning (anyonyāśraya) in proving its non-self-luminosity. Nor does it follow that the inclusion of the "I-sense" (ahamartha) in the reflective awareness "I slept" would be untenable; for its status as a reflective awareness is not established with respect to that [egoic] component. Even so, how it possesses the character of a reflective awareness with respect to the component of ignorance has already been demonstrated below.

Although the self-reflection "I slept" and so forth is not distinct from that cognition, nevertheless, since the referent of "I" was not experienced during the time of deep sleep, the reflection ultimately culminates in the Self alone, which was experienced at that time as the substrate of ignorance. For this very reason, the possibility of the reflection taking the form "consciousness slept" or "itself slept" is refuted, because the form "I" is logically accounted for through the association with the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) experienced at that time.

As for what was stated in the *Vivaraṇa*: "We maintain that recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) pertains only to the Self as qualified by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), and not to stainless consciousness (*niṣkalaṅkacaitanya*), because that which exists in the state of liberation is cognizable solely through scripture (*śāstra*). This does not constitute a contradiction here; for, by stating the reason "because that which exists in the state of liberation is cognizable solely through scripture," and by negating recognition in "stainless [consciousness]"—meaning that which is devoid of mere limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*)—the term "internal organ" is intended to signify merely the limiting adjuncts.

And likewise, even in deep sleep, it is the Self as qualified by ignorance that is apprehended. Furthermore, there is no contradiction, because the denial of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) applies to the Self as characterized by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), whereas the denial of simple cognition (*abhijñā*) does not; for it has been stated that in deep sleep, simple cognition alone occurs. Nor should it be argued that if the "I-sense" (*ahamartha*) were not reflected upon, there would be doubt—"Was I asleep for this long, or was it someone else?"—rather than the certainty "It was I myself"; understand rather that this is due to the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of identity with the Self experienced during the time of deep sleep.

Just as there is no doubt regarding Caitra—whom one has experienced as non-different from Devadatta experienced on a previous day—as to whether "this is he" or not, but rather the certainty that "this is indeed he"; furthermore, when certainty exists, there is a rule of the absence of doubt, but it is not the case that when certainty is absent, there is a rule of doubt. As it has been said: "When there is a superimposition (*āropa*), one seeks its cause; it is not the case that because a cause exists, there is a superimposition."

Nor should it be argued: "In the case of 'I was awake' following the thought 'for so long I was seeing a dream,' there is an experience of the awareness (*parāmarśa*) regarding the element 'I'; how then can there be a lack of awareness (*aparāmarśatva*) in the case of 'I slept'? This is because, due to the superimposition of identity with the self being reflected upon, there arises the conceit (*abhimāna*) of awareness regarding that which is distinct from it. Nor should it be argued: "The superimposition of awareness upon what is not awareness is never observed. For we observe the superimposition of awareness even upon that which is experienced as distinct from it, yet in its true nature [as being the self].

For this very reason—the objection that if the referent of "I" were other than the Self, there would arise the cognition, "He who was previously different from me and was in deep sleep has now become 'I'," just as one might say, "He who was previously in pain has now become happy"—is refuted; because whereas there was previously knowledge of [the Self] by way of its being in pain, there was no such prior knowledge of it by way of its being other than "me. Just as the referent of "I" is not manifest in deep sleep, its being other [than the Self] is likewise unmanifest.

And thus, because there is no apprehension of prior non-existence and because it is apprehended as non-different from what was apprehended at the previous time, there can be no cognition of birth in relation to the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra); for such a view would lead to an undesirable consequence for those who possess discernment.

Nor should it be argued that there is a circular dependency—namely, that the superimposition of identity with the Self being reflected upon is established only once the difference between the "I-sense" (*ahamartha*) and the Self is established, and that this difference is established by the non-manifestation of the "I-sense" during deep sleep once that superimposition is established—for we have already proven the non-reflection of the "I-sense" prior to the establishment of its difference from the Self. Since we accept that the very cognition "I slept well" (*ahamasvāpsam*) constitutes a reflection upon the Self, there is no lapse of what is observed nor the necessity of postulating what is unobserved.

For this very reason, there is no room for the objection that "if the referent of 'I' were manifest during deep sleep, it would have to be remembered as being like yesterday"; furthermore, there would be the retrospective reflection: "For so long a time, I existed while identifying myself as 'I'. Nor can it be argued—on the grounds that "the manifestation of the referent of 'I' does not necessarily produce such identification, just as touching the ear does not cause the movement of the hip"—that this is a problem only for you [the opponent]. This is indeed your own position.

Because the "I-sense" (ahamartha) alone is required, and because its conceit (*abhimāna*) and its manifestation (*prakāśa*) are co-extensive, the production of a mutual reflection through their mutual manifestation is not misplaced. Nor does this entail for you the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of the reflection "he existed conceiving himself as the Self," since the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) is the necessary condition (*tantra*) there; in its absence, such a reflection cannot be produced. As for the claim that the "I-sense" indeed shines forth even in deep sleep—

The claim that the reflection on ignorance in the form "I did not know anything at all" has as its object an ignorance distinct from the ignorance regarding the Self and so forth, or an ignorance distinct from the ignorance regarding the *ahamartha* (the "I-sense"), because otherwise there would be a contradiction—that is merely the manifestation of that [very] ignorance. For the witnessing consciousness (*sākṣivedana*) is not opposed to ignorance. Furthermore, it has already been stated how the *ahamartha* does not manifest during deep sleep. Moreover, the scriptural text, "He does not know that he exists," is also an authority for the non-cognition of the *ahamartha* at that time.

Furthermore, this scriptural passage—"neither [knowing] itself nor others"—is not intended to convey a lack of knowledge regarding specific distinctions, as is the case with the scriptural texts concerning the ignorance of the Self during deep sleep. It is not logical to interpret it as referring to a lack of knowledge of specific distinctions, because that would contradict other scriptural passages that teach the awareness of the Self, such as: "Every day they go to Brahman; having become united with it, they do not know. However, in the present context, such a contradiction does not exist.

As for the argument: "The referent of 'I' (ahamartha) is, first of all, the rememberer. And is that [rememberer] consciousness delimited by ignorance (*avidyā*), or is it consciousness delimited by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*)? In the first case, there would be a contradiction with experience, since one has the experience: 'I, who performed [the action], am the same I who remembers the ignorance and so forth of deep sleep. In the latter case, however, the status of being the experiencer must be attributed to the very referent of 'I', because the causal relationship between experience, its latent impression (*saṃskāra*), and memory exists only when they have a single locus, and because of the recognition: 'I, who experienced [it], am the same I who remembers it.'"

That is not so, for an answer has already been given. For it has been stated that consciousness delimited by ignorance (*avidyā*) is the experiencer, and that very same [consciousness], when delimited by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), is the rememberer; thus there is no disparity between the two. Nor should it be argued that even for consciousness delimited by ignorance there is no unity, because of the difference caused by the distinct limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) in the form of the internal organs; for the delimitation by the internal organ occurs precisely within that which is already delimited by ignorance.

Nor should it be argued that—nevertheless, due to the distinction between the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) consisting of ignorance (avidyā) and the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), there would be a distinction in the conditioned [Self] (upahita), just as there is between the space within a hut and the space within a jar situated therein—for the illustrative example is unestablished. It is only those two adjuncts which bring about a mutual distinction in the conditioned that do so by not being themselves conditioned by one another. Otherwise, the space within a jar would be something entirely different from the space delimited by the neck as cut off by a turban.

Nor does it follow that, in the absence of the referent "I" during deep sleep, activity for the sake of deep sleep would be impossible due to the desire "May I be free from suffering," for such activity is logically established—just as in the case of [the thought], "I, who am thin, shall become fat. Nor should it be argued that in that instance, for those possessed of discrimination, the body alone (as distinguished from thinness and so on) is the intended object as the locus of fatness; for in the present case as well, the intended object of that desire is precisely the self as distinguished from the internal organ and the rest.

Now, an objection may be raised: "The recognition that 'I who was asleep am now awake,' or 'I who did this yesterday am doing it today,' would be untenable because the referent of the term 'I' (ahamartha) is distinct [in different states]. Furthermore, there would follow the loss of what was done and the acquisition of what was not done, since the agent and the enjoyer—the referent of 'I'—would be different. Moreover, since agency and the like do not exist in the non-dual consciousness itself, nor can they be superimposed upon it, such recognition would also be impossible; and finally, there would be the over-extension [of this principle] to the body and other such things. If this is argued, we say no. For all these difficulties are resolved by accepting that the very same entity which existed in deep sleep in the form of its cause arises [again]. Thus, everything is logically consistent.

Nor should it be argued that "the cessation of the ego (ahaṅkāra) does not occur because the scripture beginning with 'Now, when this person sleeps' and continuing with 'the eye is withdrawn, the ear is withdrawn, the mind is withdrawn,' etc., mentions only the cessation of the mind and other faculties"—for when the mind ceases, the cessation of the ego follows by necessity. Indeed, the ego is the substrate of the experience associated with the self, such as "I experience," and of agency and so forth associated with the non-conscious, such as "I am the doer"; for it is superimposed as being of the nature of a synthesis of consciousness and the unconscious.

When that insentient internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) ceases, there is cessation [of the ego]. Furthermore, the scriptural passage—"Now, therefore, the instruction regarding the ego; now, therefore, the instruction regarding the Self"—is also proof for their distinctness, because of the separate teaching.

Now, an objection might be raised: even if, according to your view, there is identity between the *ahaṃkāra* and the *bhūman* taught in the passage "That indeed is below," a separate teaching of them is nonetheless appropriate. Nor can it be argued that—since the *bhūman* and the Self are established by perception as distinct, their separate teaching must be for the purpose of establishing their identity (because it is impossible for both to be the universal self)—whereas the separate teaching of the *ahaṃkāra*, which is established by perception as identical with the Self, must be for the purpose of establishing a difference; for [in your view], the Self, which is other than the referent of "I," is distinct from the Brahman called *bhūman*.

If it is argued: "Since those two [the body and the senses] are not established by perception, their instruction is for the purpose of differentiation; however, since the 'I-sense' (ahamartha) is established by perception as distinct from Brahman, why could the instruction regarding those two not be for the purpose of establishing identity?"—we say no. Although the self's difference from the ego (ahaṅkāra) is not established by perception, its non-difference from it is likewise unestablished. Therefore, given that the instruction of both as being the Self of all (sārvātmya) is otherwise untenable, it is appropriate that this scripture intends their non-difference, especially in the present context.

Furthermore, there is a contradiction in [your claim that the text] has non-difference as its primary purport, because identity between the insentient and the sentient is impossible. Nor should it be argued: "In your own view, since the Bhūman, the ego (ahaṅkāra), and the self can all be established as pure consciousness (cinmātra)—the Self limited by the adjunct of ignorance (avidyopādhika) which stands in the relation of the original object (bimba) and its reflection (pratibimba) like a face and its reflection—the distinctness of the ego from the individual soul (jīva) is not proven. This is not to be said, because after the description of the nature of the Bhūman in the passages "where one sees nothing else" and "he himself is below," etc., there is the mention of a locus and a subject in the word "where" (yatra), and the use of the demonstrative pronoun "he" (sa) indicates a state of remoteness (pārokṣya).

Since the contingency of [the Self] being other than the seer (draṣṭṛ) arises, in order to prevent that, when the "Full" (bhūman) is indicated by means of the "I-maker" (ahaṅkāra) in the passage, "Now, therefore, the instruction regarding the I-maker," and since the I-maker is seen to be used indiscriminately with respect to the aggregate of the body and so forth, the contingency of non-difference from that [aggregate] arises; therefore, taking up the nature of the pure Self as distinct from the I-maker, the difference from the seer is stated in the passage, "Now, therefore, the instruction regarding the Self. Since the purpose is such, the analogy of the reflection and the reflected object is impossible here.

Alternatively, the statement that the individual soul (*jīva*), conditioned by ignorance (*avidyopādhika*), is the ego (*ahaṅkāra*) follows the analogy of the "gross Arundhatī" (where one first points to a nearby star to indicate the faint one). For this very reason, the concluding statements such as "He alone is all this," "I alone am all this," and "The Self alone is all this,"—along with their openings such as "He alone is below, I alone am below, the Self alone is below," and the Smṛti texts such as "You pervade everything, therefore You are everything"—are intended to establish his omnipresence (*sarvagatatva*), and not to establish his identity with all (*sārvātmya*), which would otherwise [imply] for the word "I" (*ahaṃpada*)...

The objection that [the Upanishad] would instead be teaching the supremacy of a consciousness from which the ego has been extracted, or that omnipresence is possible even for many [individuals], or that the intermediate instruction on the ego is useless because the identity of Brahman and the Self is established solely through the teachings on the "plenum" (bhūman) and the Self—this is all refuted.

Following the question, "O Blessed One, on what is that established?", is it asked whether there is merely a state of being supported by something, or whether there is an actual dependence upon something in the ultimate sense? In the first case, having stated "in its own glory," and in the second case, intending to show that nothing exists apart from the *bhūman* (the Infinite), and since it has been determined—following the previous statement "for one thing is established in another"—that the passage beginning with "That indeed is below" also refers to the universal selfhood (*sārvātmya*) within a single sentence; [the following is said].

This is because no other meaning is postulated by means of the assumption of an "attack" (upakrama) and so forth; because that which is being postulated does not establish the subject matter at hand; because, under the view that the genus (*jāti*) is omnipresent, it is possible for the "plenum" (*bhūman*)—just like the all-pervading genus—to be presided over by another; and because the Smṛti passage beginning with "You pervade everything" has been established as having the intent of teaching the identity of all things (*sārvātmya*). Nor is the instruction regarding the "I-maker" (*ahaṅkāra*) in the middle [of the text] useless, since the identity with the "I-maker" is stated for the sake of making Brahman directly manifest (*āparokṣya*).

Nor should it be argued: "In your own view, since the Self, whose nature is the inner subject (*pratyag-artha*), is of the nature of immediate, non-dual experience, its immediacy is established simply by stating its identity [with the ego]; therefore, it is improper to speak of 'omnipresence' (*sārvātmya*) regarding the ego, as that quality does not actually exist in it. This is not to be said, because although the immediacy of the ego is indeed established through its identity with the Self—since the ego becomes immediate precisely through its connection with the Self—nevertheless, because the immediacy of the ego is so well-known in common experience, the mention of the ego is not improper. As it is said: "The *bhūman* (the Infinite) is known as Nārāyaṇa; He alone is remembered as the *ahaṅkṛti* (the creative I-maker).
That which resides within the individual soul (*jīva*) as Aniruddha is called *ahaṅkāra* (the ego)."

[The opponent argues: "Even though the Lord Vāsudeva is the supreme, all-pervading one, his being the Self (ātman) is stated [in scripture], yet by such Smṛti as 'He is all-pervasive,' the meaning of the Śruti is not that he is the Self of all (sārvātmya), but rather that he is omnipresent (sarvagatatva). This is not so; for, in contradiction with Śruti, the Smṛti itself has the sense of being the Self of all, and it is not the case that Śruti is to be interpreted otherwise by means of Smṛti. Nor [is this view supported] in the Mokṣadharma...
For Aniruddha, the Great Self, who is higher than the highest, is indeed present in all worlds;
he, having attained a manifest form, created the Grandfather (Brahmā).

It should not be argued that the statement "He is called *ahaṅkāra*, for he consists of all splendor," along with the sūtra "That [Self] indeed [is] the Truth, etc.," establishes that *ahaṅkāra* is the Self, because otherwise the assertion of its pervasiveness would be untenable; for the Śruti says, "The *ahaṅkāra* and that which is to be made the object of 'I'," and the Smṛti says, "The great elements and the *ahaṅkāra*. Since it is impossible for *ahaṅkāra* to be all-pervasive, the word "I" in passages such as "I was Manu" refers to the pure consciousness of the *ahaṅkāra* (the *ahaṅkāra-caitanya*) extracted from its adjuncts.

Now, one might object: the subject matter of these two [scriptural] authorities, Śruti and Smṛti, is the principle of *ahaṅkāra*—designated by terms such as "ego"—which is the cause of the mind and other faculties and is an effect of the principle of *mahat*, being threefold according to its divisions such as the *vaikārika*. It is not, however, the referent of the word "I" (*ahamartha*). Thus, the Smṛti says:
"From the principle of *mahat*, undergoing transformation and impelled by the potency of the Lord, the threefold *ahaṅkāra*, which is the power of action, came into being."

This is because the passage beginning with "ityādi" is consistent when interpreted in this way. If one were to assume a contradictory meaning, then in the verse "buddhiravyaktameva ca," since consciousness (*saṃvit*) is denoted by the word "intellect" (*buddhi*) as part of the field (*kṣetra*), it would follow that consciousness itself is the field.

Nor should it be said that while the word *buddhi* has multiple meanings, the word *ahaṅkāra* does not have as its referent something other than the Self; for in such passages as "joined with deceit and *ahaṅkāra*," the term is used to denote the body, the notion of "I" regarding the body, and pride. Furthermore, since the lexicographical definition states "pride, self-conceit, and *ahaṅkāra*," there is no rule that it must exclusively denote the referent of "I. Thus, the word *aham*, which denotes the Self, is established by the word *asmad* (the base of the personal pronoun), whereas the word *ahaṅkāra* denotes that which is not the Self.

If it is argued that the word *aham* is a synonym for that [Self] and is an indeclinable ending in *m*, we say no; for it is improper to postulate a difference in meaning based merely on the distinction between ending in *m* or *d*. All of these words have as their object only the *ahaṅkāra* (the principle of ego), since they are observed to be used as synonyms. As for its usage with respect to a Self distinct from the *ahaṅkāra*, that occurs through secondary figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*), because the observation of the word *aham*—when not determined by whether it ends in *m* or *d*—being used for the *ahaṅkāra* serves as the restrictive rule. As it is said: "For Aniruddha, the Great Self, higher than the highest, is indeed among the worlds."

"He who, having attained manifestation, created the Grandfather (Pitāmaha)—he is called Ahaṅkāra, for he consists of all splendor. In this passage, the word *ahaṅkāra* refers to the Self (*ātman*) by way of metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*). As for the claim that the perception of the attributes of both Self and non-Self in the referent of "I" (*ahamartha*) is unestablished—on the grounds that agency and so forth are attributes of the Self—we shall explain there how agency and the like are not attributes of the Self.

Now, one might object: "Even if agency and so forth are not properties of the Self (*anātmadharma*), and even if their substratum does not appear [as such], let agency and the like nevertheless appear in the Self, just as in the cognition 'I am fair,' the fairness residing in the body appears [in the Self]. This is not so, because the example is unestablished; for even in that case, although it does not appear as the body, its cognition occurs through its being fair, human, and so forth.

And the inference is as follows: the referent of "I" (ahamartha) is non-self, because it is the object of the cognition "I," like the body. Nor is there a deviation [of the reason] with respect to the consciousness that serves as the substratum included within the referent of "I," since even that [consciousness], insofar as it is the object of that cognition, is non-self in that form; for while it is not the object of the cognition "I" in its own essential nature (svarūpa), there is no deviation [in the reason]. Furthermore: the referent of "I" is other than the Self, because it is denotable by the word "I," like that which is denotable by the word "ego-sense" (ahaṃkāra).

Nor is there a lack of proof here, since the state of being synonymous has already been demonstrated. Nor should it be argued: "Even by you, it has been stated that the 'I' (the *ahamartha*) is the locus for the superimposition of the non-self in such expressions as 'I am fair'; that it is the object of supreme love through such [desires] as 'May I not cease to be, may I exist'; and that the self is self-luminous because its own existence is never dissociated from manifestation. All of this would be untenable if the 'I'-referent were not the self. This objection cannot be maintained, because we have stated that it is the locus in the sense of being the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) of the locus, just like the "this" (*idam*) in the case of an illusion.

The status of being the object of supreme love belongs to the "I-sense" (ahamartha) due to the superimposition of identity with the Self (ātman). Nor is there a circularity in this, because the difference [between the "I-sense" and the Self] is established through the contrast between their manifestation and non-manifestation during the state of deep sleep (suṣupti). Furthermore, it is not the case that no love other than the love for the "I-sense" is experienced, since there exists the experience of such love during deep sleep as established by subsequent recollection (parāmarśa).

Nor should it be argued that even when love is observed to arise through the perception of the beneficial in what is actually harmful, one does not observe the superimposition of the status of being an object of valid cognition (*pramāspadatā*) upon that which is not an object of valid cognition (*apremāspada*). We reply: we maintain that the status of being an object of love in the referent "I" (*ahamartha*) is based on the superimposition of identity with the Self (*ātman*), and is not intrinsic; we do not, however, claim it is a superimposition of the status of being an object of love itself.
