Furthermore, even though there is a difference between the referent "I" and the Self, the fact that the manifestation of the referent "I" is never absent cannot be accounted for without its connection to the self-luminous Self; thus, this too serves as a proof for that [identity], and there is not even a trace of irrationality here.
Nor is it the case that the locus must possess the form of the superimposed object.
But by means of the form of the object, that which is superimposed is not itself possessed of form.

It should not be argued that, according to the statement of Vācaspati, there would result the cognition of the very quality of being a non-object of love residing in the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) as belonging to the Self; for, is it being proposed that a property residing in the substrate (adhiṣṭhāna) fails to appear in the superimposed object (āropya), or that a property residing in the superimposed object appears in the substrate? It is not the first case, because there is no such rule in the present instance: namely, that when a substrate is known as possessing a certain property, the superimposed object ceases [to be perceived], and therefore that property necessarily fails to appear in the superimposed object. This is not the case here.

Not the second [alternative], because there is no contradiction in the case at hand even if that which belongs to the superimposed (āropya) appears in the substrate (adhiṣṭhāna), provided it does not contradict the properties residing in the substrate. Since the status of being an object of love is possible at the very time of the superimposition of identity with the Self, the absence of the status of being an object of love is not perceived in the superimposed object either; how then could its perception occur in the objective field? Just as, at the very time of the superimposition of silver upon "this" (idaṃ), the non-this-ness (anidantva) of the silver is not perceived.

As for what is refuted by some—namely, that the cognition "I experience pleasure" and the like occurs precisely as a distinction between the Self, whose nature is the experience of pleasure, and the referent of "I"—that is not so, because the experience of sensory pleasure is distinct from the Self. Nor should it be argued: "In liberation, since the referent of 'I' is absent, liberation would result in the destruction of the Self, which would lead to the fallacy of the materialist (Bāhya) view; for in your own view as well, the referent of 'I,' which is the object of love, is destroyed, while in their view, something else—a void—is not destroyed. This is not to be said.

If, through the destruction of the object of love that is conditioned by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), one were to fall into the position of the external (non-Buddhist) systems, then this would also follow upon the destruction of the body. Even if, to this extent, the referent "I" (*ahamartha*) is not connected with liberation, the scriptural passages such as "Make me immortal" (*mām amṛtaṃ kṛdhi*) and "May I become light, stainless, and free from evil" (*jyotir ahaṃ virajā vipāpmā bhūyāsam*) likewise take as their object immortality residing in consciousness itself; just as the desire "May I be nourished" refers to the nourishment occurring in the body existing at that very time.

Nor should it be argued that liberation would result in something undesirable because no desire for the liberation of the Self alone is observed—unlike the desire for the nourishment of the body alone, expressed as "May the body be nourished. For, although at the time of the desire there is a superimposition of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) [upon the Self], such that the desire for liberation does not pertain to the Self alone, nevertheless, by means of the intended discrimination (*vivakṣita-viveka*), the desire for the liberation of the qualified entity (the Self as associated with the adjuncts) results in having the liberation of the substrate alone as its object; thus, its desirability is established.

Nor can it be argued that if the "I-sense" (*ahamartha*) were merely a knot of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), the cognition "my mind" would be impossible; for since the ego (*ahaṅkāra*) is a knot of consciousness and the unconscious, while the internal organ is the unconscious alone, the use of the genitive case (expressing distinction) is justified. Furthermore, one should not object: "In that case, the experienced difference between the cognition 'I' and cognitions such as 'the mind manifests' or 'the mind exists' would not occur, because there is no distinction in their being objects of the conjunction of consciousness and the unconscious. This is not a valid objection, because "conjunction" (*saṃvalana*) does not mean mere relation, but rather manifestation through identity (*tādātmya*).
And since that [identity] is absent in those other cases, there is a distinction.

Now, an objection is raised: "Is it not the case that every error has a twofold object, since otherwise one would fall into the error of having no substratum at all? Furthermore, the twofold nature of the cognition 'I' is not experienced. If you postulate it, then one might as well postulate a twofold nature for the cognition of the Self. If this is said, we reply: No. What is this "having a twofold object"? If it means "having both a substratum and a superimposed object," then we grant your point; for the falsity of the referent "I" (ahamartha) itself serves as the proof for its being the second part of the object.

Regarding the [notion] "Self," however, there is no such means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) for its having a dual-aspected object, by which it might be so postulated. Nor does having a dual-aspected object mean having as its object a superimposed thing qualified by distinct and distinct modes; for this would lead to a fallacy (vyabhicāra) in the cognition "this is silver," which is based on the superimposition of the relation of "silverness."

For even in the case of silverness (*rajatatva*), no qualifier (*prakāra*) appears therein, because there is no evidence for postulating that silver and so forth function as qualifiers there; such a postulation is unnecessary, and if one were to so postulate it, it would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) and lack of logical necessity (*aprayojakatva*). Alternatively, here too, the two-fold nature (*dvy-aṃśatā*) certainly shines forth in the forms "I shine" and "I am," just as it does in "silver shines" and "silver exists."

However, this is the distinction: there, the substrate is the manifestation delimited by "this-ness," and thus the cognition is "this is silver"; here, however, the substrate is manifestation alone, and thus the cognition is simply "I am manifesting. Nor is it improper for the error itself to be the substrate because it is superimposed; you are mistaken, for we speak of consciousness (*caitanya*) as the manifestation, not of the mental modification (*vṛtti*) of ignorance and so forth. And thus, perception is not a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for the "I-sense" being the Self.

Nor is there inference [to prove this]. For instance: "The referent 'I' (ahamartha) is connected with liberation, because it is the locus of the activity that accomplishes it, like [the consensus]. In this case, regarding the specific pervasion (*viśeṣavyāpti*), there is an absence of an example; for nowhere is it accepted that the locus of an activity is connected with liberation. Furthermore, regarding general pervasion (*sāmānyavyāpti*), there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) because the priest (*ṛtvij*), who is the locus of the activity that accomplishes heaven, is not himself connected with heaven.

In the argument "The referent of 'I' (ahamartha) is the locus of the cessation of misfortune, because it is the locus of misfortune, like the [self] admitted by both parties," there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) with respect to the body. Nor is the property of being the locus of misfortune unestablished (*asiddha*) in that case; for just as "I am ignorant" is a cognition regarding the "I," so too "I, who am fat, am ignorant" is a cognition regarding the body. Otherwise, the fallacy of the unestablished reason would follow. Furthermore, in the argument "Non-selfhood (*anātmatva*) does not reside in the referent of 'I,' because it resides only in non-selves, like pot-ness (*ghaṭatva*)," the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) is "not residing in the locus of purposeful action (*kṛti*)."

Nor is it [the case that the "I" is the individual soul], because in such passages as, "When which [element] has departed shall I depart? Or when established in which shall I be established? He created the vital breath (prāṇa); 'Come now, let me enter these three deities,'" the state of being "I" is mentioned prior to the creation of the vital breath and the mind within the cause of the universe; and because in the passage, "Then he knew only himself: 'I am Brahman,'" the state of being "I" is attributed to the pure Self through this definitive realization; and because the mention of the term "I" refers to the faultless Brahman, as stated: "He who is to be known as 'I' alone is celebrated as the individual soul (jīva)."

"He is the one who suffers and he is the one who rejoices; he alone is the vessel for bondage and liberation"—since such passages state the connection [of the self] with liberation, these scriptural texts are authoritative. This is because the word *aham* (I), which denotes a qualified entity, is employed through secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) to refer to the pure consciousness that is stripped of the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*). The logical inconsistency that serves as the seed for this secondary signification has already been stated. By this, Smṛti passages such as "Those who take refuge in Me alone" are also explained.

For this very reason, even in cases such as "That which I am, He is," one must resort to secondary signification, since it is necessary to apply secondary signification to the substratum (*viśeṣya*) of that which was established as denoting a qualified entity.
Thus ends the demonstration that the referent of "I" is not the Self in the Advaitasiddhi.

Now, one might object: "If agency were a property of the non-Self (anātmadharma), how could it appear in the Self? Nor can it be argued that agency—residing in the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa)—is superimposed upon the Self, as the redness of a hibiscus flower is superimposed upon a crystal, and is not real, because that would contradict the scriptural texts on the changelessness [of the Self], and because we observe the absence of agency when the intellect is absent during deep sleep. This should not be said; for if that were so, there would occasionally be a perceptual cognition that "the mind is the agent," just as one says "the flower is red," whereas [the cognition] "the crystal is red" [is merely an illusion].

If it is argued that there would be the delusion that consciousness (caitanya) is the agent, we say no; for there is no such perception because the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), qualified by agency, is superimposed (adhyāsa) as being identical with consciousness, whereas in the case of a flower, there is no superimposition as being identical with a crystal—thus there is a difference between the two cases.

Nor should it be argued that—since there is no superimposition of the intellect (buddhi) endowed with agency and other attributes upon the conscious self (cidātman) without an adjunct (upādhi), such as the un-superimposed hibiscus flower which stands in place of the locus (adhiṣṭhāna)—there would be no "conditioned" (sopādhika) nature [of the illusion], because no second quality of frightfulness is superimposed upon the rope [when it is mistaken for a snake] as there is no second agency superimposed upon the self. For, in fact, it is precisely a second agency that is superimposed upon the self.

In that case, there would not be a distinct perception of the two types of agency, because of the superimposition of identity between the Self and the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). This [superimposition] is not a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), as in the case of a rope-snake and the like, where another snake of higher reality might exist in relation to the snake qualified by cruelty and other attributes being superimposed; therefore, it is without a limiting adjunct (*nirupādhika*). However, here, since there exists no other entity of higher reality qualified by attributes such as agency in relation to the internal organ being superimposed, the internal organ itself is the limiting adjunct; thus, there is no inconsistency in its being "with a limiting adjunct" (*sopādhika*).

Nor should it be argued that even so, the mind is not non-manifesting (asphuraṇa), but rather manifesting (sphurat); for if there were a cognition of their difference at that time, there would arise—just as in the cases of "the flower is red" and "the crystal is red"—the respective cognitions "the mind is the agent" and "consciousness is the agent. This is not to be said, because it is precisely the apprehension of a difference that is opposed to the superimposition of identity which serves as the cause of that [cognition], and in the present case, such an apprehension of difference is absent.

As for the claim that even at a time when non-difference is grasped, there might arise the cognition "the mind is the agent" and "consciousness is the agent"—just as one might have the cognitions "this snake is terrifying" and "I am fair-skinned, the body is fair-skinned"—that is not so; for since the very apprehension of identity acts as an obstacle, the cited example itself is inadmissible.

Furthermore, as for the objection that—having proposed two positions regarding the nature of being "conditioned" (*sopādhikatva*)—either (1) that the condition (*upādhi*) or its property must possess the same level of reality (*samasattākatva*) as the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*), or (2) that both must possess a higher level of reality than the object superimposed—and then asserting that neither of these two is possible in the present case—that is a criticism of what was not stated. For in the case of being "conditioned," the essential factor is simply the absence of any other locus for the property that possesses a higher level of reality than the [superimposed] object, which is perceived as following the presence and absence (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of that [condition].

Nor would the cognition of the properties of milk—based on the superimposition of the identity [of water] with water mixed with milk—be "conditioned" (sopādhika) in this way; for if that were conditioned, it would be an accepted consequence (iṣṭāpatti). Now, one might ask: is the agency residing in the intellect superimposed upon the referent of "I," or is that which resides in the referent of "I" superimposed upon the Self?

If [the self] were the first [of the two types], then even though an undesirable thing (anartha) is superimposed upon it, since that [undesirable thing] would not reside in the self, it would follow that the self could not be the locus of bondage and liberation. If [it were] the second, then since the cognition "I am the agent" could be accounted for even without superimposition, what is the use of superimposition? [Reply: This is not so; for the ego (ahaṅkāra) has two parts by virtue of being a knot between consciousness (cit) and the non-conscious (acit). Among these, although agency exists in the non-conscious part—the intellect (buddhi)—the cognition "I am the agent" is impossible without the superimposition of identity with consciousness upon that intellect as qualified by that [agency]; therefore, superimposition is necessary.
By this, the objection—that if even superimposed agency were absent, the self would lack the status of being the locus of bondage and liberation—is refuted.

Nor is there any contradiction with the section [Brahma Sūtra 2.3.33], "The agent [is the self], because the scriptures have purpose," where you yourself, having raised the Sāṅkhya position that agency belongs to the intellect (*buddhi*), established as the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) that it belongs to the living self (*jīva*) alone.

Nor should it be argued that "the state of being grounded in the individual soul (jīva) is not based on non-discrimination (aviveka), because non-discrimination exists even in the Sāṅkhya system"; for [the text] first establishes the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that agency belongs to the intellect (*buddhi*) while the capacity for enjoyment (*bhoktṛtva*) belongs to consciousness (*caitanya*), and then states that since there is a rule of co-occurrence (*aikādhikaraṇya*) between agency and the capacity for enjoyment, agency must be accepted just as the capacity for enjoyment is. It does not, however, mean that the intellect is non-agential or that agency is the soul's inherent nature.

And because, in the subsequent section (*uttarādhikaraṇa*) beginning with "Just as the carpenter in both ways" (*yathā ca takṣobhayathā*), the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that the self's agency mentioned in the preceding section is inherent was refuted by establishing that it is merely adventitious (*aupādhika*); therefore, there is no contradiction with that section.

As for the objection: "If the intellect (*buddhi*) is the agent, how can it also be the instrument?"—that too is untenable, because elsewhere it is established that the very same intellect, while being the agent, can also function as the instrument with respect to perception. Nor should it be argued: "Since bondage, which consists of evils such as agency, resides in the intellect, liberation would likewise follow as being connected to it, because there is a rule that evil and its cessation must reside in the same substrate. This is not to be said, because agency and the like are evils only insofar as they reside in the conscious self (*cetana*); thus, the intellect is not the locus of these evils.

Nor does it follow that if suffering (anartha) residing in consciousness implies that consciousness itself must be included within the category of suffering; for according to all schools of thought, the self would likewise have to be abandoned simply because suffering is to be abandoned on account of its connection with the self. Since suffering is not characterized as such by virtue of being superimposed [upon the self], there is no circular reasoning.

Nor should it be argued that the pure Self is never perceived as the locus of misfortune (anartha), because at the time of error one perceives "I am the enjoyer," while at the time of valid cognition one perceives "the intellect is the enjoyer"; for even though the pure Self is not the locus of such misfortunes as being an enjoyer, since there is no natural difference between the conditioned (upahita) Self and the pure Self, the co-location (sāmānādhikaraṇya) of bondage and liberation is logically established.

By this [argument], the following objection is refuted: "Since the intellect (*buddhi*) is the agent of hearing and so forth, liberation (*mokṣa*)—which is its fruit—must also belong to that [intellect] alone; for according to the maxim 'the fruit of the scripture belongs to the performer,' otherwise there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). This is refuted because of the counter-examples of the *jāteṣṭi* and the *pitṛyajña*. Nor is it the case that having a purified son or having a father who attains heaven is a fruit residing solely in the agent, for those are not heard of as being the fruit [of the rites].

Nor should it be said that such "sonship" is a connection with the fruit, but not the fruit itself; for if this were so, then by means of conjunction-inherence (*saṃyuktasamavāya*) and other relations, that fruit would belong to someone other than the father as well, since there is no difference in their lack of scriptural basis (*aśāstrīyatva*).

Nor should it be argued that—just as the purity and other benefits pertaining to the son for the sake of the father are the fruit for the father who performs the rite because he intended it for him—here, too, the Self is not for the sake of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), such that liberation residing in the Self would be what is intended by it. For although the Self is indeed not for the sake of the internal organ, since it resides within the "I-sense" (ahamartha), nevertheless, because experience shows that the fruit must be intended, and because the "I-sense" consists of both the Self and the non-Self, the status of being intended does not fail to apply even to the fruit residing in the Self.

Alternatively—agency common to both the superimposed and the non-superimposed is itself the determinant for the experience of the fruit, and that [agency] certainly exists in the self. Nor does it follow that the body would also experience the fruit by virtue of having superimposed agency, because since [the body's agency] is non-existent until the fruit is reached, it is impossible for it to experience the fruit. For we do not state a rule that the agent must necessarily experience the fruit; rather, we state a rule that the experiencer of the fruit must necessarily be the agent, because [otherwise] there would be deviation in the case of one who performs an action whose fruit has not yet been produced, and because [the former rule] would lack causal efficacy.

Now, it may be objected: agency does not belong to the mind, because its being the object of action and its being an instrument—both of which are contradictory to [agency]—are established by scripture and other authorities, and because agency is heard of even in the absence of the intellect (buddhi).

For instance: in passages such as "He made that mind," the mind is the object of the act of creation (*kṛti*); in Vedic texts such as "The wise, hearing with the ear, [perceiving] with the mind," and in Smṛti texts such as "Whatever action a person undertakes with body, speech, and mind," the mind is an instrument (*karaṇa*); and in Vedic texts such as "When the mind departs, he remains as if blinking, eating and drinking," the self (*ātman*) is the agent even during the departure of the mind. Likewise, [it is said]: "Having reached the supreme light, he emerges in his own true form; he moves about there."

If it is argued that even in supreme liberation, which consists in the manifestation of one's true nature—as seen in passages such as "eating, playing, and rejoicing"—there is agency, because of scriptural texts like "The agent is the knowing self who knows 'let me smell this,' he is the Self" and "The wise one is the enjoyer of bliss," and thus the intellect (*buddhi*) is not the agent; we say no. For although there is a contradiction regarding the mind being the agent of its own actions—given the scriptural text "Consciousness performs the sacrifice"—nevertheless, in that context, with respect to perception, [the mind] is the object of the Lord's action.

And because there is no contradiction in [the Lord] being an instrument, since it is possible for Him to possess an activity (kṛti) of that nature, just as He possesses knowledge and desire in the form of a modification of ignorance (avidyāvṛtti).

Nor should it be argued that the word "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) refers to Brahman on the basis of the supplementary passage: "If one knows consciousness as Brahman, and if one does not become negligent because of that, having cast off all evils from the body, one enjoys all desires. This is because it is certain that the "consciousness" presented here as the agent is something other than the pure Brahman—the object of knowledge for those seeking liberation—mentioned in the supplementary passage, since the latter cannot possibly be the performer of a sacrifice; furthermore, this case shares the same logical status as the passage, "One meditates on food as Brahman."

This being the case, it is because of such Smṛti passages as, "He who, due to an unrefined intellect, perceives the Self alone as the agent does not see," and "Actions are performed by Prakṛti," and so forth; nor do these two [passages] intend to teach that agency is denied to the Self independently, for there is no sublation to a general denial. For this very reason, the word "as it were" (iva) is used in passages such as, "It meditates, as it were; it moves, as it were."

Nor can it be said that the word "eva" (only) in the phrase "as if he were the lord" does not signify mere dependence regarding the soul's agency—as it does in the case of [the phrase] "as if the lord"—because here there is no such sublation [of the literal sense]. Furthermore, it should not be argued that the intellect's agency is impossible because scripture declares the Self to be the agent even in the absence of the intellect.

Whether the intellect (*buddhi*) is the agent or merely the producer [of action], in either case, since it is intended to reside in the living self (*jīva*), it must depend upon the volition (*kṛti*) attributed to that self; thus, in the absence of such volition, even in your own view, the term denoting agency would have only a figurative meaning. Furthermore, this contradicts scriptural passages that teach the self's qualitylessness (*nirdharmakatva*), changelessness (*nirvikāratva*), and actionlessness (*niṣkriyatva*).

Nor should it be argued that the scriptural declaration of "being devoid of attributes" (*nirdharmakatva*) does not intend its literal meaning, because there would be a contradiction between the existence and non-existence of the attribute consisting in the absence of attributes; and because, just as in the case of "knowing-ness" (*jñānatva*) and "witness-ship" (*sākṣitva*), knowing-ship (*jñātṛtva*)—whether real or unreal—is possible only in the Self. This is not to be said, because the absence of attributes, being of the nature of the non-existence of attributes, is not distinct from the very essence of Brahman, and thus lacks the status of being an attribute itself; consequently, no contradiction arises.

As for the statement that the status of being a knower—whether real or unreal—is possible even in the Self, that is indeed accepted; for we do not deny agency in the Self even when it is superimposed.

Nor should it be argued that "changelessness" (nirvikāratva) refers to the absence of transformation into the form of another substance (*dravyāntara*), rather than the absence of specific modes (*viśeṣākāra*), and that this is not contradictory even if the Self possesses agency and other such qualities; for even though this statement prohibits transformation into the form of another substance, it—following the scriptural texts on the Self being devoid of attributes (*nirdharmaka*)—is intended only to prohibit specific modes, since the prohibition of specific instances follows necessarily from the prohibition of the general category.

Nor should it be argued: "If [the Self] is inactive, what is this 'activity'? Is it physical motion (*parispanda*), or the meaning of a verbal root (*dhātvartha*)? In the first case, it is an admitted consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*). In the second case, [the reason is] unestablished (*asiddhi*), because existence (*sattā*) and so forth—in the form of the meaning of roots such as *as* (to be)—exist even in the Self. This is not to be said, because Brahman alone is of the nature of Being (*sad-rūpa*), and thus even existence and the like are absent from it; furthermore, the word "activity" (*kriyā*) here refers to volitional effort (*kṛti*). For this very reason, in deep sleep (*suṣupti*), when the mind is absent, agency and other such qualities are not observed.

Nor should it be argued that even then the state of being the agent of breathing and so forth is indeed observed, because the Śruti states, "In deep sleep, one breathes out 'bhūḥ, bhūḥ'"; for by such Śruti passages as "There is not a second," there is an absence of even breathing with respect to him (the Self), making agency all the more impossible. Alternatively, since the internal organ, which consists of the vital breath (prāṇa), exists even then due to the predominance of the power of action (kriyā-śakti), agency conditioned by that [organ] exists even then; thus, the Śruti passage has another purpose.

Furthermore, perception has as its object breath and so forth, which are constructed by the ignorance of the seer; and this is established only within the doctrine of *dṛṣṭisṛṣṭi* (creation upon seeing). The scriptural passage beginning with "Desire, resolve... and ending with "...shame, intelligence, fear—all this is indeed the mind" is also intended to show that the mind is the agent (*kartṛ*), and not merely that it is the instrumental cause (*nimitta*).

Nor should it be argued that the mind possesses the status of an instrument (karaṇa) based on such scriptural passages as "In the beginning, one wills with the mind," or "The wise say that the Self, when joined with the senses and the mind, is the enjoyer"; for since nothing other than the mind can be the locus of volition (saṃkalpa), the scripture stating "with the mind" must be understood in a figurative sense.

Nor should it be argued that the self’s status as an agent is established by such inferences as: (1) "The self possesses effort directed toward the means of liberation, because it is connected with the fruit thereof, like [a person] commonly agreed upon"; (2) "Ignorance has the same locus as knowledge, because it is removable by knowledge, like the prior non-existence of knowledge"; and (3) "The experience of suffering and so forth has the same locus as liberation, because it is bondage, like [what is] commonly agreed upon. This is because, regarding the first inference, is the probandum (*sādhya*) "possession of effort" in general—whether superimposed or non-superimposed—or is it "possession of non-superimposed effort"? In the first case, it is an admission of what is already accepted (*iṣṭāpatti*).

In the second [inference], there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) with respect to that which is connected to the fruits produced by the *jāteṣṭi* and *pitṛyajña* sacrifices. Regarding the second inference as well, does [the reason] consist in residing in the locus of a cognition that is common to both superimposed and non-superimposed [objects], or in residing in the locus of a non-superimposed cognition? In the first case here, it would be an admission of the desired conclusion (*iṣṭāpatti*). In the second case, "being distinct from beginningless positive entities" (*anādibhāvabhinnatva*) constitutes a limiting condition (*upādhi*). In the third inference, if there is co-occurrence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with liberation (*mokṣa*) through a relation common to both superimposed and non-superimposed [objects], it is an admission of the desired conclusion.

If there were co-referentiality through a relation that has not been superimposed, the probandum would be unestablished; therefore, it is proven that the agency of the mind is superimposed upon the self.
Thus ends the demonstration of the superimposition of agency in the Advaitasiddhi.

Now, an objection might be raised: "If the referent of 'I' (ahamartha) were not the Self, then the perception 'I am a Brahmin, I am one-eyed,' etc., could not serve as a proof for the superimposition of identity between the Self and the body, senses, and so forth; for in that cognition of identity, the Self would not be its object. This is not so. Since the notion of "I" has two parts, just as there is a superimposition of identity with the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) qualified by agency and other attributes within the conscious part (cidaṃśa), it is possible for the cognition of identity with the body, senses, and so forth—qualified by Brahminhood, being one-eyed, and the like—to have the Self as its object through the superimposition of identity.

Thus, the superimposition of identity between the self and the body, senses, and so forth, is indeed logical. Nor does it follow that, because the identity of the body and the self is thus perceived, inference and scripture contradicting it would lose their authority—just as in the case of inferring the coldness of fire, or the scriptural statement "The sacrificer is the sacrificial grass-bundle" regarding its literal meaning.

And thus, it should not be argued that the distinction between the body and the self would remain unestablished; for, by means of examples such as the inference and scripture contradicting the perception of the moon's size, the validity of examined scripture and inference—which contradict perception—has been established, and therefore the establishment of their distinction remains possible even so.

Nor should it be argued that there can be no simultaneous superimposition of identity upon the body, senses, and so forth—which are ascertained to be mutually distinct—just as there is no simultaneous superimposition of identity between silver and a conch-shell, both of which are ascertained to be distinct; for although the superimposition of identity such as "I am the body" or "I am the sense-organ" is impossible due to the cognition of difference in the form "the sense-organ is other than the body" and "the body is other than the sense-organ," yet [such superimposition does occur] because of the absence of a cognition of difference in the form "the blind man is other than the Brahmin" and "the Brahmin is other than the blind man."

"I am a Brahmin" and "I am one-eyed"—in such cases, the superimposition of identity is possible because only a cognition of difference possessing the same mode (*samānaprakāraka*) acts as its sublator.

Now, an objection may be raised: for you, who maintain that even mere difference is superimposed, the difference between the body and the self is likewise superimposed; therefore, like the non-difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman, that [non-difference between body and self] would have to be real (*tāttvika*). For falsity (*mithyātva*) consists in being the counter-correlative of an absolute non-existence that is not sublated by the knowledge of the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna-jñāna*). This is impossible even if there exists the counter-correlativity of an absolute non-existence that *is* sublated by such knowledge.

And since non-difference (*abheda*) is the absolute absence of difference (*bhedātyantābhāva*), how could it be that non-difference is not real when difference is false? Nor should it be argued that—because the body is also superimposed—the self has neither difference nor non-difference with respect to it; for we observe a difference between the shell and the silver (which is superimposed) that is not sublated by the knowledge of the shell itself. To this we say: no, even if difference is false, non-difference is not ultimately real, because it has already been established that both existence and non-existence are equally false.

However, this is the distinction: here, non-difference is sublated by inference and other means whose status as valid cognition has been examined at the time of empirical usage; but difference between the body and the self is not sublated by those [means], but rather by the final cognitive state (*caramavṛtti*). Nor should it be argued that, in this case, there would not be the cognition "I am the possessor of a body" (*dehī*)—as there is in the case of "the owner of a house"—but rather the cognition "I am the body" (*deho 'ham*); for both cognitions, "I am a Brāhmaṇa" and "I am the possessor of a body," are possible because the difference is grasped through the property of being a body, while the difference is not grasped through properties such as being a Brāhmaṇa.

Even when there is a cognition of difference, such as "Yajñadatta is other than Devadatta," one observes the error of non-difference (*abhedabhrama*) in the form "this is he" regarding Yajñadatta with respect to Devadatta presented as the true reality (*tattvena*).

Now, an objection: How can [cognitions] such as "I am a Brāhmaṇa" or "I am a human" be of the nature of superimposition (*adhyāsa*), given that since humanity, Brāhmaṇahood, and so forth reside in the self as qualified by the body, it is possible for them to be valid cognitions (*pramātva*)? As it has been said:
"For us, [cognitions] such as 'I am a Brāhmaṇa' or 'I am a human' are indeed valid."
For it is associated with the distinction of bodies, as expressed by such terms as "Brāhmaṇa" and so forth.

If it is argued thus, we say no; for if humanity (*manuṣyatva*) and so forth were to reside in the self as qualified by the body, they would not be perceivable by the eyes and other senses, because the self as qualified by the body is not accessible to the eyes. Nor should it be said that "the universal residing in the qualified [substratum] is grasped by the eye because one part [of that substratum] is accessible to the eye," because the rule is that only when both [relata of a relation] are fit [for perception] is there fitness [for the perception of the relation itself], which is a relation of collective occurrence (*vyāsajyavṛtti*). Otherwise, there would be perceptibility even for things such as duality of conjunction, which resides in both sensory and non-sensory [entities].

Because subsistence by way of distribution (vyāsajyavṛttitva) has never been observed in a genus (jāti), there would be the consequence of confusion (saṅkara) with earth-ness (pṛthivītva) and other such properties; furthermore, according to your own view, since the self is atomic, if [the genus] were to reside in it, it would follow that it is beyond the senses (atīndriya). Nor does this lead to the undesirable consequence of such cognitions as "the body is a Brāhmaṇa" or "the body is a human," because the very defect that generates the error of co-referentiality with "I-ness" (ahaṃtva) acts as the obstacle to such a cognition.

Because there is no other possible recourse when the [notion of "I"] resides in the body due to the aforementioned subverting arguments, and because in cases such as "I am thin" or "I am fat," the superimposition of identity with that which is qualified by thinness and so forth is necessary. Nor can it be argued that this is a figurative usage (aupacārika), like saying "I am thin" when one's son is thin; for it has been said:

"In instances such as 'I am thin' or 'I am dark,' the thinness and so forth residing in the body are metaphorically attributed to the Self, just like the thinness residing in a son or similar relative."

This must be stated: for if this were so, the Vedic scripture stating, "It is indeed as 'it exists' that He is to be perceived," which establishes the existence of a self distinct from the body and so forth, would become a mere restatement (anuvāda); furthermore, there would be no decisive criterion to distinguish between the non-figurative sense of "my body" and the figurative sense of "I am fair-complexioned," and so on.

Now, one might object: this is the decisive argument—namely, that for an animal or similar being immediately after birth, the cause of its activity and so forth is the inference of "being a means to a desired end" (iṣṭasādhanatā) based on the drinking of mother's milk. This inference is supported by the recollection of a pervasion such as, "the drinking of mother's milk in a previous body was a means to a desired end. However, such a recollection of pervasion is not possible if there is no recollection of another body. Nor can the cognition of identity—"I had another body in the past"—possibly arise in one who does not remember [that other body].

But [one might argue]: "For one who perceives the Self as permeating many bodies, like a thread running through many gems, there is here a cognition of difference arising from itself"—if this is said, we reply: no; for even without the memory of a previous body, the memory of the pervasion (vyāpti) which is the cause of inference is possible. Indeed, unlike the initial experience of pervasion, at the time of remembering the pervasion there is no requirement for the knowledge of an instance (dṛṣṭānta), such that for that purpose the memory of that [previous] body would have to be required.

Nor should it be argued: "Even so, how could one who—preceded by the cognition of the difference between bodies—synthesizes one's own identity, thinking 'I who experienced my parents in childhood am the same I who experience my grandchildren in old age,' or 'I who was a tiger in a dream am now this human body,' not know the difference [between those states]? For even if a cognition of difference arises from the cognition of a mark (liṅga) consisting of contradictory attributes, there is no contradiction with respect to an immediate (aparokṣa) delusion of non-difference.

Nor should it be argued: "In the case of a perceptible subject (*dharmin*), the perception of a differentiator is pervaded by the perception of difference; however, here, since the persistence (*anuvṛttatva*)—which is the differentiator from the body and so forth residing in the intellect as excluded entities—is established by the perception of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) in the Self, and since it is only the perception of the differentiator that opposes the immediate error of unity, and because it cannot be said that [this perception] is not obstructed by the observation of specific qualities due to its being free from adventitious conditions (*nirupādhika*), how then can there be an error of unity? This is not to be said, because [the objection fails to account for] the perception of the differentiator...

This is because it is unestablished that there is a contradiction between the direct perception of difference and the superimposition of identity through pervasion; for in the case of "the crane is blue," even though the crane-ness—which differentiates it from the blue—is perceived, we observe the absence of a direct perception of difference from the blue and the presence of a direct perception of non-difference. Nor can it be argued that this occurs there due to the intensity of a defect (doṣa), while in the present case it does not occur due to the intensity of a defect—by whom was such a thing asserted to you?

In this way, even scriptural injunctions such as "A Brāhmaṇa should sacrifice" serve as the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding that [self], for they enjoin the self which has undergone the superimposition of identity with the body—the locus of Brāhmaṇahood—since that body, being insentient, cannot itself be enjoined. Nor can the status of being enjoined be established by assuming some other relation between the self and the body characterized by Brāhmaṇahood, because it is impossible to specify such a relation that does not over-extend to all bodies. To explain: first, it cannot be conjunction (*saṃyoga*), because since the self is omnipresent (*vibhu*), it is common to all bodies.

Nor is the relationship one of owner and owned, because that would apply equally to cattle and other such things. Nor is the relationship one of direct owner and owned, because it is impossible to predicate "directness" of the owner-and-owned relation as it exists in the body and so forth, which is distinct from the case of cattle and the like. Nor is it the state of following the will [of another], because that is absent in the case of a body paralyzed by rheumatism (āmavāta). Nor is it the state of being the locus of that person's sense organs; for does this mean being the locus of sense organs connected to that person, or being the locus of sense organs that generate cognition for that person? Not the first, because it leads to over-extension (atiprasaṅga).

The second alternative is not tenable: if the word "knowledge" (*jñāna*) refers to the consciousness of one's own nature (*svarūpa-caitanya*), it is impossible [for it to have a relationship with the body]; if it refers to a modification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa-vṛtti*), then superimposition (*adhyāsa*) is still necessary for the sake of establishing a connection even with that. Therefore, it is better to say that the body itself has a relationship based on superimposition. For this very reason, the following views are refuted: that the relationship consists in being the locus of action directly produced by effort, or being the substratum for its enjoyment, or being acquired through its karma; for the quality of being acquired through its karma is common to sons and other such things as well.

Nor should it be said that in those cases, ownership alone is produced by unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*), but not the son and so forth; for, since a son is not already established like a village or similar objects, his production is necessary even for the sake of producing ownership. Otherwise, one might as well claim that in the case of one's own body, pleasure, and so forth, unseen merit produces only ownership and not the body itself. Thus, the distinction is this: in the case of what was not previously produced, it is produced by unseen merit together with ownership; but in the case of what was previously produced, only ownership [is produced].

By this [it is meant]: Does the word *brāhmaṇa* found in the scripture refer, through metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*), to one who possesses the superimposition of identity with a particular body? Or does it refer to the relation with a particular body? Since no other relation is possible, that relation is indeed the superimposition of identity. Alternatively, does it refer to the particular body itself? [In this case,] the self proceeds [to action] because of the superimposition of identity with that [body].

Not the first, because figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) is inappropriate in a primary injunction; for if one accepts the superimposition (adhyāsa) that "I am myself impaired or complete" when one's son, friend, and so forth are impaired or complete, it would follow that a Śūdra who has a Brāhmaṇa friend would possess the qualification [for Vedic rites], while a Brāhmaṇa who has a Śūdra friend would lack the qualification. Nor the second, because other types of relations—such as being the locus of those [friend's] sense organs—are indeed possible.

"The third [alternative] is not tenable because, being insentient (*jaḍa*), it cannot be subject to an injunction"—this is refuted. The objection raised against the final position is a "criticism of what was not stated," since only the first and second positions were accepted as withstanding scrutiny. Furthermore, since figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is observed in injunctions such as "Mix the *matsara* with cows," and since superimposition (*adhyāsa*)—which is evidenced by universal experience, distinguished from [the case of] sons, friends, and so forth, and based on the non-recognition of ownership—is the motivating factor, it does not apply to the aforementioned instance.

There is no risk of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) or non-application (*aprasaṅga*). Since such a superimposition (*adhyāsa*), occurring only occasionally, is the very cause for the application of the term "Brāhmaṇa," it is logically consistent that injunctions such as "A Brāhmaṇa must not be killed" apply even to one who is in deep sleep (*suṣupta*). Likewise, they also apply to one who is liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*); for although there is an absence of superimposition based on the power of concealment (*āvaraṇa-śakti*) in such a person, superimposition based on the power of projection (*vikṣepa-śakti*) is still possible.

Nor does this imply that, if superimposition were always the cause [of eligibility], there would be the undesirable consequence of eligibility even for one who has lost his Brahminhood through a mortal sin (*mahāpātaka*); for in that case, it is the mortal sin itself that causes the lack of eligibility, not the absence of Brahminhood, since the very absence of that [Brahminhood] is non-existent—as evidenced by the common usage "the fallen Brāhmaṇa. Thus it is stated in the Bhāṣya: "All scriptures of injunctions and prohibitions have their root in superimposition."

The impossibility of [the self's] being a knower (*pramātṛtva*) and so forth otherwise than through superimposition (*adhyāsa*) is also a proof for superimposition. This refutes the objection: "Since superimposition is sometimes the motivator [of the notion of knowerhood], how can the superimposition of identity be the motivator there, given that knowerhood is observed even in deep sleep when superimposition is absent, and even at the time of perceiving objects like jars when [the superimposition of the Self as the body] is absent? As it is stated in the *Bhāṣya*: "Knowerhood and so forth have their root in superimposition. For this very reason, there is the popular assertion among the Cārvākas and others—who do not take into account powerful scripture or inference—that the body alone is the Self.

Otherwise, for one who maintains that perception alone is a valid means of knowledge (*pratyakṣa-prāmāṇyavādin*), such conventional usage would be untenable. Nor should it be argued that the Cārvāka and others, having developed a delusion of the identity of the body and the self through a fallacious inference (*anumānābhāsa*), merely have a conceit of it being perceptual; for once difference has been grasped by perception, it is impossible for a fallacious inference or the like to produce a cognition of non-difference. Thus, this delusion of identity is indeed perceptual. For this very reason, pointing to the body with a finger, one says, "This is I."

For this very reason, even the scriptural texts negating the identity of the body and the self become intelligible; otherwise, they would entail the fallacy of negating what has never been proposed. Nor can it be argued that such texts merely negate a view obtained from false doctrines (*kusamaya*), for there is no room for a false doctrine that contradicts direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Therefore, it is established that from the common experience of cowherds (*ābhīra*) such as "I am fair-complexioned," the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of the body and its attributes upon the self occurs through the superimposition of the unity of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) with the self.
Thus ends the demonstration of the superimposition of the identity of the body and the self in the *Advaitasiddhi*.

Now, even if ignorance (*avidyā*) and the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) based upon it are thus established, its indeterminability (*anirvacanīyatva*) is not yet proven, due to the absence of both a definition (*lakṣaṇa*) and a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). To explain: what is this indeterminability? It cannot be the absence of verbal expression, nor the absence of the knowledge that causes such expression, nor the absence of the object that causes such expression, nor the absence of the general category that causes such expression. In the first case, there is a contradiction with the very term "indeterminable" (*anirvācya*), as well as with the expression "this is silver" (*idaṃ rūpyam*).

In the second case, since the result in the form of verbal designation exists, it is impossible to speak of an absence of its cause. For this very reason, the third [alternative] is not tenable; furthermore, the object is not the cause for its verbal designation. Precisely because the result exists, the fourth is also not tenable. Nor is it the case that being distinct from the existent while being distinct from the non-existent [constitutes reality], for it could be explained even if it were of the nature of both existent and non-existent.

Therefore, it is not the case that the absence of non-existence follows from the absence of existence; thus, [if you argue] there is an impossibility of a definition—[we reply: no, for a faultless definition is possible, such as: "being distinct from the existent while being distinct from the non-existent, and being distinct from both the existent and the non-existent"; or "being incapable of withstanding inquiry in terms of existence and non-existence, while being incapable of withstanding inquiry in terms of both existence and non-existence"; or "being sublated within the locus in which it is apprehended," and so forth.

Nor should it be argued that there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) because even an existing entity is distinct from another existing entity; for the meaning of the term "distinctness from existence" (*sad-vailakṣaṇya*) is the difference delimited by existence (*sattvāvacchinna-bheda*), which is the cause of the cognition "it is not existent. Indeed, even though one existent is distinct from another existent, the cognition "it is not existent" does not arise; therefore, there is no *siddhasādhana*. Likewise, being devoid of existence while being devoid of non-existence, and being devoid of both existence and non-existence, is also well-established.

It might be argued as follows: Is existence (*sattva*) the universal "Being" (*sattājāti*), or the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*), or non-sublatability (*abādhyatva*), or being established by valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇikatva*), or non-emptiness (*aśūnyatva*), or being Brahman (*brahmatva*), or that which is accepted by the opponent (*parāṅgīkṛta*)? It cannot be the first or the second, because it would follow that there is a difference from "Being" in the pure Self, and an absence of difference from "Being" in the phenomenal world (*prapañca*).

The third [alternative] is not tenable; for in your own view, since even the void (*tuccha*) is non-sublatable, it is impossible for it to possess the distinction from the real (*sadvailakṣaṇya*), while the indeterminable (*anirvācya*)—being sublatable—cannot possess the distinction from the unreal (*asadvailakṣaṇya*). Nor is the fourth; for valid cognition (*pramā*) is a modification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇavṛtti*), and since its objecthood exists even in the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), it would follow that the distinction from the real would be absent there (i.e., the world would be real). Nor is the fifth; for since that [distinction] exists even in the phenomenal world, it would follow that the world lacks the distinction from it (i.e., the world would be indeterminable).

It is not the sixth [alternative], because it would entail the undesirable consequence that its distinctness from them exists in the world. It is not the seventh, because since existence as accepted by the opponent consists in the absence of non-existence, it is impossible to speak of its being distinct from both. For this very reason, the claim that the absence of these [existence and non-existence] consists in non-existence is refuted.

Now, is this non-existence (*asattva*) a state of being indefinable (*nirupākhyatva*), or is it a state of lacking intrinsic nature (*niḥsvarūpatva*)? It cannot be the first, because [the object] is already being manifested by terms such as "non-existent" (*asad*). Nor can it be the second, because if negation were applied to the intrinsic nature itself, then even things like "silver in a mother-of-pearl shell" would lack intrinsic nature, making it impossible for them to differ from the non-existent. If you say this is not so—because what is intended here are existence and non-existence as conceived by the opponent, and not the technical definitions [of the Advaitins], and therefore there is no unwanted consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*) in stating their difference from the non-existent and the existent respectively—nor [is there a problem] because those two are mutually contradictory.

It should not be argued that "the difference between two things in one locus is contradictory because the negation of one necessarily implies the affirmation of the other"; for there is no contradiction, as we accept that the conjunction of negations is non-real (*atāttvika*). Indeed, there is no opposition between mother-of-pearl and illusory silver. And if that is so, how can there be a statement regarding its difference from "Being" (*sat*) and so forth? [The answer is: it is merely to manifest the fact that each respective counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) is indefinable (*durnirūpa*). For when a thing is indefinable in its own nature, not even a single real form can possibly exist in it.

Now, [an objection may be raised]: even if the absence of *sattva* and so forth is not ultimately real (*atāttvika*), if indeterminability (*anirvācyatva*) consists merely in the fact that *sattva* and so forth are difficult to define, then in the case of the cessation of ignorance—which is of the fifth kind—the prohibition of indeterminability in the statement "nor is its destruction indeterminable" would be inappropriate. Furthermore, if the absence of *sattva* and so forth is as unreal as *sattva* itself, then since the proofs for *sattva* and so forth have been refuted, it would be improper to speak of their absence.

If it is argued that one must accept the non-reality (*atāttvikatva*) of the very combination of injunctions (*vidhi-samuccaya*) for the sake of non-contradiction—this is not so. In the view that the cessation of ignorance (*avidyā-nivṛtti*) is of a fifth kind, this "indefinability" (*anirvācyatva*) does not consist merely in being distinct from the three categories [of existence, non-existence, and both], but rather in being accompanied by the property of not persisting at the time of liberation. Thus, the negation of indefinability is appropriate in the case of the cessation of ignorance which persists until the time of liberation. However, regarding the absence of [the qualities of] existence and so forth, there is simply no statement of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) whose object is an uncontradicted reality; a mere mention of an indicator (*jñāpaka*) is uncommon (*asādhāraṇī*) with respect to that aspect.

Therefore, this [argument] is for the purpose of dispelling the disagreement among disputants. As for the consequence of an unreal conjunction of positive prescriptions (*vidhi*), that is indeed acceptable; for unreal existence and non-existence do not contradict one another even when there is a conjunction of negations (*niṣedha*). As for the objection that, under the view that the conjunction of positive prescriptions is unreal, there would be no distinction between error (*bhrānti*) and sublation (*bādha*), that is not so; because it is precisely due to their unreality that error and sublation do not exclude the negation of existence, and since existence itself is unreal, that [distinction] is possible.

Now, is the unreality of the collection of negations due to the unreality of both, or due to the unreality of each individually? Not the first, because the unreality of both is as contradictory as the reality of both, and because it would entail the reality of the collection of affirmations.

If it is argued that the second [position] is also untenable because it would entail the reality of each individual counter-positive—since only that which is the counter-positive of a real absolute non-existence is unreal—we say no; for precisely because both are unreal, their conjunction as a negation is also unreal. Nor is the unreality of both contradictory in one place, just as the reality of both is, since we observe the unreality of both "being a post" and "being a person" in a single location such as an anthill.

Nor is it contradictory for both [properties], which consist in mutual exclusion, to be unreal in the same locus, since we observe that both a jar and its prior non-existence can be unreal in the same place, such as a thread. Nor is this rule restricted solely to a counter-positive and its absolute non-existence, because there is no restrictive principle and we do not accept it. In reality, however, existence and non-existence do not consist in mutual exclusion, but merely in being pervaded by mutual exclusion.

Nor should it be said: "We have no objection to the statement regarding such a technical distinction between existence and non-existence. For existence (*sattva*) is defined as non-sublatability (*abādhyatva*), and non-existence (*asattva*) is the unfitness for being perceived as existent; and since this distinction between both is not accepted by you regarding the world, how can there be room for the concession that this is what you desire? And if this were indeed desired, how would there not be a destruction of your own tenet? Precisely for this reason, [the properties of] permanence and impermanence—consisting in the connection with an existence characterized by or not characterized by destruction—cannot apply to that which is devoid of existence.

They say that, as in the case of non-existence regarding universals (*sāmānya*) and so forth, eternity (*nityatva*) consists in the absence of a subsequent limit, while non-eternity (*anityatva*) consists in possessing the cessation of what is other than existence; the absence of both of these, like prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), is the absence of both existence and non-existence in certain false things such as silver. This is because, although the aforementioned existence and non-existence are mutually exclusive (*parasparavirahavyāpyatva*), they are not of the nature of mutual exclusion (*parasparavirahānātmakatva*), just like the aforementioned eternity and non-eternity.

Now, it was stated that this [definition] is the joint exclusion (*vyatireka*) of both eternality and non-eternality, and that it exists in both universals (*sāmānya*) and prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*); however, that is incorrect. For eternality consists in being a non-counterpositive of destruction that follows after a universal, whereas non-eternality consists in being a counterpositive of such [destruction] that follows after a prior non-existence. Furthermore, for prior non-existence as well, destruction is simply its own counterpositive; for it is accepted that the negation or cessation of a positive entity (*bhāva*) is itself a negative entity (*abhāva*), whereas the negation of a negative entity is itself a positive entity.

One might argue: "Just as existence and non-existence coexist in universals (*sāmānya*) and the like, so too would permanence and impermanence—defined respectively as the absence of existence characterized by destruction and the absence of existence not characterized by destruction—coexist in the same locus. If this is said, we reply: No, for we do not assert the coexistence of existence and non-exclusion (non-existence) in a single locus merely on the basis of an example; otherwise, by pointing to the presence of our technical definitions of permanence and impermanence in universals and the like, one would have to conclude that existence and non-existence themselves coexist in the same place.

It is said that [the subject] exists; however, when a combination of negations is established by means of valid cognitions (*pramāṇa*), we employ as an illustration the combination of negations regarding both eternity and non-eternity in relation to the exclusion of universals (*sāmānya*) and so forth. And thus, even if the combination of negations regarding eternity and non-eternity—as asserted for the persistence of universals and the like—does not serve as an illustration, there is no harm.

For this very reason it has been said: "In the case of superimposition (*adhyasta*), the absence of both existence and non-existence is not contradictory, just as [the absence] of both permanence and impermanence [is not contradictory]. This is because, since the substratum itself is merely imagined (*kalpita*), there is no contradiction even between two contradictory properties. Nor does this entail a contradiction with the acceptance of the impermanence of the imagined; for although there is an absence of ultimate (*tāttvika*) impermanence, there is no contradiction in accepting the presence of an impermanence that possesses the same degree of reality (*samasattāka*) as the substratum.

Nor should it be argued that there is a contradiction between the reason (*hetu*)—which is "being imagined" (*kalpitatva*)—and the probandum (*sādhya*)—which is the absence of real attributes (*viruddhadharmābhāva*)—due to their respective existence and non-existence; for there is no contradiction in establishing the absence of a real attribute by means of the presence of a non-real reason.

For this very reason, the statement of the ancients—that nothing whatsoever can be a real form for that which is difficult to define in its own nature (*svarūpato durnirūpa*)—is also consistent, since the absence of a real conventional form is established by the very reason of being conventionally difficult to define.

For this very reason, the following objection is refuted: "If the reason—consisting in the difficulty of being defined—and the probandum—the absence of a real nature—are unreal (*atāttvika*), then there is the fallacy of unestablishedness (*asiddhi*) or contradiction (*bādha*); if they are real (*tāttvika*), then there is a logical inconsistency (*vyāghāta*). This is because, since the reason, the probandum, and so forth possess an existence equal in reality to that of the subject (*dharmin*), there is no unestablishedness or similar fallacy; and since the reason and so forth lack ultimate reality (*tāttvika*), there is no logical inconsistency. Furthermore, being difficult to define in its own nature (*svarūpataḥ*) is precisely what constitutes being imagined (*kalpitatva*).

By this [it is asked]: is this "indefinability in its own nature" [meant] in some way or another? Is it "indefinability by some [specific] way," or "by a way other than that"? Is it by way of existence or non-existence? Or is it "indefinability by some [specific] way," or "by a way other than that," or by way of existence and non-existence? The first [option] is not [tenable], because there is a contradiction between "indefinability by some way" and "definability by that very way."

For this very reason, the second [alternative] is not tenable, because it involves a contradiction between being "indefinable" (durnirūpa) and "not being definable" (adurnirūpa) in any manner whatsoever. For this very reason, the second is not tenable: because "being undefinable in any manner" is distinct from "being undefinable in some other manner," and because that which is imagined as "unreal" (mithyātva), etc., is indeed definable. Nor is the third [alternative] tenable, because its distinction from both the real and the unreal lacks a basis in reality—this is refuted, moreover, because the third position cannot withstand scrutiny.

For instance—the difficulty of defining [an object] in terms of existence or non-existence consists precisely in its being sublated by both of those [opposites]. And that [sublation] is the reason for the unreality (*atāttvikatva*) of the substratum as qualified by its attributes. Thus, why should the distinctness from both the existent and the non-existent (*sadasadvailakṣaṇya*) not also be a reason for the unreality of that [substratum]? Nor should it be argued that, in this way, a conceptualized entity would also be excluded from such categories as being visible or invisible, sublatable or unsublatable, difficult to define or easy to define; for in the case of a conceptualized entity, there is indeed an exclusion from all real attributes such as visibility and the like.

Because it is accepted; for there is no contradiction even in this way, since non-real properties such as visibility and the like are admitted by conventional means of knowledge (*vyāvahārikapramāṇa*) according to their respective contexts. However, conventional invisibility and so forth simply do not exist. We indeed admit that this [invisibility] is merely apparent (*prātibhāsika*). And thus, just as in the view of the Naiyāyikas (*tārkika*) there is no contradiction between conjunction and its absence, or as in the view of the Bhaṭṭas between difference and non-difference, there is likewise no contradiction between existence and the absence of existence.

And it should not be argued that, in this way, there would likewise be no contradiction between existence and non-existence; for while we accept the absence of contradiction between two things that are not ultimately real (*atāttvika*), since we do not admit a collection of negations (*niṣedhasamuccaya*) as being ultimately real, it is impossible to establish a collection of affirmations (*vidhisamuccaya*) as ultimately real by analogy with that. Nor can such an implication be made on the strength of the example of ultimate conjunction and its absence, because even in the case of the illustrative instance, ultimate reality is not admitted.

Now, is not "inexpressibility" (anirvācyatva) simply the inability to withstand analysis in terms of existence, non-existence, and so forth? And that [inability] cannot mean merely "not being a locus of existence and so on," because that would result in over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to non-existent things and to Brahman, since Brahman is devoid of attributes (*nirdharmaka*). Nor can it be said that [the definition is] "being a locus of imagined existence," for since that [imagined existence] exists in the world as well, it would result in under-extension (*avyāpti*) there.

Nor can it be the state of being the locus of the absolute non-existence of existence (*sattva*) and so forth; for, since Brahman is devoid of attributes (*nirdharmaka*), there is no absolute non-existence of existence in it—just as there is no existence—and since even in the "void" (*tuccha*) there is no absolute non-existence of non-existence—just as there is no existence—it may be that over-extension (*ativyāpti*) is somehow avoided. However, because both the void and Brahman are devoid of attributes, the very fact of possessing attributes would result in being the definition of the "indefinable" (*anirvacanīyatva*). Furthermore, since even the scripture stating that Brahman is "without distinctions" (*nirviśeṣa*) cannot negate all attributes without contradiction, the absence of existence in Brahman implies the presence of its absolute non-existence.

[The opponent objects: "Because it is impossible to exclude [Brahman]; nor is it the absence of the nature of existence (*sadrūpatva*) and so forth, for if Brahman lacked existence, it would lack the nature of existence, and thus the definition would over-apply (*ativyāpti*) to it. Nor is it the state of not being an object of valid cognition (*pramāṇāgocaratva*) in the sense of [being defined by] existence and so forth, because even Brahman—which is known solely through the Vedāntas that have an undivided meaning (*akhaṇḍārtha*)—is not an object of valid cognition characterized by the mode (*prakāra*) of existence and so forth. [The author replies: No, for "incapability of withstanding inquiry (*vicārāsahatva*) in terms of existence and so forth" means being the locus of the absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) of existence and so forth.

Nor is there the fault of over-extension (*ativyāpti*), because in Brahman, just as existence (*sattva*) is absent, so too is its absolute non-existence; otherwise, there would arise a contradiction with scriptural texts such as those concerning its being "without distinctions" (*nirviśeṣa*). Nor can the scripture be interpreted as having another meaning due to a contradiction arising from the presence or absence of the distinction consisting in "being without distinctions," for since that distinction is merely imagined (*kalpita*), its non-existence is not real; thus, by the absence of the existence of that [imagined] distinction, there is no contradiction, just as in the case of a dream-elephant and its absence. For this very reason, the claim that "even in the absence of existence, its absolute non-existence is necessary" is refuted.

Now, one might object: "In that case, let indefinability (*anirvācyatva*) consist in possessing particularities (*viśeṣavatva*) or possessing attributes (*dharmavatva*). If so, we reply: no; let this friendly advice rest for now, because the definition as previously stated has been established. Alternatively, indefinability may mean the inability to withstand analysis in terms of existence (*sattva*) and so forth, which is the absence of being of the nature of existence (*sadrūpatva*) and the like. Even in the absence of the attribute of the nature of existence, it has already been demonstrated below how Brahman possesses the nature of existence; therefore, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) of the definition to Brahman.

Nor should it be argued that, if Brahman were thus of the nature of existence (*sat*), words such as "existent" (*sat*) found in the Vedas would not be figurative (*lākṣaṇika*); for while those words denote that which is qualified by the attribute of existence, their application through indication (*lakṣaṇā*) to the attribute-less [Brahman] is necessary. Indeed, there is no word whatsoever whose primary denotation is a nature devoid of attributes. Now, one might object: the absence of existence and other attributes cannot be merely illusory (*prātibhāsika*), because if it were, then the silver and the phenomenal world would have to be considered ultimately real (*pāramārthika*), like Brahman; nor can it be of the same ontological order as the substrate (*dharmisamasattāka*), because that which is known through sublation cannot possibly be identical to what is established by error.

Nor is it conventionally real; for if the world were conventionally real and the silver were illusory, the aforementioned defects would follow, and if the silver were conventionally real, it would entail that the world is ultimately real, resulting in the loss of non-duality (advaita). If this is argued, we say no, because we accept the absence of existence and so forth as having the same level of reality as the substratum itself.

Nor is it improper for that which is sublated by a sublating cognition (*bādhaka*) to be equated with what is established by error; for since the sublating cognition has as its object only the underlying substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*), the absence of existence in the silver-like [object] is itself established by the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*), and thus it does not constitute something to be sublated. Furthermore, this does not contradict the perception of existence, because even that [existence] is admitted to be non-ultimate (*atāttvika*).

Nor should it be argued that this results in the definition being reduced merely to the absence of real existence—where "reality" means non-sublatability—and thus "sublatability" alone could serve as the definition; for sublatability, being employed as an adjunct to another term, cannot be construed with the subject (the definiendum), and it is impossible to maintain that by taking that [sublatability] alone, the other terms would be redundant.

Nor should it be argued: "How can you establish 'indefinability'—defined as being distinct from both the existent and the non-existent, or as being pervaded by that [distinction]—while refuting such difference through both scripture and reasoning? Do not despair; for we are establishing that very [indefinability] only in its non-ultimate (atāttvika) sense, whereas its sublation has already been established at the time of defining falsity (mithyātva). Therefore, there is no inconsistency in the definition of indefinability that applies equally to the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell and to the phenomenal world.
Thus ends the definition of indefinability in the Advaitasiddhi.

The means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are perception, inference, verbal testimony, and presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*). First, regarding perception, there is the experience: "silver appeared falsely," and so forth. Now, the word "false" (*mithyā*) is not a synonym for "non-existent" (*asan*); for, according to the reasoning to be stated later, it is impossible to attribute a non-existence that is common to things like a "man's horn" to the silver and other objects currently being manifested. Nor is there a contradiction with the experience, "for all this time, non-existent silver appeared," because this [experience] is satisfactorily explained as having for its object the absence of existence—which is but one aspect of its indeterminability (*anirvacanīyatva*).

Nor can it be argued that in the case of the text "Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, Infinite" (*satyaṃ jñānamanantaṃ brahma*), the term "Truth" (*satyam*) is likewise explained solely as having the exclusion of non-existence (*asattva-vyatireka*) as its object; for since the nature of Brahman as Being (*sadrūpatā*) has already been established, it is inappropriate to assume that the term refers merely to the exclusion of non-existence. Thus, because the cognition of "Being" with respect to Brahman and the cognition of "non-Being" with respect to a shell-silver differ—due respectively to the absence of a sublater of existence and the presence of a sublater of existence—the two cases are not equivalent in their logical implications (*prasaṅga*).

And the inference is as follows: "The subject of dispute, being devoid of existence while being devoid of non-existence, is devoid of both existence and non-existence, because it is sublatable or because its appearance is caused by defects; for whatever is not so is not thus, like Brahman. Nor is there the fallacy of an unestablished qualification (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*), because that [qualification] is established in a general sense by the following: 'Existence and non-existence are the counter-correlates (*pratiyogin*) of absolute absences that coexist in the same locus (*samānādhikaraṇa*), because they are properties (*dharma*), like color and taste; or, existence does not reside in that which is not the locus of non-existence, or non-existence does not reside in that which is not the locus of existence, because they are properties, like color.'"

Nor does the partial establishment of one part of the probandum constitute the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*), because—as in the case of the argument "qualities and so forth are both different and non-different from the substratum of qualities, because they are co-referential"—the absence of *siddhasādhana* has been demonstrated by the force of the desire to prove (*siṣādhayiṣā*). Nor should it be said that the probandum is contradictory because existence and non-existence are mutually exclusive; for this has been resolved by showing that they are not ultimately real and do not consist in mutual exclusion.

Since it is precisely the reality of difference that is to be refuted, there is no contradiction with that [scriptural authority]. Nor is there the fallacy of proving something already established (*arthāntara*), because even in the absence of *sattva* (existence) like Brahman, its non-illusory nature (*anirvācyatvābhāva*) is established by its being of the nature of Being (*sad-rūpatva*). This is because the world, being devoid of *sattva*, lacks any evidence for being of the nature of Being, and thus such a claim would be sublated (*bādha*). Furthermore, in the case of Brahman, the very fact that it would otherwise result in nihilism (*śūnyatā*) serves as the proof for its being of the nature of Being.
