Nor should it be argued that there is an equality of fallaciousness (ābhāsasāmya) because the subject of dispute (vimata) is not both existent and non-existent, since it is sublatable (bādhyatvāt), like Brahman; nor should it be argued that there is a counter-inference (satpratipakṣa) such as "the subject of dispute is non-existent, because it is not the locus of existence, like a human horn. This is because there will be stated a subverting tarka (reductio ad absurdum) against the contrary position, characterized by the impossibility of accounting for manifestation and sublation otherwise, and thus both the equality of fallaciousness and the counter-inference are absent.

Nor is there a contradiction with perception in the form "it was not even non-existent silver that appeared," because it has been stated that the term "non-existent" (asat) has as its object the absence of existence (*sattvābhāva*), otherwise the theory of misapprehension (*anyathākhyāti*) would be untenable. For this very reason, the claim that the word "false" (*mithyā*) is a synonym for "non-existent" is refuted. Furthermore, it does not follow that the notion of "non-existent" would apply to Brahman as well due to the absence of existence; for while a cognition whose object is the absence of the attribute "existence" in the attributeless (*nirdharmaka*) Brahman is accepted, there is no basis for a cognition whose object is absolute non-existence (*tucchatva*).

Nor does it follow that, because of the absence of non-existence, there would be the consequence of perceiving the world as "existent" [in the same way]; for this is an accepted consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*). Nor should it be argued that no distinction is experienced between this [cognition] and the cognition of the non-existence of a human horn; for by this much, let it be granted that the latter also has the absence of existence as its object, but not that the former has "insubstantiality" (*tucchatva*) as its object on account of the latter, since there are subverting arguments (*bādhaka*) against such insubstantiality here, and because it has already been shown that even two cognitions of identical form can have diverse objects.

As for that which was stated—regarding the alternatives of existence and non-existence: in the first and second [alternatives], there is sublation (*bādha*) in the world with respect to the aspect of the absence of existence, and in the case of silver and the like, with respect to the aspect of the absence of non-existence; in the third and fourth, with respect to the aspect of the absence of non-existence in both cases; in the fifth, with respect to the aspect of the absence of existence in both cases; and likewise in the seventh, according to the aforementioned reasoning, with respect to the aspect of the absence of non-existence in both cases—the same applies to the voidness of non-sublatability (*abādhyatva-śūnyatva*) and the voidness of momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva-śūnyatva*). However, in the sixth [alternative], there is no such sublation, because it can be accounted for even by means of existence in the form of non-sublatability.

That it is a different matter is not so, because by adopting the non-existence previously mentioned, objections such as partial sublation (*bādha*) and proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) have been avoided. Likewise, this [argument] which establishes indeterminability (*anirvācyatva*) in a general sense should also be understood as having that very purpose. The avoidance of contradictions and other such issues is likewise explained in this manner.

Now, regarding the inference for the sake of establishing the probandum (*sādhyaprasiddhi*): existence and non-existence "are not the counter-correlates (*pratiyogin*) of absolute absences (*atyantābhāva*) residing in the same locus (*samānādhikaraṇa*), because they are mutual absolute absences of one another, like potness and non-potness."

If it is argued that "non-existence (*asattva*) does not reside in what is not the locus of existence, because it is of the nature of its negation—just as impermanence (*anityatva*) does not reside in what is not the locus of permanence (*nityatva*)"; and that likewise, taking "existence" (*sattva*) as the subject, one should formulate the argument [to show] counter-balanced opposition (*satpratipakṣatā*), and that the "not being of the nature of mutual exclusion" (*parasparavirahānātmakatva*) is the limiting condition (*upādhi*)—[we reply: no, because the reason (*hetu*) is unestablished (*asiddha*) since it has been stated that existence and non-existence are indeed of the nature of mutual exclusion, and because the limiting condition pervades the probans (*sādhanavyāpaka*), given the impossibility of otherwise accounting for manifestation and sublation (*khyātibādhānyathānupapatti*).
Because there is no room for either a counter-qualification (*upādhi*) or a counter-argument (*satpratipakṣa*) due to the reasoning that sublates the opposing side.

As for the objection that the examples of "eternal" and "non-eternal" lack the probans (*sādhanavaikalya*), that is incorrect; for it has been stated by the opponent that "eternality" and "non-eternality"—defined respectively as being non-counter-correlates of destruction and being its counter-correlates—are mutually exclusive in nature. Furthermore, the charge of similarity to fallacious arguments (*abhāsasāmya*)—namely, that "pot-ness and non-pot-ness are counter-correlates of absolute absences co-located with their own substrata, because they are properties, like color and taste," and "fictitiousness does not reside in that which is not the locus of non-fictitiousness, because it is a property, like color"—is likewise baseless.

"The [probandum] does not reside in that which is not the locus of being different from the existent (*sad-vilakṣaṇatva*), being different from the non-existent (*asat-vilakṣaṇatva*), being imagined (*kalpitatva*), and not being imagined (*akalpitatva*), because it is a property (*dharma*), like color (*rūpa*). This [inference] is also similar to a fallacious argument (*ābhāsa*).

[Objection: "In the case of [the properties] being distinct from the real (*sad-vilakṣaṇatva*), distinct from the unreal (*asad-vilakṣaṇatva*), imagined (*kalpitatva*), unimagined (*akalpitatva*), visible (*dṛśyatva*), invisible (*adṛśyatva*), indefinable (*durnirūpatva*), and non-indefinable (*adurnirūpatva*), there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*)—respectively for the first, second, and third [cases]—with respect to being distinct from the unreal and being distinct from the real, as well as with respect to being knowable (*jñeyatva*), being expressible (*vyavahāryatva*), and so forth. [Reply: That is not so. Just as in the inference "The earth has an agent, because it is an effect, like a pot," there is either a similarity to a fallacious argument (*ābhāsa-sāmya*)—such as "A sprout has an agent, because it is an effect"—or a deviation in the case of the sprout and similar instances.

There is no fault; for me, who establishes by means of the reason "being a property" (*dharmatva*) that [the subject] is the counter-positive of an absence co-located with itself, there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*), since the probandum (*sādhya*) exists in the case of potness, non-potness, and so forth, and thus the reason is not fallacious. Indeed, being a property of something non-contradictory (*aviruddhadharmatva*) and the like is not the necessary condition for the existence of such a probandum; rather, it is merely being a property (*dharmatvamātra*). For it is not impossible for properties such as "visibility" (*dṛśyatva*) to be absent anywhere at all.

As it has been said: "For that which is indefinable in its own nature cannot possess even the slightest real form. Therefore, there is no deviation [of the reason] even with respect to being the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) of absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*). Nor is there the fallacy of proving what is already established (*arthāntara*) by means of being the counter-positive of an absolute non-existence residing in the self (*ātman*), because the self is devoid of attributes (*nirdharmaka*) and thus even such an absolute non-existence does not exist; or else, because the term is qualified by "residing in what is not the self" (*anātmaniṣṭha*).

Nor is there a parity with the fallacious argument (ābhāsa-sāmya) that "being imagined" is not the counter-positive of an absolute non-existence residing in the non-self—which is itself the locus of the absence of being unimagined—because it is the counter-positive of an absolute non-existence residing in the non-self, just like "being unimagined"; for this undesirable consequence is actually accepted [by us]. Just as there is no deviation (vyabhicāra) regarding falsity (mithyātva) due to the property of being visible (dṛśyatva) and so forth which establish falsity, so too, against a specific opponent, there is no suspicion of the probandum being unestablished (sādhyāprasiddhi) by means of proving only a portion [of the reason].

For instance: against the proponent of *satkhyāti* (the theory that the object of error is real), [it is argued] that the subject under dispute, which is distinct from the non-existent, is distinct from the existent, because it is sublated, like the connection between mother-of-pearl and silver. Against the proponent of *asatkhyāti* (the theory that the object of error is non-existent), the subject under dispute, which is distinct from the existent, is distinct from the non-existent, because it is the object of immediate cognition, like a jar. The establishment of its indeterminability (*anirvacanīyatva*) follows by the force of the property residing in the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*). And how there is no such fault as proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) or contradiction (*vyāghāta*), has been explained below.

Thus, the property of being the counter-correlative of an absence residing in the phenomenal world (prapañca) resides in both existence and non-existence, because it resides only in that which is the counter-correlative of an absence residing in the phenomenal world, just like the state of being expressible in linguistic usage (vyavahāryatva). Furthermore, the property of residing in both existence and non-existence resides in the counter-correlativity of an absence residing in the phenomenal world, because it resides in everything that resides in that which possesses both existence and non-existence, just like the counter-correlativity of difference (bhedapratiyogitva). Any lack of probative force will be refuted by stating the favorable reasoning (anukūlatarka). Therefore, inference is the means of valid knowledge (māna) in this matter.
Thus ends the inference establishing indeterminability (*anirvācyatva*) in the *Advaitasiddhi*.

The justification for the impossibility of appearance and sublation otherwise (*khyātibādhānyathānupapatti-samarthanam*): Presumption (*arthāpatti*)—in the form of the impossibility of appearance and sublation otherwise—is also a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in this regard. To explain: if the disputed silver and so forth were real (*sat*), it would not be sublated; if it were unreal (*asat*), it would not be perceived. Yet it is both sublated and perceived; therefore, because it is distinct from both the real and the unreal, it is indeterminable (*anirvacanīya*). [Objection]: But surely [qualities such as] the universal of existence (*sattājāti*), causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*), and so on, are contradicted by your own non-acceptance [of them], and they are also inconclusive (*vyabhicārin*) in your system.

Nor can it be argued that being unsublated during the state of empirical transaction (*vyavahāra*) is what must be established; for if that were so, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the world—which is unsublated during the state of empirical transaction by the scriptural negation "not here, not manifold" (*neha nānā*)—would fail to be established as indeterminable (*anirvacanīya*), since logical sublation (*yauktika-bādha*) is observed even during the state of empirical transaction.

[The opponent argues: "Existence (*sattva*), defined as the state of being non-sublated (*abādhyatva*), is [too] broad when applied [to all things]. However, being established by valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇikatva*)—as found in the case of the featureless nature (*nirviśeṣatva*) residing in Brahman, which is known through the Vedas that reveal reality—is subject to deviation (*vyabhicārin*) because it applies to things distinct from Brahman that are themselves sublatable. Thus, existence cannot be defined. [The author replies: Not so. For here, "existence" is simply "being established by valid means of knowledge," and "validity" is the quality of revealing reality (*tattvāvedakatva*). This [validity] belongs to the Vedānta passages that, through metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*), convey pure Brahman, but not to those passages that set forth attributes such as featurelessness. Therefore, there is no deviation in that regard.

Nor should it be argued that, since Brahman—which is pure consciousness—is self-luminous, there would be no apprehension of the pervasion (*vyāpti*) between being an object of valid knowledge (*prāmāṇikatva*) and being non-sublatable (*abādhyatva*), because the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) do not operate upon it due to their futility; on the contrary, since being an object of valid knowledge exists only in things distinct from Brahman, its pervasion would be with subtableness alone. This is not so, because even though Brahman is self-luminous, the operation of the means of knowledge is fruitful for the purpose of removing the ignorance that obstructs worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*).

For this very reason, there is no pervasion (*vyāpti*) between being sublated and being non-authoritative (*aprāmāṇikatva*), because of the deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of Brahman and because of contradiction. Indeed, for that which makes known the reality (*tattva*), there is no such thing as making known the unreality (*atattva*). Now, an objection might be raised: "If the sublater (*bādhaka*) of silver and the like were to make known the reality, then non-duality (*advaita*) would be lost; if it does not make known the reality, then the lack of authority (*aprāmāṇikatva*) of the silver and so forth—which is based upon that sublation—would not occur. This is not so. Even if the sublater does not make known the reality, its very capacity to serve as the cause for the lack of authority of the silver and so forth remains intact. This is because the criterion for something being a sublater is precisely that its own existence (*sattā*) is not inferior to that of the object to be sublated (*bādhyānyūnasattākatva*). Thus, even if the sublater pertains to the level of phenomenal appearance (*vyāvahārika*), it is sufficient to invalidate the silver which exists only at the level of illusory error (*prātibhāsika*). Therefore, the sublation of silver and the like by the cognition of shell-silver (*śukti-rajata*) is established. Consequently, the lack of authority of the silver and so forth is proven by their being sublated. Hence, the pervasion between being sublated and being non-authoritative is established. Thus, the definition [of falsity] is free from defects. Therefore, the definition of falsity is established. Q.E.D. For this very reason, it is refuted [by the opponent] that even though silver and the like are sublated by empirical means of knowledge (*vyāvahārika-pramāṇa*) which do not reveal reality, they should possess ultimate reality (*pāramārthikatva*) due to their own intrinsic validity (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*), just as non-duality (*advaita*) does; nor can it be argued that this [silver] is not sublated by the non-dual Śruti which reveals reality, because that [Śruti], like the Śruti concerning difference, is explained as merely restating the negation of the empirically obtained silver. Furthermore, it is refuted because, under the view that the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) is not itself the negation, it is established that the negation of duality (*dvaita-niṣedha*) is likewise merely empirical.

However, some [hold] that here "existent" (*sat*) is intended as being distinct from the non-existent (*asat*) alone. Nor should it be argued that the restriction "of the non-existent alone" results in the non-establishment of the *reductio* (the *āpādaka*), because the meaning would terminate in "if it were not distinct from both existent and non-existent," and thus the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) would be unestablished; for the establishment of the counter-correlate has already been proven by inference prior to this. Nor does the aforementioned dilemma regarding what constitutes "existence" apply here to the phrase "if it were not distinct from existent and non-existent," because there is no room for objection if existence is defined as being grounded in valid cognition (*prāmāṇikatva*).

Nor does the impossibility of explaining the appearance [of silver] follow from the proof of its being inexpressible (*anirvācyatva*) due to sublation (*bādha*); for that [proof] constitutes a separate *arthāpatti*. As for the mention of "oneness" (*ekatva*) in the authoritative texts (*ākara*), it is said to be based on both explicit statement and implied intent (*tātparya*) from the statement of purpose. Alternatively: existence (*sattva*) is simply non-sublatability (*abādhyatva*). Nor does this result in a lack of distinction between the probandum and the reductio (*apādyāvaiśiṣṭya*); for non-sublatability consists in not being the counter-positive of a negation across the three periods of time. By means of that, the absence of being the object of a contrary cognition is what is being reduced to absurdity; thus, there is no lack of distinction between the probandum and the reductio. Or, since conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) is the thing being reduced to absurdity, there is likewise no lack of distinction between the probandum and the reductio.

Nor should it be argued that the remaining [reasons] are redundant because the exclusion of the non-existent (*asadvyāvṛtti*) is established by sublation alone, which results in the establishment of indeterminability (*anirvacanīyatva*); nor should it be said that the statement "it would not be perceived" is improper because the distinction from the existent (*sadvailakṣaṇya*) is established by perceptibility (*dṛśyatva*) in the counter-case (*viparyaya*). For although it is possible for each of these two—sublatability and perceptibility—to establish both exclusions (from the existent and the non-existent), nevertheless, at the stage when one perceives that each [reason] pervades only one part [of the respective exclusion], both are effective.

Even though each [reason] individually pervades both [sides], it is presented as establishing only one part; for, against one who proposes this, the fact that each establishes only one part does not constitute a defect. Alternatively, these two are two distinct *arthāpattis* (presumptions); the mention of their being "one" is based on the impossibility of establishing both [conclusions] by means of either one alone within the system of the opponent, who accepts that the non-existent is sublated and that the existent Self is visible.

Now, an objection is raised: regarding the statement "it would not be sublated," does "sublation" mean cessation by means of a sublating cognition (*bādhaka-jñāna*), or is it a negation throughout the three periods of time (*traikālika-niṣedha*)? It cannot be the first, for that would be an acceptance of what is already desired (*iṣṭāpatti*). As for the second, if it were sublated according to the position that [the object] is distinct from the non-existent (*asadvilakṣaṇa*), it would result in the opposite conclusion—that it is indeed sublated. If this is argued, we say no, because there is no fault in either case. Nor is it an acceptance of what is already desired in the first instance, because it has been stated that being removable by knowledge (*jñānanivartyatva*) is in accordance with the Śruti and other authorities.

In the second case as well, there is no failure to reach a contrary conclusion by virtue of being distinct from the non-existent; for since it is impossible for that which is non-existent to be the counter-positive of a negation residing in a locus already apprehended, it is precisely the distinction from the non-existent that serves as the determinant for reaching the contrary conclusion.

Regarding the phrase "if it were non-existent" (*asaccet*), even here, although non-existence does not mean the absence of the universal *sattā* (existence), for that would lead to a logical deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of universals (*sāmānya*) and so forth, which lack *sattā*. As for the objection raised by others—that there is a deviation in the case of the Self (*ātman*)—that is not correct; for in their view, since existence (*sattā*) exists in the Self, the very ground for the consequence (*apādaka*) is absent; and in our view, since the property of being perceptible (*dṛśyatva*) is itself absent there, the thing to be established (*apādya*) is likewise absent. Nor does it mean "being sublated" (*bādhyatva*), because that would result in a deviation in the case of the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell and similar instances. Nevertheless, non-existence consists in being indefinable (*nirūpākhyatva*) or being devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvarūpatva*).

Nor should it be said that "being indefinable" (nirupākhyatva) means the absence of manifestation (khyāti-abhāva), for in that case the consequence would be indistinguishable from what is to be proven; rather, being indefinable consists in not being an object of the function of words (pada-vṛtti).

Objection: Is it not the case that "being devoid of intrinsic nature" (niḥsvarūpatva) means being the counter-correlate of negation by way of its own nature, and since this is common to the entire phenomenal world (prapañca), there is a fallacy of deviation (vyabhicāra) therein? Nor should it be said that the negation occurs in the form of ultimate reality (pāramārthikatva) and not by way of the phenomenal world's own nature; for even in the attributeless Brahman, there is negation by that [ultimate] form, which would result in its being false as well. Reply: No. For it has already been stated that, due to the qualifying phrase "in a locus where it is perceived" (pratipannopādhau) in the definition of falsity, there is no over-extension (ativyāpti) to that [Brahman].

Even in that view where there is a negation of the world (prapañca) by way of its own nature (*svarūpa*), "lack of own-nature" (*niḥsvarūpatva*) consists in being the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) of a negation by way of its own nature, provided that no limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) has been apprehended. This [lack of own-nature] does not exist in the world, such that there would be no conclusion in the contrary case (*viparyaya-paryavasāna*) that it is therefore not non-existent.

Now, as for the objection that "it would not be cognized," it is first argued that the absence of any cognition whatsoever is being attributed [to the non-existent]. This is incorrect, because even a non-existent thing, such as a "hare's horn," is indeed cognized through sentences like "the hare's horn does not exist. Otherwise, it would be impossible to have a cognition of its distinction from the existent, and it would be impossible to refute the cognition of the non-existent. Furthermore, if the word "non-existent" were meaningless, there would be no possibility of communication, since words employed together cannot produce an effect unless they possess denotative power. Moreover, if the non-existent were not cognized as non-existent, the conventional usage of the term "non-existent" would be untenable. As it has been said: "In order to cognize that which is distinct from the non-existent, the non-existent itself must indeed be known."
Therefore, how can the perception of a non-existent object be prevented by that?

If it is argued thus, we say no; for even in the absence of actual perception, everything is accounted for by mere conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), such as "the non-existent horn of a hare. As it has been said: "Conceptual construction is that which follows upon the cognition of words but is devoid of a real object. Nor can it be asked: is conceptual construction a function other than knowledge—like desire and so forth—or is it a specific type of knowledge? In the first case, there would be contradiction with experience and the impossibility of its being perceived; in the second case, the perception of the non-existent is already established.

Regarding the phrase "devoid of a real object" (*vastuśūnya*), one must ask: does this mean it does not depict anything at all, or that it depicts what is non-existent (*asad*)? If the first, there is a contradiction with experience; if the second, it is an admission of what we already accept. This is because there is no subverting argument (*bādhaka*) against the view that conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is a function other than [perceptual] cognition, and furthermore, because there is no such awareness as "I am experiencing a rabbit's horn. Being "devoid of a real object" means the non-depiction of properties (*dharma*) that possess designations (*sopākhyā*); therefore, there is no fault whatsoever. If, however, conceptual construction is considered a form of cognition (*jñāna*), then its lack of being an object of any cognition other than itself must be established.

Furthermore, since it is untenable for silver in a mother-of-pearl shell and the like to be objects of cognition if they were non-existent, or objects of a cognition other than conceptual construction (vikalpa), their indeterminability (anirvācyatva) is established. Alternatively, the very absence of being perceived as existent is what should be adduced as the consequence.

[Objection: But surely, it is precisely what we desire that such a cognition—which has the form of a valid means of knowledge (*pramā*)—be brought about as non-existent. For no one maintains that the apprehension of a non-existent thing as being existent constitutes a valid means of knowledge (*pramā*). Nor can the absence of such an error, or the absence of such a cognition in general, be established as the goal; for we observe that even in a person who has not realized the absence of horns on a hare, an error arises from the sentence "the horn of a hare exists," just as it does from the sentence "the horn of a cow exists. Indeed, in this case, the words do not fail to present the referents (*padārtha*), as is the case with words like *ghaḍhadhaṣa*; nor is it the case that...

If it is argued that [the sentence] lacks the capacity to convey a syntactic connection—just like "The pot, the goat-skin," and so on—because there exists either an absence of the cognition of incompatibility or an illusion of compatibility accompanied by the causal complex of expectancy and the rest, and otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence of the absence of comprehension and so forth; we say no, because this [sentence] also has an indescribable object, just like the perceptual illusion "This is silver."

Nor should it be said that if this [silver] were also indescribable (*anirvācya*), there would be no difference between it and the [illusory] silver; for who is intent on distinguishing one indescribable thing from another indescribable thing, such that you thus object? Rather, [the distinction is made] from that which is devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvarūpa*). And how it is not the case that [the cognition] has a thing devoid of intrinsic nature as its object by virtue of being existent has been stated previously.

Nor does the indeterminability (*anirvācyatva*) of things such as a rabbit’s horn entail the loss of its naturelessness (*niḥsvarūpatva*); for even if the cognition "there is a rabbit’s horn" has an indeterminate object through the superimposition (*āropa*) of a horn upon a rabbit or the superimposition of belonging-to-a-rabbit, the rabbit’s horn conceptualized immediately after hearing the sentence "the horn of a man is non-existent" is not of an indeterminate nature, but rather possesses naturelessness. Nor is there a conceptualization here of naturelessness and so forth, because that has already been answered.

Nor should it be argued that—according to your own view, which holds that "a word indeed produces knowledge of an object even if that object is absolutely non-existent"—despite the fact that the existence superimposed [upon the hare's horn] is indeterminable (*anirvacanīya*), the word "hare's horn" must still convey the non-existent itself in the sentence "the hare's horn exists," just as it does in the sentence "the hare's horn is non-existent. This is because, since the existence is indeterminable, the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of that existence must necessarily be denoted by the two words "hare" and "horn."

Since that which is absolutely non-existent cannot serve as a substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*), there is no apprehension of it through the words "hare's horn"; however, in the sentence used as an illustration, nothing indeterminable (*anirvācya*) is perceived, and thus there is no requirement for knowledge of a substratum—this constitutes the difference. As for the statement that "there is cognition even of the absolutely non-existent," etc., this refers to the word "non-existent" (*asat*) as denoting its own meaning when not co-occurrent with "hare's horn," just like the verb "is" (*asti*).

Nor should it be argued that the Śruti passage, "Now some say: 'In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent,'" implies the perception of the non-existent as having existence; for how this text does not establish the existence of the non-existent has already been explained in the definition of falsity (*mithyātva*).

The logicians (*tārkikas*), however, maintain that words such as "hare's horn" and the like are simply meaningless (*apārthaka*). [They argue: there is no contradiction with experience—extending up to actual activity—at a time when there is an absence of certainty regarding the lack of syntactic connection (*ananvaya*); for it is only at the stage of certainty regarding the lack of connection that one speaks of their non-expressiveness (*abodhakatva*). Thus, even in the absence of such certainty, they do not express an indivisible (*akhaṇḍa*) hare's horn or the like; rather, they produce either a cognition having existence-in-general (*sanmātra*) as its object with a discordant qualifier (*vyadhikaraṇaprakāraka*), or a cognition having the non-existent as its object under the guise of existence (*saduparāgeṇa*). This is because the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) for the manifestation of a purely non-existent entity is absent.

This has been stated in the *Bauddhādhikāra*: "Because there is no apprehension of a conventional relation (*saṅgati*), words such as 'hare's horn' are non-denotative. Nor is it the case that derivative (*yaugika*) words do not require a separate conventional relation beyond the relation of their parts; for when a meaning is conveyed through the predominance of the powers of the parts, they are incapable of conveying an indivisible (*akhaṇḍa*) non-existent entity, since the parts do not produce cognition without placing their own respective powers forward. Indeed, a word such as *pācaka* ("cook") does not convey its meaning without first conveying the act of cooking (*pāka*) and so forth.

In that case, it is not the case that sentences such as "the horn of a rabbit is non-existent" or "there is no horn of a rabbit" lack cognitive efficacy; for they do indeed convey the absence of a horn in a rabbit. This cognitive efficacy, however, does not reside in the word "rabbit-horn" alone, but rather in its co-occurrence with the word "is not. Therefore, there is no room for the fallacious doubt that the word "is not" is redundant. Alternatively, the intended consequence (*āpādya*) is the absence of immediate (non-conceptual) cognition.

Nor should it be argued that direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is necessarily required for the knowledge of pervasion (*vyāpti*)—namely, that "whatever is non-existent is not perceived"—and therefore even a non-existent thing must be perceptible; otherwise, there could be no cognition of the non-existence of even a non-existent thing, such as a hare's horn, and thus it would follow that even such things are indeed perceptible. This is because [the definition of perception] includes the qualifiers "directly" and "as something not to be negated," which specify that it must be an object of immediate (*aparokṣa*) cognition. In the case mentioned, however, since the object is both an object of cognition and an object of negation, there is no impossibility regarding the qualified absence (*viśiṣṭābhāva*) that is to be established.

Alternatively—the absence of being an object of immediate cognition (*aparokṣapratīti*) by way of existence (*sattva*) is what is to be established as the consequence. Nor should it be argued that in cases such as "this is silver," something absolutely non-existent (*atyantāsadeva*) is cognized as existent through error; for there is a lack of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) for an absolutely non-existent thing to be the object of such a cognition. Indeed, sensory contact (*indriyasannikarṣa*) is the general causal complex for perception, and that does not exist in the case of a non-existent thing.

Nor should it be argued that, on the view that [silver and the like] are merely phenomenal (*prātibhāsika*), since they do not exist prior to their cognition, how can there be the possibility of the causal complex for perception consisting of sense-object contact? For in this system, regarding silver and the like—which exist solely through being known and are directly manifest to the witness-consciousness—there is no requirement for contact as the instigator of the mental modification (*antaḥkaraṇavṛtti*) that destroys ignorance. Indeed, even for you, contact is not the cause for every instance of perception, including that of the Lord.

Nor should it be argued that the cause of valid cognition (*pramā*) is the contact of a faultless sense organ, whereas in the case of error (*bhrama*), it arises from the sense organ alone accompanied by a defect; for sense-contact is a general causal condition (*sāmānyasāmagrī*) just like the sense organ itself, and it has already been stated that a sense organ devoid of that [contact] is not a producer [of cognition].

In that case, one might ask: since the general causal complex for verbal cognition lacks the knowledge of compatibility (*yogyatājñāna*) and so forth, how can there be a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) of something beyond the senses? For it is the absence of the knowledge of incompatibility (*ayogyatājñānaviraha*), not the knowledge of compatibility itself, that constitutes the general causal complex; this is because the absence of the knowledge of incompatibility—in the form of a non-apprehension of non-relation—is necessary for any qualified cognition (*viśiṣṭajñāna*). And this [absence] certainly exists even in a sentence that conveys a non-existent thing. Indeed, one who knows that "non-existence does not belong to a rabbit’s horn" does not thereby apprehend that "the rabbit’s horn is non-existent.
It is precisely on this basis that there is such an aversion toward direct perception (*aparokṣapratīti*) in such cases.

By this [reasoning], it is established that immediate cognition (aparokṣajñāna) whose object is pure existence (sanmātra) has non-existence as its object, because it is a cognition whose object does not reside in existence, like a mediate cognition (parokṣapratīti) whose object is non-existent. Nor is there a lack of locus (āśrayāsiddhi) here, even if "existence" is intended in its sense common to both the apparent (prātibhāsika) and the real.

It has been refuted [by others] that the term "only" (*mātra*) is redundant when one intends to speak of that which exists in the ultimate sense (*paramārthasat*), because without this term, the fallacy of an unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*) would be difficult to avoid, since even mere error (*bhramamātra*) must have as its object that which exists ultimately as its substratum. This refutation is rejected for the following reasons: first, because there is a sublation [of such a claim] due to the absence of the necessary causal conditions (*sāmagrī*); second, because "being verbal" (*śābdatva*) is a limiting condition (*upādhi*); and third, because it shares the same logical flaws as fallacious arguments (*ābhāsa*), such as: "Dharma and so forth are objects of immediate perception (*aparokṣapratīti*), because they are objects of cognition (*pratītiviṣayatvāt*)."

Furthermore, if a non-existent silver were the object of immediate perception (*aparokṣapratīti*), then even things such as a hare’s horn would likewise become objects of immediate perception, since there is no distinction [between them]. If a distinction were admitted, it would contradict their non-existence. Now, one might argue: "Because existence and non-existence are distinguished by their having a nature or being devoid of a nature respectively, there can exist among things like a man’s horn and a hare’s horn a distinction—established by the intellect and not inconsistent with non-existence—consisting in their being the objects of indirect cognition (*parokṣapratīti*) and conventional usage through their respective words, 'man’s horn' and 'hare’s horn'."

Nor should it be argued: "How can there be a relation between the non-existent, which is devoid of all capacity, and existent cognition? For it is impossible to predicate 'object-ness' (viṣayatva) of it, and because there is a contradiction in such things as its being the agent or the object in expressions like 'it shines' or 'it is perceived'. This is not a valid objection, because [the existence of an object] is logically established just as the past and so forth are objects of memory, inference, and the like.

If it is argued that one should not say, "In that case, only the word *pratīti* (cognition) and so forth possess the status of being the object, and by that alone there is the conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) of 'object-ness' therein"—and that this is the same for me as well—do not say so. For when the word *śaśa* (hare) is in a state of error regarding a man, just as the horn of a man is cognized by the word *nṛśṛṅga* (man-horn), it is also cognized by the word *śaśaśṛṅga* (hare-horn); thus, it is impossible to state any mutual distinction such as "being cognized by the words *nṛśṛṅga* and so forth" [versus others].

Nor should it be argued that because the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of a silver object assists [the cognition] while the latent impression of a rabbit's horn does not, the latter is not the object of immediate error; for otherwise, why would another equally indeterminable (*anirvācya*) thing not arise there for you as well? This is because a latent impression does not have a direct utility in the production of the cognition itself, as that would result in the cognition being a memory (*smṛti*); rather, its utility is through the production of the object. Thus, the restriction of the latent impression applies only to the position of indeterminability (*anirvācyatā*), and not to the position of having a non-existent object (*asadviṣayatā*).

In reality, however, in every philosophical system, it is the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) alone—having as its object real silver and the like—that serves as the cause for the initial error regarding silver and so forth. And that [impression] is common to all things, including non-existent silver, the horns of a hare, and so on, since there is no difference in their not being the objects of that [impression]. Thus, how could it be a restrictive factor? [The answer is:

because the occurrence of purposeful activity (*pravṛtti*) would otherwise be inexplicable. In this way, the inexplicability of the occurrence of purposeful activity is itself the proof [for the existence of the object], since it has been demonstrated that the causal complex is absent when the "this" portion (*idamaṃśa*) is perceived in the form of a non-existent silver.

Now, an objection: regarding that which is illusory (*prātibhāsika*) and devoid of this-worldly form, these two—namely, "this-ness" (*idantva*) and empirical existence (*vyāvahārikasattva*)—are not real, for that would contradict non-duality (*advaita*). Nor are they indeterminable (*anirvācya*); for if they were so, then in order to distinguish them from the non-existent (*asat*), they must be perceived as existent in order to be illusory. And if that existence itself is indeterminable, then it too must be perceived as existent, leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Thus, their non-existence must be asserted. As it has been said: "Otherwise, non-existence is what is perceived in illusion."
For in this way, the cognizedness of an entity that is non-existent must indeed be accepted.

"If it were indefinable (*anirvacanīya*), there would indeed be an infinite regress (*anavasthiti*). Even in the *Ṭīkā*, it is stated that since existence (*sattva*) is incompatible with "this-ness" (*idaṃtva*), if [the silver] were indefinable, activity would be impossible because one could not perceive it as "this"; and if it appeared as existing, there would be an infinite regress due to the proliferation of the same alternatives (existence, etc. regarding that [existence] as well; therefore, "this-ness" and empirical existence (*vyāvahārika-sattva*) are non-existent. If this is argued, we say no. For if those two were non-existent, they could not be objects of immediate perception (*aparokṣapratīti*), since obstacles such as the absence of causal conditions have already been stated. Therefore, they are simply indefinable (*anirvacanīya*).

Nor should existence (*sattva*) be conceived in that way [as requiring another existence], for that would lead to an undesirable consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*). Nor does this result in an infinite regress (*anavasthā*), because when existence is perceived as "existent," no further existence beyond it is required; otherwise, even in your own position, since silver is non-existent, the existence that is perceived in it could not logically belong to it, and if it were non-existent, activity toward it would be impossible upon such a perception, and there would likewise be an infinite regress in perceiving it as existent.

And it should not be argued: "Even if there is indifference toward both existence and non-existence regarding what exists, our position faces no inconsistency because activity is possible through the cognition of a non-existent thing as existent; and even if the existence of that which is cognized in a non-existent thing is not cognized as such, its non-existence is established. For you, however, even if activity were possible despite the non-cognition of the existence of silver and so forth as existent, their appearance-ness (*prātibhāsikatva*) would be untenable. This is because, in that case, that existence would not be existent by way of its own nature (*svarūpataḥ*), owing to its being a void (*tucchatva*); nor would it be existent by way of consciousness (*vijñānataḥ*).

Because it is not perceived as existing [ultimately]. And if it were non-existent, how could there be linguistic usage based upon it? Nor should it be argued that if it exists at the time of its appearance, it could not be the counter-positive of a negation in terms of its own nature; nor that if it were the counter-positive of a negation in terms of ultimate reality, there would be an infinite regress, and thus silver and the like must simply be non-existent. For it has already been stated that even if it exists at the time of perception, there can be a negation of it in terms of its own nature, and that the infinite regress is avoided even when the negation is in terms of ultimate reality.

Nor should it be argued that, because the nature of being either one or the other is untenable, the object must possess both natures; for this has already been answered, and because error would otherwise be impossible. Furthermore, it cannot be maintained that error exists in your view simply because its object is indeterminable (*anirvacanīya*), such that here too error might exist by virtue of having as its object that "existence" which constitutes the nature of being both existent and non-existent; for if that were so, the form of the cognition—"the silver is both existent and non-existent"—would become unavoidable.

Nor should it be argued: "Just as the sublation (*bādha*) has as its object the difference from the real (*sad-vailakṣaṇya*)—in the sense that 'silver is indeed non-existent'—let the error (*bhrama*) 'this is real silver' also have as its object only the difference from the non-real (*asad-vailakṣaṇya*); and thus, let even 'prātibhāsika' existence not exist. For if that were the case, since the sublation would not remove the existence of the object of the error, the conventional usage of the term "sublating" (*bādhaka*) would be abolished; furthermore, one perceives "this silver is real" even without having apprehended its non-existence. Indeed, there is no cognition such as "the non-real silver appeared," because sublation is necessarily preceded by a prior manifestation (*prasakti*).

Now, one might object: "If it were not different from the non-existent (*asat*), it would not be sublated; if it were not different from the existent (*sat*), it would not be perceived. Therefore, by this very inconsistency, why should the absence of indeterminability (*anirvācyatva*) itself not be established? Nor should it be argued that existence and non-existence are the determining factors for sublation and perception due to parsimony (*lāghava*), rather than being different from the non-existent and different from the existent, because of complexity (*gaurava*). To this we reply: When there arises a desire to know the determining factors for sublation and perception—which are the first things to present themselves—it is the states of non-existence and existence that are postulated as those determining factors, because of parsimony.

Furthermore, because it is the first to present itself, and not because of "being different from the real" (*sad-vilakṣaṇatva*) and so forth—which would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*)—and because it presents itself last; and since its non-appearance is subsequently established simply by the absence of the conditions for its appearance, there is no need to postulate any other causal factor.

If it is argued that there is no sublation (bādha) even in the case of a human horn and the like because there is no prior manifestation (prasakti), do not say so. Existence (*sattva*) is certainly not the cause of manifestation, for otherwise it would follow that silver is never manifested according to either philosophical system. Nor is non-existence (*asattva*) the cause of sublation, because sublation is not observed in the case of an absolute non-entity (*asat*) established by both systems; furthermore, the non-existence of silver is as yet unestablished, and on the contrary, its logical inconsistency will be demonstrated later. Thus, complexity (*gaurava*) is accepted as being consistent with valid cognition (*prāmāṇika*).
Therefore, it is established that indeterminability (*anirvācyatva*) follows from the otherwise inexplicability of manifestation and sublation.

Thus ends the section on the "Inexplicability of Appearance and Sublation" (*khyātibādhānyathānupapatti*) in the *Advaitasiddhi*. Some, however, assert that because sublation is inexplicable whether [the object] exists or does not exist, it must be "indefinable" (*anirvācya*). It should not be argued that, just as there is the state of being the counter-positive of destruction (*dhvaṃsapratiyogitva*) in something past—which does not exist at that [past] time—there could likewise be the state of being the counter-positive of absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāvapratiyogitva*) even for that which is never-existent; and thus, sublation would not be incompatible with absolute non-existence. For although the existence at one time is of no utility toward existence at another time, the state of being the counter-positive of destruction occurs in a jar or the like precisely during the state of its current existence.

Because of the cognition "the pot exists as impermanent," it is not the case that the pot possesses the state of being the counter-positive of its own destruction at the time of that destruction; for at that time, the pot and other such things have already ceased to exist. Nor does it follow that there would then be the cognition "the pot is not the counter-positive of destruction"; for if that were so, it would absurdly follow that the pot must also be "possessed of color" (at that time). If you argue that this is not the case because color persists as long as the substance exists, then the same applies to the present instance as well. In reality, even at the time of destruction, the pot is indeed perceived as having the state of being the counter-positive of destruction in the cognition "the pot is destroyed."

If it is argued that even if [the world] is indeterminable (*anirvācya*), its being a counter-correlative (*pratiyogitva*) and so forth remains untenable—this is true. What serves as the basis for [the impossibility of sublation] there is existence (*sattva*) in the sense of not being sublated at some time or other, and not existence in the sense of not being sublated at all three times; for the latter involves unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*). Nor does it follow that, in that case, sublation would be untenable in the case of what exists; understand that this is not so in the case of mere existence (*sanmātra*), but rather in the case of ultimate reality (*paramārthasat*). Thus, there is no inconsistency in the position of indeterminability.

If that is so, how can there be the counter-correlativity of being distinct from non-existence in the case of what is non-existent, or how can there be the scriptural negation "non-existence was not"? Non-existence (*asattva*) is simply the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*). Distinctness from that is the state of having existence as its intrinsic nature (*satsvarūpatva*), and that is indeed devoid of a counter-correlative. The meaning of the scripture is precisely that; thus, there is no apprehension of counter-correlativity.

Nor should it be argued that the rabbit’s horn is experienced as the counter-correlate of negation through perception itself in the case of a non-existent thing; for the apprehension of absence is effected by the non-perception of what is perceptible (*yogyānupalabdhi*). Furthermore, the perceptibility of such things as a rabbit’s horn must be said to consist in a causal complex involving defects. In that [defective state], there is no non-perception; and when there is non-perception, that [perceptibility] does not exist. Thus, because *yogyānupalabdhi* is impossible in this case, it has been said: "The perceptibility of a rabbit’s horn and the like consists in a defective causal complex for its apprehension; in that [state], there is no non-perception, nor does that [non-perception] exist."

Nor should it be argued that "only non-apprehension (anupalabdhi) which is incompatible with the existence of the counter-positive (pratiyogin) is the apprehender of that [absence], and such [non-apprehension] certainly exists in the present case"; for while it is possible to entail the apprehension of a *piśāca* within the nature of a pillar by means of the sublation of its fitness (*yogyatva*), the existence of a rabbit’s horn is not pervaded by fitness—on the strength of which its apprehension could be entailed. Thus, there is no non-apprehension here that is incompatible with the existence of the counter-positive. For this very reason, the difference (*bheda*) of *piśācas* and the like is perceptible, but their absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) is not.

Nor should it be argued that horns and the like are necessarily pervaded by perceptibility (*yogyatā*); for by that much alone, the possibility of non-perception of the perceptible (*yogyānupalabdhi*) applies only to the absence of a horn, not to the absence of a non-existent (*alīka*). Thus, even for the cognition that "the horn of a rabbit does not exist," the object is simply the absence of a horn in the rabbit. Likewise, for the cognition "the horn of a rabbit does not exist in a cow," the object is the absence of the property of belonging to a rabbit in the horn whose locus is the cow; this is because there is no other possible recourse.

For this very reason, there is no non-inherence (ananvaya) even in a cow, because, according to the method of the logicians (*tārkika*), it is stated that since things such as a hare's horn are not present [in cognition], their absence cannot be apprehended. Consequently, since the negation of a seventh category is impossible, the categories are indeed six; thus, the interpretation of the phrase "only six" [as implying a seventh] is a forced construction (*kusṛṣṭi*).

Nor can it be said that the object of the cognition "the jar is not" is merely the absence of the relation with the jar, and not the absence of the jar itself; for since the jar previously existed there, its absolute absence (*atyantābhāva*) is impossible. Furthermore, prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and destruction (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*) cannot occur at the time of the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*), because the distinction between the removal and non-removal of the jar remains the same. Moreover, the relation itself is not real, as prior destruction and so forth are untenable in the case of the counter-positive; rather, it must be stated that the relation is simply non-existent.

Regarding this, the teacher Udayana has stated: "For whatever is the basis of the cognition of X, the absence of that very thing is the basis for the cognition of the absence of X. In this case, the cognition of the existence of a jar is based on conjunction (*saṃyoga*), and the cognition of its absence is based solely on the absence of conjunction. And that conjunction is indeed real. Nor is there any dilemma concerning destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) and so forth, because prior to the bringing of the jar, there is the antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of conjunction, and once the jar has been removed, there is the destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) of conjunction."

For when a jar is moved elsewhere, there is no conjunction of that jar with the previous location, by which [an argument] such as prior non-existence would be contradicted. Thus, even if one accepts an absence whose counter-positive is a relation, there is no failure to establish an absence whose counter-positive is a non-existent.

In reality, however, since negation is experienced precisely as having the jar as its counter-positive (*pratiyogin*), it cannot have conjunction as its counter-positive. This being the case, one must accept either (1) an absolute negation (*atyantābhāva*) qualified by a particular time, or (2) a fourth kind of relational negation (*saṃsargābhāva*) characterized by arising and perishing, or (3) a "negation of the qualified" (*viśiṣṭābhāva*) resulting from the absence of the qualifier in the case of a jar already conjoined with the ground.

Nor should it be argued that here, in the case of the potsherd, the usage [of "the pot does not exist"] is accounted for by an absolute absence (*atyantābhāva*) that relates to a time other than the one when the pot existed—such as its destruction today; for just as the three distinct usages "he has a staff," "he is fair-complexioned," and "he moves" have as their respective causes the three distinct categories of substance, quality, and action, so too here, since the three distinct usages "it is not," "it is destroyed," and "it will be" cannot be explained by a single absolute absence, the existence of three distinct types of absence is established.

And the connection with a particular time is either the very nature [of the object] as delimited by that time, or it is the destruction of the conjunction and so forth. Nor should it be argued that the cognition is necessarily accounted for by the destruction of the conjunction and so forth alone; for it has already been stated that such an explanation fails to account for the experience [of the absence] as having the jar as its counter-positive (*pratiyogin*). Nor should it be argued that even in the case of the potsherd, the destruction of the jar and so forth may serve as the locus of the relation, and thus a single absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) could suffice for all conventional usage; for this objection has already been answered by the fact that it fails to account for the three distinct types of conventional usage.

For this very reason, the second and third positions are also unable to withstand scrutiny, because the experience of [the absence] having the pot as its counter-correlate cannot otherwise be accounted for. By this, the following argument is refuted: "In the case of a staff-bearer, even when the staff exists, the absence of the staff-bearer is observed due to the absence of the person; thus, let there be an absence of the qualified entity (*viśiṣṭābhāva*) there. However, here, while conjunction exists, no absence of the conjoined object is observed; therefore, it is not an absence of the qualified entity, but rather an absence of the qualifier alone. This is refuted because the experience is of that which has the conjoined object as its counter-correlate.

"Indeed, the blessed consciousness alone is the refuge in the apprehension of reality. Therefore, even by the impossibility of otherwise accounting for its being the counter-correlate of negation, the indeterminability [of the world] is established. Thus ends the demonstration of indeterminability through the impossibility of its being the counter-correlate of negation in the *Advaitasiddhi*.

The scriptural passages beginning with "Neither non-existence existed nor did existence exist" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.7) are also authorities for its indeterminability (anirvācyatva). Nor should it be argued that here the words "existent" (sat) and "non-existent" (asat) refer to the five elements, because they are used in reference to the elements in such passages as "It is called neither existent nor non-existent," and because of the scriptural statement: "That which is other than air and the intermediate space is 'existent,' while air and the intermediate space are 'non-existent. This is because, when it is possible to accept the well-known meanings, it is improper to assume an unfamiliar sense.

For the words "existent" (*sat*) and "non-existent" (*asat*) are not conventionally established with respect to what has come into being (*bhūta*), but rather only with respect to the ultimate (*pāramārthika*) and the non-ultimate (*apāramārthika*). Nor does there arise the fault of negating something unestablished in the phrase "there was neither non-existence" (*nāsad āsīt*); for when "there was not existence" (*no sad āsīt*) expresses the state of being distinct from existence, the possibility of non-existence also follows. Nor is the term "then" (*tadānīm*) redundant, since it is connected specifically to the negation of *rajas* and so forth—as in "there was neither *rajas* nor sky"—for it is not the case that *rajas* and the like are eternally non-existent.

Nor is it the case that, since the negation of *rajas* and the other qualities is already established by the very statement "it was not existent" (*no sad āsīt*), a separate negation would be redundant; for in the phrase "it was not existent," the word "existent" (*sat*) refers to ultimate existence (*paramārthasat*), and therefore the negation of *rajas* and the rest—which belong to the conventional level of reality (*vyāvahārika*)—is not obtained from that [statement].

If it is argued that, because of the supplementary statement "That One breathed, windless, by its own power" (*ānīdavātaṃ svadhayā tadekam*), Brahman also would necessarily be indescribable—just as ignorance (*avidyā*) is from the statement "Darkness existed" (*tama āsīt*)—we reply: no, because in order to avoid contradiction with other scriptural passages, the meaning must ultimately conclude that the one existent Brahman always was, and not something distinct from both the existent and the non-existent. Thus ends the section on the presumptive implication of the meaning of the scripture beginning with "Neither non-existence existed" (*nāsadāsīt*) in the *Advaitasiddhi*.

The refutation of the theory of the manifestation of the non-existent (*asatkhyāti*): Therefore, only the theory of the manifestation of the indeterminable (*anirvācyakhyāti*) is established by the existence of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), and not the theory of the manifestation of the non-existent as something else (*asad-anyathākhyāti*), because it lacks any supporting evidence. Nor is perception a proof for the manifestation of the non-existent in the form "this is the appearance of a non-existent silver," since, by the refutation just mentioned, such a cognition would have as its object merely the difference from the existent. Furthermore, this is not even a case of perception, for even you yourself admit that an existent thing is perceived in its aspect as non-existent.
Nor does the cognition here—"the silver, which was the object of a prior manifestation, is non-existent"—take an existent thing as its object in its aspect of non-existence.

Nor can it be argued that the following inference is the proof for that [non-existence]: "The object of dispute is non-existent, because it is not the locus of existence, like a hare's horn; the cognition under dispute is invalid and has a non-existent object, because its object is not the locus of existence, and because while having existence alone as its object, it possesses an object, like the indirect (parokṣa) cognition produced by sentences such as 'the human horn is non-existent'. This is because there is sublation (*bādha*) in that case by the reasoning stated previously, and because in the first inference "being cognizable solely through scripture" is the limiting condition (*upādhi*), while in the second and third, "indirectness" (*parokṣatva*) is the limiting condition.

Furthermore, by accepting the theory of the manifestation of the non-existent (*asatkhyāti*), one falls into the Buddhist position. Nor can it be argued that the presence of a real substrate (*saduparāga*) serves as a distinction, for even so, the consequence of *asatkhyāti* remains unavoidable. Nor should it be said that this consequence would apply to the Logicians (*Tārkikas*) as well, since they too accept the manifestation of a non-existent relation (*saṃsarga*); for if they were to accept it in that way, the same consequence would apply to them as well. In reality, however, even for them, the emphasis lies solely on the manifestation of a relation with something real.

Since, in the error of silver, nothing other than the mother-of-pearl, the silver, and their identity is the object, and since these [three] are real, there is no lack of justification for its being an error; for it is an error precisely because it possesses a qualifier that resides in a different locus (vyadhikaraṇaprakāraka).

Nor should it be argued that because a relation having silver as its counter-correlative does not reside in the mother-of-pearl, there could be no "having a non-resident qualifier" (vyadhikaraṇaprakārakatva) unless there were an appearance of a non-existent relation; for what, O long-lived one, is this non-existent relation resident in the mother-of-pearl, such that you must accept its being the object [of cognition] for the sake of having a non-resident qualifier? Therefore, being the counter-correlative of a manifested relation is not "qualifier-hood," but rather a specific kind of essential relation (svarūpasambandha) between the cognition and its object.

And as for that relation of essential identity (*svarūpasambandha*), whether it appears as a real connection (*saṃsarga*) or as unreal, it is exactly the same in both cases. Nor does it follow that you yourself fall into the error of "apprehension of the non-existent" (*asatkhyāti*), because you have admitted that even in the case of sentences such as "the horn of a hare is non-existent," there is a mediate cognition (*parokṣapratīti*) despite the object being unreal; for it has been stated that in such instances there is no actual perception, but merely a conceptual construction (*vikalpamātra*). Therefore, there is no apprehension of the non-existent. Thus ends the refutation of *asatkhyāti*.

Refutation of Anyathākhyāti: Nor can there be "misapprehension" (anyathākhyāti) due to the appearance of silver situated elsewhere, because the impossibility of a sensory contact that serves as the cause for immediate perception is equal even for that which exists elsewhere, since it is absolutely non-existent [in the locus of its appearance]. Furthermore, the latent impression (saṃskāra), memory (smṛti), and defects (doṣa) cannot constitute the "proximity" (pratyāsatti), because it is established that conjunction with silver (*rajata-saṃyoga*) is the cause for all perceptions of silver; for it is impossible to claim that a perception of silver arises in the absence of that [conjunction] even when other forms of proximity exist.

Furthermore, it is not the case that only worldly valid perception (*laukikapramārūpapratyakṣa*) serves as its cause, because this distinction is appropriate only for one's own students, because it entails unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*), and because it lacks generality with respect to indeterminate perception (*nirvikalpaka*). Moreover, it would be impossible for a cognition of silverness as a qualifier (*rajatatvaprakārakajñāna*) regarding silver—produced by sensory contact with silver—to be an error (*bhrama*). Even though sensory contact with silver exists in the error "these are turmeric and silver," it does not function as the producer [of the cognition], just as in the case of inference, an object may exist in some instances but not serve as the cause.

Now, if it is argued that inference would result in being a form of perception (*pratyakṣatva*) because it is produced by its object, then there is the subverting argument (*bādhaka*) that inference would not occur regarding past or future objects; and if the perception of silver were produced by contact with silver, there would be the subverting argument that it would be a valid cognition (*pramātva*), whereas if there is no contact, that perception would not occur—this [argument] applies equally to the case at hand as well.

If, however, by the power of a defect (*doṣa*), the contact with silver were the cause of the "red cloth" (*raṅga*)-cognition component, and the contact with the red cloth were the cause of the silver-cognition component, then—because that [silver] cognition-component would not be produced by its own [corresponding] contact—it would follow that it lacks the status of valid knowledge (*pramātva*), and likewise, it would lack the status of perception (*pratyakṣatva*). Therefore, the cognition "these" (*ime*) alone is produced by the sense organ, whereas "the red cloth and the silver" (*raṅgarajate*) consists of recollection (*smṛti*), being of the nature of an illusory mental modification (*avidyāvṛtti*) due to its indeterminability (*anirvacanīyatva*); this is explained in detail elsewhere. Thus ends the refutation of the theory of misapprehension (*anyathākhyāti*).

And that [silver] has indeterminable ignorance as its material cause and is destroyed by the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*). Now, an objection: if this were so, there would be the undesirable consequence of a cognition such as "the silver has arisen and perished," and there would be no perception of its negation throughout the three periods of time. To this we say: no; is this perception of arising and destruction urged against us at the time of the illusion, or at the time of sublation (*bādha*)? Not the first, because in that case, the very apprehension of the previously arisen and undestroyed mother-of-pearl as non-different [from the silver] acts as an obstacle, and furthermore, because the silver is not destroyed due to the non-arising of a contradictory cognition.

Not the second [alternative], because the apprehension of absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) acts as an obstacle to the apprehension of its production and destruction, just as it does to the apprehension of its counter-positive (*pratiyogin*). Indeed, there is never, anywhere, an apprehension of production or destruction in that which is perceived as the locus of absolute non-existence.

Nor can it be asked: "How is the cognition of destruction obstructed by the cognition of absolute non-existence regarding the three [entities], since there is no sentient being [to perceive them]? Or, why is the cognition of absolute non-existence not itself obstructed by the cognition of destruction? One must say that this is because there is no restrictive factor; for, by the force of the result, the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) for the cognition of absolute non-existence alone possesses greater strength, and thus it is that which serves as the decisive factor (*vinigamaka*).

And if that is so, how can there be absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) regarding the locus of origination and so forth? Observe the cognition: through the impossibility of otherwise accounting for direct perception and the like, the status of being the counter-correlate (*pratiyogitva*) of a negation across the three periods of time is made the object of that [cognition] which has established origination and so forth as its content.

Alternatively—it is not the case that [the object] is the counter-correlate of a threefold negation (*traikālika-niṣedha*) by virtue of its own nature (*svarūpeṇa*), but rather by virtue of its mode of ultimate reality (*pāramārthikatvākāreṇa*). Nor should it be argued that since even ultimate reality is perceived at the time of appearance, it cannot possibly be the counter-correlate of a threefold negation, and that this contradicts experience because [the silver] is experienced as the counter-correlate [of negation]. For even the ultimate reality perceived at the time of perception is itself merely phenomenal (*prātītika*); thus, it is not that which is negated, but rather its existence elsewhere. Therefore, it is in that specific mode [of ultimate reality] that [the negation applies].

Since it is the silver itself that is negated, there is no contradiction with experience even regarding its being the counter-correlate [of negation]. Now, one might object: although "presupposition" (prasakti) is indeed a cognition—and that takes the form of a memory which exists for ultimate reality—nevertheless, there is no presupposition of the phenomenal (prātibhāsika) silver in the form of "ultimate reality," which is the necessary condition for being negated. To this we say: no.

For this absence has as its counter-positive a property delimited by a different locus; and in the cognition of that [absence], the apprehension of the qualified entity is not the intended objective, since the cognition of it is established through the apprehension of each [constituent] individually. The claim that the cognition of an absence arises from indeterminate perception (nirvikalpaka) is to be refuted simply by the admission that such a consequence is undesirable.

Alternatively—the negation there applies to both empirical and ultimate silver across all three periods of time. Nor does it follow that, for the sake of the negation "not here, not manifold" (*neha nānā*), one must accept another ultimately real world-phenomenon (*prapañca*); for in the case of the negation "not here, not manifold," because of the inclusion of the word "anything" (*kiñcana*), a negation of everything as it is perceived is necessary, making the postulation of another world-phenomenon as the object of negation cumbersome due to its complexity. In the present case, however, since no counter-positive is specified by way of "everything," this is like the negation of silver found in a marketplace.

Therefore, it is more reasonable to assume the negation of something that has not even been perceived due to its necessity [in the cognition]. Nor can it be argued: "How can there be a negation of that which has not arisen at all for fear of *anyathākhyāti* (the theory of misapprehension)? For even in the absence of direct perception (*aparokṣatva*), such an arising is possible in the form of a memory. By this, the following view is also refuted: that "ultimate reality" (*pāramārthikatva*) residing in the cognition is the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*), whereas the cognition of the non-delimiting appearance (*ābhāsa*) is the cause of the cognition of negation.

Nor should it be argued that the cognition of negation is necessarily preceded by superimposition (*āropa*), for since there is no superimposition [in this case], how could there be a cognition of its absence? This is because there is no evidence for superimposition being the cause; rather, the cognition is established simply through the recollection of the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) and the perception of the locus (*adhikaraṇa*). For this very reason, there is also no intentional superimposition. Otherwise, since the theory of misapprehension (*anyathākhyāti*) has already been refuted—just like the theory of the apprehension of the non-existent (*asatkhyāti*)—due to the absence of its causal conditions, and because superimposition is produced by the non-perception of distinctions, it cannot be intentional.

Furthermore, the very occurrence of an appearance (*ābhāsa*) is itself the occurrence of that [object]. Now, one might object: since there is no actual connection between the appearance and the non-appearance, the "occurrence" of the appearance must be explained as occurring through the form of silverness (*rajatatva*) even though there is no real connection; yet this is untenable, because there is no single commonality (*sāmānya*) shared by both, and because even if a commonality were accepted as a means of proximity (*pratyāsatti*) for grasping pervasion (*vyāpti*) on the strength of the result, such a commonality would be absent here due to the risk of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) elsewhere. To this we say: no, for if there were no commonality—whether perceptual (*prātītika*) or worldly (*āpaṇika*)—between the silver in the mother-of-pearl and the silver in the marketplace, the activity of one desiring that [silver] would be inexplicable.

Because a single universal common to both [the silver in the shop and the silver in the shell] is necessary, we do not say that there is a cognition of the shop-silver through that universal as a means of proximity (*pratyāsatti*). Rather, a cognition whose qualifier is the delimiting condition of the counter-positive (*pratiyogitāvacchedaka-prakāraka*), even if it does not have the counter-positive itself as its object, has become useful for the apprehension of non-existence (*abhāva*). Therefore, there is no room for the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) resulting from the dependence on a universal as a means of proximity.

As for the claim that, having accepted generalization (*sāmānyapratyāsatti*) as the means for grasping pervasion (*vyāpti*), one subsequently refuses to accept it elsewhere due to the fear of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), this is like thrusting a finger into the mouth of a venomous serpent and then feigning fear of a scorpion. For the ancients have stated that the very act of grasping pervasion involves such an over-extension, namely: "One who determines pervasion by means of knowability (*prameyatva*) would thereby become omniscient. This has been stated here in accordance with the literal reading of the ancient texts.
However, one must not forget that the status of empirical-ultimate silver as the object of negation was previously explained by taking mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) as the basis.

Nor does the state of having material cause (*sopādānatva*) entail the consequence of having an agent (*sakartṛkatva*), for that is an accepted conclusion. Now, even so, how can ignorance (*ajñāna*) be the material cause of silver? For it is not perceived as being permeated by that [ignorance], but rather it is perceived as being permeated by the "this" aspect (*idamaṃśa*), and because of the pointing with a finger and the binding of the hem of the garment, one should accept that the "this" aspect itself undergoes illusory transformation (*vivarta*) in the form of a false modification, without contradicting its real modification—[if you say this], we reply: no, for the causality of the ignorance of the mother-of-pearl is necessary on the basis of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).

Let that very thing be the material cause (*upādāna*) as well; for the postulation of that [ignorance] alone is more appropriate, since no other material cause is established. Furthermore, the cognition of mother-of-pearl, in destroying ignorance, also destroys the silver. And this is not possible without its being the material cause, because the destruction of an efficient cause (*nimitta*) is not a necessary factor for the destruction of its effect, and because there is no rule that a material cause must be perceived in its product—since we do not perceive "the color is the pot" or "the shard is the pot," and any kind of perceived continuity could occur here too through qualities such as insentience (*jaḍatva*).

The cognition of the "this" portion as being permeated by that [the universal] is precisely the cognition of it as being interwoven with the "this" portion, since there is no delimitation [of the two]. Because of the non-difference between cause and effect, even such things as pointing with a finger are logically consistent. Nor should it be argued: "Since even indirect (parokṣa) knowledge destroys ignorance, once ignorance has been destroyed by the inference of whiteness, the error of yellowness would not arise due to the absence of its material cause"; for ignorance residing in the object is not destroyed by indirect mental modification (vṛtti).

Nor should it be argued that even though a non-mediated mental state (*aparokṣavṛtti*) has the power to destroy ignorance, there would follow the undesirable consequence that no error could arise from a fallacious statement such as "this is a cloth" regarding an object directly perceived as "this is a jar. For in this case, unlike the example "he sprinkles with fire," there is no presentation of something that contradicts the logical connection (*anvayavirodhin*), which might grant scope to the acceptance of the undesired consequence.
