Indeed, when the nature of being a jar (*ghaṭatva*) is understood as being contradictory to the nature of being a cloth (*paṭatva*), then the perception of that [jar] is precisely the perception of its contradictory; so how can there be scope for the acceptance of the undesired consequence? When [the nature of] the jar...

Since it is not [the object] because of its opposition to cloth-ness (*paṭatva*), then even though that ignorance is destroyed by the cognition of pot-ness (*ghaṭatva*), there still exists an ignorance regarding the unperceived particular due to its opposition to cloth-ness; therefore, the error has precisely that as its material cause (*upādāna*), and thus there is no inconsistency whatsoever.

Nor should it be argued that the superimposition of the nature of the absence of knowledge (*jñānābhāvatva*) or the nature of the absence of pain (*duḥkhābhāvatva*) upon pleasure (*sukha*) and so forth—which are known by the witness-consciousness (*sākṣi*)—would not occur because of the absence of ignorance (*ajñāna*) as their material cause (*upādāna*). For the knowledge of the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna-jñāna*), which removes error, functions through [the cognition of] being distinct from the absence of pain, being distinct from the absence of knowledge, possessing attributes contradictory to "pain-ness," or possessing attributes contradictory to "ignorance-ness. Furthermore, such opposition, difference, and so forth are not accessible to the witness-consciousness, but are rather accessible through non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*).

And thus, that very ignorance is the material cause of error. Nor should it be argued that indirect superimposition (parokṣādhyāsa) would not be removed by indirect knowledge, because [indirect knowledge] does not remove ignorance; for it has been stated that in the case of indirect superimposition, the material cause is precisely the ignorance residing in the knower, and that this ignorance is indeed removed even by indirect knowledge.

Nor should it be argued that for a person who has desisted from the silver upon seeing it, the cognition of that silver is unavoidable because—due to the absence of knowledge of the reality of the substratum—the ignorance (avidyā) that is the material cause of both the silver and its cognition has not ceased, and thus the causal complex for that cognition remains present; for as soon as the silver and its cognition have arisen, they dissolve into their material cause by means of the subsequent sublating cognition. However, the cessation of that material cause itself does not yet occur, owing to the absence of knowledge of the reality of the substratum.

The arising of a subsequent cognition of silver occurs precisely because of the existence of an internal mental modification (*antaḥkaraṇavṛtti*) bearing the form "this," which prevents the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of the reality of the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna-tattva*). In the absence of that [modification], there is a delay [in the realization] due solely to the delay in its occurrence; thus, there is no inconsistency whatsoever. Consequently, since all cognitions are authoritative regarding their own objects, the existence of the silver at the time of its perception is established.

Nor should it be argued that its reality (*tāttvikatva*) would likewise be established, since that too is merely apparent (*prātītika*); for it has already been stated that direct perception (*aparokṣa-pratīti*) cannot take reality—in the sense of being uncontradicted throughout the three periods of time—as its object. Even if reality were taken as an object by indirect cognition (*parokṣa-pratīti*), it remains merely apparent, because its unreality may still occur through contradiction at another time. Thus is established the production of illusory silver (*avidyaka-rajata*).

Therefore, there is a modification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa-vṛtti*) regarding the substrate-portion (*adhiṣṭhānāṃśa*), and a modification of ignorance (*avidyā-vṛtti*) regarding the superimposed portion (*adhyastāṃśa*). And because identity (*tādātmya*) is manifested within that [ignorance-modification], there is no lapse into the theory of non-apprehension (*akhyāti-mata*).

Now, one might object: "In this way, even this [substratum] would be twofold by virtue of being superimposed as 'this,' and the cognition 'this is silver' would be threefold; furthermore, the cognition 'this is silver' in a dream would be fourfold. We say: no. Even if "this-ness" (*idantva*) is superimposed, it is not twofold in the form of "not-this," because the substratum of "this-ness" and so forth is self-luminous (*svaprakāśaka*). For we do not maintain that every superimposition is twofold in nature; rather, we hold this only in cases where the manifestation of the substratum depends upon a modification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇavṛtti*).

For this very reason, the [judgment] "this is not silver" does not possess a threefold nature; however, the suspicion of a fourfold nature in the case of a dream is entirely untenable, because both "this" and "silver" are objects of superimposition, and because the substrate, which is consciousness limited by ignorance (*avidyā*), is self-luminous. Nor is there a contradiction with the experience of visual perception in the form "I see silver," even though the cognition of silver is not visual; for it is metaphorically designated as "visual" because it is a transformation of ignorance residing in the consciousness delimited by the visual modification (*vṛtti*) of "this. Furthermore, even in the case of mere experience, we observe the expression "I see myself."

If it is argued: "Since the cognition of silver is a modification of ignorance (*avidyā-vṛtti*), it is illusory (*prātibhāsika*); because an illusion necessarily involves appearance, and because a cognition whose object is superimposed is itself necessarily superimposed, even this modification of ignorance must be known by a consciousness reflected in another modification of ignorance. Thus, for that too, and for that too as well, there would be an infinite regress"—this is true. However, there is no infinite regress, because within the consciousness that manifests the modification of ignorance, the modification of ignorance itself serves as its own limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) and thus does not require another modification [to manifest it].

Now, an objection may be raised: since the cognition of "silver" can be accounted for either by the transformation of ignorance into the form of the cognition itself, or by the analogy of a cognition whose object is past, it is not logical to postulate a transformation of ignorance into the form of silver. This is not so; for if the cognition were to possess its object solely through its own internal form, it would entail the consequence of *sākāravāda* (the theory that cognition possesses forms). Furthermore, even if one were to account for it as being like a past object, it has already been stated that direct perceptuality (*aparokṣatva*) would then be untenable.

Nor should it be argued: "Since defects (*doṣa*) are the cause of excellence (*atiśaya*) precisely within their own substratum, how could an error produced by a defect located in the eye not be visual (*cākṣuṣa*)? Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that even for one with closed eyes, errors such as [seeing] a yellow conch or silver would arise when the conch is grasped by the skin and the similarity to silver is grasped by the eye. This argument cannot stand, because the very premise that "defects produce excellence only within their own substratum" is unestablished, as there is no restrictive rule (*niyāmaka*) to prove it.

Nor has the aforementioned over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) been stated as a restrictive factor, because no such over-extension occurs by accepting that [the cause] produces its effect in relation to its own correlate. Furthermore, the relationship consists in being the object of a cognition produced by something that is generated by the locus of itself (*svāśraya*). And since that [relationship] does not exist in the case of a substrate-cognition produced by a sense organ that grasps an object which is the content of a latent impression (*saṃskāra*)—because such a cognition is the cause of an immediate error (*aparokṣabhrama*)—and because there is no evidence for the existence of an "idam" (this-ness) mental modification (*vṛtti*) in cases where one closes one's eyes after having perceived similarity with the skin, it is impossible to charge us with the fault of over-extension.

If that [oneness] exists, then we simply accept the consequence (iṣṭāpatti). Now, one might object: "In this way, there would be a contradiction with the experience of the difference between the mental modifications (vṛtti) and the oneness of the cognitions. Nor should it be said that the oneness of the two cognitions is merely figuratively attributed because the two objects have attained oneness through the superimposed non-difference; for even if such a formal argument (prayoga) establishing oneness were supported, the contradiction with experience would remain unresolved. This is not so, because when there is a superimposition of non-difference between the two objects, the superimposition of non-difference between the two cognitions is precisely what is meant by the term 'figurative attribution' (upacāra), and thus there is no contradiction with experience.

Nor should it be argued that, in that case, there would be the undesirable consequence of superimposing unity upon successive cognitions (*dhārāvāhika-jñāna*), because the cognition of the identity of the object—which serves as the basis for superimposition—is present; for a superimposition cannot be established merely by the presence of its causes. Nor should it be argued that the identity of the object has never been observed to be the cause for the superimposition of the identity of the cognition; for once the difference between cognitions is established by the previously mentioned reasoning, there is no fault even in postulating something unprecedented.

Alternatively, just as the silver appears as "this" because it is a transformation of ignorance residing in the consciousness delimited by the aspect "this," so too the cognition of silver appears as the "cognition of this" because it is a transformation of ignorance residing in the consciousness delimited by the mental modification (antaḥkaraṇavṛtti) in the form of "this. Nor does it follow that, upon sublation, there would be a perception of a difference between the two cognitions just as there is between the two objects; for it is impossible to draw such a conclusion, since the perception of a difference between objects and the perception of a difference between cognitions possess distinct causal conditions (sāmagrī).

However, some say that while at the time of error there is a rule regarding the apprehension of the identity of the object, there is no such rule for the apprehension of the identity of the cognition; for even without that, the occurrence of purposeful activity and so forth is possible. And likewise, at the time of sublation, there is also no rule for the apprehension of their non-identity.

Nor should it be said that because this mental modification (*vṛtti*) exists solely through being known, there is no ignorance residing in the consciousness delimited by it; for although there is no knowledge regarding that [modification] since it is cognizable by the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*), nevertheless, ignorance regarding the object delimited by the mother-of-pearl exists in the consciousness delimited by that [modification]. Thus, the actual state of affairs is that this mental modification is the delimiting adjunct of the locus (*āśraya-avacchedikā*), but not the delimiting adjunct of the object (*viṣaya-avacchedikā*).

For this very reason, the objection that for one who knows the reality of the mother-of-pearl (*śuktitattva*) but does not know the reality of the mental modification (*idaṃ-vṛtti*), there would follow the persistence of that ignorance even when the silver has ceased, is refuted; because the ignorance of the reality of the mother-of-pearl itself is the cause of both transformations, and it has been stated that these two—the "this" aspect (*idamaṃśa*) and the mental modification in its form—are merely the limiting adjuncts (*avacchedaka*) of the substrate. Nor does this contradict the experience of the unity of uncontradicted cognition, since the absence of sensory contact with the superimposed object is precisely what constitutes sublation (*bādhaka*).

Furthermore, sensory contact (*sannikarṣa*) is not the causal complex (*pramāsāmagrī*) [for valid cognition], because instruments are necessarily restricted to acting through direct contact (*prāpyakāritva*), and thus contact itself is merely a general condition (*sāmānyasāmagrī*). For it is never observed that a cutting occurs by means of an axe separated from the wood; the details of this are found elsewhere.

As for the claim that the mother-of-pearl itself may be the locus of the illusory appearance (*vivarta-adhiṣṭhāna*) and not the "this" (*idam*), that is not correct; for it is a rule that the locus must be real because it is not imagined by the ignorance (*ajñāna*) that produces the error, whereas the mother-of-pearl is false. Alternatively, due to its being veiled by ignorance (*avidyā-vṛtti*), it does not possess the nature of cognition (*jñānatva*); therefore, there is the notion of the identity of cognitions, since the property of being a cognition resides only in that which sublates ignorance.

Nor should it be argued that, in the case of a continuous stream of cognition (*dhārāvāhana*), the status of being a "cognition" (*jñānatva*) would not belong to the second and subsequent cognitions; for even those [subsequent cognitions] remove ignorance by apprehending what was previously unapprehended, insofar as they grasp their respective objects as qualified by their specific times. In reality, however, there is no inconsistency whatsoever, because the principle holds that "as many cognitions as there are, so many are the ignorances," and thus ignorance is removed by both the intervening cognition and the immediately preceding one.

Even in the case of an imperceptible object, there is indeed the cessation of ignorance residing in the knower; therefore, the cognition "I know" arises. Because of the apprehension of non-difference from that [cessation], the cognition "I know" occurs even in the case of an imperceptible error.

Nor does this constitute a contradiction with the *Vivaraṇa* when the term "knowledge" (*jñāna*) is applied to the mental modification (*vṛtti*), because the *Vivaraṇa* intends to state that the application of the word "knowledge" to the modification is based on its luminosity (*prakāśatva*), and not that the application of the word "knowledge" based on its capacity to remove ignorance (*ajñānanivartakatva*) is merely figurative. Thus, wherever the word "knowledge" is used for a modification of nescience (*avidyāvṛtti*), it is strictly figurative.

Nor should it be argued that if ignorance (*avidyā*) is a modification (*vṛtti*) consisting of non-knowledge, it would contradict the principle that knowledge possesses intrinsic validity (*autsargika-prāmāṇya*), because such a rule is possible only when there is no exception. For the statement regarding "intrinsic nature" is made with the intention that any modification whatsoever which produces desire is considered "knowledge. Alternatively, even though there is a difference between the two modifications, there is the cognition of a single knowledge because the result is one, since both the "this" (*idam*) and the "silver" (*rūpya*) are manifested by the consciousness delimited by the "this"-aspect.

Nor should it be argued that in the case of an indirect error (*parokṣa-bhrama*), since there is an absence of identity with the fruit—which is immediate, unitary consciousness (*aparokṣaikarasa-caitanya*)—how can there be an experience of the identity of knowledge based upon that [identity of the fruit]? For the distinction is simply this: in that case as well, the identity of knowledge is metaphorically attributed (*upacāra*) by first metaphorically attributing the identity of the fruit.

But surely, in your own view, how can there be unity of the fruit (*phalaikya*) given that there is a difference in the fruit delimited by the object of cognition (*vedyatva*), whether it be due to the reflections in the internal organ-vrtti and the ignorance-vrtti (respectively) having the forms of "this" and "silver," or due to the consciousnesses underlying the substrate of "this" and the substrate of "silver" being delimited and undelimited by the aspect of "this"? For the non-difference from pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), which has become unconditioned and dissolved, is the same everywhere.

If it is argued that even in the "this" (idam) portion, the consciousness limited by that [portion] alone cannot be the material cause due to the fallacy of self-dependence (ātmāśraya), nor can consciousness unqualified by the "this" portion be the material cause for silver, because the cognition "this is silver" would otherwise be untenable—[we reply: no, for a modification of ignorance (avidyāvṛtti) does not destroy ignorance; rather, it is a modification of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇavṛtti) having the form of "this. Thus, the very consciousness manifested by that [modification] manifests the silver, and therefore the identity of the result (phalaikya) is possible.

For there is no difference in the result due to a difference in the delimiting adjunct (*avacchedaka*), but rather due to a difference in the manifestor (*vyañjaka*). Thus, the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the superimposed cognition is ultimate reality-consciousness (*paramārthasaccaitanyam*). And that [reality] is of two kinds: empirical reality (*vyāvahārikasat*) and apparent reality (*prātibhāsikasat*). As it has been said: "Because it has for its object empirical reality prior [to sublation], perception is not sublated by scripture. Including ultimate reality, existence (*sattva*) is thus threefold. In this way, the dual nature of the mental modification (*vṛtti*) in error is established.

Objection: In this way, the threefold division of existence is not tenable, because dream-illusory silver—which is inferior even to the *prātibhāsika*—and the cessation of ignorance (*avidyānivṛtti*), which is superior even to the *vyāvahārika*, both exist as real entities. Reply: This is not so, because there is no evidence for the inferiority of the dream-illusory to the *prātibhāsika*. For instance, being *prātibhāsika* means existing solely through appearance, and that is the same for both dreams and waking states.

If it is objected: "In the waking state, the 'this'-aspect (*idamaṃśa*), which serves as the delimiting factor of the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*), possesses a higher degree of reality (*adhikasattākatva*); whereas at the time of dreaming, even that [aspect] is merely illusory (*prātibhāsika*), and thus is inferior"—we say no. For in a dream, the 'this' does not function as the delimiting factor of the substrate, since it is projected (*āropya*) in exactly the same manner [as the object]. In that case, it will be explained that the substrate is simply consciousness (*caitanya*) delimited by ignorance (*avidyā*). Furthermore, according to the view that the cessation of ignorance (*avidyānivṛtti*) constitutes a fifth category of existence, this division pertains only to the reality belonging to the period of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*); thus, there is no deficiency.

Alternatively—since the cessation of ignorance (*avidyānivṛtti*) lacks positive existence (*sattva*), there is no fault based on its non-inclusion within the classification of existence. In reality, however, the cessation of ignorance is either the very nature of Brahman or indefinable (*anirvacanīya*); thus, there is no deficiency in the classification. Nor should it be argued that if this classification were real, it would contradict your own tenets, or that if it were unreal, the threefold division would be lost; for one who asserts that everything other than Brahman is unreal accepts the unreality of this classification as well.

In that case, there is no loss of the threefold nature as being ultimately real; for who asserts that this threefold nature is ultimately real? Rather, it is merely conventional (*vyāvahārika*). Nor should it be asked: "How can a division, which is understood through sublation (*bādha*) from the ultimately real Brahman and from the illusory silver in a mother-of-pearl shell—which is not ultimately real—be itself non-ultimately real? For being cognizable by sublation is not the determinant of ultimate reality; rather, it is non-sublatability (*abādhyatva*). And that [non-sublatability] does not reside in anything other than Brahman, because it is sublated by such [scriptural texts] as "There is no diversity here" (*neha nānāsti*).

Nor does the acceptance of the threefold existence (trividhasattva) contradict our own doctrine that "Brahman alone is real" (brahmaiva sat), for that statement is intended to mean that Brahman alone is the ultimately real (paramārthasat). By this, the objection that one might similarly raise such dilemmas and find fault with [the doctrines of] the falsity of the universe (viśvamithyātva) and the attributelessness of Brahman (brahmanirviśeṣatva) is also refuted.

Now, is it intended here that only the ultimately real (*paramārthasat*) is truly existent, while the other two [categories]—though distinct from the existent—are merely appearing as existent despite being of a different nature from existence, their distinction being due to the delay or lack of delay in sublation; or rather, is it that there is a subordinate internal division within existence itself? It cannot be the first, because in your own view, just as the cognition of "silver" would be impossible in the absence of silver, so too the cognition of "existence" would be untenable in the absence of existence.

Because if there were never any existence of entities, production and so forth would be impossible, as they would be like a void; and because, since there is no difference in terms of objective reality between the empirical and the apparent, it would follow that causal efficiency and the like do not exist in the former, and thus the validity of the scriptures—which have that [causal efficiency] as their object—would be undermined. On the contrary, just as the cause of the illusion of blue sky leads to the certainty of invalidity, the cause of the error regarding objects would likewise result only in the determination of invalidity.

It is not the latter [position], because there is no common general property (*sāmānyadharma*) shared by both the superimposed (*āropita*) and the non-superimposed (*anāropita*); and because, if the conventional were a specific instance of the non-superimposed, it would result in the acceptance of what is already desired. If this is argued, we say no, because the second position alone is incapable of withstanding scrutiny. To explain: non-sublatability (*abādhyatva*) is the common property shared by both the superimposed and the non-superimposed. Otherwise, even in the case of the sublatable, that property would be possible for the superimposed as well, simply by virtue of its being unsublatable at its own time. Furthermore, it has been stated that if there were no single common property for both the superimposed and the non-superimposed, the occurrence of purposeful activity (*pravṛtti*) and so forth would be untenable. For this very reason, it has been said: [The cited verse follows.]

"In space and so forth, there is one kind of reality; in the pure self alone, there is another kind of reality; and through their conjunction, there is yet another reality therein. It is with reference to this [latter] that the word 'real' (satya) is conventionally established."

Just as in illusory silver there is one "silver-ness" (rajatatva) that exists only when known (*jñātaikasat*), and in empirical, ultimate silver there is another "silver-ness" that exists even when unknown (*ajñātasat*), and the object of the word "silver" is a "silver-ness" common to both that pervades them both and is shared by the superimposed and the non-superimposed; so too, in space and other such things, there is one superimposed reality (*satyatā*), and in the conscious self (*cidātman*), there is another non-superimposed [reality], and yet another distinct "transactional reality" (*vyāvahārikī satyatā*) common to both of those, which is the referent of the word "truth" (*satya*). This is the intended meaning.

Even though the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) possesses reality (*sadvaiśeṣya*), it does not possess the quality of being a non-superimposed reality (*anāropitavaiśeṣya*), such that there would be room for the objection of "proving what is already accepted" (*iṣṭāpatti*); for reality (*sattva*) does not consist in the nature of being non-superimposed. Precisely because reality is admitted, there is no contradiction with [the doctrine of] origination and so forth either.

Nor should it be argued: "Sublatability in its own nature does not exist even in the phenomenal world (prapañca), for that would entail its being a non-entity (tucchatva); yet sublatability in the form of ultimate reality exists even in Brahman because it is devoid of attributes (nirdharmaka). Thus, how can the status of being 'empirical' (vyāvahārika) and so forth be established by taking sublatability as the criterion?"—for this objection has already been answered in the very definition of the probandum (sādhya) consisting of falsity (mithyātva).

As for the argument that—only knowledge possessing a mode (*saprakāraka*) can be the sublater of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), because it is impossible for that which lacks a mode (*niṣprakāraka*) to be a sublater; and thus, such a mode must necessarily be real (*tāttvika*)—that is not so. For it has already been stated previously that even in the absence of a mode, a cognition whose object is the essential nature (*svarūpa*) as characterized by its defining attributes (*upalakṣaṇa*) and which possesses an excluded form (*vyāvṛttākāra*) is indeed a sublater. Furthermore, it has also been explained below how there is no loss of the quality of being "indivisible in meaning" (*akhaṇḍārthatva*) despite the fact that the excluded form is based upon the defining attributes of the essential nature.

Now, an objection: since there is no difference between the empirical (*vyāvahārika*) and the apparent (*prātibhāsika*) in terms of their sublation (*bādhyatva*), what is the basis for their distinction? It cannot be based on being "illusory" (*māyika*) versus being "ignorance-born" (*avidyaka*), because there is no difference between *māyā* and *avidyā*, and because such a distinction is untenable in the absence of any difference in the objects themselves. Nor can the distinction be based on the capacity or incapacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*), since we observe causal efficiency—such as the fetching of water—in dream-objects like jars and the like.

Furthermore, "empirical" (*vyāvahārika*) cannot be a qualification for causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), because that would involve mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*), and because it would result in over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to illusory cases such as the embrace of a woman in a dream, which produces empirical pleasure. Nor can there be a distinction based on being sublated by the knowledge of Brahman versus being sublated by a different kind of knowledge; for in your own view, even things like silver are sublated by the cognition of Brahman as delimited by the mother-of-pearl, and there is the fault of over-extension to illusory properties such as momentariness—which are superimposed upon Brahman—since these too are sublated by the cognition of Brahman.

Nor is there a distinction based on being sublated by the cognition of Brahman versus being sublated by a cognition other than that, because according to your own view, only the knowledge of Brahman possesses the status of valid cognition (*pramā*). Nor is there a distinction based on being sublated by valid cognition versus being sublated by error, because even Brahman is subject to sublation by error [in the view of the opponent]. Nor is there a distinction based on being sublated by a cognition whose object is ultimately real versus being sublated by a cognition whose object is merely empirical (*vyāvahārika*), because this would involve the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*).

Nor can they be established through "mutuality" (*anyonya*) and "otherness" (*itaratva*), because in the absence of a differentiator, otherness itself is impossible, and because it would involve mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*). If this is argued, we say no; for difference is possible through the following distinctions: being sublated by a cognition with qualifiers versus a cognition without qualifiers; or being sublatable by the cognition of the pure Brahman versus a cognition other than that; or being sublatable by the cognition produced by a Great Sentence (*mahāvākya*) versus a cognition other than that; or being sublatable by a cognition that sublates itself versus being sublatable by a cognition other than that.

By the word "pure" (*śuddha*), it is intended here merely the substratum devoid of attributes (*nirdharmaka-adhiṣṭhāna-mātra*). Nor should it be argued: "Even at the time of error, that [substratum] is in reality devoid of attributes; if what is intended is a cognition qualified by 'being devoid of attributes' or indicated by it, then its status as having an undivided meaning (*akhaṇḍārthatā*) would be lost, and there would be the consequence that the attribute 'being devoid of attributes,' the absence of a second, and so forth, would become ontologically real. This is not to be said, because [the intention is] a cognition whose object is precisely that which is in reality devoid of attributes.

Because that [nature] is intended to be expressed, and because it is absent at the time of error; furthermore, properties such as being devoid of attributes (niṣdharmakatva) serve merely as a means for the cognition of that [reality], but they do not constitute its object in that cognition. Therefore, there is neither a loss of the status of being an indivisible referent (akhaṇḍārthatā) nor the consequence of [the qualifiers] becoming ultimately real. Even though it is devoid of qualifiers (niṣprakārakatva), its capacity to remove doubt and the like has already been established. Consequently, it is proven that the world, having ignorance as its material cause, is illusory (mithyā). Indeed, "perceptibility" (dṛśyatva)—which is free from counter-examples based on limiting adjuncts (upādhi) and lacks any opposing evidence, and which relies upon the sublation of the contrary and scriptural authority—is a firm and unassailable proof for establishing the illusoriness of ether and the rest.

Thus, since the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) that is perceived is false, the Vedic statements of the Upanishads—which are established upon the partless reality (*akhaṇḍārtha*) consisting of Brahman as distinct from that world—are the revealers of the supreme reality (*paratattva*). Everything whose object is a qualified entity (*sakhaṇḍārtha*) is merely a non-revealer of reality (*atatvāvedaka*). Although this definition of the empirical (*vyāvahārika*)—applied here to the illusory (*prātibhāsika*) object of an error immediately preceding the knowledge of Brahman—is over-extensive (*ativyāpta*), [it remains valid for its intended scope].

Furthermore, the definition of the apparent (prātibhāsika) is under-extended; nevertheless, being produced by a defect associated with the instrument [of cognition] and being produced by a defect dissociated from that [instrument], respectively, are the faultless definitions of those two. Thus is established the threefold nature of existence.
Upon the removal of the dense bondage consisting of ignorance and its effects, there remains that non-duality which is real, consisting of pervasive supreme bliss, and immortal.
Those of noble intellect worship the Infinite One, who shatters the fear of worldly existence;
salutations eternally to that Hari, the Lord of all the Vedas. || 1 ||
Its nature is beginningless bliss, it is entirely free from all that is visible,
it is eternally infinite, and its manifestation is self-evident.

The ultimate reality throughout the three periods of time, whose nature is empty of the threefold distinctions—this has been imparted to me by hundreds of scriptural revelations; therefore, I am that full Hari. || 2 ||

Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Determination of the Falsity of the World along with its Appurtenances," in the *Advaitasiddhi* composed by Śrī Madhusūdana Sarasvatī, disciple of the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ācārya Śrī Viśveśvara Sarasvatī. 1.
In this regard, the justification for the definition of having an impartite meaning (*akhaṇḍārthatva*) is as follows:
Having first defined that which is to be abandoned— namely, bondage— and the means for its cessation,
that knowledge which is the basis for such cessation is now stated to be what possesses an impartite meaning and is to be accepted.

And that [knowledge] of the impartite reality (*akhaṇḍārtha*) is of two kinds: one based on the meaning of a word (*padārthaniṣṭha*), and the other based on the meaning of a sentence (*vākyārthaniṣṭha*). Each of these, in turn, is twofold through the distinction between Vedic and worldly. The Vedic type based on the meaning of a word is also twofold: that which is based on the meaning of the word *tat* (That) and that which is based on the meaning of the word *tvam* (Thou). Among these, "Truth, Knowledge, Infinite," and so forth, is based on the meaning of the word *tat*; "This person consisting of consciousness among the vital breaths, the light within the heart" (*yo 'yaṃ vijñānamayaḥ prāṇeṣu hṛdyantarjyotiḥ puruṣaḥ*), and so forth, is based on the meaning of the word *tvam*.

Expressions such as "exalted light" (*prakṛṣṭaprakāśa*) pertain to worldly objects; however, Vedic statements such as "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*) pertain to the meaning of a sentence, while worldly examples such as "This is that Devadatta" also pertain to the meaning of a sentence.

On this point, they say: What is "having an undivided referent" (*akhaṇḍārthatva*)? It cannot mean "having a referent devoid of distinctions," because if being devoid of distinctions were something cognizable by words, then—whether as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) or as a secondary indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*)—it would result in having a divided referent (*sakhaṇḍārthatā*), just as in the case of the statement "the ground is devoid of jars. On the other hand, if it is not cognizable by words, then even those sentences describing the qualified (*saguṇa-vākya*) that, in reality, refer to Brahman which is devoid of distinctions, would incur the status of having an undivided referent. Nor can it mean "having as its purport only that which is, in reality, devoid of distinctions."

This is because there is no over-extension [of the definition] to sentences such as "supreme light" (*prakṛṣṭaprakāśa*), since these refer to an entity possessing a difference that has the same ontological status as the substrate (*dharmisamasattāka*); thus, they do not ultimately reside in an object that is devoid of difference. For this very reason, they also do not have the non-differentiated (*nirviśeṣa*) as their meaning. Nor does it mean that synonymous words terminate in the mere sense of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), for there would be an over-extension to cases such as "water and fire possess cold and hot touches," which refers to multiple meanings of several nominal stems.

Nor should it be argued that there is no lack of intent toward a collective meaning here, but rather that each [word] individually intends its own respective meaning because they are definitional statements (*lakṣaṇavākya*), and thus there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*). For even so, this definition fails to apply to Brahman; for it is impossible for Vedāntic sentences to culminate in Brahman—which is unrelated [to other words]—either through primary denotation (*abhidhā*) or through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*). For this very reason, neither does the definition consist in intending a single qualificandum (*ekaviśeṣyaparatva*); for this would result in over-extension to sentences such as "blue lotus," which convey a single qualificandum qualified by those attributes, and one would then have to accept that as the intended definition.

As for that which has been stated: the definition of *akhaṇḍārthatva* (the state of having an indivisible meaning) is either the capacity of non-synonymous words to produce a valid cognition whose object is not a relation, or their culminating solely in the meaning of a single nominal stem (*prātipadika*). This was said by the authors of the *Pañcapādikā*: "The connection of words—whose meanings are not mutually delimited and which have no further expectancy—is with the mere meaning of a single nominal stem, which is an undifferentiated, unitary essence. And it was also said by the authors of the *Tattvapradīpikā*: "That which is the cause of a correct cognition untouched by relations among words is called *akhaṇḍārthatā*; or else, it is the state of being the meaning of that [single] nominal stem."

That is not so; for in the first case, there is an over-narrowness (*avyāpti*) in the definition of conjunction (*saṃyoga*), such as in the statement "conjunction is the reaching together of two things that were previously unjoined. Now, if what is intended is "the state of not being a means of valid cognition regarding the relation between the objects signified by the words recalled by the words [of the sentence]," even then there is an over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in the sentence "Eat poison," which is directed toward the injunction "One should not eat food containing poison," since this sentence does indeed convey the relation between the objects signified by the words recalled by the words within the context of the scriptural injunction. Nor can it be argued that because the injunction "One should not eat food containing poison" is rooted in scripture, this [sentence "Eat poison"] does not over-extend, as it conveys a relation between objects signified by words recalled by words that are themselves scriptural; for its root is in reasoning (*yukti*), and thus its status as being rooted in scripture is unestablished.

Now, if it is intended here that [verbal testimony] does not cause the cognition of a relation between the objects sought to be communicated, even in that case there is an impossibility; for the referents of words such as "moon" or "Brahman," being known by their own nature, are not what is sought to be communicated in themselves, but rather are sought to be communicated precisely as the correlates of a specific relation. For this very reason, the second definition is also untenable. Thus, because the definition is impossible, the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is also impossible, since it is impossible to set forth a means of valid knowledge when its definition has not been established.

To this it is replied: what is intended here by the term "relation" (*saṃsarga*) is something over and above that which is recalled by the word's own function (*padavṛtti*). Thus, the first definition results in the following: the capacity to produce a valid cognition whose object is something over and above that recalled by the word's own function with respect to non-synonymous words. Consequently, there is no lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) in the case of conjunction (*saṃyoga*), because that is recalled by the word's own function. Nor is there an over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in the case of the prohibition against eating with an enemy, because in that instance the relation of being a means to an undesirable end—which is the thing to be communicated—is not recalled by the word's own function.

In the case of the statement, "Water and fire possess the qualities of cold and hot touch," non-differentiation (*akhaṇḍārthatva*) is indeed intended. Nor should it be argued: "How can non-differentiation, which cannot tolerate the relation of attribute and substrate (*dharmadharmibhāva*), tolerate a difference between substrates? For the inability [to tolerate something] in one instance does not constitute a reason for its inability everywhere; furthermore, there is a difference in the meaning of the sentences: "Water possesses cold touch" and "Fire possesses hot touch. As for the impossibility [of the definition], it will be refuted when the failure of the reason—namely, that [the definition applies only to] answers to questions concerning that alone—is cleared away.

And here, in order to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to expressions such as "ghaṭaḥ kalaśaḥ" (pot, jar), which convey a single meaning but do not produce knowledge of a relation between distinct entities, the phrase "of synonymous words" (*aparyāyaśabdānām*) is included. Even there, because the plural number conveys the sense of conveying a single meaning collectively, there is no over-extension to expressions such as "dhava-khadira-palāśāḥ" (the dhava, khadira, and palāśa trees). If one were to say merely "cognized by the word," then by implication (*arthāpatti*), one would include the fact that [eating] poison is a means to an undesirable end (*aniṣṭasādhanatva*)—which is cognized by the word [in the sentence "eat poison"]—and thus there would be over-extension to the sentence "viṣaṃ bhuṅkṣva" (eat poison); to prevent this, the term "function" (*vṛtti*) is added.

Nevertheless, since in the theory of "expression of the related" (anvitābhidhāna) the relation constituting the sentence-meaning is made known by denotative power (śakti), and in the theory of "relation of the expressed" (abhihitānvaya) it is made known by secondary signification (lakṣaṇā), there would be over-extension (ativyāpti) to all authoritative sentences; to exclude this, the word "recalled" (smārita) was stated.

In the first alternative, because a "crooked" (kubja) power is admitted, and in the second alternative, because it is admitted that *lakṣaṇā*—which resides in the word-meaning (*padārtha*)—is indeed a function even when unknown, the relation (*saṃsarga*) is not something "recalled by the word," but rather something "to be experienced" (*anubhāvya*); thus, the over-extension (*ativyāpti*) is avoided. In this way, the second definition is also perfectly correct. There too, "oneness" (*ekatva*) refers to the fact that the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*) is the object of the function (*vṛtti*) as delimited by a single property, and not merely the state of being a single individual (*ekamātravyaktitva*).

Therefore, there is no lack of pervasion (avyāpti) in cases such as the answer to the question regarding a descendant of Upagu (*aupagava*)—where the etymological meaning is involved—as in "the descendant of Upagu is dark-complexioned, tall, and red-eyed," nor in answers to questions concerning things consisting of multiple parts, such as a forest (*vana*) or an army (*senā*), as in "the trees standing in one place constitute a forest. Furthermore, the statement "water and fire possess cold and hot touch" is certainly included, because each term refers to a single individual object. As stated by the authors of the *Kalpataru*:
"That which is revealed by several words that are not distinct synonyms—in this way, those proficient in Vedānta have established the partless (*akhaṇḍa*)."

[Objection: Is it not the case that synonymy is avoided only when there is a difference in the grounds for the application (*pravṛttinimitta*) of words? Yet such a difference is impossible in the case of terms like "infinite" (*ananta*), because they reside solely in the pure Brahman; therefore, the definition [of a word] does not apply to the Vedāntas. [Reply: This is not so, because we shall explain how terms such as "infinite," by means of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), have the pure Brahman as their referent precisely by accepting a difference in their grounds for application. Nor should it be said that even secondary indication is impossible because there is no relation in the pure [Brahman]; for secondary indication is established by means of a non-ultimate (*atāttvika*) relation.

Just as there is a secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) of the word "silver" with respect to mother-of-pearl through the relation of silver as perceived in error, so too, since the Pure [Brahman] alone is the substratum of all conceptual constructions, there is no impossibility of a superimposed relation in the Pure. And just as it will be explained later that even though words such as "infinite" are used figuratively, there is no consequence of finitude and the like in Brahman, so it is here. Thus ends the first section: "The Establishment of the Definition of Indivisible Meaning" in the *Advaitasiddhi*.

Thus, when the definition [of Brahman] is established, the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is likewise established; for instance: "The sentence beginning with 'Truth' (*satya*) has as its purport an indivisible object (*akhaṇḍārtha*), or it has as its purport the nominal stem-meaning of 'Brahman', because it is a defining statement (*lakṣaṇavākya*), or because it is an answer to a question regarding that alone, like the sentence 'The moon is the most excellent light'. This is an inference establishing that the subject matter of the word-meanings is an indivisible object.

The inference that the sentence "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*) and others have as their object an indivisible reality—that is, they reside solely in the nature of the Self—is as follows: such sentences reside solely in an entity that is neither cause nor effect, because they possess grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) while residing solely in an entity that is neither cause nor effect, or because they are answers to questions concerning that alone, just like the sentence "This is that" (*so 'yam*). Nor is it unestablished that the sentence beginning with "Truth" (*satya*) and so forth is an answer to a question concerning that alone.

"By knowing Brahman, one attains the Supreme"—since the knowledge of Brahman alone is the means to the desired end, there is a desire to know that alone, and thus that alone is the subject of the question. Nor is there a deficiency of the probandum (*sādhyavaikalya*) in the statement regarding "the most excellent" (*prakṛṣṭa*); for, taking that very statement as the subject (*pakṣa*), its restriction to the moon alone is established by relying on a general pervasion (*sāmānyavyāpti*), because it serves as the answer to that specific question.

Thus, even in the case of sentences such as "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*), it is not unestablished that they are answers to questions concerning that alone; for since the very nature of the Self is the object of the question "Who am I?", an answer exceeding that [nature] would be improper. Nor is there a failure of the illustrative example here, because [the answer] proceeds when only the nature of Devadatta is asked about. Nor is the reason (hetu) ineffective, because that would result in a lack of coordination (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) between the question and the answer, and because there exists a subverting tarka against the contrary position.

Nor should it be argued that the probandum—“the state of being a producer of a valid cognition whose object is not a relation”—is unestablished (*aprasiddha*), because even through perception and other means, only a valid cognition whose object is a specific relation (in the form "this is thus") is produced. For those who accept indeterminate (*nirvikalpaka*) cognition, this [probandum] is established in that very [cognition]; for others, however, its establishment is general, as follows: “The property of being a valid cognition (*pramātva*) resides in that which does not have a relation as its object, because it resides in all valid cognitions, just like nameability (*abhidheyatva*).”

Although even here the possibility of the reason being inconclusive (*aprayojakatva*) may be suspected, nevertheless, the establishment of the probandum (*sādhyaprasiddhi*) in the form of a doubt is not difficult to obtain; in fact, that establishment has already been demonstrated in the very sentence concerning "the supreme" (*prakṛṣṭa*) and so forth.

Nor should it be argued that the status of being a defining statement (*lakṣaṇavākyatva*) is unestablished in the case of the sentences beginning with "Truth" (*satya*), because truth and so forth are universal and particular classes (*jāti*) and thus lack exclusivity since they exist elsewhere; nor should it be argued that such [truth] exists in Brahman only in a real sense (*tāttvika*)—since that would contradict the scriptures on non-duality (*advaitaśruti*)—while in other cases it is equal [only] in a non-real sense (*atāttvika*), because being of the nature of ultimate truth and so forth constitutes the defining characteristic of the very essence of Brahman.

In our view, although any one term such as "truth" (*satya*) is intended to define the essential nature (*svarūpalakṣaṇa*) of Brahman—since everything other than Brahman is merely a semblance of it—nevertheless, even by others, truth is admitted [as a property] of something other than Brahman; likewise, knowledge (*jñāna*) is admitted as true, and bliss (*ānanda*) is admitted as true. Even by the Śūnyavādins, Brahman is admitted to consist of knowledge and bliss devoid of existence (*sattva*). Therefore, since the definitive establishment of Brahman is not possible without these combined, the definition is a composite one.

Nor does the fact that the qualified [Brahman] serves as the definition (lakṣaṇa) entail the consequence of its having a determinate meaning (sakhaṇḍārthatva); for even though the denoted meaning (vācya) may have a determinate meaning, the indicated meaning (lakṣya) remains partless (akhaṇḍa). Although the single, undifferentiated Brahman is the sole indicated meaning of all words such as "Being" (satya) and so forth, nevertheless, there is no redundancy of the other words because each eliminates a different portion of what must be negated. Therefore, since the qualification of the denoted meanings serves as a means to the realization of the partless [Brahman], it is not in contradiction with that [realization].

If it is objected: "But this is contradictory, because there is a rule that a sentence whose purpose is a definition (lakṣaṇa) consisting of a unique property (asādhāraṇadharma) must necessarily have a determinate meaning (sakhaṇḍārtha)," we reply: No, for the rule is not established since all definitional sentences terminate in the essential nature (svarūpa) alone; moreover, while a definition by means of a property might contradict the partless nature (akhaṇḍatva), a definition by means of the essential nature does not contradict it.

Nor is there an impossibility of the relation between the characterized (lakṣya) and the characteristic (lakṣaṇa) in the absence of difference, because both are established through a distinction of forms based on the modifications of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇavṛtti), just as in the case of being veiled and not being veiled; otherwise, the distinction between an essential characteristic (svarūpalakṣaṇa) and an incidental characteristic (taṭasthalakṣaṇa) would not exist.

Nor is there a determination [of permanence] based on whether a property exists as long as the substance exists; for by that much alone, there would be a determination of permanence or non-permanence, but not one regarding the nature of the essence and so forth. Furthermore, in your own view, this definition of the essential nature (*svarūpa-lakṣaṇa*) would be over-narrow (*avyāpti*) with respect to the color and other qualities of earth, and because Brahman lacks any property that exists as long as the substance exists. In reality, however, the intention in a definition lies in its being a means (*dvāra*); this does not contradict the fact that the thing to be defined (*dvārin*) is an impartite whole (*akhaṇḍārtha*).

Nor should it be argued that because the knowledge of the essential nature (*svarūpa-jñāna*) has already arisen in a general sense prior [to the specific inquiry], there is no dependence on this [definition] for its cognition; for although this [definition] does not serve as a means for mere cognition in general, it is required as a means for that cognition which removes doubt and the like. Nor is there a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of sentences defining things with parts, such as mountains, since the presence of the probandum (*sādhya*) is established even there. Nor is there a deviation in the sentence "the most excellent light" (*prakṛṣṭaprakāśa*), which is the answer to the question "What is the definition of the moon?"—a question concerning a unique property (*asādhāraṇadharma*).

For in that case, the sentence does not have as its primary object the nature of the moon itself; rather, it has as its primary object the nature of that light which is the locus of excellence. Thus, since it merely conveys the specific individuality of light characterized by excellence, there is no contradiction in its being a statement of an undivided meaning (*akhaṇḍārtha*). For this very reason, the objection that "when a property (*dharma*) is asked about, it is not appropriate to state the nature of the moon" is refuted; for it is the nature of the property itself that is stated, otherwise there would be a lack of coordination (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) between the question and the answer.

[Objection: But surely this [position] is refuted; for, since the injunction to investigate the Vedāntas—on the grounds that it would otherwise be inexplicable as a means toward the knowledge with a specific mode that depends on the cognition of the subject (*dharmin*) and which removes doubts and the like possessing a specific mode—is the cause of liberation, one must ascertain the absence of the probandum (i.e., the lack of a specific mode) in the Vedāntic statements. [Reply: This is not so, because the removal of doubts and the like regarding falsehood and so forth is established by the very cognition of the excluded form (*vyāvṛttākāra*) that negates falsehood and the rest, and thus [the requirement of a specific mode] is superfluous (*anyathāsiddha*). For it is not the mere possession of a specific mode (*saprakārakatva*) that is the essential factor there.

If a cognition that persists during the time of an error were to remove doubt and the like simply by virtue of possessing a mode (*saprakāraka*), the very phenomenon of error would be abolished. A cognition removes ignorance solely by having the same object as that ignorance, not even by having the same mode, because that would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*). Furthermore, the object of ignorance is pure Brahman, since it is impossible for anything other than that—which is imagined by ignorance—to be the object of ignorance.

And thus, the mental modification (*cittavṛtti*) having the form of pure Brahman is indeed devoid of any specific mode (*niṣprakārikā*), and it alone is the remover of ignorance; for since every mode is merely imagined by ignorance, the mental modification cannot have that [mode] as its object, and therefore it lacks the same object as ignorance. Just as knowledge whose objects are ignorance and its effects does not remove them, this has been demonstrated previously.

Furthermore, since the fact that cognitions of forms such as substance (*dravya*) possess forms such as pot (*ghaṭa*) is refuted by experience, there is no undesirable consequence of the cognition of the form of a pot being sublated by a cognition of the form of a substance; this is because substance-ness (*dravyatva*) and pot-ness (*ghaṭatva*) are distinct, and thus their objects are different. Moreover, as we have demonstrated in our *Vedāntakalpalatikā*, one cannot achieve a solution even by taking recourse to the condition of having the same mode of presentation (*samānaprakārakatva*); this is the general direction of the argument.

Now, let it be granted that there is a counter-argument (*satpratipakṣa*), for instance as follows: The object intended by the sentence "satyam" etc. is either of the nature of a related entity (*saṃsṛṣṭarūpa*) or of the nature of a relation (*saṃsargarūpa*), because it is the object intended by a valid statement (*pramāṇavākya*), like [the object intended by] a consensus (*saṃmata*). Furthermore, the sentence "satyam" etc. intends a relation that is not sublated by the cognition which is its own intended object, or it intends a relation defined by categories that are objects of a valid cognition produced by its own instrument, which is not sublated by the cognition which is its own intended object; because it is a valid statement, like the statement regarding the *agnihotra* sacrifice and so forth.

In cases such as "Eat poison," although there is no intention toward the connection between the literal meanings (*vācyārtha*), there is no deviation [from the rule] because there is an intention toward the connection between the objects that are the targets of the valid cognition produced by one's own words. Furthermore, in cases such as "The sky is a hole" or "A cuckoo is a *pika*," since these terms have nearly identical referents, grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) would be impossible; therefore, there is an intention toward the connection of the hole, the cuckoo, and so forth with being the denotable objects (*vācyatva*) of the words "sky" and "*pika*. If this is argued, we reply: No. In the first inference, if the probandum (*sādhya*) is "in the form of a connected entity," then [the reason applies to] the connection; if the probandum is "in the form of a connection,"... [the argument continues].

Furthermore, there is deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of an object whose nature is a composite (*saṃsṛṣṭarūpa*), because both of those [types of objects] are the intended referents of authoritative statements (*pramāṇavākya*). In the second inference, since the property of being an authoritative statement can be accounted for merely by its having as its object that which is non-sublated, or merely by its having as its object that which is the content of a valid cognition (*pramiti*), the specific probandum (*sādhya*) is irrelevant (*atantra*) and thus lacks logical necessity (*aprayojakatva*); moreover, the property of not being a sentence defining a *lakṣaṇa* (*alakṣaṇavākyatva*) constitutes a limiting condition (*upādhi*).

Nor can it be argued that the valid cognition (*pramā*) produced by Vedāntic statements possesses a qualifying mode (*saprakārikā*), because it is produced by inquiry (*vicāra*) or because it sublates doubt, just like the knowledge produced by the ritual section (*karmakāṇḍa*) [of the Veda]. One might offer a counter-argument (*pratisādhana*) as follows: "The valid cognition produced by the Vedānta has Brahman as its object qualified by a mode, because it opposes doubt regarding the nature of Brahman or because it is produced by the inquiry into Brahman; for whatever is thus, is so, just like the certainty produced by the ritual section. However, this should not be said, because in your own view, all knowledge whatsoever necessarily possesses a qualifying mode.

The two properties of "being produced by reflection" (*vicārajanyatva*) and "being opposed to doubt" (*saṃśayavirodhitva*) are redundant and lack probative force; for doubt and the like can be removed even by a cognition devoid of any specific mode (*niṣprakāraka-jñāna*), and the property of "not being produced by the defining statement" (*lakṣaṇavākyājanyatva*) is a limiting condition (*upādhi*). For these very reasons, the second inference is also refuted, as there is no corroborating example (*dṛṣṭāntābhāva*) for proving that [the cognition] has as its object a mode residing in Brahman. Furthermore, in all counter-arguments (*pratisādhana*), one should recognize a counter-reasoning (*pratikūlatarka*) based on the resulting mismatch between the question and the answer (*vaiyadhikaraṇyāpatti*).

Now, an objection may be raised: there is a deficiency of the probandum (*sādhyavaikalya*) in the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*). To explain: the sentence "the supreme light" (*prakṛṣṭaprakāśa*, etc. does not, first of all, have as its object an indivisible reality (*akhaṇḍārtha*) by way of primary denotation (*abhidhā*), because primary denotation does not apply to an indivisible entity in the case of words such as "supreme," and because you yourself do not accept this. Nor does it do so by way of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), because there is no justification for the syntactic connection (*anvaya*) of either a substance or a quality that is "supreme light" with the moon; thus, the seed of secondary indication—namely, the impossibility of syntactic connection—is absent. If this is argued, we reply: No, because in common worldly usage, as in the case of "Bring in the staff-bearers" (*yaṣṭīḥ praveśaya*), and in the Vedic case of "The sacrificial cakes consist of strength" (*tarasamayāḥ puroḍāśāḥ*), [secondary indication is well-established].

Just as in the Veda—in passages such as "They become" (*bhavanti*)—even though a literal syntactical connection is possible, figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is resorted to for the words "staff-bearer" and "sacrificial cake" (*puroḍāśa*) because the syntactical connection intended by the purpose (*tātparya*) is untenable; so too here, since it is established that the sentence has an indivisible meaning (*akhaṇḍārtha*) through figurative indication caused by the untenability of the intended syntactical connection, it is appropriate that the answer, which refers solely to that [indivisible reality], be given when asked, "What is the moon? regarding the very nature of the moon.

Now, an objection is raised: if the nature of the moon is already known, a question regarding it is not appropriate; yet if it is unknown, there arises the problem that the desire to know (*bubhutsā*)—which is accomplished by the knowledge of the substratum (*dharmijñāna*)—and the doubt would be impossible. Furthermore, the question "What is this? after restating "the moon" would be improper because, due to ignorance of the meaning of the word "moon," it would not function as a nominal stem (*aprātipadikatayā*), and consequently, the case-ending (*sub-vibhakti*) following it would be unjustified. It is also not tenable to argue that although the nature of the moon is known, its unconfused (*asaṅkīrṇa*) nature remains unknown, for there are not two distinct forms within that single entity.

If it is argued that [the nature of the moon] is not known because it is not known as being non-confused (*asaṅkīrṇatvena*), then the conclusion is that the sentence aims at a cognition whose qualifier is non-confusion. And that [cognition] consists either in the qualification by the differentiator (*vyāvartaka*) or the qualification by the exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*); in either case, there would be a destruction of the status of having an undivided meaning (*akhaṇḍārthatva*). If this is said, we reply: no, because of a misunderstanding of the point. To explain: precisely because it is admitted that the essential nature of the moon is already known, there is no room for the defect based on its being unknown.

Moreover, even when [the object] is known, a question is indeed appropriate at a time when a cognition opposed to error has not yet arisen, for the purpose of bringing about such an arising; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the total abolition of questioning everywhere. Now, if it is argued that a cognition in a state of non-habituation is not opposed to error, this applies equally to the case at hand, because it is an established tenet in all systems (*sarvatantra-siddhānta*) that it is only a specific type of cognition—despite having the same object—that possesses the power to remove error.

In such indirect (parokṣa) cognitions as "the conch is white, not yellow," the nature of whiteness or the nature of the absence of yellowness appears exactly as it does at the stage of being the object of direct (aparokṣa) cognition; thus, it is that very [nature] which opposes error. Therefore, it is said to be "unmixed" precisely when it is endowed with the fruit that opposes error. Furthermore, whether there is this endowment with the fruit or its absence depends on the presence or absence of specific defects, respectively; this is another matter.

And thus, a single essential nature (svarūpa) is both mixed and unmixed according to the distinction of its particular states; consequently, the simultaneous occurrence of knowledge and non-knowledge is established during the state of mixture. For this very reason, the definitions that "unmixedness consists in the qualification by exclusion" or "the qualification by the differentiator" are rejected, because even when both [exclusion and differentiation] are present in the cognition "the conch is white, not yellow," one observes a state of mixture characterized by the absence of opposition to error.

"Even though I already know that whatever is the moon possesses moonhood (*candratva*) and the exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) of darkness, stars, and so forth, nevertheless, the true nature (*svarūpa*) of the moon itself is not known"—based on this experience, since the possession of the exclusion by the differentiator (*vyāvartaka*) is not what is sought to be known (*ajijñāsita*), it is entirely consistent that the sentence "The moon is the most excellent light" (*prakṛṣṭaprakāśaś candraḥ*) makes known precisely the nature of the moon as it is sought to be known (*jijñāsita*), thereby generating a specific cognition that is the opposite of error (*viparyaya-virodhijñāna-viśeṣa*). What is there that is untenable here? [This is so] because of the exclusion (*vyāvṛtteḥ*).

Even though [the exclusion] is the result of verbal cognition, there is no contradiction of its being a non-differentiated entity (akhaṇḍārtha), because it is not the object of that cognition, and because there is an absence of any word expressive of it. Nor is it the case that the exclusion appears in the verbal cognition through secondary signification (lakṣaṇā); for that would be redundant, and since there is no intended meaning (tātparya) directed toward it, secondary signification is untenable.

To explain: does the exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) convey a universal (*candra-jāti*) or a particular individual (*vyaktiviśeṣa*)? Not the first, because even when one has the cognition "that which is mother-of-pearl is distinct from silver," one still observes ignorance of the true nature of the mother-of-pearl and the resulting error; likewise, even when one has the cognition "the moon is distinct from darkness and so forth," one still observes ignorance of the true nature of the moon and the resulting error.

As for the second alternative, since it is necessary, let only the particular individual be conveyed; what is the use of an exclusion that is not presented by the word itself, since the [desired] result is established simply through the cognition of the particular individual? Indeed, there is no indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of fire in the sentence "there is smoke."

Therefore, the following [objection] is refuted: "Exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) appears in verbal cognition even without *lakṣaṇā* (indication), just as 'being other than perforated' (*chidretaratva*) does in the sentence 'Bring water with a jar'. For although "being other than perforated" is the intended meaning of the word because it cannot be obtained through any other means, exclusion is not likewise [the intended meaning]; this is because, like [the cognition of] avoidance or acquisition, exclusion is obtainable through another means, namely, as a result (*phala*).

Even the state of being other than the apertures (*chidretaratva*) is not an object of verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) without recourse to secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*), for otherwise, the very utility of *lakṣaṇā* would be abolished; rather, it exists in reality as a means for fetching water within the scope of the verbal cognition—this has been explained at length elsewhere. For this very reason, it is stated in the authoritative treatises (*ākara*): "Exclusion from others arises from the meaning, not from the word. Nor is the question "What is the moon? a question regarding a property (*dharma*), because when one has control over the use of words, it is improper to employ a purposeless *lakṣaṇā*; furthermore, even in the case of such a cognition, the fact that the sentence possesses an indivisible meaning (*akhaṇḍārthatva*) has already been established.

Now, one might object: since all definitional statements (*lakṣaṇavākya*)—in reality—generate cognitions whose objects are merely the respective individual word-meanings (*prātipadikārtha*) distinct from one another, and thus lack the capacity to generate cognitions possessing a qualifier (*saprakāraka*), the respondent should employ only the word "moon" (*candra*) and so forth found in the question, which conveys the mere substantive (*viśeṣya*); why then use words such as "excellent light" (*prakṛṣṭaprakāśa*)? If this is asked, we say no; for even though the thing-in-itself (*svarūpa*) alone is the object of knowledge, it is only when the cognition of that thing-in-itself is dependent upon those [qualifying] word-meanings that [the definition functions].

This is because all words possess their fruitfulness by having the exclusion of other referents (*padārtha-itaravyāvṛtti*) as their result; otherwise, it would be established by experience that doubt and other such states would persist.

Now, an objection might be raised: if the subsequent statement lacks the intention (*tātparya*) to convey a cognition qualified by excellence and so forth, then—since it would merely communicate "whatever is the moon"—anything at all would in fact possess the nature of being the moon. Furthermore, regarding the object of that intention, because there would be no distinction between the subject (*uddeśya*) and the predicate (*vidheya*) in the form of "this is the moon" (as a definition), the desire to know the moon would not be satisfied, and the question "What is the moon? would remain unanswered. If this is argued, we say: no; for just as in the case of the [statement] "The bank of the Ganges," even though there is no intention to convey something qualified by its connection with the Ganges...

In reality, the bank is indicated by the word "Ganges" precisely because it is connected to the Ganges; or, as in the case of "He sprinkles the rice-grains" (*vrīhīn prokṣati*) and similar injunctions, since the prescription of sprinkling and so forth would be purposeless with respect to the mere nature of the rice-grains themselves, even when there is an indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of being connected to the *apūrva* established by sentences such as "One should sacrifice with rice-grains," in actual fact, only those individuals that serve as the substrata of the property of being rice-grains (*vrīhitva*) and so forth are indicated by the words "rice-grains" and the like. Similarly, in the present case as well, by the two words "excellent" (*prakṛṣṭa*) and "light" (*prakāśa*), in actual fact, only that which serves as their own substratum [is indicated].

An individual instance (*vyakti*) is indicated, but not just any instance whatsoever; thus, even in the absence of a specific intended meaning (*viśiṣṭatātparya*), the previously mentioned defect does not apply. Furthermore, although there is no relation of the "defined" (*lakṣya*) and the "defining characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*) in the expression "this is the moon," since the two terms that convey both [the moon and "this"] present a single identical form, the relation of subject (*uddeśya*) and predicate (*vidheya*) is possible. Consequently, the cessation of the desire to know (*bubhutsā*) and the state of being subsequent are both possible. Moreover, it has already been established above that even a cognition devoid of a qualifying mode (*niṣprakāraka*) can dispel doubt and other such cognitive states.

This is the extracted conclusion: first, the question and answer concern only the referent of the nominal stem *candra*; and the referent of the nominal stem *candra* is the unique individual that serves as the substratum of "excellent light" and functions as the substantive (*viśeṣya*), rather than being qualified by "excellent light. This is because the co-occurrence of the expressions "excellent light" and "moon" would otherwise be untenable. Furthermore, since the individual that is the substantive is partless (*akhaṇḍa*), it follows that [the sentence] has an impartite meaning (*akhaṇḍārthatā*).

[Objection: But surely—just as in the case of "Bring the cow" (*gām ānaya*), because the bringing is enjoined with reference to the cow, *gotva* (cowness) possesses the status of a qualifier (*prakāratva*) despite not being connected with the act of bringing (since it is the delimiting factor of the objecthood, *uddeśyatāvacchedaka*), so too in the present case, although the "excellent light" (*prakṛṣṭaprakāśa*) is not connected with the meaning of the nominal stem *candra*, it must unavoidably possess the status of a qualifier because it is the delimiting factor of the objecthood; for in "Bring the cow," there is no connection [of the sentence] without *gotva*. [Response: This is not so, because [the status of being a qualifier] depends on being the delimiting factor of the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārthatāvacchedakatva*).

Since it is restricted to being the meaning of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), it is impossible to assert that it serves as a delimitor (*avacchedaka*) for something that is not the meaning of a nominal stem; and thus, if "intense light" were the delimitor of the meaning of a nominal stem, its status as the meaning of a nominal stem itself would be unavoidable.

If it is argued: "In cases such as 'earth is that which possesses earth-ness' (*pṛthivītvavatī pṛthivī*), there is no lack of syntactic connection (*ananvaya*) between earth-ness and the meaning of the nominal stem *pṛthivī* (earth), because earth-ness is indeed the meaning of the nominal stem *pṛthivī*. As for their co-occurrence, the word 'earth' is intended to convey the conventional usage (*vyavahartavyatā*) of that [entity]; thus, there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) from the rule"—we reply: No. For one who does not know the entity qualified by the universal earth-ness as being the meaning of the word 'earth', the universal would not be presented by the term 'earth-ness,' and thus there would indeed be a lack of syntactic connection.

The hearer must necessarily have previously grasped that the meaning of the word "earth" is that which is qualified by the universal (jāti) of earthness (*pṛthivītva*). Consequently, the statement would otherwise be futile; thus, as there is no other recourse, the answer is resolved in the sense that "earth is that which possesses a universal co-located with odor, as excluded from water and the like."

Furthermore, since the possession of a genus co-located with fragrance (*gandha-samānādhikaraṇa-jāti-mattva*) and so forth is not the denotation of the word "earth" (*pṛthivī*), how could there be no [lack of] syntactic connection (*anvaya*)? Moreover, the attempt to justify the co-usage [of the two words] through the definition of being the object of linguistic usage (*vyavahartavyatā-lakṣaṇā*) is incorrect; for in the case of being the object of linguistic usage, there would be an exclusive indication (*jahat-lakṣaṇā*), which entails the abandonment of the primary meaning (*svārtha-hāni*). However, in the case of the essential nature (*svarūpa*), there is an inclusive-exclusive indication (*jahadajahat-lakṣaṇā*), wherein the primary meaning is retained; thus, an inclusive-exclusive indication is alone appropriate for the essential nature.

This has been stated by the authors of the Bhāṣya in the section beginning with "And because of the pervasiveness [of the relationship], it is consistent": "Even in the case of figurative indication (lakṣaṇā), there exist proximity and remoteness. Regarding the passage, "One should meditate on this syllable Om as the Udgītha," when the intention is to determine whether the meaning is "the Udgītha similar to the syllable Om" or "the syllable Om which is a part of the Udgītha," the indication of the part (avayava-lakṣaṇā) is superior to a figurative application (gauṇī vṛtti), because in the latter the primary sense is abandoned; it was determined therein that this is so due to its proximity.

By this [it is shown]: since the subject, the moon, is known in a general sense, and since the distinguishing attribute and the exclusion [of it] from stars and so forth are already known in relation to jars and other things, both the question and the answer concern a qualified object. Even if the questioner’s direct desire for knowledge were directed solely toward the exclusion as a qualifier, nevertheless, because it would be impossible to state each specific exclusion even with a thousand verses, he expresses the qualification by the distinguishing attribute itself—just as one speaks of smoke when desiring to know fire—and not otherwise.

The sentence "there is smoke" does not have its primary purport (tātparya) on the smoke itself for the sake of cognizing fire; nor does the sentence "that which belongs to Agni," which implies a sacrifice, have its purport on the relationship between the substance and the deity.

However, when—having realized that it is impossible to state the exclusion of this or that [particular]—one asks specifically about the possession of the distinguishing property (*vyāvartaka-dharma*), then it is all the more evident that both the question and the answer refer to the qualified entity (*viśiṣṭa*); thus, the [opponent's] position is refuted. For in the first case, there would result a lack of grammatical coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) between the question and the answer; and in the second case, there would result the abandonment of the literal meaning of what was heard. Even in the first case, the abandonment of the literal meaning remains established. Nor can one accept the abandonment of the literal meaning as a last resort, since another way has already been stated.

[Objection: "But surely, this would result in a lack of grammatical coordination (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) between the question and the answer; if there is indication (*lakṣaṇā*) regarding the essential nature (*svarūpa*), then in the case of the answer 'there is smoke' to the question 'where is the fire?', let there be indication regarding the fire. [Reply: No, because when the inferential mark (*liṅga*, i.e., smoke) is directly understood through the primary power (*śakti*) by the sentence "there is smoke," the cognition of the fire is established from that very [mark] alone.
