Moreover, since the element of "that-ness" (*tattā*) is not mentioned in the cognition of the word-meaning, and because postulating the loss of that [element] here would involve excessive complexity (*gaurava*) by violating the rule that such mention is mandatory, [the cognition is established as distinct].

And thus, word-meanings (*padārtha*) are said to be "denoted" (*abhihita*) when they become the objects of a cognition that is distinct from both the recollection produced by words and direct experience. And such meanings, according to the requirements of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and other factors, bring about the experience of their own mutual connection; therefore, the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*) is said to be "indicated" (*lakṣya*). This is because of the rule: "That which is made known by a word is its primary meaning (*śakya*); that which is made known by the word-meaning is its indicated meaning (*lakṣya*). For this very reason it has been said: "It is our settled position that the sentence-meaning is everywhere indeed indicated."

Although there is a distinction in that, in the case of a riverbank (*tīra*) and the like, being indicated by a word (*lakṣyatva*) consists in its being remembered through the meaning denoted by the word, whereas in the case of the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*), it consists in its being experienced (*anubhāvyatva*), nevertheless, the designation "indicated" (*lakṣyatvavyapadeśa*) is applied by taking into account the fact that it is made known by the word-meanings. For this very reason, when one word-meaning indicates another word-meaning, there is a requirement for knowledge of a prior relationship, because that [other word-meaning] is to be remembered; however, in the indication of the sentence-meaning, there is no such requirement, because since that [sentence-meaning] is to be experienced, it does not depend on knowledge of a prior relationship.

In the case of the indication of word-meanings (*padārtha-lakṣaṇā*), it is simply the knowledge of the prior relationship; in the case of the indication of sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha-lakṣaṇā*), it is simply expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and so forth. Thus, both are restrictive factors independently of one another. Consequently, the objection—“How can there be indication when the sentence-meaning is unprecedented (*apūrva*) and impossible to know as being related to anything expressible?”—is refuted, because such a condition applies only to the indication of word-meanings. And thus, since the power of a word is exhausted merely in the presentation of its own meaning, and since the presented word-meanings bring about the experience of their mutual connection (*anvaya*), there is no inconsistency in the Vedānta sentences being the means for the experience of connection, even if they function through the indication of all their constituent words.

It might be argued as follows: "Let there be no inconsistency in the theory of the expression of the related (*abhihitānvaya-vāda*); however, it does arise in the theory of the expression of the already-related (*anvitābhidhāna*). For in that view, the very capacity of words to produce the experience of a relation is called 'power' (*śakti*). The presentation of the meaning of each individual word, by contrast, is of the nature of memory (*smṛti*) and is not accomplished by power. This is because the recollection of one related member from the knowledge of another related member is common to all cases, such as [the recollection of] an elephant-driver [from seeing an elephant], and because the fundamental relation, which consists in the capacity to generate the experience of the connection, remains present."

Precisely for this reason, since the presentation of the word-meaning—which is not accomplished by the power of the word—is common to other forms of memory, and because there is no evidence for postulating a distinct class (*vaijātya*) for it, there is *arthādhyāhāra* (supplying the meaning) alone when there is no sublation, and not *padādhyāhāra* (supplying the word). For example: the word *spṛhayati* [is supplied] after *puṣpebhyaḥ* for the sake of grammatical correctness; the word *svargakāma* [is supplied] after *viśvajitā yajeta* for the sake of obtaining the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*); and in the mantra "I offer what is pleasing to Agni" (*agnaye juṣṭaṃ nirvapāmi*) used in the *saurya* oblation, which is extended from the archetype (*prakṛti*), [the word *sūryāya* is supplied] because the archetype contains a denotative word.

Even if the word *sūrya* is supplied (*adhyāhāra*) to obtain a denotative term in place of the sublated term *agni*, where the auxiliary function has already been established, there is no dependence on it for either the recollection of the word-meaning or the experience of the sentence-meaning. Furthermore, verbalness (*śābdatva*) belongs to the experience of the relation [of connection] precisely by virtue of being an experience of connection produced by a word, and not by virtue of being an experience of connection produced by what is presented (*upasthiti*) by a word-produced [recollection], because that would be unnecessarily cumbersome (*gaurava*).

For this very reason, even though properties such as "being other than a hole" (*chidretaratva*), which serve as delimiters of compatibility (*yogyatāvacchedaka*), are not presented by the word, they possess verbalness because they are objects of the experience of connection produced by the word; others also accept that the same applies to properties such as "favorability" (*anukūlatva*) and "counter-correlativity" (*pratiyogitva*).

Thus, in worldly usage such as "This is Caitra," and in Vedic usage such as "One desiring cattle should sacrifice with the Udbhid," words like "Caitra" and "Udbhid" are construed as proper names (*nāman*) precisely because they are presented through direct perception; otherwise, if one were to postulate that "this [person] denoted by the word 'Caitra' [is related] to the sacrifice denoted by the word 'Udbhid'," it would entail the fault of metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*), since such indication is impossible for a word whose relationship [to its meaning] has not been previously grasped.

Just as in the case of the negative particle (*nañ*) in the expression "the pot is not a cloth," one must postulate a distinct rule of linguistic usage (*vyutpatti*) for the connection with a name such as "this is Caitra" that does not depend on the mediation of a case-meaning; otherwise, if the connection with the negative particle required the mediation of a case-meaning, the monists (*advaitavādins*) would be victorious, since—just as in the case of "a blue, fragrant, large lotus"—the non-difference relation between the pot, the cloth, and the meaning of the negative particle would be established. Furthermore, if the connection with a name required the mediation of a case-meaning, the status of being a name (*nāmadheyatva*) could not be established in the Veda; thus, the prima facie opponent (*pūrvapakṣin*) would be victorious.

Just as in the case of "one should sacrifice with Soma," where a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*) is established through the indication of possessive meaning (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*), so too in cases such as "one should sacrifice with the *udbhid*," the status of being a qualified injunction is justified. Even though the indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is equal in both instances, it is more appropriate to regard it as a true injunction because it produces a specific course of action. As for the Vārttikakāra, however, since the presentation of word-meanings is accomplished through the power of words, he accepts the supplementation (*adhyāhāra*) of a word in every case to achieve that end; nevertheless, in the case of the connection with a name (*nāmadheya*), there is indeed the recourse to a different process of linguistic derivation (*vyutpatti*). This has been explained by him himself in the section on Names (*nāmadheyādhikaraṇa*); so, enough of this digression.

Let us return to the subject at hand: this being the case, if even a word with a secondary (lakṣaṇika) meaning were to convey the syntactic connection (anvaya), then since the capacity to generate the experience of that connection is itself what constitutes "power" (śakti), even a word with a secondary meaning would possess it; consequently, there could be no distinction between primary and secondary meanings. Furthermore, this would contradict the *Liṅgādhikaraṇa* [of the Mīmāṃsā-sūtras].

In that regard, having raised the doubt whether mantras such as "I cut the grass, the seat of the gods" (*barhir devasadanaṃ dāmi*) are applied by virtue of their indicative power (*liṅga*) to both the primary and secondary meanings, or only to the primary meaning, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that since they are verbal in nature, they are applied to both. However, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that they apply only to the primary meaning. As it is said: "The status of being subsidiary (*śeṣabhāva*) belongs to mantras because of their connection with the expression of meaning; therefore, their connection with the meaning is based on their origin, due to the eternal association [between word and meaning]."

In the case of mantras such as "I cut the grass, the seat of the gods," which are not assigned by direct Vedic statement (*śruti*), their application as subsidiary elements (*śeṣabhāva*) would arise from the indicative power (*liṅga*) consisting in the capacity to express a meaning. This capacity resides in the primary sense, not in the secondary one; for a meaning presented through the power of the word itself is called "primary" because it is like a face, being immediate. However, that which is presented through a connection with the primary meaning is called "secondary" because it is like the back, being mediated.

And thus, even by one who asserts the application [of a word] to a secondary meaning, the primary presentation must be stated for the sake of that [secondary] presentation. Consequently, the origin-connection (*utpatti-sambandha*), which is the connection with its own form (*svabhāva-sambandha*)—namely, the connection with the denotation of the meaning—would alone be the applicator (*viniyojaka*), because that [primary connection] is fixed to the meaning, and because the injunction regarding Vedic study (*svādhyāya-vidhi*) achieves its purpose through that much alone. However, the primary connection is not an indicative mark (*liṅga*), because there is no fixity of meaning due to many things being primarily connected, and because it is the last [in the order of consideration]. This is the meaning of the Sūtra.

Therefore, it is a universally established tenet (*sarvatantra-siddhānta*) that when the primary sense (*mukhya*) is possible, metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) should not be resorted to. For word-potency (*śakti*) resides in the word itself, whereas metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) resides in the word-meaning; moreover, the latter is of many kinds, as is well known elsewhere. When the requirement for a correlate in the syntactic relation (*anvaya-pratiyogin*) has been fulfilled by the presentation of a meaning through a word used metaphorically, only that which remains—namely, the potency residing in the word itself—is the actual cause of the experience of the syntactic relation. Even though all the words in an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) are metaphorical, it is only the injunctive word (*vidhi-pada*) with which they form a single syntactical unit that is the cause of the experience, according to the maxim: "Because they form a single syntactical unit with an injunction, they serve the purpose of praising the injunctions."

If it is asked, "In that case, since all words such as 'Being' (sat) and the rest would be figurative (lākṣaṇika), how can the experience of their syntactic connection (anvaya) be accounted for?", this is not a fault, because we accept that the experience of syntactic connection pertains precisely to the primary meaning (śakya). The figurative indication (lakṣaṇā), however, involves merely the abandonment of a portion [of the primary meaning], and not the presentation of an entirely non-primary (aśakya) object, as in the case of [the statement] "The cow is eternal" and so forth. For this very reason, it was stated previously that this figurative indication belongs to expressive words themselves with respect to their own meanings. But, one might object: if a "figurative indication involving the abandonment of the primary meaning" (jahallakṣaṇā) is accepted, how can there be an experience of syntactic connection? For even a single part of the primary meaning is absent therein. As it has been said in the *Saṃkṣepaśārīraka*:

"If, on the other hand, the word *brahman* denotes knowledge accompanied by appearance (*sābhāsa-jñāna*), and likewise the word *aham* denotes the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*), then in that case there is the *jahatī* (exclusive) indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

In this view, since the theory of *anvitābhidhāna* (the denotation of related meanings) is not accepted, there is no fault. However, the recourse to both views [of *jahatī* and *ajahatī*] occurs only in the case of *jahadajahallakṣaṇā*. And so it has been shown in that very same place:
"When there is the theory of the expression of the related (abhihitaghaṭanā), then at that time a pair of recollections and cognitions arise regarding each word;
but in the theory of the expression of the related (anvitābhidhāna) as seen by others, first a pair of recollections arises from the pair of words.

Thus, the author of the *Tattvapradīpikā* and others have adopted only the theory of the expression of the related (abhihitānvaya), because it is in every way consistent with their established doctrine; therefore, there is nothing objectionable. Furthermore, the fact that the position of the Logicians (Tārkikas) falls outside both theories has been explained in the *Vedāntakalpataru*, so we shall desist here. Thus ends the second section: "The Establishment of the Indivisible Nature of Subordinate Sentences such as 'That Thou Art' in the Advaitasiddhi."

Thus, the inference based on the great sentences (mahāvākya) such as "That thou art" (tat tvam asi) is also free from defects. Nor is the example "This is that Devadatta" deficient in the probandum (sādhyavikala), because it is impossible to convey an identity between two distinct qualifiers.

To explain: what is it that is being established here? Is it the possession of this place and time by that which is qualified by that place and time? Or is it the possession of that place and time by that which is qualified by this place and time? Or is it the identity of those two qualifiers? Or is it the identity of the two things qualified by them? The first [alternative] is not tenable, because since the possession of that place and time is not perceived, it cannot be the object of the proposition; furthermore, it would entail that the time of that [past event] and so forth exists at the present moment. The second is not tenable, because it would entail that the time of this [present event] and so forth exists at another time. The third is not tenable, because it is contradicted by experience (*bādhāt*).

For this very reason, even the fourth [type of relation] is not possible; for since the qualifier is distinct, the qualified entity—which consists of the qualifier, the qualificand, and their relation—is itself distinct. Even if it were something additional, its distinction would necessarily follow from the distinction between the qualifier and the distinction between the qualificand. Thus, by setting aside both qualifiers, only the non-distinct qualificand is understood; therefore, its status as having an undivided meaning (*akhaṇḍārthatva*) is established. As it has been said: "Even when two qualified entities arise from two non-contradictory qualifiers, their identity is not possible; how much less so when they possess forms that are the opposite of that."

For when, in cases such as "the man with a staff" (*daṇḍī*) or "the man with earrings" (*kuṇḍalī*), there is no contradiction because the staff, the earrings, and so forth exist at the same place and time, yet there is still no identity between the two things qualified by them—since that would entail the identity of the qualifiers themselves—then what need is there to mention the case of "this is that" (*so 'yam*)? In that instance, because the properties of "that-ness" (*tattā*) and "this-ness" (*idantā*) necessarily do not coexist at a single time and are thus mutually contradictory, how could there be identity between the two things qualified by them? However, the communication of identity through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is the same in both cases.

Even though [terms] like *daṇḍin* (staff-bearer) or *kuṇḍalin* (wearer of earrings) possess defining characteristics (*lākṣaṇika*), they are not conventionally treated as having an indivisible meaning (*akhaṇḍārtha*) because their intention (*tātparya*) is directed toward a qualified entity. However, in the case of "this is that" (*so 'yam*), since the object of inquiry is the mere non-difference—which is the subject of doubt and error such as "Is this him or not? or "This is certainly not him"—the intention is directed toward that alone; thus, it possesses an indivisible meaning. For it has been stated that it is not appropriate to explain one thing when another is what is sought to be known.

Even though perceptual recognition (*pratyabhijñā-pratyakṣa*) has no object beyond the essential natures presented by the two cognitions (*abhijñā*), it serves to dispel error by making known the non-difference through the mediation of the presentation of both; and since this sentence has the same meaning as that [recognition], it does not have a qualified entity (*viśiṣṭa*) as its primary referent.

Just as there is a difference in the result between two types of supernormal cognition (*abhijñā*)—even though there is no difference in the object of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*)—due solely to the difference in the knowledge residing in the specific means (*dvāra*), so too is there a difference between the presentation of the referents of the words "that" and "this," which takes the form of memory, and the comprehension of the sentence-meaning, which takes the form of experience. And thus, the statement of the ancients—"Co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is the state of two [words] having different grounds for application (*pravṛttinimitta*) while being intent upon the cognition of a single object"—is all the more easily established in the case of a [cognition] devoid of qualifiers (*niṣprakāraka*).

Now, an objection: this recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) in the form "this is that" cannot have an undivided entity as its object; for in that case, there is no operation of words—either primary or secondary (*lakṣaṇā*)—in perception. Furthermore, since it involves the mention of both "that-ness" (*tat-tva*) and "this-ness" (*idantā*), its being devoid of any qualifying attributes (*niṣprakārakatva*) is contradicted by experience. If those attributes were not mentioned, it would be impossible for it to differ in object from mere cognition (*abhijñā*).

And likewise, verbal recognition is also such, because it informs another person of what has been understood through one's own recognition. If this is argued, we say no; for even though perception does not depend on a mental mode (*vṛtti*), when its object is a qualified non-difference, sublation acts as an obstacle, and thus [perception] has only the non-difference of the essential nature (*svarūpa*) as its object. Furthermore, non-difference is not a qualifier (*prakāra*), because it is primary as the essential nature itself. Nor do "that-ness" (*tattā*) and "this-ness" (*idantā*) possess the status of qualifiers, because they lack the state of being the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) of the qualified relation whose form is the non-difference that appears.

For this very reason, that [perceptual cognition] does not possess the mention of "that-ness" and "this-ness"; however, when there is a verbal expression of it, such a mention occurs through the conventional usage arising from two successive acts of recognition (*abhijñā*). And in that case, metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) has indeed found its footing. This is the principle in every instance where a non-conceptual cognition is verbally expressed. Nor is there any lack of distinction between [two instances of] recognition, for they are distinguished precisely by having a qualifier (*saprakāraka*) and lacking a qualifier (*niṣprakāraka*), respectively. As for the difference in their results, it has already been stated.

For this very reason, since the intended meaning is that Devadatta, as characterized by "this-ness" (idantā), is identical in essence with the absence of difference whose counter-positive is characterized by "that-ness" (tattā), the instruction is also logically consistent with one's cognition. Furthermore, the absence of difference is not some distinct attribute, but rather the essential nature itself; and that alone is what is called "oneness."

Nor is there this rule that one must communicate to another exactly as one has understood it oneself; for we observe that even through a cognition of a whole (samūhajñāna), instruction regarding a single part desired by the listener occurs, since instruction is accomplished by mere knowledge and follows the desire to know. Thus, even from a cognition whose object is qualified, the teaching of the undivided (akhaṇḍa) is possible. The distinction between qualifiers (viśeṣaṇa) and indicators (upalakṣaṇa), etc., is clear elsewhere and is not elaborated here. And just as the illustrative example is not deficient in the probandum (sādhyavikala), so it should be understood in the case of the great sentences (mahāvākya) such as "That thou art" (tattvamasi).

Now, an objection is raised: if it is argued that there is no contradiction in the realization of the identity of pure consciousness with pure consciousness, this would be an instance of proving what is already accepted (*iṣṭāpatti*) and a negation of what was never suspected (*aprasaktaniṣedha*). Furthermore, if non-difference is the very nature of that [consciousness], then because it is eternally established by virtue of being self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*), instruction would be useless; and if it does not manifest, then the desire to know it and so forth could never cease. Moreover, since this [identity] is established by the intermediate sentence alone which purifies the meanings of the terms *tat* and *tvam*, the Great Sentence (*mahāvākya*) would be redundant; and since it is established by a single word alone, the other words would be superfluous.

If it is argued that there would be no cessation of the delusion of difference from the Great Sentence because of the failure to realize the object known at the time of the delusion, we say: no, for even though consciousness (*caitanya*) is eternally established, the knowledge of its essential nature as characterized by omniscience and so forth—which serves to remove ignorance and the like—is something yet to be accomplished (*sādhya*). Nor does this entail having a specific qualifier (*saprakāratā*), because omniscience and the rest are not qualifiers in the relational cognition (*anvaya-bodha*)—just as "that-ness" (*tattā*) and so on are not—and because such knowledge cannot be attained through any other means, the faults such as the futility of the instruction (*upadeśa-vaiyarthyādi*) do not apply.

This is because the mere cognition of the essential nature (svarūpa) as qualified by the two—namely, the delimitors of the counter-correlativity (pratiyogitāvacchedaka) and the delimitors of the locus of the delusive difference (bhedāśrayatāvacchedaka)—serves to remove the delusion of difference; thus, even though there is no difference in the object, there is a difference in the result (phala). This is seen in the case where, although the subject matter is equally the whiteness of a conch shell, the yellow delusion—which cannot be removed by inference—is observed to be removed by its direct perception (pratyakṣa).

Therefore, it has been stated in the *Vivaraṇa*: "There is no difference between recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) and direct cognition (*abhijñā*) in terms of their object (*prameya*), because what is already known through direct cognition—the identity of Devadatta—is precisely what is grasped by recognition as well. For the identity of Devadatta with himself does not fail to appear in direct cognition; nor is there any other identity of his that remains unknown and is subsequently recognized."

If it is argued that the relation of a single object to two different times is the object of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), we say no; for if there is identity, the relation to the two times is established by the two acts of direct perception (*abhijñā*) alone. Therefore, since both [cognitions] are equally concerned with the identity of the object related to the two times, it is recognition itself—by virtue of its reference to both times—that dispels the delusion of difference in the object, and not direct perception.

Thus, although the sentence "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*) does not differ from sentences such as "He is real" (*satyaḥ*) or from the word "That" (*tat*) in terms of its object of knowledge (*prameya*), it possesses validity because it removes the delusion of difference by reflecting upon two attributes. And it has been stated by Kātyāyana: "But [the word] is established [as a means of knowledge] because it effects a negation.

It might be argued: even though through recognition (*abhijñā*) one grasps the connection of a single entity with two times and the non-difference of Devadatta, recognition (*pratyabhijñā*)—by grasping either that "one thing is connected to two times" or that "the one connected to two times is a single entity"—differs in its very object of knowledge (*prameya*).

Indeed, the cognition "this" (*idam*), even when it apprehends non-difference from mother-of-pearl in reality, does not have the form "this is precisely the locus of non-mother-of-pearlness," as would be the case with the cognition "this is mother-of-pearl. Otherwise, there would be no distinction even in terms of the result, since the reflection upon two points of time exists even in the error of difference. The same applies to the statement "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*). It is replied: It is not the opinion of anyone that oneness is a qualifier (*prakāra*) in recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), because oneness is its very essence (*svarūpa*) and thus functions as the substantive (*viśeṣya*).

Since both [theories] are equal in having the non-different essential nature (*abhedasvarūpa*) as their object, it is your view that this [cognition] has both "that-ness" (*tat*) and "this-ness" (*idam*) as its modes (*prakāra*), whereas it is my view that it is entirely without modes. Furthermore, oneness (*ekatva*) is not the numerical category of unity (*ekatvasaṅkhyā*), because such a quality does not exist in [entities like] *guṇa* and so forth, and because the cognition of such a quality would not oppose the delusion of difference; rather, it has been stated that it is the essential nature consisting in the absence of difference. Otherwise, even the sentence expressing it would be "This is one" (*so 'yamekaḥ*), and not "This is that" (*so 'yam*).

In the sentence "This is that" (*so'yam*), the status of identity as a qualifier (*prakāratva*) is dismissed from afar precisely because there is no word in the sentence that expresses it. Furthermore, even when two points in time are referred to within the error of difference (*bhedabhrama*), the distinction in the resulting cognition—such as its being the substratum of the difference perceived in the error and so forth—is indeed logically consistent. For this very reason, the *Kalpataru* states: "That [sentence] by which a single object, differentiated by various limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), is conveyed would also have an undivided meaning (*akhaṇḍārtha*), just as 'the great ether' (*mahat kham*) and 'the pot-ether' (*kumbhakhaṃ*)."

The Vārttika statement, “Just as the cognition of identity arises from the expression ‘the pot-space is the great space’,” is also faultless. Thus, it is said that the sentence *tat tvam asi* has an indivisible (akhaṇḍa) meaning, because it establishes identity in an object differentiated by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), like the sentence “the pot-space is the great space. And so, the statement of Citsukhācārya—“‘Being, consciousness,’ and so forth, is a means of valid knowledge regarding an object distinct from the relation between these [qualities], because it is a means of valid knowledge, like the sense of sight and other means of valid knowledge”—is also correct.

The intended probandum (sādhya) here is stated with emphasis: that this sentence concerning truth and so forth is a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) regarding an object distinct from the relation between the meanings of its constituent words. Therefore, because validity is admitted even with respect to the related entities themselves—which are distinct from their relation—there is no "proving what is already established" (siddhasādhana). The removal of objections (kaṇṭakoddhāra) is as before. In this manner, the formulations of others should also be explained accordingly.

Therefore, O dull-witted one, you weep in vain; for this suffering of yours arises solely from delusion. It has been dispelled by the means of valid cognition; it is strange that it does not please you!
The Vedānta texts establish the nature of the Self as devoid of attributes (nirguṇa) because they reveal it as an indivisible consciousness;
and its attributelessness has been declared by the Śruti, supported by reasoning. (2)
In this world, a wretched man of poor intellect, claiming to speak the truth about what is not the truth, loudly prattles forth a spurious refutation at an improper time;
what wise person would offer a reply to him? For does a lion ever mimic the howl of a village dog? 3.
Thus ends the demonstration of the impartite nature (*akhaṇḍārthatva*) of the great sentences (*mahāvākya*), such as "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*), in the *Advaitasiddhi*.

By the scriptural testimony of *kaivalya* (isolation), the Self is indeed devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*). But [one might object]: "Its attributes are vast," according to scripture; and: "Even by the gods beginning with Brahmā and Īśāna acting together, and even by those who constantly explain it, a fraction of its qualities cannot be fully determined."

If it is argued that Brahman possesses attributes of its own level of reality (svasamānasattāka) based on the Smṛti passage, "Brahman, like Dharma, [possesses attributes] because it is an entity," and by such inferences as these, we say: not so. First of all, the possession of attributes (saguṇatva) is not established by Śruti, because passages situated within a context concerning attributes serve merely to provide qualifiers for the object of an injunction for meditation (upāsanā), and thus lack the status of being the primary purport (tatpara). Nor can there be an intention regarding qualifiers such as "having true desires" (satyakāma) and so forth, simply because they are something previously unknown (apūrvatva).

Even if it is something not previously established (*apūrva*), it is observed that what is subordinate to another (*anyaśeṣa*) lacks *tātparya* (final purport), just as in the case of "One should offer with a gruel of wild sesame (*jartila-yavāgū*) or one should offer with a gruel of *gavīdhuka*," where the status of the wild sesame gruel as a means for the oblation and its subsequent censure—"Wild sesame and *gavīdhuka* are indeed not offerings"—lack final purport because they form a single syntactical unit with the injunction "One offers with goat's milk. The same logic applies here as well.

However, those [passages] situated in the section concerning the *nirguṇa* (devoid of qualities) are otherwise established as serving to provide the objects required for the negations that are conducive to the realization of the non-dual Brahman. Nor should it be argued that the mention of specific things is redundant since all things other than Brahman are already presented by general terms such as "anything whatsoever" (*kiñcana*); for its purpose is to dispel the misconception that [these specific things], being beyond the senses, are the objects of knowledge derived from the Vedic sentences.

For this very reason, the following objection is refuted: that if there were a prohibition by scripture of what has been established by scripture, then the statement "one shall not injure" (*ahiṃsā*) would prohibit the injury involved in the *agniṣomīya* sacrifice; the statement regarding non-grasping would prohibit the grasping of the *ṣoḍaśin* cup; the statement "it is non-existent" (*asad vā*) and so forth would prohibit the reality of Brahman; and the statements concerning difference would prohibit oneness. This is because, in the present case, there is no such thing as being established by scripture. For "being established by scripture" does not mean "being occasioned by it," as that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*); nor does it mean "being cognized by it," since that is absent in the present case.

The statement regarding non-violence (*ahiṃsā*) does not share the same scope as [the injunction to sacrifice], because its subject matter is restricted to non-scriptural violence; for if they shared the same scope, an option (*vikalpa*) would result, as in the case of the injunctions to "take" or "not take" [the soma]. However, although the two statements regarding taking and not taking do indeed share the same scope, the relationship of sublation (*bādhyabādhakabhāva*) is impossible between them because neither possesses superior force; otherwise, one would be forced to abandon the very concept of an option. Furthermore, the two statements concerning the unreal and the difference do not negate the reality and unity of Brahman, because those two statements which convey reality and unity possess greater authority due to their being devoted to that very purpose.

Nor is inference capable of establishing real attributes (*tāttvika-dharma*) in Brahman. To explain: Brahman, as the subject (*dharmin*), possesses attributes co-existent with its own existence, or possesses attributes in the form of positive entities (*bhāva-rūpa*) co-existent with its stated existence, or possesses attributes that persist as long as its own nature persists, or possesses such attributes in the form of positive entities, or possesses attributes not sublated by its own cognition, or possesses such attributes in the form of positive entities, or it does not remain devoid of attributes or attributes in the form of positive entities, because it is an entity (*padārthatvāt*), or because it is a positive being (*bhāvatvāt*).

Like a pot: Brahman possesses attributes that are not sublated by its own cognition, or rather, it possesses attributes that exclude what is superimposed upon it and are not sublated by its own cognition, because it is the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*), like a mother-of-pearl shell. Brahman possesses attributes that exclude suffering and are not sublated by its own cognition, because it is non-suffering in nature (*aduḥkhātmakatva*), like a pot. Brahman is the substantive qualified by attributes that are not sublated by its own cognition, because it is an object of doubt, because it is an object of inquiry, or because it is an object of ascertainment, like a post.

Brahman possesses the mode that is the object of the purport of the Vedānta, because it is the subject matter of the inquiry into the Vedānta; whatever is thus, is so, just as Dharma is the subject matter of the inquiry into the Karma-kāṇḍa. God is one who eternally possesses all auspicious qualities, because while He always desires them, He is also capable of attaining them; whoever, at whatever time, desires something and is capable of it, possesses that thing at that time, just like Caitra.

In the following inferences—such as "Īśvara is one who has eternally abandoned all defects, because while he always desires to abandon them, he is capable of doing so; and whoever is thus [is so], like Caitra"—if the terms *dharmin* (the subject) and *svapada* (the word "himself") refer to some arbitrary subject or some arbitrary related entity, there is the fallacy of *siddhasādhana* (proving what is already established), since [the subject] would possess imagined properties (*kalpitadharma*) of the same ontological status (*samasattāka*) as a jar or other such things. If, however, they refer to Brahman, there is the fallacy of *sādhyāprasiddhi* (the unestablished nature of the probandum), because it is unestablished that the properties of a jar or similar objects have the same ontological status as Brahman, and so forth.

Nor should it be argued that—in the illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*), when defining the probandum (*sādhya*), that very [world] is the subject (*dharmin*), whereas in the thesis (*pakṣa*), when defining it, Brahman alone is the subject; for terms such as "subject" (*dharmin*) and "its own word" (*svapada*) refer to what is co-referential (*samabhivyāhṛta*). This is because the introduction of the nature of words is irrelevant to inference. Furthermore, if the term "own-nature" (*svarūpa*) likewise refers to Brahman, there is the fallacy of the unestablished probandum (*sādhyāprasiddhi*); if it refers to pots and so forth, there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*).

The refutation—that the nature of sound (*śabda*), when mentioned in conjunction [with other properties], is not a valid probans for inference—is as before. As for the statement "it does not exist without attributes" (*dharmair vinā nāvatiṣṭhate*), its meaning is that Brahman is pervaded by attributes. In that case, there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*); for at whatever time or place Brahman exists, attributes necessarily exist there as well. Indeed, neither time nor space is devoid of attributes, since the connection between *māyā* and consciousness (which constitutes time) does not coexist with liberation (*mukti*).

In the expression "not sublated by its own cognition" (*svajñānābādhya*), there is likewise the same alternative regarding the meaning of the term "its own" (*sva*) as before. For this very reason, the definition "possessing a property not sublated by its own cognition which excludes what is superimposed upon itself" is refuted; furthermore, in the definition "possessing a property that excludes suffering and is not sublated by its own cognition," there is again the same alternative regarding the meaning of "its own" as before. Moreover, [the argument] would result in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) because [the subject] possesses properties that exclude suffering. Finally, in the phrase "within the scope of the purport of the Vedānta," there is proving what is already established if one takes into account the intermediate purport (*avāntaratātparya*).

Furthermore, when stating the primary intended meaning (*tātparya*), there is a lack of establishment of the probandum (*sādhyāprasiddhi*) because the mode of the object of the primary intention of the Vedāntic statements is not well-known. Nor can the establishment of the probandum be achieved by following the words "that which" (*yat-tat*); for such verbal accompaniment is of no use for inference. In the case of the statement "God is one who has eternally attained all auspicious qualities," we also accept that He possesses attained qualities throughout time; for indeed, if He were devoid of attributes (*nirdharmakatā*), there could be no connection with time.

Furthermore, if the pure [Brahman] is made the subject (*pakṣa*), the reason (*hetu*) is unestablished (*asiddha*); if that which is conditioned (*upahita*) is made the subject, there is a shift in the subject matter (*arthāntara*). Moreover, because it possesses all auspicious qualities non-different from itself, it is impossible for it to possess those same qualities as attributes (*sadharmakatva*), and there is also the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*), since you yourself cannot maintain that the auspicious qualities such as bliss are eternal, nor can you maintain the desire to obtain them or the capacity for that purpose. For this very reason, the argument that "the desire to obtain [them] and so forth [is present] because of its being a mass of consciousness" is refuted.

If "the state of having abandoned all defects at all times" is what is to be proven, the reason is unestablished (*hetvasiddhi*), because there is a lack of capacity for such abandonment until the very final moment of mental modification (*caramavṛtti*). However, when that capacity exists, the abandonment of defects is precisely what is desired. Furthermore, if "possessing a mode" (*prakāravattva*) and so forth are the properties to be proven, the reason is also irrelevant (*aprayojaka*).

Nor is the impossibility of [the world] being a locus (*adhiṣṭhāna*) due to its being doubtful and so forth the favorable argument (*anukūlatarka*). For it has been stated that in the case of being a locus, what is essential is the possession of a differentiator superimposed by oneself, which is common to both the imagined (*kalpita*) and the non-imagined (*akalpita*); thus, there is no impossibility of that [being a locus] without a property qualified by non-sublation by one's own cognition. Furthermore, even "doubtfulness" is established simply by the fact that [the object] is not ascertained in the form of a differentiator—whether imagined or non-imagined; therefore, even that does not have an impossibility without a property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) that is itself unascertained.

Thus, the fact that suffering is non-self must be stated as being established solely by its nature as that which excludes suffering; otherwise, an infinite regress would result. For even the property that acts as the differentiator cannot be a purely positive (kevalānvayin) one, such that it could reside in itself. And so, if that [differentiator] were established even without another differentiating property, it would not suffice to prove [the original point]. If, for fear of infinite regress, one rests upon some property [as the ultimate limit], then "being a category" (padārthatva) would likewise be inconclusive (vyabhicārin).

Nor is there a lack of deviation [in the reason] because a thing cannot reside in itself; for that would entail the fallacy of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*). Nor does it follow that the reason "being an object of perception" (*dṛśyatva*) suffers from the fallacy of partial unestablishedness (*bhāgāsiddhi*) due to its non-residence in itself; for even in the absence of residence in itself, the condition that renders it unestablished—namely, being the counter-positive of an absolute non-existence residing in itself—is absent here. Therefore, inference is not a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding a property that possesses the same level of reality as Brahman.

Furthermore, scripture concerning the lower Brahman (*apara-brahman*) must have a distinct object, because a difference in subject matter is necessary to avoid contradiction with the scriptural texts stating that Brahman is devoid of attributes (*nirdharmaka*). Nor should it be argued that the higher Brahman (*para-brahman*), as distinct from the qualified (*saguṇa*), remains unestablished even now—since in your own view there exists no other entity possessing real attributes—and thus one must ask what the object of the scriptures on the qualified Brahman is. For the scriptures on the qualified Brahman do not take as their object the reality of those attributes (i.e., their ultimate existence), and the pure Brahman is established by the scriptural texts on its being devoid of attributes.
As it was stated by the authors of the *Kalpataru* in the *Antaradhikaraṇa*:
Those who are dull-witted and unable to directly realize the supreme Brahman, which is devoid of distinctions, are shown compassion through descriptions of Brahman with attributes.

"When their minds have been brought under control through the practice of the Brahman with attributes (saguṇa-brahman), that very [Brahman] manifests directly, free from the conceptualization of limiting adjuncts (upādhi).

For this reason, there is no contradiction with the Smṛti and the Sūtra. Nor should it be argued: "In the case of the Brahman with attributes, the Smṛti states 'the highest of the high' and so forth, implying a state even higher than the highest; how then can passages concerning the Brahman with attributes have the lower Brahman as their object? This is because, in comparison to the insentient (jaḍa), the limited knower (kiñcijjña) is "higher"; in comparison to him, the omniscient one is higher; and in comparison to the pure (śuddha) Brahman, even the lower Brahman is "higher."

Nor should it be argued that the two scriptural passages, "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1) and "In the beginning, this was Non-being" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.7), refer to the higher and lower Brahman respectively; for since the word "this" here refers to the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) which is the subject under discussion, it is impossible to say they refer to Brahman. Therefore, these two [passages] have as their object the fact that the phenomenal world itself existed previously in the form of its cause and did not exist in the form of its effect.

Nor do the statements regarding the taking (*grahaṇa*) and non-taking (*agrahaṇa*) concern the sacrifice (*yāga*), because—just as in the case of "He takes the *aindravāyava* cup" and so forth—the statement concerning the taking of the *ṣoḍaśin* cup may indeed have the sacrifice as its object, whereas the statement concerning non-taking has no such status, as it merely conveys the absence of that [taking].

Now, one might object: "In this way, even the scriptural passage, 'If he knows Brahman as non-existent, he himself becomes non-existent,' does not aim at establishing non-existence; rather, it must refer to the supreme liberation consisting in the attainment of emptiness (*śūnyatā*). If this is argued, we say no, because emptiness is not a human goal (*apuruṣārtha*), and because it contradicts the teachings that define liberation as the attainment of bliss (*ānanda*). Alternatively, there is no contradiction between the statements that [Brahman] is "with attributes" now and "without attributes" in another state.

Nor should it be said that by this much there is merely the impermanence of the qualities, but not the establishment of their falsity (mithyātva) as you intend; for even the reality (tāttvikatva) intended by you remains unestablished. Furthermore, the recourse to another means [of proof] is the same [for both sides]. As for the objection that Brahman would then fall into the position of being existent now and non-existent at another time, that is not so; for just as its qualitylessness (nirguṇatva) is understood at another time, its non-existence is not cognized, and thus the contingency does not arise.

Nor should it be argued that [Brahman] possesses qualities (saguṇatva) because scriptures such as "Knowledge is eternal, action is eternal, and power is eternal for the Supreme Self," and "This is the eternal majesty of the Brāhmaṇa," establish the eternality of Brahman-knowledge and so forth; for knowledge and the like, being the very nature (svarūpa) [of Brahman], cannot be established as mere attributes (guṇa). As for those [qualities] distinct from the essential nature, their "eternality" is merely figurative, insofar as they persist until the final direct realization (caramasākṣātkāra), just like the "immortality" mentioned by the Purāṇas, which—as stated in the commentary on passages such as "We have drunk Soma, we have become immortal"—is defined as the state of immortality lasting until the dissolution of all beings (abhūtasamplavasthāna).

For this very reason, it is refuted that the statement from the Taittirīya recension, "This is His eternal greatness," etc., has as its purport the eternality of qualities; for the statement from the Bṛhadāraṇyaka, "He is 'not this, not this,'" establishes a greatness consisting of a nature in which all limiting adjuncts have been negated, pertaining to a person who has renounced all desires, and thus lacks the purport of qualities residing in Brahman.

Nor should it be suspected that, because Brahman is the subject under discussion in passages such as "the controller of all," the text refers to qualities residing in Brahman; for, by way of restating the nature of the individual soul (jīva) as described in the passage beginning "this one who consists of consciousness among the vital breaths," the intent is to reveal its identity with Brahman, and thus there is no reference to qualities belonging to Brahman. Furthermore, if the word *brāhmaṇa*—which is derived from the suffix *aṇ* prescribed by the rule "one who studies that or knows that"—were taken to mean Brahman itself, it would result in the fault of metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*), since it actually denotes the knower of Brahman.

Furthermore, there is no contradiction between the statements regarding [Brahman] possessing qualities and the scriptural texts concerning its natural qualitylessness, because those former statements have as their object qualities that are adventitious (*aupādhika*). Nor should it be argued that if this adventitiousness consists in being superimposed (*adhyasta*) by means of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), it would result in the invalidity of scripture; nor that it contradicts the scriptural texts on truth (*satyatva*) which will be cited later; nor that if it consisted in being imagined (*kalpita*) by limiting adjuncts, it would contradict the scriptural texts on eternity; nor that before the creation of the limiting adjuncts such as the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), the scriptural mention of "being a seer" (*īkṣitṛtva*) and so forth would be impossible due to the non-existence of such adjuncts. For [these qualities] are like the words describing the illusions shown by a magician, which merely repeat what is seen.

This is because, since it does not inherently produce error, invalidity would not result; because the scriptural declaration of its reality is not to be interpreted otherwise; because the meaning of the scriptural declaration of its eternity has been explained otherwise; and because, even though the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) did not exist prior to creation, the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) consisting of ignorance (*avidyā*) was present. Nor is there a contradiction with the statement, "His power of knowledge and action is innate," if it is held to be adventitious through a limiting adjunct; for that is called "innate" in the sense that it is not adventitious through a material adjunct as it is in the case of people like us, nor is it acquired through yoga as it is in the case of yogis.

Nor is there an absence of a restrictive factor (*saṅkocaka*), for the very statement regarding the absence of qualities (*nirguṇavākya*) serves as that restriction. Nor is there a contradiction with the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) with "natural knowledge" (*svābhāvikajñāna*); because by the word "knowledge" (*jñāna*) one intends precisely that which has evolved from ignorance (*avidyā*) in the form of omniscience and so forth, one accepts a difference in form (*vairūpya*) despite the co-occurrence, depending on the presence or absence of a sublater—just as in the expression "the Brahmin is fire" (*pāvako brāhmaṇaḥ*). Furthermore, statements concerning qualities (*saguṇavākya*) do not have the function of making known the reality of those qualities, since "reality" (*satyatva*) is not the meaning of the constituent words (*apadārtha*).

Nor should it be argued that its establishment [as Brahman] follows from the force of the statement of its eternity, because validity—characterized by non-sublation of the object—is the rule (*autsargika*), and because of scriptural texts such as "True is that majesty of His," which establish it by way of its essential nature (*svarūpa*). For the first point has already been shown to be otherwise established; the reasoning known as the "rule" (*utsarga*) was demonstrated only with respect to non-sublation within empirical usage (*vyavahāra*). Furthermore, in passages such as "True is that majesty of His," there is no contradiction because majesty is of the very nature of the essence (*svarūpa-rūpa*); however, if it were a mere attribute (*dharma*), [the argument would fail].

The application of the term "real" (*satya*) is justified by its association with the quality of not being sublated by anything other than the direct realization of Brahman. Nor should it be argued that, if this were so, the reality of Brahman, its identity [with the individual soul], and so forth—as stated in such scriptural passages as "Brahman is real, consciousness" (*satyaṃ jñānam*) and "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*)—would likewise not be ultimately real; for there is no contradiction with the scriptures concerning the attributeless (*nirguṇa*) Brahman in this case, just as there was none in the previous instance.

Now, it may be objected: when there is a conflict between two scriptural texts (*śruti*), it is not the case that one of them has a non-ultimate subject matter; for in the *Pūrvatantra* (Mīmāṃsā) and in Grammar, it has been established that when there is no contradiction with scripture, the authority of both is maintained through methods such as restriction (*saṅkoca*) or option (*vikalpa*). To illustrate: in the tenth chapter [of the Mīmāṃsā], regarding the extended application (*codaka*) formulated in the form "one should act as in the archetype" (*prakṛtivat kuryāt*) when there is a sublation of what was obtained, the restriction (*saṅkoca*) itself takes the form "except for the threshing (*avaghāta*) in the case of *kṛṣṇala* beans," and so forth.

Thus, even in the third [case], where there is no sublation by non-attainment (*aprāptabādha*), the mantra containing the word "Indra" must be understood as having a secondary (*gauṇa*) sense with respect to the *gārhapatya* fire, in accordance with the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) in the accusative case: "the *gārhapatya*. Even in grammar, where a sublation of the preceding by the subsequent, or of the occasional (*anitya*) by the obligatory (*nitya*), and so forth, is taught, that too is merely a restriction (*saṅkoca*).

In the tenth [book of the Mīmāṃsā-sūtra], regarding the sentence "He does not choose a *ṛṣi*" found in the context of the *mahāpitṛyajña*, which is a modification (*vikṛti*), it is stated that because it forms a single syntactical unit with the phrase "one should act as in the archetype, excluding the choice of an *ṛṣi*," its purpose is indeed an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) based on its unity with the term "as in the archetype" (*prakṛtivat*) pertaining to the *mahāpitṛyajña*.

However, in cases such as "He does not perform those two at the animal sacrifice" (*na tau paśau karoti*), which occurs in proximity to the injunction for the *ājyabhāga* offerings situated within the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the archetypal *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices—where, because a syntactic unity with the word "like the archetype" (*prakṛtivat*) from the animal-sacrifice section is impossible, an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) cannot be intended—it has been stated that the purpose must be a direct prohibition (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*) through a split in the sentence (*vākya-bheda*), namely: "One should act according to the archetype, but one should not perform the *ājyabhāgas*. In that case, since the *ājyabhāgas* are not applicable to the animal sacrifice by any other means, and because there can be no total sublation of what is established by scripture, it is said that there is an option (*vikalpa*). Thus it has been stated:
For what investigator would say that when two scriptures contradict each other,
one should be authoritative while the other is unauthoritative?

If this is argued, it is not so; for in that case, since the two scriptures possess equal status as authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), absolute sublation of either one is impossible, and thus their authority was accepted as being partial through either restriction (*saṃkoca*) or option (*vikalpa*). Here, however, there is a disparity: because one [scripture] is stronger due to its being devoted to that [ultimate reality], while the other is weaker due to not being devoted to it.

As for the statement that an option (*vikalpa*) is taught in passages such as "He does not perform those two at the animal sacrifice" (*na tau paśau karoti*), that is not the case; for the passage situated within the context of the animal sacrifice (*paśu-prakaraṇa*) serves the purpose of an exclusion (*paryudāsa*), being syntactically unified with the term "according to the archetype of the animal sacrifice" (*pāśuka-prakṛtivat*); whereas the passage situated within the context of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa-prakaraṇa*) serves the purpose of praise (*stuti*), meaning "the two butter-portions (*ājyabhāgau*) do not exist at the animal sacrifice, but they do exist here. Even if the author of the *Vārttika* accepts an option, there is no fault, because there is a distinction due to the presence of a specific intended meaning (*tātparya*) in both cases.

As for the argument that—in passages such as "If it be said [the Self is not Brahman] because of the word 'modification,' no, because of abundance," "If it be said [it is not Brahman] because of the difference in instruction, no, because there is no contradiction in either case," and "Because a figurative sense is impossible"—when there is a conflict between two scriptural texts, it is stated that they intend a different, ultimate reality, and not that they have a superimposed meaning; otherwise, in the sections concerning "seeing" (īkṣati) and so forth, since qualities like "seeing" which establish the final conclusion could be superimposed upon the *pradhāna* (primordial matter) favored by the Sāṅkhya and others, the refutation of the *pradhāna* would not be established—that is not so.

In passages such as "on account of the word for a modification" (*vikāra-śabdāt*), the meaning is not that there is a contradiction [with scripture] and thus the text intends a different, ultimate reality; rather, the meaning is that the word "tail" (*puccha*) is employed because it is impossible for Brahman—which is its own primary subject—to be a limb. This is stated in the *Ṭīkā*: "The locative case is used in reference to the tail. Furthermore, regarding the sūtra of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) which states "because of the impossibility of figurative application" (*gauṇy-asambhavāt*), the meaning is that the scriptural text "from the Self, space was produced" (*ātmana ākāśaḥ saṃbhūtaḥ*) is figurative because a cause for the production of space is impossible; it does not mean that the text has a different, ultimate reality as its object.

Regarding the passage beginning with "upadeśabhedāt" (due to the difference in instruction), since the locative and ablative cases in the expression "divi divaḥ" convey respectively the sense of a locus and a point of departure, one might initially conclude that there is no recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) of the previously mentioned Brahman because of this difference in instruction. However, the meaning is as follows: even in the case of a single hawk, we observe such expressions as "the hawk is on the top of the tree" (*vṛkṣāgre śyenaḥ*) and "the hawk from the top of the tree" (*vṛkṣāgrācchyenaḥ*); thus, there is no contradiction in both modes of description applying to the very same Brahman. It does not, however, imply that there is a difference in the actual ontological reality (*tāttvikārthāntara*).

Furthermore, the act of "seeing" (*īkṣaṇa*) cannot be superimposed upon the Pradhāna, because superimposition is observed only when there is a degree of fitness (*yogyatā*). For instance, while one may superimpose the status of a king upon a minister, one does not superimpose it upon a pillar or similar objects. Thus, since the capacity for seeing is observed only in a conscious being, it is logical that this [seeing] is superimposed upon the conscious Brahman and not upon the unconscious; therefore, there is no damage to our established conclusion (*siddhānta*). Moreover, since the text can attain its authoritative status as a single syntactical unit by merely providing the object to be negated, it is not proper to assume that it establishes attributes through a split in the sentence (*vākya-bheda*).
For this very reason, there is no contradiction with the statement beginning with "For what Mīmāṃsaka... and so forth.

Now, an objection might be raised: "Just as the rule *na ktvā seṭ* functions as a negation of a negation (i.e., it negates the prohibition of the suffix *ktvā* when it is *seṭ*), why should statements concerning the qualified [Brahman] (*saguṇa-vākya*) not likewise sublate the statements concerning the unqualified [Brahman] (*nirguṇa-vākya*)? If this is asked, the answer is: No. In the illustrative example, according to the principle of the section on *paryudāsa* (exclusion), the rule *mṛḍamṛdetyādi*—though prescribed subsequently—is intended to negate the absence of the *seṭ* suffix and the *apratyaya* status (the lack of a suffix) for the root *mṛḍ*, thereby forming a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*). Consequently, it is not conceived as a negation of a negation through a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*). Thus, the case is not analogous.

Nor can it be argued that even in the present context [of the Upanishads] the term has the sense of a *paryudāsa* (exclusion); for since the repetition "not this, not this" (*neti neti*) negates everything that might be suspected [of being Brahman], it is impossible to resort to *paryudāsa*, as there is no possibility of leaving any specific thing remaining.

As for the falsity of the universe, the reality of Brahman, and the identity of the individual self and Brahman—which are respectively implied by the denial of omniscience and other attributes necessitated by [Brahman’s] being the creator of the world; which are implied by [Brahman’s] being the locus of the superimposition of the world through its being negated by knowledge as heard in scripture; and which are implied by the universal selfhood of the individual self and Brahman as heard in such texts as "He alone is all this," "The Self alone is all this," "Two birds..."; these are what are to be denied by the statements "the universe is real," "or rather non-existent," and "two birds of beautiful plumage. It is therefore by the statement "not here, no diversity" that [the text] affirms the truth [of the aforementioned].

It might be argued that [the passage] "jñānam" and "tattvamasi" are restated here; however, that is not so. For in the passages "viśvaṃ satyam" and "dvā suparṇā," there is no word indicating negation, and thus they cannot function as negators. Furthermore, although the negative particle *nañ* is present in "asadvā," it cannot function as a negator because it is conjoined with a noun. Moreover, since "dvā suparṇā" is explained in the *Paiṅgi-rahasya-brāhmaṇa* as referring to the intellect (*buddhi*) and the individual soul (*jīva*), it does not convey a difference between the individual soul and Brahman. Consequently...

Because there is a disparity between the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) and the subject of the example (*dārṣṭāntika*) in establishing the nature of negation. To explain: even if omniscience were false by virtue of being the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) of its own negation, there would be no inconsistency in its implying [other properties], since the agency of creating the world—which serves as the impeller—can be established even through a superimposed (unreal) form. However, if the falsity of the universe, the reality of Brahman, and the identity of the individual self with Brahman—once implied—are themselves negated, then the three impellers, such as "being removable by knowledge" and so forth, would become impossible; for that which is real cannot be removed by knowledge, and that which is unreal...

This is because [the Absolute] cannot be a substratum, and because if there were difference, its being the self of all would be impossible. By this, the following view is refuted: that the scripture of non-duality, or another scripture concerning the absence of qualities (*nirguṇa*), merely restates the very qualitylessness already established through the full comprehension of its intended meaning (*tātparya*) in order to negate it by means of a statement regarding qualities (*saguṇa*). For if the qualitylessness has already been established through the full comprehension of the intended meaning, it is illogical to repeat it for the sake of negation.

Now, one might object: since qualities such as being the seer are enjoined by such passages as "The Witness is consciousness, absolute, devoid of qualities," there can be no negation of them by that [text]; for that reason, the statement regarding the possession of qualities is not a mere restatement (anuvāda). Otherwise, even omniscience and other such attributes would lack even a conventional (vyāvahārika) status; for there is no intermediate intention (avāntaratātparya) regarding prohibited acts such as the killing of a Brahmin.

If it is argued that the omniscience and other attributes of the Brahman taught in the Upaniṣads are not established by inference or other means of knowledge, we say no; for, since these [attributes] are mentioned as restatements of the status of being a witness—which is itself established through nescience—they serve, by way of an indirect definition (taṭasthalakṣaṇa), to point toward Brahman and do not have those qualities as their primary purport. Thus, it is logically consistent that they negate such qualities.

Nor should it be argued that, just as there is no subordinate intention (*avāntara-tātparya*) regarding prohibited acts such as the killing of a Brahmin, so too here, in the absence of such an intention, even conventional omniscience would not exist; for in the case of the corporeal form of a deity and similar matters, which are accepted as means for injunctions and praises, there is neither contradiction with nor prior attainment by other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Just as those [forms] are established merely by not being abandoned, so too here, omniscience and the like—which are accepted as being conducive to the prohibitions and are not attained through other means of knowledge—are not contradicted by conventional means of knowledge.

In the state of empirical transaction (*vyavahāra*), its status as empirical is established merely through non-abandonment [of the conventional]. However, the distinction is that acts such as the killing of a Brahmin are already established by other means of knowledge (*māna*). Nor is the capacity to convey that [meaning] necessarily restricted to its primary purport (*tātparya*); for even though a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*) conveys the qualifier, it lacks purport regarding the qualifier itself, since the qualified entity is something distinct. Furthermore, if there were purport regarding omniscience and so forth when these are mentioned as subordinate elements, it would result in a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*). Nor, then, can there be purport regarding both the fact that meditation (*upāsanā*) is an action to be performed and the fact that Viṣṇu is the Self within a single injunction such as "one should meditate on the Self."

It should not be said that there is a contradiction with the *smṛti*, because, according to the principle of the *devatādhikaraṇa*, the intent in both cases is the establishment of both [the attributes and the substrate], since the *smṛti* is not an independent means of valid knowledge (*apramāṇa*). Even in passages such as "He who is omniscient," although they do not occur within a context of meditative worship (*upāsanā*), their intent is to establish Brahman by way of an incidental definition (*taṭasthalakṣaṇa*); thus, there is no intent regarding the qualifying attributes. Otherwise, there would arise a contradiction with the initial proposition that through the knowledge of one, all is known.

Nor should it be argued that in the passage "One should meditate [on the Self] as the Self," non-duality (advaita) would fail to be established because it is subordinated to meditation as its object of worship; for the word *upāsti* here does not denote an action, since it has the same meaning as the verb *vid* (to know) in the subsequent sentence, "By this, all this is known. Furthermore, there can be no injunction regarding knowledge, as such an injunction will be refuted later. Nor is the scriptural mention of an injunction purposeless, as it serves to turn the mind away from external objects and direct it toward the inner Self (pratyagātman).

Furthermore, by considering the subsequent statement, "He who worships another deity," which is intent upon censuring the perception of difference, there is no suspicion at all that the passage is concerned with worship (*upāsti*). Nor can the conclusion be interpreted in accordance with the introduction; for the conclusion is more authoritative, as it does not contradict the initial proposition that "by knowing this one, all this is known," which asserts that through the knowledge of a single thing, everything is known.

As for the argument that, in the section on the "Combination of Attributes" (*Guṇopasaṃhārapāda*), under the sūtra "Bliss and so forth belong to the Principal" (*Ānandādayaḥ pradhānasya*), it is stated that bliss and other qualities mentioned in such scriptures as "Brahman is bliss" are to be combined; and under the sūtra "Interchange" (*Vyatihāra*), because the Lordship of the Lord in the individual soul, or the individuality of the individual soul in the Lord, is taught as an object of meditation—as seen in the *Uttaratāpanīya* and other texts where the meditation on the attributeless (*nirguṇa*) is taught—just as there is the establishment of the identity of bliss and so forth with the attributeless, so too let there be the reality (*tāttvikatā*) of [qualities] such as having true desires (*satyakāmatva*). That is not so.

Because the sūtra *ānandādayaḥ* (Brahma Sūtra 3.3.11) effects a synthesis of the literal meanings of the constituent words for the sake of establishing the indivisible sentence-meaning (*akhaṇḍavākyārtha*) of the indicated sense (*lakṣya*), it does not state that [the attributes] are objects of meditation (*upāsya*).

Furthermore, regarding the sūtra on "mutual exchange" (*vyatihāra*; BS 3.3.37), which concerns the meditation on the non-difference of the Lord from the individual soul—as expressed in the text, "He who is I, He is that; He who is that, He is I"—or the meditation on the non-difference of the individual soul from the Lord, this is intended solely to show that the non-difference of the individual soul and the Lord, though taught in scriptural passages situated within the context of meditation, must be firmly established even by way of meditation upon the qualified Brahman (*saguṇopāsana*). Thus, although unity (*aikya*) may be an object of meditation, its lack of ultimate reality (*atāttvikatva*) is not established merely by that, as is the case with [attributes] such as having true desires (*satyakāmatva*).

Furthermore, qualities such as "having true desires" (*satyakāmatva*) and so forth do not possess ultimate reality in the same way that oneness does, because there is a distinction between those qualities being taught by statements intended for that purpose within a context of meditation (*upāsanā*) and those not so taught; for in the *Uttaratāpanīya* and other texts, the meditation mentioned is subordinate to knowledge (*jñāna*), and since meditation has a qualified object, it cannot have the attributeless (*nirviśeṣa*) Brahman as its object.

As for the claim that—just as when qualities such as "having true desires" (*satyakāma*) are taught even for the purpose of meditation, the Lord (*Īśvara*) is established as possessing those qualities, so too is unity established—this is not the case upon careful consideration of the commentary. There, the meaning is that the Lord is established as being *with* qualities (*saguṇa*), but it does not mean that the qualities themselves are established; for, in accordance with the scriptural texts concerning the qualityless (*nirguṇa*), the intention lies solely in the *atadguṇasaṃvijñāna-bahuvrīhi* interpretation [where the qualities are not understood as belonging to the subject].

And thus, upon the establishment of oneness, it is the Lord who serves as the illustrative example, not the quality. We do not disregard that which is established by the very fact of the matter. The commentary should be interpreted as follows: "Because of the teaching of qualities such as 'having true desires,' the Lord and others are established as possessing those qualities."

Now, one might object: "Since there is an equality between the passages concerning bliss (*ānanda*) and so forth and the passages concerning having true desires (*satyakāma*) and so forth—in that both are not contradicted by other means of knowledge, are not already established by them, do not explicitly mention an injunction for meditation, and are equally opposed by the scriptures on the attributeless (*nirguṇa*) Brahman—how can it be determined that qualities such as bliss are real (*tāttvika*), whereas qualities such as having true desires are unreal (*atāttvika*). If this is asked, we reply: No, because the fact that qualities such as bliss are the very nature of Brahman serves as the determining factor for the absence of contradiction with the scriptures on the attributeless Brahman.

Nor should it be said that, on the basis of such scriptural texts as "The Blessed Lord consists of knowledge" and "The Blessed Lord consists of strength," as well as "He consists of all auspicious qualities," there is non-difference [of the Lord] from Brahman even in the case of powers, strengths, and so forth; for we too harbor an aversion to the existence of qualities distinct from Brahman, and because the acceptance of the relation of quality and qualified in a state of non-difference is merely a technical convention.

As for the objection that if the meditation on the qualified Brahman (*saguṇopāsti*) were an error, then the meditation on the unqualified Brahman (*nirguṇopāsti*) would likewise be an error, resulting in the non-attainment of the perfect fruit and the non-realization of Brahman; and as for the rebuttal that—although the meditation on the unqualified is indeed an error—it nevertheless yields the perfect fruit, like the error of perceiving a gem in the luster of a gem; as it has been said: "Just as even an error, when it corresponds to reality, bestows the perfect fruit, so too does the meditation on the reality of Brahman bestow the fruit of liberation. [This is not so. For in that case, since the meditation on the unqualified is an error, its result would be the attainment of a gem, whereas the result of the meditation on the qualified is the attainment of the reflection of the gem. Thus, there is no equality between the two. Furthermore, the meditation on the unqualified is not an error at all, because it is established by the scriptures (*āgama*). Moreover, the meditation on the unqualified is not an error, because it is the object of a valid cognition (*pramā*). This is because the scripture, which is the means of knowledge for supersensuous objects, establishes the existence of the unqualified Brahman through the negation of all attributes. Therefore, the meditation on the unqualified is not an error. Consequently, the objection that the perfect fruit and the realization of Brahman would not occur is baseless. Thus, it is established that the meditation on the unqualified is the cause of the supreme goal. Hence, it is concluded that the meditation on the unqualified is superior to the meditation on the qualified. Therefore, the meditation on the unqualified is the most excellent among all meditations. Nor should it be argued that there is no failure to establish Brahman because, even if meditation (*upāsana*) is an error, the knowledge arising from the Word (*śabda*) is valid (*pramā*); for the same consequence would apply here as well, since in this case too, just as with the "jewel-nature" in the luster of a jewel, Brahman lacks falsity, and thus meditation also has the real Brahman as its object. That is not so; for while meditation on the qualified (*saguṇa*) Brahman is an error because it has a qualified object, meditation on the unqualified (*nirguṇa*) Brahman and the like is not an error, as it has the indeterminate (*nirviśeṣa*) as its object.

In the same way, this applies to verbal cognitions of both the qualified (*saguṇa*) and the unqualified (*nirguṇa*): although a statement concerning the qualified has as its object the reality of the substantive portion (*viśeṣyāṃśa*), it nonetheless has as its object the unreality of the qualifying portion (*viśeṣaṇāṃśa*). For this very reason, the objection that—since meditation on Brahman (*brahmadhyāna*), which is produced by verbal cognition of Brahman and generates direct intuition (*aparokṣadhī*) of It, would itself have as its object something other than Brahman—the same would follow for hearing (*śravaṇa*) and the other means is refuted; because those [means] do not have the qualified as their object, whereas meditation (*upāsti*) does have the qualified as its object. Nor is it the case that in the sūtra *īkṣatikarma* (BS 1.3.13), "the object of seeing," seeing (*īkṣati*) and meditation (*dhyāna*) are identical, since they stand in a relationship of cause and effect.
The general rule is that [scripture] has reality as its object, because it is seen to be so.

Thus, one should not say that there is a contradiction with the *Bhāmatī*, which states: "He beholds the Person dwelling in the city, higher than the high" (*parāt paraṃ puriśayaṃ puruṣamīkṣate*), because by declaring that the Supreme Brahman alone—the object of the act of beholding—is to be meditated upon as the "Person higher than the high," it is shown that there is no contradiction, since the object of meditation is described as qualified by the adjunct of support in the three-measured *oṃ* syllable, and thus lacks the status of being the pure [Brahman]; furthermore, by taking the substantive element [the Person], it is logically possible for it to have the same object as the act of beholding.

As for the objection that the meditation on identity and so forth constitutes a stream of invalid cognitions, and the subsequent claim that it is equivalent to the meditation on the qualified (saguṇa) Brahman—that is incorrect.
