For the knowledge of identity produced by sentences concerning identity found within the context of the qualified [Brahman] has a qualified object, as it is subsumed under the meditation on the qualified Brahman; whereas the knowledge of identity produced by independent [texts on] identity has the non-qualified (nirviśeṣa) as its object, and thus differs from the meditation on the qualified which has a qualified object.

Nor should it be argued that—since oneness and so forth are conveyed by two types of sentences consisting of injunctions and non-injunctions, just as there is both the state of being an object of meditation (*dhyeyatva*) and the state of being an object of knowledge (*jñeyatva*)—omniscience and other qualities, though subjects of injunctive worship, must also be objects of knowledge because they are conveyed by non-injunctive sentences such as "He is omniscient" regarding the true nature of reality. For those [qualities] serve merely as indirect indicators (*taṭastha-lakṣaṇa*) for the realization of the Supreme Brahman, and thus, unlike [the identity taught in] "That thou art," they lack the status of being the primary purport (*tatparatva*).

For this very reason, the objection that—since agency and other attributes must be superimposed upon Brahman and subsequently sublated—the causal statements regarding Brahman cannot be shown to have a unified meaning (samanvaya) even in the case of Brahman (just as they cannot in the case of names), and thus the first chapter on *Samanvaya* would fail to begin—is hereby refuted. This is because, although names do not possess a unified meaning with Brahman due to being its modifications (*vikāra*), Brahman itself is not a modification and is the object of knowledge for those seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*). Consequently, it is possible for the causal statements to have their ultimate purport (*tātparya*) directed toward Brahman alone by way of teaching agency and other attributes as its "indirect" or "circumstantial" characteristics (*taṭastha-lakṣaṇa*); since the unified meaning is therefore necessary, the commencement of that chapter is indeed possible.

Nor should it be argued that [the Self] is an object of knowledge because, starting from the passage "The Self which is free from evil," it is heard that "He who is of true desires and true resolves is indeed to be sought, He is to be understood," whereby qualities such as having true desires are to be known together with qualities such as being free from evil.

Although qualities such as being free from evil (*apahatapāpmatva*) enter the scope of what is to be investigated (*jijñāsya*) as part of the essential nature (*svarūpa*), qualities such as having true desires (*satyakāmatva*) cannot be objects of investigation because they fall outside the essential nature. Therefore, they are not referred to by the word "that" (*tat*). If they were not part of the essential nature, then since they too would not be referred to, there would be a reference only to the substantive (*viśeṣya*) itself, just as in the example: "Bring that man who has brindled cows and much wealth."

Therefore, the following argument is refuted: that because attributes such as "He is the Lord of all, He is the sovereign of beings" are stated, and because these are declared to be objects of knowledge for those seeking liberation in passages such as "Brahmins desire to know Him through the study of the Vedas," and because after stating "He who is all-knowing, all-perceiving, whose glory is on earth," it is said "The wise behold Him through the realization of that," thereby indicating that He is the object of immediate valid cognition (*aparokṣapramā*), and because of the scriptural testimony regarding the omniscience of the Fourth State (*turīya*) in the passage "The Fourth is the all-seeing Being"—it follows that omniscience and other such qualities are established as real.

As for the objection that if qualities such as being free from sin (*apahatapāpmatva*) were the objects of meditation, they could also exist in the elemental ether (*bhūtākāśa*), which would contradict the *Daharādhikaraṇa*—which establishes that the small ether (*daharākāśa*) is Brahman—that is not so; for although the absolute absence of attributes belonging to a conscious being, such as the lack of sin and so forth, might possibly exist in an insentient thing, it is impossible to conceive of desires, volitions, and the like in an insentient entity, and thus there is no contradiction.

As for the statement, "True is that greatness of his," since it prescribes truthfulness (*satyatva*) by referring back to the greatness mentioned in the direct Vedic declaration (*śruti*)—"He [is] that"—in the same way that the *āhavanīya* fire is prescribed in reference to the mere act of *homa*, omniscience and other such qualities are also true. Furthermore, although the passage beginning with "True is that greatness of his" occurs within the *Aindra-sūkta*, the term *brahman* is used in the verse, "I seek that [power], O thou of heroic strength; that is the *brahman*, for the sake of ancient thought," and thus [it is said]: "Indra caused the sun to shine."

[The opponent argues: "Because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of illuminating the sun found in the passage beginning with 'For in Indra all beings are centered,' and by the logic of the *Jyotir-adhikaraṇa*, it is established that this hymn refers to the Supreme Lord. This is not so, because the greatness of the essential nature (*svarūpa*) alone is stated to be real in view of its contradiction with the scriptural texts on the absence of qualities (*nirguṇatva*); because the use of the genitive case is merely figurative (*upacarita*); and because even the attributes are said to possess only empirical reality (*vyāvahārika-satyatva*). Nor is the existence of Brahman (*brahma-sattva*) likewise [merely empirical].

This is because the expression "the truth of truth" would contradict the demonstration of an unsurpassed reality (*niratiśaya-sattva*), and because it would be impossible for [Brahman] to be the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*). Nor does this imply that it possesses distinctions (*saviśeṣatva*); for its being without distinction (*nirviśeṣatva*) has already been established as the true nature of reality (*tattva*). Furthermore, [this is not contradicted by] such scriptural passages as "He who knows the Self as distinct," and so forth, nor by the statement: "To him who knows me as free from all defects and enriched with the totality of all qualities, I, being pleased, shall grant liberation, and not otherwise."
Knowing Me as the enjoyer of sacrifices and austerities, the Great Lord of all worlds,
and the friend of all beings, one attains peace.

It must not be argued that because liberation is declared in such Smṛtis to arise from knowledge possessing attributes (*saviśeṣa-jñāna*), therefore only knowledge with a specific mode (*saprakāraka-jñāna*) is the cause of liberation; for those passages are merely *arthavādas* intended to enjoin the meditation on the qualified (*saguṇa-upāsanā*) as a means to purify the *sattva*, which in turn serves as an auxiliary to the direct realization of the attributeless (*nirguṇa-sākṣātkāra*)—the actual cause of supreme liberation—and they do not establish that [qualified knowledge] is itself the direct cause of liberation. Nor is the scriptural statement regarding liberation from the knowledge of the attributeless to be interpreted in the same way; for there is a difference between those two cases based on whether the text is intent upon that subject (*tatpara*) or not, and furthermore, because other fruits are heard to result from the knowledge of the qualified.

Although the hearing of other fruits—such as "in his family there is no one ignorant of Brahman"—is common even to the knowledge of the attributeless (nirguṇa), and the justification of these as being for the sake of praise is likewise the same, and the statement that both yield fruits according to the principle of the distinctness of conjunctions (saṃyogapṛthaktva-nyāya) is also the same; nevertheless, there is a distinction between the knowledge of the attributeless and the knowledge of the qualified (saguṇa) due to whether or not they penetrate the reality of the substratum, and because the liberation produced by the knowledge of the qualified is merely an intermediate liberation (avāntara-mukti).

Nor should it be argued that because of the statement "having shaken off merit and demerit," which speaks of the cessation of all karma, this must be the state of supreme liberation (*paramamukti*); for this [passage] refers to karmas other than those that cause the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of the reality of Brahman, and since there is no destruction of ignorance (*avidyā*), the status of supreme liberation is not established. Nor should it be argued that even a liberation produced by the knowledge of the attributeless (*nirguṇa*) is merely intermediate, while the emptiness (*śūnyatā*) described in the Śruti passage "He is indeed non-existent" is the supreme liberation.

Because emptiness (*śūnyatā*), being of the nature of non-bliss, would not constitute a human goal (*apuruṣārtha*), and because the statement "it is simply non-existent," etc., does not establish emptiness. As for the claim that a sentence negating the manifold (*niṣprapañca-vākya*)—which stands in proximity to injunctions regarding specific qualities—cannot negate those enjoined qualities, that is not so; for a sublation occurs through the contraction [of a general rule] only when the negating authority is of equal status [with the injunction], which is not the case here.

As for the objection that, because it occurs merely within a context of meditative worship (*upāsanā*), the infinity (*anantatva*) and other qualities mentioned in the scripture "This is that Infinite" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.9.1)—which reside in the meditation on the *udgītha*—are merely objects of worship in the case of the elemental ether (*bhūtākāśa*), and thus it would be improper to declare Brahmanhood based on such marks as infinity in the *Ākāśādyadhikaraṇa* (Brahma Sūtra 1.1.22–23), that is not so. For even though these qualities reside in a context of worship, since there is no contradiction with the scriptures concerning the attributeless (*nirguṇa*) Brahman, their reality is accepted. And since those qualities cannot possibly exist in the elemental ether and the like, the commencement of that specific section (*adhikaraṇa*) is indeed justified.

As for the claim that qualities such as "having true desires" (*satyakāmatva*) are heard in a context not concerning meditation (*anupāsti-prakaraṇa*), that is not so; for it is possible that they are to be extracted from their context—just like the mantras for addressing Pūṣan and others—or that they serve a merely laudatory purpose (*stāvakatva*), just like the statement regarding the twelve *upasads*.

As for the argument that because there is a difference in meaning due to piercing and so forth, the principle stated regarding the extraction of mantras such as "I pierce everything" (*sarvaṃ pravidhya*) from the context of meditation would apply by analogy to sentences concerning Ananta and the rest—and that if those sentences were intended for meditation or for the nature of reality, then sentences concerning the qualified Brahman (*saguṇa-vākya*) would likewise be so—that is not correct.

In such statements as "Knowledge is its own nature, the supreme truth, infinite," and so forth, there is no purpose for the excellence of infinity and other qualities because they exist by their very nature; furthermore, since such passages are intent solely upon the reality of the thing itself, they lack the dual character (of referring both to the nature and the qualities). Even though a passage concerning infinity situated within a section on meditation might possess that dual character, a statement regarding qualities cannot possess it here due to its contradiction with the scriptures concerning the attributeless (nirguṇa) Brahman.

Nor does it follow that omniscience and the like would thereby become merely apparent (prātītika), as in the case of the "cow of speech" (vāgdhenu) and so forth; for while the "cow of speech" and such are indeed apparent because they are objects of intentional superimposition, qualities such as having true desires cannot exist in anyone other than God, and thus they are not objects of intentional superimposition.

[Objection: But surely, meditation on the non-existent is not possible, because of such Smṛti passages as: "The Vedas do not speak of what is non-existent; nor do the followers of the Veda meditate [on it]. Alas, those who destroy themselves do not practice meditation on the non-existent," and also because of the prohibition in the Saṅkarṣaṇa-sūtra: "Inanimate objects, the unreal, and the unworthy are not to be meditated upon, due to the absence of fruit and the occurrence of the opposite. [Reply: This is not so, because the Smṛti and the Sūtra are intended to prohibit meditation on that which is absolutely non-existent, and thus there is no contradiction with [the present case of] "one should meditate on Speech as a cow" and similar instances.

Furthermore, it is observed that even that which is merely apparent (prātītika) can be an object of meditation. Nor should it be argued that in those cases the word "cow" in the other scriptural passage, "One should meditate on the night as a cow approaching," is used figuratively; or that in the passage, "One should meditate on the woman as fire," the word "fire" is used figuratively because she is the locus for the offering in the form of semen—as supported by the scriptural statement "offering semen"—or that it is etymological according to the method stated in the Commentary, rather than being a case of superimposition (āropa). For when superimposition allows for the primary (mukhya) sense of a term, it is improper to resort to a figurative (gauṇa) interpretation.

Nor does this entail the abolition of figurative usage; for where no meditation is heard of, figurative usage is appropriate because superimposition would be purposeless, and because it is improper to assume a derivative meaning when the conventional meaning is somehow possible.

By this [it is meant]: in the passage "Nāma Brahma," the word *brahma* is used figuratively (*gauṇa*) with respect to the name and so forth—which are the substrates (*adhiṣṭhāna*)—based on the very traditional teaching (*smṛti*) that says, "One should meditate on Hari as Brahman, and Uṣas is the one who identifies with Name. In this context, the nominative case in *nāma* may signify the locative case, as in the expression "Vasanta is the Māruta," or the nominative in *brahma* may signify the ablative case, as in the expression "The Brāhmaṇa was his mouth," according to the rule *supāṃ suluk...* Otherwise, [one would contradict the fact that] from those like the Blessed One we have heard: "He crosses over..."

The argument that it would be improper to speak of the worship of a name to Nārada when he had asked, "What is sorrow?"—and that even in the case of an image, the fruit arises only from the cognition of the deity's true essence and not from the cognition of the non-essence of the deity, because [the scripture] prohibits the notion of a stone being the deity with such statements as "the cognition of a stone is a cognition of earth for the purpose of sacrifice"—is refuted; for when primacy can be established through superimposition (*āropa*), it is improper to resort to a secondary sense (*gauṇatva*), and because if there were an absence of grammatical coordination (*samānavibhaktikatva*), it would result in a syntactical inconsistency (*ananvaya*) of the words.

Likewise, even in the case of images and the like, since they are treated as the deity itself through superimposition (*āropa*), it is indeed improper to regard that [superimposed] status as secondary (*gauṇa*). Nor can it be argued that such a view is precluded by the prohibition, "The worship of the earth is not [the worship of] the Deity" (*bhauma ijyadhīḥ*); for that [prohibition] aims at dispelling the delusion that there is no conscious deity other than the earth, and thus does not prohibit superimposition. Furthermore, the meditation on what is non-Self (*anātma-upāsti*) was introduced merely as a means to teach the primary Brahman, according to the analogy of the branch and the moon; for it is said, "Know that alone to be Brahman, not this which they worship [as qualified by attributes]" (*tadeva brahmatvaṃ viddhi nedaṃ yadidamupāsate*), referring to the object of worship as characterized by qualities.

And because of the negation of Brahman-hood [in the case of the individual soul]. It should not be argued that in the scriptural passage, "It is indeed other than the known, and also other than the unknown," there is a negation of non-scriptural knowledge or of incomplete knowledge; and therefore, in passages such as "That alone is Brahman," there is likewise a negation of non-scriptural meditation or of incomplete meditation, but not a negation of the object of worship being Brahman—otherwise, it would contradict the scriptural text, "From meditating upon that... For in the passage beginning with "It is indeed other," the term "known" refers to an object of cognition (*prameya*).

Because your stated point lacks a supporting example, as it aims to establish self-luminosity by contrast with non-cognizable things such as a jar or a rabbit's horn; furthermore, even if the status of Brahman were denied in the object of worship, there would be no contradiction with the Śruti passage, "By meditating upon Him" (*tasyābhidhyānāt*), since the word *abhidhyāna* denotes *nididhyāsana* (reflective meditation), and even if it refers to *dhyāna* (meditation), there is no contradiction because it serves the purpose of gradual liberation (*kramamukti*). Therefore, Brahman is devoid of attributes (*nirguṇa*) due to the absence of evidence for its having attributes, and because there exists evidence that contradicts its being endowed with attributes (*saguṇa*).

Nor is there a lack of proof, because the scriptural texts concerning falsity (*mithyātva*) and the texts concerning the absence of qualities (*nirguṇa*) possess subverting power; for the manner in which the scriptural texts on falsity would fail to subvert has already been refuted in both the *Mithyātva-vāda* and the *Akhaṇḍārtha-vāda*. Now, one might object: "What is the determining factor here that the statement regarding the absence of qualities subverts the statement regarding the possession of qualities, but not vice versa? Nor can the statement regarding the absence of qualities be considered stronger simply by virtue of being a negation, for that would lead to the absurd conclusion that a statement such as 'Non-existent indeed was this in the beginning' would be stronger than a statement such as 'Being alone, my dear, was this in the beginning'. If this is raised, we say no, because the superiority [of the latter] has already been explained according to the logic of the "successive disqualification" (*apacchedanyāya*).

Furthermore, [the Nirguṇa texts] possess greater authority because they are prohibitions; whereas in the passage "or non-existent" (*asadvā*), the word "non-existent" refers to the unmanifested [state] and thus is not a prohibition, so it does not have greater authority by this same logic. This is because the Nirguṇa statements, culminating in the supreme human goal, possess greater authority as being *tatpara* (intent upon that); whereas the Saguna statements, being recited in proximity to them, must be interpreted in conformity with them according to the maxim "that which is near to what has a fruit [is subordinate to it]. Nor can knowledge of the Saguna Brahman be the cause of liberation, since that has already been refuted.

For this very reason—the impossibility of a combination due to the contradiction between having qualities (*saguṇatva*) and being devoid of qualities (*nirguṇatva*), and because an option (*vikalpa*) is impossible regarding an established reality as it is in the case of ritual performance—when one must be sublated by abandoning its perceived meaning, it is appropriate that it be the *nirguṇa* statement, and not the stronger *saguṇa* statement; thus [the opponent's view] is refuted, since the strength [of the latter] is unestablished.

Nor should it be argued that the statement regarding the qualified [Brahman] (*saguṇavākya*) possesses greater force—due to its lack of contradiction according to the principle of the section on the opening statement (*upakramādhikaraṇanyāya*), because the scriptural text concerning the unqualified (*nirguṇaśruti*) is delayed by its dependence on the knowledge of its counter-correlate (*pratiyogijñāna*), whereas the inferential mark (*liṅga*) proceeds more swiftly than scripture, and because the qualified statement has a specific scope like the rule "one offers in the footstep" (*pade juhoti*). This is because the principle of the section on the opening statement applies only to cases where the concluding portion (*upasaṃhāra*) is otherwise established, and such a case does not exist here.

Because a sentence containing a specific quality (saguṇavākya) possesses strength due to its rapid application by way of presenting its own counter-correlate, it would follow that even a sentence concerning the grasping [of the moon] would possess such strength; consequently, there would be no room for optionality (vikalpa). This is because a sentence concerning a particular is stronger only when it stands on an equal footing with a means of knowledge (pramāṇa) whose object is general, and in the present case, that condition is absent.

By this, the argument that [the scripture concerning the Self] possesses superior authority due to its lack of scope—similar to the injunction "one should recite at the *dīkṣaṇīyā* sacrifice"—is refuted; for the scripture regarding the attributeless [Self] has scope within the qualities such as *sattva*, just as in scriptural and traditional texts like "The divine power of the Self is concealed by its own qualities" and "For this divine [nature] consists of the qualities. Furthermore, the maxim of "that which has scope versus that which lacks scope" applies only to cases where the two items are of equal status. For this very reason, superiority cannot be established even on account of multiplicity, according to the maxim: "Even a hundred blind men do not see."

Nor does the strength of those words—such as "Brahmā" and so on—which convey attributes (guṇas), arise from their being depended upon for the negation of attributes performed after designating the substratum (dharmin) by means of words that require a ground for application (pravṛttinimitta). This is because the grounds for application are not intended to be significant as qualifiers of the subject, just as in the case of the singularity of the cup (grahaikatva). Furthermore, it is not a settled rule under the principle of the singularity of the cup that once the essential nature of the subject has been established, whatever is additional to that is precisely what is not intended; otherwise, even the "cup-ness" (grahatva) would have to be unintended.

Therefore, it must be said that in the *Havirārti-nyāya*, it was stated: "We tolerate the qualification by the oblation (*havis*), but we do not tolerate the state of being both. This principle applies where the word *yat* presents the locus (*dharmin*) by imparting its basis for application (*pravṛttinimitta*); however, where it presents [the locus] through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), this principle does not operate.

Nor should it be argued that even by means of a word used in a secondary sense (*lakṣaka*), the nature of the reality must be indicated as being exclusively excluded from others and unmixed; otherwise, there would be a negation of some attribute or other [rather than the intended object]. For, just as in the case of "the Ganges" (*gaṅgāyām*) and so forth, one obtains the riverbank which is excluded from other rivers, here too, since the object itself is inherently excluded, it is possible for that very reality to be the subject of indication (*uddeśya*). What, then, is the use of providing a specific attribute? Nor should it be argued—on the analogy of the "goat-sacrifice" (*chāgapaśu*) rule—that a statement regarding the absence of qualities (such as "devoid of the three qualities" or "without... [is merely figurative].

It should not be said that there is a restrictive inclusion (*viśeṣopasaṃhāra*) of specific qualities and so forth by means of [the phrase] "by means of defects such as qualities" and so on; for, since the negation of everything that has been suggested is understood through the force of the repetition (*vīpsā*) in "not this, not this" (*neti neti*), it is impossible to leave behind only a few specific [qualities].

For this very reason, just as in the case of the injunction "curd must be protected from crows," the prohibition of the three qualities (*traiguṇya*) and so forth has a general scope; because there is no contradiction since scripture is not an authority regarding omniscience (*sārvajñya*) and the like, here too—just as with the word "crow"—there is an equal reliance on the support of other means of knowledge (*mānāntara*). Nevertheless, if one were to restrict [the prohibition] to specific cases, it would follow that the general rule "one should not harm any living beings" would be restricted to the specific instance "a Brāhmaṇa is not to be killed. This is because, just as there is an absence of an injunction regarding useless violence, there is likewise an absence of an injunction regarding qualities such as omniscience; thus, the symmetry of the prohibition is logically established.

Therefore, the following argument is refuted: that because the scripture states, "seeing the dharmas as separate," and by the maxim *saviśeṣaṇe hi* ("for when there is a qualification"), the separateness of the qualities alone is prohibited, it is logical that the same prohibition applies elsewhere by analogy.

This is because the maxim *saviśeṣaṇe hi* operates only when there is an obstruction to the primary object (*viśeṣya*), whereas in the present case there is no such obstruction; furthermore, the scriptural testimony of omniscience has been shown not to constitute an obstruction, and since the negation of separateness leaves only Brahman remaining, this would merely be a statement of non-dualism under a different name.

As for the argument that—since there is no exclusion of either one when knowledge (*jñāna*) and bliss (*ānanda*) are non-different, there is likewise no exclusion of either the attribute (*dharma*) or the substratum (*dharmin*]; otherwise, liberation would not be the supreme human goal (*apumartha*) due to the absence of either the manifestation of bliss or of knowledge—that is not so; for the term "either one" (*ekatarā*), which implies difference, cannot apply to the two individual instances (*vyakti*) of knowledge and bliss. This is because, in your own system, the non-difference between the quality (*guṇa*) and the qualified individual (*guṇin*) is possible, rendering such a definition merely a technical convention (*paribhāṣāmātra*).

As for the argument that because qualities are mentioned both before and after the passage "The Witness, the Consciousness," even the statement regarding the absence of qualities situated between them must be interpreted as being subordinate to those qualities—according to the logic of the *upāṃśuyāja* sacrifice—that is not correct. For, having set aside the qualities as incidental, these passages have Brahman as their primary purport, and thus there is no intentionality (*tātparya*) regarding the qualities. Therefore, the objection that the term "devoid of qualities" (*nirguṇa*) cannot logically negate all qualities whatsoever—on the grounds that it would contradict the injunctions of "being a witness" and so forth contained in words like "the Witness"—is refuted. This is because even here, the purport does not lie in [affirming] "being a witness" and the like.

And thus, this very nature of the object—consisting of the form of Brahman as characterized by being the seer and so forth—is the actual meaning of the scripture, since the authority of the scripture is possible only therein. Consequently, such statements as "Wherever a meaning of the scripture is perceived as both reasonable and unreasonable, there the reasonable meaning alone should be accepted" are more appropriately established within our own system. Therefore, since the principles of *upakrama* (initial statement) and so forth pertain to other subjects, the possession of qualities (*saguṇatva*) cannot be established on their strength.

As for the argument that the existence of qualities (*saguṇatva*) is established because the various attributes are respected in such sūtras as "On account of the teaching of those qualities within" (*antastaddharmopadeśāt*) and "On account of the designation of those qualities in the inner ruler with respect to the divine, etc. (*antaryāmyadhidaivādiṣu taddharmavyapadeśāt*), as being the means of proving the respective conclusions of those sections—that is not so; for the establishment of the conclusion is possible by taking up qualities that are merely superimposed and related to Brahman alone, since [the sūtras] remain indifferent to the ultimate reality of those qualities.

As for the claim that—just as in the case of the two statements regarding non-violence (*ahiṃsā*) and the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice—the possibility of non-contradiction through having different scopes applies here too, yet the statement of the saguṇa texts being non-authoritative arises from "friendship toward the Saugatas" (Buddhists)—that is not so. For even though sublation is necessary because the nirguṇa text is stronger due to its being devoted to that [reality], the assertion of the saguṇa text's authority is nothing more than hostility toward the proponents of Brahman. Therefore, due to the sublation by the nirguṇa texts, the saguṇa text is not intended to convey the ultimate reality.

Experience is without distinctions because it is experience; this negative inference (*vyatirekyanumāna*) is also a subverting proof (*bādhaka*). Nor is there the fallacy of an unestablished qualification (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*) here, because there is general establishment based on the principle that whatever, in its absence, leads to the occurrence of the undesired, is fit for valid cognition. Furthermore, "particularity" (*viśeṣatva*) is the delimiting factor of the counter-correlate (*pratiyogitāvacchedaka*) of absence, because it resides only in things that are themselves counter-correlates of absence, just like "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*); thus, it exists even specifically. Nor is there self-contradiction (*svavyāghāta*), because "absence of distinctions" is accepted as being the very nature (*svarūpa*) [of experience] and is not admitted to be a "distinction" itself.

Nor can it be argued that inference is redundant because the essential nature (*svarūpa*) is already established prior [to the inference], for knowledge is intended as its object precisely in that form. Nor is there any sublation by scripture (*śrutibādha*), since that has already been refuted; on the contrary, there is support from a great many scriptural passages. For this very reason, there is no parity with fallacious arguments (*abhāsasāmya*). Nor is the reason unestablished (*aprayojakatva*), because the impossibility of the relation between attribute and substratum (*dharmadharmibhāva*)—due to the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) and infinite regress (*anavasthā*) that would follow if they were either different, non-different, or related otherwise—serves as a subverting argument against the contrary position.

Nor can it be argued that there is no infinite regress because the relation, like its own falsity, is self-establishing; for in the doctrine of non-difference (*abheda*), it is impossible to speak of anything additional [to the substrate]. Nor should it be said that this is mere sophistry due to the contradiction arising from the presence or absence of the nature of a property (*dharma*) consisting in the absence of properties; for since we accept the existence of the absence of properties precisely as the essential nature (*svarūpa*) [of the substrate], there is no contradiction. Furthermore, even in the case of non-difference, you yourself accept the conventional usage of the relationship between property and property-possessor (*dharmadharmibhāva*) through the conceptualization of difference (*bhedakalpanā*).

Nor should it be argued: "If bliss (*ānanda*) were merely knowledge, then even the knowledge of suffering would be bliss; if they were distinct, its indivisibility (*akhaṇḍatva*) would be lost. Likewise, if the world were non-different from Brahman, it would follow that it is false; if it were different, the reality of difference would result. Such arguments based on logic (*tarka*) would undermine your intended Brahman as well. Thus, since these logical arguments are equally fallacious due to their contradiction with scripture (*śruti*), [the objection does not apply]. This is because the knowledge of suffering is of the nature of a mental modification (*vṛtti*), whereas bliss does not exceed eternal pure consciousness (*nityacinmātra*).

Because there is no risk of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*); because, according to the logic of the section on "clinging" (*ārambhaṇādhikaraṇa*), the world does not exist apart from Brahman, leaving no room for the dilemma of difference or non-difference; because it is improper to claim that the scriptural texts concerning the qualified Brahman (*saguṇa-śruti*) equally subvert the scriptures by being non-literal; and because the scriptural texts concerning the unqualified Brahman (*nirguṇa-śruti*) are indeed literal, and thus the reasoning supported by them is not "dry" (i.e., devoid of scriptural foundation).

As for the objection that the claim of being "without attributes" (nirviśeṣatva) involves self-contradiction—whether by affirming or denying it—just like saying "I am mute": if one argues that even the specific attribute consisting of "attributelessness" is negated by this very statement, then this act of speaking is likewise negated by the very statement "I am mute," and thus the cases are equal. That is not so. For if "attributelessness" were itself of the nature of an attribute, its negation in the form of an attribute would be as logically consistent as the negation of a second thing in the form of the absence of a second, as expressed in the sentence "non-dual" (advitīya).

Otherwise, the cognition of a negation delimited by the property of being a particular would be untenable. Furthermore, if [the particular] were not distinct from its absence, it would not be distinct from its own nature; thus, as in the case of "I am mute," there would be no contradiction in one's own statement. In the case of "I am mute," a contradiction is indeed possible because there is no negation of both speakerhood and its absence in a single form.

If it is objected: "In the absence of specific attributes that differentiate Brahman from the void (śūnya) and the indescribable (anirvācya), there would follow its own insignificance (tucchatva) or falsity (mithyātva); whereas if such attributes exist, Brahman would possess distinctions (saviśeṣatva)," we reply: Even in the absence of attributes possessing the same ontological status as the things to be excluded (vyāvartya), both its distinctness and its being without distinction are established by means of a property possessing the same ontological status as the cognition of that exclusion. For this very reason, if Brahman were without distinction, it could not be the object of inquiry. Knowledge in the form "this is thus" is the purpose of the desire to know (jijñāsā).
Indeed, the "being-thus" (itthaṃbhāva) is a property (dharma) of the thing; if it did not exist, there could be no counter-correlativity (pratiyogitā).

This is refuted, because at the time of inquiry (*vicāra*), there is the possibility of superimposed attributes (*āropita-dharma*). Furthermore, after inquiry, the conventional usage of "it is thus" (*ittham*) and the exclusion of the thing's own nature (*svarūpa-vyāvṛtti*) are both possible by taking recourse to an imagined distinctness (*kalpita-pārthakya*). Now, an objection is raised: even for the purpose of superimposing attributes, some attributes must be accepted as real, since we observe the superimposition of silver and the like only upon that which is already known through such [perceptions] as "this. As it has been said: "The superimposition of attributes occurs indeed when there is the perception of common attributes and so forth; for where is the superimposition of attributes ever seen in that which is devoid of all attributes?"

If it is argued thus, we say no: for even "this-ness" (*idantva*) and the like are not admitted to be real; furthermore, superimposition (*adhyāsa*) has been demonstrated to occur even with respect to the pure [Self]; and the possession of attributes distinct from those of the object of superimposition is explained solely by its connection with beginningless ignorance (*anādyavidyā*). For this very reason, the argument that "if negative attributes are accepted, then positive ones must also exist, since there is no difference in their being established by valid means of knowledge" (*prāmāṇikatva*) is refuted; because we do not accept even a negation that is distinct from the essential nature (*svarūpa*), and because the notion of "being established by valid means" regarding mere attributes has already been rejected. Therefore, the Supreme Brahman is devoid of distinctions (*nirviśeṣa*).
Thus ends the demonstration of the featurelessness and qualitylessness of Brahman in the Advaitasiddhi. 4.

Now, if it is asked: "What is the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding that which is devoid of attributes?"—is this question concerning the means of knowledge for the sake of its manifestation (*sphūrti*), or for the sake of the removal of ignorance (*ajñānanivṛtti*)? In the first case, the means of knowledge are redundant because [the Self] is self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*). Nor does this lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), since one cannot claim self-establishedness (*svataḥsiddhi*) regarding something about which there is disagreement; for there is a distinction based on the presence or absence of a means of knowledge that makes known the exclusion of non-existence (*abhāvavyāvṛtti*). In the second case, the Upanishads themselves are the means of valid knowledge. For this very reason, there is no room for alternatives such as whether it is perception (*pratyakṣa*) or inference (*anumāna*).

Now, one might object: how can the Upaniṣads be a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) in that regard? For, since there is an absence of any basis such as genus (*jāti*), quality (*guṇa*), or action (*kriyā*), primary denotation (*mukhyavṛtti*) is impossible and is not admitted [by you]. Furthermore, a cognition whose object is based on a superimposed basis cannot have validity regarding that which is devoid of distinctions (*nirviśeṣa*). This is because secondary denotation (*gauṇī*) presents its own meaning only by way of being connected with the qualities of the primary meaning, and metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) presents its own meaning only by way of possessing a form that delimits the relation to the literal meaning. Moreover, a word presents its own meaning through a form that delimits its capacity for syntactic connection (*anvayitāvacchedaka-rūpa*); thus, it is impossible for it to apply to that which is devoid of distinctions.

[Objection: The Upaniṣads are not a means of valid knowledge regarding the featureless [Brahman], because they lack connection with mere verbal forms (vṛtti), whether by way of words (*pada*) or sentences (*vākya*), and because they do not have the relation of syntactic connection (*saṃsarga*) as their object. [Reply: This is not so, because even when primary (*mukhya*) or secondary (*gauṇī*) denotation (*vṛtti*) is impossible, figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is possible. Furthermore, there is no rule that a word functioning through indication must necessarily present its meaning as possessing a form delimited by its connection to the primary meaning, or as possessing a form delimited by its capacity for syntactic connection with every word in the sentence; such a requirement applies only to those words situated within a sentence that convey a relation of syntactic connection.

Nor is it the case that, because [the Vedānta] does not have association (*saṃsarga*) as its object, it cannot be a valid sentence; for its status as a means of knowledge (*prāmāṇya*) is established by its capacity to produce a cognition that is neither doubtful nor erroneous, and its status as a sentence is established by its possessing expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and so forth, even though it is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*). Furthermore, the author of the *Vārttika* has demonstrated that the Vedānta sentences possess validity regarding the indeterminate (*nirviśeṣa*), even without a [verbal] function (*vṛtti*), just like a sentence that awakens one from sleep. As it is said: "Even without grasping the relationship between the denoter and the denoted, those awakened by others from deep sleep wake up, casting off their slumber."
For no one perceives a connection in deep sleep as they do while awake.

By this passage and others, the validity of a sentence has been established even in the absence of a [literal] connection. Even on the view that [meaning is obtained through] secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), the avoidance of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) must be stated as resulting precisely from the non-apprehension of a specific intention (*tātparya-viśeṣa*). Since a relation with the primary meaning (*śakya-sambandha*) is possible in many places, the apprehension of a specific intention belongs only to a particular person and not to everyone; the distinction residing in the person consists in the purity of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa-śuddhi*), which is the absence of obstacles (*pratibandhābhāva*).

The fact that sin, which consists of impurity of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), acts as an obstacle [to knowledge] is established by such scriptural passages as: "Knowledge arises for men through the destruction of sinful karma. Thus, when the obstacle has been removed, the direct realization of the Self occurs even for a Śūdra without [the need for] a formal connection [to the Veda]; this is beyond reproach. This has been explained by us at length in our *Gītā-nibandhana*.

Nor should it be argued: "Since inquiry (*vicāra*), which depends on the knowledge of the subject (*dharmin*), is the generator of a certainty (*niścaya*) whose mode (*prakāra*) is an undetermined single alternative, how can the knowledge of a Vedānta sentence occurring simultaneously with that inquiry be devoid of a mode? For the fruit of inquiry is precisely that knowledge capable of removing doubt; and since such [removal] is possible even from the knowledge of the subject as qualified by the exclusion of the contradictory alternative, there is no necessity for it to be established by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Nor is there any weight [to this objection], because weight is only justified when it possesses a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Nor should it be argued that since a cognition whose object is the indeterminate (*nirviśeṣa*) is devoid of modes (*niṣprakāraka*), the indeterminate nature itself would remain unestablished; therefore, for the sake of establishing that [indeterminate nature], it is necessary for the cognition to have as its object a "mode" consisting in the absence of specific attributes (*viśeṣābhāva*). This is because the absence of specific attributes is the very nature (*svarūpa*) of the thing, and thus its manifestation does not depend on a means of knowledge. It is sufficient merely for it to be an object of the presentation of distinct categories of entities conducive to the establishment of the indivisible meaning (*akhaṇḍārtha*).

Because the occurrence of specific conventional usage [is possible]. Therefore, since there is an absence of proof for its possessing qualities (*saguṇatva*) and the presence of subverting arguments against it, whereas for its being devoid of qualities (*nirguṇatva*) there is an absence of such subverting arguments, it is established that Brahman is indeed devoid of qualities. Thus ends the fifth section: the establishment of the evidence for the qualitylessness of Brahman in the *Advaitasiddhi*.

Thus, [the Brahman] is also formless. But surely [it is argued that it is not], for by such scriptural passages as "Of the color of the sun, beyond darkness," "When the seer sees the golden-colored one," "The Truth, the Reality, the Supreme Brahman, the Person, dark and tawny," "Eyes on all sides," and "A thousand heads," as well as by smṛti passages such as "Behold my forms, O Pārtha," and "That [Brahman] has hands and feet everywhere," and by inferences such as "Brahman possesses a body, because it is a creator, because it is a protector, because it is a teacher," and so forth.

If it is argued that this establishes a physical form (*vigraha*), we say no; for the passage "of the color of the sun" is consistent with its purpose of establishing the self-luminous nature of the Lord as distinct from ignorance, and also with its purpose of being an object of meditation. Nor does the mention of being "beyond darkness" preclude its being an object of meditation; for what is described as being beyond darkness is the Lord as characterized by the meditated-upon form, and not as possessing that form as a qualifying attribute.

Nor should it be argued that because the passage "this golden person is seen within the sun" describes the object as being present and thus a subject of immediate perception (*aparokṣajñāna*), it cannot be a superimposition; for one does not say "the fire-nature of the woman is seen. This is because, although there is no rule regarding the direct realization of the object of meditation in the case of symbolic meditation (*pratīkopāsana*), in the case of meditation on the qualified Brahman (*saguṇopāsana*), the direct realization of the object is mandatory—as established by the scripture "He may become this"—and it is precisely this [realization] that is denoted by the word "seeing."

This is because scriptural and traditional texts such as "Eyes on all sides" (*viśvataścakṣuḥ*) and others are appropriately explained as restating the eyes, hands, head, and so forth of the bodies of the individual souls who are to be governed [by the Lord], since He is the Self of all and the inner controller of all; whereas attributes such as having hands and feet everywhere (*sarvataḥpāṇipādatva*) are impossible [in that sense]. Furthermore, you yourself must admit this very point; otherwise, your own presentation of supreme liberation as being delimited by a specific location, as well as your arguments regarding [the Lord's] being the goal of movement and entering [into things], would be inconsistent. The same applies to inference: there, too, the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) occurs.

If it is argued that [the Lord cannot be the cause] because He lacks organs, we reply: "That has already been explained. This is because there is no contradiction, as the transformation of ignorance—which serves as the locus of the instruments—is admitted [as the means].

As for the argument that the all-pervading Brahman’s status as an “enterer” and an “object of attainment”—established by such scriptural passages as "He entered into that very [being]" and "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme"—is not tenable without a physical form, that is not so; for the meaning of the word "entrance" (anupraveśa) is simply manifestation within an effect created by oneself, since a literal entrance is impossible for that which is omnipresent. Furthermore, although [Brahman] is attained by its very nature, it is figuratively spoken of as being "attained" with reference to the cessation of concealment by ignorance (avidyā), and thus this does not necessitate the existence of a physical form.

As for the argument that because the Śruti passage beginning with "He who knows Him thus becomes immortal here" refers by means of the pronoun *tat* specifically to the one possessing a form (*savigraha*), the very knowledge of Him as such must be the cause of liberation, and therefore He possesses a form—that is not so; for that [knowledge] is otherwise established as being for the sake of gradual liberation (*kramamukti*) in the case of qualified knowledge (*saguṇavidyā*). In the view that [knowledge] directly produces liberation, it is the knowledge of the Self characterized (*upalakṣita*) by that [form] which is the cause of liberation.

For this very reason, such Smṛti passages as "Even the gods constantly long for a vision of this form" are also explained. Furthermore, is the body material (bhautika) or non-material (abhautika)? If it is non-material, is it illusory (māyika) or non-illusory (amāyika)? If it is non-illusory, is it different from Brahman or not? If it is not different, [the body would be Brahman itself]. Even if it were both material and illusory, would it be acquired through one's own karma or through the karma of another? In the first case, there would be the consequence of being a transmigrating soul (saṃsāritva); in the second case, it would be an accepted conclusion (iṣṭāpatti).

If [the body] were different from Brahman, there would be a contradiction with your own established tenet (*apasiddhānta*), a contradiction with the scriptural text "Not this, not this" (*neti neti*), and a contradiction with scriptural texts such as "Without hands or feet. If one accepts a body that is non-material, illusory, and non-different from Brahman, there is a contradiction with the aforementioned scriptures, an entry into the Cārvāka doctrine, and a lack of valid evidence (*pramāṇābhāva*). And there is a lack of valid evidence.

Nor does the statement "from the navel arose the intermediate space" establish that [the deity] is non-material (abhautika) by asserting it as the cause of the elements; for, upon considering such scriptural passages as "Agni is the head," which present the intermediate space and so forth as the navel and other limbs to describe the body of Virāj, this does not establish that the body is the cause of the elements. Furthermore, passages such as "beyond the darkness" refer to Brahman as indicated by the body of Virāj, and thus do not establish that the corporeal form exists beyond the darkness.

Nor can the existence of a permanent body be established for Nārāyaṇa on the basis of the Śruti passage, "There was neither Nārāyaṇa, nor Brahmā, nor Śaṅkara," which speaks of Nārāyaṇa's presence during the great dissolution (mahāpralaya); for, in accordance with the Śruti, "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone," the word *nārāyaṇa* refers to Brahman as conditioned by Māyā, and thus lacks reference to a physical body. Nor does this imply that [the status of being the creator] is common to other sentient beings; for it is precisely the state of being conditioned by indivisible Māyā that serves as the differentiator.

Nor does the statement, "He is the eternal among the non-eternal, the conscious among the conscious," contradict the mention of a specific [eternal] form (*vigraha*) in the absence of an actual body, for this is consistent even without accepting a formal body, as it is explained by taking the consciousness of His essential nature (*svarūpa-caitanya*). Nor is an eternal form established by the statement, "At the end of the previous aeon, having internalized His own created [world], though it was transformed," etc., which speaks of the body's direct existence during the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*); for the meaning of the word "internalizing" (*udarīkṛtya*) is the subsistence of ignorance—the root cause of all transformations—in the form of a latent impression (*saṃskāra*).

Nor is there an abandonment of the primary meaning, for even you must state this very point; otherwise, the dissolution of the entire universe would not be established merely by its entry into that [Brahman]. As it is said: "All bodies of that Great Soul are eternal and everlasting, consisting of a mass of supreme bliss and always composed of pure knowledge."

If it is argued that there is a contradiction with the direct statement of its eternity in such passages, that is not so; for [the text] refers to a body whose primary nature is knowledge and which serves as a non-receptacle for the experience of suffering persisting until the dissolution of the universe, and thus lacks the status you intend for it. For this very reason, it is insentient and distinct from that [Self].

Nor should it be argued that, although there is no difference [between Brahman and its attributes] according to such scriptural texts as "That which shines as immortal, whose form is bliss," "All is indeed bliss unto the very tips of the nails," "Joy is the right wing," and "The Blessed Lord consists of that which the individual consists of; of what nature is the Blessed Lord? He is of the nature of knowledge, of the nature of sovereignty," etc., the possession of a physical form (vigrahavattva) is nonetheless established by the force of specific distinctions through the analogy of the serpent and its coils. This cannot be maintained, because those passages are intent upon establishing that the Self is of the nature of knowledge and bliss, and do not aim to establish a physical form.

This is because statements such as "The ancient Puruṣa possesses manifold powers" and the Sūtra "And so too in the Self, for [powers] are manifold" establish the variety of the power of *māyā*, rather than establishing a power inherent in the Self; furthermore, the passage beginning with "down to the very tips of the nails" is logically consistent with the Self not being an experiencer of suffering and the like, given its limitation by the body assumed for sport (*līlā-vigraha*). Finally, the passage beginning with "Joy is the southern [quarter]" establishes the sheath consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya-kośa*) and thus lacks the status of referring to Brahman.

For the form of Brahman as a body does not follow merely from its being mentioned in scripture; otherwise, by such scriptural passages as "Brahman indeed is all this" and "The Person indeed is all this," it would follow that Brahman also possesses the nature of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*). This is because the conceptualization of a "body" is merely a technical designation for that which is eternal and independent, just like its own essential bliss. Furthermore, even in my view, it is accepted that whatever is distinct from Brahman—even if considered to have an existence equal to the existence of Brahman—is negated within Brahman.

Nor should it be argued that the Self possesses a physical form (vigrahavattva) because of the statement that "this wisdom is not to be attained by reasoning" (*naiṣā tarkeṇa matirāpaneyā*), which declares the Self to be inaccessible to logic; for that statement declares only the featureless Self (*nirviśeṣātman*) to be inaccessible to logic, and does not state that the Self's possession of a physical form is inaccessible to logic. Furthermore, since a formless entity cannot possibly be perceived by the eye, any attempt to justify its non-perception on the grounds of a power of invisibility—like that of a *piśāca* or similar being—would be an argument for something that never even arose as a possibility. Moreover, in the case of a physical form, there would be a contradiction with scriptural texts such as "without hands or feet."

Nor should it be argued that—just as in passages such as "neither pain nor pleasure" there is a negation of ordinary pleasure, so here too there is a negation of ordinary limbs; otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the supplementary statement "he hears, he sees"—because while there is a restriction [of the meaning] in that case due to its contradiction with Śruti texts establishing that [the Self] has the nature of bliss and so forth, there is no cause for such a restriction here. Furthermore, there is no contradiction with those [scriptural statements], since hearing and seeing are accounted for simply by [the Self's] being the witness of sound and form.

Otherwise, even in your own view, since you do not admit that knowledge produced by the eyes and other senses applies to Brahman, the contradiction with that [scriptural] teaching would be difficult to avoid. For this very reason, the claim that the statement "it is formless and non-material" (from the Smṛti) explains the sense of the scriptural passage on being formless—such that the phrase "not formless" (in the Śruti) is a negation of form in general—is refuted; for there is no reason to restrict the Śruti, which teaches the Brahman to be known, on account of a Smṛti whose purpose is merely the object of meditation, especially since the Śruti and Smṛti are not of equal authority. On the contrary, it is by such passages as "that which is invisible" and so forth...

Furthermore, this contradicts the demonstration that the object of supreme knowledge (*paravidyā*) possesses a physical form (*vigraha*). Moreover, the Lord’s form is not eternal, because it possesses color-and-form (*rūpa*) while being large, or because it is a physical form; for it has already been stated that the scriptural passages intended to establish its eternity can be explained otherwise. Nor is "being composed of primordial matter" (*prākṛtatva*) a valid limiting condition (*upādhi*), as it pervades the probans (*sādhana*). Furthermore, it cannot be eternal because it possesses parts (*sāvayavatva*). Nor can anything possessing parts be eternal on the strength of scripture, since it has been stated that such scriptures can be explained otherwise.

[Objection: "But surely—if it is the *upādāna* (material cause) that constitutes a part (*avayava*), such parts do not exist at all in the body of Brahman. If, on the other hand, you mean a mere 'portion' (*ekadeśa*), there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of space and the Self, since those two also possess portions. Nor is it the case that a 'portion' distinct from the material cause does not exist, for we experience in the cutting of cloth, for instance, a portion consisting of a measurement of one cubit or span that is distinct from the constituent threads which are the material cause. [Reply: This is not so, because we experience the very threads that serve as the material cause as possessing measurements such as a cubit or a span.

As for the proof of [properties] such as being a conjunct in the case of space and so forth by means of [the reason] "being a conjunct," that is indeed acceptable to us, since we admit both having parts and impermanence in those cases.

As for the attempt to prove that [pleasure and pain] reside in the same locus because they are perceived in the self as having spatial distinctions, that is not correct; for pleasure and pain reside in the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), and thus do not reside in that [self]. Nor should it be argued that there is a deviation [from the rule] because the primordial nature (*prakṛti*)—though beginningless and eternal according to such scriptural passages as "The cow is without beginning or end"—is seen to have parts consisting of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*; for there is no eternality in *prakṛti* [in the sense intended here], and furthermore, there exists no *prakṛti* other than ignorance (*avidyā*).

Nor is there any deviation [in the rule] regarding ignorance (*avidyā*) alone, since even that is not subject to deviation because it too is impermanent. Nor [is there a flaw], for even though the individual souls (*jīvas*) are described as partial manifestations—as in "Droṇa was the portion of Bṛhaspati; the son of Droṇa arose from a portion of Rudra; Durvāsas was a portion of Śaṅkara"—and as it is said:
"I bow to that Imperishable One, whose very nature is the Supreme Brahman, in even a ten-thousandth part of a ten-thousandth part of whom the power of the universe resides."

One might argue that because the Lord’s own "parts" (aṃśa) are mentioned in such passages as, "Pervading this entire world, I stand with one part," there is a deviation between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara). This should not be said, because a part of the Self is merely adventitious (aupādhika) and lacks intrinsic nature (svābhāvikatva); for according to your own view, since individual souls are atomic in form, they lack an intrinsic part, and thus only a conceptual (kālpnika) part can be spoken of. By this, the eternality of the world of the Blessed One and so forth is also refuted. Nor [should you say]: "Therefore, indeed, the Vaiṣṇava worlds are eternal, and they consist of sentient beings."
By my grace, you shall attain supreme peace and the eternal abode.

Thus, there is no contradiction with such scriptural passages, as they refer to [Brahman's] state during the intermediate dissolution (*avāntara-pralaya*). Therefore, it is established that Brahman is devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*) and devoid of form (*nirākāra*). Thus ends the sixth section, "The Proof of Brahman’s Formlessness," in the *Advaitasiddhi*.

I know no reality higher than Kṛṣṇa, whose hand is adorned with a flute, who possesses the luster of a fresh rain-cloud, who wears yellow garments, whose lips are like the ruddy bimba fruit, whose face is as beautiful as the full moon, and whose eyes are like lotuses.

Now, an objection: if Brahman is indeed devoid of attributes (*nirviśeṣa*), then it is not tenable that Brahman alone is of the nature of knowledge, of the nature of bliss, non-dual, eternal, and the witness (*sākṣin*). To explain: in that regard, what is this "cognitivity" (*jñānatva*)? Is it a specific genus (*jāti*)? Or is it the capacity to directly produce empirical usage (*vyavahāra*)? Or is it opposition to the insentient (*jaḍa*)? Or is it difference from the insentient? Or is it opposition to ignorance (*ajñāna*)? Or is it having the nature of illuminating objects? Or is it something accepted by others? It cannot be the first [a specific genus], because [cognitivity is absent] in mental modifications (*vṛtti*), reflected cognitions, and the semblances of cognition (*jñānābhāsa*).

Even if that [relation] were possible, it would be untenable in the case of the knowledge of Brahman as an indivisible whole. Not the second [alternative], because the presence of the fruit (phalopadhāna) is absent in states such as deep sleep, and because even the natural capacity (svarūpayogyatā) in the form of power (śakti) and so forth is absent in liberation. Not the third, because since the knowledge of the essential nature (svarūpajñāna) is eternal, its opposite—the insentient—would necessarily be eternally negated. Nor the fourth, because it contradicts the statement in passages such as "Truth, Knowledge" (*satyaṃ jñānam*) that the exclusion of the unreal (*anṛtavyāvṛtti*) is merely implied. Nor the fifth, because it would entail the eternal negation of ignorance (*ajñāna*).

It is not the sixth [alternative], because in liberation there is no mention of any other object, and if there were a mention of its own nature, it would follow that it has itself as its object. It is not the seventh, because in your view, universals (jāti) accepted by others, or the state of being a cause for linguistic usage, and so forth, are impossible. If this is argued, we say: no, for the very nature of knowledge is "the illumination of an object" (arthaprakāśatva). Even in the absence of an object in liberation, the state of being an illumination conjoined with that [object] does not perish, since it was once connected with an object. For this very reason, the following objection is refuted: "How can Brahman have the nature of knowledge, which consists in the illumination of an object? Because in liberation there is no other object, and because it does not even know itself by itself."

As for the following [alternatives]: Is bliss (ānandatva) a specific universal (jāti)? Or is it being experienced as agreeable? Or is it the state of being an agreeable experience? Or is it mere agreeableness? Or is it simply having the nature of knowledge? Or is it being opposed to suffering? Or is it a nature characterized by the absence of suffering? Or is it that which is accepted by others? The first [alternative] is not tenable, because that [universal] is absent in the partless nature of bliss. The second is not tenable, because in liberation there is no cognizer, and because the Self is not an object of cognition.

Furthermore, being "conducive" (ānukūlya) implies dependence on something else; since it is not logical for that to exist in relation to another, it must be said to exist only in relation to oneself, which results in the fallacy of its having attributes (saviśeṣatva). For this very reason, the third [definition] is not tenable. Moreover, if the "conduciveness" were inherent as something additional to the nature of consciousness, it would result in the fallacy of the Absolute Being being composite (sakhaṇḍatva); if it were adventitious (aupādhika), it would result in the possibility of bliss ever ceasing. The fourth [definition] is also untenable, because "conduciveness" is impossible according to the reasoning already stated. For this same reason, the definition—"Bliss is the state of being desired without any limiting condition" (nirupādhīṣṭatvam)—is refuted.

It cannot be the fifth [alternative], because it would follow that even the cognition of suffering and so forth would be bliss (*ānanda*). If it is argued that only a cognition which does not refer to an object is thus [blissful], we say no; for cognition is necessarily characterized by having an object, and furthermore, since the exclusion of suffering is already established by the term "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) alone in such passages as "Brahman is consciousness and bliss," the term "bliss" (*ānanda*) would be rendered redundant.

It is not the sixth [alternative], because if contradiction were of the nature of being a sublater (*nivartakatva*) and so forth, it would follow that suffering is eternally ceased; and if it were of the nature of being unfit for identity (*tādātmyāyogyatva*), it would follow that even a jar and the like possess bliss, and it would be impossible to say that in passages such as "Brahman is consciousness and bliss," the exclusion of suffering is merely implied. It is not the seventh [alternative], because, as in the liberation of the Vaiśeṣikas, even when your defined suffering is absent, there would be no fulfillment of human purpose due to the absence of bliss, which would result in your own concept of liberation being likewise useless.

Nor is the eighth [alternative] valid, because in your own view, qualities such as being "desirable as such" (nirupādhyanukūlavedanīyatva) without qualification are impossible for that which is accepted by others. If it is argued: "Even if the nature of bliss (*ānandatva*) and so forth is difficult to define, if Brahman—the substratum of those qualities—is itself uncontradicted and consists of bliss, then even if the nature of reality (*satyatva*) and so forth is difficult to define, the world—the substratum of those qualities—should likewise be uncontradicted and consist of existence (*sattva*)," we say no; for the nature of bliss consists in being desired as such without qualification (*nirupādhikeṣṭatvarūpatva*).

Nor is there an over-extension [of the definition] to the absence of suffering, because even the absence of suffering is a subordinate element of happiness, since it is accepted that an absence is a distinct positive entity (bhāvāntara) that is opposed to its counter-positive. Nor does it follow that bliss would vanish when desire ceases in the state of liberation, because the essential nature (svarūpa), which is characterized by being the object of desire, does not perish; and furthermore, the presence of that characterizing desire is irrelevant with respect to the characterized essence itself.

Nor should it be argued: "Is this 'being desired without qualification' (nirupādhikeṣṭatva) natural or adventitious? It cannot be the latter, because that would entail that Brahman is of the nature of bliss (ānanda). In the first case, is it distinct from knowledge or non-distinct from it? In the first sub-case, there would be the consequence of Brahman being composite (sakhaṇḍatva); in the second, the term 'bliss' (ānanda) would be redundant. This objection is not valid, because even though knowledge and bliss are non-different, the employment of two terms is purposeful due to their exclusion of different superimposed attributes, based on a distinction between imagined universals (kalpitajāti).

By this, it is also established that knowledge devoid of any objective content (*viṣaya*) is itself bliss (*ānanda*), since the necessity of objective content within knowledge has already been refuted. Thus, because the nature of bliss is well-defined, the world cannot be reduced to the nature of pure existence (*sat*) by that same logic. Furthermore, there are subverting arguments (*bādhaka*) against the world having the nature of existence and so forth, such as its being an object of perception (*dṛśyatva*); however, these do not apply to bliss, because bliss is non-different from the seer (*dṛg*). By this, it is said: "Bliss is considered to be that which is cognized as being favorable and free from limiting adjuncts (*nirupādhi*)."

The claim that "Brahman, being without distinction and unknowable, cannot be of the nature of bliss" is refuted; for it is known as the object of supreme love, and because there is no difference between the bliss and its cognition, it is impossible to argue that it is not bliss due to a lack of cognition. Now, is non-duality (advitīyatva) the state of being qualified by the absence of a second, or is it being characterized by it? In either case, if the absence of a second—whether as a qualifier or a characterizer—is established by valid means of knowledge (prāmāṇika), then Brahman would become "with-a-second" (sadvitīya) by virtue of that absence. If, however, it is not so established, then Brahman would still be "with-a-second" by virtue of that second [which remains].

Nor can it be argued that even if a second non-existence (*abhāva*) exists, there is no loss of the doctrine of the non-duality of existence (*bhāvādvaita*), because—just like non-existence—there is no sublation (*bādhaka*) against the view that perceived entities such as attributes (*dharma*) are likewise established by valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇika*). This is not so; for according to the Prābhākara school, since the non-existence of a second entity is not distinct from its locus (*adhikaraṇa*), even if it is established by valid means, it does not entail the state of having a second (*sadvitīyatva*).

Nor should it be argued that it is improper to state that non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) is a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) because it does not transcend the objects of knowledge (*prameya*); for such a statement is made only from the perspective of those who maintain that negation (*abhāva*) is a separate category, and even when a separate negation is not admitted, its status as a valid cognition is established insofar as it produces a cognition characterized by the mode "negation-ness" (*abhāvatva*). Furthermore, there is no consequence of the reality of difference (*bheda*) resulting from the fact that the exclusion of the untrue (*amṛta-vyāvṛtti*) is also nothing but Brahman; for this is an accepted conclusion (*iṣṭāpatti*), since being defined by the untrue is itself false due to the falsity of the untrue.

Difference is indeed real because it is non-different from Brahman. Nor should it be argued that, in the Prābhākara view, a specific qualification such as "aloneness" (kaivalya) must necessarily be predicated of the locus in order to exclude the locus as being possessed of the counter-positive; for if that were so, that [qualification] itself would be the absence, otherwise even their [notions of] absence would be untenable. Rather, "aloneness" is simply the non-difference consisting in the essential nature (svarūpa) of that in which there is never any connection with a counter-positive.

And when that [absence] also exists in something at some time, then that locus is delimited by a time different from the time containing its counter-positive; thus, there is no over-extension of isolation (*kaivalya*) beyond its locus, nor is there any logical inconsistency. Nor should it be argued that, according to the view asserting the non-difference of quality and qualified, attributes such as power (*śakti*)—being positive entities like whiteness and the like—must also be non-different from Brahman; for there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to establish non-difference between Brahman and power and the rest.

Or, let "non-duality" (*advitīyatva*) be the essential nature characterized by the absence of a second; even if that [absence] is established by valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇika*), its counter-correlate—the second—does not thereby attain the status of being established by valid means, just as in the case of swallowing things experienced in a dream.

By this, the following is also refuted: if the absence of a second were a prior absence (*prāgabhāva*) and so forth, there would only be non-eternality of the second, but not its falsity (*mithyātva*); if, however, it were an absolute absence (*atyantābhāva*), it could not function as a defining characteristic (*upalakṣaṇa*), because it is eternal. If it were a defining characteristic despite not being connected to any effect such as being the intended object of the scripture's purport, then the absolute absence itself would remain unestablished. And thus:
The objection—"If the absence of duality were real (*tāttvika*), then there would be a second entity;

if it were unreal (*atāttvika*), then duality would follow"—is refuted. This is because that cognition [of non-duality] cannot be the intended object (*uddeśya*) since it does not transcend the essential nature (*svarūpa*) [of Brahman]; because such an understanding is possible in some way through a secondary intention (*avāntaratātparya*); because if it were real, it would not be distinct from Brahman; and because if it were unreal, the logic of "swallowing a dream" has already been stated. Furthermore, this has been established in detail previously. All is well.

Now, an objection: Is that which is intended as the eternity of Brahman its relation to all time? Or its freedom from limitation by time? Or its non-counterpositiveness to destruction (*dhvaṃsa*)? Or its freedom from both temporal limits? Not the first two, because they over-extend (*ativyāpti*) to ignorance (*avidyā*) and to time itself; for since ignorance is the material cause of all time, it is necessarily related to it, and thus, being free from such limitations as "only now" or "not at other times," it would possess those characteristics. Nor is the third, because it over-extends to destruction itself.

Nor should it be argued that even destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) cannot itself be the counter-positive of a destruction, for while the non-reemergence of the counter-positive is logical—just as the prior absence (*prāgabhāva*) does not reemerge even when the pot, which consists in the cessation of that prior absence, has ceased—it would follow that in liberation (*mokṣa*) some destruction other than the self must be asserted; therefore, for the sake of parsimony (*lāghava*), it is more appropriate to maintain the eternality of the primordial destruction itself.

Nor should it be said: "Even though destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) is eternal, Brahman alone is eternal among existing things (*bhāva*)," because, since it lacks a counter-correlate (*niṣpratiyogika*), existence itself—such as the state of being destroyed (*dhvaṃsatva*)—would necessarily also have to be eternal. Nor is the fourth [position] tenable; for even under such a convention, the result—that Brahman alone is eternal—would fail to establish the absence of anything else in liberation (*mukti*). If this is argued, we say no, because the fourth position withstands scrutiny.

Nor should it be said that "the non-existence of anything other than Brahman at the time of liberation is not established because it lacks a final limit," for another qualification is indeed established. Precisely for this reason: "If there exists a permanent time, unconditioned by time, and a destruction that is itself indestructible, how can your view—that only Brahman is eternal—be maintained?"

This is refuted: because time itself is of the nature of nescience (*avidyā*), it possesses a final limit; and because even though destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) has no subsequent destruction as its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), it nevertheless possesses an initial limit. Nor does this imply the existence of a second entity (*sadvitīyatva*), for even in this case, there is no second entity that is ultimately real (*tāttvika*). Nor does being unreal in this way entail the cessation of the destruction, for that is precisely what we accept. Nor is there a resurgence of the counter-correlate, because the essential nature (*svarūpa*) characterized by such a destruction is itself the obstacle, just as in the case of antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) with respect to the destruction of its counter-correlate and so forth.

Now, one might ask: how can Brahman, whose nature is pure consciousness (*dṛgrūpa*), possess the status of a witness (*sākṣitva*) consisting in being a direct seer? If it is argued that this follows from the grammatical rule, "the term *sākṣin* [is used] for one who sees directly," [we reply: it is because only consciousness reflected in either ignorance (*avidyā*) or its effects possesses the status of a witness. Thus, even though its nature is pure consciousness, it becomes a seer by means of an adjunct (*upādhi*).

Nor does this lead to a logical fallacy such as circularity, since the adjunct itself is a product of phenomenal ignorance (*prātītikāvidyā*) whose establishment depends upon the witness; for there is no obstruction to their arising or their cognition, as both the witnessing subject characterized by ignorance and its adjunct are beginningless.

Now, an objection is raised: Is the witness (sākṣin) part of the category of the individual soul (jīva), or part of the category of Brahman, or is it pure consciousness (cinmātra) common to both? It cannot be the first, because according to the view that the individual soul is atomic and has the intellect (buddhi) as its limiting adjunct (upādhi), it would be impossible for the silver in a shell—which is an object of knowledge delimited by the "this" aspect—to be known by the witness, which would lead to the fallacy of a circular argument (cakraka).
