Furthermore, even under the view that the soul is all-pervading and has ignorance (ajñāna) as its limiting adjunct, there is a mutual dependence (anyonyāśraya), since ignorance itself depends upon the witness for its establishment.

The second [alternative] is not tenable, because it would lead to the opposite conclusion—that the cognition of pain and so forth, which are known by the witness-consciousness, belongs to Brahman alone and not to the individual soul (jīva). Otherwise, there would likewise be the cognition of unconditioned bliss belonging to the jīva. Furthermore, according to the view that the consciousness of Brahman is the illuminator of objects such as jars, [the jīva cannot have such cognitions] because of the absence of such a mental modification (vṛtti) that manifests the non-difference of that [Brahman-consciousness] from the jīva-consciousness through the suppression of ignorance.

Not the third [alternative], because even if the suffering of transmigrators is not perceived as residing in pure consciousness (cinmātra) by that consciousness—as it is not by Īśvara—there is nonetheless the disappearance of the affliction consisting in the manifestation of suffering and so forth for that portion of pure consciousness which is liberated.

If it is argued that—just as the friendliness of a sleeping Maitra is perceived by him as belonging to Maitra—it would follow that the suffering of a waking Caitra would also be perceived by the sleeping Maitra as belonging to Caitra, which would render impossible the subsequent reflection, "I did not experience suffering for all this time"; we say no, because we accept the existence of a Witness (sākṣin) distinct from pure Brahman and distinct from the individual soul (jīva) conditioned by the intellect (buddhi), and thus the fault mentioned in that [opposing] position does not apply.

Likewise, consciousness reflected in a modification of ignorance (avidyāvṛtti) is the witness (sākṣin), since it was stated previously that a modification of ignorance is admitted even in deep sleep (suṣupti). Nor is there a circular dependency (anyonyāśraya), as this has already been refuted; furthermore, since pure consciousness lacks the status of being a witness, there is no possibility of the consequence that liberation would entail the disappearance of the afflictions (upaplava).

As for the objection that [if the witness-consciousness were one], Caitra would have the experience of grasping the suffering of Maitra while asleep, and thus there would be a contradiction with the subsequent reflection, "I did not perceive suffering for all this time"—that is not so; for although the witness-consciousness is common to all living beings, it manifests as non-different from the consciousness of each specific individual, and thus, by being the illuminator of the suffering and so forth of that particular individual alone, there is no over-extension of the principle.

As for the objection that pleasure and so forth cannot possess "existence solely through being known" (*jñātaikasattva*) if they are objects of consciousness reflected by a modification of ignorance (*avidyāvṛtti*) occurring immediately after them—that is not so, because this same difficulty applies equally to the view that maintains their mental nature (*mānasatva*). For in that view as well, there is no "existence solely through being known" distinct from "existing only while being known"; moreover, existence solely through being known is established even by a modification arising at the same time as the pain and so forth. Therefore, it is proven that Brahman is of the singular nature of knowledge and bliss, non-dual, eternal, and the witness (*sākṣin*).
Thus ends the demonstration of Brahman’s nature as knowledge, bliss, non-duality, eternity, and witness-hood in the Advaitasiddhi. 7.

Objection: If Brahman is indeed devoid of attributes (*nirviśeṣa*), how can it alone be both the efficient cause (*nimitta*) and the material cause (*upādāna*)? How, then, can the world have a non-different efficient and material cause? For only a cause that undergoes modification is a material cause, whereas Brahman is changeless; otherwise, there would be a contradiction with such scriptural passages as "changeless, imperishable, pure. Reply: This is not so. Even in the absence of being a material cause through the process of transformation (*pariṇāma*), its status as a material cause is possible by virtue of being the substratum of illusory manifestation (*vivartādhiṣṭhānatva*). And this state of being the substratum of illusory manifestation is precisely the state of being the object of the ignorance (*ajñāna*) which is the cause of that illusion. As stated by the authors of the *Vārttika*: [The relevant verse from the Vārttika follows.]
"That ignorance which is the material cause of this illusory net of duality—depending upon that, Brahman is called the cause.

Nor is there an absence of the definition of a material cause, because the very nature of being the cause for the production of an effect within itself constitutes the definition of a material cause, and because that [definition] is common to both types of causes: the transformative (*pariṇāmin*) and the non-transformative (*apariṇāmin*).

Now, is it that Brahman alone is the material cause, or is ignorance also? In the first case, if Brahman were the material cause, its resulting reality would entail a contradiction with the postulation of ignorance as the material cause. In the second case, is it intended that both Brahman and ignorance are material causes with equal primacy—just as a rope [is the cause] for the perception of a snake—or that the scripture concerning the "changeless" refers only to Brahman alone? Or is it intended that Brahman, possessed of the power of *māyā*, is the material cause, while the scripture concerning the "changeless" refers to Brahman as unconditioned by that [power]? Or...

Is it intended that Brahman is the cause through the medium of *māyā*, just as thread is the cause of a cloth through the medium of its strands, while the scriptural texts concerning changelessness (*nirvikāra*) deny change that is not mediated by such a medium? The first alternative is untenable: since both [the *māyā* and the *brahman*] would be equally subject to modification, it would be improper to specifically describe Brahman as changeless; furthermore, just as a cloth woven from white and black threads possesses both white and black qualities, there would result the simultaneous presence of both ultimate reality (*pāramārthikatva*) and indeterminability (*anirvacanīyatva*) in the world. Moreover, if the ultimate reality, which is the very nature of Brahman, were to reside solely in the cognition of the effect (*upādeya*), [it would follow that Brahman itself is not ultimately real].

Even if ignorance (*avidyā*) were of an indefinable nature, it would follow that it must reside solely within the intellect (*dhīmātra*), because if being derived from that alone were the cause of its respective existence, then its very indefinability would be lost due to the absence of being derived from that alone. In the second case, if Brahman undergoes modification in dependence upon the advent of a cause called *māyā*, it would result in its being subject to transformation (*pariṇāmitva*), like clay and other such materials; if the qualified entity [Brahman-with-māyā] were Brahman itself, there would be a contradiction with the scriptural texts stating that Brahman is changeless (*nirvikāra*); and if it were not Brahman, then the fact that Brahman is the cause of the world could not be established.

Furthermore, for that which is qualified (*viśiṣṭa*), there would be a loss of the doctrine of illusory manifestation (*vivarta-vāda*), because it would involve a transformation (*pariṇāma*) consisting in the attainment of another form whose reality-level is equal to that of the substrate (*dharmin*), just as in the case of clay and the like. Nor can it be argued that "transformation is with respect to the qualified [entity], while illusory manifestation is with respect to the pure [entity]," because even in the case of the pure [entity], a superimposed modification must necessarily exist for the sake of illusory manifestation; consequently, it would follow that the scriptural texts concerning its being changeless (*nirvikāra*) could not have that as their intended meaning.

If that [sentence] were intended to mean the absence of real modification (*tāttvika-vikāra*) in the substantive (*viśeṣya*), then it would be illogical to speak of modification in the qualified entity (*viśiṣṭa*), because there is no contradiction between a superimposed modification and that which is truly changeless. Nor is it the third [option], because Brahman is not the material cause (*upādāna*) with respect to Māyā, just as a part is not the material cause with respect to its thread. If this is argued, we say: No. For we accept that both are causes by virtue of neither undergoing modification; thus, there is no room for the defects mentioned in the case of those [other] positions, since we do not accept causality through the modification of both, but rather [causality] belongs to ignorance (*ajñāna*) alone.

For this very reason, Brahman is also immutable by virtue of its uniqueness. For even when accompanied by ignorance (*avidyā*), Brahman does not undergo transformation (*pariṇāma*), but rather illusory manifestation (*vivarta*). Nor does it follow that [the world] would be real simply because it is a transformation of ignorance; for "reality" in the sense of having the same degree of existence as the transforming material cause (*pariṇāmī-upādāna*) is what necessitates being a transformation. Since [the world] lacks the same degree of existence as Brahman, it is not a transformation with respect to Him. Furthermore, Brahman's immutability is established because He is not the cause of any modification that possesses the same degree of existence as Himself.

Nor does it follow that [the world] must be real simply because its material cause is real; for we observe that only the properties of a transforming material cause—such as "clay-ness" or "gold-ness"—persist in the effect, and thus it is logically possible for something to have a real material cause while itself being unreal. Furthermore, one should not object that there can be no single entity called "material causality" that encompasses both real and unreal things, just as there is no single "smoke-ness" common to real and unreal smoke; for it has already been stated that [material causality] consists in being the cause of the production of an effect residing within itself.

For the dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) between being real and being unreal does not contradict similarity (*sādharmya*); otherwise, if any dissimilarity whatsoever were to contradict similarity, it would follow that the discussion of similarity would be utterly destroyed. Furthermore, properties such as "being the object of a cognition produced by a mental impression (*saṃskāra*) whose content is non-apparent" are common to both apparent and non-apparent things, and thus exist even in the corroborative instance (*dṛṣṭānta*).

Now, one might object: "The hypothesis that ignorance (*avidyā*) is the material cause (*upādāna*) is not tenable, because Brahman alone can possibly be the material cause of silver, ether, and so forth; furthermore, the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of ignorance is otherwise explained as being merely instrumental (*nimitta*). If this is argued, we say no. Since we observe that objects such as jars and earrings require a transforming material cause (*pariṇāmy-upādāna*), it is necessary that ignorance also serves as the transforming material cause for ether and other such things.

Nor should it be argued that because an unreal entity such as silver has no need for a transforming substrate (pariṇāmin) that assumes its real form, there is no rule requiring dependence on such a substrate in every case of an effect (upādeya). For by the phrase "assuming a real form," what is intended is simply the state of being [the effect] without depending on an ignorance (ajñāna) regarding itself. Indeed, when ignorance regarding Brahman assumes the state of silver and so forth, an ignorance regarding that [silver] does not act as an intervening obstacle. Furthermore, ignorance is postulated as the material cause (upādāna) precisely because of its capacity for modification.

Nor should it be argued that such a conceptualization [of transformation] is unnecessary because modification can occur in Brahman itself as something non-real; for unless a modification is understood as a transformation of ignorance (*avidyā*) directed toward that [Brahman], its non-reality cannot be established. Furthermore, ignorance is the material cause (*upādāna*) by virtue of being a material cause possessing a level of existence equal to that required by its effect. This equality of existence is established either through the two-fold nature of existence found in the case of illusory silver, or by taking "phenomenal reality" (*prātibhāsikatva*)—defined as being sublated by anything other than the knowledge of Brahman—as the criterion.

Therefore, the following objection is refuted: "Even if both the silver and its identity [with the shell] are modifications of ignorance, how can there be a modification of this [shell] consisting in its assuming the form of silver? For it is not perceived that 'this has assumed the form of silver,' and because superimposition is impossible without another superimposition. This is refuted because we do not admit that the "this" assumes the form of silver merely by being the delimiting adjunct (*avacchedaka*) of the consciousness that serves as the substrate for the ignorance transformed into the form of silver.

As for the question, "What is this nature of being the material cause (*upādānatva*)? Is it (1) being the object of the cognition of the attainment of another form; or (2) being the object of the cognition of non-difference from another form; or (3) being the object of the cognition of non-difference from the effect? The first [option] is not tenable, because it is unestablished (*asiddhi*); for there is no such cognition as "the mother-of-pearl has attained the state of silver" or "Brahman has attained the state of space. The second [option] is not tenable, because it would result in the status of material cause and its product (*upādāna-upādeyatā*) falling upon the referents of the words *tat* and *tvam*, as well as upon milk and water, or a bald man and the universal "cowness" (*muṇḍa-gotva*).

The third [position] is rejected because it is a criticism of what was not stated; for even when a similar cause is present, there is the possibility of the delusion that the effect is non-different [from it], which results in over-extension (*ativyāpti*). As for the claim that Brahman cannot be the material cause (*upādāna*) by virtue of being the locus of error (*bhrama-adhiṣṭhāna*), since past and non-existent things—which are not material causes—are seen to be loci of error, and since substances like mother-of-pearl, though loci of error, are not conventionally treated as material causes—that is incorrect, because consciousness alone is the locus [of superimposition], whereas the past and so forth are not loci.

Furthermore, the absence of a thing is not established merely by the absence of its conventional usage; for instance, although the term "earth" is not applied to trees and the like, the nature of earth (*pṛthivītva*) still exists in them. As for the objection that—under the view that Māyā is the material cause (*upādāna*), Īśvara is the efficient cause (*nimitta*), and pure Brahman is the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*)—the status of Brahman as both the non-different efficient and material cause is absent in your system, and thus the *Prakṛtyadhikaraṇa* and other sections would be untenable—that is not so. For it is one and the same [Brahman] that, being conditioned by ignorance (*avidyopahita*), serves as the material cause, while simultaneously being the locus of the desire and volition that effect the transformation of ignorance.
Because the status of being a material cause is also possible [for Brahman]. Thus ends the demonstration of Brahman’s being the material cause of the world in the *Advaitasiddhi*. 8.

Now, an objection might be raised: "In this way, agency would be defined as possessing effort directed toward a material cause, like a potter and so forth; and that [definition] is not tenable if the effect is merely imagined (*kalpita*), because we observe agency only in the case of non-imagined objects, such as a potter with respect to a [real] pot, and because we do not observe the agency of either a deluded person or anyone else with respect to imagined things like silver [in a shell]. If you say this, we reply: No, for even in the case of a pot produced by a potter, its non-imagined nature is not universally admitted, and furthermore, the lack of agency in the case of silver [in a shell] is unproven, since in that instance too, it is the Witness (*sākṣin*) alone who is the agent.

Because of [the world's] being an effect; for the agent cannot be denied merely on the grounds of non-perception, since that would lead to the undesirable consequence that even in your own system, an omniscient creator remains unestablished.

By this it is also shown that being an agent does not consist in being a presiding director (*adhiṣṭhāna*), because if that were so, there would be no possibility of stating the co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of agency and material causality (*upādānatva*), as there would be no material cause distinct from the agent. Nor does it consist in being a witness to superimposition like one who is deluded, because a deluded person lacks the kind of agency that is consciously and deliberately superimposed. Nor does it consist in being a witness to superimposition like one who is deluded, because a deluded person lacks the kind of agency that is consciously and deliberately superimposed.

Nor is agency merely the state of being a deluder, as in the case of a magician; for if the living beings to be deluded are not seen, there is an absence of deluding, and if they are seen, it would result in the occurrence of an illusion [on the part of the magician]. Furthermore, since the state of being a deluder is itself superimposed, there would be the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*). Moreover, the scriptural text, "Let me differentiate name and form," would be untenable; for a magician does not act after forming the resolve, "Let me create the world and so forth," but rather acts after forming the resolve, "Let me show [it]."

Regarding the view of others—that in all three positions (the views of the Mīmāṃsakas, the Naiyāyikas, and the Advaitins), the sūtra *śāstrayonitvāt* was intended to manifest the omniscience and other attributes already implied by the sūtra *janmādy asya yataḥ*—that position would be refuted; for omniscience cannot be obtained [in Advaita] through such notions as being the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of error. Nor can there be the possession of effort directed toward the material cause (*upādāna*) and so forth, because that is incompatible with respect to a superimposed (*kalpita*) object. Therefore:
"In the substratum, in the object of error, and in the deluder, there is no agency.
Worldly agency, consisting in the possession of volitional effort (*kṛti*), is never seen with respect to a superimposed object."

Thus [the objection] is refuted, because the intended fourth position has been established. As for what was said regarding the third position—that if the living being were the deluded observer, it would follow that he is subject to error—that is actually an ornament [to our position], because one who knows an error is not himself erroneous. Furthermore, as for the claim that the scriptural statement "I shall manifest" is untenable because no magician is seen to act preceded by such a resolve, that is not so; for such a resolve is not admitted in the case of a magician.

As for the claim that the sūtra "Śāstrayonitvāt" (Because [Brahman] is the source of the scripture) reveals the omniscience established by the meaning of the sūtra "Janmādyasya yataḥ," and thus there would be a refutation of the opponent's view—that is not so; for even while possessing Māyā, Brahman attains omniscience by being the substratum for the transformation of the *sattva* aspect of Māyā into the form of the universe to be created. Therefore, Brahman is both the efficient cause and the material cause. Thus ends the ninth section: "The Proof of Brahman’s Agency over the Universe" in the Advaitasiddhi.

The status of Brahman as the material cause (upādānatva) is established by the direct scriptural statement (śruti) of the ablative case prescribed for the source of an originator according to the rule *janikartuḥ prakṛtiḥ* in the passage, "From which indeed these beings are born," and by the indicative mark (liṅga) of being the substratum of both persistence and dissolution in the passage, "Into which they enter when they depart. Furthermore, its status as the agent (kartṛtva) is established by its being the substratum of volition and so forth, as seen in the passage, "It thought: 'May I evolve [the world]'."

Now—it was stated that in the *Vṛtti*, because the ablative case is seen even when there is no explicit mention [of the source], as in "joy arises from a son" (*putrāt pramodo jāyate*), the word *prakṛti* (source) refers merely to a cause in general; and in the *Nyāsa* as well, relying on this very point, it is said: "If the mention of *prakṛti* were not made, the technical designation *apādāna* would apply only to the material cause (*upādāna*), due to proximity, and not to any other."

It is stated [in the Mahābhāṣya] that because the term *prakṛti* (source-material) is employed, the designation *apādāna* (ablative/point of departure) is established even when the word *apādāna* itself is not explicitly mentioned, on the grounds that the rule applies to any cause whatsoever. Furthermore, in the Mahābhāṣya, it is argued that this rule (*A 1.4.29*) need not have been composed; for by the rule "that which is fixed (*dhruva*) in a process of separation (*apāya*) is the *apādāna*," the designation *apādāna* would be established simply because hair (*loman*) and the like serve as the point of departure (*avadhi*) for durva grass and the like—as in the example: "durva grass grows from cow-hair, goat-hair, and sheep-hair; they emerge and depart from them. Thus, since the designation is already established by that [earlier] rule, this present rule should not have been undertaken. This refers to the rule [under discussion].

This has been refuted. Kaiyaṭa also, having raised the objection that the perception of an effect in the case of hair and the like is not possible if they serve as the limit of departure, demonstrated that they do indeed function as the limit; for just as a long-bodied serpent emerging from a hole is perceived there in its delimited state, so too is the effect, such as *dūrvā* grass, perceived there.

If it is argued that, consequently, in both views the restriction—that the ablative case ending (*pañcamī*) occurs only for the material cause (*upādāna*) by the rule *janikartuḥ prakṛtiḥ*—is not established, we say: not so. For just as in the injunction *paśunā yajeta* ("one should sacrifice with an animal"), although the word *paśu* denotes animals in general, it is understood to refer to a specific type of animal (the goat) in accordance with the supplementary passage (*vākyaśeṣa*) "of the goat's omentum" (*chāgasya vapāyāḥ*), so too here, even though the term refers to causes in general, its reference to the material cause is logically justified.

In the case where the ablative denotes a limit (*avadhi*), as in "an arrow from a horn" (*śṛṅgāccharaḥ*) and so forth, there is no restrictive factor for the word "horn" (*śṛṅga*); thus, even though it could denote the cause (*nimitta*), in the present instance, because a restrictive factor exists, it does not denote the cause. For this very reason, in cases such as "from the Self, space was produced" (*ātmana ākāśaḥ saṃbhūtaḥ*), the ablative is one of origin (*prakṛti*). This is because the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the subsequent phrase "it became both *sat* and *tyat*" (*sacca tyaccābhavat*), as well as with the passage found in another recension, "He desired" (*so'kāmayata*), serves as the restrictive factor.

Nor can it be argued that the Śruti passage—"He performed austerity; having performed austerity, He created all this; having created it, He entered into it; having entered into it, He became the manifest (*sat*) and the unmanifest (*tyat*)"—and so forth, lacks authority for Brahman being the material cause because it merely describes the manifestation of the Supreme Lord's qualities such as *sattva* (existence), following the creation and entry into the world, and thus cannot logically constitute the creation of the world itself. Otherwise, how could it be said that "He became"? For a mother-of-pearl shell does not [become silver].

It should be stated that it is said "silver came into being" because the very coming-into-being as existence (*sad-ādi-bhavana*) constitutes the creation of the world; thus, there is no temporal sequence [between Brahman’s becoming and the creation]. Furthermore, the phrase "having entered into that" is logically consistent, just like the expression "having opened his mouth. Nor is there a redundancy with the statement "He created all this," for that [latter] is intended solely to dispel the misconception that [Brahman] is merely the efficient cause (*nimitta*). As for the claim that one never observes silver coming into being from mother-of-pearl, that is due to the fact that mother-of-pearl is not its material cause (*upādāna*); therefore, such a non-observation cannot serve as a valid example.

Nor should it be suspected that the words *nirukta* and so forth are redundant because the expansion (*prapañca*) of the formed (*mūrta*) and the formless (*amūrta*) has already been expressed by the two words *sat* and *tyat*; for this is justified as being a detailed exposition of what was previously stated in brief. Now, one might object: the sentence "He desired, 'May I be many'" does not express a concomitance with created things such that the Lord's identity with them would be perceived; rather, it expresses the Supreme Lord’s resolve to become manifold through infinite forms that impel those infinite categories of objects established in such Śruti passages as "Though unborn, he is born in many ways" and "That which is one, the unmanifest."

Nor is there any inconsistency in the creation of the world through the resolve for multiplicity by means of His own infinite forms—expressed as "He created all this"—because the manifestation of multiple forms as the controller necessarily depends upon the existence of those to be controlled; thus, it is logically consistent that after creating everything to be controlled, He enters into it by means of His forms as the controller.

If it were otherwise, the expression "may I be" (*syām*) used by the sentient being would be impossible; furthermore, since the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) does not exist prior to creation, the referent "I" (*aham-artha*) qualified by that organ would also be absent, making the use of the first person singular (*uttama-puruṣa*) untenable. If this is argued, we say no. By the word "may I be," there is no impossibility of referring to a future state of existence, just as one says "may I be happy" and so forth. Otherwise, it would be impossible for it to be the object of a volition (*saṅkalpa*), because desire cannot exist toward what is already established.

This very point serves as the decisive factor (*vinigamaka*) for establishing that the term "much" (*bahu*) refers to the objects of creation; for even in your own view, the regulating forms are established as non-different from God. Thus, in your view as well, the will ultimately terminates in that which is regulated. Consequently, the argument—that the creation of fire and so forth follows from the will having fire and so forth as its object, just as one creates disciples after resolving "May I be a teacher"—is refuted. This is because the resolution "May I become much" does not terminate in fire and so forth, but rather in the state of being the Self who is the subject of the will. Therefore, the creation of fire and so forth occurs by virtue of their being the objects of the will, just as the creation of disciples occurs by virtue of their being the objects of the will following the resolution "May I be a teacher. Thus, the objection is set aside.

As for what was stated—that the use of the first person singular (uttama-puruṣa) is untenable—that is not so; for the use of the first person singular is tenable because it can occur in reference to that which is qualified by such a transformation of ignorance as "I. In this very same way, the scriptural authority for such statements as "It thought: May I be many" should be understood.

But surely—it must be stated that you become manifold by becoming those things to be created, such as fire and the rest. However, since it is heard in scripture that fire and the others possess the qualities of being observers, creators, and the very selves of deities, they are conscious. And if it is argued that a conscious entity cannot be a material cause (upādāna), this is true; yet, because it is impossible for the things to be created themselves to possess observation and so forth, the words "fire" and the rest—which designate the agents of observation and other functions—actually signify the Self as delimited by fire and the other elements.

Because that very [Self], as delimited by each preceding effect, serves as the cause for each subsequent effect; thus, there is no room for objections based on consciousness regarding the delimiting factors such as light and so forth. Furthermore, such passages as "In the beginning, this was non-existent; from that, indeed, the existent was born; it made itself by itself" are authoritative evidence for the stated meaning. Nor is there any inconsistency in the statement of existence in the phrase "it made itself," even when the Self is being produced in the form of ether and so on, because its existence in its own essential nature (svarūpa) is established.

For this very purpose, even though it is not explicitly stated in the text, the meaning is inferred that "He made Himself into the nature of space and so forth. In the same way, in Smṛti passages such as "Thus I create myself," it should be explained as "into the nature of a body for the sake of establishing Dharma. Nor should it be argued that the phrase "Himself" (tadātmānam) is redundant because Brahman—referred to by the word "that" (tat) in the passage "From that, indeed, Being was born"—is already established prior to the origin of the universe; for even though His status as the efficient cause is obtained from the preceding sentence, this [phrase] is meaningful insofar as it makes known His status as the material cause.

Now, as for what was said—that Brahman alone is the material cause because of the scriptural teaching that creation dissolves into Brahman—that is not so; for we observe that the dissolution of threads occurs in the spider, which is merely the efficient cause of the threads. For instance, although the constituent matter of the father's body is the material cause with respect to the son, the father is not its material cause but merely the efficient cause; likewise, although the substance of the spider is the material cause of those [threads], it is only the efficient cause. This is because Brahman’s role as the destroyer is also like that of the spider, as stated in the passage beginning with "as the spider [creates and withdraws its web]."

If it is argued that [the world] arises from hearing [of Brahman as its cause], we say no. Even though the spider (*ūrṇanābhi*) is not the material cause (*upādāna*) of the threads—since the threads are perceived even when the spider has perished, and rather [arise] from its consumed food—nevertheless, there is no dissolution (*laya*) of the thread therein; rather, there is merely the entry of that which was external into the interior. For this very reason, it is said: "Just as the spider emits and withdraws [its web]. Nor should it be said: "By the statement that Brahman is the destroyer according to that same principle, let it be just like that [spider]."

Because dissolution (*laya*) is heard of there in passages such as "That from which [beings] arise, into which they dissolve" (*tajjalān*), and because that [dissolution] serves as an illustration for mere disappearance (*tirobhāva*); furthermore, because complete identity is not required for something to function as an illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*). Moreover, its status as the material cause (*upādānatva*) is established by the scriptural statement [calling it] the "womb" (*yoni*) in the phrase "the womb of those elements" (*tadbhūtayoni*).

Nor can it be argued that because the word *yoni* is used in passages such as "O Indra, at your seat" (*yoniṣṭa indra sadane*) even when referring to a mere cause, its status as the material cause is not thereby established; for according to the maxim "the primary sense follows the natural force of the word," even if the term is occasionally used in some secondary sense as a cause elsewhere, there is no reason to abandon its default primary meaning in the present context. Furthermore, the scriptural statement that "by the knowledge of one, all is known" is also evidence for [Brahman’s] being the material cause. And how this cannot be accounted for by either similarity or predominance has already been explained.

The scriptural statement of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), "All this, indeed, is Brahman," is also an authority on this point. Nor should it be argued that this scripture lacks authority because it has been otherwise explained by the Smṛti text, "You pervade all, therefore You are all"; for the reason for employing the word "all" is the fact of being the pervasive substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of everything. Otherwise, the term "all" would inappropriately apply even to space (*ākāśa*). Furthermore, since it would contradict the *Prakṛtyadhikaraṇa* [of the Brahma-sūtras] if it were not the material cause (*upādāna*), it must be the material cause.

In this regard, the inference supported by scripture (*śrutyanugṛhītānumāna*) as stated in the *Vivaraṇa* should also be understood. For instance: "The great elements have Being (*sat*) as their material cause (*prakṛti*), because, while being permeated by the nature of Being, they consist of various modifications, just like a jar and other objects which are permeated by clay. Nor is there any inconsistency regarding the status of Being as the material cause in the theory of illusory manifestation (*vivarta-vāda*), nor is there the fallacy of proving what is already established (*arthāntaratā*), since the fact of Being being the material cause has been established at the very outset.

There is no fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*), because the non-existence of *prakṛti* as a real entity has already been proven; nor is there the fallacy of proving something irrelevant (*arthāntaratā*), because its being the material cause [of the world] was established at the very outset, and because there is no room for an irrelevant conclusion once the non-existence of *prakṛti* as a real entity has been demonstrated. Nor is there the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in cases such as "the spotted cow" or "the hornless cow," where the spottedness and so on are permeated by "cowness" (*gotva*), because the intended meaning is "being a modification of Being (*sat*) while being permeated by that [Being]," and because we do not admit the existence of "cowness" or similar universals as entities distinct from Being.

For this very reason, the objection that—on the analogy of the cognition "the jar is existent"—one would have to conclude that a jar or a human horn is composed of non-existence (asat-upādāna) based on cognitions such as "now the jar is non-existent" or "a human horn is non-existent," is refuted.

Nor can it be argued that there is a counter-argument (*satpratipakṣatva*) based on such reasons as: "Brahman is not the material cause of the world, because it is conscious, like Caitra"; or "The world does not have bliss as its material cause, because it is not permeated by that nature; for whatever is not permeated by the nature of something else is not caused by that, just as cloth and the like, which are not permeated by the nature of a pot, are not caused by a pot. Although these arguments appear equal in terms of their universal concomitance (*vyāpti*) and presence in the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*), the establishing argument is stronger because it is supported by scripture (*śruti*).

In the second inference, there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) with respect to a jar that is not colored by the nature of its shards, because the cognition "the shard is the jar" does not occur. Nor should it be argued that it is nonetheless colored by [the nature of] clay (*mṛttva*), for here too, being colored by existence (*sattva*) is equally present. And thus, since the world has the nature of an effect produced through prior deliberation, like pleasure and pain, it follows that Brahman is established as the non-different efficient and material cause.

Nor is the qualification "useless," because the intention lies in the two reasons: "because it is preceded by deliberation" and "because it is an effect. Nor should it be argued that, according to your view, there is a deficiency in the probandum (*sādhyavaikalya*) since suffering and the like have the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) as their material cause; for in our view, although the internal organ is the transformative material cause (*pariṇāmy-upādāna*), its status as the illusory material cause (*vivarta-upādāna*)—as the substratum of ignorance transformed into the form of the internal organ—is not lost. Furthermore, regarding the reason "because it is an effect," [the qualification is necessary] to exclude the conjunction of the pot with time, which is the efficient cause (*nimitta-kāraṇa*) of all effects.

Furthermore, there is the availability of an example accepted by both disputants. Nor can it be argued that there is a counter-argument (*satpratipakṣatva*) such as: "The world is not the material cause nor the agent, because it is a material cause of a substance, like clay; or, the creator of the world is not the material cause of a substance, because he is an agent, like a potter," and so forth; for such arguments are of inferior strength due to their contradiction with scripture. Moreover, in the first inference, "insentience" (*jaḍatva*) is the limiting condition (*upādhi*), while in the second inference, "being the inner controller of all" (*sarvānantaryāmitva*) is the limiting condition. Even if these were "otherness of the subject" (*pakṣetaratva*)—which is not a fault—here they are faults precisely because they are brought forth by sublation (*bādhonnītatayā*).

Therefore, it is established that Brahman is both the material cause and the agent of the world. Thus ends the demonstration of the evidence for Brahman’s status as the non-different instrumental and material cause of the world in the Advaitasiddhi. || 10 ||

Now, an objection is raised: it must be stated that [Brahman] is the material cause by virtue of being the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*) for evolving ignorance; however, substratehood cannot belong to that which is not itself known, because if there were a dependence on a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to know it, there would be the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*). Nor can it be said that substratehood depends precisely upon its self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatā*), for such self-luminosity is impossible to establish.

For instance: what is this "self-luminosity"? Is it (1) not being pervaded by a mental modification (*vṛtti*), or (2) not being pervaded by the fruit [of cognition], or (3) being the object of immediate linguistic usage while being unobjectified [by cognition], or (4) possessing the fitness for such usage, or (5) not being the locus of the absolute non-existence of that fitness? The first is not correct, because even Brahman is pervaded by the final mental modification in order to remove its veil. The second is not correct, because it over-extends (*ativyāpti*) to past objects and to things that are eternally beyond the senses. The third is not correct, because it does not apply (*avyāpti*) during deep sleep and similar states, due to the absence of linguistic usage.

Nor is it the fourth [alternative], because since the property consisting of "fitness" (yogyatva) is absent at the time of liberation, there would be a lack of pervasion (avyāpti) regarding Brahman at that time. Nor is it the fifth, because "not being a locus" (anadhikaraṇatva) is itself a property, and since that too is absent during the state of liberation, there would be a lack of pervasion. For this very reason, it cannot even be that which is characterized by such non-locusness, because if that too were a property, it would be absent in liberation. If this is argued, we say no; for only the fifth position withstands scrutiny.

Nor is there non-pervasion (avyāpti) in the case of liberation (mokṣa), because the state of not being a locus (anadhikaraṇatva), being its very nature (svarūpa), exists even then. Nor is it improper for that which is the nature [of a thing] to function as a definition (lakṣaṇa); for in your own system, just as there is the conventional usage of "quality" (guṇatva) with respect to bliss and so forth which are non-different from Brahman, there is likewise the conventional usage of "definition" with respect to the state of not being a locus, even though it is the nature [of the thing].

Nor should it be argued: "In your view, since even fitness (*yogyatva*) is false with respect to Brahman, its absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) must also be admitted; and if that is so, how can Brahman be the non-locus of that absolute non-existence? This objection is invalid because what is intended is the absolute non-existence of that which is contradictory to fitness. For the absolute non-existence residing in its own substratum—which is the very cause of falsity—is not contradictory [to the substratum] precisely because it resides in that same substratum. Alternatively, what is intended is the conventional absolute non-existence (*vyāvahārikātyantābhāva*); and since the absolute non-existence of fitness in Brahman is of the nature of Brahman itself, it is ultimately real (*tāttvika*).

Nor can it be said that there is no definition of "unknowability" (*avedyatva*), for its essence is simply the state of not being pervaded by the fruit (*phala*). This is because, upon the destruction of the veil (*āvaraṇabhaṅga*), consciousness (*cit*) itself constitutes the fruit. Furthermore, one should not object: "In this way, since objects like a jar are known through a mental modification (*vṛtti*), they lack the status of being objects of the fruit; and since things like silver (in an illusion) or pleasure are fit for immediate (*aparokṣa*) discourse, the aforementioned definition would be over-extensive (*ativyāpti*). This is because, while it has been established that objects like a jar are indeed pervaded by the fruit, and although silver, pleasure, and the like are fit for immediate discourse due to being manifested by the witness-consciousness (*sākṣibhāsya*), they are nonetheless [immediate] only insofar as they are produced by a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

Because it lacks the status of being an object of a mental modification (*vṛtti*). And thus, since the definition—namely, "the state of possessing that [mental modification] while being co-located with the non-pervasion by the fruit" (*phalāvyāpyatva*)—is established, all objections are refuted. Nor is there an impossibility regarding Brahman as well, on the grounds that it is illuminated by the fruit consisting of consciousness reflected in the mental modification; for, being of the nature of the fruit itself, it does not possess the status of being its own object.

Nor is it impossible for the teacher Citsukhācārya to have stated that even manifestation (*sphuraṇa*), which is of the same nature [as consciousness], has that [object] as its object; for that statement of the teacher is based on a metaphorical designation of "having that as its object" insofar as it is the object of the linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) produced by that [manifestation]. This is the essential point here: the state of being "object-pervaded by the fruit" (*phalavyāpyatva*) consists either in possessing a specific excellence produced by consciousness reflected in a mental modification (*vṛtti*), or in being the object of the foundational consciousness (*adhiṣṭhānacit*) manifested by the mental modification or by the consciousness reflected therein.

Furthermore, the excellence [of consciousness] is neither the destruction of an obstruction nor the intended empirical usage; rather, it is the relation of consciousness with its obstruction destroyed. And that [excellence] exists in objects such as a jar, but not in the Self, because a relation necessarily involves duality (*bheda*). Thus, it is established in the *pratikarmavyavasthā* (the determination of objects according to their respective cognitions) that even the state of being an object of the aforementioned consciousness is constituted by duality and exists in objects like jars, but not in the Self. Nor is the empirical usage of the term "immediate" (*aparokṣa*) difficult to explain, since what is intended is merely the employment of the word "immediate."

Nor is there an over-extension [of the definition] to such things as *dharma* and *adharma*, which are objects of extraordinary perception (*alaukikapratyakṣa*), by virtue of their being associated with such conventional usage; for we do not admit any extraordinary means of proximity (*alaukikapratyāsatti*) other than that produced by yoga (*yogajadharma*). Even that [yoga-born dharma] possesses the capacity to bring about [cognition] only regarding what is proximate to its own [perceiver], but not regarding *dharma* and the like. As it has been said: "Even where an excellence is observed," and so forth.

By this [it is meant]: what indeed is this so-called "empirical usage" (*aparokṣavyavahāra*)? Is it (1) that which is produced by immediate cognition (*aparokṣajñāna*), or (2) that which has an immediate object as its domain, or (3) that which has the form "it is immediate"? Not the first, because there is over-extension (*ativyāpti*); for empirical usage produced by the after-cognition (*anuvyavasāya*) of a yogi’s immediate cognition, or by the cognition of pervasion (*vyāptijñāna*), exists even with respect to *dharma* and the like. Not the second, because if the immediacy of an object consists in its being the object of immediate cognition, then it would follow that the Self (*ātman*) is also something to be known (*vedyatva*), just like a jar or other objects.

If it is argued that [the definition] is "being the object of immediate empirical usage" (*aparokṣavyavahāraviṣayatva*), this is refuted because, regarding the immediacy of both the thing and its empirical usage, there would be a circularity (*anyonyāśraya*) due to their mutual dependence. Nor is the third [option] tenable, because for an empirical usage produced by Vedānta texts—which have as their purport an indivisible reality (*akhaṇḍārtha*) and have as their object the formless, pure Brahman—it is impossible for it to take the form "it is immediate. This is not so, because by the word "empirical usage" (*vyavahāra*) what is intended is verbal expression; thus, even if the final modification (*vṛtti*) does not take that form, there is no deficiency.

Nor is there an over-extension [of the definition] to non-existence (abhāva), which—though not an object of knowledge through non-apprehension (anupalabdhi) and thus not directly perceived—is nonetheless present in worldly discourse; for what is intended here is discourse that is grounded in valid means of knowledge (prāmāṇika).

Objection: Is it not the case that fitness for immediate (aparokṣa) empirical usage does not apply to everyone, since Maitra lacks it with respect to Caitra’s ignorance? Nor does it apply to cognition itself, because cognition is not an agent of empirical usage. Nor does it apply to the substratum of cognition, because consciousness (cit) is non-dependent. Reply: This is not so; for what is intended is fitness for immediate empirical usage only with respect to some particular cognizer (pramātṛ). And the cognizer is universally accepted as being none other than the referent of "I" (ahamartha).

As for what was stated—that there is no practical usage (*avyavahāra*) by Maitra regarding Caitra’s cognition—does this mean that Maitra’s lack of usage is caused by Caitra’s cognition, or does it mean that Maitra’s lack of usage concerns the object of Caitra’s cognition? In the first case, even if Maitra lacks usage due to Caitra’s cognition, since direct usage (*aparokṣavyavahāra*) regarding a jar or Brahman is possible through one’s own cognition alone, there is neither the fault of a redundant qualification nor the impossibility [of the usage].

Moreover, in the case of Caitra’s second cognition, there is no deficiency even though such conventional usage does not occur; for according to us as well, it is consciousness alone (*cit*) that is self-luminous (*svaprakāśā*), and not even consciousness as conditioned by a mental modification (*vṛtti*) designated as "Caitra’s cognition," because the modification itself is not self-luminous. And thus, its fitness to be the object of such conventional usage with respect to all cognizers is indeed consistent.

[Objection: Is it not the case that being the object of non-remote (aparokṣa) linguistic usage while being unobjectifiable (avedyatva), or the fitness for such usage, is contradictory? For, in the case of such non-remote usage, the manifestation (sphuraṇa) having that [object] as its content is the cause. [Reply: No, because although elsewhere a manifestation having a certain object as its content generates linguistic usage regarding that object, a manifestation that does not have itself as its content generates linguistic usage regarding itself due to a difference in its own nature (svabhāvabheda).

Nor should it be the case that the same applies to jars and the like; for since they are not of the nature of manifestation (asphuraṇarūpatva), there is no other restrictive factor for their being objects [of cognition] except through being the objects of that [manifestation]. Furthermore, regarding the "after-cognition" (anuvyavasāya) postulated by the logicians, it is more parsimonious to assume that the linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) of "cognition of a jar" is caused by the property of being a "cognition of a jar" itself, rather than by the property of being a "cognition of the cognition of a jar."

[Objection: "Surely, for fear of infinite regress (*anavasthā*), one should accept that [consciousness] has itself as its own object, since it is improper to abandon the rule governing that objectivity which is established elsewhere; otherwise, since the property of being an object of knowledge (*prameyatva*) could—without even residing in itself—generate the linguistic usage 'it is an object of knowledge' by its own nature alone, this would entail the collapse of its status as a purely positive (*kevalānvayi*) universal. [Reply: No, for just as one abandons a further manifestation due to infinite regress, so too [one must abandon the notion of objectivity] in the case of non-difference, because [objectivity] is necessarily bound to difference.

Since the relationship between the subject and the object is also untenable, its abandonment is logically justified; for it is accepted that [the property of] being an object of knowledge (*prameyatva*) and so forth would lose their status as purely positive (*kevalānvayi*). Nor should it be argued that, in this way, motion (*gati*) might produce its own effect within itself just as it does in a village; for since the distinction [of identity] remains the same, it would follow that clay, like a thread, could also produce a cloth. And the resolution based on the difference in intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is the same in all cases.

Alternatively, self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*) is simply the state of having consciousness as one's own nature (*cid-aviṣaya-svarūpatva*). Since everything other than consciousness is an object of consciousness, and since the void (*tuccha*) lacks any nature at all, there is no fear of over-extension (*ativyāpti*). Nor is there any lack of possibility (*asambhava*), because—just as an act of cutting cannot cut itself due to the contradiction of an action operating upon itself—it is impossible for something to be known by itself. And it should not be argued that, on these grounds, the inference of falsity (*mithyātva-anumiti*) would also result in not having itself as its object; for there is a distinction here, in that the inference possesses a single, common factor of "objectivity" (*viṣayatā-niyāmaka*) applicable to both itself and others.

For this very reason, just as in the case of cutting and so forth, the conjunction with an axe is not common to both itself and another—thus there is a contradiction regarding its occurrence in itself—so it is in the present case as well. Nor should it be argued that, in that case, just as the effect of cutting (the cut) does not reside in the cutting itself, the empirical usage produced by consciousness would not reside in consciousness; for the observation of the result itself is what determines the difference in nature relative to the cutting.

Alternatively—self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*) consists in either the independence from any consciousness other than itself in its own manifestation, or the independence from a consciousness delimited by itself. Nor is there an inconsistency in our intended luminosity on the grounds that it would involve being known by itself; for since self-knownness (*svavedyatva*) is sublated, it is impossible to establish [the definition] by resorting to that.

[Objection: "But if the property of self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*) is real (*tāttvika*), there is a contradiction with non-duality (*advaita*); if it is unreal, then by implication non-self-luminosity itself becomes real, which would sublate the inference and other means of proof for that [self-luminosity]. [Reply: This is not so, because its being the very nature (*svarūpa*) has already been stated. Nor is this desired by the opponent, for the opponent does not admit a nature that is the opposite of being an object of cognition (*vedyatva*). Thus ends the demonstration of the definition of Brahman’s self-luminosity in the *Advaitasiddhi*. 11.

Nor is there an absence of proof, because the very reason of "being an experience" (*anubhūtitva*) serves as a negative inference (*vyatirekin*) that constitutes proof. Now, it might be argued: "In this case, the probandum (*sādhya*) is unestablished; nor can it be said that its general establishment occurs through the inference: 'Objectivity (*vedyatva*) is the counter-positive of an absolute non-existence residing in some locus, because it is a property (*dharma*),'—for even if objectlessness (*avedyatva*) were established in general, the specific probandum would remain unestablished."

Nor can it be established merely by being "experience" (*anubhūti*). For if "knowability" (*vedyatva*) consists in being pervaded by a mental modification (*vṛtti*), then its absence is contradicted in the final experience that is itself pervaded by a modification. If, however, it consists in being pervaded by the fruit (*phala*), then its absence is well-known in things other than the subject of the thesis—such as a pot for me, dharma for you, and the illusory silver in a mother-of-pearl shell; thus, it would result in the fallacy of being an uncommon inconclusive reason (*asādhāraṇānaikāntika*). If, finally, it consists in not being self-luminous (*asvaprakāśatva*), then it is simply unestablished due to the non-existence of its counter-positive (*pratiyogin*).

Furthermore, if it is argued that "the state of being the counter-positive of absolute non-existence" (atyantābhāvapratiyogitva) is excluded from something, then there would be a deviation (vyabhicāra) in that very instance; yet if it is not excluded here, there is no deviation—this is not so. For when self-luminosity (svaprakāśatva), defined as having consciousness as its own nature and not being an object of consciousness, is established through the probandum of being an experience (anubhūtitva), then "knowability" (vedyatva)—which is simply the state of being an object of consciousness—is the subject (pakṣa), existing only in things other than consciousness; and the probandum is the state of having the nature of being the counter-positive of absolute non-existence.

Furthermore, it has been demonstrated that the state of being an object of consciousness reflected through a mental mode (vṛtti) exists in things such as a jar but not in Brahman; thus, there is no lack of pervasion (asādhāraṇya) nor any sublation (bādha). Nor is there any deviation (vyabhicāra) in the case where the counter-positiveness of absolute non-existence (atyantābhāva-pratiyogitva) is itself the counter-positive of an absolute non-existence; for since the counter-positiveness of absolute non-existence is itself false, it resides only in that which is the counter-positive of an absolute non-existence, and thus that which possesses such counter-positiveness cannot be a purely positive entity (kevalānvayi).

Nor should it be argued that, even if Brahman is an object of consciousness (*cidviṣaya*), there is a shift in the subject matter (*arthāntara*) because the absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) of such objectivity is possible [in Brahman], or that there is the fallacy of being over-exclusive (*asādhāraṇya*) because the probandum exists likewise in jars and other things; for the probandum consists in being the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) of an absolute non-existence that is contradictory to being an object of consciousness. Thus, there is neither a shift in the subject matter nor over-exclusiveness, since those two [properties] coexist in jars and the like without contradiction, whereas they are contradictory in the case of Brahman. Nor, in that case, does the inclusion of the "contradictory" element lead to a lack of prior establishment (*aprasiddhi*).

Cognizability (*vedyatva*) is the counter-positive of an absolute absence that is contradictory [to it], because it is the counter-positive of an absolute absence, like a jar; thus, the establishment [of the reason] is possible. However, when self-luminosity—defined as the fitness for immediate empirical usage while being uncognizable—is the probandum (*sādhya*) in the previous inference, then cognizability in the sense of being pervaded by the fruit of cognition (*phalavyāpyatva*) is the subject (*pakṣa*), and the probandum is the state of being the counter-positive of an absolute absence residing in some thing that possesses the fitness for immediate empirical usage.

Thus, since "knowability" (*vedyatva*) is generally established as being co-located with "fitness for immediate empirical usage," there is neither the fault of an unestablished qualification (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*) nor the fault of being over-exclusive (*asādhāraṇya*). Furthermore, the defects arising from the dilemmas—such as whether "being the counter-correlative of absolute non-existence" means "being the counter-correlative of an absolute non-existence residing in something"—are already avoided. By this, the establishment of the probandum (*sādhyaprasiddhi*) is also achieved through the *mahāvidyā* inference: "This jar is other than that which is not the locus of knowability while being different from this jar, because it is a category (*padārtha*)," and so forth.

Nor is there any failure to define "knowability" (*vedyatva*); for if being of the nature of self-luminosity consists merely in not being an object of consciousness (*cid-aviṣayatva*), then being an object of consciousness (*cid-viṣayatva*) is precisely what constitutes knowability. However, according to the first position, knowability is simply the state of being pervaded by the fruit [of cognition]. Furthermore, in that case, there is no fallacy of proving the already established (*siddha-sādhana*) or the fallacy of proving something other than the intended subject (*arthāntara*) by means of the qualification "other than supersensuous" (*atīndriyānyatva*), because what is intended is precisely that which is co-located with the state of being the object of immediate empirical usage (*aparokṣa-vyavahāra*).

Nor is there the fallacy of *prakaraṇasama* (neutralization by counter-argument), as in: "This jar is not [this jar], because it is not the locus of being other than that which is not the locus of being cognizable while possessing the nature of this jar, since it is an entity (*padārtha*). This is because the original position possesses greater strength due to the presence of favorable reasoning in the form of scriptural testimony (*śruti*) and so forth; furthermore, even if there is doubt regarding the probandum (*sādhya*) based on the opposing argument, the establishment of the probandum in the form of a mere possibility (*saṃśaya-rūpa*) cannot be prevented. Nor is there the fallacy of the unestablished (*asiddhi*), because the universal (*jāti*) of "experience-ness" (*anubhūtitva*) exists even in the pure [consciousness] by taking into account the imagined difference between individuals.

Furthermore, there is no rule that a universal (*jāti*) must depend upon an individual (*vyakti*) possessing a difference of the same ontological status (*samasattāka*) as the substratum (*dharmin*); for since the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) is avoided simply by the universal's dependence on an individual possessing a difference whose ontological status is not lower than its own, the requirement of dependence on an individual possessing a difference of the same ontological status as the substratum would be redundant (*gauravakara*). This is because "sameness" (*samatva*) signifies neither less nor more.

Nor is it the case that the status of being an experience (*anubhūtitva*) is untenable in the absence of an object to be experienced, for that status is established simply by the existence of an object to be experienced at some time; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that cognitions produced by sentences such as "it was" would not be experiences. Furthermore, one should not argue that the status of being an experience does not exclude the counter-example (the non-self), because the term "experience" applies to the non-self; for the non-self lacks the very quality of being denotable by the word "experience," since the word "experience" is used figuratively with respect to the mental modification (*vṛtti*), just as the word "knowledge" (*jñāna*) is used figuratively in that context.

Therefore, the objection that there is a contradiction (*bādha*) if indirect experience (*parokṣānubhava*) is taken as the subject (*pakṣa*), and a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) if direct experience (*aparokṣa*) is taken as the subject, is refuted; for what is intended is experience in its nature as consciousness (*cittva*). Nor is the reason unestablished (*aprayojakatva*), because it is supported by scripture (*śruti*). Furthermore, one should not say that there is a contradiction with perception (*pratyakṣa*)—which grasps the self’s state of being an object of knowledge in the form "I know even my direct experience directly"—nor with the scriptural text "He knew only Himself" (*tadātmānamevāveda*); for the former is a witness-experience (*sākṣyanubhava*) whose object is an experience of attributes in the form of a mental modification (*vṛtti*).

Nor should it be argued that "I know" is experienced as having the act of cognition (*jñapti*) itself as its object; for since the referent "I" (*ahamartha*) cannot be the locus of cognition, the word "knowledge" (*jñāna*) is used figuratively in that context. Furthermore, even in cases such as "I know pain," what is intended is merely a modification (*vṛtti*) of ignorance (*avidyā*) bearing the form of pain and so forth. Moreover, the second [cognition] has the referent "I" as its object, and its non-selfhood has already been stated. Finally, since scripture (*śruti*) apprehends the object of consciousness as being the object of a mental state (*vitti*) produced by the Upanishads—namely, a modification—it does not take as its object the "being reached by the fruit" (*phalavyāpyatva*), which is the state of being an object of pure consciousness (*cidviṣayatva*).

Nor is experience the object of manifestation, because it is the object of immediate linguistic usage (*aparokṣa-vyavahāra*), like a jar. [Thesis: Caitra’s experience is the object of an immediate cognition capable of being the subject of Caitra’s immediate linguistic usage, because it is the object of Caitra’s immediate linguistic usage, like a jar. Furthermore, Caitra’s experience does not fail to be the object of an immediate cognition capable of being the subject of Caitra’s immediate linguistic usage, because it is devoid of non-manifestness with respect to Caitra, like Caitra’s desire; thus, there is a counter-argument (*sapratipakṣatva*).

Since I also accept that the nature of being an object (*viṣayatva*) consists in possessing a linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) prompted by manifestation (*sphuraṇa*), there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*). Furthermore, any [objectivity] other than that is sublated by the contradiction of its own occurrence within itself, because insentience (*jaḍatva*) serves as a limiting condition (*upādhi*), and because if it were cognizable by another, there would be an infinite regress, whereas self-cognizability (*svavedyatva*) is contradictory [to such a regress].

Now, one might ask: how is it that being known by itself (*svavedyatva*) is contradictory in relation to itself? It is not so because [the self] is not in contact with the sense organ that produces its own cognition, nor because it is not produced by such an organ; for the state of being an object of eternal consciousness exists in things like jars even without those two [conditions]. Nor is it so because the relationship of object and subject must reside in two distinct entities; for since we observe knowledge of the past, of superimposed things, and of absolute non-existents, that relationship does not necessarily reside in both. Nor is it so because of a contradiction between the nature of an action and the nature of its object, since we see that specific types of actions, such as volitional effort (*kṛti*), possess the character of being effects (*kāryatva*) and so forth.

Nor can the subject be the object, for that would entail the agent becoming the object; moreover, we observe that even in the case of the inference of falsity and the like, it is the subject itself that becomes the object. Furthermore, since we observe the experience "I know myself," and because the Śruti text "He entered into himself alone" shows no contradiction between the agent and the object, [the opponent argues: "Thus, being the object does not consist in possessing the fruit of an action inherent in another, but rather in being the object of an action and so forth; and this is possible even in the case of identity. [The author replies: Not so.

Since the relationship between object (*viṣaya*) and subject (*viṣayin*) is necessarily dependent on difference, it is contradictory for something to be cognized by itself. Indeed, in the aforementioned cases of the past and so forth, difference does not fail to exist. For this very reason, an action is an object only with respect to another action, a desire with respect to another desire, a linguistic usage with respect to another usage, and a denotation with respect to another denotation; it is never an object with respect to its own self. Thus, there is no example whatsoever for self-objectification (*svaviṣayatva*).

Now, one might object: "Even though movement and the like do not have another instance of movement as their object, since things possess diverse natures, consciousness (*anubhūti*) may likewise have itself as its object—just as action (*kṛti*) and the like can have another instance of action as their object. Otherwise, it could not even produce linguistic usage regarding itself; for if the knowledge of pervasion (*vyāpti*), inference (*anumiti*), and so forth did not have themselves as objects, there would be no pervasion that encompasses all cases, and inference would be false. This is not so.

Rather than postulating that [cognition] has itself as its own object for the sake of accounting for its empirical usage (*vyavahāra*), it is more parsimonious (*lāghava*) to postulate that even while not having itself as its object, it possesses the nature of generating its own empirical usage; for this much alone suffices to account for it, and because it has already been stated that in the case of pervasion (*vyāpti*), inference (*anumiti*), and so forth, such a status arises from the attainment of identity between the delimiters (*avacchedaka*). Furthermore, there is no self-cognizability (*svavedyatva*) in itself due to the contradiction between being an action (*kriyā*) and being its own object (*karman*). Nor does the inference of falsity (*mithyātva*) have itself as its object, because that which is indirect (*parokṣa*) cannot be an object.

As for the claim that the agent itself is the object (*karman*), that is incorrect; for the aforementioned inference of falsity (*mithyātva*) and so forth are not objects, and in cases such as "I know myself" (*mām ahaṃ jānāmi*), the witness (*sākṣin*) is the agent while the referent of "I" (*ahamartha*) is the object. Furthermore, in cases such as "He [the Self] knows Himself" (*sa ātmānam...*), the referent of "I" is the agent and consciousness (*cit*) is the object; yet, when there is non-difference (*abheda*), those two are not observed. Therefore, the definition of an object as consisting of difference is not abandoned; however, being the objective domain of an action (*kriyāviṣayatva*) is not what constitutes being an object, for otherwise even actions such as sitting would result in being transitive (*sakarmaka*), since they too have a locus (*ādhāra*) as their objective domain.

Now, if it is argued that [the doctrine of Brahman’s unknowability] is refuted by counter-arguments such as: (1) a contradiction arising from whether the proof establishing unknowability is itself known or unknown; (2) the impossibility of the Vedāntas being authoritative regarding Brahman; (3) the futility of the injunction to investigate Brahman; and (4) the impossibility of the cessation of ignorance regarding Brahman—[we reply: no, for "unknowability" means either not being an object of consciousness (*cid-aviṣayatva*) or not being pervaded by the fruit [of cognition] (*phalāvyāpyatva*). Since this [unknowability] is not contradicted by its being known through a mental modification (*vṛtti*) produced by the very means of knowledge that establish it, [unknowability remains intact] merely by virtue of [Brahman] being the object of such a modification.

Furthermore, because there is the possibility of [establishing] the inquiry into the authority of the Vedānta, the injunction for such inquiry, and the removal of ignorance. By this, the objection that "if the authority of the Vedānta were based merely on its capacity to remove ignorance, it would follow that the Self remains unestablished" is refuted, since the Self is self-established (*svataḥ-siddha*). Now, an objection may be raised: if "self-established" means "by itself alone," then it follows that the Self is its own object; if it means "without any means of knowledge," then it follows that it is unestablished, as no other means has been proposed; otherwise, it would absurdly follow that even things like a human horn would be established. This is not so, because the meaning of the term "self-established" is simply establishment that does not depend upon any means of knowledge (*māna*).

Nor does such an undesirable consequence apply to things like a "man's horn," because there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that results in the exclusion of its non-existence; whereas in the present case, it exists merely by virtue of being an object of occurrence (*vṛtti-viṣayatā*). Furthermore, the conventional usage "established in the self which is of the nature of establishment" is figurative (*gauṇa*), since it is an object of usage prompted by establishment. Nor does this imply an impossibility of being a consciousness (*vittitva*) in liberation due to the absence of an object of knowledge (*vedya*), for the logic of "experience" (*anubhūti*) applies here as well.

Nor is it impossible for [a cognition] to remove doubt regarding its own object when it does not itself have that as its object; for, by its very nature, it is logically consistent for it to oppose doubt and so forth with respect to its own substratum, just as it brings about linguistic usage. Nor is there a lack of uniformity [in the definition], because, just as in your own view regarding "objectness" (*viṣayatā*), that which is non-uniform can still serve as the regulator; and furthermore, even in the absence of being its own object (*svakarmatva*), linguistic usage and the like with respect to itself are possible through its self-establishing character (*svanirvāhakatā*).

Nor is there a contradiction with the statement that [the self] is both the agent and the object of the act of establishing itself through the very term that establishes it; for it is metaphorically designated as "self-establishing" merely by its independence from any establisher other than itself. This is like the designation of "one's own servant" in expressions such as "the poor man is his own servant," where one is so called merely due to the absence of a servant distinct from oneself.

Nor should it be argued that—just as in the case of the light of a lamp, which is the means for fulfilling the injunction to study, the capacity to produce its own effect is pervaded by being its own object, so too must it be here—the reason being that in the injunction to study, there is no room for self-dependence (ātmāśraya) since it is based on a single unifying determinant (avacchedaka), and because in the case of a lamp’s light, being its own object is not established. As it is stated in the *Khaṇḍana*: "In the rule 'gāṅkuṭādibhyaḥ', the bahuvrīhi compound performs its own function even with respect to 'kuṭa', though it is not its own object; so it is here as well."

Nor is it the case that, according to Kaiyaṭa’s statement—"A collection in which the distinction between its parts is manifested is the meaning of a compound"—the object of a *bahuvrīhi* is exclusively a collection composed of *kuṭa* [bricks]; and while it is another matter whether for Grammarians and Mīmāṃsakas this is through primary denotation (*śakti*) and for others through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), just as in the example "Let those belonging to Caitra’s house be brought," even Caitra—who is merely an incidental indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*)—is the referent of that word because he resides in his own house, so too is the *kuṭa* included within the collection that constitutes the external referent (*anyapadārtha*), just like the *kuṭa*-bricks themselves.

It should not be argued that the example is unestablished because [the term "sva"] can logically be understood as a *bahuvrīhi* compound; for the phrase "not having itself as its object" means "different from the referent of the other word, which is the default object. Thus, just as there is a result in that case [of the example] even with respect to the referent of the word "self" (*sva*)—as if it were elsewhere due to its connection with the referent of "self"—so too is there a result for consciousness (*cit*) with respect to itself due to its connection with itself, as if it were elsewhere; this is how the example is to be understood.

Or rather, it is because, although [the object] is an object in the sense of being the form that constitutes the aggregate distinct from its own individual parts, it is not an object in the sense of being the form that constitutes the members of that aggregate; thus, there is no contradiction with the statement that it is not its own object.

Now, an objection is raised: by this much, the conclusion reached is that for the production of a linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) regarding something other than itself, the state of being its object (*tadviṣayatva*) consists in non-difference from itself; yet this is incorrect, because one can easily say everywhere that this rule applies only to things other than the subject (*pakṣa*). For even when there is non-difference from itself, [the following properties] exist in the self without being the state of being its own object, just as they do in the object: in hatred, the opposition to desire; in ignorance, the state of obscuring itself; in indirect knowledge such as memory and the like, the production of a linguistic usage regarding itself; and in the consciousness of Maitra...

Furthermore, in deep sleep, although there is an absence of both ultimate and conceptual difference between Caitra and consciousness, one does not observe the generation of linguistic usage [based on that distinction]. Also, regarding the cognition "I know myself," since there is an experience of self-referentiality (*svaviṣayatva*) within the knowledge that is non-different from the self, [you argue that this proves self-cognition]. If you say this, it is not so; for then, in the case of hatred and the like, even though there is non-difference from the self, self-referentiality is not observed, and thus the same would apply to the present case as well.

Now, if it is argued that—because the fruit in the form of empirical usage (*vyavahāra*) is observed—the capacity of non-difference from itself (*svābheda*) to determine its own object-sphere (*svaviṣayatāniyāmakatva*), even though this is not seen elsewhere, is postulated only in the case at hand; then the same solution applies: because the fruit in the form of self-usage is observed here alone, non-difference from itself possesses the capacity to produce its own effect (*svakāryajanakatāniyāmakatva*) precisely here, and not in hatred (*dveṣa*) and so forth, since such a fruit is not observed there. Thus, the resolution is equal.
