Nor should it be argued that, since the apprehension of its object is here abandoned silently, this consequence would apply everywhere; for the reason for abandoning the status of having that as its object—the subverting proof (bādhaka)—has already been stated, and that [proof] is absent in all other cases. As for what was said regarding "Maitra’s consciousness" and so forth, that is not correct, because at a time when that [object] is absent, even the expression "Maitra’s consciousness" does not exist, since it is accepted that the manifestation of empirical usage occurs through the witness-consciousness (sākṣicaitanya). And even if the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) were to persist in the form of a latent impression (saṃskāra), it would still be a differentiator, because difference itself would indeed exist.

As for what was stated regarding "the self" (*ātmānam*) and so forth, that too is not correct, because in that case there is the experience of [the self] being the object of a cognition whose mode of operation (*vṛtti*) is based on the referent "I" (*ahamartha*). Nor is there any parity with the fallacious argument, "A jar is self-luminous, because it is a jar," since that has been refuted by rejecting the [fallacy of] being a mere motivator (*prayojakatva*); and furthermore, because there is no parity [between the self and a jar], as in the case of a jar, the absence of the non-difference from manifestation (*sphuraṇa*) and the absence of being its object would entail the impossibility of linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*).

Now, one might object: "If the mental modification (*vṛtti*) is the subject (*pakṣa*) by the term 'experience' (*anubhūti*), there is a contradiction (*bādha*); if it is something other than that, there is a lack of proof for the locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*). This is not so, because since the mental modification is insentient and thus non-luminous, the subject is precisely that in which luminosity finds its ultimate rest; furthermore, in the very context of the determination of objects according to their respective functions (*pratikarmavyavasthā*), the experience distinct from the mental modification is established.

And thus: "Your cognition of [the Self] as being fit for immediate empirical usage (*aparokṣa-vyavahāra-yogyatva*) is not the locus of being an object of knowledge (*vedyatvānadhikaraṇa*), because it is a cognition, like my own cognition. Also correct is: "The cognitions under dispute are not the loci of being objects of knowledge, provided they are other than the cognition of a jar, because they are cognitions, like the cognition of a jar. Nor is it the case that: "Your cognition is not the locus of non-objectivity (*avedyatvānadhikaraṇa*), provided it is fit for your immediate empirical usage, because it is a cognition, like my own cognition."

"Cognition of a jar, being different from cognition of a cloth, does not reside in that which is not an object of consciousness, because it is a cognition, like the cognition of a cloth. Furthermore, one should state that this is a case of "balancing the reason" (*prakaraṇasama*) as appropriate; however, since a subverting argument against the contrary position has been stated, the original proof possesses greater force. Thus ends the demonstration of the self-luminosity of experience in the *Advaitasiddhi*.

In this way, the self-luminosity of the Self, which is non-different from consciousness (*cit*), must also be established on the grounds of its being of the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpatva*). And just as there is no lack of proof for the Self’s being of the nature of consciousness, so it has been demonstrated; and it will also be demonstrated by means of scripture (*śruti*). Nor is there any contradiction with the scriptural text, "The knower is never known," because that text—contrary to many other scriptures to be cited later—is intended to mean that [the Self] is the substratum of knowledge in the form of a mental modification (*vṛtti*). As for what Vidya-sāgara stated: "The subject under discussion, knowledge, has a different substratum and object, because it is knowledge, like any other knowledge."

The argument for self-luminosity—"The subject of dispute is not directed toward its own substrate, because it is a quality (guṇa), like the heat of fire"—is according to the perspective of others. In our own view, since the nature of being knowledge (jñānatva) does not exist in the Self when it is self-luminous, and since such knowledge lacks the status of being a quality, there is no contradiction; for the perception "I know myself" is explained as having the mental modification (vṛtti) as its object.

Nor should it be argued that [self-luminosity] is irrelevant because, like ignorance (*ajñāna*), its status as having itself as both its locus and its object is logically possible; for if the self were an object of cognition, there would be an absence of cognition regarding the self, which would entail the possibility of doubt, error, or the ascertainment of its non-existence with respect to the self during states of ignorance. Furthermore, no one doubts whether the self is "I" or "not I," nor does anyone err by thinking it is someone else, nor do they ascertain its negation by thinking "it is not I"; thus, there exists a subverting argument against the view that the self is not self-luminous.

Nor should it be argued that, in your own view, because the referent of "I" (*ahamartha*), which is not an object of doubt and so forth, is non-self (*anātman*), while doubt and so forth do exist in the Self—which is distinct from that and accessible only through verbal testimony—this [objection] remains equally unproving; for the referent of "I" is a knot of consciousness and unconsciousness (*cid-acid-granthi*), and thus, just as there is an absence of doubt and so forth in the unconscious portion delimited by "I-ness," there is likewise an absence of doubt and so forth in the conscious portion as well.

Nor should it be argued that "knowability" (*jñānatva*) is an erratic property in the case of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), its objects, and its modifications, which are produced by sound; for that term signifies "manifestation" (*sphuraṇa*). Nor is there an erratic deviation of the second reason—namely, luminosity (*tejas*)—in respect to its own substrate, as light dispels darkness even where it resides (just as it does in a jar), because color, unlike cognition and the like, lacks an object. Furthermore, scriptural authority such as "In this [body], this person is self-luminous" (*atrāyaṃ puruṣaḥ svayaṃjyotiḥ*) is also proof in this matter.

For instance, in the passage beginning with "When the sun has set, O Yājñavalkya" and ending with "What light does this person have?", it is asked how the individual soul (jīva) can manifest in the absence of external means of knowledge such as light; in response, its self-luminosity is declared through statements such as "The Self alone is his light" and "He is self-luminous," showing that it does not depend on anything other than itself. Nor can the word "Self" (ātman) here refer to the Supreme Self (paramātman), because the preceding section establishes the connection of the channels (nāḍīs) with the [individual] Self.

Furthermore, in the subsequent passage—"Which is the Self? It is this one consisting of consciousness, which is the light within the heart among the vital breaths"—the term refers to the individual soul (jīva) by virtue of the "sandance" (sandamśa) principle resulting from the consideration of that later statement. Nor can it be argued that the word "Self" (ātman) has its primary sense in that context alone according to the logic of the *dyubhvādyadhikaraṇa* (Brahmasūtra 1.3.1), because the word "Self" is used as a reason for the purpose of refuting non-Selves such as Pradhāna, as stated in the Sūtra "Because of the word 'own'" (sva-śabdāt). This is not intended to establish its primary sense, since the individual soul is not even a candidate for being refuted here, and because primacy is common to both [the individual soul and Brahman].

For this very reason, the interpretation that the concluding statement—"In this, this person is himself his own light"—has the sense that "this" (referring to the Lord) is the very light and cause of knowledge for the individual soul (*jīva*) by means of supplying the word "this" (*asya*), is refuted; for such an interpretation contradicts the introductory context according to the reasoning already stated.

Nor should it be argued that—because of the use of the word "light" (*jyotis*) in the sense of speech as a means of knowledge in the passage, "By speech alone as his light he sits," the word "light" here too must refer to a means of knowledge and not to knowledge itself—it cannot be so argued; for just as the word "light," which is conventionally established in its worldly sense, is applied to speech by virtue of being a means of knowledge, so too here it can be applied to that which opposes ignorance by virtue of its nature as the opposite of darkness.

Nor is the word "here" (*atra*) redundant in the scripture because [the Self] is always self-luminous; for while the light of the sun and other sources exists in the waking state, making [the Self's luminosity] difficult to distinguish, it is easy to distinguish in this state. Thus, the qualification "here" is purposeful. Nor does the genitive case in "of this" (*asya*) denote being an object, because—as in the expression "one's own servants" (*svayaṃ-dāsāḥ*)—it refers to the state of not being known by another. Nor does this result in the meaning being secondary, for such a thing is acceptable since a primary object [in that sense] is impossible.

Furthermore, the conventional usage of "self-luminosity" does not apply to things like a lamp by virtue of their being their own objects; rather, the basis for that usage there too is simply the state of being a light that is not illuminated by another light of its own kind. For this very reason, there is no over-extension of the term to non-luminous things such as jars.

And the Vivaraṇa’s inferences are as follows: the Self is self-luminous because it is never devoid of manifestation while it exists, because it is the locus of manifestation, and because it is the agent of manifestation, like a lamp.

But surely—it may be objected: if "unknowability" (*avedyatva*) is the probandum (*sādhya*), there is a deficiency of the probandum (*sādhyavaikalya*); if it is "not being illumined by a light of the same class," that is a different matter (*arthāntara*), since this is possible even for objects like jars which are not self-illuminating; furthermore, there is a failure to establish the "illumination" inherent in the light of knowledge (*jñāna-prabhā*). Moreover, the first reason (*hetu*) is inconclusive (*vyabhicāra*) with respect to suffering and the like, which exist only when known; as for the second and third reasons, they are unestablished (*asiddhi*) because, in your own view, the Self is indeed luminous. If this is argued, we reply: no, because self-luminosity has been refuted, and the subject (*pakṣa*) is qualified by the absence of such illumination.

Because there is no other meaning [to the term], the probandum (*sādhya*) is simply the state of being a light that illuminates what is of its own kind (*sajātīya*) while not being illuminated by it. And thus, unlike a jar or similar objects, it is not tenable for it to be non-self-illuminating (*asvaprakāśa*); for by [the definition] "not being illuminated by what is of its own kind and not illuminated by itself," one obtains the quality of being unobjectifiable (*avedyatva*), since that which is of a different kind (*vijātīya*) is not luminous. Furthermore, the nature of luminosity (*prakāśatva*) inherent in both cognition and light is the capacity to overcome concealment (*āvaraṇābhibhāvakatva*). And whether this belongs to cognition by virtue of its being consciousness (*cittva*) or to light by virtue of its being a particular kind of radiance (*tejoviśeṣatva*) and so forth is another matter altogether.

Furthermore, the nature of being an obscuration (*āvaraṇatva*)—consisting in the obstruction of the practical engagement with objects—is common to both ignorance (*ajñāna*) and darkness (*tamas*). This is the case directly for ignorance, while for darkness it occurs through the mediation of obstructing knowledge; this is another matter. Nor is there any deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of pain (*duḥkha*), because in its momentary state it possesses the absence of light, and because [the definition] is qualified by the term "light" (*prakāśatva*). Nor is the second or third [reason] unestablished (*asiddhi*), as they are stated according to the perspective of the opponent, and because it is logically consistent that a reflection, being dependent on and resting upon the original object (*bimba*), serves as the cause for the knowledge of that original object.

For this very reason, it is also sound to argue that the self is not the locus of a manifestation that arises immediately after itself, because it is a locus of manifestation, like the sun. Nor is this a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*), for you yourself accept that knowledge having objects such as a jar is produced.

And as stated by Ānandabodha: "The consciousness under dispute does not lack the absence of practical activity (vyavahāra) caused by the absence of a cognition whose locus is identical to its own, whose time is identical to its own, and which has itself as its object, because it is consciousness, like immediately preceding or succeeding consciousness. Nor is there the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) on the grounds that [consciousness] is self-cognizable; for this argument is directed against those who accept that it is cognizable by another, and because, by the power of the qualification of the subject (*pakṣaviśeṣaṇa*)—namely, that it is not an object of itself—it results in a conclusion you do not accept.

Furthermore, the unknowability (*avedyatva*) of Brahman is indeed established by scripture (*śruti*). Nor does this mean it is unknowable in its entirety, for there is no reason to restrict [the scope of the scriptural statement]. By this, the view that [consciousness] is inferable from the mark of "cognizedness" (*jñātatā*) is refuted; for if that were so, the direct experience "I know," which is analogous to "I am happy," would be contradicted. Moreover, in the Guru’s system (*gurumata*), if the cognition "this is a jar"—which is itself produced—were to have itself as its object, it would follow that it must be the locus of the sense-contact that produces it. Furthermore, this would contradict the experienced distinction between the primary cognition (*vyavasāya*) and the subsequent reflective cognition (*anuvyavasāya*).

In the Nyāya view, if even the after-cognition (*anuvyavasāya*) were cognizable by another, then since cognition is a specific quality of the self that is perceptible, it would necessarily be cognized like desire and so forth; this would lead to the undesirable consequence of experiencing an infinite series of cognitions (*jñānadhārā*). Furthermore, if the series were interrupted, the final cognition would lack any means of valid knowledge (*niṣprāmāṇikatva*), as there would be no presence of a universal (*sāmānya*) to serve as a means of cognitive connection (*pratyāsatti*). Thus, it is established that there exists an eternal cognition which has itself as its object and takes as its scope the primary cognition (*vyavasāya*), pleasure, and so on.

Furthermore, in its status as having itself as an object (*svaviṣayatā*), it does not depend on a sense-contact (*sannikarṣa*) or other factors that produce it, just like the Lord’s eternal knowledge which has all things as its objects and does not depend on sense-contact or the like. Thus, the formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: "Caitra’s pleasure, pain, and so forth, are objects of Caitra’s own eternal and immediate knowledge, because they exist only when known by him; for whatever exists only when known by someone is an object of such [immediate] manifestation for that person, just like the effort of the Lord. Once the existence of eternal knowledge is established, [the following is argued]: "That [eternal knowledge] has itself as its object, because it is eternal knowledge."

"Because it is independent of anything else in its own operation, and because it is the antithesis of its own doubt and so forth, like the knowledge of God"—thus [it is argued]. Therefore, knowledge, which is an eternal attribute of the self, is self-luminous in the sense that it has itself as its object; and the self, too, is its object, because it is non-different from that [knowledge] which exists as long as the substance [the self] does, and because of the experience "I know myself. Furthermore: "Consciousness, being the very nature of the self, has itself as its object, because it is the object of the linguistic usage produced by itself."

The argument—"Cognition has itself as its object, because it is opposed to doubt whose qualifier is selfhood and whose locus is co-extensive with itself, or because it is opposed to error possessing the aforementioned qualifiers"—is refuted.

In the first inference, there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*), because [the self] is already established as the object of eternal, immediate knowledge in the form of a witness (*sākṣin*). Furthermore, even by means of a cognition arising simultaneously [with the object], the existence [of the object] is possible only when it is known; thus, that [simultaneous cognition] lacks the capacity to prove the ultimate conclusion regarding the eternity of the cognition itself. Nor is it the case that, in the absence of such a cognition in Caitra, the subsequent reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) upon waking from sleep would be inexplicable; for that is explained by means of a mental impression (*saṃskāra*), and moreover, an eternal cognition would be contradictory to such a reflective awareness.

Furthermore, in the inference that [knowledge] has itself as its object, the corroborative instance (*dṛṣṭānta*) is unestablished, because even in the case of God, eternal knowledge having itself as its object is not established; moreover, the reason is non-conclusive (*aprayojakatva*), since practical activity and the like have been shown to be possible even when [knowledge] does not have itself as its object. Furthermore, if Caitra’s eternal knowledge were to have itself as its object, there would be no single determining factor for this, since in the Nyāya system it is possible for God’s knowledge to have all things as its objects—just as He is the locus of all things (*vastutva*). Nor can identity be the determining factor, because it is absent in the case of suffering and so forth.

Nor can there be co-referentiality (*samānādhikaraṇatva*), because it is absent in the case of the self (*ātman*) and present in the case of qualities (*dharma*) and so forth; thus, that which is to be expressed is simply non-universal (*ananugata*). And so, what has been wronged by the Guru, who maintains that determinate cognition (*vyavasāya*) is self-luminous? For even if contact (*sannikarṣa*) is the regulating factor in other cases, non-difference (*abheda*) is possible in its own case. Furthermore, the dispute regarding experience—consisting in the experience or non-experience of distinctness—is equal in your own view as well. Therefore, let the cause for linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) itself be non-universal.

Why this insistence on following up with its cause? Because even subsequently, one arrives at the very same lack of such correspondence. Thus, it is established that self-luminosity does not consist in having itself as its own object, but rather in being non-cognizable while remaining fit for uninvestigated worldly usage. This concludes the demonstration of the self’s self-luminosity in the *Advaitasiddhi*. 12.

Brahman, being devoid of attributes (*nirdharmaka*) and being unknowable (*avedya*), is that which is indicated (*lakṣya*) by words such as "bliss" (*ānanda*), but it is not directly denotable (*vācya*), because there is an absence of any ground for the application (*pravṛttinimitta*) of a word to it. Now, an objection: if it is expressed by the word "indescribable" (*avācya*), then its denotability is established; if it is indicated, how can there be indication (*lakṣaṇā*) when the primary meaning (*mukhyārtha*) in the form of "indescribability" does not exist? Or, if it does exist, then Brahman would not be indescribable, but rather merely something related to the primary meaning of "indescribability," like the word "bank" (*tīra*).

If it is argued that even if [the term "Brahman"] lacks a primary meaning (*mukhyārtha*), it could still indicate Brahman through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), then even the word "pot" would indicate a pot; this is not so, because although there is no primary meaning in the form of something non-denotable, the word denoted by the term co-occurring with the negative particle (*nañ*) results in the final determination of the essential nature (*svarūpa*) precisely through secondary indication, by means of conveying the absolute absence of denotability. The same applies to the term "without attributes" (*nirviśeṣa*); for the rule that a primary meaning must necessarily exist applies only to the case of indicating an indivisible word (*akhaṇḍapada*).

Now, one might object: "If Brahman is thus a 'designatum' (*lakṣya*) by virtue of being indicated, then like the riverbank (*tīra*), it would follow that Brahman is not actually the Ganges; thus, Brahman would end up being non-designatable. This is not so, for this is precisely what we accept. This is because Brahman is entirely devoid of attributes (*nirdharmaka*). Furthermore, the conventional usage of the term "designatum" is based solely on the absence of being a "directly expressed meaning" (*vācyatva*). This was established previously regarding the designating words. Nor does the absence of being a designatum imply that the conventional usage of "expressed meaning" would apply [to Brahman], for even that [usage] is accepted here in a figurative sense (*gauṇa*). Moreover, since words such as "Truth" (*satya*) and "Knowledge" (*jñāna*) denote imagined attributes (*kalpitadharma*), they function as indicators (*lakṣaka*) of the individual essence that is Brahman; thus, their status as denoting an undivided reality (*akhaṇḍārtha*) remains intact.

Nor should it be argued that—since [Brahman] lacks the status of being a *lakṣya* (the object to be indicated) by virtue of being the substratum for attributes such as existence (*sattva*)—Brahman, as the *lakṣya*, would consequently fall into non-existence and so forth merely by its connection with existence and the like, just as a person who is the *lakṣya* is not a "bed" merely by his connection with a bed; for here too, there is no occurrence of non-existence, just as the imagined universal of "moon-ness" does not lack the nature of being a moon due to its identity with the ultimately real individual moon. As it has been said: "The individual that is the *lakṣya* is also Brahman."
For this very reason, the argument that "the doctrine of Brahman is well-established because whatever is desired as Brahman—such as self-luminosity and so forth—is not actually Brahman" is refuted.

Furthermore, it is impossible to claim that words such as *nirviśeṣa* (without distinction) lack denotative power because—being compound words—or words such as *lakṣya* (the indicated) lack it because—being etymological (*yaugika*)—they are equivalent to sentences; for, according to the theory of *anvitābhidhāna* (denotation of the related), even these [words] possess denotative power. Moreover, even under the theory of *abhihitānvaya* (relation of the denoted), since it is accepted that relation occurs only within a sentence, and since the base and suffix denote what is already related, even that which is equivalent to a sentence possesses denotative power. Consequently, if Brahman were of the nature of a relation between word-meanings (*padārtha-saṃsarga*), it would result in its being "determinate" (*sakhaṇḍa*); therefore, it must be a word-meaning itself.

[The opponent argues: "Because its status as something to be denoted (*vācyatva*) has not been avoided. That is not so; for even if it is indicated by a word (*padalakṣyatva*), its status as not being a word-meaning (*apadārthatva*) is established, since it has already been demonstrated that even in the case of an indivisible [reality], there can be the status of being a sentence-meaning (*vākyārthatva*). Furthermore, in the theory of *anvitābhidhāna* (denotation of the related), even that which denotes the related [meaning] is accepted as having a secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) with respect to its own form. Nor does this result in the failure to establish its non-denotability; for while non-denotability and so forth were initially set aside as a means to establish the indivisible Brahman, they are subsequently established as a corollary (*anuṣaṅgika*) because there is no longer any obstacle to them.

Furthermore, scriptural passages such as "from which words turn back" and "without sound, without touch" should be considered here; for there is no contradiction even in the word "aśabda" (without sound), just as there is none in the word "avācya" (inexpressible). Nor is this scripture intended merely to express wonder, since there is no sublation when its literal meaning is accepted. Nor can it be argued that because the phrase "from which words turn back" is heard along with "together with the mind," it is improper to deny the activity of speech entirely regarding Brahman—which is pervaded by the modifications of the internal organ—just as one might deny the activity of the mind; for by accepting *lakṣaṇā* (indication), only the primary power (*śakti*) of the word is negated.

Nor should it be argued that, in view of the fact that [terms] such as "bliss" (*ānanda*) have multiple primary referents, it is more logical for them to cease [their denotative function] and for the non-primary status of the single term's referent alone to prevail; for since Brahman is devoid of attributes (*nirdharmaka*), there is no capacity [for denotation] therein, and thus multiplicity is irrelevant. Furthermore, because the terms aim at an undivided referent (*akhaṇḍārtha*) precisely by means of an object that is contrary to what is denoted, the contradiction remains as it was.

Therefore, there is no contradiction between those two [scriptural and traditional texts], because the expression "being denotable" in such passages as the Śruti, "For this very reason it is called the Supreme Brahman," and the Smṛti, "And it is also called the Supreme Self," refers merely to being cognizable by those respective words, and not to the intention that it possesses the status of a primary denotation (śakyatva). If it is argued that Brahman is denotable because it is the intended object of the [Veda's] purport, because it is a real entity, and because it is something to be indicated (lakṣya)—just like a riverbank—[we reply: no, for its denotability is sublated by its being devoid of attributes (nirdharmaka), and because there is the possibility of adventitious conditions (upādhi) such as possessing attributes, which are inferred from that [alleged denotability].

Nor can it be argued that "the term beginning with 'paramārthasatya' (ultimate reality) denotes something [other than itself], because it is a word"—for what constitutes "word-ness" (*padatva*) here? It cannot be "ending in a nominal suffix (*suP*) or a verbal suffix (*tiṅ*"), because this would be fallacious (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of compound words (*samāsa*) such as *rājapuruṣa*, since a compound word lacks [independent] denotative power (*aśaktatva*). Nor can it be "possessing denotative power," because that would be no different from the probandum (*sādhyāviśeṣa*). If it is claimed that a compound word possesses denotative power by way of its constituent parts, then that is precisely what we accept. Furthermore, the argument that "the sentence 'truth, knowledge, etc. possesses a referent for its intended meaning, because it is a sentence" is also fallacious, as it fails in cases such as "Eat poison."

[Objection: But surely, if it is inexpressible (*avācya*), its being denotable by indication (*lakṣyatva*) is untenable, because only that which is known as being related to a denoted meaning can be indicated; and knowledge of that [relation] cannot be obtained through anything other than words, since it is accessible through the Upaniṣads alone; nor can it be known through self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatayā*), because if it were eternally established, words would be useless. Furthermore, since the word "inexpressible" itself must be admitted to be indicative, if it too were to be known as being related to a denoted meaning, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). [Reply: This is not so; for such knowledge is useful only when [the object] is already present [to the mind].

Since Brahman is present by its own nature through self-luminosity, what need is there for it? Nor is the word [denoting it] useless, because it is useful for the mental modification (*vṛtti*) that suppresses the veil [of ignorance]. For this very reason, there is no infinite regress. Therefore, because the ground for its application (*pravṛttinimitta*) is difficult to define, it is inexpressible. As it has been said: "Qualities, actions, universals, and relations are observed to be the causes of words;
since none of these exists in the Self, the Self is not denoted [by them]."

Nor is there denotability by virtue of being the locus of superimposed qualities, because that [superimposition] is not the object of the primary purport (*tātparya*), and thus non-denotability remains established with respect to the actual object of the purport. Furthermore, there is no circularity—whereby the absence of a ground for denotation would be established once the words "Real" (*satya*) and so forth are proven to be figurative (*lākṣaṇika*), and the figurative status would depend on that absence of a ground—because the absence of such a ground is already established by the very sentence devoid of attributes, namely "not this, not this" (*neti neti*).

Nor should it be argued that if a statement regarding the absence of attributes (nirviśeṣavākya) were intended solely to convey the essential nature (svarūpa), there would be no contradiction with the grounds for its application (*pravṛttinimitta*); or that if it were intended to convey [Brahman] as qualified by "absence of attributes," then because that very [qualification] exists, it would follow that Brahman is itself denotable by the word "nirviśeṣa. This is because [the qualification] is merely a means of approach (*dvāra*) and thus involves a contradiction between itself and its own subject, and because it is impossible for that which is "without attributes" to be denotable. Therefore, precisely because of the absence of attributes, the non-difference of the individual soul and Brahman is established, since no differentiator is possible. And so it is said: "The wise man who perceives denotability in Brahman, which is itself inexpressible..."
Let him, being shameless, be awakened by the absence of those signs.
Thus ends the demonstration that Brahman is inexpressible by words in the Advaitasiddhi. 13.

It might be argued: "This is untenable, because difference (*bheda*) is established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Nor should it be said that—since difference, if it were the very nature (*svarūpa*) of things, would result in being independent (and thus not a property), which would lead to an infinite regress; and since the apprehension of the mutual difference between a pillar and a jar depends upon the apprehension of their reciprocal difference, there is circularity (*anyonyāśraya*); and thus difference remains unestablished. For is it that there is no cognition of difference at all? Or is it produced without a cause? Or does it have a sublated object (*bādhyaviṣaya*)? It is not the first, because [difference] consists of the form of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) and so forth."

Because it would lead to the collapse of conventional discourse (*vyavahāra-viplava*); for a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) does not arise from that which is unknown as distinct. Nor is the second [alternative] tenable, because the production of an effect without a cause is a contradiction, which would entail its eternity, thereby necessitating the abandonment of the means to liberation (*mokṣopāya*) intended to remove it. Nor is the third [alternative] tenable, because the aforementioned "dry logic" (*śuṣka-tarka*) lacks sublativeness (*abādhakatva*). Otherwise, if oneness were the very nature (*svarūpa*) [of things], it would follow that it is independent; if it were a property (*dharma*), non-duality (*advaita*) would be lost. By such arguments, even the cognition of oneness would have a sublated object (*bādhita-viṣaya*).

Nor should it be said: "For me, as a mere caviller (*vaitaṇḍika*), only the other's position is to be refuted"; for if that were the case for you even while your own position exists, there would be no contradiction in that being the case for me as well. Nor does the mere refutation of the opponent's position by me establish the identity that constitutes my own view, since it is possible for me too to establish the difference that constitutes my own view by that much alone.

Nor should it be said: "In my case, you are merely engaged in the refutation of difference, and thus you are a mere caviller (*vaitaṇḍika*)," for it is possible that even in my case you might be merely engaged in the refutation of unity; moreover, a neutral observer is not dependent upon you. If you argue, "When you maintain that unity must be refuted by you using only arguments that do not contradict your own position, then it would likewise follow that difference must be refuted by you using only arguments that do not contradict your own position," this is not so. For we do not deny the nature or the cause of the cognition of difference.

However, we maintain that the subject matter [of the opponent's position] is sublated; for difference is sublated by Śruti, Smṛti, and sound reasoning (tarka) that are not of secondary intent and are accompanied by pervasion (vyāpti). Since the contradiction with perception has been resolved through the distinction of objects and so forth, there is no figurative meaning (upacaritārthatva) in the Śruti and other texts. As for the claim that non-difference is likewise refuted [by those same means]:

Furthermore, it is argued that because the arguments refuting non-difference would themselves fail to establish their own non-difference from themselves, they are fallacious due to self-contradiction; and since the arguments refuting difference likewise contradict themselves by being non-different from the very arguments that adorn them (the *bhūṣaṇa-yukti*), this defect applies equally to both. This is not so, because although the arguments refuting difference do indeed negate difference in the ultimate sense (*tattvataḥ*), they do not negate conventional difference (*vyāvahārika-bheda*), and thus it is logically consistent that they do not involve self-contradiction.

Nor does the real negation of the difference of the unreal from Brahman entail its identity with it; for in cases where there is an error regarding the difference of one imagined pot from another [real] pot, their identity is not observed. Nor, likewise, should non-difference itself be negated in reality, for in that case, failing to arrive at the essential nature [of Brahman], one would fall into the doctrine of nihilism (*śūnyavāda*). Furthermore, for us, there is no unity whatsoever apart from Brahman; and to negate that [unity] in such a manner would contradict the Śruti.

Nor should it be argued: "I have no difference distinct from the pot; therefore, its negation would contradict perception," for it has already been stated that perception does not contradict [the non-dual reality] because its object is not ultimate existence (*pāramārthika-sattva*). Now, an objection may be raised: "The sublater of difference cannot have difference itself as its object, for that would result in its being a prover of difference. Nor can it have non-difference as its object, for in that case, the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) must be said to be either 'other than that,' 'contrary to that,' or 'the absence of that'."

And in every way, difference is difficult to avoid; for if there were non-difference from that [entity], it would be impossible for it to be either contradictory to it or its absence, and because even the cognition grasping the absence of difference perceives the absence as distinct from its counter-positive, and because, like the cognition "this" in one who acts with indifference, it would not be sublated—[if you argue thus], we say no, because only that which has as its object the absence of difference in its ultimate (pāramārthika) form is sublatable.

Nor is it difficult to avoid [the charge of contradiction] regarding difference, because it is possible to establish the states of being contradictory to that [non-difference] and being its absence by means of conventional difference alone, according to the maxim: "The offering corresponds to the spirit. It is thus established that knowledge whose object is the reality which is the substratum of the error of difference is the sublater of that error, since—according to the manner explained—the apprehension of that [reality] is possible as distinct from difference.

As for the objection that one must state a subverting cognition (bādhakajñāna) of the form, "This is not a difference; there is no difference here; something else has appeared as having the nature of a difference"—just like the cognition "this is not silver"—and that since this [cognition] apprehends difference in every respect, how could it be a subverter in that case: that is not so, because the apprehension of that [difference] as a counter-correlative (pratiyogitayā) does not conflict with its being a subverter.

Nor should it be said that the cognition "there is no difference here" does not in any way apprehend the absence of difference; for if difference exists elsewhere, that very difference must necessarily exist here as well, and thus the statement "there is no difference here" would ultimately mean "it does not exist anywhere at all. Consequently, one must consider the subverting argument (bādhaka) such as: "the One alone appeared as manifold," and so forth. Furthermore, as has already been stated, the status of this [cognition] as a subverter is established because the two alternatives (koṭi) are grasped as possessing that [absence of difference] through a conventional difference. By this, it is also addressed whether the sublating cognition (bādhadhī) apprehends its own object as distinct from difference or not.
In the first case, the difference is stable; in the latter case, however, it would not be that which sublates the difference.

Thus, [the objection] is refuted; for even if there is stability in terms of its own nature (*svarūpa*), instability is possible from the perspective of ultimate reality (*tattvataḥ*). And in this way, because the object has not been established, objections such as mutual dependence (*anyonyāśrayatva*) arise; and once they have arisen, they cannot be considered mere fallacies (*ābhāsa*). Furthermore, this appearance of an objection is directed against those who maintain that things can be defined (*nirvacanavādin*), not against us. For we say that whatever difference appears is inexpressible (*anirvacanīya*)—either by being included within or excluded from the categories of essential nature (*svarūpa*) and so forth, or by some other distinct attribute.

Nor does the appearance of a pseudo-reasoning (tarkābhāsa) lead to the consequence that oneness is likewise indeterminable; for it has been stated that the sublation of difference is not a pseudo-reasoning, and there is a distinction between oneness and difference based on whether or not they are supported by scripture.

If it is argued that the exclusion of untruth and so forth from Brahman must be something not sublated by the knowledge of Brahman—since in the case of non-self objects like a pot, which are distinct from emptiness and the like, one observes a difference from emptiness that is not sublated by the knowledge of those objects themselves—the answer is no. This is because of the distinction between Brahman and the pot based on their being the substrate and the superimposed respectively; and since untruth is itself illusory, it is logical that its exclusion [from Brahman] is also illusory, making the fact of being sublated by the knowledge of that [pot] equally applicable to both.

Nor should it be argued that, in this way, the exclusion of illusory silver and the like would also result in being illusory, and consequently, the distinction between error and sublation (*bādha*) could not be maintained; for we accept such illusoriness because the distinction between sublation and error is established by whether [the cognition] is produced by the perception of a specific feature (*viśeṣadarśana*) or not. Furthermore, it does not follow that a statement such as "Being is" (*satyam*), which conveys the exclusion of the unreal (*anṛta*), would lose its validity; for that exclusion is merely implied (*ārtha*).

Nor should it be argued: "In this way, since absolute non-existence (atyantābhāva) whose counter-correlate (pratiyogin) is false—like a mere exclusion (vyāvṛtti)—is itself false, it would follow that it cannot possess falsity, defined as being a counter-correlate of an absolute non-existence that is not sublated by the knowledge of the substratum (adhiṣṭhāna-jñāna). This is not to be said, because "being sublatable by the knowledge of the substratum" is not a qualifying attribute in that case. Nor should it be argued: "In this way, if the difference between the body and the self were sublatable within the self, then the identity of the body and the self would not be false. This is not to be said, because it has already been stated that the falsity of a difference does not entail the non-falsity of the identity with its counter-correlative.

Nor should it be argued that the knowledge of the discrimination between eternal and non-eternal entities—which is included within the fourfold means—is an error, and that consequently there would be no inclination toward the eternal by way of abandoning the non-eternal; for since a cognition that apprehends the forms conducive to rejection and acquisition possesses empirical validity (*vyāvahārikaprāmāṇya*), empirical rejection and acquisition cannot be overturned.

By this, the following [objections] are refuted: (1) that if the difference from Being (*sadvailakṣaṇya*) in the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) were false, it would result in the identity of all with Being; and (2) that the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the falsity of the world would then fail to reveal reality (*atattvāvedaka*). This is because the answer to these has already been stated in the definition of falsity (*mithyātva*). By this, the following is also refuted: that since non-difference depends on difference, if difference is absent, both [difference and non-difference] must be sublated by the arguments used to sublate either one of them. This is because, even in the absence of real difference (*tāttvikabheda*), the systematic arrangement of things is possible through imagined difference (*kalpitabheda*).

Nor is it impossible for a conceptualized entity to obstruct the effect of a non-conceptualized one, since we observe that ignorance obstructs the effects of Brahman—which is self-luminous by nature—and we also observe that a conceptualized beloved obstructs the effect of separation.

Now, an objection: even for the sake of establishing the conventional reality (*vyāvahārikasattva*) of difference, you must resolve the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*) and so forth; for there is no conventional activity either that is mutually dependent—indeed, conventional clay does not depend upon the jar produced from itself. Furthermore, it is not by means of mere difference or the mere perception thereof that the charge of mutual dependence is leveled; if it were so, those two [difference and its perception] would fail to be established even as conventional realities.

Nor does that consequence follow from the reality of that cognition, for it is logically consistent—just as the object of a final mental state may be real even if the state itself is unreal—and because the pervasion is unestablished, as mutual dependence is not observed in cases of what is real. Nor can that consequence be established by means of a cognition in the form of valid knowledge (*pramā*), since you have already stated that mutual dependence applies to cognition in general, and thus no such defect exists when one reaches the level of validity (*pramātva*).

Nor can it be argued that the [non-existence] of that [difference] is established because the cognition of it depends upon a substratum (dharmin) and a counter-correlate (pratiyogin), for by that much, there is merely the cessation of its dependence on those two. If this is said, we reply: no, for us, all such logical inconsistencies are resolved through the power of avidyā. Indeed, there is nothing impossible within māyā; thus, it will demonstrate even mutually dependent things, like a magician’s trick.

Nor should it be argued that such [distinctions] could be real by virtue of God’s power; for, just as in the case of illusory magic (indrajāla) admitted by both parties, one observes effects that transgress the established order of causes and so forth, yet this is not seen elsewhere, and even where it were seen, it would ultimately resolve into being false. Furthermore, the logical consequence (*āpādana*) is as follows: if difference and its cognition were not illusory, they would not transgress all established orders; however, they do indeed transgress all established orders.

Therefore, because [the opponent's position] culminates in the conclusion that [difference] is illusory (*māyikī*), the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is established by the observation that in an illusory thing there is a transgression of the established order. Since difference is sublated by the aforementioned scripture and by reasoning that does not contradict itself, whereas non-difference is not so sublated, the hatred for difference alone—while both self-non-difference and self-difference are equal in their conventional status—is not without cause. Thus ends the general refutation of difference in the *Advaitasiddhi*. 14.

As for the objection raised—that if the nature [of Brahman] were independent (*nirapekṣa*), then dependence (*sāpekṣatva*) would be untenable—that is indeed incorrect. For in both of your systems, the cessation of ignorance and the identity of the individual soul with Brahman (*jīva-brahmaikya*) are established; furthermore, we observe that when a mere genus is perceived as dependent on an individual, it takes on the form of a dependent universal, just as "bluer" is dependent on its substrate. Likewise, in cases such as "Brahman exists," we see that knowledge—which consists in the illumination of an object—and the non-difference from Brahman within Brahman, as well as existence (*astitva*) which depends on time, take on the form of the independent Brahman-individual and so forth. Thus, dependence is not incompatible with an independent essence.

If it is argued [that there is a contradiction], we say no; for since the dependence [of the cognition] upon the cessation of ignorance and the identity of the individual soul (*jīva*) with Brahman is itself *avidyaka* (unreal), it does not contradict their ultimate independence. This is because mere universals (*jāti*) are not established as non-different from individuals, and because that [dependence] is absent in cases such as "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*), which possesses the same ontological status (*samānasattāka*) as the individual pot. Furthermore, in the case of universals such as "existence" (*sattā*), whose ontological status is not the same as the individual, the dependence is merely conceptual (*kālpnika*). Since there is no evidence to establish that "blueness" and the like are of the nature of the individual, there is no reason to deny the identity of knowledge—which consists in the illumination of objects—with Brahman.

This is because dependence is merely conceptual. The same applies to such statements as "Brahman exists" and so forth. Thus, since grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) cannot be established for that which is in reality independent, there is no proof of the pervasion [of the reason] by the fallacy of reasoning (*tarkābhāsa*). For this very reason: if identity were not the essential nature [of the two], non-duality would be lost; if it were false, it would follow that difference is real. Furthermore, wherever something is superimposed, its opposite there is not sublated by the knowledge of that [superimposition], just as the absence of silver is not sublated in mother-of-pearl.

The argument—that wherever identity is sublated, there its difference is not sublated by the knowledge of that [identity], as in the case of the difference between two trees standing at a distance; or that wherever something is superimposed, there its opposite is real, as in the case where untruth is superimposed on Brahman and thus truth is real—has been refuted. This is because identity with Brahman is not admitted to have any difference from Brahman, and because the pervasions (vyāpti) are unestablished, since all things that conform to their opposites are merely imagined in Brahman and are therefore sublatable by the knowledge of Brahman.

Now, an objection may be raised: "If identity were independent [of other factors], then the sentences defining the referents of the terms *tat* and *tvam*, such as 'Being, a mass of consciousness,' etc., would be redundant, because they would lack syntactic unity with the Great Mahāvākya which expresses identity. This is not so. Although identity—being non-different from self-luminous Brahman—is independent in its existence and apprehension, there still exists a state of syntactic unity among the sentences defining the essential nature [of the Self], because those sentences depend upon the word-meanings for the production of a mental modification (*vṛtti*) that removes the delusion regarding the difference between the indicated meanings (*lakṣyārtha*). Thus, they do possess syntactic unity.

Because difference is dependent upon its counter-correlative (pratiyogin) which possesses a distinct form, the conventional usage of "dependence" applies to it. Nor is there a reversal of this principle in the case of the negation of identity—as in "the jar is not the cloth"—where the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) is the negation of identity, just as it is difference; for if identity consists of the unique properties residing in that [object], then difference does not depend on non-difference. And if identity has the form of non-difference, then because difference is required for that [non-difference], identity itself does not depend on it. Furthermore, this does not entail the contingency of unity being dependent, since such dependence is accepted only in the case of conceptual constructs.

For this very reason, the following is refuted: "Just as with the destruction of ignorance, just as with the cognition of the nature of Brahman, and just as with non-difference, it is indeed logical that difference, even though it is one's own nature (*svarūpa*), should be dependent. This is refuted because, for you, those two forms of dependence would be real, and thus there is a disparity with the illustrative examples. Nor can it be said that the same applies to difference; for since difference is heard of in scripture as the counter-positive of negation, it lacks the nature of Brahman. Furthermore, there is no scriptural statement regarding non-difference in that case [of difference].

By this [argument], the following is refuted: "Just as non-difference (*abheda*), though independent in its own nature (*svarūpa*), is dependent insofar as it is 'non-difference,' let the jar also be dependent insofar as it is 'difference' (*bheda*), even though it is independent in its own nature; for just as there can be both having a counter-correlative (*sapratiyogitva*) and not having a counter-correlative (*apratiyogitva*) due to a difference in limiting adjuncts (*avacchedaka-bheda*), so it is here. [This is refuted because] if difference were independent in its own nature and devoid of a counter-correlative (*niṣpratiyogika*), then, being indistinguishable with respect to itself just as it is toward others, it would result in self-contradiction (*svavyāghāta*).

Nor does it follow that, if this were the case, non-difference (*abheda*) would likewise be perceived as such by others just as it is by oneself; for such a consequence is accepted (*iṣṭāpatti*). Difference is merely imagined (*kalpita*) through attributes such as "pot-ness" and so forth, whereas in its own nature (*svarūpataḥ*), there is indeed non-difference. This being so, only "otherness" (*paratva*) is contradicted, not its essential nature (*svarūpatva*) either.

As for the argument that the distinction between having a counter-correlate (*sapratyogika*) and lacking a counter-correlate (*niṣpratyogika*) is established such that whatever, in its cognition, depends upon the cognition of a counter-correlate by virtue of being delimited by the specific ground for the application of its own designator, is "with a counter-correlate," while anything else is "without a counter-correlate"—that is not correct; for if difference were the very nature (*svarūpa*) [of the thing], then its being "other than that" (*tadanyatva*) would be unestablished.

By this [argument], the following is refuted: "Just as a single object may be independent when characterized by lightness, hardness, and so forth, yet dependent when characterized by weight, fluidity, and so forth; likewise, although 'jar' is independent when characterized by that [specific] description, its dependence is established when characterized by the description 'difference'. This is refuted because there is experience of both dependence and independence even without the mention of words, and because the analogy is unconvincing—just like the case of dissolution (*laya*) and so on—since mere non-mention of the negative particle (*nañ*) does not suffice for a valid comparison.

Nor should it be argued: "Since we observe that for a single act of going, there is dependence on an object (*sakarmakatva*) and independence (*nirapekṣatva*) through the verbal expressions *gacchati* and *calati*, and for a single effort, there is dependence and independence through the verbal expressions *karoti* and *pravartate*—which are prompted by the nature of the words themselves—so too here, dependence and independence should exist through the verbal expressions *ghaṭa* and *bheda*. This must not be said, because properties such as transitivity (*sakarmakatva*) residing in the meaning do not depend upon the nature of the words.

On the contrary, these two [the action and the result] are observed within the very same verbal root (*dhātu*) through a distinction in meaning, as seen in such instances as *tapati ṛṣiḥ* ("the sage heats"), *tapati pṛthivīm savitā* ("the sun heats the earth"), and so forth. Thus, in the examples, there is indeed a difference in meaning; for according to the view that the result is the meaning of the verbal root, there is a difference in meaning in the form of "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*).

According to another view, however, the meaning of *gam* (to go) is motion delimited by posterior conjunction (*uttara-saṃyoga*), the meaning of *cal* (to move) is motion resulting in prior disjunction (*pūrva-vibhāga*), the meaning of *kṛ* (to do) is effort conducive [to an action], and the meaning of *yat* (to strive) is effort in general. Nor should it be said that "it is only the property of being a difference (*bhedatva*) that is dependent [on a counter-correlative], but not the difference itself"; for experience shows that it is the qualificandum (*viśeṣya*) alone that is dependent, otherwise there would be the verbalization: "the property of being a difference having a jar as its counter-correlative."

By this, the following [objection] is refuted: "Since it consists of both existence and non-existence, difference is not something separate from mutual negation (*anyonyābhāva*); rather, difference is merely the essential nature (*svarūpa*) itself. Furthermore, because it has been stated that "difference is mutual negation, and that is non-different from the entity as possessing specific attributes," the claim that "the jar and so forth themselves are the difference by virtue of being of the nature of both existence and non-existence" is rejected. For in the case of a jar and its absence, since existence and non-existence are contradictory, how can there be identity between their substrates? Nor can one argue: "In the case of the cessation of ignorance (*avidyānivṛtti*) and non-duality (*advaita*), how could there be identity with Brahman? [The answer is that our position does not entail such contradictions.]

It must be said that, in our view, there is no contradiction because non-existence (*abhāvatva*) in that case is merely conceptual and thus illusory (*māyika*); for you, however, since both are real (*tāttvika*), the contradiction is difficult to avoid.

For this very reason—whether it be the unfitness for identity with that [object], or not being the object of a cognition of identity with that, or the state of being opposed to the superimposition of identity with that where there is the perception of that, or the nature of being that which resides in something not possessing any of its own attributes, or the nature of being that which possesses an attribute residing in something not possessing any of its own attributes—this difference is its essential nature (*svarūpatva*). And "not being a substratum" (*anādhāratva*) means the absence of being a substratum, and not being something other than a substratum.

The claim that there is no mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*) has been refuted: for if difference were the very nature (*svarūpa*) of the object, its being dependent [on a counter-correlate] would be untenable; if it were something additional (*atireka*), there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*); furthermore, absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) and mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) would result in being identical; and finally, because it would be constituted by the perception of the cognized object and so forth, it would follow that it is not accessible to the eyes and other sense organs. Moreover, if difference were the nature of the jar, then its defining counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) would also have to be of the nature of that jar; for the jar is not merely the form of difference, but rather the form of difference having cloth as its counter-correlate.

Is it not the case that this is not a fault? For the counter-correlate of difference (*bhedapratiyogin*) is a mere secondary characteristic (*upalakṣaṇa*), and thus does not participate in the essential nature (*svarūpatā*). Otherwise, since the cessation of suffering is the human goal (*puruṣārtha*), suffering itself would also be a human goal; if the absence of defects (*doṣābhāva*) is the cause for being an instrument of proof, then a defect would also be a cause for being an instrument of proof; if the exclusion of falsehood (*anṛtavyāvṛtti*), the cessation of ignorance (*ajñānanivṛtti*), and knowledge whose nature is the illumination of ignorance and so forth are identical with Brahman, then falsehood and the rest would also be of that same nature; and if the cessation of ignorance were liberation, then ignorance itself [would be so].

And there would be the status of liberation [as a qualifier]. Nor can it be argued that because we observe the connection of ears and so forth as qualifiers in cases such as "long-eared" (*lambakarna*), the same must hold here; for why should it not be the case that it is exactly the same in examples like "the owner of brindled cows" (*citragu*) due to the lack of such a connection? Otherwise, there would be no understanding in the cited instances. Nor does it follow that if the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) were merely an incidental indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*), then even when that is unknown—as in the case of knowing a house despite not knowing the crow—the cognition of it would arise; for this is an accepted consequence, and otherwise, there would be no understanding in the cited examples.

Some, however, say that even when the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) is not included in the positive concomitance (*anvaya*), as in "sound is non-eternal" and so forth, the counter-correlate functions as a qualifier; they claim that here too [the counter-correlate] functions as a qualifier. This is not correct, for we do not thereby cause the cloth to become the nature of the jar simply because it is a counter-correlate entering into the positive concomitance as the object of determination, nor merely by being a determiner through its status as a counter-correlate; rather, [we do so] by its being a determiner through its status as a counter-correlate with respect to the nature that is the object of a co-referential cognition.

[The difference] is like the counter-correlative (pratiyogin) that determines non-difference. Furthermore, the cessation of ignorance and so forth are not objects of a co-referential cognition, whereas difference is the object of a co-referential cognition such as "the jar is not the cloth. Otherwise, being the object of a co-referential negative cognition would not constitute the definition of difference. By this [it is shown that]: just as suffering is not included within the human goal [of happiness], nor is ignorance within Brahman, nor delusion within liberation, so too a jar and the like are not included within a cloth.
"The cognition of difference does not occur when jars and the like are not perceived even while [the self] remains neutral,
just as the loss of that [ignorance] and so forth is not perceived when ignorance itself is not perceived"— this [argument] is refuted.

Furthermore, if difference (*bheda*), which is by nature disintegration, were the very essence of the jar, then the jar itself would undergo disintegration, as would its constituent parts; thus, even the atom would not be a unity, leading to the consequence of universal voidness (*śūnyatā*), because in the absence of the one, the many—which is a collection of unities—would also be non-existent. Now, if non-difference (*abheda*), which is by nature non-disintegration, were the essence of Brahman, then since the ultimate Brahman is not subject to disintegration even by the empirical, the apparent, or the void, its oneness would likewise be subject to such non-disintegration.

If it is argued: "The identity with the living self (*jīva*) alone is the essential nature (*svarūpa*), whereas identity with a jar or other objects is not; likewise, here too, difference from jars and so forth is the essential nature of the cloth, but not difference from itself—thus the cases are equal," we say no. For if difference were the essential nature, then given that its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) is known without being obstructed by the knowledge of itself, it would necessarily entail self-annihilation, just as non-difference does by virtue of being the essential nature, due to the rule that it must have itself as its own counter-correlate. This is because, among the attributes of a jar, there exists the state of being a difference whose counter-correlate is a cloth, as well as the state of being a difference whose counter-correlate is the jar itself.

This is because it is accepted [as a fact], and because the cognition that "the pot is different from the pot" is as indelible as a diamond-stone (vajralepa) as the cognition that "the pot is different from the cloth. As for the argument that if something were to split itself, the parts would merely become subtle through division and not reach non-existence (*śūnyatva*), since nothing is ever produced from the conjunction of a void—that is incorrect. For "dividing-ness" does not mean "splitting," but rather "being opposed to oneness. Thus, when oneness is absent, multiplicity is all the more absent, and the result is necessarily a state of voidness.

By this it is shown that if difference (*bheda*) is the very nature (*svarūpa*) [of a thing], then a saw, a chisel, or the like would not cut its own self—that is, its cutting power would reside only in what is related to itself, and not in itself. Furthermore, difference does not possess the quality of cutting, because "cutting" (*vidāraṇa*) is derived from the verbal root in the sense of an action (*bhāva*).

And thus, it is refuted [by the opponent] that there would be no splitting of a jar by means of a difference in its own nature (*svarūpabheda*), because that would involve a contradiction of its own existence; however, this is rejected because difference consists in the nature of splitting, which is essentially division (*vibhāga*). Since division is necessarily resident in that which is being divided, there would be an infinite regress of parts, resulting in the consequence of emptiness (*śūnyatā*); therefore, that situation remains as it was. Consequently, difference is not of the nature of splitting, which is division, but rather is mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*), because verbal roots have multiple meanings. As it has been said: "In order to express their action, each individual meaning is demonstrated; for verbal roots have multiple meanings, which must be followed according to usage."

The argument that "otherwise, there would be no conventional usage of two conjoined things as being distinct" is refuted; for if difference were essentially the nature of mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*), then a difference whose counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) is the form of the substrates such as the potsherds would, by virtue of having the form of the substrate such as the jar as its own nature, become the locus of a difference from itself. Consequently, the unity of the potsherds and so forth would be destroyed, resulting ultimately in a void due to an infinite regress of parts.

For this very reason, the following objection is refuted: "It is not logical to negate plurality by means of a difference that inheres in the same object as unity, and then use that [difference] to further negate unity, because it would contradict what it depends upon (upajīvya-virodha). This is because the absence of oneness is established merely by the existence of a difference whose counter-correlate is itself, without even touching upon plurality. Therefore, the Teachers have stated: "Because there is a contradiction between unity—inhering in the same object as non-difference—and difference."

As for what was said—that there is a contradiction regarding its own occurrence—that is not so, because we do not accept an operation consisting of division and the like; rather, an operation consisting of opposition to others and so forth exists everywhere. Furthermore, if difference were of the nature of the thing's own essence (svarūpa), there could be no doubt or the like [regarding it], because when the locus is known, there would be no ignorance of the difference, and if that [difference] were unknown, the very cause [for such cognition] would be absent.

[Objection: But surely, even for you, the impossibility of doubt and so forth is equally applicable if non-difference (*abheda*) is also the very nature (*svarūpa*) [of reality]; and if it is because of the non-cognition of non-difference as such that this occurs, then for me too it would occur because of the non-cognition of difference as such. [Reply: No, for if difference were the very nature [of reality], then by the argument leading to emptiness (*śūnyatā*), all conceptual alternatives (*koṭi*) would be utterly destroyed. And it should not be said: "Even for you, if non-difference were the very nature [of reality], the alternative of difference would be destroyed. For doubt is possible by taking recourse to a conceptually constructed (*kalpita*) alternative. Nor is the alternative of the existence of a differentiator (*bhedaka*) and so forth constructed for you either, since it has already been stated that this would result in the consequence of emptiness.

As for the objection that—even though consciousness (*caitanya*) is self-luminous—there might still be a non-manifestation of unity and unconditioned bliss (which are non-different from it), just as there is a non-manifestation of difference (though it too is non-different from the substrate); and furthermore, that if unity were manifest, there would be no disagreement regarding it and its teaching would be purposeless—that is not so, because although unity and the rest are of the nature of self-luminosity, they are not in contradiction with ignorance, its effects, or disagreements.

This is because there is no lack of justification for the cessation of the functioning that is opposed to its object-domain. Nor should it be argued that, in that case, there would also be disagreement regarding the inner self (*pratyagartha*), since even the Cārvākas and others are seen to hold such views. Therefore, while ignorance does not veil the manifestation of the inner self—which serves as the substrate for ignorance and so forth—it certainly veils the aspect of identity and the like; it is with respect to that [aspect] that disagreements and so on arise.

Nor should it be said that, in this way, the aspect of difference is also veiled here due to defects such as similarity, for one who maintains the theory of superimposition (*āropavādin*) cannot admit that, since the alternative possibility (*koṭi*) has not been presented prior to the primary [superimposition].

As for the difference in essential nature (*svarūpa-bheda*), it indeed appears as difference itself, since for the most part everything is perceived precisely as distinct; otherwise, there would be doubt regarding every possible alternative. In that case, various attributes such as having "pot" as its counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*)—which remain ungrasped due to similarity and other factors—will become the objects of doubt. Nor does it follow that difference, which is defined by multiple relata, becomes manifold simply because of the multiplicity of its defining relata; for we observe unity even in such cases, such as the non-duality (*advaita*) defined by the plurality of dualities in the knowledge of the Lord (*īśvara-jñāna*), and so forth. One...

And because it is observed that the prior non-existence and the destruction of a determinable object are not identical—that is incorrect. We do not assert a difference [of non-existence] based on a difference in the determiner; rather, a difference in non-existence is necessary due to a difference in the delimitors of the counter-positive (*pratiyogitāvacchedaka*). Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the identity of the four [kinds of non-existence], such as destruction, which all have a single jar as their counter-positive. Nor is it the case for those who maintain that non-existence is of the nature of its locus that non-existence differs merely by a difference in locus; for if that were so, there would be the consequence of the identity of destruction and prior non-existence, which would result in the impossibility of distinct linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) regarding them.

Nor is there any inconsistency regarding non-duality even in this case, because the delimiting factor of the counter-correlativity—namely, "being other than Brahman"—is one and the same, and because the distinction or non-distinction of the counter-correlate is irrelevant. As for the claim that the cognition of difference does not oppose error, but rather it is the cognition of a property contradictory to the superimposed object within the substrate that opposes it—that is incorrect; for it would follow that a verbal error regarding non-difference could not be removed by a verbal cognition of difference.

As for what has been said by some—that the cognition of something as having a certain nature when it is not cognized as such, being rooted in a defect, constitutes the definition of a difference in essential nature (svarūpabheda), and since the non-cognition of a mother-of-pearl in its true nature as mother-of-pearl is rooted in a defect, there is no over-extension [of the definition] to that case.

As for the claim that although "having no basis in defects" (*adoṣamūla*) cannot function as a qualifier for the locative [term], it nonetheless functions as such by virtue of being a qualifier for the qualified [whole], that is incorrect. For if there is no cognition [of the object] in its specific form, then since the cognition is common to both identity and difference, one must state that the cause for the linguistic usage of difference is the knowledge extending up to the point of "having no basis in defects. In that case, since "having no basis in defects" is to be inferred solely from its result, the difference would not be visual (*cākṣuṣa*), because it would be constituted by the cognition; furthermore, at the time when there is no such cognition, difference would not exist.

Furthermore, at the time of the cognition of a shell as having the nature of silver, the difference between them would not exist there; for the term "not rooted in a defect" lacks the capacity to exclude under-extension when used as a qualifier of negation, since that which does not reside in the locus of the qualificand can even less reside in the locus of the qualified whole. Indeed, a man with a staff cannot exist where a man is absent. Nor can the phrase "not rooted in a defect" serve as a qualifier of the counter-positive (the defect) in order to include sublated cases—just as "body" is a qualifier of the counter-positive in the expression "not produced by a body"—because a negative particle compounded with another term cannot be construed with a term that is not itself compounded.

For by the statement "one who is not a Brāhmaṇa is not correct," the absence of a correct Brāhmaṇa is not understood. Furthermore, when stating the absence of a cognition of identity with the cause of error (adoṣamūla), since there is no cognition of the shell as having the nature of silver at the time it is not so cognized, and since there is no cognition of it as having the nature of a shell [either], the same predicament arises due to the resulting difference from itself (svabhedāpatti) because of the lack of causal conditions (sāmagrīviraha). Thus, the situation remains exactly as it was.

Nor should it be argued that even then, the state of being perceived as having the nature of the mother-of-pearl (śukti) exists by taking into account the cognition of the Lord; for if that were so, the term "being perceived" would be redundant, as there is no occasion when it is not being perceived. Nor is that [difference] the nature of mutual non-existence (anyonyābhāvatva), because that cannot be defined. As the Teachers have said:

"Because it is relative, because it has a limit, because if it were real it would entail the consequence of non-duality, because it is the absence of one, and because there is no doubt [regarding its identity], difference is not the form of a real entity."

Furthermore, if the pot were of the nature of difference (*bhedatva*), it would entail the consequence of the reduction to either one or the other. Now, [the opponent objects]: "The consequence of the reduction to either one or the other is equally applicable to you as well, since oneness, consciousness, and bliss are the very nature of Brahman; nor can this be accepted as a desired conclusion because the reality is one, for the same logic applies here too. We reply: No, because by the consequence of the reduction to either one or the other, one would arrive at the absence of distinct linguistic usage such as "pot" and "difference," which are of different characters.

Nor can that [distinction] be established on the basis of the difference between the two grounds for application (*pravṛttinimitta*), namely "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*) and "difference-ness" (*bhedatva*), because "difference-ness" itself cannot be defined. To explain: it cannot first be a *jāti* (universal), because it would then be common to universals and so forth; nor can it be an *upādhi* (accidental property), in the form of "the state of being an absence whose counter-positive is delimited by identity," because if identity were of the nature of the absence of difference, there would be circularity (*anyonyāśraya*). If, on the other hand, it were of the nature of a unique property residing in that [difference], it would be over-extensive (*ativyāpti*) with respect to absolute non-existence whose counter-positive is delimited by that [property]; and if that [non-existence] were also of the nature of its own essence (*svarūpa*), [the same problem would persist].

Because it would result in the impossibility of following conventional linguistic usage; nor should it be argued that "in that case, there would be no distinct usage even regarding cognition, bliss, and so forth," for that is explained by resorting to a difference in imputed properties (*kalpitadharma*). Nor should it be argued that "difference itself may likewise be [imputed]," for if that were so, you would be beyond refutation. Furthermore, if difference were the very nature (*svarūpa*) of an object, there could be no cognition of it as a relation, such as "this is different" or "this is the difference of that."

Nor is the argument "Ānanda is not Brahman" tenable; for when identity is established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), the conventional usage of difference is assumed to be figurative (*aupacārika*), as in the case of "the head of Rāhu. But that is not the case here, because there is no evidence for identity and, on the contrary, there are subverting arguments (*bādhaka*). Nor can one adopt an alternative position simply because another alternative is untenable; otherwise, since neither existence nor non-existence is possible for things like a hare's horn, one would have to accept one of them.

Nor can there be an establishment of falsity in both cases due to sublation; for in the present case as well, an establishment of the nature of being illusory (*āvidyaka*) is possible due to sublation in both instances.
