Now, [it may be argued]: there is a cognition of difference as being the very nature [of the object], such as "the pot is not identical with the cloth"—where difference, in the form of the negation of identity with the cloth, is perceived as non-difference through its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the pot—and likewise, there is the inferential mark (*liṅga*) consisting in the fact that when either of the two, the pot or the difference, is cognized, the other is necessarily cognized.

If it is argued that there is scriptural authority for this, such as "The truth is that difference is the very nature of things; there is no doubt about this," we say no. This is because statements such as "A jar is not of the nature of a cloth" have as their object mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) as a form of difference, and thus do not concern the identity of difference and non-difference. Otherwise, even a statement like "The jar is blue" would result in having the identity of color as its object.

Furthermore, since the non-difference of the *liṅgin* (the subject) has not been established prior [to the inference], and because the universal concomitance (*sāmānyavyāpti*) is fallacious in the case of genus (*jāti*), individual (*vyakti*), and so forth—which are cognized by a single cognition—and because even in the case of a specific concomitance (*viśeṣavyāpti*), there is a fallacy regarding the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), and because scripture (*āgama*) intends to establish non-existence apart from the substratum;

moreover, is the difference from the cloth the nature of the jar alone, or is it the nature of all things such as the jar and the wall? In the first case, the wall and so forth would not be different from the cloth. In the second case, since individual natures are not uniform (*ananugata*), there could be no uniform cognition of the difference from the cloth.

Nor should it be argued that, just as there is a uniform linguistic usage regarding cognition of a cloth, desire for a cloth, and so forth, based on the commonality of having the cloth as their object (*viṣayatva*), there is likewise a uniform usage here based on the commonality of having the cloth as their counter-correlative (*pratiyogikatva*). For by this much, just as there is a uniformity in the aspect of "having the cloth as object" in cognitions and desires—such that one speaks of "cognition of the cloth" or "desire for the cloth"—there would only be uniformity in the aspect of "having the cloth as counter-correlative," and not even in the aspect of difference (*bheda*). And it has already been stated that "difference-ness" (*bhedatva*) is also not a single [entity].

Furthermore, whether one apprehends difference as "this is different from that" or as "the difference of this from that," there is mutual dependence (parasparāśraya) because the apprehension of difference is constituted by the subject (dharmin) and the counter-correlate (pratiyogin). For, the knowledge of difference depends on the knowledge of the subject and the counter-correlate, and once that [difference] exists, there arises the knowledge of the distinct subject and counter-correlate expressed as "this from that. This is the case even when apprehending that "the jar and the cloth are different," whether the difference is grasped as a qualifier of the jar and the cloth or as their substantive object. In all such cases, there is indeed mutual dependence.

In the cognition of a jar and a cloth, there is the apprehension of their difference by way of their being the qualificands (*viśeṣya*) and so forth; and when there is the apprehension of difference, there is the cognition of the jar and the cloth as delimited by duality (*dvitva*). Nor should it be argued: "Since difference is the very nature (*svarūpa*) [of things], the cognition of difference is nothing other than the cognition of that nature itself; thus, because there is no second cognition, the aforementioned fault does not arise. This objection cannot stand, because even if the cognition of the nature [of the object] lacks a second [cognition], there is still a requirement for a second cognition of the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), which is distinct from the cognition of the nature itself.

Nor should it be argued that—because one observes the absence of the erroneous cognition "this is of the nature of everything"—one experiences the object as generally excluded from everything (i.e., as not being of the nature of everything), and thus there is no mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*) since there is no requirement for the knowledge of a specific counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*). For in the case of the statement "it is not of the nature of everything," is "everything-ness" (*sarvatva*) the delimiting property of the counter-correlate, or is it "everything-ness other than itself"? In the first case, if it were distinct from itself, it would follow that the self is unestablished. In the second case, the mutual dependence is evident.

Nor should it be argued: "Just as in the passage 'All this, indeed, is Brahman,' all that is not perceived as having Brahman as its self is denoted, so too here, by the word 'from all,' all that is not known to have that [Brahman] as its self is intended. This cannot be said, because prior to one's own apprehension, even oneself is unknown as one's own self, which would result in oneself being the counter-correlative (pratiyogin); furthermore, you do not accept that the word 'all' is unrestricted in the cited example.

Nor should it be argued that—in reality—the cognition of that which is the locus of difference, when not known as non-different, is the cause [of the cognition of the counter-correlate] by virtue of being a cognition [of it], and not by virtue of being a cognition having "difference" as its qualifier; for if this were so, there would be no illusion of duality regarding the moon, since in reality there is an absence of difference.

If it is argued that—just as in cases such as "I do not know this which exists" or "All this is indeed Brahman," where there is a cognition of the non-difference of the object from its ignorance along with all factors including time established by the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*), so too here there is a cognition of exclusion together with the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) established by the witness-consciousness, and thus there is no mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*)—we say no; for even if a qualified cognition is not produced by a cognition of the qualifier, a determinate cognition (*savikalpaka*) of the counter-positive is, through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), the cause of the cognition of the absence.

Furthermore, since the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*) does not apprehend the counter-correlate—such as a cloth—without depending on a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) as distinct from the locus (*dharmin*), how could the apprehension of difference be possible through a counter-correlate established by the witness? As it is stated in the *Cintāmaṇi*: "Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that even from indeterminate perception (*nirvikalpaka*), the cognition 'the jar does not exist' would arise."

Nor should it be argued that, by this much, one need only seek a cognition having "cloth-ness" (*paṭatva*) and so forth as the qualifier of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*), but not a cognition extending up to the difference from the locus (*dharmibhinnatva*); for if the difference [of the property] from the locus is not known, there is an absence of the very status of being the determiner of non-existence (*abhāvanirūpakatva*) by way of being the qualifier of counter-correlativity. Furthermore, when there is a cognition of the mutual difference between properties, the cognition of the difference of the pillar from the jar occurs upon the specific cognition of the difference of the jar from the pillar; thus, the fault of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*) remains as it was.

Objection: Even in your view, since the reflected Brahman (*pratibimba-brahma*) is non-different from the original object (*bimba*), the individual soul (*jīva*), there would arise such cognitions as "this is non-different from that," "the non-difference of this from that," or "the non-difference of these two. And since the cognition of the relation between a substratum and a counter-correlate (*dharmi-pratiyogi-bhāva*), as well as the cognition delimited by duality (*dvitva-avacchinna-dhī*), are dependent upon the cognition of difference, the cognition of non-difference—which is opposed to them—would be impossible. Reply: This is not so, because a conceptual cognition of difference, which merely serves to account for the cognition of the relation between substratum and counter-correlate and the cognition delimited by duality, cannot obstruct the cognition of real non-difference (*tāttvika-abheda*).

Furthermore, in the cognition of non-difference, there is no dependence on the cognition of the substratum or the counter-correlative (pratiyogin), because that [non-difference] is the very nature of the thing itself, devoid of a counter-correlative; the conventional usage of it as having a counter-correlative, however, occurs by virtue of the counter-correlativity of the difference that serves as its defining condition (nirūpaka).

For this very reason, the following [objection] is refuted: "The individual soul (*jīva*) can only be the determiner of non-difference from Brahman by being known as non-different from it; thus, there is a circular dependency (*anyonyāśraya*), because only that which is perceived as non-different from a substratum (*dharmin*) can be its counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) of non-difference. Otherwise, even fire would have to be the counter-correlative of non-difference from ice. Furthermore, the apprehension of difference acts as an obstacle in that regard.

For this very reason—namely, to avoid the contingency that the specific entity denoted by the term *tvam* in the statement "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*) would be the counter-correlate of identity with Brahman—the established doctrine of others is formulated as follows: when no obstacle exists, the cognition of the existing non-difference in the form of the mind's fitness for non-difference is the cause of the realization of non-difference; however, in the case of the error of difference, a defect acts as an obstacle, and thus the realization of non-difference does not occur. [This is stated] having postulated this doctrine, even in the view that difference is essential (svarūpa-bheda), where two things such as a jar and... are in reality mutual counter-correlates.

The proposed resolution—based on the parity that, when the cloth and its own nature (paṭasvarūpa) are perceived respectively as "potness" and "clothness," which are capable of being mutual counter-correlates, a qualified cognition arises through their mutual counter-correlation provided there is no obstruction; and likewise, even in the view that difference is a property (dharma), the perception of the existing difference in the form of "blueness" and "yellowness," which are capable of being differences, serves as the cause of difference provided there is no obstruction; whereas in the case of trees at a distance, the defect of distance acts as an obstruction so that no cognition of difference occurs—is refuted, because a lack of parity has already been stated.

Now, an objection: just as in cases such as "a cow is similar to a gavaya," the difference of the gavaya and so forth from the cow and so forth—which is already existent—is the cause for its being a counter-correlate (*pratiyogitva*), and not something that must be known; for even the perceptual cognition "a cow is similar to a gavaya" is not invariably experienced as being preceded by the thought "the gavaya is different from the cow," much less so in the case of verbal cognition, since there is no word denoting difference therein; so it is in the present case as well.

Otherwise, there would be a circularity regarding all categories that possess counter-correlates (sapratiyogika), such as the cognition of Caitra’s sonship toward Maitra occurring only when Maitra’s fatherhood toward Caitra is already known, or the cognition that "the cow is similar to the gavaya" occurring only when the gavaya’s similarity to the cow is already known. If this is argued, we say no, because such a consequence is accepted; for this very reason, it is our established doctrine (*siddhānta*) that difference, similarity, and so forth are difficult to define—whether as possessing a counter-correlate or lacking one—since there are objections against every such definition.

As for what was said—that the rule of being preceded by the apprehension of the distinction between the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) and the locus (*dharmin*) is not experienced—that is precisely what we accept, because that very [rule] acts as a sublation when [the object] itself possesses a counter-correlate. For it is only in the case of the perception of an object possessing a counter-correlate that the charge of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*) can be leveled; whereas the absence of a word denoting difference in verbal cognition (*śābda*) is no fault in our view. And thus, the mere cognition of a counter-correlate is not the cause of the cognition of difference, since that would entail its occurrence even from the indeterminate (*nirvikalpaka*) cognition of it; rather, it is [the cognition of it] as a counter-correlate (*pratiyogitvena*).

Even in that case, [the cognition] does not have "otherness" as its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), but rather "difference. Thus, there would be the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*). Nor can this be the case for similarity and the like, which do possess counter-correlates, because we accept that very point; furthermore, it has already been stated that non-difference (*abheda*) does not possess a counter-correlate. As for the claim that where both the locus (*dharmin*) and the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) are present, there is a simultaneous cognition of the existence of the locus, the existence of the counter-correlate, and their difference—just as in the case of "this is similar to that"—[that is incorrect].

Likewise, there is a simultaneous cognition of the qualifier-qualified relationship, as in the case of "these two are similar. This is because, when all [objects] are capable, it is possible for a single cognition of all objects to arise simultaneously through sensory contact. Indeed, in my view, even the cognition "one who possesses a staff" (*daṇḍī*) is not produced by the cognition of the staff. And this has been stated: even where one of the two—the locus (*dharmin*) or the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*)—is not present, a cognition arises in exactly this same way through sensory contact aided by mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), just like the cognition "this is similar to that," and so forth.
Otherwise, even the cognition of non-difference would not be possible; and thus there would be a circular dependency. As it has been said:

"If the state of being the locus (dharmitva), the state of being the counter-correlate (pratiyogitva), and their absence were to occur simultaneously, then the qualifier, the qualified, and their very absence would be grasped [at once]."

That is not so; for even when a jar is known by way of its "knowability" (*prameyatva*) and so forth, there is no cognition that "the jar is absent. Since the jar must necessarily have been previously known by way of its "jar-ness" (*ghaṭatva*) and so forth, the cognitions of the locus (*dharmin*), the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), and so on, cannot be established simultaneously. Nor is it the case that, because the jar must necessarily have been previously known by way of its "jar-ness," the cognitions of the locus, the counter-correlate, and so on, fail to be established simultaneously.

Nor should it be argued that "the delay there is due solely to the delay in the causal complex for the cognition of jar-ness and so forth, and since that [complex] is present, the desired consequence follows. For even with this, the objection that an absence-cognition could arise without having the counter-positive as its object remains unrefuted. Nor is such a causal complex for grasping the counter-positive the cause [of the absence-cognition], because the cognition of the counter-positive itself is simpler than that.
[Objection: But if otherness is not grasped, how can the aforementioned circularity be established?
And if otherness were already established, how could there be circularity?

If it is argued that "this is a rope with snares on both ends," we say no; for we do not deny the cognition of difference even as something functional within empirical usage, but rather we maintain that it is untenable if it is not rooted in ignorance (avidyā). Furthermore, since difference is known only through the relation of qualifier and qualified, and since the cognition of those respective entities depends upon the cognition of difference—as seen in cases such as "the staff" and "Caitra"—there would result an infinite regress of successive cognitions of difference.

Nor should it be argued: "It is the same for you as well that the initial cognition of non-difference (or the like) cannot occur, because even in cases such as 'Brahman is non-different from the individual soul' or 'the world is illusory,' there is the requirement of a cognition of difference to serve as a qualifier for the non-difference, which would lead to an infinite regress. This is not to be said, because it is possible for something to function as a qualifier even if its difference [from the qualificand] is merely imagined by ignorance (*avidyā*) and remains uncognized.

But this is not the case for you as well, because there is no difference between the distinction (*bheda*) and the thing distinguished (*bhedya*) in their own nature, since the distinction is not distinct from its locus. As for the position that "distinction is a property" (*dharma*), even if the infinite regress regarding the cognition (*pratīti*) is avoided, it results in the unavoidable consequence of an infinite regress regarding the object (*viṣaya*). Nor is there the defect of infinite regress and so forth even in the view that distinction is illusory (*avidyaka*), for such irrationality is an ornament [to the doctrine].

Therefore, the objection that—in the statement "Brahman is non-different"—it is impossible to convey the non-difference of Brahman from ignorance (avidyā), which is known as something different and serves as a qualifier, because that cognition of prior difference acts as an obstacle—is refuted; for the knowledge of an indeterminable (anirvacanīya) difference does not obstruct the knowledge of real (tāttvika) non-difference.

Furthermore, regarding the position that difference is a distinct category (*dharmabheda*), does perception take difference alone as its object, or does it also take the entity itself? Not the first, because there is no cognition of "difference" alone. As for the second, does it take the entity preceded by difference as its object, or difference preceded by the entity, or both simultaneously? Not the first, because there is no cognition of "difference" alone, and because a cognitive operation cannot be interrupted (*viramya-vyāpāra*). For this very reason, not the second; nor the third, because it has been established that the apprehension of the entity is what generates the apprehension of difference.

Nor can there be a simultaneous apprehension of both [the object and its difference] by means of a qualified cognition (viśiṣṭajñāna) that arises immediately after the cognition of the mere thing (vastumātra), because the cognition of difference has as its cause only that which is already known as a counter-correlative (pratiyogin) and so forth; otherwise, the employment of the ablative case (pañcamī) and similar grammatical usages would be untenable. And in that case, the aforementioned fault remains.

For this very reason, the following [objection] is refuted: "If one holds the view that a qualified cognition (*viśiṣṭadhi*) is produced by the cognition of its qualifier (*viśeṣaṇajñāna*), then the possibility of a subsequent cognition—'these two are distinct'—is established; whereas if it were not produced by the cognition of the qualifier, such a cognition having both as its object could occur simultaneously. This is rejected because, in cases such as 'the difference between these two' (*anayor bhedaḥ*), the apprehension of difference must necessarily precede the grasping of the relation indicated by the genitive case; thus, an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) is unavoidable.

Furthermore, there is no parity with such conceptual alternatives as: "Why would perception and verbal testimony—which grasp the non-difference between the reflection and its original (bimba-pratibimba) or between the individual soul and Brahman (jīva-brahman)—not have non-difference itself as their object? For since non-difference is the very nature of the thing, there is no room for such conceptual alternatives. Moreover, if difference were mutual non-existence (anyonyābhāva), then because the identity of the two counter-correlates—the pillar and the jar—is unestablished by any means of valid cognition, mutual non-existence itself would be unestablished.

Nor does the lack of epistemic warrant for duality and the like entail the lack of epistemic warrant for its absence; for in the view that [the absence] is distinct [from its locus], this is an accepted consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*), while in the view that it is not distinct, the epistemic warrant of the locus itself is the necessary condition for the epistemic warrant [of the absence], such that its epistemic warrant is established even when the counter-positive lacks epistemic warrant. Nor should it be argued that "in the case of mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) as well, let it be accepted in that way under that view," because it has already been stated that if that [mutual non-existence] were of the nature of the locus, it would lead to the consequence of nihilism (*śūnyavāda*) and so forth.

As for what has been asserted by others—that even that which lacks epistemic warrant can be the counter-correlate (pratiyogin) of a negation—we do not deny that; however, we maintain only that such a negation is itself epistemically unwarranted when it is distinct from its locus (adhikaraṇa).

Now, one might object: "In this case, the counter-positive of the negation is not the identity of both the jar and the pillar; rather, it is the identity with the pillar—which was cognized in the pillar—that is being negated as residing in the jar. Thus, there is no lack of a validly established counter-positive. If you say this, we reply: No, for if identity-in-general were the counter-positive of the negation, then after the sublation [of the error], just as one might have the cognition "these two are trees" regarding two distant trees, so too would there arise the cognition "these are mother-of-pearl and silver," which is absurd.

Nor is there a distinction based on proximity; for even by that much, the cognition "this is mother-of-pearl" or "that is silver" would result. As for the definition of mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*) and relational absence (*saṃsargābhāva*)—namely, that where the negation is apprehended after superimposing the delimiting property of the counter-positive upon a locus, that is mutual absence; and where the appearance of negation occurs after superimposing the counter-positive itself upon a locus, that is relational absence—that is not correct, because it lacks pervasion (*avyāpti*) in the case of supersensible difference and relational absence according to that [opponent's] own view.

Furthermore, because there is deviation in the case of the cognition of absence produced by words, superimposition (*āropa*) is not the cause for the cognition of absence. Moreover, since difference must be described as the difference from that which is other than itself, there would be either a contradiction of self-residence (*svavṛttivirodha*) or an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Nor should it be argued: "Even in the case of non-difference from Brahman, the same problem of self-residence applies because non-difference must also be described [as the non-difference from itself]"; for you should understand that non-difference is self-establishing (*svanirvāhaka*).

Nor is it the case that [difference] is thus [self-referential], because if the linguistic usage of difference residing in a locus of difference were established by its own nature (*svarūpeṇa*), then even in the case of a jar, such a state would obtain, resulting in the impossibility of a difference whose locus is a property (*dharma*). Furthermore, in the case of difference, "difference-ness" (*bhedatva*) must be stated as either an imposed characteristic (*upādhi*) or a universal (*jāti*); in that case, difference must again be stated, otherwise there would be no difference of difference-ness from something else. And thus, through mutual occurrence or occurrence in itself, the same contradiction arises as in the case of self-residence (*svavṛtti*).

Nor should it be argued: "Even in the case of non-difference (abheda), its 'state of being non-difference' (abhedatva) must be stated; there too, non-difference must again be stated, otherwise it would not possess non-difference with itself, which would lead to the same consequence [of infinite regress] there as well. For if the mutual occurrence of properties such as "knowability" (prameyatva) and "nameability" (abhidheyatva) is not considered a fault in the case of non-difference, then the same applies to difference. We reply: this is not so, because for us, both mere non-difference and the state of being non-difference are non-different from Brahman; thus, since the very notion of "mutually" does not exist, it is impossible to even raise the charge of mutual occurrence.

In that case, there is no futility of the Vedāntas regarding the non-difference of the pot from the pot, or the non-difference of the individual soul (jīva) from the soul, or the non-difference of the soul from Brahman; for it has already been stated that the great sentence (*mahāvākya*) is indispensable for the mental modification (*vṛtti*) that removes the delusion of difference. As for the claim that in cases such as "knowability" (*prameyatva*), since it is itself known, its occurrence in itself is not a fault—that is not so, because even there, "being known" is unestablished due to the faults of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*) and the like. For this very reason, there is no purely positive (*kevalānvayin*) probans.

Furthermore, does difference reside in that which is different or in that which is non-different? In the first case, there is either self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*) or mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*). In the second case, there is a contradiction. Nor should it be argued that this same dilemma—whether non-difference, indeterminability (*anirvācyatva*), and so forth, reside in that which possesses them or in that which lacks them—applies here as well; for since non-difference is the very nature (*svarūpa*) of the thing, there is no room for such a dilemma therein, and because this very dilemma serves our purpose by acting as the ground for the indeterminability of [the opponent's] position regarding indeterminability and the like.

Nor is difference itself the essential nature [of the object], since that has already been refuted. Nor should it be argued: "Difference exists in that which is capable of being its locus, and this capacity is to be inferred solely from the fruit in the form of valid cognition (*pramā*). For it is impossible to speak of such capacity without difference; for there can never be such capacity in what is non-different, since even another property (*dharmāntara*) does not serve as a determinant of capacity unless it is preceded by difference. Furthermore, without first recognizing difference and non-difference, one cannot recognize the distinction between the fruits in the form of error and valid cognition; thus, the capacity for difference cannot be inferred from the distinction between the fruits in the form of valid cognition.
By means of valid rejoinders that do not contradict one's own position and which differ in their generic character, the distinction [of the opponent] is refuted;
thus, by taking up that very distinction, the non-difference of one's own self is established.
Thus ends the specific refutation of difference in the Advaitasiddhi. || 15 ||

Now, it may be argued: "For us, difference is not merely the essential nature [of things], but rather mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*); and that is non-different from the entity as possessing its specific qualities; therefore, because of this non-difference, there would follow the consequence of non-distinction and so forth."

If it is argued that because a "particular" (*viśeṣa*) exists as a substitute for difference (*bheda*), there is no synonymy (*paryāyatva*) and so forth, and that this particular—even in the absence of difference—serves to resolve issues such as the non-exclusion of one [of two identical things]—we say: no. For if one accepts a particular distinct from the essential nature (*svarūpa*) as the cause of the cognition of synonymy and so forth, then since that very thing is itself a difference, it is illogical to speak of a difference in properties (*dharmabheda*). Furthermore, the difference of the particular must also be said to be either non-different from the particular itself or possessed of further particulars; and thus, the fault of infinite regress (*anavasthā*) remains exactly as it was.

Nor can that [Brahman] possess a "particularity" (*viśeṣa*) as postulated by the Vaiśeṣikas, such that it could function as its own and others' means of establishment; for there is a lack of evidence for such a particularity. Now, one might object: "In your own view as well, since it is impossible to accept that consciousness, bliss, and so forth—as understood from scriptural passages such as 'Brahman is consciousness, bliss'—possess difference, or both difference and non-difference (given that they are *akhaṇḍārtha*, or impartite in meaning), and because this would contradict Śruti texts such as 'It should be viewed as one alone,' you must necessarily admit a 'particularity' as a substitute for difference in order to account for meanings such as non-synonymy."

If it is argued that presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) alone is the means of valid cognition—no, for just as there is a contradiction with the scriptural teaching of non-duality (*aikarasya*) in the case of difference, here too that same defect persists. Furthermore, even though the indicated meaning (*lakṣyārtha*) is non-different, the non-synonymy resulting from the difference in the denoted meanings (*vācyārtha*), as well as the non-futility resulting from the difference in what is to be excluded (*vyāvartya*), are established in quite another way.

Furthermore, let the non-synonymy [of the terms] reside in you as well, simply due to the difference in their limiting adjuncts (*nimitta*), such as "knowledge" and "bliss"; what is the need for a *viśeṣa*? Nor should it be argued that this is not so because the Śruti text "Thus are its attributes" prohibits the difference between those two [attributes] as well; for in that case, since the *viśeṣa* too is dependent and thus an attribute, its difference would also be prohibited by that same text, and thus [the objection] remains untenable.

Nor should it be argued that a specific substratum in the form of the manifestation of an object and the desire for it without qualification is necessary for the two properties of cognitivity (*jñānatva*) and blissfulness (*ānandatva*), which consist respectively in the manifestation of an object and being desired without qualification; for cognitivity and blissfulness are universal classes (*jāti*), and thus they lack the aforementioned nature [of being dependent on such substrata].

Nor should it be argued that—since the terms "space" (*ākāśa*) and "substratum of sound" (*śabdāśraya*) would become synonyms due to the non-difference of their grounds for application (*pravṛttinimitta*), some distinction must be stated to avoid this—it need not be so stated, because even if they are synonyms, their simultaneous usage is justified by their relationship as commentary and the subject of commentary (*vyākhyānavyākhyeyabhāva*). Nor should it be argued that—by thus leaving only one of the two, knowledge (*jñāna*) and bliss (*ānanda*), there would be no manifestation of bliss in liberation—it need not be so argued, because since there is no difference between the two, the very status of being "one of the two" (*ekataratva*) does not exist; for the suffix *-tara* is prescribed only when two things are mentioned.

By this, the following [objection] is refuted: "There is no difference between the unity [of the self] and the purified meaning of the word *tat* (That), nor is there both difference and non-difference; rather, there is absolute non-difference. Furthermore, if particularity (*viśeṣa*) is not admitted, then when self-luminous consciousness manifests, it would follow that unity does not manifest. Even if the manifestation of that [consciousness] is not opposed to the delusion of difference, the manifestation of unity is opposed to it. Moreover, while that [consciousness] is independent, it is not tenable for unity to be dependent. [This is refuted] because everything is logically consistent when one takes into account the portions fabricated by the concealing ignorance (*āvarakājñāna*).

Nor should it be argued that if a single mother-of-pearl shell were both covered and uncovered, there would necessarily be a difference between its parts; for there is no result that could justify the postulation of such parts.

Now, one might object: "Let the scripture stating 'thus are its attributes' (*evam-dharmā*) be the authority here; for after describing the attributes of Brahman, difference is negated. Moreover, in the absence of a correlate to difference, it would not be logical for there to be a relationship of attribute and substrate, nor for the plurality of attributes. If this is argued, we say no. The phrase "its attributes" is a restatement of what has already been negated, and thus it lacks any intentionality regarding [the reality of] attributeness or plurality. Furthermore, the attributes of Brahman are not established by any means other than scripture, since they are established solely through the witness-consciousness (*sākṣi*) as being merely products of nescience (*āvidyaka*).

Now, [the opponent may argue]: "If there were non-difference between quality and the possessor of quality, then upon perceiving a jar, one would not perceive its whiteness and so forth. Even in the view of difference-and-non-difference, a relation of inherence (*samavāya*) must be accepted to avoid contradiction between the two. Furthermore, even in the view of absolute difference, a 'particularity' (*viśeṣa*) must be admitted for the sake of uncontradicted worldly usage—such as 'existence exists,' 'ultimate particularity is distinct,' 'time always is,' and 'space is everywhere. Moreover, in the case of non-existence and the like, existence and so forth are not different from non-existence itself; and since they are not included among qualities and the rest, there are exactly six categories of reality."

If it is argued that [the existence of existence] must be accepted there as well—lest there be the fallacy of violating the rule (niyamabhaṅga)—and even in the case of no fixed rule (aniyamapakṣa), since there would be another existence within existence, leading to the fallacy of infinite regress; we say: no, for everything is accounted for by the very particularity of intrinsic nature (svabhāvaviśeṣa). Nor should it be said: "In that case, by accepting a particularity, you have entered into my own position"; for the meaning of the term 'particularity of intrinsic nature' is precisely the unique, specific essence (asādhāraṇasvarūpa) of each respective thing, and thus the 'particularity' mentioned by you is not what is being asserted here. This is because inherence (samavāya) and the like are self-establishing through their own respective unique forms.

Therefore, the following argument is refuted: "Self-establishment (*svanirvāhakatva*) indeed means being the agent of an establishment that has itself as its object, and since this is contradictory in a single entity, one must admit a 'particularity' (*viśeṣa*) to explain it. This is rejected because the word "self-establishing" merely signifies being the object of linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) without depending on anything other than itself; otherwise, since you yourself accept that even a particularity is non-different from the thing due to the fear of infinite regress (*anavasthā*), the aforementioned refutation would apply, and the defects such as the "survival of only one side" (*ekatarapariśeṣa*) stated regarding the position of essential difference (*svarūpabheda*) would remain unavoidable.

Nor should it be argued that, as in the case of ultimate particularity (*antyaviśeṣa*), this [universal] is established by the very means of cognition that apprehends its locus as having such a nature, and thus no further questioning is appropriate; for there is a disparity, since—as in the case of the example itself—you yourself do not admit any nature over and above the thing's own essence in the case of the subject of the proposition.

As for the claim that a *viśeṣa* (particularity) is postulated only where there is an absence of difference and yet a function of difference is perceived—and not by resorting to a *viśeṣa* to abandon difference in the case of jars, cloths, and so forth, where difference is already established—this is not correct. For, just as in that [other] case, here too there is no factor determining primacy; since both the *viśeṣa* and difference terminate in their own essential natures (*svarūpa*), there is no room for the quibbling of your words.

Furthermore, it would follow that difference itself should perform its own function, and that a substitute for it should exist for the sake of the function of non-difference; moreover, there is no absence of cognition of difference in cases such as bliss, just as there is none of non-difference, since both are equal in the case of the extraordinary (*alaukika*).

Now, an inference is the means of knowledge here; for instance: the absence of the exclusion of either one between consciousness (*vijñāna*) and bliss (*ānanda*), which constitute the very nature of Brahman, as well as their non-difference from Brahman, [is established]; or else, properties such as being an object of knowledge (*prameyatva*) and so forth, or the state of being supported by itself (*svāśritatva*) and so forth, must be governed by something other than difference (*bheda*), because while not being governed by difference, they are nonetheless governed [by something]. Whatever is governed while not being governed by X is governed by something other than X, just as is commonly accepted.

Or rather, [Brahman] consists of the nature of Brahman, such as consciousness, bliss, and so forth; for it possesses a state that is established by the non-removal of one or the other [of its attributes], while being devoid of difference. Whatever is devoid of difference and possesses a state established by the non-removal of one or the other, must possess the capacity to establish the other, just like the agreed-upon example.

If it is argued that "the property of being an object of knowledge (*prameyatva*) and so forth, which reside in [Brahman] itself, exist because they possess a form of the relationship between locus and located (*āśrayāśrayibhāva*) while being devoid of difference, just like that which sustains the relationship between locus and located despite the absence of difference—as is commonly accepted," we say no. This is because there is the fallacy of proving something other than the intended point (*arthāntara*), as it is possible for something else—such as *avidyā* (nescience), which you yourself accept—to be the regulator in all such cases; furthermore, there is sublation (*bādha*) since [the properties] are governed by differences that are themselves products of *avidyā*, and thus the reason is unestablished (*asiddhi*).

Now, an objection is raised: even so, perception (*pratyakṣa*) is the means of valid cognition here; for instance, a distinction is indeed experienced between cognitions such as "thread" and "cloth" on the one hand, and cognitions such as "pot" on the other. And this distinction cannot be due to having a relation as their object, because they are experienced as distinct from cognitions such as "bowl" and "jujube fruit. Nor can it be due to having a relation other than conjunction (*saṃyoga*) as their object, because they are also experienced as distinct from cognitions of a pot, its cognition, and its absence.

Nor can it be by way of being the object of a relation other than essential proximity (svarūpa-pratyāsatti) or conjunction (saṃyoga), because this would result in the absence of any distinction between the cognition of the mutual non-existence of a jar and its properties and the cognition of jars, cloths, and so forth.

Nor can it be defined as having inseparable existence (*ayutasiddhi*) as its object; for inseparable existence is indeed the restriction to the relation of substrate and superstrate (*āśrayāśrayibhāva*). In that case, while at that time the relation of substrate and superstrate appears even in the case of a bowl and a jujube fruit, such a restriction does not appear even in the cognition of threads and cloth. For the cognition of threads and cloth is not of the form "the destruction of the relation between these two will not occur," nor "there will be a separation"; nor is the cognition of the bowl and jujube fruit of the form "the destruction of the relation between these two will occur," nor "there will be a separation."

Nor can it be on the basis of having inherence (*samavāya*) as its object, because according to the reasoning already stated, neither the permanence of the relation nor the inseparable existence (*ayutasiddhi*) of the relata appears therein. Therefore, the distinction must be stated solely on the basis of having non-difference (*abheda*) as its object; for in such cases as "this is a jar," "an army consists of elephants and so forth," or "the leaf itself is the earring," there is the cognition of non-difference between the cloth and the threads—which are themselves the warp and woof—just as there is between the jar and other objects present before one, and even in cases such as "a white cloth," there is the cognition of the non-difference of the cloth from the threads and so forth.

Nor should it be said that "here it is only the co-location of cloth-ness and white-ness that appears," for the identity of the cloth and the white is also included therein; otherwise, there would be no non-difference anywhere at all. Furthermore, the cognition "the pot is not a cloth" would not have difference as its object. Even in cases such as "Caitra is the staff-bearer," the non-difference of Caitra from the staff-bearer indeed appears.

Nor should it be said that in the cognition "the cloth is white" (*śuklaḥ paṭaḥ*), what is perceived is precisely "that which possesses whiteness" (*śuklavān*); for here, what is perceived is exactly that which is [perceived] in the case of "white color" (*śuklaṃ rūpam*). Otherwise, just as in the case of "one with a staff" (*daṇḍī*), there would have to be the form "white-possessor" (*śuklī*) here as well. The postulation of the elision of the *matup* suffix and so forth pertains to linguistic usage regarding words, but not to the cognition itself. Furthermore, the cognition "the whiteness of the cloth" (*paṭasya śauklyam*) does not have difference as its object; rather, being an object of relation, it is established even in the absence of difference, just like [the cognition] "existence" (*sattā*) and so forth.

Furthermore, if the cloth were distinct from the threads, there would be the consequence of two separate weights; moreover, the cloth could not reside within the threads, because it is a contradiction for corporeal objects to occupy the same location. However, distinctions such as linguistic usage and causal efficiency are appropriate, as in the case of a leaf or an earring. Therefore, the cognition of "threads" and "cloth" has non-difference as its very object. Yet, if it were thus directed solely toward non-difference, it would not produce the usage of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), since one does not employ expressions such as "pot" and "jar" [as if they were identical].

From this it is known that there must be an additional object of cognition for this [perception]. Nor is this [additional object] mere difference (*bheda*), because that would lead to the undesirable consequence of the mental representation being "the pot is not white," and because a *viśeṣa* (particularity) is necessary to avoid the contradiction between difference and non-difference. Therefore, that which is the additional object is the *viśeṣa*. If this is argued, we say no; for even when non-difference exists, such conventional usage can be accounted for by resorting to an imagined difference, and thus the *viśeṣa* remains unproven.

Nor does the cognition "the cloth is not white" follow as a consequence, because—on the strength of the observed result—it is postulated that a conceptual difference serves merely to sustain linguistic usage such as grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*); thus, it cannot be a cause for a contrary apprehension.
Therefore, my friend, this distinction is not an object of valid cognition;
abandon your despondency, for through the ignorance established by me, all things are consistently integrated.
Thus ends the refutation of the particular (viśeṣa) in the Advaitasiddhi. 16.
Since you thus refute only that difference which is established through direct perception,
what can be said of your position regarding the non-perceived difference between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara), and so forth?

For instance: since God is not perceptible, it is impossible to apprehend a difference that has Him as its locus (*dharmi*) or as its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*). Now, one might object: even if a difference having God as its locus is imperceptible to the individual soul (*jīva*), a difference having oneself as its locus is nevertheless perceptible, because of such experiences as "I am not omniscient" and "I am not free from suffering."

Nor should it be said that "having a fit counter-positive" is the determinant for the fitness of an absence; for while this may be the case for relational absence (saṃsargābhāva) on the strength of perceptual results such as "the pillar is not a piśāca," in the case of mutual absence (anyonyābhāva), the determining factor is simply the fitness of the locus itself.

In reality, however, fitness (yogyatā) does not consist merely in the absence of a relation; for otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of perceiving the absence of "fitness-qualifying earthness" even in a water atom. Rather, where the existence of something is incompatible with non-perception, the absence of that thing is "fit" (yogya) in that locus. Thus, fitness is restricted to the locus and is common to all absences. And this [fitness] certainly exists in the present case as well; otherwise, the scriptural statement regarding non-difference would result in the fallacy of negating what was never even suggested.

Furthermore, because of the scriptural teaching of difference, it could not be a mere restatement of the difference established by the perception you have described. Even regarding the difference between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (Īśa), [the scripture says]: "I know all those, but you do not know them, O scorcher of the foe."

If it is argued that this is established by direct perception inferred from His own words beginning with "But the Supreme Person is another," we say no; for the aforementioned experience consists of the consciousness delimited by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) apprehending a difference relative to the undelimited consciousness, and thus does not apprehend a difference relative to pure consciousness (*śuddhacaitanya*) characterized by freedom from suffering and so forth. Even the scripture merely restates the difference between the delimited [consciousnesses]. As for the scriptural negation of difference, it is intended to negate the difference that might otherwise be suggested by inference and other means.

Nor should it be argued that there is a perception of difference in the pure Self—which is recognized through its non-difference from the internal organ at the time of deep sleep and through its non-difference from the locus of ignorance and so forth—as expressed in the thought, "I who slept, for me there was ignorance, transmigratory existence, and so on; that same I am now free from suffering. For our dispute concerns only the difference between the substratum of transmigratory existence and that which is not its substratum, not the difference between consciousness and consciousness itself. To this we reply: by this much, the apprehension of difference occurs only in that which is delimited by ignorance, and not in the pure [Self].
Indeed, at the time of deep sleep, there is no lack of delimitation by ignorance, just as there is no lack of delimitation by the internal organ.

As for the claim that there is no difference between consciousness and consciousness, that is favorable to us, because we hold that non-difference is the very nature of consciousness and constitutes our secret doctrine; yet it is contrary to your own position. For you do not maintain that the consciousnesses of Caitra, Maitra, and others are one. Furthermore, as was stated previously, the "I-sense" (ahamartha) is not the pure Self. Since the perception of the witness (*sākṣipratyakṣa*) is common to all superimpositions and the like, the mere fact of its being established by that perception cannot possibly constitute an uncontradicted proof of difference.

By this, the claim that perception is the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding the mutual difference between individual souls (*jīva*) is refuted; for [perceptions] such as "I am not Caitra" have as their object a difference limited by adjuncts (*avacchinna-bheda*). Since perceptions such as "The pot is not Brahman," "The pot is not a cloth," and "I am not a pot" have as their objects differences that are merely imagined (*kalpita*), a real difference (*tāttvika-bheda*) is not established. Therefore, perception is not a means of valid knowledge regarding the fivefold difference. Thus ends the section on the refutation of perception regarding the fivefold difference in the *Advaitasiddhi*. (17)

Nor is there inference [to prove difference]. In the argument, "The individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara) are distinct, because they are substrata of contradictory properties, like fire and snow," there is a failure of the essential nature of the reason (*svarūpāsiddhi*), since suffering and so forth are attributes of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and not of the self. Furthermore, since it is observed that the absence of suffering and the presence of suffering can coexist in one and the same substrate through a distinction of limiting adjuncts (*avacchedaka-bheda*), this does not prove a difference in the substrate itself. If one intends to prove mere difference, the argument is superfluous (*siddhasādhana*). If one intends to prove real difference (*tāttvika-bheda*), the reason remains unestablished. Thus: "Brahman is in reality different from the individual soul, because it is omniscient; by way of negative concomitance... [the argument fails].

In the argument "like the individual soul" (*jīvavat*), the qualification is unestablished (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*). If the probandum (*sādhya*) is formulated as "Brahman possesses a difference whose ontological status (*sattā*) is equal to the ontological status of the substratum (*dharmin*)," it suffers from the fallacy of being over-exclusive (*asādhāraṇya*). In the argument "Selfhood (*ātmatva*) resides in multiple individuals, because it is a universal (*jāti*), like earthness (*pṛthivītva*)," it is unestablished (*asiddhi*) against one who maintains the oneness of the Self; furthermore, it results in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) if one considers it to reside in imagined (*kalpita*) individuals. In the argument "Suffering (*duḥkha*) is supported by a locus distinct from that which shares its genus through a subordinate universal of the class 'quality' (*guṇatvāvāntarajāti*), because it is a quality, like color (*rūpa*)," there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) with respect to sound (*śabda*).

Furthermore, since suffering and the like are established as properties of the internal organ (*antahkarana*), there is the fallacy of proving what is already proven (*siddhasādhana*). Moreover, in the argument—"The bodies under dispute possess as many selves as their own number, because they are bodies, like [ordinary] agreed-upon bodies"—there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) with respect to the body of a yogi.

Furthermore, [the following arguments are fallacious]: "The self possesses a difference whose counter-positive is the self, which has the same ontological status as the existence of the subject (dharmin), because it is a substance, like a jar"; and "The self is manifold by virtue of a genus pervaded by substantiality, because it is the locus of specific qualities that are not audible, like a jar. In these cases, the reason is unestablished (*asiddhi*) because the self is devoid of qualities; moreover, there is a parity of fallacies (*ābhāsasāmya*), as in: "Caitra possesses a difference whose counter-positive is Caitra himself, for the stated reason, like the aforementioned example."

By this, even the following new inferences are refuted: "God possesses a real difference having the individual soul as its counter-correlative, because He is omnipotent, because He is omniscient, because He is the agent of all effects, or because He is independent; for if it were otherwise, He would be like the individual soul."

Or [the argument may be stated as]: "The individual soul (jīva) possesses a real difference from Brahman, because it has limited power, limited knowledge, limited agency, or because it is subject to transmigratory existence; otherwise, like Brahman. In such cases, there is a sublation (*bādha*) of the proof of possessing that [difference], because difference is [already] the very nature (*svarūpa*) of the thing. Nor can this be established by taking a "particularity" (*viśeṣa*) [as a distinct property], because since that particularity does not exceed the nature of the thing itself, it cannot produce the state of "possessing" it; furthermore, this would result in the fallacy of having an unestablished qualifier (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatā*).

Nor should it be argued that—due to the undesirable consequence [of contradiction] arising from the non-difference of the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman—it is impossible for the probandum (sādhya) to be amenable to valid means of knowledge, just as it is impossible for a substance to be distinct from the eight substances, or for self-luminosity (svaprakāśatva) as established by you [to be so]. For even though there is a transcendence of real difference (tāttvika-bheda), all undesirable consequences can be avoided through a difference imagined by limiting adjuncts (upādhi-kalpita-bheda).

Nor should it be argued that there is a general establishment of the probandum (sāmānyataḥ sādhyaprasiddhi) by means of the inference: "The individual soul or Brahman is the counter-correlate of a difference not sublated by the knowledge of some property-possessor and its counter-correlate, because it is an underlying substrate (adhiṣṭhāna), like mother-of-pearl. This is because, while such a thing may be the counter-correlate of a difference not sublated by the knowledge of a jar or other object—which is the counter-correlate of some non-existence—there is no proof of a difference [in this case] that is not sublated by the knowledge of the Self. Furthermore, if the probandum were "being the counter-correlate of a difference not sublated by the knowledge of its own counter-correlate," then in the example (the mother-of-pearl), the word "its own" would refer to the mother-of-pearl, whereas in the subject of the argument (the soul), the word "its own" would refer to the Self. Thus, the two cases would not correspond.

Because the apprehension of pervasion (vyāpti) is impossible based on that statement. As for the claim that the probandum (sādhya) is simply "distinct from the individual soul" (jīva), and that the charge of proving what is already established (siddhasādhana) by means of a false distinction will be refuted later—that is not correct, because the means of such refutation will itself be refuted.

Nor is it the case that the probandum (sādhya) is simply "Brahman possesses a difference whose ontological status is equal to the ontological status of the substratum (dharmin) that stands in opposition to the individual soul (jīva). For if by the term "substratum" Brahman itself is meant, the fallacy of an unestablished qualification (aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva) remains as before. If any arbitrary substratum is meant, there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (siddhasādhana), since such a difference would have the same ontological status as a substratum like a jar. Furthermore, in the absence of a specific counter-argument (vipakṣabādhaka) to rule out the contrary, the previously mentioned fallacy of being over-exclusive (asādhāraṇya) would result.

As for the claim that Brahman does not possess a real identity (tāttvikābheda) with the individual soul (jīva), that is not correct; for even so, since a real identity would be established by its absence as something unreal, it results in proving what is already established (siddhasādhana). Furthermore, if one adds the qualification "real" to the absence itself, the same problem of the subject being unestablished (aprasiddhi) remains.

Now, an objection might be raised: since the real difference (tāttvika-bheda) here has the nature of mutual non-existence (anyonyābhāva) with respect to the individual soul (jīva), the fault of the unestablished nature of the probandum (*aprasiddhi*) does not apply. For, in cases where the absence of the reason is apprehended as pervading the absence [of the probandum], it is there that the establishment of the probandum is a necessary factor. Here, however, what is to be apprehended is the pervasion of the absence of the reason by the identity with the individual soul; since its absence is what is to be proved by the reason, what is the need for the establishment of the probandum? Even without that, the apprehension of pervasion is possible, and there is no requirement for it even to fulfill the status of the subject (*pakṣatā*) in the form of doubt.

If it is argued that—because this [desire to know] consists in the absence of a proving means of knowledge conjoined with the absence of a desire to prove, it does not involve doubt; and because even when the doubt "Is Brahman in reality different from the individual soul (jīva) or not? is absent, the doubt "Does the difference between the individual soul and Brahman possess ultimate reality or not? is possible, just like the doubt "Is knowability the counter-correlative of an absolute non-existence residing in this [Brahman] or not?"—we say: no, for in that case, just as the difference from other well-known things exists in earth, so too would the difference from the well-known individual soul exist in Brahman.

Let it be granted that [the reason] is established; however, even the reality of that [difference] residing therein is not proven, because the absence of the pervader is capable of proving only the absence of the pervaded, otherwise there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Furthermore, as for the suspicion that the reality of difference resides in the locus (*dharmin*), that too is flawed due to the unestablished nature of the probandum (*sādhyāprasiddhi*). Nor is it the case that Brahman is different from the individual soul (*jīva*) because it is not an experiencer of suffering, like a jar; such an affirmative (*anvayi*) inference is invalid, because the reason is unestablished (*asiddha*) in one who is the experiencer of all.

If the qualification "residing in itself" (*svaniṣṭha*) is used, there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) with respect to the individual soul (*jīva*), because suffering resides in the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*); furthermore, there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) due to the existence of illusory difference (*mithyābheda*). Nor should it be said: "When difference is the probandum, it is improper to speak of proving what is already established by means of an objectless illusion (*arthaśūnyabhrānti*)," because an illusion is precisely not devoid of a real entity (*vastu*). This has been stated in the doctrine of the indeterminable (*anirvācyavāda*).

Nor can it be argued that this [reality] is established as being grounded in valid cognition (*prāmāṇika*) simply by virtue of being the object of an inference; for being the object of an inference is not the determining factor for being grounded in valid cognition. Furthermore, in the case of an inference regarding falsity (*mithyātva*) and so forth, there is no risk of the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanāpatti*) by means of a fabricated falsity, etc. Is "fabricated-ness" intended here to mean "empirical reality" (*vyāvahārikatva*) or "illusory appearance" (*prātibhāsikatva*)? In the first case, we accept the consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*). In the latter case, since the reason (*hetu*) proves a probandum (*sādhya*) that possesses the same ontological status as itself, there is no possibility of the probandum being merely illusory.

By this, the following [arguments] are refuted: (1) "Brahman possesses a difference from the individual soul (*jīva*) that has the same ontological status (*samasattāka*) as the existence of the locus (*dharmisattā*), because it does not experience suffering, because it is non-erroneous, and because it is not subject to transmigratory existence (*asaṃsāritva*), like a jar"; or (2) "The individual soul possesses such a difference from Brahman, because it lacks omnipotence and other [attributes]. For if the conditioned (*upahita*) entity is taken as the subject (*pakṣa*), then even if its having the same ontological status as the locus is established, its ultimate reality (*tāttvikatva*) is not proven; thus, the argument commits the fallacy of proving what is already admitted (*siddhasādhana*).

If the purified referents of the terms *tat* and *tvam* were taken as the subject (*pakṣa*), there would arise the fallacy of sublation (*bādha*), because those two lack the status of being a substratum (*dharmin*). Nor can it be argued that there is a contradiction between being a substratum and not being a substratum; for since Brahman is by nature the negation of everything, no such contradiction exists. Furthermore, the word "substratum" (*dharmin*) does not intend to denote a mere locus (*āśraya*), because even the status of being a locus is absent therein, just like the status of being a substratum.

As for the claim that, because the word *dharmin* (the subject) is a relative term like the word "father" and so on, it denotes something whose existence is equal to that of some [particular] subject, and therefore there is no "proving what is already established" (*siddhasādhana*), that is not correct; for the introduction of the intrinsic nature of a word is of no use with respect to inference. By this, the proposal to substitute the word "self" (*sva*) in place of the word "subject" is also refuted, as it shares the same logical status as the word "subject."

For this very reason, it is refuted that one should provide the qualification "ultimately real" (*pāramārthika*), or "persisting as long as its own nature," or "not an effect of its own ignorance," or "unsublated by its own knowledge" in place of the term "having the same ontological status as the locus" (*dharmisattāsamānasattāka*); for it is established by linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*) that the word "own" (*sva*) refers to whatever specific object is being co-referentially mentioned. Furthermore, in the first case, there is a deficiency of the probandum (*sādhyavaikalya*).

Nor should it be argued that—“the pot possesses a difference that is not sublated by a cognition whose counter-correlate is the individual soul (jīva), because it is not the counter-correlate of a non-sublated identity whose locus is the individual soul; for whatever is not the counter-correlate of an identity with respect to a certain locus that is not sublated by a certain cognition, it possesses a difference with respect to that counter-correlate that is not sublated by that cognition, as in the case of one of two distant trees”—because the pervasion (*vyāpti*) cannot be grasped in a reason (*hetu*) whose property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) involves the non-universalized term *yat* (whatever).

For when pervasion (*vyāpti*) is apprehended in a general form such as "subject-ness" (*dharmitva*) or "counter-positive-ness" (*pratiyogitva*), it is impossible to establish [the probandum] in a specific manner. Nor should it be said: "In that case, what is the recourse for [arguments] such as 'distinct from its own prior non-existence' (*svaprāgabhāvavyatirikta*)? For even there, the intention lies either in a negative inference (*vyatirekin*) or in another type of inference, since this same objection applies there as well.

Nor should it be argued: "It is not the case that Brahman is non-different from the individual soul (jīva) in reality; thus, there is not even the suspicion of a deficiency in the probandum (sādhyavaikalya), because even in your own view, just as there is no real difference between an imagined pot and an imagined soul, there is likewise an absence of real non-difference. This must not be said, because it has already been stated that there is a *siddhasādhana* (proving what is already established) due to the absence of real non-difference by means of an unreal [non-difference].

Nor should it be argued: "The individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara) possess a mutual difference that is not sublated by the knowledge of the substratum (dharmijñāna), because they are the loci of contradictory attributes, like fire and snow; and 'contradiction' consists either in being the absolute absence of one in the other, or in being pervaded by such absence, or in the incapacity for coexistence even at different times; furthermore, since there is no coexistence of conjunction and its absolute absence according to either philosophical system, there is no deviation (vyabhicāra) in the locus of these properties"—this cannot be maintained, because the flaw remains when the term "substratum" (dharmin) is taken into account.

This is because it has already been stated [that such a distinction is untenable], and because there is a fallacy (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of substrates for non-pervasive entities such as suffering, sound, and so forth; furthermore, since the identity of the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman is established, the contradiction—defined as the unfitness for co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) regarding independence, dependence, and so on—is itself unestablished, resulting in a failure of the essential nature of the reason (*svarūpāsiddhi*); and finally, because the regulation of imagined attributes such as omniscience and non-omniscience is explained solely through imagined difference—just like the regulation of shortness and length in a letter—and thus does not serve as a proof for an intrinsic difference.
Nor can one argue: "Limited power, non-omniscience, dependence, and incompleteness... [and so on].
The state of being a dependent is "jīvatva" (the nature of a living being), while the opposite of that is "īśatva" (lordship).

"Of those two, this [nature] is innate; it is not otherwise in any way. By such scriptural passages, the innate nature of omniscience and other attributes is stated, thereby establishing that they are not merely imagined (*kalpita*). This is because their being "innate" is predicated on the fact that they are established by beginningless ignorance (*anādyavidyā*) and thus lack any state of being merely contemporary. Furthermore, the word "that" (*tat*) refers specifically to the two [Brahman and the individual soul] as qualified (*upahita*). There is no contradiction in the statement regarding their innateness there, for even in the qualified [state], omniscience and so forth are not adventitious (*āgantuka*). Nor is Brahman possessed of a difference whose counter-correlate is the individual soul (*jīva*) which is not sublated by its own knowledge, because it is a category of existence (*padārthatva*), like a pot.

It should not be argued that "consciousness (*cetanatva*) resides in that which possesses a difference which is not sublated by the knowledge of the locus whose counter-correlativity is delimited by *jīvatva* (the state of being a living soul), because it resides in all conscious beings, or because it lacks the property of residing in non-conscious things, like the meaning of the word [‘conscious’]"; for this would suffer from the same lack of consistency regarding the non-universality of the terms "self" (*sva*) and "locus" (*dharmin*), the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of *jīvatva* as the final reason, and the lack of probative force (*aprayojakatva*) due to the existence of the limiting condition (*upādhi*) of "residing in non-conscious things" and the absence of any sublation of the contrary position. Furthermore, if Brahman were to become subject to transmigratory existence (*saṃsāritva*) like the individual soul (*jīva*), one would simply have to accept that as the desired conclusion (*iṣṭāpatti*).
Alternatively, the resolution must be made through the distinction established by conceptual construction (*kalpitabheda*). As it has been said:

"In no way can inference operate upon the immeasurable (*aprameya*); however, because the measurable (*prameya*) is not the Self, a distinction is inferred therein. The meaning is that inference does not extend to pure consciousness (*śuddhacaitanya*), as it is not the locus of any attributes (*dharma*). Where it does extend, there is the acceptance of what is desired (*iṣṭāpatti*). Nor should it be argued: "In that case, how can there even be an inference of identity? For it could be said of your verse: 'How can there be an inference of that identity? This is not to be said, because the identity of pure consciousness is accessible through scripture alone (*śabdaikagamya*), and thus its non-inferability is accepted.
Nor, then, is the presentation of the inference for identity purposeless, because its fruit is merely the removal of the delusion that difference is real. Therefore:

"Because the specific property [of the probans] is unestablished, and because it can be explained otherwise, difference is not the basis for [the distinction between] 'omnipotent' and 'limited power,' and so forth."
Thus ends the refutation of the inference of the difference between the individual soul and Brahman in the Advaitasiddhi. || 18 ||

In this same way, there can be no inference of mutual difference among living beings (*jīva*s). For instance, consider the following argument: "Caitra possesses a difference from Maitra that is not sublated by the cognition of the substratum (*dharmin*) having Maitra as its counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*), or rather, Caitra does not possess a real (*tāttvika*) identity with Maitra as its counter-correlative, because he does not experience the pain experienced by Maitra, because he does not remember everything remembered by Maitra, and because he does not perceive everything perceived by Maitra, like a jar. In this case, regarding the first probandum (*sādhya*), there is a dilemma concerning the term "substratum" (*dharmin*); and regarding the second probandum, [there is a problem] with respect to real identity versus unreal difference.

[This is] because it would result in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanāt*); because if that which is conditioned (*upahita*) is the subject (*pakṣa*), there is the fallacy of shifting the topic (*arthāntara*); because if mere consciousness (*caitanyamātra*) is the subject, the reason (*hetu*) is unestablished (*asiddhi*); and because it is possible for a part of the proof (*sādhanaikadeśa*), such as non-connection (*ananusandhāna*), to constitute a limiting condition (*upādhi*). The disputed destruction of bondage (*bandhadhvaṃsa*) resides in something distinct from that which is not sublated by the knowledge of its counter-correlate, where the counter-correlate is related to a substratum delimited by the delimitor of its own counter-correlation; because it is the destruction of bondage, like a [previously] accepted instance.

The living self (jīva)—whether as the transmigrating being, or as the substratum for the destruction of transmigration—is possessed of a difference whose counter-correlate is a living self not sublated by its own knowledge, or possessed of a difference whose counter-correlate is the transmigrating being and which is not sublated by its own knowledge, or possessed of a difference whose counter-correlate is a substratum for the destruction of transmigration not sublated by its own knowledge; because it is an ontological category (padārtha), like a jar.

[The argument] "Ānanda is different from what is dissimilar [to him], because he possesses a property pervaded by being opposed to the suffering residing in himself, and because this difference is of the same class as its counter-positive and is not sublated by knowledge of itself; for he is opposed to suffering, like the absence of suffering," etc., is fallacious due to the *arthāntara* (proving too much) resulting from the existence of *dhvaṃsa* (destruction) in time (*kāla*) and other things which possess a difference having bondage as their counter-positive; furthermore, because "bondage" cannot be established as a common property shared by both suffering and shackles, and because the term "self" (*sva*) lacks uniformity (*ananugama*).

Furthermore, there is parity with fallacious arguments (ābhāsa-sāmya), such as: "The destruction of Caitra's bondage resides in something distinct from the locus of Caitra's bondage, because it is the destruction of a bondage, like [the destruction of] a [similarly accepted] bond"; and because there is no subverting evidence against the contrary position. Moreover, "bondage-ness" (bandhatva)—which is the delimitor of the counter-correlativity of destruction—is not a single property common to multiple bondages, because it lacks the status of being a universal (sāmānya).

By this [it is argued]: 1. The self (*ātman*) is distinct from the mere self; it possesses a difference that is not sublated by its own cognition having the self as its counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*), because it is an entity (*padārtha*), like a jar. 2. Under the view of the all-pervasiveness of the self, space (*ākāśa*) is distinct from an all-pervasive substance possessing specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*) that are the substratum of a difference not sublated by the cognition of the locus having the self as its counter-correlative, because it is a substance (*dravya*), like the earth. 3. Earth-ness (*pṛthivītva*) is distinct from the genus directly pervaded by substanceness (*dravyatva*) that is other than water-ness, fire-ness, air-ness, and mind-ness, because it is knowable (*prameya*), like water-ness.

The argument that, in the case where "the nature of space" (*gaganatva*) is the genus (*jāti*), "being other than that" is also a qualifier—namely, that existence (*sattā*) is other than the genus residing in itself that is other than substantiality (*dravyatva*), or that substantiality is other than the genus residing in itself that is other than existence, because it is knowable (*meyatva*), like a pot—or that, according to the view that the self is atomic, the self possesses a genus pervaded by substantiality because it is a non-omnipresent substance, like a pot, and so forth, whereby the genus "selfhood" (*ātmatva*) is established and the real distinction between selves is thereby proven—is refuted.

In the first [inference], insentience (*jaḍatva*) is the extraneous condition (*upādhi*); and by substituting the word "Caitra" for the two terms "self" (*ātman*), there is also a similarity of fallacy (*ābhāsa*). In the second, the fact of not being the substratum of sound (*śabdānāśrayatva*) is the extraneous condition; furthermore, by adding the qualification "being other than the nature of the aesthetic determinants" (*vibhāvātmānyatva*), it would lead to the undesirable consequence of proving that [the self] is an all-pervading entity possessing specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*) distinct from the self and space. In the inferences where the universal (*jāti*) is the subject, since that universal is established even through the distinction of imagined individuals, it results in proving something else (*arthāntara*) because it ultimately rests upon a real distinction of individuals.

Nor should it be argued that "it is impossible for a universal (jāti) to exist without a difference that is not sublated by the knowledge of its substratum; otherwise, the non-difference of individuals would never be a sublater of a universal. This is because, given the rule that a universal must possess the same ontological status as the difference between its individuals, an illusory difference cannot establish a conventional universal; thus, the non-difference of individuals can indeed function as a sublater of the universal. Thus ends the section on the Refutation of the Inference of the Difference between Jīvas in the Advaitasiddhi. 19.

[Objection: "But surely—if there were identity of self, Caitra would experience the connection with all [others'] suffering and so forth. [Reply: No, for the lack of such connection is logically established by the difference caused by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). [Objection: "But since we observe a connection even when there is a difference in adjuncts such as hands and feet, the mere difference of adjuncts is not the determining factor. Nor is it the case that a *disconnected* difference of adjuncts is the cause there, because otherwise it would follow that the fetus should experience the pleasure and so forth of the mother.
