As stated in the *Mahābhārata*: "Even headless trunks (*kabandha*), whose staff-like arms were raised with weapons and who saw with their own fallen heads and eyes, struck down their enemies in battle."

If it is argued that this is not so because [the texts] state that there is a connection even when there is a separation, as in the passage beginning with "ityādi," we reply: no, for we do not say that any mere limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) is the cause of non-connection; rather, we mean the distinction between limiting adjuncts consisting of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) or the distinction of ignorance (*avidyā*). Such a distinction does not exist at all in the case of the headless trunk (*kabandha*) or the yogi. Therefore, there is connection in those cases, whereas there is non-connection in the case of Caitra and Maitra.

By this, the objection that the difference in limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) consisting of the body is the cause for the lack of recollection—on the grounds that there would otherwise be no memory in youth of what was experienced in childhood, no memory by a *jātismara* of what was experienced in a previous birth, and no memory by a yogi of what was experienced in various bodies—is refuted; for in those cases, the difference of the body is irrelevant, as there is a unity of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) in the cases of the yogi and the one who remembers past births.

Nor should it be argued that, given the unity of consciousness (*caitanya-ekya*), the difference in internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa-bheda*) cannot be the cause of the lack of recollection (*ananusandhāna*), since we observe recollection even when there is a difference in external instruments such as the eyes; for although such recollection is observed despite the difference in other instruments, the difference in the internal organ is postulated as the cause of non-recollection in a case where identity has been superposed upon it. Otherwise, since the unity of the individual soul with Brahman is established by scripture, it would follow that all [souls] would possess recollection [of one another].

Nor should it be argued that because the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) dissolves every day during deep sleep (*suṣupti*), there would follow the impossibility of recollecting what was experienced on a previous day; for since the internal organ persists in the form of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) and is subsequently awakened, there is no difference in the internal organ in that regard.

Nor should it be argued that, in this way, there would be the undesirable consequence of those who are in deep sleep, those merged [in Brahman], and those liberated experiencing the suffering of transmigrating beings—due to the absence of a distinction in their internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*) which is the cause for such non-recollection; for they lack the causal complex consisting of the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of the identity of the internal organ, which is the cause for recollection. Indeed, the absence of an effect does not result from a mere obstacle, but rather from the absence of the causal complex as well.

Nor should it be argued that, in this way, even the experience of the bliss of one's own nature would not belong to the liberated one; for since that [bliss] is unproduced, it does not depend upon the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), and because both the coordination and non-coordination [of experiences] are possible through the difference or non-difference of the ignorance that constitutes the limiting adjunct (upādhi) dividing the individual soul (jīva).

Nor should it be argued that—just as with the prior absence of knowledge (*jñānaprāgabhāva*)—difference and non-difference are irrelevant to ignorance (*ajñāna*) in this context; for if one holds the view that there are as many ignorances as there are cognitions, it would follow that even in a single individual soul (*jīva*), there is a lack of synthetic awareness (*anusandhāna*) due to the distinctness of the various ignorances regarding Brahman. This objection is invalid because, since the prior absences of cognition and the corresponding number of ignorances do not serve to differentiate individual souls, they are irrelevant to synthetic awareness and the like.

As for the objection—that there would be the undesirable consequence of the liberated soul experiencing the miseries of saṃsāra, and that if it did not experience the distinctions of limiting adjuncts (upādhi) consisting of ignorance, it would follow that its own essential bliss could not be experienced—that is not so; because while such adjuncts are required for the experience of worldly pleasures and the like, they are not required for the manifestation of the self-luminous essential nature.

Now, an objection: if it is argued that since the connection with manifold ignorance and the misfortune consisting of the experience of suffering reside in the qualified [Self], then bondage and liberation would fall into different loci (vaiyadhikaraṇya); whereas if they are said to reside in the pure [Self], then how can there be a distinction between experiencing and not experiencing, given that the very pure Self which experiences Caitra’s suffering is the same that experiences Maitra’s suffering? If this is asked, we reply: no, because even though liberation—which consists in the cessation of the bondage whose nature is ignorance—resides in the pure [Self], [the distinction remains].

Since the property of being the substratum of suffering and so forth resides in the conditioned (upahita) state, it is impossible for it to produce a difference in the pure (śuddha) Self. Nor does it follow that Brahman would become a transmigrating being (saṃsārin) if saṃsāra were located in the pure Self; for the distinction between being a transmigrator and not being a transmigrator is established through adventitious limitations (aupādhika-bheda), just as there is a distinction between whiteness and blackness in a reflection and its original, between the limited space within a jar and the infinite great space, or just as the single ether becomes the sense of hearing (śrotra) in various places due to the limitation of various ear-cavities. Thus, the systematic arrangement of saṃsāra and non-saṃsāra is logically consistent.

For this very reason, the objection that—since the evil consisting of the persistence of suffering resides in the conditioned (upahita), it is merely imagined, and thus there is only the cessation of the bound one, but not liberation—is refuted; for although the adjunct (upādhi) ceases because it is imagined, the thing conditioned (upadheya) does not cease because it is unimagined, and thus its connection with liberation is logically established.

Nor should it be argued that the reflection is like a shadow—a distinct entity—and thus, since even in your own view space (*ākāśa*) is a product-substance (*kāryadravya*) and therefore possesses parts, and since the auditory organs, being products of the *taijasa-ahaṃkāra*, are inherently distinct [from one another], the example is unestablished; for the status of the reflection as a distinct entity will be refuted, the nature of space and the auditory organ is used as an example according to the opponent's own system, and according to the scripture, "The wise say that the Self, when joined with the body, senses, and mind, is the enjoyer," it is the qualified [Self] alone [that is intended].

Even according to the method stated in the *Kaumudī*, the distinction [between the selves] is established because of their being enjoyers and because they are distinct, and thus the occurrence of both connection with and non-connection with [experiences] is logically possible.

For this very reason, the following [objections] are refuted: (1) that if [difference] resides solely in pure consciousness (*śuddhacinmātra*), then because difference is not perceived therein, even imagined difference would be non-existent; or (2) if it were present, then difference—which, like heat in fire, performs its own function in the form of a fixed determination (*vyavasthā*)—would be something not sublated by the knowledge of the substratum (*dharmijñāna*), whereas non-difference—which, like non-heat, does not perform its own function in the form of a fixed determination—would be false; and (3) that for one liberated and devoid of the difference born of ignorance (*āvidyaka*), there would follow the experience of the suffering of transmigratory existence. This is refuted on account of the nature of fixed determination.

Because an effect that possesses a difference coexistent with its own existence cannot entail a difference possessing a higher level of existence; and because non-distinction from pure consciousness is not an effect of the lack of regulation (avyavasthā), it is impossible to attribute falsity to it on the grounds of its failure to produce that [non-distinction], since in this case, the identity of the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) alone is the determining factor. Furthermore, is the recollection (*anusandhāna*) being attributed to the individual souls (*jīva*), which are portions imagined through the limiting adjuncts, or to the whole, Brahman? It cannot be the first, for there is no recollection of the pain and so forth of one part delimited by the foot by another part delimited by the hand.

Nor should it be argued: "We do not assert a confusion (*sāṅkarya*) of the seats of experience (*bhogāyatana*), such that there would be no [distinction between] 'pain in my foot' and 'pleasure in my head'; rather, we maintain mere unification (*anusandhāna*). And this [unification] certainly exists among the parts [of a single body]. Otherwise, just as Maitra does not exert himself to extract a thorn stuck in Caitra's body, there would be no activity of the hand to extract a thorn stuck in the foot. This is not to be said, because it is just like the non-production of pain delimited by the foot within that which is delimited by the hand.

The non-arising of the recollection (*anusaṃdhāna*) of Caitra’s suffering and so forth in Maitra is due to the absence of the unity of the limiting conditions (*upādhi*) that cause such recollection—just as there is an absence of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) that produces suffering in the hand [when it is not the locus of the self]. Thus, since recollection certainly exists with respect to the hand (as delimited by the self), there is no contingency of an absence of activity (*vyāpāra*) therein. Nor is the latter [alternative] tenable: because that [Self], being a non-enjoyer (*abhoktṛ*), the experience of pleasure and pain would not follow; and because mere knowledge of suffering and so forth is accepted even for that omniscient [Self].

Nor does it follow that Brahman itself becomes an enjoyer by virtue of being non-different from the individual soul (jīva) who is the enjoyer, because the distinction is established through the analogy of the original object and its reflection; furthermore, since the experience of continuity resides only in the conditioned [soul], it cannot be attributed to the pure Brahman. Nor does this entail a lack of co-location between bondage and liberation, because bondage—consisting of ignorance—is admitted to reside in the pure [Brahman], thus establishing their co-location. Even though the conditioned soul is the experiencer of continuity, it is accepted that the pure [Brahman] is the experiencer by way of the ignorance that permeates all three states, as evidenced by the scriptural text: "By this living soul... and so forth.

Furthermore, just as when a sound delimited by one's own ear-cavity is perceived, there is no perception of sounds residing in other parts [of space], so too are the perception and non-perception of pleasure, pain, and so forth. Nor should it be argued: "If there were a plurality of selves, the ear-cavities would have a restrictive rule of belonging to this or that self; however, in the doctrine of a single self, since all bodies are 'one's own,' there is an absence of such a restrictive rule of belonging, and thus the systematic arrangement [of experiences] is untenable. This should not be said, because for me, the systematic arrangement is established through the distinction of limiting adjuncts (avacchedaka) such as cognition, just as you establish it through the distinction of selves.

Furthermore, one who asserts difference on the basis of "distinction" (*vyavasthā*) must be asked: what is this "distinction"? It cannot be a difference in properties (*dharma-bheda*), because that is inconclusive due to the observation of pleasure and pain in a single [subject]; nor can it be the statement of properties residing in different substrata, because that would involve circular reasoning; and as for the statement of contradictory properties, if contradiction consists in the impossibility of coexistence, that is unestablished; if it consists in the relation of sublated and sublator, that is untenable because such a relation can exist within a single substratum and thus does not prove difference.

Nor do [the notions of] connection and non-connection [prove a difference], because it has already been stated that, since those two are possible through the distinction of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) in the manner described, they do not establish a difference in the Self (*ātman*). For this very reason, the systematic arrangement of bondage, liberation, and so forth, does not prove an inherent difference; for that arrangement is established precisely through the acquisition and relinquishment of their respective limiting adjuncts. Nor is there any fault such as circular reasoning (*ātmāśraya*), on the grounds that the adjunct itself resides in that which is conditioned by it; for since the adjunct is not a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and does not depend upon another individual instance, there is no room for the four types of faults beginning with circularity.

By this, the following objection is refuted: "If [liberation] consists in abiding in purity, is liberation the removal of each individual limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) one by one, or the removal of all limiting adjuncts? It cannot be the first, because it would follow that there is always liberation and never bondage. Nor can it be the second, because it would follow that there is currently bondage and no one is ever liberated. This is refuted because, according to the doctrine of the plurality of souls (*nānājīvavāda*), liberation is defined as the removal of that very limiting adjunct by which a particular consciousness was delimited; thus, there is no room for the aforementioned defects.

In the doctrine of a single soul (*ekajīvavāda*), liberation is defined solely as the removal of all limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*); therefore, it is currently accepted that there is no liberation [for others]. Now, one might ask: how can a limiting adjunct be a differentiator? To explain: does the adjunct connect with only one part [of the object], or with the whole? In the first case, according to your own view, since there is no inherent part [to the object], its being "limited" (*aupādhika*) would have to be asserted; thus, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). In the second case, there is no power to differentiate, because the whole is already seized by a single adjunct. Even in the case of space and so forth, if there were no inherent parts, there could be no connection with adjuncts such as a jar. As it has been said:

If the connection with the limiting adjuncts occurs in only one part, then it would not be all-pervading; if it were all-pervading, then there would be no distinction [between the self and the adjunct].
If it were in only one part, there would be an infinite regress; if it were all-pervading, it could not be a differentiator.

If this is argued, we say no; for it has already been established that an adjunct (*upādhi*), being itself false because it cannot withstand any conceptual analysis (*vikalpa*), is the cause of the appearance of false difference. Furthermore, as the authors of the *Bhāṣya* have elaborated at length, the impossibility of establishing a systematic distinction among all-pervading selves (*ātman*) is likewise demonstrated. Thus ends the section "The Refutation of Arguments Favoring the Difference between Jīvas" in the *Advaitasiddhi*. (20)

Thus, there is no evidence for the reality of a difference between the insentient and the Lord, nor for a difference between the insentient and the individual soul (*jīva*). [Objection: Brahman or the *jīva* possesses a difference that is not sublated by the knowledge of the locus having as its counter-correlative something other than itself, because it is an entity (*padārthatvāt*), like a jar. Or, Brahman or the *jīva* possesses a difference that is not sublated by the knowledge of the locus having as its counter-correlative a jar, because it is related to a time that is not related to a jar, because it is related to a space that is not related to it, or because it is not produced by what produces it, like a cloth. Or, Brahman or the *jīva*...

[The argument that] "the Self possesses a difference that is not sublated by the cognition of a substrate having an insentient counter-correlate, because it is not of the nature of the insentient; for whatever is thus, is so, as in the case of one of two distant trees," etc., does not escape the previously mentioned defects. This is because limitedness (*paricchinnatva*), insentience (*jaḍatva*), and being produced (*janyatva*) are [merely] adventitious conditions (*upādhi*), and because the reason is inconclusive (*aprayojaka*). Furthermore, there is parity with fallacious arguments such as: "The individual soul (*jīva*) or Brahman is the locus of such a difference having the Self as its counter-correlate, because it is a category (*padārtha*)."

Nor should it be argued that—because the jar is non-different from Brahman—the Vedānta scriptures would be redundant since the jar is established by the very establishment of Brahman; nor that Brahman would incur the defects of insentience and impermanence; nor that the individual soul (*jīva*), which is the substratum of bondage co-extensive with liberation, would incur cessation like an insentient object; nor that cognitions such as "I am fair" would become valid knowledge (*pramā*)—for these counter-arguments against the opposing view prevent any charge of fallacious similarity. This is because, even though Brahman is established through its self-luminosity and its being the object of all cognitions, [the scriptures are necessary] for the sake of the knowledge that removes ignorance along with its manifestations.

Because the fruitfulness of Vedānta has been stated in many ways: just as in the case of a jar and so forth, although there is an absence of non-imagined difference [from the substrate] due to another imagined individual, there is neither identity with that imagined individual, nor cessation through the perception of its specific nature as being merely apparent (*prātibhāsika*), nor the validity of a cognition of oneness with another imagined individual; likewise, in the present case as well, even though there is an absence of that [oneness] due to an imagined insentient object, there is no such thing as identity with it or the like. Thus, there is no scope for a subverting argument (*bādhaka*) against the counter-example either.
In this way, even regarding the mutual difference among insentient things, there is no inference [to prove non-difference].

A pot is, in reality, not non-different from mother-of-pearl, because it is not related to the time at which the mother-of-pearl is related [to its own properties], and because it is not produced by that which produces it, like silver superimposed upon it. Since you yourself accept a conventional (vyāvahārika) difference, there is no inconsistency regarding the subject (pakṣa), the example (dṛṣṭānta), and so forth; otherwise, there would be a contradiction with one's own activity due to the identity between the establishment or non-establishment of difference and the presence or absence of defects.

In this context, because the counter-positive—consisting of non-difference from the real mother-of-pearl—is unestablished, the probandum itself is unestablished; furthermore, if "in reality" (*tattvataḥ*) were a qualifier for "not" (*na*), it would be even more unestablished; moreover, since the reason is accounted for by mere difference existing at the same level of reality as a jar and so forth, it lacks logical necessity (*aprayojakatva*); and finally, there is sublation (*bādhāt*), because it has already been stated that if difference were real, it would be contradicted. [Thesis: The non-self (*anātman*) possesses an internal difference sublated by a cognition that does not reside in its own locus of attributes, because it is a category (*padārthatvāt*), like the self (*ātmavat*).

As for the objection that, in the case of the contrary [position], the perception grasping the non-difference between two distant trees or between mother-of-pearl and silver would have to reveal reality (*tattvāvedaka*), and that there would follow a confusion between liberation and saṃsāra, and so forth—that is not so; because there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of the many jars imagined upon a single jar, which possess a difference that is not sublated by a cognition of a jar that does not possess the properties residing in itself.

If the statement means "not being the locus of any of its own inherent properties," there is the fallacy of *arthāntara* (proving something irrelevant), because the difference [of the self] from cloth—which is not the locus of potness—is sublated by the knowledge of the self, yet is not sublated by the knowledge of the cloth. If it means "not being the locus of all its own inherent properties," then in your own view, since even Brahman is denotable (*vācyatva*), it would be a locus of purely positive (*kevalānvayi*) properties; thus, the probandum (*sādhya*) would be unestablished (*aprasiddhi*). Furthermore, just as there is an absence of real difference (*tāttvika-bheda*) along with the imagined [difference], there is likewise an absence of real non-difference (*tāttvika-abheda*); consequently, in the case cited, there would be no occurrence of the confusion of the capacity to reveal reality (*tattvāvedakatva*) and so forth.

As for the argument regarding the mutual real difference between the self and the non-self: "The non-self is the locus of a difference that is not sublated by the cognition of its counter-correlative, where that counter-correlative is the locus of a property residing in itself; and whatever is the locus of a property residing in itself is the locus of a difference not sublated by the cognition of its counter-correlative, where that counter-correlative is the locus of a property residing in itself, because it is a category [of existence], like the self. In this syllogism, the subject (pakṣa) is the locus of a property residing in itself, namely the self; the establishment of the probandum (sādhya) consists in its being distinct from another self that is different from it.

Furthermore, in the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), the locus of the property residing in itself (*svāvṛttidharmādhikaraṇa*) is insentient (*jaḍa*); therefore, the existence of the probandum (*sādhyasattva*) is established by its being distinct from another insentient thing different from it. This is not so, because the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is unestablished due to the lack of consistency (*ananugama*) between the subject (*pakṣa*) and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) regarding the referents of the terms "self" (*sva*) and "counter-correlate" (*pratiyogin*); because "non-insentience" (*ajaḍatva*) is a limiting condition (*upādhi*); and because there is a counter-argument (*satpratipakṣa*) by means of a negative inference (*vyatirekin*) based on "insentience" (*jaḍatva*).

Furthermore, regarding the real difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman, and between the soul and the insentient (*jaḍa*): Earth is the locus of a difference that is sublated by the knowledge of the substratum having Brahman as its counter-correlative, yet it is not the locus of water-ness and so forth; therefore, it possesses a difference whose counter-correlative is not sublated by the knowledge of the counter-correlative [Brahman], because it is a real entity (*vastu*), like water. By the phrase "water-ness and so forth," properties residing in the insentient and distinct from earth-ness—which are established for each respective proponent—are intended.

[The opponent argues: "In the subject (pakṣa), the probandum is established as being distinct from a self that is different from Brahman; whereas in the example (dṛṣṭānta), it is established as being distinct from an earthen object that is different from Brahman. [Reply: That is not so. For, by adding the qualification "not being the locus of the nature of a living soul" (*jīvatva*), just as one adds the qualification "not being the locus of water-ness" (*aptva*) and so forth, there would follow the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of proving a self that is distinct from both the living soul and Brahman. Furthermore, there is the possibility of a counter-argument (*satpratipakṣa*) based on a negative inference (*vyatirekin*) such as "being the substratum of odor" (*gandhādhāratva*). Moreover, the defect rooted in the various alternatives regarding the term "subject" (*dharmipada*) remains as it was.

By this—namely, regarding the difference of the individual soul (*jīva*) from Brahman and other souls, and the difference of the insentient (*jaḍa*) from the soul—the very same previous syllogism is presented as an inference, with the qualification "like internal difference" added to the phrase "not having water-ness as its locus," for the purpose of establishing the difference of the soul from other souls. And in this case, the establishment of the probandum (*sādhya*) is by way of being different from the soul which is itself different from Brahman and from one another; whereas in the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), it is by way of being different from the earthen [substance] which is itself different from Brahman and from one another. Thus, [the objection] is refuted.

Regarding the difference of the individual soul (*jīva*) from Brahman and other souls, and the difference of the insentient (*jaḍa*) from the individual soul, Brahman, and the insentient—[the following inference is stated]: "Earth is the counter-correlative of that difference which resides in a subject known by a cognition not sublated by [the knowledge of] Brahman, and which does not reside in [the property of] 'waterness' (*aptva*), while possessing internal mutual differences; provided that it possesses a difference residing in a subject known by a cognition not sublated by [the knowledge of] its own counter-correlative, and is not the counter-correlative of a difference residing in a non-transmigrating subject known by a cognition not sublated by [the knowledge of] 'waterness' and so forth, because it is a real entity (*vastu*), like water. This is for the purpose of establishing the difference of Brahman even from the insentient.

The qualification "not being the locus of fluidity (*aptva*) and so forth, yet not being a transmigrating being (*asaṃsārī*)" is superior to the previous one. In this position, Brahman—which is the non-locus of fluidity and so forth, and which is non-transmigrating—is established as the probandum (*sādhya*) by virtue of being the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) of a difference whose locus is that [Brahman]. As for the example, however, it is understood as being the counter-correlate of a difference whose locus is an earthen object that is the non-locus of fluidity and so forth, and which is non-transmigrating. In this regard, because the property of "not being the locus of jīva-hood" is used as a qualifier for "not being the locus of fluidity," there is a parity with the fallacious argument (*ābhāsa*) as before; furthermore, there is a counter-argument (*satpratipakṣa*) based on [the reason] being the locus of color produced by baking (*pākaja-rūpa*) and so forth; and finally, the argument is swallowed by the dilemma of alternative interpretations regarding terms such as "dharma" (*dharma*).

Thus, even with respect to mere difference (*bheda*), there is no inference [to prove it]. For instance, one might argue: "Brahman does not exist as devoid of difference, or rather, it possesses a difference that is not sublated by its own knowledge, because it is an entity (*padārthatva*), like a jar. This is rejected because "not coexisting with liberation" and "insentience" (*jaḍatva*) serve as limiting conditions (*upādhi*), and because the argument is swallowed by the dilemma of the term "its own" (*sva-pada*). By this same reasoning, the following is also refuted: "The non-self (*anātman*) is the locus of a difference not sublated by the knowledge of something other than itself, because it is an entity, like the self (*ātman*)."

In the argument "The difference from Brahman (brahmabheda) is not the counter-positive of the absolute non-existence residing in all things, because it is definable by Brahman, like the non-difference from Brahman," the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) is "not subsisting in what is non-different from Brahman. Furthermore, since the non-difference from Brahman is not definable by anything other than Brahman, the reason (*sādhana*) lacks the required property (*vaikalya*). In the argument "The cognition of Brahman has as its object a difference that is not sublated by itself, because it is a cognition, like the cognition of mother-of-pearl," the limiting adjunct is "having ignorance or the self as its object."

If "knowledge of Brahman" is stated by its own term (*svapadena*), there is a lack of establishment of the probandum (*sādhyāprasiddhi*), because a difference that is not sublated by that [knowledge] is unestablished. If "knowledge of mother-of-pearl" is stated, there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*). In the inference: "A jar is the counter-positive of an absolute negation (*traikālikābhāva*) residing in a cloth, etc., whose counter-positiveness is not delimited by a relation with the jar, because it is a substance, like a cloth"—there is *siddhasādhana*, since even a conceptual negation (*kālpānikābhāva*) can possibly exist throughout the three periods of time. By adding the qualification "not delimited by identity" (*tādātmyānavacchinna*)—just as one added "not delimited by a relation with the jar" (*ghaṭasaṃsargānavacchinna*)—[the same fault remains].

There would also be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of this [reason] proving the non-existence of the fifth category (abhāva), since the absence of a subverting argument against the contrary (vipakṣabādhakābhāva) exists in both cases. Difference (bheda) is ultimately real (paramārthasat), because it is not the locus of appearance-ness (prātibhāsikatva) while being the locus of the non-existence of non-reality; because it is the direct object of a valid cognition (pramā) whose scope does not include its own non-existence; because it possesses a superimposed falsity (mithyātva); because it is devoid of a creator (kalpaka); and because it precedes the direct perception (sākṣātkāra) that has itself as its object.

The difference between Brahman and the individual soul (jīva) is ultimately real, because it is beginningless, like the self; the difference between pleasure, pain, and so forth as cognized by the witness-consciousness (sākṣin) is ultimately real, because it is not sublated and is directly the object of knowledge not produced by defects; the difference between dharma, adharma, sacrifice, charity, and so forth is ultimately real, because it is the intended object of the Śruti—[these arguments] have "consciousness" and other such qualities common to the self as their limiting adjuncts (upādhi), and they are countered by the opposing argument (satpratipakṣa) based on "insentience" and other such qualities, which establish [the world's] falsity.

Furthermore, there is sublation by those [arguments] because their superior strength has already been stated. Regarding the first [reason], if "phenomenality" (*prātibhāsikatva*) consists in being an appearance caused by a defect, it is unestablished (*asiddhi*); if it is defined as being sublatable by knowledge other than that of Brahman, there is an inconsistency (*vyabhicāra*) with respect to a phenomenal object immediately preceding the final cognitive state (*caramavṛtti*). Regarding the second reason, since the status of being the object of such valid cognition depends upon the establishment of the ultimate reality of difference, it results in a lack of distinction from the probandum (*sādhyāviśeṣa*). Regarding the third, the property of having falsity sublatable by something other than the final cognitive state serves as a limiting condition (*upādhi*).

In the fourth [reason], there is a lack of proof because of the existence of the one who imagines forms through ignorance (*avidyā*). In the fifth, there is a lack of proof under the view that the world is a creation of perception (*dṛṣṭisṛṣṭivāda*), while in other cases, the reason is inconclusive (*aprayojakatā*). Furthermore, "beginninglessness" is deviant (*vyabhicārin*) with respect to ignorance and the like. There is also a lack of proof regarding the claim that "knowledge not produced by a defect is the intended object of the Śruti," because the mental modification (*vṛtti*) that delimits the witness-consciousness is itself produced by a defect, and because the primary intention of the scripture does not reside therein. Therefore, the fivefold difference is not an object of inference.
Thus ends the refutation of inference in the *Bhedapañcaka* section of the *Advaitasiddhi*. 21.

[Objection: "But surely, if difference were real, the following scriptural passages would be the authority: 'Two birds...'; 'He who dwells in the self...'; 'The eternal among eternals, the conscious among conscious beings...'; and 'One unborn [soul] lies near, enjoying her, while another unborn [soul] leaves her after she has been enjoyed. [Reply: No, for in the first half of the verse 'Two birds...', difference is not the object of knowledge (*prameya*), because it is neither the meaning of a word (*apadārtha*) nor the meaning of a sentence (*avākyārtha*). This is because duality is invariably co-located with a difference whose counter-positive is its own substratum."

If it is argued that even a distinction which is understood through presumption based on the duality heard in scripture is itself scriptural, we say no; for this can be accounted for by an imagined distinction—just as in the case of "two moons"—and thus does not necessitate a real distinction. For this very reason, the latter half of the verse also cannot have a real distinction as its purport. In fact, since this scriptural passage has been explained in the *Paingi-rahasya-brāhmaṇa* as referring to the intellect (*buddhi*) and the individual soul (*jīva*), it is impossible to assert that it refers to a distinction between the individual soul and the Lord (*jīveśa*).

In passages such as "He who dwells in the self," the relationship of locus and located (*ādhārādheya-bhāva*) can be explained by resorting to a conceptual distinction; likewise, the selection [of one from many] in "the conscious among the conscious" and the designation of difference in "another, unborn" are also compatible with a conceptual distinction, as they do not result in the reality of difference. Furthermore, this is because such an interpretation would contradict other scriptural texts. Nor can it be argued that the very scripture [in question] has another purpose due to a contradiction with [other] scriptures, for the scriptural texts concerning difference are weaker in authority as they merely restate the difference already established by perception.

Nor does the statement [of the difference between the individual soul and the Lord] lack the status of a restatement (*anuvāda*) simply because the difference between the individual soul as delimited by the property of being a living being (*jīvatva*) has not been previously established—unlike the injunction "one should not kill" (*na hiṃsyāt*), for instance. This is because the difference between the individual soul and the Lord is established by perception; and since the difference between the individual soul as delimited by *jīvatva*—which is established through the necessary implication (*arthāpatti*) of that [perceived difference]—is of an equal degree of certainty as what is established by perception, it is logical that the Śruti text communicating that [difference] functions as a restatement. In the case of "one should not kill," there is not even a suspicion of it being a restatement, because there is no determining factor to establish that "A Brāhmaṇa is not to be killed" and so forth serves as its prior authoritative source (*purovādaka*).

Nor should it be argued that its meaningfulness is directed toward a specific individual, like an injunctive statement found in another recensional branch (*śākhā*); for it is impossible for a single person to study multiple recensions, and because perception—being common to all persons and having primacy—is capable of being said to be meaningful even with respect to a specific individual.

Nor should it be argued that—just as in the case of "they lead two [fires]" (*dvayoḥ praṇayanti*) and so forth—the perception, which grasps only the present, establishes a difference that remains unsublated throughout the three periods of time; for in passages such as "the other is indeed unborn" (*ajo hyanyaḥ*), there is an absence of words indicating unsublatability across the three times.

Nor should it be argued that the scriptural texts on difference serve to strengthen the non-difference by possessing the sixfold marks of intentionality (*tātparya*); for even if they possess a purpose there, they cannot avoid being mere restatements (*anuvāda*), like the statement "fire is the remedy for cold."

Nor can it be argued that this is for the purpose of a counter-exception (pratiprasava), as in the case of the injunction "one should say 'twenty-six'"; for a counter-exception is impossible here because [the scriptural statement] is weaker than that [perception], and since the scriptural text prohibiting difference has the purpose of negating the reality of difference, it is impossible for it to be a counter-exception to a sentence that establishes the very nature of difference. Furthermore, it is not the case that if perception were invalid, the scripture could not be a restatement of what is established by it; for its status as a restatement is justified simply by its making known what was already known.

Nor should it be argued that—even so—the status of being a valid cognition (*pramātva*) is established for [the second and subsequent cognitions in] a continuous stream (*dhārāvāhika*), because they are restatements (*anuvāda*) independent [of prior knowledge]; for mere restatement, whether independent or dependent, is not in itself a cause for invalidity. Furthermore, the illustrative example (the second cognition) is dissimilar, as its object is a temporal moment not previously apprehended, since it pertains to a distinct point in time. Nor can it be maintained that, like the statements of those who know [the truth], it possesses its own objective import (*svārthaparatā*) by virtue of being a purposeful restatement; for although such a statement conveys its own meaning, it lacks the status of having its own objective import insofar as its function is merely to produce the number "two."

Nor is it improper for this to be a restatement of a prohibition, because there is an absence of any indicative mark (liṅga) for restating a prohibition—such as "that which is" and so forth—and because another thing to be enjoined is heard; for even though "that which is" and so on possess the marks of a restatement, they lack pervasion over all restatements, since a restatement can be inferred by other means as well, and because in cases such as "Brahman is not to be killed," we observe a restatement of a prohibition even in the absence of the words "that which is. Furthermore, when there is another thing to be enjoined, although there is no restatement of the meaning of the prohibition, the status of being a restatement of its meaning cannot be avoided.

Nor is there a rule that an explanatory restatement (*anuvāda*) for the purpose of an injunction must be ultimately real (*tāttvika*), because in cases such as "bring that which is silver," we do not observe ultimate reality when there is an explanatory restatement of something established by error for the sake of another injunction. Nor should it be argued that even in the case of an explanatory restatement, there is no loss of validity (*prāmāṇya*) in the form of correspondence with reality (*yathārthatva*); for that [validity] is contingent upon the absence of a sublater (*bādhaka*), and such an absence is impossible in the present context.

Now, an objection may be raised: "Since Brahman, as taught in the Upanishads, is not established by any means other than the scriptures, how can a difference—whether having that Brahman as its locus or as its counter-correlative—be established by perception and other means independent of the scriptures? We reply: No, for although perception requires the scriptures for the sake of apprehending the counter-correlative (the Brahman), it is nonetheless possible for perception to establish difference, since there is no rule that perception must be preceded by a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) regarding an object identical to its own.

Even though difference having God as its locus is not apprehended by perception, nevertheless, since that very difference—though established through the presumption of the meaning of scripture (śrutārthāpatti) based on the fact that the difference between the individual soul and God, established by perception, would otherwise be inexplicable—is logically consistent with being "established by perception," just as it is "scriptural" [in the sense of being established by the presumption of scriptural meaning], so it is established. Thus ends the section on the non-reiterative nature of the scriptures concerning difference in the *Advaitasiddhi*. 22.

Alternatively, even in the absence of being a mere restatement (*anuvādaka*), the scripture is justified by its having as its purport the conventional distinction (*vyāvahārika-bheda*). Nor does this result in a loss of authority (*aprāmāṇya*); for it is justified like an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), and because the lack of authority is actually desired in the case of the perceived meaning when it contradicts the scripture of non-duality. Nor is there a contradiction with the scripture of non-duality on the grounds that it has as its purport only undivided pure consciousness (*akhaṇḍa-cinmātra*), since it contradicts it by taking up the meaning that serves as the means to that [consciousness]. Nor can the reverse be maintained, because of the distinction between what is already established and what is not yet established.

Nor should it be argued that the scripture concerning identity is invalid because it contradicts perception, since—as in the case of matters established by other means of knowledge—the contradiction itself serves as a ground for its weakness; for when there is a contradiction, the validity of the contradicting [scripture] does not require the validity of that which establishes its status as a mere restatement (anuvādaka). Furthermore, the scripture concerning identity possesses superior authority because it is endowed with the sixfold marks of interpretative intent (*tātparya-liṅga*).

Nor should it be said that those [scriptural passages] do not establish the actual state of the object because they merely indicate the intended meaning (*tātparya*); for they are useful indirectly by making known that the scripture has that as its purport, and furthermore, they provide greater force by establishing the absence of purport in any scriptural passage heard that contradicts this.

Nor can it be argued that even here there exists a mark of purport (*tātparyaliṅga*)—such as the logical reasoning that "the Supreme, being full, eats without eating, whereas the multitude of individual souls (*jīvasaṃgha*) is indeed incomplete," or the repeated statement "True is the difference, true is the difference, true is the difference"—and that therefore the scriptural texts on difference are also intent upon establishing that difference; for the statements "he eats" and "is incomplete" are merely restatements (*anuvāda*) of the individual soul (*jīva*) for the purpose of enjoining its identity with the full Brahman, and thus they do not constitute a logical proof for difference.

The statement "truth is difference" does not imply the practice of [accepting] difference, because this sentence lacks authoritative validity (*aprāmāṇikatva*); or, even if it were authoritative, it would ultimately result in non-difference through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) when faced with sublation. Now, one might object: "The scripture concerning difference is indeed more powerful, because it arises without prior contradiction, because it is corroborated by perception and other means of knowledge, and because it has no other scope. This is not so, because the scripture concerning non-difference has already arisen as its contradicter; because perception and the like are not valid means of knowledge, their corroboration cannot serve as a factor for establishing superiority; because of the maxim "even a hundred blind men [cannot see]" (regarding those who rely on such perception); and because the scripture concerning difference has its own scope by having empirical difference (*vyāvahārika-bheda*) as its subject matter.

[Objection: "But surely this difference is not merely conventional (*vyāvahārika*), because even in liberation (*mukti*), difference is established by both Śruti and Smṛti. [Reply: No, because that liberation is only an intermediate one. [Objection: "But surely it is conventional, since even in liberation, difference is established by Śruti and Smṛti. [Reply: No, because that liberation is only an intermediate one. [Śruti says: "Having taken refuge in this knowledge, they have attained my own nature;
they are not born even at the time of creation, nor do they suffer at the time of dissolution. (Gītā 14.2)
Because such Smṛti passages state the absence of creation and so forth:
"Where there is no Māyā, much less others [bound by it], O Hari— therein abide those who are devoted to Him and worshipped by gods and asuras."
Dark-complexioned yet radiant, with eyes like lotus petals,
they were dressed in saffron-colored garments, possessing a divine luster and exquisite beauty.

This is because Māyā is negated in the Smṛti, and because in the passage, "He who knows [Brahman] hidden in the cave enjoys all desires together with the wise Brahman," the fruit of the knowledge of the pure Brahman is stated to be suchness (tattva).

Even in the case of the Bhūmavidyā, which you yourself have accepted as having pure Brahman as its object, at the point of stating its fruit, there is the mention of distinctions such as "He moves at will in all worlds, fivefold and sevenfold," and the mention of the manifestation of one's own nature in passages such as "Having reached the highest light, he appears in his own form" and "There he moves about, laughing, playing, and rejoicing. Likewise, in the passage: "The knower, having shaken off merit and demerit, stainless, attains the supreme equality."

And because of the statement regarding the exhaustion of karma; for in such passages as, "When he sees the other, the Lord, whom he loves, and His majesty, then he is freed from grief," and "Having known the Self and the Impeller as distinct, being loved by Him, he thereafter attains immortality," liberation is stated to result from the knowledge of difference.

If it is argued that even in your own view, since the fruits such as differentiation and enjoyment—which are situated in the final quarter of the *Phalādhyāya*—must be described as the very fruit of the previously introduced knowledge of pure Brahman (*śuddha-brahma-vidyā*) in the sūtras "except for the activity of the world" (*jagadvyāpāravarjam*), "but that [occurs] from mere resolve, because of scripture" (*saṅkalpādeva tu tat śruteḥ*), and "because of the indicative mark of equality in respect to enjoyment alone" (*bhogamātrasāmyaliṅgāt*), these must therefore be the state of supreme liberation (*parama-mukti*), we say no; for even one who has gone to the world of Brahmā (*brahmaloka*) through the meditation on the qualified Brahman (*saguṇopāsanā*) is declared by such scriptural texts as "He does not return again" (*na sa punarāvartate*) to be free from connection with the daily cycles of creation and so forth.

This is because it is logically consistent even with the state of intermediate liberation (*avāntaramukti*) through such instruction. Furthermore, in the *Smṛti* passage beginning with "There is no illusion there" (*na tatra māyā*), the word "illusion" (*māyā*) refers to envy and so forth; thus, there is no indication of an absence of primordial illusion (*mūlamāyā*). Otherwise, a contradiction would arise with the statement "dark and bright" (*śyāmāvadātatva*). In the verse "He who knows it as hidden," the attainment of all desires—which is the fruit of the knowledge of pure Brahman—is not of the nature of worldly enjoyment; rather, it means that for this very bliss, all other beings [are merely parts].

Because the Śruti statement, "subsisting on the measure," declares that [the attainment of all desires] is included within the bliss of Brahman, it is intended to refer to that [bliss]; therefore, by the force of that statement, the attainment of various desires does not constitute the fruit of pure knowledge. This is because, at the occasion of describing the fruit of the Bhūmavidyā, the fruit consisting of "moving at will in all worlds" and "becoming manifold in many ways"—which was previously stated as the fruit of the Prāṇavidyā—is explained as being merely a eulogy for the Nirguṇavidyā, just as the twelve *upasads* mentioned in the context of the Jyotiṣṭoma are understood to be a eulogy for the Ahīna sacrifice. This applies even in passages such as "self-luminous" (*svayaṃjyotiḥ*).

Because [the state of] eating and so forth implies differentiation (*bhedagarbha*), it is intended as being sublated by such expressions as "as if eating" or "as if playing"; since the highest liberation (*paramamukti*) is described therein, your preferred forms of play and the like—which imply differentiation—cannot constitute the highest liberation. Furthermore, in the passage "having shaken off merit and sin," because the supreme equality (*paramasāmya*) takes the form of identity (*aikya*), the destruction of karma results in liberation in the form of identity; thus, it cannot result in a liberation that implies differentiation. Finally, in the passage "being enjoyed" (*juṣṭam*), the word "other" (*anya*) refers to the Self as distinct from the body, senses, and so forth.

This is because there is no state of being other than the Lord for the individual soul (*jīva*). Thus, it is understood from this that the knowledge of difference is the cause of liberation. In my view, this is because, in the sections beginning with "By mere resolve alone, on account of the scriptural statement" (*saṅkalpādeva tacchruteḥ*) up to the end of the chapter—which concern those [texts] devoted to difference, enjoyment, and so forth—the fruit of *saguṇa* (qualified) knowledge has been described, and not the fruit of the knowledge of the pure Brahman. Therefore, since difference does not apply to supreme liberation, and its status as merely conventional (*vyāvahārika*) is thus established, it remains settled that the scriptural texts concerning difference have a conventional purport.
Thus ends the demonstration that the scriptural texts concerning difference have as their purport conventional difference within the Advaitasiddhi. 23.

Now, an objection is raised: In the second chapter of the *Pūrva-mīmāṃsā-sūtra*, the distinction between ritual acts (*karma-bheda*) was established by means of "difference of words" (*śabdāntara*) and other criteria; by those very same criteria, the distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*) is also proven. To illustrate: (1) there is the difference of words consisting of verbal forms derived from roots with contradictory meanings, such as "this very one awakens the individual soul" (*eṣa eva jīvaṃ prabodhayati*) and "from this the individual soul arises" (*etasmāj jīva uttiṣṭhati*); (2) there is repetition (*abhyāsa*) in the form of a restatement where the subject is recognized, such as "the Supreme is eternal, the individual soul is eternal" (*nityaḥ paraḥ, nityo jīvaḥ*); and (3) there is number (*saṅkhyā*), as in "two birds [of beautiful wings]" (*dvā suparṇā*).

If it is argued that there is a distinction because of the presence of other differentiating qualities such as "soundless" and "not eating," because of other contexts such as "from which words turn back," and because of the two designations "the individual soul" (jīva) and "the Lord" (īśa), we say no; for although terms like "another word" and so forth serve as differentiators when they stand on the same footing as perception and other means of knowledge, they do not contradict ultimate non-difference.

Furthermore, you, O Mīmāṃsaka, are a sight unseen: you postulate that word-difference (*śabdāntara*) and the other criteria established as grounds for the difference of actions or scriptures are the grounds for the difference of conscious agents. For that which causes the difference of one thing cannot be the cause of the difference of another; otherwise, it would follow that even the difference of a qualifier—which causes the difference of a qualified whole—would itself be a differentiator of the qualificand. This would lead to the absurdity of a difference [of the agent] even in such cases as: "Devadatta stands up," "he instructs his pupil," "he sacrifices," "he gives," or "he offers oblations."
A difference in words does not constitute a difference in the agent. Thus ends the section on the absence of difference in the self due to difference in words and the like, in the Advaitasiddhi. 24.

Now, an objection: how can the difference, which is known through scripture endowed with the six marks of purport (*tātparya-liṅga*), be unreal? To explain: in the *Atharvaṇa*, there is the opening statement, "Two birds..."; the conclusion, "he attains the highest equality"; the repetition (*abhyāsa*), "of these two, one eats while the other does not eat; the other is the Lord"; the novelty (*apūrvatā*), since a difference that is sublated by neither of the three times and which has as its counter-correlative the Lord—who is knowable solely through scripture—cannot be established without scripture; the fruit (*phala*), "having shaken off merit and sin"; and [the glorification], "his greatness... [is seen].

The explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) consists of praise; the logical justification (*upapatti*) is "he eats while not eating. And here, as in passages such as "this duality is mere illusion" (*māyāmātram idaṃ dvaitam*), the word *dvi* itself denotes difference, or it implies it, or the number two itself—which is the antithesis of oneness—constitutes the opening statement concerning difference.

Similarity (*sādṛśya*) consists precisely in the possession of many attributes belonging to that [object] as qualified by its difference from it, and not merely the object itself [as the qualificandum]. This is because, in such expressions as "This is not that, but similar to it" and "This is not similar to that, but that itself," there is a negation of one term in order to establish the other, regarding either similarity or identity. As for statements such as "The sky has the form of the sky," they are intended to negate the existence of any other object similar to it, or they refer to the similarity between a portion of the sky and a portion of that [other object]; thus, even the conclusion concerns only difference.

Even in the case of repetition (*abhyāsa*), it is the identity of meaning alone that constitutes the criterion for unity, not verbal identity, because otherwise there would be over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). If it is argued that in the phrase "another Lord" (*anyam īśam*), the repetition is possible because the living being (*jīva*) under discussion—the subject of the verb "sees"—is connected as the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) by way of the "foot-rule" (*padinyāya*) with respect to the otherness residing in the Lord; [Response: This is not so. For in this case, the word "other" (*anya*) is used in relation to the Lord who is the object of the act of seeing, and not in relation to the subject of the sentence. Furthermore, since the word "Lord" (*īśa*) is mentioned only once, its repetition is impossible. Moreover, the word "other" (*anya*) does not denote the Lord himself, but rather something distinct from Him. Therefore, the repetition of the term "Lord" is not established here. Consequently, the principle of repetition (*abhyāsa*) cannot serve as a ground for the oneness of the purport in this instance. Thus, the argument based on repetition is refuted. || 1.3.30 || *Āvṛttyadhikaraṇam* (The Section on Repetition). || 1.3.31 || *Prāṇādhikaraṇam* (The Section on Vital Breath). || 1.3.32 || It is not so; for in the first *muṇḍaka* of the *Atharvaṇa*, following the question of Śaunaka—"O Blessed One, when what is known does all this become known?"—two types of knowledge (*vidyā*) are introduced with the words "Two knowledges are to be known. After describing the lower knowledge characterized by the *Ṛgveda* and the others, the text proceeds to explain the object of the higher knowledge—the Imperishable (*akṣara*)—in accordance with the question, beginning with "Now, the higher [knowledge] is that by which that Imperishable is attained, which is unseen, ungraspable, without lineage, without caste," and so forth; thus, non-difference alone is the subject introduced at the outset.

Otherwise, it would be impossible for [the subsequent passages] to be its sequel. For in the second Muṇḍaka, there is a reference in the middle: "The Person alone is this universe; Brahman alone is this most excellent. Furthermore, at the end of the third Muṇḍaka, the conclusion is made with the fruit characterized by identity: "In the highest imperishable, all become one; he who knows that supreme Brahman becomes Brahman itself. Thus, since the Upaniṣad consisting of the three Muṇḍakas is established as being intent on identity, [the principle applies]: "That which is not connected [with another context belongs to the main context]."

By logical principle, just as in the case of the "approaching" (*abhikramaṇa*) and other rites, since it is possible for the intervening passage beginning with "Two birds... (*dvā suparṇā*) to be concordant with that [teaching of non-duality], there is no absence of the commencement of non-difference through the postulation of a contrary intention that would contradict the great context (*mahāprakaraṇa*). Furthermore, by the previously stated reasoning, the statement "He attains the highest equality" (*paramaṃ sāmyam upaiti*) has non-duality as its purport; thus, there is no absence of the conclusion of non-difference.

Therefore, by the passage beginning with "not eating" (*anaśnan*), there is no practice of real difference (*tāttvika-bheda*); nor is a difference—whether having the Lord as its counter-correlate or as its locus—newly established by the scripture, since even if such a difference were required for the mere knowledge of the Lord, it is already established through perception and through means of knowledge equal in status to that [scripture]. Furthermore, even under the view that the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) regarding the results mentioned by you support non-difference, they cannot serve as a unique mark (*liṅga*) for proving difference, because passages such as "not eating" can be explained through conceptual difference and thus lack the capacity to establish real difference.

Now, an objection: the Antaryāmibrāhmaṇa is a statement endowed with the sixfold marks of interpretive intent (*tātparya-liṅga*), and it is a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for [establishing] difference. To explain: "Do you know, O Kāpya, that inner controller? is the introduction; "This is your self, the inner controller" is the conclusion; the repetition twenty-one times of the phrase "This is your self," etc., constitutes the repetition (*abhyāsa*); the status of being the inner controller is something not previously established, and thus constitutes novelty (*apūrvatā*); "He indeed is the knower of Brahman," etc., is the result (*phala*); and [the passage], "If you, O Yājñavalkya, do not know that thread and that inner controller... [constitutes the corroborative reasoning].

If it is argued that there is a deprecatory explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) such as "O Brahmin-cow, you shall perish; your head will fall off," and an illustrative reasoning (*upapatti*) such as "He whose body is the earth, whom the earth does not know," we say: not so.

In this four-chapter work, which serves as an exposition of the Brahmavidyā enunciated in the aphorism "One should meditate [on the Self] as 'I am the Self'," [the text] begins with the declaration that through the knowledge of one thing all things are known—"For by this all this is known"—and proceeds by way of non-difference, stating: "In the beginning, this was indeed Brahman; it knew only itself, thinking 'I am Brahman'; therefore, it became all. Then, at the conclusion of the sixth chapter, in the form of a summary within the Maitreyī-brāhmaṇa, it says: "But where for him everything has become the Self alone, then by what and whom [should he see]?"

Since the conclusion of the four chapters is established as being solely concerned with non-difference—beginning with the passage "He saw" (paśyet) and so forth—it is certain that they aim at non-difference. Consequently, the portion situated within them which sets forth the *sūtrātman* and the intermediate worlds of Brahmā must, in accordance with the primary context (*mahāprakaraṇa*), be understood as conducive to the realization of the Supreme Brahman—the innermost Self free from all attributes—which is the subject matter of the subsequent Brāhmaṇa; it cannot therefore have as its purport a difference that contradicts that primary context. Even if the indicative marks (*liṅga*) you have cited were to determine a purport of difference, they would do so only by referring to a difference that is merely imagined (*kalpita*).

Because [the scriptural texts concerning difference] do not contradict the non-difference that is the ultimate reality. For this very reason, there is no contradiction with the Sūtra: "Nor the embodied one, for both [groups of texts] teach him as distinct," nor is there any inconsistency with its commentary. Thus ends the section on the refutation of the sixfold marks of purport regarding the scriptural texts on difference in the *Advaitasiddhi*. (25)

Now, an objection: Is oneness (*aikya*) the very nature of the Self, or something else? It cannot be the first, because it would entail the consequence of the reduction of one of the two [Self and oneness] to nothingness, and because oneness, being relative, cannot logically be the absolute, independent Self. Nor can it be the second, because if it were real, non-duality (*advaita*) would be lost; and if it were false, statements such as "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*) would fail to reveal reality. If this is argued, we reply: the first position alone is faultless.

Just as there is no consequence such as the reduction of one of the two to nothingness despite the identity of knowledge (*jñāna*) and bliss (*ānanda*)—due to the fact that attributes such as "being imagined" belong to bliss—so too is it possible in the present case. This is because identity was previously stated to be knowable (*abhijñeya*); since that [knowability] is also independent, it does not contradict the nature of the Self being independent. Furthermore, although the nature of the Self appears as the substratum of ignorance and so forth, the cycle of transmigration (*saṃsāra*) remains tenable because the specific mental modification (*vṛtti-viśeṣa*) directed toward that [Self], which would remove ignorance, is currently absent.
As for the faults in the latter position, they are merely criticisms of what has not been stated.

For this very reason, it is rejected [by some] that oneness is something additional—neither the number one, nor the possession of all attributes residing therein, nor the possession of unique attributes residing therein, because these are absent in the attributeless Brahman; nor is it the absence of difference, because difference consists in the absence of oneness, leading to a circular argument; nor is it the non-substratum-ness of attributes not residing in it, because that would result in even the void (śūnya) being identical with Brahman. This is refuted by the fact that oneness is the essential nature (svarūpa) as characterized by the non-substratum-ness of attributes not residing in it.

Because the void (*śūnya*) is devoid of any form, the void cannot possess the nature of unity. Nor should it be argued that by negating attributes not residing in it, there follows the affirmation of attributes residing in it—on the grounds that the negation of a specific [attribute] has as its result the tacit permission of the remainder—for such a principle of "affirming the remainder" is not universally accepted. Otherwise, the statement "there is no blue color in air" would absurdly follow as an affirmation of whiteness.

Now, an objection is raised: Do non-difference-ness, ultimate reality, distinction from the non-existent, and so forth, exist in reality within non-duality, or not? If the first [alternative is true], it would entail the consequence of having a second entity; if the second, there would be a loss of non-difference-ness and the rest. This is not so, because the non-loss of the nature of non-duality and non-duality itself is established precisely through those qualities which are, in reality, identical with its own essential nature (*svarūpa*).

Nor should it be argued that—since non-difference thus culminates in the nature of the Self as something uncontradicted, and since that nature of the Self is accepted by others as well, it would not be the subject matter of your scripture; for others do not accept a nature of the Self characterized as being the substratum of properties that do not reside in the individual soul (*jīva*). Thus, when the non-difference between the individual soul and Brahman has been stated in this way, such scriptural texts as "That thou art" and "This very Self is Brahman" serve as the authority. This concludes the demonstration of the nature of unity in the *Advaitasiddhi*. (26)

Objection: How can the identity between two things characterized by such opposites as omniscience and non-omniscience be taught by the cited scripture, since it is contradicted by logical impossibility (*ayogyatva*)? Reply: It is not so, because—as in the case of "this is that" (*so 'yam*)—the scripture teaches the identity of the pure form (*śuddhākāra*) by setting aside the contradictory forms. Objection: Is this setting aside of the contradictory forms merely due to a lack of intention to express them (*avivakṣā*), or due to their being non-eternal (*anityatva*), or due to their being false (*mithyātva*)? It cannot be the first, for even if the contradictory form is not intended to be expressed, it does not thereby cease to exist.

For it is not possible to easily assert the identity of Brahman with the void or the insentient merely on the grounds that the Śrutis such as "In the beginning this was non-existent" (*asad vā idam agre āsīt*) and "All this is indeed Brahman" (*sarvam khalvidam brahma*) do not intend to express existence and emptiness, or consciousness and insentience, respectively. Nor is the second [position] tenable: because it would result in the instruction "Thou shalt become That" (*tattvam bhaviṣyasi*), the use of the present tense "Thou art" (*asi*) would be inappropriate; furthermore, you yourself do not accept that difference and non-difference could coexist by virtue of a distinction in states, and because the soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara) possess the attributes of independence and dependence, which are eternal.

The third [alternative] is not tenable, because it is impossible for two contradictory properties—established by the witness of flawless scripture—to be false; if this is argued, we say no, because the contradiction is abandoned precisely by not intending to emphasize that aspect. This abandonment consists in the property not being an object of the experience of Brahman, not in its destruction, since destruction is accomplished only by the final direct realization (*caramasākṣātkāra*). Thus, just as "that-ness" and "this-ness" do not contradict the non-difference of the substratum even though they are inseparable, so too omniscience and non-omniscience do not contradict the non-difference of the locus. And this lack of intention to emphasize is for the sake of establishing the primary object of knowledge (*pradhānaprameya*).

Nor should it be argued that in the expression "this is that" (*so 'yam*), there is no abandonment of the aspects of "that-ness" (*tattā*) and "this-ness" (*idantā*), because these two are not contradictory in a single locus when occurring sequentially. For in this context, which aims at non-difference (*abheda*), the identity of the two qualifiers necessitates the abandonment of those [sequential aspects], even if they exist in one place in succession. This is unlike cases such as "all this is indeed Brahman" (*sarvaṃ khalvidaṃ brahma*) or "the unreal," etc., where there is no resulting identity between the void and the real, or between the conscious and the insentient; for in those cases, there is no persisting form—like that of the individual soul and Brahman (*jīva-brahman*)—which remains after the abandonment of their contradictory forms.

"Because that which is non-existent lacks intrinsic nature, and because that which is insentient has a nature subject to sublation"—this is the proof for the non-difference of the individual soul and Brahman in the *Advaitasiddhi*.

Now, an objection may be raised: by means of the scriptural texts on identity (*aikya-śruti*), must the Brahman-hood of the individual soul (*jīva*)—already established by perception—be taught; or must the individual-soul-hood of Brahman—established by scripture—be taught; or must non-difference be enjoined by restating both? In any case, there can be no authoritative validity regarding identity because it contradicts that upon which it depends. For by perception, the individual soul is known to be distinct from Brahman, and by scripture—which apprehends Brahman as possessing omniscience and other such attributes—the Brahman is known to be distinct from the individual soul who is experienced as dependent upon it.

Nor can Brahman be established through inference, because even that [inference], by making Brahman its object through attributes such as omniscience, leaves the contradiction with the foundational [perception] as it was; if this is argued, we say no. For although those two [perception and inference] are foundational for the apprehension of word-potency (*śakti*) and so forth, they are not foundational regarding their own specific objects of knowledge (*svaprameya*). As stated in the *Vācaspatya*: "That which is foundational is not sublated; that which is sublated is not foundational. If being foundational were based merely on some kind of dependence, then even in the case of the cognition "this is not silver," the cognition "this is silver" would result in being foundational for it.

Now, an objection: for when X depends on Y, and upon the sublation of X there follows the sublation of itself, then X is dependent upon Y; and in the present case, since that which apprehends the substratum (dharmin) and so forth is precisely what apprehends its own validity, if that [substratum-apprehension] were sublated, its own sublation would follow. However, this is not the case in a context where there is the presentation of a thing to be negated (niṣedhya).

If it is argued that the invalidity of the knowledge of the negandum does not entail the invalidity of the knowledge of the negation—just as the invalidity of the knowledge of the substrate (the nature of Brahman) does not entail the invalidity of the knowledge of oneness—because that would lead to the abolition of the scriptures of negation; [we reply: True, but the substrate is not, for the time being, characterized by omniscience and so forth, but rather the mere nature of Brahman. For the validity of the knowledge of the substrate qualified by such attributes is not required for the validity of the knowledge of oneness; rather, only the validity of the knowledge of its essential nature is required.

Otherwise, since even the cognition "this is silver" would be a cognition of the locus (*dharmijñāna*) and thus a prerequisite (*upajīvya*), the validity of the sublation-cognition would entail the validity of the cognition of "this" as qualified by silverhood. This is because, just as the qualification by silverhood does not necessitate [the status of] being the locus, the same applies here: the qualification by omniscience and so forth likewise does not necessitate it.

Now, an objection might be raised: "If Brahman is not intended as the subject (*uddeśya*) by way of being delimited by unique attributes such as omniscience (*sārvajñya*), then it must be intended either by way of a common attribute or by its own essential nature (*svarūpa*). In the first case, there is the acceptance of what is already established (*iṣṭāpatti*), since we too accept the identity of the common attribute such as 'consciousness' (*cittva*). In the second case, the oneness of Brahman is not established, because only the common essential nature is intended. To this we say: no.

Regarding the claim that "the identity with Brahman cannot be established," if by the word "Brahman" you mean that which is qualified by omniscience and other such attributes, then we grant your point; for it has already been established that the cognition of identity pertains only to the two referents (padārtha) indicated by the words "Thou" and "I. Consequently, the objection—that because the unique nature of Brahman cannot be presented by the word without its unique attributes, there remains the same problem of contradicting a prior premise—is refuted; for the unique attribute serves merely as an indicator (upalakṣaka) in conveying the object to be designated.

Nor should it be argued that "if there is an absence of a delimiter for being characterized (*upalakṣyatāvacchedaka*), then being characterized is unestablished; and if consciousness-ness (*cittva*) were that [delimiter], it would result in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*). This is because, in the case of a characterization by way of essential nature (*svarūpopalakṣaṇa*), a delimiter for being characterized is not required. As for the claim that "if there is identity through consciousness-ness, it results in proving what is already established," that is not so; for even if identity of consciousness-ness is accepted, the identity of their substrates is not accepted by you, and if that were accepted, there would be no dispute.

For this very reason, it is refuted [by the opponent] that there is no attainment of the desired result through indication (lakṣaṇā) here—as there is in the case of "He winnows the husks with the cake-potsherd" (*puroḍāśakapālena tuṣān upavapati*), where the desired result is achieved through indication based on a substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna-lakṣaṇā*) by enjoining the winnowing of husks not otherwise established—because even though the unity of consciousness (*cittva-ekya*) is already established, the unity of the substratum (*āśraya-ekya*) remains unestablished and must be brought about by indication; for even in the case of "This is that" (*so 'yam*), the aforementioned mode [of indication] must necessarily be asserted.

Nor should it be argued that "thatness" (tattva) qualified by [the property] is not the intended object (*uddeśyatā*) there, because the cognition of the relation of one thing to another occurs only when that thing is known as possessing that [property], since "thatness"—meaning the status of being a qualifier—is possible in respect to "thatness" and so forth; for this has already been answered.

[Objection: But surely, in cases such as "the atom has parts," "God is not omniscient," or "the sacrificial post is the sun," there would be no contradiction with a more fundamental authority (*upajīvyavirodha*); nor would there be a contradiction with a statement regarding the origin of a qualified entity (*saguṇotpattivākya*) in the case of an injunction concerning a quality for something already produced. For in those instances too, it could easily be argued that what is qualified by "atom-ness" and so forth is not the subject (*dharmī*), but rather its mere essential nature (*svarūpamātra*). [Reply: This is not so. Because even in the case of atoms and the like, if they were the subjects (*dharmī*) for properties such as "having parts" even in their essential nature (*svarupeṇa*), then "atom-ness" and so forth would have to possess the same ontological status (*samānasattāka*) as the subject itself.

It would not apply to atoms and the like, because their having the same ontological status [as the whole] depends upon the predominance of that which makes them possess parts; yet there is no inference for such predominance, and on the contrary, such a statement is weak as being a delusive utterance. In the case of "The sacrificial post is the sun," non-difference is not the object of cognition.

Because there is no remainder [of meaning] through the door of praise (*stuti*), and because praise is possible even through qualities not contradicted by perception (*pratyakṣa*), it is illogical to postulate a meaning that contradicts perception; furthermore, if one were to enjoin a quality for something already produced, then the word *āmikṣā* (curd-mixture) situated in the originative injunction (*utpattivākya*) would result in being redundant, since the general category of substance (*dravyasāmānya*) is already obtained merely through the injunction of sacrifice (*yāgacodana*)—by means of the pronoun *asya* included within the sense of the secondary derivative (*taddhita*), and by the principle that "the act enjoined by the sacrifice involves a substance and a deity."
