In the present context, because [the text] is powerful due to not being subordinate to anything else and because it is a statement of authoritative means of knowledge, and because it is most appropriate as a definition of essential nature (*svarūpalakṣaṇā*) by way of establishing identity which contradicts that [prior notion].

Now, one might object: although the scriptural text presenting the difference—which presents the silver as the object to be negated—is weak because it lacks examination despite being required, since mere dependence does not entail strength; nevertheless, in this case, the scriptural text presenting the difference and the witness-consciousness (sākṣipratyakṣa) are both strong because they are faultless and have been examined. Therefore, due to opposition to them, how can there be a focus on identity? If this is argued, we say no, because even for a faultless scripture, there is an absence of any intent toward difference.

Because the contradiction [of that] is established by the impossibility of [the identity] in the scriptural texts on unity; for a scripture cannot have as its purport a meaning devoid of the sixfold marks of intention (tātparya-liṅga) such as the introduction (upakrama), since there would be no regulator thereof, and otherwise there would be an over-extension (atiprasaṅga). Furthermore, even the witness-consciousness (sākṣin) lacks the status of being "examined" merely by virtue of being faultless, because it would follow that even superimposed pleasure and the like within the absence of pain would possess scriptural authority. In my view, everything that is merely phenomenal (prātibhāsika) and established by the witness is false; thus, even regarding the witness— [The text continues: ...even regarding the witness— [the argument holds].

Furthermore, it has already been stated that non-sublation is not established because [the cognition] is colored by a defect in its arising that is itself faultless. Moreover, the distinction between valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and their absence is determined by whether or not they are produced by defects associated with the instruments [of perception]; and the empirical (*vyāvahārika*) [cognition] is produced by the defect of ignorance (*ajñāna*) residing in pure consciousness alone.

Therefore, since there is no contradiction with that which must be accepted as foundational (*upajīvya*), and on the contrary, because the scripture teaching non-difference is the basis for all and thus the foundation for the scripture teaching difference, the latter must be interpreted in a manner consistent with the former despite its apparent contradiction; consequently, the statement "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*) and similar texts are free from all contradiction. Thus, it is established that they have non-duality as their primary purport. This concludes the section on the absence of contradiction with the foundational [texts] regarding the scripture of non-duality. //27//

Objection: In that case, there would be figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in both words; therefore, following my own view, one should resort to figurative indication in only a single word. For instance, in passages such as "Two birds, united together," since the individual soul (*jīva*) is described as being in association with Brahman, it is designated by that [name of Brahman] due to such association—just as the *Mahābhāṣya* states that the word "spring" (*vasanta*) is used for the study [of the Vedas] associated with spring in the rule *vasantādibhyaṣṭhak*; and because of the complementary passage, "All creatures have Being as their root, Being as their abode."

Or rather, it is designated as "that" because it is well-known to be dependent upon that; for in the sūtra "A rule concerning words applies when they are semantically connected" (*samarthaḥ padavidhiḥ*), the Mahābhāṣya states that a word-rule depends on the usage of semantically connected words, and because of the supplementary statement [of the Upaniṣads]: "O dear one, all these creatures have Being as their root."

Alternatively, the use of that term [for the individual soul] is due to its being well-known as "born from that," as in the passage, "Of this [sacrifice], Brahman was the mouth," and as stated in the Bhāṣya on the rule *igyaṇaḥ saṃprasāraṇam*: "The letter produced from *saṃprasāraṇa* is called *saṃprasāraṇa*. Or, the use of that term is due to the individual soul’s dependence upon Him (the Lord), since the supplementary portion of the text, "For the mind, my dear, is bound to the vital breath (*prāṇa*)," declares the soul’s subordination to the Lord; this is like the use of the word "grain" for rice in the mantra, "Thou art grain, prosper! (*dhānyam asi dhinuhi*).

Alternatively, the use of that term [for something else] may arise from similarity (*sādṛśya*), as stated in Jaimini’s Sūtra: "In cases such as 'the sacrificial post is the sun,' it is due to similarity. Furthermore, in the Brahma Sūtra—"But that designation [of the individual soul] is because its essence consists of the qualities of That"—it is stated that the designation for the individual soul (*jīva*) is based on its connection with the qualities of Brahman. And in the Mahābhāṣya, under the rule *bahu-gaṇa-* etc., it is shown that even without the suffix *-vat*, the sense of *-vat* is understood, as in the expression "like a number" (*saṅkhyāvat*).

If it is argued that [the statement] "He said 'Brahmadatta' to one who was not Brahmadatta" implies we consider him to be like Brahmadatta because of that speech—this is not so. For when the intended meaning (*tātparya*) is determined to be identity (*abheda*), there is no fault in the multiplicity of secondary indications (*lakṣaṇā*) required to sustain it. Indeed, the abandonment of the intended meaning should not occur merely for the sake of conforming to a single secondary indication. As it has been stated in the *Nyāyacintāmaṇi*: "The function [of a word] arises from the intended meaning, but the intended meaning does not arise from the function."

Furthermore, since it is improper to assume a meaning such as "being associated with" when the primary sense is possible through the *jahadajahallakṣaṇā* (the indicative function that both excludes and includes), and just as there was no lack of expressive power regarding the primary sense of non-difference, so it was stated previously. In passages such as "Two birds, inseparable companions," it is not the soul's association with Brahman that is being described, but rather its association with the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*); therefore, there is no well-known tradition of such association [with Brahman] based on that.

Nor is the dependence of the individual soul (jīva) upon that [Brahman] established by such passages as "Beings have their root in Being," because the word *prajā* denotes that which is being born, and thus does not refer to the eternal soul. For this very reason, the term is not applied to the soul on the grounds of its being produced from Brahman either. Just as the statement "A Brāhmaṇa is the mouth" is said correctly on the basis of his being born from the mouth, so too the expression "The soul is Brahman" would be valid [only in a similar figurative sense].

Thus, even the Smṛti is effectively non-Smṛti, because it contradicts the Śruti. As for the claim that the connection of the individual soul (jīva) with the attributes of Brahman was stated [in the Sūtras] by the passage beginning with "because its essence consists of those qualities" (tadguṇasāratvāt), that is not so; for the intent of that Sūtra is simply that the soul possesses subtlety—due to its association with the subtlety of the qualities of the intellect (buddhi)—just as Brahman does. By this same reasoning, the use of the term "thou" (tvam) with respect to Brahman, which resides within the soul, is justified—just as one might say "the moon is in the branch" when the moon is near the branch, or as the Śruti says "abiding in the self," or as the text states "the Brāhmaṇa is indeed all the deities."

The argument that the designation "Thou" (*tvam*) refers to Brahman—either because Brahman is the locus of the individual soul (*jīva*), or because of Brahman’s status as the universal agent (just as in the case of "The sacrificer is the sacrificial grass-bundle," where the identity is established through a secondary sense)—is refuted.

Now, one might object: "In the case of *jahadajahallakṣaṇā* (indication with partial exclusion), there is a re-acceptance of that which was previously present in the intellect as part of the denoted meaning but was abandoned due to a sublater; whereas in *jahallakṣaṇā* (pure indication), there is the acceptance of that which was not even present in the intellect and was never abandoned. It is better to accept what was not present in the intellect than to accept what was abandoned. This is not so. For even when the qualifying attribute (*viśeṣaṇa*) is abandoned due to logical inconsistency, the substratum (*viśeṣya*) portion is not abandoned.

By this [it is meant]: from the word *tat*, the third case and subsequent case endings may undergo substitution by the first case singular (*supām suluk...* etc. or elision; thus, the meaning would be "by that you stand," or "born from that," or "you belong to that," or "in that you [stand]," as is clear from the remainder of the passage: "Pervaded by this living self, he stands drinking and rejoicing... all these creatures have their root in Being, my dear; this whole world has that as its essence."

And likewise, the Mīmāṃsakas, in the passage "But they recite the Sāmidhenīs where they press [the Soma]" (*uta yatsunvanti sāmidhenīstadanvāhuḥ*), accepted that the nominative case of the words *yat* and *tat* carries the sense of the locative; thus they explained it as: "Wherever they press [the Soma], there, standing at the Havirdhāna shed, one should recite the Sāmidhenīs."

And it is refuted that it is logical to sacrifice the natural sense of a single, accommodative, primary case-ending for the sake of the natural sense of multiple, non-accommodative, primary nominal stems; for just as in the case of *prodgātṝṇām*, where the nominal stem is interpreted otherwise in order to preserve the natural sense of the case-ending, here too, the nominal stem itself must be interpreted otherwise.

Nor should it be argued that because the genitive plural cannot be shifted elsewhere—since it is not prescribed for other contexts as the nominative singular is—it is impossible to interpret it otherwise, and therefore the primary nominal stem (prātipadika) must be taken figuratively (lakṣaṇā) to refer to the *chandoga* singers such as the *prastotṛ* and others in accordance with the plural number. For, as in the case of "he offers the groats" (*saktūn juhoti*), shifting [the meaning] elsewhere is indeed possible. Furthermore, the expressive word does not lack scope; for the case-ending has scope regarding the qualified object (*viśeṣya*), just as it has regarding number.

Nor is predominance [the criterion], because predominance belongs only to the suffix that expresses the predominant meaning. As it has been said: "The base and the suffix together express the meaning; of these two, the suffix [expresses it] by way of predominance. Nor is the multiplicity of nominal stems (*prātipadika*) a necessary factor for naturalness (*svārasya*), since we observe a lack of naturalness even when there is multiplicity, as in the case of "in the deep river" (*gabhīrāyāṃ nadyām*). If you argue that this is so there due to the force of the intended meaning (*tātparya*), the same applies in the present case as well.

As for the claim that in the injunction "one should sprinkle the sacrificial oblations with the remnant of the *prayāja*," there is an inconsistency with the instrumental case-ending (*tṛtīyā-vibhakti*)—meaning one would instead be throwing the *prayāja* remnant into the oblations—and that in cases such as "one offers the groats" (*saktūn juhoti*), there is likewise an inconsistency with the accusative case-ending (*dvitīyā-vibhakti*), this is accepted only out of necessity. This is because in the case of "with the *prayāja* remnant" and similar instances, no other mode of action is possible apart from the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of what has already been used; whereas in the case of "the groats" and similar instances, since they lack utility either in the past or the future, they cannot be objects of refinement (*saṃskārya*).

By this, the view that "tasya tvam tattvam" is a compound word (*samasta-pada*) is refuted; for since the meaning is established by the uncompounded form itself—which is devoid of the indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the genitive sense and so forth—a genitive compound is improper, otherwise it would result in a contradiction with the *Sthapati-adhikaraṇa*.

Now, an objection may be raised: in the passage "All this has that as its self (aitadātmyam); That is the Truth; That is the Self; Thou art That," the word "That" (tat) does not refer to the Self, but rather to "aitadātmyam. This is because of its neuter gender. The term *aitadātmyam* means "this is its self" (*eṣa cāsāvātmā ca etadātmā*, tasyedam aitadātmyam*). Thus, the meaning would be "Thou art this thing belonging to That," and not identity. For if the meaning were "that which has That as its self is aitadātmyam," the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) would be rendered meaningless. Therefore, it is better to resort to another interpretation, according to the saying: "The formation of taddhita derivatives is indeed manifold."
He is the creator, the destroyer, the controller, and the protector;
Hari pervades all this, and therefore they know it to be "this-ness" (aitadātmya).

If it is argued that this is because of the traditional rule (*smṛti*), we say no; for the suffix *ṣyañ* is not prescribed in the sense of "this belongs to that" (*tasyedam*), nor is such usage observed. However, it is seen used in its own sense (*svārtha*), as in the expression *saukhyam* (happiness). Thus, *aitadātmyam* means "that which has this Being (*sat*) as its self (*ātman*)"—that is, everything whose self is this. Its state is "being of this self" (*aitadātmyam*). Furthermore, there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) either because the suffix is used in its own sense, or by metaphorically treating the state and the thing possessing the state as non-different, as in the passage: "That which is the Plenum (*bhūman*), that is happiness.

As for the statement in the *smṛti* that speaks of "being of this self" (*aitadātmya*) in terms of pervasiveness, that is not tenable, because it would contradict the promise of knowing all through the knowledge of one.

[Objection: But surely, since words denoting bodies—such as *deva* (god) and *manuṣya* (human)—are seen to extend to the embodied being, the term [for the individual soul] denotes the living being who is the body of Brahman; thus, the designation "That thou art" (*tattvam asi*) is based on the relationship between body and embodied being, according to such scriptural texts as "He whose self is the body. Therefore, in our view, both terms are primary. [Reply: No. Does this "extending to the embodied being" mean that they indicate (*lakṣaka*) it? Even so, does it mean they have a direct denotative power (*śakti*) toward it, or do they function toward it solely through their primary application to the body?

Or does it mean "denoting that [body]"? Not the first, because the primary sense [of the word] cannot be established. Not the second, because the designation "of those denoting the body" would be inappropriate as an uncommon (asādhāraṇa) reference, and because it has already been stated that the genus (jāti) such as "human-ness," which serves as the basis for the application [of the word], does not reside in the embodied being. Not the third, because the application of a word to one object is useless for another; therefore, it must be said that this usage is based on the non-difference established by beginningless delusion between the body and the embodied being.

Likewise, even here this application is based solely on non-difference; the distinction, however, is that here non-difference is real because there is no sublation. As for the claim that the statement "That thou art" is intended for the purpose of meditating upon the individual soul as Brahman—just like [the statement] "The sun is Brahman"—that is not so, because the illustrative example is dissimilar due to its occurrence in a context not concerning meditation, and because it is improper to abandon that [meaning of non-difference] when it is possible for it to be grounded in reality according to the method already stated.

Now, one might object: in the statement "That art thou" (*tat tvam asi*), the word-division should be "thou art not that" (*atattvam asi*), just as in the case of "sound is impermanent," the word-division is "impermanence" (*anitya*) according to the analogy of a jar; likewise here too, it should follow the analogies of the bird, the thread, and so forth.

For indeed, there is no identity between the bird and the string mentioned in the first section—where it is said, "Just as a bird is bound by a string"—nor between the salt and the water mentioned in the sixth section—beginning with "This water is salty"—nor between the man and the land of Gandhāra mentioned in the seventh section—beginning with "O dear one, [lead] a man from Gandhāra"—nor between the thief and the stolen object mentioned in the ninth section—beginning with "He has taken it; he has committed theft."

If it is argued that in the example of the thief and the stolen goods, the harm to the knower of oneness is clearly evident—since the thief is one who falsely identifies with the Brahmanhood belonging to another, rather than one who simply lacks knowledge of his own existing Brahmanhood—that is not so. For in examples such as the bird and the string, even though a difference exists, it does not necessitate the word-break (*padaccheda*) "not-that" (*atad*); the example is established even without that [word-break]. Furthermore, the pot-example is dissimilar, as it cannot be logically sustained as being eternal.

For instance, just as one afflicted by diseases such as fever finds rest upon recovery and regaining health, so too does the individual soul (jīva) abide in its true nature as the divine Self (devatātman) to dispel the exhaustion produced by the activity of the organs during the waking and dreaming states; this is the meaning of the analogy of the bird and the string, which is established in quite another way, in accordance with the Vedic scripture: "He becomes merged in his own [Self]" (*svam apīto bhavati*).

If it is argued: "The word *sva* (own/self) applied to Brahman does not intend non-difference from the individual soul (*jīva*), but rather signifies 'one's own' or intends 'independence,' according to the traditional teaching that 'it is called *sva* because of its independence'; furthermore, the phrase *apīto bhavati* means 'having become concealed, he has arrived [at it],' and not that he is non-different—since the prefix *api* denotes concealment, the root *i* denotes motion, and the past passive participle suffix (*niṣṭhā*) is established as having an agentive force; moreover, there is an absence of both etymological derivation (*yoga*) and conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) for the sense of identity"—we say: no.

Because a word is primary (*mukhya*) when referring to its own form, whereas if it were intended to refer to another object, it would necessarily result in being either secondary (*gauṇī*) or indicative (*lakṣaṇā*); and because, even though there is no absence of etymological derivation (*yoga*) or conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) in the case of non-difference, the meaning consisting of the attainment of the essential nature—obtained through a consideration of the prefix, root, and suffix—culminates in non-difference. For this very reason, the objection that "even if the meaning is identity, since the root *apīta* is intransitive, there is an inconsistency with the heard accusative case and the necessity of postulating an unheard instrumental case" is refuted.

For this very reason, the objection—that there is a contradiction because another Śruti passage concerning deep sleep uses the distinct analogy of a hawk or a falcon flying about in the sky and, becoming weary, folding its wings and remaining for the sake of rest—has been refuted; for total similarity is not a necessary requirement for something to serve as an illustrative example (dṛṣṭānta).

Nor should it be argued that there is a contradiction with the scriptural text regarding deep sleep—"He is embraced by the conscious Self"—since even in your own view, this text speaks of difference; nor with the sūtra "In deep sleep and departure [there is] difference," since in your position too, just as in the waking state, you accept a difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman based on ignorance (*avidyā*) even during deep sleep. This is because the statement regarding the attainment of one's own true nature is intended to mean that there is no more distinct manifestation of limitation (*vikṣepa*) than in the waking and dreaming states, rather than intending absolute non-difference; otherwise, [the following would be the case]:

Because otherwise, there would result the undesirable consequence that deep sleep and liberation would be indistinguishable. To the objection—"If [Brahman] is the root of the real world, why is it not perceived?"—the example of salt dissolved in water is given to clarify this point: that even an existing thing may not be perceived, whereas it is perceived under other conditions; for even in that case, it is perceived differently.

If it is argued that, just like salt, the root of the world—though not perceived by the senses—is capable of being perceived through another means, and that one might therefore ask what the means for perceiving that very root is, the answer given is the illustration of the man from Gandhāra to state the means, namely, "A person who has a teacher knows [the truth]"; however, even in that case, the illustration is applicable in quite a different way.

Likewise, when the doubt arises as to what that sequence is by which the wise man possessed of a teacher becomes united with the True (Sat), the example of the thief and the non-thief is given in order to state that one who is intent on truth attains the goal, while one who is intent on untruth meets with misfortune. Even in that case, however, the matter is established in quite another way. Furthermore, there is no inconsistency in citing "He committed theft" as an illustration, since the examples of truth and untruth are not intended to be exhaustive; rather, they are not separate illustrations because the latter is subsumed under the former as its explanatory basis.

Now, an objection is raised: it is certainly not possible to assert the identity between the various tree juices mentioned in the ninth section in the passage beginning with "the juices of various trees," and the river and ocean mentioned in the tenth section in the passage beginning with "these, my dear, are rivers. For the juices of various trees do not attain identity with the honey already established there by abandoning their mutual distinctions; nor do they, having previously been objects of the illusion of difference, later cease to be such objects. Rather, like threads in a cloth, they remain mutually distinct.

They produce honey from what was previously non-existent, yet this is not consistent with the illustrative examples. Even regarding the example of the river and the ocean, is there an identity between the two wholes—the river and the ocean—or between their constituent water-atoms? Or is there the production of a different substance? It cannot be the first or the second, because even though they become mutually mixed—just as when beans are thrown into a heap of beans, or when water is poured into milk—an identity between those things that were previously distinct cannot occur later on.

If it is argued that "in the third case there is indeed a difference, and thus there is conformity with the examples (dārṣṭāntika)," we say: no. For the examples were cited with the intention of showing the absence of a manifest difference due to the lack of a clear delimiting factor (avacchedaka), and since they maintain neutrality regarding whether a real difference or non-difference exists in the example, the multitude of objections you have raised is not to be counted. For this very reason, the claim that the example refers merely to the non-cognition of an existing difference is refuted; for [the examples] maintain neutrality regarding the actual existence of difference.

Nor is this lack of clarity regarding the object of distinction useless in the case of absolute non-difference; for it is possible that it serves a purpose by generating a conceptual cognition (*sambhāvanā-buddhi*)—namely, that just as that which is delimited by subtle adjuncts (*upādhi*) attains identity with that which is delimited by a great adjunct, so too, upon the dissolution of those [subtle adjuncts], that which was delimited by them attains unconditioned identity.

For this very reason, in the passage "They enter into the ocean itself, and he becomes the ocean itself," when the transformation of the rivers under discussion into the ocean is enjoined, there would have been the designation "they become the ocean itself," just as in the expression "gold becomes a bracelet."

Therefore, rivers go forth from the ocean—which consists of an indefinite mass of water—and enter back into it; yet the ocean remains exactly as it was. The meaning is either that these [rivers] do not possess the nature of the ocean, or that the ocean itself does not attain the state of being a river. These two examples illustrate the very ignorance of mutual distinction even while things exist.

Therefore, the following objection is refuted: that in the illustrative passage concerning the manifold flavors (*nānārasa*), "In this very way, my dear, all these creatures, upon reaching Being, do not know 'we are reaching Being,'" and in the illustrative passage concerning the rivers and the ocean, "Having come from Being, they do not know 'we are coming from Being,'" it is stated that evil results from the ignorance of the distinction of Being itself (in the form of "they [become] tigers here," etc.). This is because those passages are intended as illustrations based on the absence of a clearly manifest distinction.

As for the claim that the scriptural passage concerning the tiger and so forth refers to the calamity of assuming the form of a tiger based on the ignorance of difference—that is not so. Because of the proximity of the phrase "having attained [the Self] in Being" (*sati sampadya*), the statement "they do not know" (*na viduḥ*) expresses the lack of knowledge regarding the attainment of Being, and not the ignorance of difference. Thus, since the attainment of Being is not preceded by [such] knowledge, the passage intends to show that one comes to exist in the state of a tiger or other such beings precisely through their respective latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
Therefore, because the primary intent of these illustrative examples is not the existence of difference, it is clear that there is no contradiction with those [other] passages.

[Objection: "Is it not the case that [the reading] *atat* (not that) is indeed the correct division? For in the eighth section, by means of the illustration of deep sleep—which is not a ground for suspecting independence—with the words, 'O gentle one, understand from me the end of dream'; and in the eleventh, by stating the method of positive and negative concomitance with the words, 'When the living self leaves one branch...'; and in the fifteenth, by means of the illustration of death—which is not a ground for suspecting independence—with the words, 'O gentle one, when a person is afflicted by illness...'; the subordination to the Lord has been declared. Therefore, *atat* is appropriate. [Reply: No, because the passage beginning with "the end of dream" (*svapnāntam*) refers precisely to the state of deep sleep.

Because it was brought down by Uddālaka with the intention, "I shall show my own form as a deity, which is free from the state of being a living soul," it lacks the quality of being dependent on a Lord (Īśvara). Furthermore, the destruction of waves, ripples, foam, and bubbles—which arise from water and return to that same state—is observed.

In response to the doubt as to how there can be no destruction of living beings—who daily attain their true nature—and of death and dissolution, the illustration of the tree branch was stated as a refutation; for that illustration intends to show that "the body presided over by the living being lives, and when abandoned by it, it dies, but the living being does not die," as evidenced by the complementary passage: "Verily, this [body] alone dies when abandoned by the living being; the living being does not die."

Just as in the case of the passage "O dear one, [he approaches] one suffering from heat," there is no intention to establish dependence on the Lord, because that passage aims at demonstrating the sequence by which a wise person possessing a teacher attains *sat*, in response to the inquiry regarding that very sequence.

As for the claim that in the eleventh [chapter], in the passage "pervaded by the living self (jīva), drinking deeply and rejoicing, he remains," the word *jīva* refers to the Lord because the term "rejoicing" (*modamāna*) is stated separately from the transmigrating soul—that is not so; for since "rejoicing" functions as an attribute of the tree introduced as a simile, it does not refer to the transmigrating soul, and thus there is no reason to abandon the literal meaning of the word *jīva*.

And as for the statement in the twelfth [section], "O dear one, this great banyan tree stands within this very subtle (aṇiman) [entity]," here the word *aṇiman* refers to the subtle Lord (*sūkṣmeśvara*). This is because that term is used for the Lord in this very scripture in the passage, "This subtle [entity]—this whole world has that as its self" (*sa eṣo'ṇimā aitadātmyam idaṃ sarvam*). It does not, however, refer to the seeds (*dhānā*), because those are indicated by the word *aṇu*—which is accompanied by the particle *iva*, is feminine, ends in the plural number, and lacks an abstract suffix—as in the passage, "What do you see here? These seeds are, as it were, minute (*aṇvya*)."

If it is argued that [the self is not atomic] because it is the opposite of that and because it is unfit for the term "aṇiman" (atomicity), we say no. For even in the case of the Lord, who is the subject of the usage "eṣo'ṇurātmā" (this self is atomic) without an abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*), we see the usage "eṣo'ṇimā" (this is his atomicity); thus, it can be said similarly regarding the grain (*dhānā*). Nor does it follow that the invisibility mentioned in the phrase "na ca tarhi nibhālayase" (yet you do not perceive it) is untenable; for the meaning is simply this: "In this very grain which has been experienced, a great banyan tree stands, but it is not known by you because it is unmanifest."

Now, an objection: if, in the fifteenth [chapter], the intention is merely to state that the knower attains Brahman, then the statement would have ended simply with "his speech merges into the mind" up to "the fire [merges] into the supreme deity"; thus, the passage beginning with "as long as his speech does not merge into the mind" would be redundant—this is not so.

The sequence of merging into Being (*sat-sampatti*) that occurs at worldly death is the very same for the wise person as well; the only difference is that it is produced by knowledge or ignorance. To establish this point, the sequence of merging into Being is presented through both positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) in the illustrative example, so there is no lack of purpose. Furthermore, in the passage "That is the True, That is the Self," the word "Self" (*ātman*) refers to the Lord (*Īśvara*) denoted by the term *aṇiman*, and not to the individual soul (*jīva*). As it is said: "Because he attains [them], because he takes [them], because he eats the objects here, and because his state is constant, he is therefore called the 'Self'."

This must be stated: because of the statement [beginning with] "What is the Self? and so forth, since the word "Self" (ātman) is well-known in common usage to refer to the individual soul (jīva), and since the quality of being the enjoyer of the objects mentioned in that statement is possible only for the individual soul, it is appropriate to accept that very [soul]. As for the conclusion reached that the one spoken of in the sentence "Know Him alone as the one Self" is not the individual soul because there is no word denoting it, that was intended on the grounds that the word "Self" is not used in its primary sense for the individual soul, but rather for the primordial matter (pradhāna) and so forth.

However, even though the individual soul (*jīva*) possesses selfhood (*ātmatva*), it is excluded [from being the creator] because its limited nature makes it impossible for it to be the creator of the universe; this is the intended meaning. Furthermore, grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with "by means of the soul" (*jīvena ātmanā*) would otherwise be untenable. Nor can the word *jīva* refer to the Lord (*Īśvara*) alone, because there is no reason to abandon its conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*), and because that conventional meaning is already established. Moreover, statements such as "I am indeed known as the *jīva*" are possible even under the view of non-difference (*abheda*). Finally, the quality of sustaining the vital breaths (*prāṇadhārakatva*) does not belong to the Lord alone, as it is common to the individual soul as well.

Nor is it impossible for the differentiation of name and form preceded by the tripartition (trivṛtkaraṇa) to occur in the individual soul (jīva); for even if it were impossible in beings such as ourselves, it is possible for Hiraṇyagarbha—who possesses the conceit of the subtle body (liṅgaśarīra) composed of non-tripartite elements—to effect the differentiation of the phenomenal world consisting of names and forms.

Nor should it be argued that, in that case, the subsequent statement regarding the entry of the individual soul (*jīva*) would be inconsistent, since consciousness was already established previously by the texts, "That fire thought," "Those waters thought," and "These three deities [thought]. This is because the purpose of the passage is to show that while Brahman is the direct cause in the creation of the unevolved elements (*avyākṛtabhūta*), it is not the direct cause in the creation of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) and so forth, but rather acts through the medium of the individual soul who is non-different from itself.

Furthermore, because the opening statement is "one only, without a second," it is not appropriate to break the compound as *a-tat* (not that) on the basis of following the analogies of the hawk and so forth; for that would contradict the proposition that by the knowledge of one, all is known, and because the identity of Brahman and the individual soul (*jīva*) has not been previously suggested, its negation would be logically untenable.

Nor should it be argued that there is a possibility of identity [between the Self and the body] based on either (1) a failure to understand the intent of the Śruti—as in passages such as "They think sacrifice and merit are the highest," etc.—or (2) an ancient false doctrine—as in "Some indeed say that in the beginning this was non-existence alone"—or (3) the fact that everyone presumes sovereignty, which consists in independence over the body, senses, and so forth, within their own selves, or (4) through direct perception; for the intent of [the Upanishads] regarding identity has been established by valid cognition, and its status as a sound doctrine has been firmly settled.

Because it is impossible to state that [the soul] has attained a state free from ignorance regarding the intended meaning (*tātparya*), and because even the mark of oneness (*aikyaliṅga*) is not merely based on conceit (*ābhimānika*), if [oneness] were to follow from that, then it would be impossible to deny it; for since the body, senses, and so forth are superimposed as one with the individual soul (*jīva*), it is impossible to speak of a universal conceit of independence toward them, and because independence toward anything whatsoever does not constitute the definition of God (*īśvara*).

By this [it is shown that] the sixfold marks of purport (*ṣaḍvidha-tātparya-liṅga*) are indeed directed toward difference (*bheda*): because the opening statement, "One only, without a second," establishes the absence of equals or superiors; because its conclusion, "This is its essence" (*aitadātmyam*), reiterates that very same point; because of the repetition nine times of the statement, "That thou art not" (*atattvamasi*); because of its novelty (*apūrvatva*), since the difference from the Lord—which is accessible through scripture alone—is not otherwise established without scripture; because of the hearing of the fruit, "Then he becomes perfected" (*atha sampatsyate*); because of the explanatory praise (*arthavāda*), "By which the unheard becomes heard"; and because it is supported by analogies such as the bird and the thread. Thus, [the opponent argues,] these marks of purport refer exclusively to difference.

— This is refuted: because in the phrase "only one" (*ekameva*), there is no lack of beginning with a statement of difference merely by the absence of equals or superiors; because even in non-difference (*abheda*), such [an absence] is possible; because it would contradict the promise that "by the knowledge of one, all is known"; and because the beginning refers only to the absence of a second. For this very reason, the repetition (*abhyāsa*) and the conclusion (*upasaṃhāra*) also do not have difference as their object; rather, regarding non-difference, it has already been stated how there is "novelty" (*apūrvatā*). Furthermore, the fruit, the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), and the logical consistency (*upapatti*) are all possible only in non-difference.

Likewise, there is no contradiction with the statements regarding non-difference found in other Vedic branches, for those situated within the context of meditative worship (upāsanā) are intended solely for the purpose of worship. Thus concludes the determination of the meaning of the statement "That thou art" (tattvamasi). || 28 ||

However, as for the passage situated in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka—“In the beginning, this was indeed Brahman; it knew only itself: ‘I am Brahman’”—since it occurs in a context not concerned with meditative worship (anupāsanā), its purpose is solely to establish non-difference. Nor is there any contradiction with the subsequent supplementary passage which appears to concern difference, namely: “Whosoever among the gods awakened to that, he alone became that; likewise among the seers, and likewise among men. For even there, having identified the person who had awakened among the gods and others, the statement “he alone became that” is intended to convey non-difference from Brahman, and does not intend to establish difference.

Nor should it be doubted that, because Brahman alone is the subject under discussion in this sentence, the identity of the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman is not established by it; for, in accordance with the supplementary portion of the text—"He who [is] of the gods"—which refers to the individual soul, the word "Brahman" here refers to the *kāryabrahman* (the conditioned or effected Brahman). Furthermore, if it were intended to refer to the pure (*śuddha*) Brahman, it would be improper to proclaim the fruit characterized by universal identity—namely, "therefore all that became that"—as being caused by the act of instruction.

Nor should it be suspected that—just as in passages such as "One should meditate on Name as Brahman" and "The sun is Brahman, such is the instruction"—the absence of identity with Name and so forth is indicated by the presence of the word *iti*, so too here the absence of difference from Brahman is indicated by the presence of the word *iti*; for since this occurs outside the context of meditation (*upāsanā*), it is impossible to claim that identity is not intended, as is the case in passages like "Name is Brahman."

Nor is the word "ca" (and) redundant; for its utility lies in refuting the notion that verbal cognition, like [the act of] knowing the Self—as in the passage "One should meditate [on Him] as the Self"—is inherently transitive by nature. Furthermore, the word "I" (aham) is primary when referring to the Inner Controller (antaryāmin), because the word "I" is employed for the Inner Controller in such passages as "I became Manu and Sūrya. Viṣṇu, the Inner Controller of all, is denoted by all pronouns;
however, He is not [denoted] in His entirety as "This is I," "You," or "That."

And as for the statement "because of this declaration," that is not so; for, according to the maxim *śāstradṛṣṭyā tūpadeśo vāmadevavat* (the teaching is by means of the vision of the scripture, as in the case of Vāmadeva), the state of being the sun and so forth is predicated of the living-consciousness of Vāmadeva precisely because of its factual non-difference from Brahman, and thus there is no intention to refer to the Inner Controller (*antaryāmin*). This is because in the preceding sentence, "Whosoever among the gods awakened to That, he indeed became That," the attainment of the state of Brahman caused by the realization of reality (*tattvabodha*) is the subject at hand; therefore, the passage beginning with "seeing, he attained" also refers to the attainment of the state of Brahman caused by such realization.

Because there is an absence of the status of being the Inner Ruler (*antaryāmin*). Even in the case of *smṛti*, since a specific power toward each respective individual self is necessary, the usage of "this is I" and so forth occurs in reference to the Inner Ruler by association with that [individual self], but not in the sense of being identical in every respect. As for the prohibition, however, because it is based on the absence of identity between the two as conditioned [entities], there is no contradiction. For this very reason, the objection—that the state of being Anasūyā and others is impossible for Vāmadeva, who is of the nature of qualified consciousness, because he is of the nature of qualified consciousness—is refuted, since it was stated from the perspective of the vision of the scriptures (*śāstradṛṣṭyā*).

In that case, it cannot be argued that the use of the first person (the *uttama-puruṣa*) is inappropriate because [the Self] does not exist as pure consciousness (*śuddha-citi*), for such usage is possible by way of referring to its prior state. Nor should it be said that [passages such as] "I gave the earth to the noble lady" are illogical because pure consciousness alone is not the giver of the earth; for these statements are justified by taking into account the consciousness as conditioned (*upahita-cit*). Furthermore, passages such as "His secret name was 'I'" are intended for meditation (*upāsanā*) of that kind and thus lack the power to determine the primary meaning of the word.

Therefore, this scripture does not intend to teach the non-difference [of the inner controller] from [the individual soul], because no difference regarding the inner controller (antaryāmin) has been raised as an issue. Nor is such an issue raised by the infinite number of things to be controlled and so forth, since we observe that even a single individual soul can be the controller of many limbs, and even a single king can be the controller of many regions.

The statement, "That which is here in the person and that which is yonder in the sun are one," does not have as its primary purpose the identity of the inner rulers (*antaryāmin*); rather, since pure Brahman is the subject under discussion—as seen in passages such as "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme"—the teaching of identity is logically justified as a means to refute the notion that the distinctions created by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) possess ultimate reality.

Nor does there arise, in this way, a contradiction with the subsequent statements concerning difference in the Chāndogya—such as "I am that person who is seen in the sun" and "He leads them to Brahman"—because those passages reside within a context of meditative worship (*upāsanā-prakaraṇa*) and are intended for the meditation on the "I-grasping" (*ahaṃ-graha*), and thus lack contradiction [with the doctrine of non-duality]. Nor should it be suspected that the identity [of the individual and the universal self] is not established even by a statement residing outside the context of worship, simply because it is not established by a statement residing within the context of worship; for the status of being subsidiary to something else (*anya-śeṣatva*) is the necessary condition for such [non-establishment], and that condition is absent here.

Furthermore, since the subsequent statement, "But he who worships another deity," is intended to censure the cognition of difference, the preceding statement cannot be taken as referring to meditative worship (*upāsanā*) in accordance with that [subsequent] context. As for the argument that the word *brahman* here means "expansive" (*bṛṃhaṇa*) and thus the identity with the Supreme Brahman is not established—and that otherwise the phrase "I am Brahman" would be redundant because the knowledge of "Brahman" was already established by the earlier statement "He knew himself alone as 'I am'"—that is not correct.

This is because the word "self" (ātman) refers back to the consciousness of the living being (jīvacaitanya) and is meaningful as having the purpose of enjoining non-difference from the consciousness of Brahman, which is characterized by such qualities as being "enlarged" (bṛṃhita). Accordingly, even such Smṛti passages as "I am Hari; all this is Janārdana" are consistent with this view.

As for the claim that the passage, "Now, he who worships another deity, thinking 'He is one and I am another,' does not know; he is like a beast," is a censure of the knowledge of a distinction between the Inner Controller (antaryāmin), that is incorrect; for the Inner Controller is not the subject under discussion here, and because the figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) of two words is adopted in accordance with the intended meaning. As for the interpretation that the meaning here is: "He who is other—the individual soul (jīva)—worships another deity, distinct [from himself], thinking 'He is the Supreme Self and I am He,' yet he does not know; he is like a beast," that is worthless, due to the fault of a remote syntactical connection (vyavahitānvaya).

This is because the word "others" (*anya*) in the phrase "I am other than those proximate to sound" is brought over [to the relative pronoun] *yaḥ*. Nor should it be suspected that proximity (*sannidhāna*) has greater force than semantic compatibility (*yogyatā*) according to the maxim "that which has a semantic connection with another," for even when the connection exists as it stands, semantic compatibility is present by the aforementioned sequence. Furthermore, this direct statement (*śruti*) does not independently negate the existence of others, as there is no word present that establishes independence in the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) of "otherness."

As for the claim made by some that—on account of the scriptural hearing of the word "upāsīta" (he meditates)—the prohibition applies only to *upāsanā* as a distinct mental state different from knowledge achieved through effort, and not to knowledge itself—that is incorrect. For in the preceding sentence, "Whosoever among the gods awakens to this," and in the subsequent deprecatory statement, "He does not know it," it is *vedana* (knowledge) alone that is mentioned; therefore, even the *upāsanā* situated between those two must have knowledge as its ultimate purport.

Thus, even this sentence from the *Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad*, "He who knows that supreme Brahman becomes Brahman itself," has as its sole purport non-difference. Nor can it be argued that the second occurrence of the word "Brahman" refers only to the individual soul (*jīva*), because that term has multiple meanings such as "genus," "living being," and "the lotus-seated one" (Brahmā), and because the word "Brahman" can be applied to the individual soul in passages such as "There are two Brahmans. Consequently, the meaning would be: "He who knows the supreme Brahman becomes the individual soul itself, and not the supreme Brahman."

Therefore, it must be said that the first use of the word "Brahman" is qualified by the term "supreme" (paramatvena). Even though the application of the word "Brahman" to the individual soul (jīva) is possible, in this context it is more appropriate to employ the term "Supreme Brahman" (parabrahma), because the state of being an individual soul and the state of not being Brahman have already been established, and thus they cannot be accomplished through the knowledge of Brahman. Consequently, by implication, the second becoming-Brahman is also qualified as "supreme."

As for the statement "he becomes Brahman," its meaning is that he comes to be pervaded by the nature of Brahman, which consists in being expanded (*bṛṃhita*), just as it is said, "Even a Śūdra may become a Brāhmaṇa by worshipping a Brāhmaṇa with devotion. For a Śūdra does not indeed become the very individual who was worshipped; rather, he becomes one who is pervaded by the genus (*jāti*) of Brāhmaṇahood. That [explanation] is incorrect, because according to the reasoning stated previously, in the present case only the non-difference of the individual is possible, and thus the illustrative example is dissimilar.

Nor is it correct to argue that, because of the supplementary statement "his greatness," only the attainment of his greatness is established and not his identity with him; for the passage has the following purpose: "He who knows [the Self] as distinct from the manifold of the body, senses, and so forth, and he who knows the manifold and its manifestation—that person becomes free from sorrow. Nor should it be said that the citation of the analogy of separate rivers and the ocean in the verse "Just as rivers flowing... is improper; for it has already been stated that the analogy is appropriate because its sole intent is the dissolution of clearly perceived difference.

The statement, "He goes to the divine Person who is higher than the high," does not intend to describe the attainment of a Brahman located in another place; for since that [attainment] is the fruit of meditation on the qualified (saguṇa) Brahman, it cannot be the fruit of the knowledge of Brahman, and thus the passage must refer to the attainment of Brahman as one's own essential nature (svarūpa).

Nor should it be argued that, in the Advaita system, it is illogical to speak of the attainment of a previously non-existent state of Brahman for one who is eternally Brahman; for we observe that in cases such as gold already on one's neck, the result is considered an "attainment of what was already attained" through the mere cessation of delusion. Nor is the cessation of superimposition non-verbal, since its verbal nature is established by being cognizable through *śrutārthāpatti* (presumption based on what is heard). Furthermore, the scriptural text, "Being Brahman indeed, he merges into Brahman," is also intended to convey identity (*aikya*).

Nor does there arise here a contradiction regarding the relationship between agent and object due to the first word "Brahman" not referring to the individual soul (*jīva*), for such a designation is possible by taking into account the difference conditioned by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) prior to direct realization. Furthermore, the statement, "In the supreme imperishable, all become one," is also evidence for non-difference. It is not as when cows become one in the cow-pen at evening; nor is it like: "All the kings, having become one, rained arrows upon the son of Pāṇḍu."

One might argue that the expression "the insect has become one with the bee" refers to a state of unification based on identity of location, identity of mind, or similarity—since such unifications are observed in cases like a cow, a king, an insect, or a bee—and that here too, unification is figurative (gauṇa) due to those very same causes; however, this must be rejected because when a primary sense is possible, a figurative sense is inappropriate. Furthermore, since the single utterance is intended solely to convey identity with Brahman, there is not even a suspicion of it having multiple meanings.

Nor can it be argued that since oneness is already established, the suffix *cvī*—which denotes the becoming of what was not previously so—is inappropriate; for even though [oneness] exists, it is equivalent to being non-existent due to its being concealed, like a treasure placed in one's own house that remains unknown, and thus the use of the suffix *cvī* is justified. Furthermore, one should not say that this involves abandoning the locative case heard in the rule *pare 'vyaye* (Pāṇini 5.4.74) and the unwarranted assumption of an unmentioned instrumental case; for, in accordance with another scriptural authority, the locative case need not be followed here.

Nor is there a contradiction between the preceding and following statements—namely, "he attains the supreme equality" and "he attains the Puruṣa who is higher than the high"—for that [objection] has already been refuted. Likewise, the statement "there is no other seer than this" found in the context of the Inner Ruler (Antaryāmin), and the statement "there is nothing else than this as a seer" found in the context of the Imperishable (Akṣara), are both authorities for their identity.

It should not be argued that by the phrase "and there is no other" (*na cātaḥ anyaḥ*), having referred back to the subject at hand—the universal controller—it follows that there is a negation of another controller who would govern Him (a *svaniyāmaka-draṣṭṛ*), rather than a negation of the seer (*draṣṭṛ*) in general; for in expressions such as "in this village, this person alone is the universal controller and there is no other man," the word "other" (*anya*) is understood to refer to something else similar to the subject under discussion, and because in the passage "the rest is the same as the Śyena sacrifice" (*samānam itarac chyenena*), the word "other" (*itara*) is stated to refer to what is similar to what was previously specified. This [objection] must be addressed as follows: ...by this [text].

This is for the purpose of establishing the previously asserted "knowledge of all through the knowledge of one" by demonstrating the non-difference [of the Self] from the individual soul (jīva), which is perceived as distinct; furthermore, because the insentient category is negated by the statements "everything else is miserable" and "not this, not this," the intended meaning of the sentence is precisely the non-difference between the individual soul and Brahman. As for the illustrative example, since non-difference was not intended there, there is no contradiction in adopting the method you have described.

Nor is there any contradiction here in the Antaryāmin passage with the preceding statement—"He who is internal to the Self, whom the Self does not know, whose body is the Self, who controls the Self from within"—nor with the subsequent statement—"This is your Self, the inner controller, the immortal; other than this, everything is afflicted. It should not be argued that, by accepting another conscious being distinct from the Supreme Self, the latter merely asserts that [other] being's lack of independence due to its being subject to affliction; for the preceding statement is fully explained by the mere distinction based on limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).

By the subsequent statement, the connection of another conscious being with suffering is not enjoined; rather, since it teaches that everything other than the Inner Controller—who is the very nature of the individual soul—is "afflicted," perishable, or illusory, there is no room for suspicion of contradiction. For this very reason, the objection regarding a contradiction with the preceding statement in the passage concerning the Imperishable—namely, "O Gārgī, by the command of this Imperishable, the sun and the moon stand held apart"—is also refuted.

Furthermore, because difference is censured as the cause of fear in the statement, "From a second [entity] indeed fear arises," non-difference alone is what is to be understood from the Upaniṣads. Nor should it be argued that the meaning is simply, "Fear arises for this [person] from a similar opposing entity," since this merely restates a worldly fact—that in the world fear arises precisely from such [an opponent]—and because we hear in the preceding passage, "Therefore, being alone, he is afraid," and in the subsequent passage, "Therefore, being alone, he does not rejoice. For [the Lord says], "Since there is nothing other than Me, why should I be afraid? and it is from that very [source] that his [fearlessness] arises.

This is because of the Vedic scripture stating, "From fear [of Him] does [the wind] blow. Since, in general, the mere perception of a second entity is the cause of fear, there is no room for assuming any specific distinction [between them]. In the preceding statement, "He who is alone fears," it is said that fear arises from that [perception of a second] for one who lacks the vision of ultimate reality; thus it is stated that "he who is alone fears. In the subsequent statement, "Therefore, he who is alone does not find delight," it is stated that there is no delight for the solitary one, because delight—which is born from union with the desired object—is absent in one who is alone.

Furthermore, since the intermediate statement concerning those who know reality is useful by way of conveying its own meaning in accordance with the statements concerning those who do not know reality, it is impossible for it to have a meaning that contradicts that [intermediate statement]. Moreover, non-difference is established through the censure of difference in the passage: "If one perceives even a slight difference in this, then fear comes to him."

Nor should it be suspected that, because of the hearing of the word "in this" (*etasmin*), this is a negation of difference inherent within [the Self] rather than a negation of difference in general; for this is due to the natural force of the word *kāra* having the sense of "small," the natural force of the word *utpatti* having the sense of "arising," and because there is no mention of [the Self] as the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*). Thus, since it is impossible to assume a negation of a specific kind of difference when the text intends a negation of difference in general, such texts as "The one God is hidden in all beings" are also authorities here for non-duality (*aikya*).

Nor should it be argued that this scripture is devoted to the identity of the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), because—as in passages such as "from which indeed these beings (*bhūtāni*) are born"—the word *bhūta* refers to sentient beings. This is because the illustrative example is unestablished; for it is impossible for a sentient being to be "born" [in the primary sense], since, as in the scriptural prohibition against harming living beings (*bhūta-hiṃsā*), the word *bhūta* denotes only those things consisting of the vital breath and body presided over by a sentient being. For this very reason, there is also the traditional teaching (*smṛti*): "For the one and only Self of all beings resides within every single being.
Thus, as long as delusion persists, there may be a distinction between the individual soul and the Supreme.
Beyond that, there is no differentiation, because of the absence of any cause for differentiation.
When the ignorance that produces the sense of difference has gone to absolute destruction,
who will create the non-existent distinction between the Self and Brahman?

From such Smṛti passages as these, it is understood that difference is perceived as being rooted in ignorance (avidyā), and thus non-difference alone is established as the ultimate reality. Furthermore, in this context, the word "difference" (bheda) does not signify discord or enmity—as in the expression "breaking of friendship" (mitrabheda)—for if it did, it would entail the fault of metaphorical indication (lakṣaṇā). This is because mutual absence (anyonyābhāva) and the like constitute the primary meaning of the word, and it is improper to abandon the literal sense of what is heard in scripture. Smṛti passages such as "And know Me also as the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) in all fields, O Bhārata," also serve as authority here. Nor does this mean, "Know Me, the omniscient Knower of the Field, in all fields."

It should not be said that by stating "the great elements, ego, etc. and concluding with "this field, together with its modifications, has been briefly described," [the Lord] intends to teach that the entire field—consisting of both the sentient and the insentient—is the body of the Lord, as stated in such scriptural passages as "He whose body is the earth. For this would result in redundancy, since the Lord's connection with all fields as their universal controller has already been established. Rather, it is more appropriate that this passage aims to establish the non-difference between the individual soul (denoted by the term *kṣetrajña*) and the Lord, in His capacity as the presiding deity (*adhiṣṭhātṛ*) of each respective field.
Therefore, [it is said]: "The fields are the bodies, and the seeds are the good and evil [karmas]."
The one whose self is yoga knows what has been heard; therefore, he is called the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña).

They call the witness of both nature and its transformations, who is devoid of qualities, the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña); but they call the individual soul (jīva) the agent, enveloped by the qualities.

In such Smṛti passages as these, although the term *kṣetrajña* refers to the omniscient Inner Controller (*sarvāntaryāmin*) of all, its application here [to the individual soul] is impossible; furthermore, it is well-established in common usage as referring to the individual soul (*jīva*). Nor does the maxim *śāstrasthā vā* apply, because that maxim concerns cases where there is a conflict between two scriptural authorities regarding a single subject. In this manner, other statements as well should be applied to the doctrine of non-duality (*aikya*) according to their possibility. Therefore, scripture (*āgama*) is the means of valid knowledge for non-duality. Thus ends the exposition of the meaning of numerous Śruti and Smṛti texts such as "I am Brahman" (*ahaṃ brahmāsmi*) in the *Advaitasiddhi*. (29)

Thus, inference (*anumāna*) is also a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) in this regard: "The individual souls (*jīvas*) do not differ from the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) in reality, because they possess selfhood (*ātmatva*), like the Supreme Self. Now, one might object: "Selfhood is a universal (*jāti*) and thus the reason; however, since non-difference [in reality] entails the destruction of the universal, this constitutes a counter-argument (*pratikūlatarka*) that undermines the reason. This is not so, because even while there is non-difference in reality, the non-destruction of the universal is established by means of empirical difference (*vyāvahārika-bheda*). Furthermore, "being a knower" (*jñātṛtva*) is also a reason here. For that [selfhood] exists in the soul as the substrate (*upadheya*), since it is not unestablished (*asiddhi*) due to its occurrence in the state of being conditioned by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇopahita-vṛtti*).

In empirical usage (*vyavahāra*), the reason is the state of not depending on a cognition distinct from itself. For you as well, the individual soul (*jīva*)—which possesses eternal cognition non-different from itself—is the object of uncontradicted empirical usage. Furthermore, "uncontradictability" (*abādhyatva*) is also a reason here. Nor is there any deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of insentient objects (*jaḍa*), because the reason is absent there due to their being subject to contradiction; and since "real difference" (*tāttvikabheda*) is non-existent everywhere, there is no possibility of deviation.

Nor should it be argued that, in this same manner, the absence of empirical difference between the individual soul (jīva) and the supreme self (paramātman) should likewise be established; for in that case, the contradiction with direct perception (pratyakṣa) serves as a subverting factor, and because of the support of scripture (śruti), there is no room for the argument that [the two cases] are equivalent as fallacious appearances.

For this very reason, the objection regarding the similarity of fallacious arguments is rejected: namely, that in the inference for the oneness of individual souls—"The disputed individual souls do not differ from Caitra in reality, because they possess the nature of being souls, like Caitra"—and in the inference for the oneness of Brahman and the individual soul—"The disputed individual souls do not differ from Brahman in reality, because they are real entities, like Brahman"—one might likewise prove as the thesis that "they do not differ even conventionally. This charge of parity of fallacy is set aside.

Thus, the bodies under dispute are presided over by Caitra, because they are bodies, like those [bodies] that are commonly agreed upon. It should not be argued: "By this much, the unity of the individual soul (*jīva*) is not established, because even if they are presided over by Caitra, it is possible for them to be presided over by another; furthermore, if they are presided over by Caitra alone, there would be a deficiency in the probandum (*sādhyavaikalya*) in the example, since [the body] is presided over by the Inner Controller (*antaryāmin*). This is not a valid objection, because what is being proven is that they are presided over by a transmigrating soul (*saṃsārī*) who is Caitra alone. Alternatively, the probandum may be stated as: "they are the substrata of the experiences of Caitra alone."

Nor should it be argued that there is a contradiction—namely, that the state of being an enjoyer belongs to that which is qualified by the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), and that this [qualified entity] differs from body to body, whereas the one pure consciousness is not the enjoyer; for even though the state of being an enjoyer resides in the qualified entity, its residence in the substantive (viśeṣya) is not thereby lost.

Nor is there a similarity of fallacy in the claim that diverse bodies are joined with a single mind, because such an arrangement is in every way untenable even if the mind were one, and because there is a distinction based on whether or not it accords with scripture, as well as because that [single mind] is accepted in the *dṛṣṭisṛṣṭi* (creation-as-perception) view. Furthermore: The Self is not manifold by virtue of being a subordinate genus of substance, because it is all-pervasive (*vibhu*), like space.

Nor should it be argued: (1) that because space differs in every kalpa, there is a deficiency in the probandum (*sādhyavaikalya*); (2) that because [the self] is limited, there is a deficiency in the probans (*sādhanavaikalya*); and (3) that even if "selfhood" (*ātmatva*) is not a genus like "atomicity" (*paramāṇutva*), the distinction between selves is established, which results in proving something other than what was intended (*arthāntara*). This is because the intended meaning is as follows: "The locus of selfhood is not manifold at the same time as a single lower genus of substance (*dravyatvāparajāti*), because it is conjoined with all corporeal things existing at the same time, like space. Furthermore, by the power of the qualification of the subject (*pakṣaviśeṣaṇa*), there is no proving of something other than the intended point.

The disputed difference is false, because it is either imagined within a single vision or because it is a difference, or because it is an object of perception—just like the difference in the appearance of the moon; or it is imagined within a single vision, because it is a difference or because it is an object of perception—just like the difference in the appearance of the moon, or like the differences imagined by the proponents of momentarism (*kṣaṇikavādin*) within a single vision. Falsity has already been established previously. Nor is there a lack of proof for "difference" as being common to what is imagined, since the very non-imagined nature of difference remains unproven.

For this very reason, the following objections are refuted: (1) that because the difference of the moon from a second, imagined moon is real, the illustrative example lacks the property to be proven (*sādhyavaikalya*); and (2) that there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of liberation being different from transmigratory existence or Brahman being different from the unreal. Nor can it be easily established that "non-difference is false because it is a non-difference, like the non-difference between the body and the self," and so forth, since that would entail the consequence of nihilism (*śūnyavāda*), as has already been stated. Likewise: "The cognition of difference under dispute is false, because it is a cognition of difference, like the cognition of the [second] moon."

Nor is there any deviation (vyabhicāra) in cases such as the perception of Brahman, falsehood, or difference, for these too are equivalent to the subject of the thesis (pakṣasama). Any semblance of parity [with the reason] is refuted precisely by the impossibility of its being perceived as real. For this very reason: "The subject of dispute is devoid of any internal real division, because it possesses magnitude;
whatever is thus is so, just like space; and since this [subject] is thus, it is therefore so."

In this regard, there is no deficiency in the probandum (*sādhyavaikalya*) because of the sky's possession of parts, since by the term "within itself" (*svāntaḥ*), something distinct from its own parts is expressed. Likewise, consciousness is devoid of natural internal differentiation, because its difference is not perceived apart from limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), like the sky. Nor is there a deficiency in the probandum, for the example is stated according to the perspective of the Naiyāyikas.

Nor should it be argued that there is a deviation (vyabhicāra) in the case of desire and so forth, because their difference is manifested through the distinction of limiting adjuncts (upādhi) such as pots and cloths; for since desire and the rest are exclusively modifications of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), the property to be proven (sādhya) exists there as well. The subject under dispute (vimata)—a difference whose counter-correlativity (pratiyogitā) is not delimited by a non-pervasive (avyāpyavṛtti) attribute—is the counter-correlative of an absolute absence (atyantābhāva) co-located with itself, because it is a difference, like the difference in the case of two conjoined objects.

The disputed difference (bheda) is the counter-correlative of an absolute non-existence that is purely positive (kevalānvayin), because it is a category of existence (padārthatvāt), like an eternal substance (nityadravyavat). Regarding its being the counter-correlative of an absolute non-existence in its own nature (svarūpeṇa), there is no "falsity" (tucchatva); regarding its being the counter-correlative of an absolute non-existence in the form of ultimate reality (pāramārthikatvākāreṇa), there is no "deviation from the truth" (arthāntara), since its nature as such is established through its identity with Brahman, as was stated previously.

The inference—"Mutual absence-ness (anyonyābhāvatva) resides in that which is the counter-positive of an absolute absence co-located with itself, because, while residing in an absence existing at all three times, it is directly pervaded by the property of being an absence (abhāvatva), like absolute absence-ness"—is intended to establish the example consisting of the difference whose counter-positive is conjoined, as previously mentioned. Nor is there the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) regarding the superimposed difference from mother-of-pearl in the case of mother-of-pearl; for you, who maintain the theory of "misapprehension of the non-existent" (*asad-anyathākhyāti*), do not accept that [superimposed difference], and thus it remains the very thing to be proven (*sādhya*).

Nor is there an inconsistency with falsity (*mithyātva*) on account of existing in all three periods of time, because the relation between *māyā* and consciousness, being temporal in nature, persists through all time and thus does not contradict that [falsity]. Nor is there the fallacy of proving something else (*arthāntara*)—as in the case of conjunction and the like—by virtue of being the counter-positive of an absolute absence (*atyantābhāva*) co-located with itself due to non-pervasive occurrence (*avyāpyavṛttitva*), since such non-pervasive occurrence is impossible here by the power of the qualification of the subject (*pakṣaviśeṣaṇa*). Furthermore, the lack of systematicity regarding recollection and so forth has already been refuted previously.

The fallacies of irrelevance (*aprayojakatva*), similarity (*sāmya*), counter-arguments (*satpratipakṣa*), adventitious conditions (*upādhi*), and so forth, are to be refuted as in the previously mentioned inference for the falsity of the phenomenal world (*prapañca-mithyātva*). Likewise, one should also consider such arguments as: "Selfhood (*ātmatva*) is pervaded by oneness (*ekatva*), because it subsists only in the Self, like the nature of Caitra. Thus ends the inference for the non-difference of the individual soul and Brahman in the *Advaitasiddhi*.

The non-difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman is established not only by scriptural texts such as "All beings are one foot of Him" (*Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad* 3.15) and by Smṛti texts such as "In the world of living beings, that which exists as the individual soul is indeed a portion of Myself, eternal," but also because of the designation of the soul as a "portion" (*aṃśa*). Although the soul’s status as a portion of Brahman cannot consist in being something produced (*ārambhakatva*), since Brahman is beginningless; nor can it consist in being a fragment (*khaṇḍatva*), since Brahman is indivisible; nor can it consist in being a member of a composite whole (*samudāyitva*), because a whole is non-different from its members, which would lead to the undesirable conclusion that even in the state of worldly experience there is no pure Brahman distinct from the transmigrating soul.

Nor can it be a substance that is both different and non-different, as that is not admitted. Nor can it be a part (pradeśa) of the whole with respect to the cloth, as in the case of a fragmentary cloth; for this is impossible with respect to Brahman, which is without parts, except through conceptual construction (kalpanā). Nevertheless, in the view that the individual soul (jīva) is a limitation (avacchedapakṣa), its status as a part—in the form of a conceptually constructed part—is possible, just as the space within a jar is a part of the great space (mahākāśa). How a part can be attributed through limiting adjuncts (aupādhika) even to that which is inherently partless has been explained previously.

But it is not the case that being a part consists in being similar while being inferior to it, for then even a fine cloth would have to be considered a part of a coarse cloth. Furthermore, the primary use of the word "part" (aṃśa) with respect to a single portion of a real entity—even when the entity itself is inherently partless—is more appropriate than postulating its use in a different sense based on a merely imagined portion.

In the sūtra, "A portion [of Brahman], because of the designation of multiplicity, and also because otherwise the state of being a fisherman, a kitava, and so forth is taught as one," the designation of difference—such as "He is to be sought, He is to be known; having known Him thus, one becomes a sage, He who dwells within the self"—and the designation of non-difference—as in the Atharvaṇa mantra, "Brahman is the fishermen, Brahman is the slaves, Brahman these gamblers are"—have both been cited; therefore, it is appropriate to accept the stated meaning.

Furthermore, if one were to accept a different meaning containing an absolute distinction [between the individual soul and Brahman], it would result in a contradiction with this very Sūtra; moreover, to assume this [distinction] everywhere merely because of its application in some other instance would lead to many logical inconsistencies. For this very reason, [it is argued]: "Is the individual soul (jīva) understood by the scripture 'A foot of Him' (pādo'sya) as being a portion of pure consciousness, or a portion of the Lord (Īśvara)? It cannot be the first, because in the scriptural passage 'A foot of Him are all beings' (pādo'sya viśvā bhūtāni), the word 'this' (idaṃ) refers to the Lord who is the subject characterized by having a thousand heads and so forth; and in the Smṛti [Gītā 15.7], 'A portion of Me alone,' the word 'Me' (asmad-śabda) is used for the Lord himself."

Not the latter [alternative], because in your view even Īśvara is conditioned (*upahita*); thus, just as the space within a water-jar cannot be a part of the space within a pot, it is impossible for the *jīva* to be a part of Īśvara. Nor can it be argued that the very consciousness delimited by the adjunct of Īśvara (like the space of a house) is again delimited by the adjunct of the *jīva* (as when that same space is further delimited by a jar); for if that were the case, one who is liberated would not possess the nature of pure Brahman. Therefore, in your view as well, there is no primary sense of being a "part," nor can it be said to be merely adventitious (*aupādhika*). Consequently, [the analogy of the sparks does not hold].

The claim that only the manner I have described is to be accepted has been refuted; for if another meaning were adopted, contradiction would result as already stated, and because the pronouns occurring in the Śruti and Smṛti refer to the Consciousness characterized by having a thousand heads and so forth, there is no room for the aforementioned objections.
