Therefore, although the non-difference between the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman is established by such scriptural passages as, "Thou art the woman, thou art the man; thou art the youth and even the maiden; thou, as an old man, totterest along with a staff; having been born, thou becomest facing in all directions; the Wise One, having fashioned all forms and created names, abides calling them forth," yet it is proven that non-difference is understood through the force of this [scripture] as well, because any imaginary notion of being a part (aṃśatva)—intended to justify designations of difference such as the "thinker" and the "object thought"—is contradicted by both Śruti and Smṛti.
Thus, in the Advaitasiddhi, the establishment of oneness even as parts is concluded. 31.

Likewise, the non-difference between the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman should be understood from their being related as an original object and its reflection, like a face and its reflection. Now, one might object: "In the illustrative example, non-difference is not admitted; for just as people standing nearby perceive Caitra and his shadow to be distinct, so too they perceive Caitra and his reflection to be distinct, and even Caitra himself perceives his own hand and its reflection to be distinct. To this we say: no.

Even though there is an initial perception of difference, the identity of the original object (*bimba*) and its reflection (*pratibimba*) is established through reasoned perception; thus, their fitness as an illustration is justified. Just as when one who is confused by a lack of knowledge regarding defining characteristics perceives Caitra standing outside as possessing certain specific features, and consequently, when he is seen inside the house, the cognition arises that "this is indeed Caitra" because he appears in that same way—so too, having determined that the face situated on the neck possesses certain specific features and that the face in the mirror possesses those very same features, one recognizes it as being exactly the same.

The common perception shared by both oneself and others—that "this is the face" and "this is the hand"—is also established by experience. Nor should it be argued that recognition is unestablished because, in the case of a somewhat translucent copper vessel or similar object, although the mere reflection of the face is perceived, the specific configuration (saṃsthāna) is not; for even if it were not perceived everywhere, the example is established by the fact that recognition does occur in the case of a clear mirror and the like.

If it is objected: "But since one lacks the initial cognition (*abhijñā*) of one's own eyeball and so forth, how can there even be a recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) of them?"—we say no. This is because the rays of the eye, struck by a mirror, come into contact with the object at its front edge; thus, the initial cognition of one's own eyeball and so forth is possible precisely at the immediately preceding moment. As for the claim that "since there is an absence of recognition in the case of a 'counter-sun' situated beside the sun, there must likewise be an absence of recognition here [in the case of the eyeball]," that is not correct. For in that case, as here, the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) is not perceived, and therefore its status as being caused by an adjunct cannot be determined.

Likewise, the knowledge that [the reflection] is based on a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) and the knowledge that it characterizes [the original object] constitute the causal complex for the direct realization of non-difference. When this complex is present, the absence of the experience "my face is attached to the mirror" is indeed contrary to actual experience. As for the claim that there is a contradiction with contrary experience—namely, that Caitra’s reflection is seen, but Caitra himself is not; rather, he is inferred by it—that is not so. For even when non-difference is known in reality, there is no contradiction in the cognition that "that which is delimited by a limiting adjunct is seen, while that which is undelimited is inferred," just as the Ganges of the rainy season is inferred from the Ganges of autumn.

Nor should it be argued that when one's own face is seen in a mirror as facing backward and so forth, the cognition of it as "my face" would not arise; nor that children would not have the delusion of another child in their own reflection. This is because both [the failure to recognize it as a reflection and the lack of delusion] are based on the non-recognition of its having its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇaka*). For this very reason, there occasionally arise both the cognition and the verbal designation "this is my face" even with respect to the reflected face.

Nor is this conventional usage figurative—like the usage of the term "one's own footprint" on a path preceded by a cognition of difference—because at the time of recognizing the object as having its own specific characteristic, the cognition of difference is as good as non-existent.

[Objection: "Surely there would be no dispute regarding the direct perception of difference; otherwise, whose error would even you declare it to be? Furthermore, one who perceives directly both the difference and the differentiator is never seen to perceive non-difference. [Reply: It is accepted that, due to the power of an adventitious condition (*upādhi*), one who perceives non-difference perceives difference—just as one perceives yellowness upon perceiving the quality of being a conch-shell pervaded by whiteness—because such experience is impossible to deny.

Nor does it follow that error would be impossible because the ignorance of identity, which is the material cause, is removed by the knowledge of identity; for the absence of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) also acts as a cooperative factor in that removal.

Nor should it be argued that, just as when that knowledge exists, the non-experience of "I do not know that" implies that ignorance—like its own prior absence—is a sublater independent of anything else; for even when the portion of ignorance that serves as the cause for the linguistic usage "I do not know" is removed, the error is still experienced. Consequently, in the case of *jīvanmukti*, just as with *prārabdha-karma*, the substrate itself acts as an obstacle, making the requirement for its removal necessary.

By this, the following objections are refuted: (1) that if this delusion of difference has *mūlāvidyā* as its material cause (*upādāna*), it would follow that it is merely empirical (*vyāvahārika*); (2) that if it does not have ignorance as its material cause, it would contradict established doctrine (*apasiddhānta*); and (3) that the difference between the original object (*bimba*) and its reflection (*pratibimba*) would consequently be real. This is because the matter is established by the reasoning already stated, and there is no inconsistency even if it is empirical.

When there is identity between the two, inference (*anumāna*) is also a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Here, although absolute dissimilarity is fallacious (*vyabhicārin*) in the case of the left and right hands and so forth, nevertheless, the reflection is non-different from the original object (*bimba*), because it possesses those uncommon properties belonging to that [object], because it is not the locus of contradictory properties [belonging to that object], and because it is not produced by what does not produce the original object. Nor is the second reason unestablished (*asiddha*), since contradictory properties such as facing the opposite direction are caused by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*); thus, the state of not being the locus of natural contradictory properties exists.

Nor is there a failure to establish a third cause for the reflection produced immediately after the original object (*bimba*), because for one who maintains their identity, "being produced immediately after the original object" is itself unestablished. If it is argued: "Surely, in accordance with the requirement for a distinct effect—as in the case of halos, rainbows, shadows, and mock suns—a separate cause must be postulated here as well; for a reflection is indeed a specific kind of shadow. Indeed, even when the sound has ceased due to the absence of the established causes such as striking a drum, the echo that is still heard is not a different sound," we say: no.

Since a reflection can occur even in light—which is opposed to shadow—it cannot be established as a specific type of shadow; furthermore, because an echo occurs at a different time, its distinction is irrelevant to the present case, and it is impossible to first state a difference in the cause when that difference must be inferred only after the distinctness of the effect has been established, since the effect exists solely through its already-established causal status. Moreover, perception is neutral regarding difference and non-difference, and by reason, non-difference alone possesses greater force. For this very reason it has been said:

In the Vivaraṇa: "In a mirror and the like, there is no other manifestation of the face, because it lacks the causes for its production, just like a horn on a rabbit's head. Thus, since the cognition of non-difference has been established, its superior strength [over the cognition of difference] is proven. The objection that "that very [manifestation] does not exist because of the absence of a cause for another manifestation" was already refuted. Nor can it be argued that, as in the case of a shadow, a cognition of difference is justified by postulating a difference in the cause; nor can it be said that, since it is not included among the well-known substances, it must be a distinct substance like darkness. For such an argument would result in the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*).

The assumption of both distinctness and the existence of separate substances and causes is based on their having a logical justification, and that [justification] resides in that very [distinction]. For this very reason, the conventional usage found in the Smṛti—“it is neither eclipsed nor situated in water”—is primary; it is not secondary (gauṇa), as in the cases of “a painted lion,” “a wooden woman,” or “a leather deer.

Nor should it be argued that even in your own view, the term “situated in water” (vāristha) is not primary, because there is no other sun in the water and it is impossible for the sun situated in the sky to be situated in water; for what is negated is the entire class of suns situated in water as presented by the notion of being “situated in water.”

If it is argued: "But surely, since the sun itself is present by virtue of being situated in the water, the non-difference between the two is neither established by perception nor is it logical; for their difference is established by such factors as having smaller or larger dimensions, being mobile or not, being conjoined with or not conjoined to limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), being perceptible or imperceptible to the sense of touch and so forth, facing toward or away from oneself, and, in the case of musk and its reflection, having fragrance or lack thereof," we say no. For the difference must be proven as belonging to the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) itself, based on its smaller dimension, its fragrance, and so on.

And thus, because the state of being located in an adjunct (*upādhi*) is imagined (*kalpita*) in the reflected object (*bimba*), the reason (*hetu*) and the subject (*pakṣa*) are unestablished (*asiddha*); furthermore, there is no dispute regarding the establishment of a probandum (*sādhya*) of the same ontological status as the imagined reason and so forth by means of such an imagined reason. Nor is it the case that:
"Just as this shadow [appears] in a person, so is this [world] spread out in Him;
just as a shadow is seen to resemble a person and to be dependent upon the person..."

Thus, it should not be said that there is difference [between them] based on the Śruti passage, "In this very way, all [beings], beginning with Brahmā, have the Supreme Self as their essence," because similarity is established by mere imagined difference; for there is no intended meaning (tātparya) of the Śruti regarding [difference's] ultimate reality, and because it contradicts numerous Śruti passages that establish non-duality (aikya).

If it is objected: "Since that which possesses its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is superimposed as being situated in the mirror, there should likewise be a cognition of it as being situated in the mirror even when it possesses its odor and so forth, just as when it possesses its color and so forth," we say no. For although it is superimposed as possessing that specific characteristic, since we do not admit that it is superimposed as possessing every one of its specific characteristics, it is impossible to bring about the cognition of its odor and so forth.

If it is asked: "In that case, since there is no face in the mirror, how can there be a distinction between the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman—such as being subject to transmigratory existence (saṃsāritva) or not being subject to it—given that an adjunct (upādhi) favors its own reflection, just as the brightness or darkness belongs respectively to the face and its reflection? The answer is: No. For while the face itself is not in the mirror, the reflection is qualified by the superimposed state of being situated in the mirror; thus, properties such as turbidity and so forth are possible in that reflection.

Nor should it be argued that since the state of residing in a limiting adjunct (*upādhisthatva*) is itself superimposed (*āropya*), how can it serve as the delimiting condition (*avacchedaka*) for the locus of impurity? For [in our view], the locus of the superimposition is precisely that which is qualified by the attributes perceived prior to the superimposition; it does not require that those attributes be real. Thus, there is no room for the defects inherent in the opponent's system.

Nor should it be argued that the reflection is not the face itself because it is experienced as residing in the mirror rather than in the face; for just as that which is conditioned by ignorance (avidyopahita) can have ignorance as its locus, so too that which is conditioned by the mirror can reside in the mirror. By this, the objection that liberation—which resides in the pure [Self]—cannot be co-located with transmigratory existence (saṃsāra), which resides in the qualified [Self] like impurity, is refuted.

Saṃsāra, for its part, has a conditioned mode of existence; thus, by taking up the conditioned portion (upadheyāṃśa), the possibility of grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) arises. Accordingly, just as the state of being the locus of the monkey’s conjunction with the tree is delimited by the tip [of the tree], so too is the impurity [of the face] delimited by its connection with the mirror. This much is the distinction: the monkey’s conjunction with the tree is natural (sāhajika), whereas the impurity in the face is adventitious (aupādhika).

Thus, the cognition of dirtiness occurs only with respect to the face as delimited by the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) [the mirror]. By this, the following objections are refuted: (1) if the dirtiness of the mirror were to reside in the face, it would follow that transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) would also reside in the pure [Self]; (2) there would be the consequence of the perception "the face is dirty" arising—just as one says "the tree is joined"—rather than "the reflection is dirty"; and (3) there would be a contradiction with the actual experience that "the face is not dirty, but the reflection is."

Now, one might object: since the reflection of musk and the like does not conform to the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the original object, how can there be identity with the prototype? Nor can their identity be established merely by having that same form; for if it were so, then shadows, imprints, statues, and the like would also possess that identity, since even here there exists a differentiator such as facing the opposite direction and so forth.

If it is argued that the cognition of facing westward is not an error, because one never experiences a reflection as being oriented toward the original object (*bimba*), we say no. For in the case of reflections in mirrors and the like, since their identity with the original object is established through the persistence of its specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), that [cognition] is merely imagined under the limitation of being a "reflection. Furthermore, there is no similarity [between a reflection and a shadow], because the possession of specific characteristics is never observed in shadows and the like. Nor is facing westward and so forth a differentiator [of the reflection from the original], because it is produced by an adventitious condition (*upādhi*), just like [the appearance of] dirtiness.

For this very reason, the cognition of that [reflection] is erroneous, just like the perception of redness in a hibiscus flower (*japākusuma*). The eye, struck by a mirror, turns back toward itself; and because it has the capacity to grasp [objects] facing itself, it is logically possible for it to grasp even a face or other objects that are facing in the opposite direction. As it has been said:
"The vision, struck by the mirror, turns back and, pervading its own face, displays the face in its inverted state by means of its orientation toward [the self]."

Nor is it the case that, upon turning back, there would be an impossibility of perceiving two faces for a person standing to the side when one perceives only one’s own face; for the restriction that "only one's own face" is perceived is unproven, since anything merely in proximity to the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) is perceived in that manner. Nor should it be argued that, because the mirror and such are exhausted by their mere function as deflectors, there would not be the perception of multiple faces even when there are multiple mirrors—as in the case of a single mirror—since the cases are dissimilar: through the multiplicity of deflectors, the eye acquires multiple focal points, thereby perceiving each individual face as delimited by its respective deflector.

Nor should it be asked how it is possible for multiple faces of contradictory forms to be perceived in a jewel, a mirror, a sword, and so forth; for you should understand that this is due to the predominance of limiting adjuncts (upādhis) established through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka). Nor should it be said that the process of the eye’s rotation is impossible in the case of the individual soul (jīva), which is a reflection of Brahman; for it has been demonstrated that this process applies exclusively to visual reflections.

Nor does it follow that water with sparse parts would fail to strike the eye, resulting in the impossibility of perceiving stones and other objects within the water; for since there is no impact [of the light] across all parts [of the water], it is possible for the eye to enter into its interior. Nor should it be argued that, if this were so, one would perceive the sun and other objects located at a great distance above even when standing behind them—since they too would be perceived despite being obstructed—because there is a distinction due to the eye’s movement back and forth.

For one who says that the eye reaches the sun situated at a great distance does not thereby imply that the eye travels by piercing through a back wall or similar obstacles. Nor should it be argued that the eye, even when struck by a stone, should turn back and grasp its own face; for then it would follow that a reflection could likewise arise there [on the stone], since our position—that the failure to do so is due to lack of transparency—is equal to yours. You maintain that a reflection arises only on what is transparent, while we maintain that the eye turns back precisely from such a surface.

Nor does it follow that by seeing a reflection one would also experience the pleasure, merit, and so forth produced by seeing the original object; for where the production [of an effect] arises solely from the sight of that [reflection] and not from anything else, there we accept the consequence as desired. And where the production is specifically qualified by being a cognition free from limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), there the reason for such a consequence is absent. Furthermore, it does not follow that a solar reflection (*sūryaka*) would also be as difficult to see as the sun itself; because at the time of perceiving the solar reflection, the direct confrontation with the sun's radiance—which is the cause of its difficulty to behold—is absent in the lens (*golaka*).

Nor does it follow that a specific configuration of a face would appear in a clear mirror or in slightly clear copper and the like; for in those cases, the very impurity and so forth—which act as the cause for the absence of extreme clarity inherent in the limiting adjunct (upādhi)—is precisely what constitutes the obstruction. Otherwise, even for you [the proponent of reflection], the difficulty of answering why a reflection possessing such a specific configuration does not arise there would be unavoidable.

[Objection: But surely, if [the Lord] exists as a reflection, there is no contradiction with your own statement that "interiority" (*antaryāmitva*) is possible because reflection is possible even when doubling [the size] through limitation (*avaccheda*) is impossible; furthermore, it would be improper to say that "the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) takes the side of the reflection. [Response: This is not so, because there is no contradiction with our own statement since the distinction imagined by the adjunct is established through the difference between being limited by all adjuncts and being limited by only one part of an adjunct.

For this very reason, in the case of a mirror, it is only denied that "there is no face [in the mirror]" due to its being conjoined with the adjunct; it is not denied in its own nature (as "this is not the face") in the same way that "this is not silver" is denied.

If it is argued that there is no contradiction even in the mirror’s location being in the reflected face—since there is no experience here of "there is no shadow of the face," but rather an experience such as "for all this time there was a sun-reflection (*pratisūrya*) here," or a traditional memory (*smṛti*) such as "like a reflection in a mirror"—and thus the shadow of the cloud is not sublated merely because one says "there is no cloud on the ground"—we say: no, for since the face and the reflected face are established as one through their having a single specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), it is the face itself [that is perceived].

Because it is possible to deny the existence of the face by denying its presence [in the mirror], whereas this is not the case for cloud-shadows, reflected suns, and the like; therefore, the denial of clouds and so forth does not entail the denial of shadows and the like. Furthermore, the traditional Smṛti text is intended as an illustration, taking into account objects that appear to exist conventionally. Nor should it be argued that such a view would result in the abolition of inferring the original object (bimba) from its reflection (pratibimba), on the grounds that the probandum would be indistinguishable [from the reflection]; for a distinction is established through the difference imagined by limiting adjuncts (upādhi).

By this, the following [objections] are refuted: (1) that the injunction "one should not look at the rising sun" would entail a prohibition against seeing even the reflection of the rising sun; (2) that by the prohibition against seeing the sun situated in water, there would also be a prohibition against seeing the sun situated in the sky; and (3) that by merely seeing the reflection, one would have fulfilled the scriptural purpose of "having seen [the sun], one should bathe. This is because the scriptural arrangement is established precisely through imagined difference (*kalpitabheda*). Furthermore, it is not the case that a non-udumbara tree, when known as being made of udumbara wood, becomes an udumbara sacrificial post (*yūpa*).

It should not be argued that this leads to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of establishing the purpose of the scripture—that the Self is to be heard through the body, hearing, and so forth, known as the Self—because when a valid means of knowledge (*pramā*) is possible, it is improper to establish that [purpose] through error (*bhrama*). [Objection: But for the beginningless individual soul (*jīva*), being a reflection dependent on limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) is not the case; rather, it is similarity while being dependent on them. And since that [similarity] is pervaded by difference (*bheda*), the reason (*hetu*) is contradictory (*viruddha*).

If it is argued that the author of the Sūtras has indeed stated, "And for this very reason, the analogy [is given] as with the sun's reflection and so forth," we say no. For dependence on a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) means existing only when the adjunct exists; and this is not incompatible with beginninglessness, since such dependence is possible even for the beginningless individual soul (*jīva*). Therefore, the objection regarding contradiction—based on taking the term "reflection" (*pratibimba*) to mean either difference or similarity—is improper as a reason. Thus, it is established:
since the identity of the reflection with the original object (*bimba*) is settled, the identity of the entire class of individual souls with Brahman is proven, because they are its reflections.
Thus ends the establishment of oneness by means of the analogy of the original object and its reflection in the Advaitasiddhi. || 32 ||

If it is objected: "How can there be non-difference of the individual soul (*jīva*) from the all-pervading Lord (*īśvara*) if the soul is atomic (*aṇu*)?", we say no. For the soul is not atomic, as established by such scriptural texts as "He is eternal, all-pervading" and "This great, unborn Self," as well as by the following inferences: [1] because it is the substratum of perceptible qualities and because it is itself perceptible, like a jar; and [2] because it possesses the nature of self (*ātmatva*) and is not a material element (*abhūtatva*), like the Lord. Furthermore, in the case of the opposite view (that the soul is atomic), there would be the subverting consequence that pleasure, knowledge, and so forth—which pervade the body—would not be perceived. Nor does the following passage contradict this: "This is the Self today which these two bind—the good and the evil."

If the tip of a hair is divided into a hundred parts, and each of those parts is further divided into a hundred, the individual soul (jīva) should be known as one such part; yet it is capable of infinity.

Thus, it cannot be said on the basis of this scriptural statement that the individual soul (*jīva*) is atomic, because such a claim contradicts numerous scriptures establishing its all-pervasiveness; furthermore, since the perception of its qualities pervading the body cannot be otherwise explained, the statement must be intended to mean that the soul is difficult to comprehend. By this, the argument—that the soul is not all-pervasive because it possesses departure, movement, and action, like the body of a bird, and that the sublation resulting from the absence of these reasons in the contrary case (the all-pervasive) is the refutation—is also rejected, as the reasons themselves are unestablished (*asiddha*).

Nor should it be argued that the reason [for the soul’s existence] is established by such Śruti passages as, "Having departed from this body, he goes to that world; from that world, he returns to this world," and by such Smṛti passages as, "The yogin, having reached the light of the moon there, returns. For the Śruti teaches that departures and so forth—which actually belong to the intellect—are attributed to the soul as conditioned by that intellect.

Nor should it be argued that because the Śruti states—“Having experienced [the fruits] on the back of the firmament (nākasya pṛṣṭhe) through their good deeds, they enter this world or one even lower; having experienced the unpleasant, they return”—that the co-location (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the experience of pleasure, pain, and so forth with the *gati* (state of transition) is mentioned, how then could that *gati* reside in the intellect? For even the experience of pleasure, pain, and so forth by the Self is conditioned by the intellect (*buddhyupādhikatva*); thus, the co-location mentioned in the context of *gati* does not prove that it is inherent (*svābhāvikatva*).

Now, one might object: "In such scriptural passages as *'He leads them to Brahman'* and in such Smṛti passages as *'Departing from there, the people who know Brahman go to Brahman'*, movement (*gati*) is stated to be co-referential with liberation; how then can its non-establishment [as a means] be maintained? If this is raised, we say no. Movement occurs only for that which is non-pervasive (*avyāpaka*) toward that which is likewise non-pervasive. Since Brahman is all-pervasive (*vyāpaka*), movement toward It is impossible. Therefore, the word "movement" here signifies the absence of distinction created by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*); consequently, these passages do not establish a co-referential relationship between movement and liberation.

Now, it might be argued: "The non-establishment [of the self's departure] is not the case, because of the scriptural statement that 'this very self departs with the light,' which establishes the self as the locus [of departure]; otherwise, even liberation and so forth would belong to the intellect alone; nor is it possible for the scripture to have as its subject the departure and so forth of the self as conditioned by the intellect, since there is the illustration of a cart as the basis for natural motion: 'Just as a well-oiled cart goes along making a sound, even so this body, mounted by the conscious self (prājña), goes along making a sound. If this is said, we reply: No, because the word "this" (*eṣa*) refers precisely to the self as qualified by the intellect.

Because it is not stated that [the soul] reaches its state of being established in the pure Self through [the cessation of] mental grasping (*parāmarśa*); because there is a disparity, since such establishment in the Self is impossible upon the cessation of the intellect (*buddhi*) in the case of liberation; because total similarity is irrelevant for the purpose of a supporting example (*dṛṣṭānta*); and because, by virtue of that [example], the conclusion that [the state] extends to being inherent (*svābhāvikatva*) remains unproven.

Nor should it be argued that, since the scripture stating "as he departs, the vital breath (prāṇa) departs after him" and so forth describes the departure of the individual soul (jīva) prior to the movement of what is called the vital breath—which is actually the intellect (buddhi)—how can the soul's departure be otherwise established by the movement of the intellect? For even though the part characterized as the vital breath, which possesses the power of action, departs later, it is possible for the soul to depart first by means of its other constituent parts.

By this, the following objection is refuted: "Since scripture states that even when the mind departs, 'the Self remains as if closed-eyed, eating and drinking,' there is no departure of the Self; how then can the Self possess motion solely through the motion of [the mind]? For there is no contradiction in the conditioned self possessing motion based on its adjuncts, while the unconditioned self—unassociated with the intellect—lacks such motion.

Nor can it be argued that liberation from name and form is merely conditional (aupādhikī), because the scripture—such as "The knower, liberated from name and form, attains the divine Person who is higher than the high"—speaks of a journey even after such liberation. For, since the Supreme Person is omnipresent, movement toward Him is impossible; thus, the expression "attains" (*upaiti*) must, as before, have a different meaning.
For this very reason, scriptural passages such as "Having reached the highest light, he appears in his own true form; he moves about there, the highest one," do not signify actual motion.

Now, an objection: does motion and so forth belonging to the intellect produce motion and so forth in the Self as delimited by that [intellect], or is it merely superimposed upon the intellect, or is it figuratively attributed to it? Not the first, because we do not observe a separate motion in the ether delimited by a jar due to the motion of the jar; otherwise, wherever there is motion of the jar or the intellect, there would be a perforation of the ether or the Self, and there would be a doubling of its presence in different locations.

Nor should it be argued that the aforementioned defect does not apply to the theory of reflection; for even if that defect is absent under the view that the reflection is a distinct entity, in your own system it is held that the visual ray, struck by the mirror, turns back and perceives one's own face. Thus, since the visual ray does not reach the original object (bimba) due to its engagement with the limiting adjunct (upādhi), it would likewise be impossible for it to reach the reflection.

It is not the case that the last two [options] are correct; for if one were to accept that the attainment of the world, which is the locus of experience, belongs not to this limited region of the agent (*kartṛ*), but rather to another region limited by the moving intellect (*buddhi*), it would entail the fallacy of the loss of what was done (*kṛtahāni*) and so forth, because the limited agent and the limited enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*) would be distinct. Alternatively, if they were non-distinct, there would be an absence of agency and so forth in the unlimited [Self]. If this is argued, we say no: the application of the term "movement" to the conditioned (*upahita*) [Self] based on the movement of the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) is merely figurative (*aupacārika*).

Nor does this entail the fallacy of the loss of what has been done (*kṛtahāni*) and so forth, because an action performed by the self as delimited by a particular cognition produces its fruit for that very same self as delimited by that cognition. For there is no spatial part (*pradeśa*) in the partless self. As for the claim that there is a difference between the agent and the enjoyer as delimited [by cognitions], that is not correct; for when the self to be delimited and the delimiting cognition are one, it is impossible to speak of a difference within that which is delimited.

Nor is there the inference that "selfhood does not reside in atoms because it is a genus directly pervaded by substanceness, like earthness," for [the property of] "not residing in the pervader" (vyāpakāvṛttitva) serves as a limiting condition (upādhi), and because it would follow that [qualities such as] touch and so forth could likewise be established [as not residing in atoms].

The soul (*jīva*) is not all-pervasive, because—while being other than the elements—it is not the substratum of the non-inherent cause of priority (*paratva*), because it is not omniscient, because it is the substratum of non-eternal specific qualities other than sound, and because it is the substratum of mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), like a mat; here, "non-selfhood" (*anātmatva*) is the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), and there is also the fallacy of unestablished middle (*asiddhi*) since non-eternal specific qualities, mental impressions, and so forth, reside in the adjunct. Likewise, it is easy to establish [the same for] largeness (*mahattva*).

The argument that "the soul (jīva) is atomic because it is the substratum of a conjunction that is the non-inherent cause of knowledge, like the mind" is untenable; for, firstly, the mind cannot serve as a valid example due to its being of intermediate dimension (madhyama-parimāṇavat), and secondly, because insentience (jaḍatva) constitutes a limiting condition (upādhi). Furthermore, in every case here, the perception of pervasive pleasure, knowledge, and so forth, serves as a counter-argument (pratikūla-tarka); moreover, since it is impossible for a single atom to be delimited by two spatially separated locations at once, there would be a contradiction with such simultaneous experiences as "pleasure in my foot" and "pain in my head."

Nor does there arise a contradiction with the inference of all-pervading pleasure and knowledge through the pervasion of their qualities—even if the substance [the self] is atomic—because it is impossible for these qualities to exist apart from the possessor of the qualities. Otherwise, the color of a jar would exist even apart from the jar itself. Furthermore, light seen elsewhere than the lamp is not a quality of the lamp, but rather a distinct substance in which touch is unmanifest.

Nor should it be argued that, just as genus (*jāti*), inherence (*samavāya*), and so forth do not exist elsewhere than in their substratum (*dharmin*), here too the quality (*guṇa*) or cognition (*buddhi*) would not be perceived elsewhere; for in that case, it would follow that they are all-pervading (*vyāpaka*) just like genus and inherence, since there would be no regulating factor for them to remain even apart from their substratum. Nor can it be said that the restriction [of perception] is due to the restriction of causes; for if the restriction were due solely to the restriction of the immediate inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*), then the consequence of their occupying every location (*sarvadeśatā*) would be unavoidable.

Nor should it be argued that the heat of fire would not be perceived externally; for if one were to claim that this [heat] belongs to a light whose form is unmanifest due to its proximity [to the fire], then the heat of fire itself could not be established. This is because, while there is an obstacle [to perception] that leads to the postulation of another light nearby, there is no such obstacle regarding the tactile sensation of heat experienced in the visible fire; therefore, it is impossible to postulate that the fire is something other than light. By this same reasoning, since fragrance is experienced all around a *ketakī* flower and the like, it follows that qualities do not depend upon a substratum (*guṇin*).

Furthermore, those fragrances do not pervade the parts of the *ketakī* flower on all sides, for that would entail the exhaustion of the substance. Nor can it be argued that there is no such exhaustion because other parts enter [the flower], as in the case of musk kept in a crystal casket; for such an entry of other parts is rejected due to a lack of evidence. For if an effect were independent of its inherent cause (*samavāyin*), it would follow that it lacks a substratum; and if, consequently, other causes based on proximity to that substratum were also eliminated, the very status of being an "effect" would be lost. Therefore, the postulation [of such entry] is itself the proof [that it does not occur].

As for the claim that in the passage "He is eternal, omnipresent, and immovable," the analysis of the compound should be "situated in the omnipresent one" and "atomic," in accordance with another Smṛti which states, "The atomic jīva is situated in Viṣṇu, who is eternal and omnipresent"—that is not correct. For it is more appropriate to follow the meaning of the Śruti texts, "And he is eternal and omnipresent like space" and "This very Self is great and unborn"; if one were to split the word as "atomic," it would result in a contradiction of those [scriptural] passages.

As for the claim that the all-pervasiveness of the atom itself is asserted through its connection with various bodies in succession, that is not correct; for there is no evidence to justify restricting the word "all" (*sarva*), which denotes everything without exception. Furthermore, as for the assertion that non-pervasiveness must be established solely on the grounds of perceptibility and so forth, that is also incorrect; for we have already stated the counter-argument (*pratikūlatarka*), and since that very argument serves as a favorable proof for pervasiveness, it lacks the status of being an "unestablished reason" (*aprayojaka*).

If it is objected: "But if the self (*ātman*) were all-pervasive, then all bodies would become the locus of experience for every self, because the bodies, sense organs, and so forth of all [bodies] are always in contact with all selves; furthermore, since actions would also be performed by bodies and the like that are common [to all], they could not be restricted to a specific individual; and even the superimposition of 'I-ness' (*ahantva*) and so on could not be restricted, as there would be no underlying relationship to serve as a regulator"—we say no, because this objection applies equally to you as well, since the Lord (*īśvara*) is also all-pervasive, and thus all bodies would necessarily result in producing His experience.

Nor can it be argued that because [the sprout] is not produced by that [specific] unseen merit (adṛṣṭa), no experience arises therein even though it is conjoined with it; for then the same would apply here as well. Nor can you ask how the actions themselves possess such exclusivity; for they are produced by previous actions of that same person, and thus there is simply beginninglessness. Otherwise, since the Lord’s nature is not understood by you, and because the sprout and so forth that produce Caitra’s experience are produced by his unseen merit, and since the unseen merit inherent in the self has no direct connection with the sprout, you must admit a connection mediated by the self; and in that case, the self's omnipresence (vibhutva) follows.

Nor should it be argued that even though sprouts and the like are not connected to the unseen merit (adṛṣṭa) through the self, they are nonetheless irrelevant because they are not produced by it—even if they do not serve as causes for Caitra’s enjoyment—since the connection mediated by the self, defined by its relation to the producing adṛṣṭa, is indeed relevant as it avoids over-extension (atiprasaṅga). For the status of being a producer is to be inferred solely from the result of the adṛṣṭa. Since this explanation suffices, there is no evidence for postulating any other relationship between the adṛṣṭa and its effect, such as those found between a counter-positive and its absence, or between a word and its denotation, or between knowledge and its object.

As for the claim that there exists a relationship between the unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*) of the *kārīrī* sacrifice and rain—consisting in being produced by an action enjoined with that [rain] as its purpose—that is not so; for even in that case, it is only through the inherence in what is conjoined (*saṃyuktasamavāya*) via the self of the sacrificer that the trickling of water and so forth are brought about. All of this has been stated according to the perspective of others; in our own view, however, the established position is exactly as previously stated.

And thus, because the Śruti states, "By the quality of the intellect and by the quality of the Self, it is indeed seen to be as small as the point of an awl," its inherent omnipresence (*vibhutva*) is established, since it is described as being the size of an awl's point by virtue of the quality of the intellect. It should not be argued that here the construction is inverted—meaning that the size of an awl's point refers to the quality of the Self and the state of being inferior refers to the quality of the intellect—because this would contradict the Śruti: "Just as the light of the minute eye is all-pervading, even so the light of this Puruṣa is all-pervading; for this Puruṣa is indeed minute."

Because this [statement] refers to the conditioned minuteness of that very [intellect], in accordance with the rule "by a quality of the intellect" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.2.28) and in view of its contradiction by numerous scriptures teaching its all-pervasiveness; and because the genitive case in the word "puruṣasya" (of the person) has a figurative meaning, as in expressions such as "the head of Rāhu"; therefore, there is no syntactical connection through transposition [of the words]. Consequently, minuteness is not a differentiator of the Self. Thus ends the refutation of the minuteness of the Self in the Advaitasiddhi. (33)
The merits or faults found in these texts have been clearly taught by my gurus; they do not belong to me as I speak the words of others.
However, there is this fruit of my labor here: that which has been [discerned] by my own intellect.
It is not the domain of the Vedas, nor of logical arguments, nor even of the words of the gurus.

Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Definition of the Self," in the *Advaitasiddhi* composed by the venerable Madhusūdana Sarasvatī, disciple of the venerable Viśveśvara Sarasvatī, the illustrious wandering ascetic teacher (*paramahaṃsa-parivrājaka-ācārya*).

Thus, once non-dualism is established, *śravaṇa* (listening) is the primary member (*aṅgin*) for its direct realization, while *manana* (reflection) and *nididhyāsana* (meditation) are to be practiced by those seeking liberation as its subordinate members (*aṅga*). As stated in the *Vivaraṇa*: "Śravaṇa is the primary member because the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) has no mediation in the comprehension of the object of knowledge (*prameya*); however, manana and nididhyāsana attain the status of being causes for the experience of Brahman through the effect of a one-pointed mental modification (*ekāgra-vṛtti*), which is perfected by the impressions (*saṃskāra*) that incline the mind toward the inner Self. Thus, they are members that assist the result (*phalopakāry-aṅga*).

[Objection: "Is it not the case that hearing (*śravaṇa*), being of the nature of inquiry (*vicāra*), is not the instrument (*karaṇa*) for verbal knowledge? For when Brahman is being known through the Veda—just as *dharma* is—the inquiry is merely a procedural requirement (*itikartavyatā*) regarding the instrument, whether that instrument be the Vedic word itself, the cognition produced by it, or the reasoning (*tarka*) involved in inference and so forth. [Reply: This is not so. Inquiry consists in the ascertainment of the power and intended meaning (*tātparya*) of the words. And since the word whose meaning has been thus ascertained is the instrument, inquiry enters into the category of the instrument; consequently, it lacks the status of a mere procedural requirement, as its primary character (*aṅgitva*) is thereby determined.

This has been stated by Vidyāsāgara: in inference, just as the knowledge of the logical mark (*liṅga*) is the instrument, so too is the knowledge of the word qualified by the speaker's intention (*tātparya*); therefore, reflection (*vicāra*), which consists in the ascertainment of that intention, possesses the status of the primary member (*aṅgin*).

Nor is it correct to argue that since the cognition of a word accompanied by expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and so forth can itself function as the instrument (*karaṇa*), the previously mentioned cognition of the intended meaning (*tātparya*)—which is merely exhausted by dispelling errors regarding that intention—would then have to enter the category of instruments; for if that were the case, reflection (*manana*) and other such factors would also have to enter that category. Likewise, if even the cognitions of expectancy and so forth were useful merely by dispelling errors such as the absence of expectancy, then expectancy itself would not be included in the category of instruments.

Nor is there a circularity (anyonyāśraya), because the apprehension of the speaker's intention (*tātparya*) is possible through a general understanding of the meaning. Otherwise, in cases such as words with multiple meanings, there would be no basis for determining the specific sense. Thus, although the knowledge of intention is not a causal factor in all instances of verbal cognition, its status as a cause must be accepted in those cases where verbal cognition occurs following a doubt or error regarding the intention—just as the perception of a distinguishing feature (*viśeṣadarśana*) is the cause of perceptual cognition following a doubt or error. For this very reason, there is no contradiction with the *Vivaraṇa* either.

[Objection: But surely, if the knowledge of the speaker’s intention (*tātparya*) enters into the category of the instrument [of verbal cognition], then because a misconception regarding the intention is possible even in the Veda, and because a correct cognition of the intention is possible even in non-Vedic scriptures (*bāhyāgama*), there would be no established distinction between the instrument of verbal cognition being defective or non-defective. [Reply: This is not so. For although in the case of the Veda there may occasionally be a misconception of the intention by someone regarding some particular point, its status as having a true intention remains intact due to its being inherently faultless. In the case of non-Vedic scriptures, however, because they are of human origin and composed by persons subject to deception and other flaws, they are defective; thus, it is not the same.

Because it is impossible to establish a distinction between being defective and non-defective [in the case of the word], the aspect of *tātparya* (purport) possesses the status of the primary factor (*aṅgin*) by entering the category of the instrument (*karaṇa*), due to its being an auxiliary that directly contributes to the connection [of meaning], just as threshing and the like [contribute to the preparation of the grain]. Nor is it the case that [the purport] is merely subordinate to the substance that serves as the instrument in the illustrative example; for total similarity is not a requirement for something to function as an illustration.

If it is argued that even though [hearing] is an auxiliary that assists by immediate conjunction (*sannipatyopakāraka*), it cannot be the principal (*śeṣin*) with respect to the auxiliaries consisting of reflection and meditative contemplation (*nididhyāsana*) which assist toward the fruit—otherwise, acts such as the *avaghāta* (threshing) would become the principal with respect to the *prayāja* offerings and so forth—the answer is no. For if it is the principal by virtue of being included within the qualified sacrifice (*viśiṣṭayāga*), we accept that as a desired consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*). However, its status as a principal in a non-common sense would require it to be an assistant toward a non-common fruit; and since hearing produces a non-common assistance in the form of the removal of specific doubts regarding impossibility (*asambhāvanā*), that status is indeed possible for hearing.

For this very reason, it has been stated by Citsukhācārya: "Because hearing is the cause of the latent impression (*āśaya*) residing in the word which has become the instrument (*karaṇa*), it possesses the status of the primary member (*aṅgin*) as an instrument; whereas reflection (*manana*) and meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*), being causes of the excellence (*atiśaya*) residing in the consciousness that serves as the auxiliary (*sahakārin*), possess the status of subsidiary members (*aṅga*) that assist toward the fruit. Nor should it be argued that, on these grounds, there would follow the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the pressing of the Soma (*abhiṣava*) and its drawing (*grahaṇa*)—which are causes of the excellence residing in the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and other subsidiaries that serve as auxiliaries to the Soma sacrifice—would also have the status of subsidiaries to those [pressings and drawings]. This is because the answer has already been given, as before.

This has been stated in the *Tattvaśuddhi*: "Because hearing is the object of the intentionality (*tātparya*) regarding the power (*śakti*) which is a property of the word that has become the instrument (*karaṇa*), it possesses the status of the primary member (*aṅgin*) by being included within the instrument."

It should not be argued that because the word [the scripture] requires both hearing (*śravaṇa*)—as well as reflection (*manana*) and meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*)—in order to produce either an unobstructed direct cognition (*aparokṣajñapti*) or an unobstructed indirect cognition (*parokṣajñapti*) when such cognitions are to be produced, all three are merely auxiliary factors contributing to the result (*phalopakāryaṅga*), and thus how could there be a mutual relationship of principal and subordinate (*parasparāṅgāṅgibhāva*) among them? For reflection and meditative absorption serve to provide the necessary auxiliaries for the word in producing the result, whereas hearing serves as the very producer (*janakatā*) of that result itself.

Because of this distinction; and where this is not the case, there is simply equal status as auxiliary parts (*aṅga*). By this, the following objection is refuted: that in the scriptural passage—"He who desires rain, he who desires food, and he who desires heaven should praise with the *saubhara*; for one desiring rain, he should make 'hīṣ' the *nidhana*; for one desiring food, 'ūrk'; for one desiring heaven, 'ū'"—there would result a mutual relationship of principal and auxiliary (*aṅgāṅgibhāva*) between the *saubhara* (as the means) and the *nidhana*-elements such as 'hīṣ' (as the results), just as there is between hearing, reflecting, and so forth. This is rejected because [the results] are distinct.

Because the causal factor (*tatprayojaka*)—consisting of the accomplishment of the nature of the instrument (*karaṇa*) and the accomplishment of the auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*)—is absent there [in the case of the final result] just as it is here [in the case of the intermediate result]. Nor should it be argued that, in this way, threshing and the like intended for the sacrifice would become subsidiary (*śeṣa*) to the production of the ultimate *apūrva* (just as the *prayāja* offerings, etc., are subsidiary to the production of the ultimate *apūrva*), because there is a distinction: both [the threshing and the *prayāja*] lack the status of being intended for the sacrifice with respect to a single fruit. Now, it may be objected: "In the world, the established fruit of a word is mediate knowledge (*parokṣajñāna*)."

If it is asked how hearing—which imparts excellence to the word—can be a subordinate factor for producing the fruit of direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*), [the answer is as follows]: Directness (*sākṣāttva*) is neither a genus (*jāti*) nor is being produced by the sense organs (*indriyajanyatva*) and so forth the determining factor; rather, the removal of ignorance (*ajñāna*) residing in the object itself is the sole determinant of immediacy (*aparokṣatva*). Thus, the removal of ignorance extends as far as the object, and since that [removal] exists here because it extends as far as the Self (*ātman*), there is no need to postulate an unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*).

And thus, its status as the primary element (aṅgin) is established even by the force of the context, because once the primacy of hearing is established through its connection with the fruit, there arises an expectancy for the procedural requirements (itikartavyatā).

Objection: Although it is observed that one-pointedness of mind (*cittaikāgrya*) is a cause for the knowledge of subtle objects, nevertheless, reflection (*manana*) is not a cause for one-pointedness of mind. This is because it is observed that reflection, which consists of the investigation of reasoning, serves only to remove doubts regarding what is unreasonable; therefore, to postulate its status as a cause for one-pointedness would result in the abandonment of what is observed (*dṛṣṭahāni*). Furthermore, it would follow that the injunction for reflection (*mananavidhi*) is an original injunction (*apūrvavidhi*), and this would contradict the traditional teaching (*smṛti*) which states, "The intellect persists as long as there is unreasonableness. Reply: This is not so. When such a doubt exists, amidst the various alternatives (*nānākoṭau*), [reflection is required].

Since it is observed that the inclination of the mind toward the object of determination reaches its limit precisely upon the cessation of that mental distraction through the application of reason—and thus there is no contradiction with direct perception, nor with the injunctions for what is not previously known—meditation (*nididhyāsana*) is universally established as the means for overturning contrary impressions (*viparīta-bhāvanā*).

If it is argued that the cessation of that [misconception] is not observed to be the cause of knowledge—since we observe the direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*) of mother-of-pearl even while the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of silver persists—we reply: no, because after the cognition "this is mother-of-pearl," there occurs the memory "that was known as silver. While this proves the existence of a latent impression whose object is that cognition, the fact that one does *not* remember "that was silver" demonstrates that the cessation of the contrary impression is present there as well.

If it is argued that, by the mark (*liṅga*) consisting of the semantic power of the word—namely, through the sentence "But then, meditating upon Him, he sees Him who is partless"—there is a connection between *nididhyāsana* and the fruit, and that by virtue of the context (*prakaraṇa*), hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth are directly auxiliary (*sannipatyāṅga*) to *nididhyāsana*, we say no. This is because the term *nididhyāsana* lacks the semantic power (*śabda-sāmarthya*) to connect with the fruit in the form of direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*), as is the case with expressions such as "The seat of the gods is the *barhis* grass. Furthermore, even in the sentence, it is *śravaṇa* itself that is supplied by ellipsis (*adhyāhriyate*) on the strength of semantic fitness (*yogyatā*).

And thus, because it culminates precisely in the favorable meaning that "by meditating upon that [Brahman] through hearing it, one perceives the partless Brahman," it follows that in the statement "It is to be seen, it is to be heard," hearing has a direct connection with seeing due to its proximity in the text as being mentioned immediately before seeing. Furthermore, if direct realization were produced by the excellence of the cultivation (bhāvanā) consisting of meditative absorption (nididhyāsana), it would result in the fallacy of its being invalid, like the direct realization of a beloved woman.

Nor can validity [be established] through the strength of the primary means of knowledge; if that is so, let that very [primary means] be the direct instrument [of realization]. What is the use of another [means] that depends upon it? By this, the view that the mind, assisted by *nididhyāsana* (meditative contemplation), is the instrument is also refuted. Thus ends the section on the status of *manana* (reflection) and *nididhyāsana* as auxiliary parts (*aṅga*) to *śravaṇa* (hearing) in the *Advaitasiddhi*. 1.

Furthermore, since hearing (*śravaṇa*) and the other means are established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) as the means for the comprehension of the object, the injunction regarding them does not constitute an original injunction (*apūrva-vidhi*), but rather a restrictive injunction (*niyama-vidhi*). If it be argued that hearing serves as a means toward the fruit of immediate realization (*aparokṣa-phala*), and since this [status] is not known from any other source, it must therefore be an original injunction—this is not so; for in the case of the study of the science of music (*gāndharva-śāstra*), the fact that inquiry is the cause for the direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*) of the musical notes such as *ṣaḍja* and others is already observed in experience.

It should not be argued that, on this basis alone, it is not established that scriptural inquiry is a cause for the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of an object in all cases, because there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of the inquiry into the *Dharma-śāstra*. For, by the force of observation, the capacity to produce direct realization is established as belonging to the inquiry into a scripture whose object is immediate (*aparokṣa*). And the Self (*ātman*) is immediate, like the musical notes *ṣaḍja* and so forth, whereas *dharma* and the like are not. Nor should it be said that inquiry is useless regarding what is immediate, for there is no rule that whatever is immediate must necessarily be inquired into.

Just as there is no rule that what is directly perceived must be investigated, so too there is no rule that it must not be investigated; for we observe that even in the case of the musical notes such as *ṣaḍja*, which are directly perceived, investigation takes place, and because, in that very same way, success is possible. Furthermore, it is only the states of being doubtful (*saṃdigdhatva*) and being purposeful (*saprayojanatva*) that serve as the grounds for investigation in all cases. By this, the claim that the means [of knowledge] is the cause for the direct realization of the meaning of the scripture—which is fit for direct realization when it has been investigated—is not tenable.

The argument that [inquiry] is purposeful because it leads to the realization of objects such as heaven or hidden treasures—which are suitable for inquiry—after some time, since such realization would otherwise not occur through inquiry alone, is refuted. For even when the direct perception of a hidden treasure or the like has not yet arisen due to a lack of sensory contact with it, the status of inquiry as its cause does not thereby disappear.

In that case, deliberation (*vicāra*) is delayed by the delay of the sense organs because it functions as their auxiliary; however, in the present context, since the result is verbal knowledge (*śābda*), there is no dependence on them. This is because the nature of the effect consists in being a direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of an object capable of being perceived, while the nature of the means consists in being a deliberation upon a scripture concerning such an object. By this, the objection is refuted: namely, that if one were to abandon the status of this [injunction] as an *apūrva-vidhi* (an original injunction) merely by postulating that a deliberation different from the present one is the cause of an effect different from the present effect, then all *apūrva-vidhis* would be subject to total annihilation.

If it is argued that a restrictive rule (*niyama*) applies only when there is a possibility of alternative means, and such a possibility exists only when other means of accomplishment are available—whereas no such possibility exists regarding the knowledge of a Self devoid of form and so forth—this is not so. Even though there is no attainment through other means of knowledge regarding the specific attributeless Self, a restrictive rule is possible because there is a general attainment of the Self [through other means]. This is just as, although methods like scratching with the fingernails are not applicable to specific varieties of rice used for sacrificial purposes (*apūrva*), the restrictive injunction "one threshes the rice" (*vrīhīnavahanti*) is valid because such methods are applicable to rice in general.

Now, it has been established in the ninth [book] that in the injunction "one threshes the rice" (*vrīhīnavahanti*), the word *vrīhi* refers to the substance that serves the *apūrva* (the transcendental result), and not merely to rice in general; otherwise, threshing would not be directly enjoined for barley, and even if it were extended by analogy to wild rice (*nīvāra*), it would be sublated due to the absence of the quality of being *vrīhi*. Therefore, it must be stated that the application of actions such as tearing with the nails occurs only in the case of substances that serve the *apūrva*.

If it is argued that otherwise, if threshing were restricted solely for the purpose of dehusking, then—just as there is a restriction on the means of acquiring wealth such as officiating at sacrifices—that [threshing] would result in being a human goal (puruṣārtha) in its own right; and consequently, one would incur sin even when crushing worldly rice grains, we say: no. For although the threshing being restricted has as its object only the substance intended for the apūrva, the restriction is established by the very fact of its application to the general category [of rice], and thus a specific application is not required.

Nor should it be argued that there is no apprehension by other means of knowledge regarding the pure consciousness (cinmātra) known through the Vedānta—which is characterized by both the featureless (nirviśeṣa) and the qualified-with-features (saviśeṣa) forms and which is reached through such means as the absence of specific qualities; for when [consciousness] is cognized as possessing features in its aspect common to both, there is indeed apprehension by other means of knowledge. If, even when there is apprehension by another means of knowledge regarding one member of a class, a restriction can be established regarding another member of that same class, then what need is there to mention that, in the case of a single self, a restriction regarding a different state is established by the apprehension of that self in a particular state through another means of knowledge?

Nor should it be argued that there is a lack of grammatical coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) when one particular is restricted by the attainment of another particular; for even in the absence of coreferentiality with the individual instance (*vyakti*), coreferentiality is accepted by resorting to a general property (*sāmānyadharma*) as a last resort.

[Objection: Is it not the case that there is another way [to resolve this]? Even in the case of rice-grains intended for the *apūrva* (unseen potency), there is the possibility of threshing, even though it does not produce the restricted unseen merit (*niyamādṛṣṭa*). For its application is not restricted to those cases where the removal of husks (*vaituṣya*) is accomplished by it; rather, it is merely a possibility based on its capacity. [Reply: No, because in this way the meaning would ultimately reduce to "its fitness" (*tadyogyatva*). And that [fitness] resides in what belongs to the same class (*tajjātīya*), but not in that specific instance itself; thus, the problem of "lack of co-referentiality" (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) remains as before. Furthermore, in the present context, since the subject is a single Self (*ekātman*) that persists through both states—namely, the qualified (*saviśeṣa*) and the unqualified (*nirviśeṣa*) forms—there is no room for the suspicion of lack of co-referentiality.

The author of the *Tattvakaumudī*, however, maintains: "Just as the requirement that recollection (*smṛti*) be accomplished by means of mantras alone is prescribed—since the knowledge of the meaning of the mantras is already established even through the *Kalpasūtras* and one's own instructional texts, and thus the status of being accomplished by mantras would otherwise be unestablished in certain cases—likewise, this is a restrictive injunction (*niyama*) intended to complete the hearing of the Vedānta and so forth, which might otherwise be unestablished in certain cases due to the availability of Smṛtis, Purāṇas, and other sources that are rooted in the Vedānta and common to women and Śūdras."

"Therefore, a Brāhmaṇa should not study what is non-Vedic," according to this Śruti, and "He should listen from the sentences of the Śruti," according to such Smṛtis, so they say. Nor should it be argued that there is a contradiction with Smṛti passages such as "One should augment the Veda by means of Itihāsas and Purāṇas," because [the Veda] cannot be augmented by that which has not been investigated; for even though there is a requirement for its investigation in order to determine the purport of the Vedānta, there is no requirement for its investigation regarding the knowledge of Brahman itself.

Nor should it be argued that, just as in the case of knowledge of ritual action, there is a dependence on Smṛti even for the knowledge of Brahman—since direct knowledge of Brahman arises even from historical works such as the Mahābhārata which concern Brahman—for in both cases, Smṛti and the like lack independent authority and serve only to determine the intended meaning (tātparya) of the Śruti. For this very reason it was said: "One should supplement the Veda," and not "one should know the meaning of the Veda."

As for the claim that such passages as "He is to be heard from the Vedic statements" intend to refer to a means of valid cognition rooted in scripture—that is not so; for when the status of being a cause indicated by the ablative case can be established directly, it is improper to assume an indirect (mediated) relationship.

Furthermore, since the ascertainment of reality (*tattva-niścaya*) is observed through historical accounts (*itihāsa*) and the like—which consist of the collection of the meanings of various scattered branches [of scripture]—and since, when that exists, there is no need for the purification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa-śuddhi*) intended for that [realization] by way of the desire to know (*vividiṣā*); and since immediate realization (*āparokṣya*) is established simply by virtue of being an object [of knowledge]; and since no immediacy greater than that produced by the Veda is experienced in the knowledge of Brahman produced by historical accounts; and since such [immediacy] cannot be accomplished by restricted unseen merit (*niyamādṛṣṭa*); and since knowledge, in the removal of ignorance, functions like the removal of its own prior non-existence (*svaprāgabhāva*).

It should not be argued that this is not a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*) because it is independent of unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*), and because there is no other [result] to be accomplished by a restrictive unseen merit; for, on the strength of scriptural texts such as "This very [Self]... by the recitation of the Vedas" (*tametam vedānuvacanena*), it is possible that all unseen merits—both those produced by sacrifices and those produced by restrictive rules—contribute solely to the purification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa-śuddhi*) through the desire to know (*vividiṣā*). Furthermore, since [purification] assists in the very nature of knowledge, it is dependent upon that [unseen merit] for the cessation of ignorance which is to be accomplished by that knowledge.

Furthermore, because there exists a distinction in the nature of the fruits produced by actions—whether conjoined with knowledge or not—as being either long-lasting or short-lasting, it is necessary to postulate a superior quality in the direct realization (sākṣātkāra) produced by the restrictive unseen merit (*niyamādṛṣṭa*) over that which is produced by the ascertainment of reality (*tattvaniścaya*) unaided by such merit; thus, its status as a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*) is possible. Therefore:

"Since there is the possibility of an excluded alternative (*vyāvartya*) to be accomplished by the restrictive unseen merit, the restriction of hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth is in every way justified. Thus [it is concluded].

For this very reason, the statement of other teachers—that the restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*) is intended to fulfill the unobtained portions by means of obtaining self-composed treatises and the like from Śūdras—is also explained. Thus ends the justification for the restrictive injunction as stated in the *Vivaraṇa*. || 2 ||

Now, what is this so-called "hearing" (*śravaṇa*)? Is it the ascertainment of the word's expressive power (*śakti*) and its intended meaning (*tātparya*)? Or is it the ascertainment of the word as qualified by those two? Or is it the ascertainment of the indicative marks (*liṅga*) that establish the intended meaning? Or is it the knowledge born from the traditional scriptures and the teacher’s instruction? Not the first, because expressive power is impossible in the case of Brahman, which is inexpressible.

Furthermore, the intention (*tātparya*) does not pertain to the subject (*dharmin*) of a doubt that is produced by an initial cognition and is to be removed by inquiry; for since that [subject] is already ascertained prior [to inquiry], inquiry—which would serve as the means to ascertain the intention—would be useless. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of doubt and so forth persisting even after inquiry.

Nor does it consist in [the knowledge of] a specific mode residing in a subject that is itself a matter of doubt, whether as qualified by that [doubt] or merely indicated by it, because this would result in the loss of the status of having an undivided meaning (*akhaṇḍārthatā*), and because you do not accept that the act of determination, being a form of cognition, can be something to be enjoined. For this very reason, the second and subsequent options are also excluded. Nor is "hearing" (*śravaṇa*) the joining of the Vedāntas with Brahman through the mouth of a teacher, since that does not exceed the first option. Nor is it "hearing" in the sense of a formal debate (*vādakathā*) consisting of the employment of specific sentences, because the word "hearing" is not used in that context.

If it is argued that for this very reason there is no injunction (*vidhi*) even for reflection (*manana*) and meditative cultivation (*nididhyāsana*), because these two are not distinct from knowledge (*jñāna*), we say no; for only the first position (*pakṣa*) is able to withstand scrutiny. Nor is the impossibility of verbal power (*śabdaśakti*) a defect in that case, because even if pure power is impossible, the qualified power—which is useful for the comprehension of that [pure meaning] and must be determined—is possible. Furthermore, although the purport (*tātparya*) is impossible there because its locus (the subject of doubt) is not ascertained, it is possible in the case of the undifferentiated reality (*nirviśeṣa*) characterized by the alternatives of doubt.

Because reflection (*vicāra*) would otherwise be purposeless. Nor does this entail the loss of the status of being *akhaṇḍārtha* (referring to an impartite reality), for it has been established that the status of *akhaṇḍārtha* is maintained because [the words] merely indicate the essential nature (*svarūpa*). Nor is the restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) non-injunctional on the grounds that it is of the nature of knowledge; for it is a distinct mental modification (*cetovṛtti*) different from knowledge, being of the nature of reasoning (*tarka*), as Sureśvarācārya states regarding hearing and so forth: "In this context, the activity of hearing and the rest must be performed with effort. In the same way, the injunctional status of reflection (*manana*) and meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*) is also to be understood.

Nor should it be argued that it is impossible for such [knowledge] to be excluded from the category of valid knowledge when there exists an object in the form of a purport (*tātparya*) and a means of proof (*pramāṇa*) in the form of the opening statement (*upakrama*) and so forth—because in cases such as the meditation on the "speech-cow" (*vāgdhenūpāsanā*), which is excluded from valid knowledge, one does not observe dependence upon a real object or a means of proof; for in my view, since the validity of an inferential mark (*liṅga*) is not admitted, the condition "when there exists a means of proof" is simply non-existent. Furthermore, even if the opening statement and so forth were accepted as means of proof, this part of the condition—"when there exists a means of proof"—is unestablished, because [the knowledge in question] occurs prior to them.

Therefore, since hearing (*śravaṇa*) and the rest are mental activities by virtue of their intellectual nature, their status as things to be enjoined (*vidheya*) is established. This is the detailed explanation found in the *Siddhāntabindu* and the *Kalpalatikā*. As for the description in the works of Vācaspati Miśra that [hearing] is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*), that does not contradict the assertion of its being an injunction, because it represents a different philosophical approach (*prasthānāntara*). Thus ends the section on the establishment of the enjoinability of hearing and the rest in the *Advaitasiddhi*. 3.

Thus, the injunction for hearing (*śravaṇa-vidhi*), which prescribes inquiry, is itself the root of the *jijñāsā-sūtra*. Nor should it be argued that this leads to the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*)—on the grounds that the injunction for inquiry would require as a qualification of the eligible person (*adhikārin*) a desire for immediate knowledge (*aparokṣajñāna-kāmanā*) dependent upon the immediate knowledge to be accomplished by hearing. For such a mutual dependence does not arise, since the qualification of the eligible person is the desire for immediate knowledge based on the immediate, though superficial (*āpātataḥ*), conceptual knowledge that arises in one who has studied the Vedas and understood the relationship between words and their meanings.

Furthermore, the inquiry (*vicāra*) mentioned in the *Jijñāsā-sūtra* does not consist of the application of logical reasoning (*nyāya*) for the purpose of determining reality; otherwise, it would be improper to state that such [inquiry] must be performed in order to establish the commencement of a treatise (*śāstra*) consisting of a systematic arrangement of logic, and because it would be untenable for anything else to constitute the procedural requirement (*itikartavyatā*) of the Veda. Moreover, "listening" (*śravaṇa*) is not of the nature of applying the aforementioned logic, as that would entail its identity with "reflection" (*manana*). Therefore, one should not say that there is no relationship of root and derivative between the injunction to listen and the *Jijñāsā-sūtra*.

Although there is no relationship of primary and secondary between the *jijñāsā-sūtra* and the injunction for hearing (*śravaṇa-vidhi*) because they do not have the same object, their relationship is nonetheless established; for it is possible for them to share a common object by taking into account the investigation of the marks of intention (*tātparya-liṅga*), such as the opening and concluding statements, which is implied by the hearing that consists in determining the power and intention of the subject matter of the injunction for hearing.

Furthermore, reflection (*manana*)—defined as the contemplation of the meaning of what has been heard through logical reasoning—is not identical to that [hearing], even though the investigation implied by the sense of the matter serves as the procedure (*itikartavyatā*). This is because the status of hearing as the principal act (*aṅgin*), as stated regarding the determination of intention, remains intact.
