As for that which is called "reflection" (*manana*) through reasonings: if it is the recollection of the purport already determined through hearing (*śravaṇa*), or of the words concerning that subject; or if it is a recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*); or if it is another act of direct knowledge (*abhijñā*) similar in form to hearing, whose fruit is the strengthening of the mental impression (*saṃskāra*); then, since that would be accomplished by the necessary repetition of hearing alone, the injunction for reflection would be redundant. For all three types of such reflection, there would be no dependence on reasonings external to hearing, as it is said: "One should hear from the Vedic sentences."

Furthermore, there would be a contradiction with the Smṛti stating that "one must reflect by means of reasonings," as well as a contradiction with the Smṛti which establishes that reflection removes the suspicion of irrationality not yet removed by hearing: "As long as there is ignorance, there is hearing; as long as there is irrationality, there is reflection. This is not so, because reflection is intended here in the sense of an inquiry into reasonings that remove doubts regarding the rationality or irrationality of the subject matter heard; thus, the faults you have mentioned find no place here.

Nor should it be argued that the first sūtra—which establishes the necessity of inquiry by means of doubt regarding what is appropriate and inappropriate, as well as doubt, prima facie arguments, and established conclusions, all of which are useful for undertaking the Mīmāṃsā system—must be based solely on the injunction to reflect (*manana-vidhi*) and not on the injunction to hear (*śravaṇa-vidhi*).

Since the investigation of the marks (liṅgas) implied by the injunction to hear (śravaṇa)—which determines the intended meaning—is more primary than the investigation that removes doubts regarding whether the subject matter of that intention is appropriate or inappropriate, it can rightly be said that [the latter] is rooted in the injunction to hear which implies that [former]. Furthermore, the investigation into what is appropriate or inappropriate is merely incidental.

Alternatively, "hearing" (śravaṇa) is the contemplation of the reasons such as the introductory passages (upakrama) and so forth, which determine the intended meaning as stated in the first chapter (samanvaya-adhyāya); "reflection" (manana) is the contemplation of the reasons that remove the doubt regarding the non-existence of the object, as stated in the second chapter.

But surely, this would contradict the statement in the *Vivaraṇa*, which, after explaining that even presumptive arguments (*arthāpatti*) are included within the first stage of hearing (*śravaṇa*) by stating, "Because the reasonings that dispel logical impossibility (*asambhāvanā*) and contrary impressions (*viparītabhāvanā*) are contained within the initial cognition," and so forth, goes on to say: "Incapacity for one-pointed mental modification (*ekāgravṛtti*) caused by the accumulation of contrary impressions regarding the identity of Brahman and the Self is 'impossibility' (*asambhāvanā'), whereas 'contrary impression' (*viparītabhāvanā') is the accumulation of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) from the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of the body [upon the Self]," and so forth—[this being said] regarding that which removes impossibility.

If it is argued that this is not so because it has been stated that reflection (*manana*) is the cause of one-pointedness of mind, which in turn is the cause for the accumulation of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) occurring immediately after the ascertainment of the meaning [of the scripture], we say no; for since the two systems follow different approaches, the contradiction with the *Vivaraṇa* is irrelevant. Furthermore, there is no consequence that the *Jijñāsā-sūtra* would partially be based on an injunction for reflection, because it is appropriate to maintain that it is based solely on the injunction for hearing (*śravaṇa*), given that the inquiry described in the *Samanvaya-sūtra* is more fundamental.

Now, [one might object]: since the word *upapatti* (reasoning) in the Smṛti passage "and it must be reflected upon through reasonings" (*mantavyaścopapattibhiḥ*), and the word *yukti* (logic) in the Smṛti passage "as far as it is not inconsistent with reason" (*matiryāvadayuktatā*), possess a general sense—just like the word *śruti* (Veda) in the phrase "it must be heard from the Vedic sentences" (*śrotavyaḥ śrutivākyebhyaḥ*)—then, according to the maxim "that which was first established by faith is later proven by logic," would not *śravaṇa* (hearing) consist merely in grasping the meaning of the Vedas from the mouth of a teacher for every sentence, based on faith alone without regard for reasoning, and only afterwards [would there be reflection]?

If it is argued that since "investigation according to logic" (*nyāyānusandhāna*) is *manana* (reflection), and thus a distinction [between *śravaṇa* and *manana*] is possible, it is improper to speak of a distinction between *śravaṇa* and *manana* only with respect to logical arguments (*yuktis*), we say no. This is because it has already been stated that the apprehension of the meaning of a sentence, being of the nature of valid knowledge (*pramā*), is not something to be enjoined. If it is further objected that if this apprehension of the meaning of the sentence is not included within the triad beginning with *śravaṇa*, it would follow that there must be a fourth [activity] to be performed by those seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*), we say no. This is because, being of the nature of knowledge, it is unfit for performance; furthermore, since it arises spontaneously through mere faith (*śraddhā*) alone, it is not dependent on human effort.

Nor does it follow that for one who has heard that meaning from the mouth of the teacher alone, the usage "this has been heard by him" (*śrutamanena*) would be untenable; for since the status of the object as something to be enjoined cannot otherwise be accounted for, its being a different entity is established, and thus this usage must somehow be explained as being figurative (*gauṇa*) or the like. For this very reason, the words *upapatti* (logical consistency) and *ayuktatā* (inconsistency) occurring in the *Smṛti* do not have a general sense.

Nor should it be argued that once the purport (*tātparya*) of the scripture, which is itself a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), has been ascertained, there is no need for reasoning (*upapatti*) to establish the existence of the object; and furthermore, while it must be admitted that reflection (*manana*) serves to remove doubts regarding the invalidity of the object—namely its non-existence—it would follow that a person who has already ascertained the validity [of the scripture] would never engage in reflection. This objection is not tenable, because such an absence [of reflection] is indeed desired for such a person, as is seen in the case of *kṛṣṇala* grains where the threshing (*avaghāta*) obtained through extended application (*atideśa*) is set aside due to the sublation of its purpose (*dvārabādha*). Therefore, the ascertainment of the purport is *śravaṇa*.

And since that [inquiry] depends upon an investigation into the marks [of Brahman], it is established that the first sūtra, which concerns the necessity of such an investigation, is rooted in the injunction for hearing (śravaṇa) and not in the injunction for reflection (manana); thus, the status of the *jijñāsā-sūtra* as being based solely on the injunction for hearing is proven.

Now, in your own view, just as the inquiry into the *karmakāṇḍa* is prompted by the injunctions for subsequent sacrifices (*uttarakratuvidhi*), why could it not be that the inquiry into the *brahmakāṇḍa* is likewise prompted by an injunction regarding the Self? For, just as the inquiry [into ritual] culminates in the determination of the object to be performed by the injunctions for subsequent sacrifices, the inquiry into the Vedānta is required for its own establishment by means of the knowledge of the Self—which is understood from passages such as "The knower of the Self crosses over sorrow"—as being the cause for the cessation of grief.

And it is logical that even though many ritual injunctions (*kratu-vidhi*) are implied [by a single text], there is still the implication of only one; if this is argued, we say no, because although the implication of a cause by its effect is possible, nevertheless, for the sake of establishing its status as being based on Vedic injunction (*vaidhatva*), its foundation in an injunction must necessarily be stated.

Otherwise, it would be improper to state that the inquiry into the ritual section (*karmakāṇḍa*) is also implied by the knowledge of rituals alone, or that it is implied by the injunction for Vedic study or the subsequent injunctions for sacrifices; for even you, who assert that [the inquiry] is rooted in the injunction for reflection (*manana*), must necessarily avoid this implication. By this, it is shown that since the application of the injunction for study—extending up to the comprehension of the meaning—is possible for the inquiry into Brahman just as it is for the inquiry into ritual action, there is no necessity for an injunction for hearing (*śravaṇa*).

Nor should it be argued that this hearing (*śravaṇa*), which has realization as its fruit, possesses repetition as its quality, and has reflection (*manana*) and so forth as its auxiliary members, is distinct from the mere hearing prompted by the injunction for study (*adhyayana-vidhi*), and therefore constitutes a separate injunction; for even though the inquiry into Brahman is prompted by the injunction for study, realization is established precisely through its having as its object the Self, which is immediate and of a single essence. Furthermore, even if repetition were accepted as an auxiliary to another injunction, it must be stated that—like the act of threshing—it possesses a visible fruit, and this applies to the section on ritual action (*karmakāṇḍa*) as well.

This is because repeated inquiry is required until the intended meaning (*tātparya*) is ascertained; beyond that point, such inquiry is no longer required even in the section concerning Brahman (*brahmakāṇḍa*). Furthermore, since reflection (*manana*) is required even in the section concerning ritual action (*karmakāṇḍa*) for the sake of determining its meaning, it is like the injunction of other subsidiaries—such as the forest (*araṇya*)—by means of another sentence in reference to the study of specific portions of the *Āraṇyaka* prescribed by the rule of study (*adhyayanavidhi*); or like the injunction of subsidiaries such as the "head-vow" (*śirovrata*) and eating on the ground in reference to the study of the *Muṇḍaka*, the *Kārīrī*, and so forth; or like [the injunction] "he takes it with four [verses]."

This is refuted on the grounds that, according to your own position, it is possible to enjoin the subsidiary elements such as reflection (*manana*) by means of restating the acquisition [of the Veda]—which is already established by implication—as a restatement of the number [of Vedas], just as one might enjoin the number [of Vedas] by restating the acquisition; for this is equally applicable to the proponent who maintains that the injunction to reflect is rooted in the injunction to study. This is because the injunction to study has the attainment of the *svādhyāya* (one's own portion of the Veda) as its fruit, and not the knowledge of the meaning, since the suffix *-tavya* in the word *adhyetavya* (to be studied), being a *kṛtya* suffix denoting the object, makes it clear that the *svādhyāya* itself is the result.

Nor does its operation extend up to the comprehension of the meaning of the fruit-bearing [text] on the grounds that it lacks human purpose (*apuruṣārthatva*), for in such cases as "one desiring cattle should sacrifice with the *citriṇī* [offering]," even the desired cattle and so forth would result in being non-fruits. If, however, they are considered fruits by virtue of being means to human purpose through a traditional sequence (*paramparā*), this is possible in the present case as well. Therefore, it is established that the injunction to hear (*śravaṇa-vidhi*) is the basis for the *jijñāsā-sūtra* which enjoins inquiry, and not the injunction to reflect (*manana-vidhi*).
Thus ends the demonstration that inquiry in the *Advaitasiddhi* is rooted in the injunction for hearing (*śravaṇavidhi*). 5.

In another system of exposition (*prasthāna*), however, it is stated that because the injunction for study (*adhyayanavidhi*) extends as far as the comprehension of the meaning, it implies the investigation of both sections [of the Vedas]; furthermore, there is no injunction regarding hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth, since their status as means to direct realization is established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).

Nor should it be argued: "Since the hearing of a scriptural transgression (*pratyavāya*) occurs in the absence of study, and since the obligatory nature (*nityatā*) of study is also understood from this, how can study have as its limit the comprehension of meaning? For even though the injunction for study has the knowledge of meaning as its purpose, in order to avoid its futility, one must rely on such restrictive rules (*niyama*) as: "Only by means of the Veda that has been studied does one come to know what is to be done, and only then is the performed ritual capable of yielding fruit. Thus, because the performance of the aforementioned obligatory and other rituals would be impossible without study, the hearing of the scriptural transgression is logically consistent.

Thus, some maintain that even for one whose purpose is the knowledge of the meaning, study is obligatory by virtue of its result. Others, however, say that although study possesses an unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) because a direct transgression is heard of in the case of not studying—just as in the case of failing to perform the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*)—the knowledge of the meaning also exists as a visible result (*dṛṣṭa*). Since this is both required and desired, it serves that purpose as well; thus, it has a dual purpose, like the animal sacrifice and the *puroḍāśa* offering.

In this regard, the opponent also accepts that the injunction for study (adhyayanavidhi), being obligatory, implies both types of inquiry; however, this is incorrect. For one who maintains that the *Jijñāsā-sūtra* is rooted in the injunction for reflection (*manana-vidhi*), such acceptance is untenable. Since even the inquiry in the form of reflection—which removes the suspicion of impropriety—is already implied by the injunction for study, the injunction [of reflection] therein would be redundant, and thus the status of the *sūtra* as being rooted in that [injunction] remains unestablished.
Thus ends the demonstration of the validity of Vācaspati’s assertion that the injunction for self-study implies the investigation [of the meaning] in the *Advaitasiddhi*. 6.

As for the claim that *śravaṇa* must be enjoined as having the very nature of the knowledge produced by words, that is not so; for such superficial perception (*āpātadarśana*) arises even without it. Nor does the knowledge of the meaning of sentences situated in various branches—distinct from that [superficial perception]—arise through the instruction of established meanings (such as "the meaning of this sentence is this") regarding every individual sentence; for the investigation of the meaning of sentences in the form of the Vedānta has already been established as a means in a general sense.

Nor should it be argued that this is an *apūrva-vidhi* (an original injunction) because the causality for the knowledge of Brahman has not been established with respect to [the inquiry] as qualified by being an inquiry into the Vedāntas—just as, for example, although the difference of a jar from other things is already established, the statement "earth differs from these" is not a case of proving what is already proven (*siddhasādhana*); and just as, according to the method stated in the *Sthāna*, *Prakaraṇa*, and *Adhikaraṇa* [sections], although the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) is obtained through the *codaka* (archetypal transfer rule) for the *iṣṭi*, animal, and *soma* sacrifices included within the *Rājasūya* individually, it is not obtained for the *Rājasūya* as a whole. This cannot be said, because [the causality] is established in a general sense.

If, disregarding the state of being a means for an already established end, one were to accept an *apūrva-vidhi* (an original injunction) by way of a specific qualification in order to establish the status of a means for what was previously unestablished, then even in the investigation of sentences such as those concerning the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, there would result the necessity of postulating yet another *apūrva-vidhi* to establish the status of a means for the knowledge of the meaning of that sentence in its specific form.

By this, it is shown that the fact that *nididhyāsana* (meditative contemplation) is the cause for the direct realization of Brahman, whose nature is unmanifest, is not obtained from any other source; thus, it is an *apūrva-vidhi* (an original injunction). Likewise, although *śravaṇa* (hearing) and *manana* (reflection) are obtained through the indicative mark (*liṅga*) alone because *nididhyāsana* is impossible regarding what is unknown and so forth, they are not obtained through that mark with respect to the specific objects of *nididhyāsana*—namely, the qualities of the subject and qualities other than those; therefore, the injunction of those two is also strictly an *apūrva-vidhi*. And thus, in the case of the portion of the qualities to be contemplated, *śravaṇa* and *manana* function by way of a visible means.

As for the claim that [meditation] is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to contemplation (*nididhyāsana*) by way of something unseen (*adṛṣṭa*), this is refuted. For hearing (*śravaṇa*) and the other stages have the attributeless (*nirguṇa*) as their object and do not have the qualified (*saguṇa*) as their object; furthermore, the opposite relationship of auxiliary and principal has been established; and finally, since it is observed that contemplation directed toward a subtle object is the cause of direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) regarding such an object, there is no question of its being an "unprecedented" (*apūrva*) result. || 7 ||

If it is asked, "What then is the status of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth heard here?", [the answer is: because they become blunt—like the sharpness of a razor applied to a stone slab—they are merely *arthavāda* (explanatory or commendatory statements), as in the case of "one should offer with wild sesame gruel" (*jartilayavāgvā vā juhuyāt*). Nor should it be argued that the injunction of knowledge is also seen in such passages as "the clarified butter is to be inspected by the wife" and "action must be performed by one who knows; therefore, one should always see"; for in those cases, since the conjunction of the sense-faculties and so forth—which are the causes of that [seeing]—are what are enjoined, metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is accepted as a last resort.

Nor is there a contradiction with the principle that "in an injunction, the primary meaning of a word is not [the one intended]," because this principle is merely a general rule (autsargika), given that even in injunctive sentences such as "Mix the soma with milk" (*gobhiḥ śrīṇīta matsaram*), figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is observed; furthermore, the principle means that in an injunction, the primary meaning of a word is not [to be accepted] when it conflicts with an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*).

Nor should it be argued that sense-contact (saṃyoga) is equivalent to knowledge because both can be indirectly accomplished by volition (kṛtisādhyatva) through the medium of an action residing in the sense organ—since even in the case of sensory contact there is an absence of being directly accomplished by volition—and because even an undesirable contact is observed to occur against one's will, just as the perception of a foul odor occurs to one who does not desire it. This is incorrect, because, unlike in the case of heaven and the like, the quality of being accomplished by a volition dependent on one’s own will—which is the determinant of being an object of injunction—is absent in the case of knowledge; whereas in the case of contact, there is a distinction precisely due to the opposite being the case.

Nor should it be argued that this contradicts the statement in the third chapter [of the *Mīmāṃsāsūtra*], which holds that in the *bhakṣa-mantras* (mantras for consumption), although the portion revealing satisfaction (*tṛpti*) is not separately applied there because satisfaction is not something to be performed—being produced as a byproduct (*anuniṣpādita*) of the act—the portion revealing the act of looking (*avekṣaṇa*) is applied to that act because looking is something to be performed. For looking, in the form of contact with the sense organ, is not a byproduct like satisfaction and so forth; rather, being something to be performed, the portion revealing it is applied to it through separate distribution (*viniyoga*).

This is because [the text] has such a primary intent. As for the claim that knowledge itself is something to be enjoined—on the grounds that when there are multiple instances of the letter *ga* perceived by a single auditory organ, one observes the cognition of the desired *ga* through the desire to know (*bubhutsā*) and effort (*prayatna*)—that is not correct. For the desire to know and effort accomplish only the turning away from undesired objects; they do not produce the cognition itself.

Nor should it be argued that because the text "Whatever one performs with knowledge" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.1.10) declares knowledge to be an auxiliary (*aṅga*), and because it is impossible for that which is not enjoined to be an auxiliary, knowledge must therefore be something to be enjoined (*vidheya*). For that passage occurs within the context of the meditation on the *udgītha*, and thus the word "knowledge" (*vidyā*) therein refers to meditation (*upāsanā*); consequently, there is no contradiction in its being an auxiliary as something enjoined. Furthermore, although the Sūtra "The non-restriction of those [meditations] bound to the auxiliaries, because they are seen for that purpose" (Brahma Sūtra 3.3.59) refutes the status of an auxiliary for knowledge when it is bound to the auxiliaries of ritual action, this does not entail the loss of its status as something to be enjoined.

If it is argued that—just as the cognition of Brahman is an object of desire even though cognitions such as those of foul odors are not; just as the cognition of Brahman is accomplished by regulated unseen merit (*niyamādṛṣṭa*) even though other cognitions are not; and just as the cognition of the pole star or Arundhatī requires such effort despite the fact that the cognition of a mountain and the like does not when the eyes are opened—so too, the cognition of the extremely subtle Brahman may possibly be accomplished through desire and effort—the answer is no.

Because it is impossible to postulate an unauthoritative distinctness based on the observation of some property that is of a different class from what has been observed by authoritative means; and because effort, both in its positive and negative concomitance, is exhausted in producing the instruments of knowledge, and since examples such as the fixed stars and Arundhatī are established through other means, it is impossible—by that same logic—to assert that the knowledge of Brahman is achievable through volitional action (*kṛtisādhyatva*).

Nor should it be argued that because the knowledge of the meaning of a treatise is invariably seen to depend on a person, and since Brahman is the subject matter of such a treatise, the knowledge of Brahman must likewise depend on a person; for even in that case, it is only the means of knowledge (*jñāna-sādhana*) that depends on a person. Furthermore, as for the observation of injunctions and prohibitions regarding praiseworthy and blameworthy cognitions, that too refers exclusively to the causes of cognition. And as for the experience of the production and cessation [of cognition] through desire and so forth, that too refers exclusively to the operation of the instruments (*karaṇa-vyāpāra*).

Nor should it be argued that if you accept that meditative worship (*upāsanā*) of Brahman upon names and so forth is something to be enjoined, then its dependence on the person (*pums-tantratva*) would not be established; for even there, one could claim that dependence on the person applies only to the fixing of the mind (*mano-dhāraṇā*) and the like. This is because, since the aforementioned incongruity regarding an injunction for knowledge does not apply there, it is impossible to claim that the acts of restraint and so forth have any other purpose [than liberation].

Nor should it be argued that hearing and the rest—which consist of the aforementioned knowledge—are to be enjoined because their being accomplished through great effort is established by experience; for it has already been stated that such experience can be accounted for otherwise.

Nor should it be argued that you, by asserting that *nididhyāsana*—which consists of a continuous stream of indirect knowledge (*parokṣajñāna*)—is something to be enjoined, must necessarily admit that the individual cognitions constituting that stream are themselves enjoined, for if those were not enjoined, the injunction of the stream would be untenable; for in this case, it is merely the connection with the quality of repetition (*āvṛtti*) that is enjoined, as in the injunction "one should repeat the Upaniṣad."

Nor should it be argued that if hearing and so forth were not themselves of the nature of knowledge, then the traditional teaching (smṛti) that "hearing is the adversary of ignorance" up to the point of [the statement] "ignorance is removed by hearing," as well as the experience that "ignorance has been removed by hearing," would be untenable; for these two—the tradition and the experience—are indeed tenable, since hearing and so forth, consisting of an inquiry into the marks such as the opening statements (upakrama), function as adversaries to ignorance and the like by means of determining the intended meaning (tātparya) which is necessary for the comprehension of the sentence-meaning through the application of the quality of repetition (āvṛtti).

In passages such as "Having understood, one should practice wisdom" (*vijñāya prajñāṃ kuryāt*), it is appropriate to take the word *prajñā* as figuratively signifying "investigation" (*vicāra*), due to the aforementioned logical inconsistency regarding the injunction of knowledge (*jñāna*). Nor should it be argued that if meditation (*dhyāna*), which you accept as the enjoined object, were distinct from knowledge, it could not produce linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) regarding its own object; for such usage regarding that object is established by means of a different kind of knowledge, which must necessarily serve as its cause. Since this [additional] complexity is supported by valid evidence (*pramāṇavat*), it does not constitute a fault.

For this very reason, the experience and recollection that "I know" regarding the object of meditation are explained as being prompted by a cognition distinct from that [object]. Although the Śruti statement "from meditating upon Him" (*tasyābhidhyānāt*) indicates that meditation brings about the cessation of ignorance known as *māyā*, that statement is intended to refer to the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) that occurs immediately after meditation; thus, there is no contradiction with that [Śruti].

As for your argument that—since you yourself accept that meditation (*upāsanā*), which begins with "one should meditate" (*upāsīta*) and concludes with "he who knows thus" (*ya evaṃ veda*), is denoted by the verbal root *vid* (to know)—meditation is understood to be knowledge; and therefore, even in other instances, being knowledge does not contradict its being something to be enjoined—that is not correct. For, due to the aforementioned logical inconsistency, the root *vid* either indicates knowledge only in a secondary sense in that context, or it possesses multiple meanings as a verbal root.

Nor should it be argued that knowledge lacks independence from the person merely because it depends on [external factors] such as the recipient of a gift, since acts like giving are also seen to depend on such things; for we do not say that something is non-dependent simply because it depends on another, but rather that it is dependent when, given a certain cause, it cannot be made otherwise by the desires of the person. Thus, the claim that knowledge is dependent on the person is refuted.

Furthermore, what is this knowledge being enjoined? Is it verbal knowledge (*śābda-jñāna*), or its repeated practice (*abhyāsa*), or meditation (*dhyāna*) having a superimposed object regardless of reality, or some other form of knowledge resulting in direct perception (*aparokṣya*)? Not the first, because—just as in the ritual section (*karmakāṇḍa*)—once the connection [between word and meaning] is grasped, it is self-evident and thus not something to be accomplished by human effort, and therefore cannot be the subject of an injunction.

Nor should it be argued that even in the *karmakāṇḍa*, while knowledge produced by mere initial encounter (*āpāta*) is self-evident (*svataḥ-siddha*), knowledge produced by investigation (*vimarśa*) is something to be accomplished through effort (*kṛti-sādhya*); otherwise, the injunction for study (*adhyayana-vidhi*) or subsequent ritual injunctions would not be capable of implying such [investigation]. This is because the very inquiry that generates that [knowledge] culminates in being something to be accomplished through effort—which is the necessary condition for being an object of an injunction—and thus this [status of being accomplished through effort] is impossible even in respect to the resulting knowledge itself.

The second [alternative] is not tenable: is that [action] enjoined for the sake of liberation (*mokṣa*)? Or for the sake of direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*)? It cannot be the first, because since it would be produced by a ritual injunction (*naiyogika*), it would follow that it is non-eternal (*anityatva*), just like heaven (*svarga*) and other such results. Nor should it be argued that even if the destruction of bondage (*bandhadhvaṃsa*) were produced by an injunction, its eternality is established because it is a destruction (*dhvaṃsatva*) and because of the authority of the Śruti and other sources; for in your system, unlike in mine, liberation is not merely the destruction of bondage, but rather the attainment of another world (*lokāntaraprāpti*). In that case, the aforementioned defect remains as it was.

Nor is there permanence [of the result] based on the scriptural statement regarding non-return (*anāvṛtti-śruti*), because the scriptural passage, "Just as here the world acquired through action perishes, even so the world acquired through merit perishes in the hereafter," makes it understood that what is produced by a ritual injunction (*naiyogika*) is impermanent. Nor can this [latter] scripture be said not to convey its impermanence due to a contradiction with the former, for the latter possesses greater force as it is supported by the logical principle: "Whatever is created is impermanent."

Not the second [alternative], for is that [knowledge] one whose fruit is seen (*dṛṣṭaphalaka*) or one whose fruit is unseen (*adṛṣṭaphalaka*)? Not the first, because the direct realization (*tattvasākṣātkāra*) of reality is not observed through the practice of indirect knowledge (*parokṣajñāna*). Not the second, because such [realization] depends upon a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). For this very reason, not the third, and because meditation (*dhyāna*) lacks the nature of knowledge. Nor the fourth, because it would follow that even verbal testimony (*śabda*) lacks validity; for [verbal testimony] possesses validity only with respect to the duty to produce the knowledge that serves as the means of valid cognition regarding Brahman.

Nor can there be authority regarding Brahman by taking recourse to a "great purport" (mahātātparya), because even such knowledge, being dependent upon a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), lacks the status of being a fruit of an injunction. Therefore, since knowledge is not enjoined even in passages such as "the clarified butter is to be looked at by the wife," and since meditation (dhyāna) is established as distinct from mere intellectual comprehension (vijñāna), and since the positive and negative concomitances (anvaya-vyatireka) regarding mental effort pertain only to the means for understanding the subtle meaning of the scriptures, it is impossible to enjoin the knowledge of the Self.

Thus, since hearing (*śravaṇa*) is of the nature of knowledge (*jñāna*), its status as something to be enjoined (*vidheya*) is untenable. Therefore, it is established that hearing—which is of a different genus from knowledge, consists of inquiry (*vicāra*) in the form of a procedural requirement (*itikartavyatā*) for the words that generate immediate realization (*aparokṣajñāna*), and has reflection (*manana*) and meditative concentration (*nididhyāsana*) as its auxiliaries—is enjoined as the primary element because it serves as a subordinate means toward the comprehension of the object of knowledge (*prameya*), having immediate realization as its fruit. Thus ends the "Refutation of the Injunction of Knowledge" in the *Advaitasiddhi*.

Objection: How can a word be the generator of immediate (aparokṣa) knowledge? [Response]: If you say "because there is no proof," we say no; for there is proof in such passages as, "He understood that from him, [as he] showed the shore beyond darkness," and "Those whose purpose is well-ascertained through the realization of Vedānta. In the former passage, it is stated that the immediate knowledge which generates that [liberation] is accomplished by instruction alone; and in the second scriptural text, the word *vi* (in *vijñāna*) conveys the sense of having a specific object, while the word *su* (in *suniścita*) expresses immediacy.

Nor can the statement beginning with "He did not know" be satisfied by a mediate (parokṣa) knowledge; for, by the natural force of the subsequent sentence, "He shows the shore beyond darkness," it is established that the intention is immediate (aparokṣa) knowledge. Nor is there a figurative usage based on indirect causality—as in saying "he shows the village" to one who points out the way to the village—since such a usage is improper here as there is no sublation of its being a direct means, and because no cause other than instruction is perceived in the narrative of Nārada and Sanatkumāra.

Nor should it be argued that this contradicts such scriptural passages as "It is not to be perceived by the mind alone," for that [passage] is intended to mean one-pointed concentration of the mind (*cittaikāgrya*). Furthermore, it should not be claimed that the attainment of its immediate (*aparokṣa*) nature follows from the second sentence—which, being devoid of any suspicion of invalidity (*aprāmāṇya-śaṅkā*), implies directness—otherwise, the objects of the Vedāntas, such as the duty to investigate, would also absurdly result in being immediately perceived. This is because the absence of suspicion regarding invalidity and so forth is already obtained by the word "ascertained" (*niścita*) itself; thus, the word "well" (*su*) does not have that as its primary meaning.

Nor does it follow that anything other than Brahman, even if cognizable through the Vedāntas, would likewise attain immediacy; for the word "object" (artha) primarily refers to the subject matter of the intended meaning (tātparya), and because the state of being cognizable through the Vedāntas culminates in Brahman alone.

Thus, inference (*anumāna*) also serves as a means of knowledge (*māna*) in this regard: "Being immediate (*aparokṣatva*) resides in the cognition produced by sentences such as 'That thou art' (*tattvamasi*), because it is not the counter-positive of an absolute non-existence residing in immediate cognition, like the nature of cognition (*jñānatva*). Nor should it be argued that the probandum (*sādhya*) could likewise be established as "residing in the cognition produced by the ritual section (*karmakāṇḍa*)," for there is a distinction based on the presence or absence of a subverting argument (*bādhaka*) against the contrary position (*vipakṣa*). To explain: if the sentence "That thou art" were not a generator of immediate cognition, the cessation of immediate error would not occur.

Nor can immediate knowledge (*aparokṣajñāna*) arise through the mind alone, because the mind lacks the status of being an uncommon instrument of valid cognition (*pramākaraṇa*) anywhere; for the self is self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*), and pleasure and the like are objects known by the witness-consciousness (*sākṣivedya*). Nor should one postulate such a capacity in the mind—similar to the word's capacity to generate immediate knowledge—where it has not been established elsewhere, for if that were so, everything would have to be postulated in the mind, which would constitute a distinction without justification. Furthermore, there is no basis for such a postulation regarding the knowledge produced by the ritual section (*karmakāṇḍa*) concerning sacrifices such as the *Jyotiṣṭoma*.

In that regard, is it to be postulated for the sake of performance (*anuṣṭhāna*) or for the sake of the fruit (*phala*)? Not the first, because that [performance] is possible through indirect knowledge alone. Nor is the second, because the attainment of the fruit follows from that very performance.

Nor can it be argued that the counter-argument—"the word under dispute is not the cause of immediate cognition, because it is a word"—is valid, for it is subject to the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in cases such as "You are the tenth. Nor should it be said that even there the sense organ alone is the instrument and the word is merely its auxiliary, since we observe that in some instances, even for one devoid of eyesight in the thickest darkness, there arises through that sentence an immediate cognition—"I am the tenth"—which removes the immediate error [of not perceiving oneself]. Even where the presence of a sense organ exists, it is simply irrelevant to the process.

Nor should it be argued that, just as in cases such as "you possess dharma" or "the mountain possesses fire," there may be remoteness regarding the qualifier even when the qualificand is directly perceived—and likewise here, there may be remoteness regarding the state of being the tenth—itself—because if there were such remoteness here, it would follow that the immediate error [of not recognizing oneself as the tenth] could never be sublated.

Now, even if this were so, is the capacity of a word to produce immediate perception (*aparokṣajñāna*) inherent in it? Or is it caused by the object being immediately perceived? Not the first, because it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Nor the second, because there would be the undesirable consequence (*āpāta*) that the inferential cognition arising from such [syllogisms] as "Individual souls are not different from the Supreme Self, because they possess the nature of self," as well as the cognition of identity produced by hearing [the Upaniṣads], by secular literary works, or by the study of the Vedānta without having previously studied them, would all result in immediate perception; and thus the rule of hearing [the scriptures] and so forth would become unnecessary.

Furthermore, the immediacy (*aparokṣya*) of an object does not consist in its being of the nature of immediate cognition; for even though this [nature] exists in the case of Brahman, it is absent in cases such as "being the tenth," and because one does not observe immediacy for Maitra through verbal testimony and so forth when Caitra possesses immediate knowledge [of that same object].

Nor can it be the state of being the object of immediate (non-mediated) linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*). For if the immediacy of usage consists in its having as its object a particular thing that is itself immediate, there would be the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*). If it consists in the form "this is immediate," then such immediacy would be absent even in the case of something veiled by ignorance (*ajñāna*), since you yourself postulate the existence of a veil precisely for the sake of accounting for such usages as "it does not manifest. If it consists in the fitness for the aforementioned usage, then there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of an immediate cognition arising from a word regarding a pot hidden behind a wall. And if it consists in being produced by immediate cognition, it is already included within the alternative position to be stated later.

Therefore, it must be stated that the immediacy (*aparokṣatva*) of an object consists precisely in its being the object of immediate cognition. In that regard, if one were to define it as "being the object of this [present] cognition," there would be the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*). If, however, the intention is another cognition, then since heaven and other such things are immediate for some people, it would follow that we too would have an immediate cognition of them through verbal testimony. If the intention is a single person's perspective, then since something was previously immediate to him, it would follow that we would now have an immediate cognition of it through verbal testimony and the like.

If it is argued that when there is the intention of [knowing] fire at one and the same time, there would be direct perception (*āparokṣya*) of it through either a logical mark (*liṅga*) or a word (*śabda*), we say no. For, regarding the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) by means of which something is to be known, the cause for the direct realization of that object is its having as its content an object non-different from that [verbal cognition]; thus, there is no room for the aforementioned fault.

Nor should it be said that, in this way, the word would be included within perception; for inclusion within perception requires the status of being an instrument of perceptual valid knowledge (*pratyakṣapramākaraṇatva*) while being distinct from words whose objects are different from the object to be known.

If it is argued that the word's status as an instrument for direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) is not based on scriptural instruction—since there is no such statement in this context establishing the mind as the instrument, as there is in passages like "It is to be seen by the mind alone"—we say no. For in passages such as "I ask you about that person who is known through the Upaniṣads," the suffix *taddhita* (in *aupaniṣada*) is prescribed in the sense of "one who is proficient in that"; thus, since proficiency implies the absence of proficiency in anything else, the authority [of the word as an instrument] rests precisely upon this scriptural statement involving a *taddhita* suffix denoting proficiency.

[Objection: Even if the mind (*manas*) is an instrument (*karaṇa*), its status as being known through the Upaniṣads (*aupaniṣadatva*) is established by another means, namely the requirement of meditative reflection (*nididhyāsana*); [Reply: No, because of the denial of the mind’s status as an instrument in the passage, “That which one does not perceive with the mind” (*yanmanasā na manute*). Nor does it follow that the word (*śabda*) is also incapable of being an instrument on account of the text, “From whence words turn back”; for, in accordance with the scriptural statement regarding its being known through the Upaniṣads, that [text] intends to mean that [Brahman] is not made known by the [word’s] power (*śakti*). As it has been said: “Even the Śruti speaks with trepidation.”

Nor should it be argued that, following the third-case (instrumental) hearing in the phrase "and it is not to be seen by the mind alone," the phrase "he does not think" is similarly reinterpreted as referring to an immature mind; for even if such a similarity were granted, there is a distinction: if the mind were the instrument, one would have to postulate more [factors], whereas if the word (the Veda) is the instrument, only a few are required.

Therefore, it is established that because the sentence "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*) and others generate immediate knowledge, hearing (*śravaṇa*), which has reflection (*manana*) and other factors as its auxiliaries, is the object of an injunction of restriction for the sake of the direct realization of Brahman—which is the means to liberation consisting in the cessation of ignorance. Thus ends the proof of the possibility of immediate knowledge from words in the *Advaitasiddhi*.
Through the grace of the preceptor named Viśveśvara, Madhusūdana attained the realization of non-duality;
indeed, his splendor was woven with immeasurable virtues, making him an unfailing ground against all refutations.
The exaltation of another's virtues is unbearable when accompanied by anxious regard,
yet it results in the ultimate loss of one's own human goals when there is no regard at all.
Therefore, the wise, disregarding such ill-willed envy, act according to this principle.
Following the dictates of necessity, show honor toward my work.

Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Exposition of Hearing and Other Means," in the *Advaitasiddhi* composed by Śrī Madhusūdana Sarasvatī, disciple of the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ācārya Śrī Viśveśvara Sarasvatī. 9.

Objection: Liberation cannot indeed be the cessation of ignorance (*avidyānivṛtti*). For instance, is that [cessation] of the nature of the Self (*ātman*) or distinct from it? Not the first, because it would follow that it is not something to be accomplished (*asādhya*). In the second case as well, is it real (*satī*) or false (*mithyā*)? If the first, there is a loss of non-duality (*advaitahāni*); if the second, it follows that it is either ignorance itself or one of its effects. Reply: This is not so, because liberation is the nature of the Self as characterized (*upalakṣita*) by the final cognitive modification (*caramavṛtti*), which consists in the destruction of nescience (*ajñānahāni*). Thus, liberation is indeed something to be accomplished, precisely through the accomplishment of the characterization.
Nor does liberation cease because its defining characteristic ceases, for we observe that even when cooking has ceased, the cook does not cease to exist. As it has been said:
"The cessation of delusion is the Self characterized by the state of being known;
even upon the destruction of the characteristic, liberation occurs, as in the case of a cook and the like."

Nor does it follow that there is a loss of that [nature] even during the time of delusion, because [the nature] exists prior as well as posterior to being characterized by the function; for that which is unestablished previously cannot serve as a defining characteristic (*upalakṣaṇa*). Indeed, one is not a "cook" before the connection with cooking, nor is one so designated. As for the claim that "cook-ness" is simply the state of being an agent of cooking: in that case, the usage [of the term] when one is not currently cooking is merely figurative, based on the principle of what was previously the case (*bhūtapūrvanyāya*).

If, however, being delimited by the delimitors of the agency of cooking, or being a locus where the absolute absence of that agency does not reside, is what is meant, then both of these exist later [in the state of liberation]. Nor can it be argued that in this way, in liberation, there is nothing other than the Self such as "fitness" (*yogyatva*) and so on, since pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) exists even prior [to liberation], and thus [liberation] would result in being non-sādhya (unattainable); for if the qualification of being delimited by a mental mode (*vṛtti*) were added—as in the case of being characterized by a crow (*kākopalakṣitatva*)—then it would follow that it possesses attributes (*saviśeṣatā*). This is not so, because even though the essential nature of the object characterized (*upalakṣya-svarūpa*) is non-sādhya, the fact that the sādhya-status resides in the characterizing attribute (*upalakṣaṇa-gata-sādhyatva*) is logically consistent.

It is like the production of space within a jar; or rather, because it is accepted that the cessation of ignorance is simply a mental state (vṛtti) opposed to it, and that destruction (dhvaṃsa) is precisely that effect which opposes the production of further effects for as long as the [original] effect persists.

Nor should it be argued that even when the action has ceased, because no other contradictory effect arises, that [state] is not a destruction since destruction exists at that time as well; for its nature as such [destruction] lasts only until the arising of a contradictory effect. Just as the destruction of a disjunction, despite being of the nature of destruction, is essentially the substratum itself, so too, although destruction takes the form of a contradictory effect until the final action occurs, the destruction of that final action is essentially the substratum itself.

Now, is this process [of the removal of ignorance] elsewhere, or here [in the case of the reflection] alone? It cannot be the first, because the cessation of the ignorance regarding the identity of the original object (*bimba*) and its reflection (*pratibimba*) must itself consist in the knowledge of that identity; thus, at the time of the cognition of their identity, it would be impossible for the ignorance—which is the material cause of the delusion of their difference conditioned by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*)—to persist. Nor can it be the second, due to the absence of any restrictive rule [to the contrary].

Nor is it the case that, because the cessation [of the world] here does not exceed what is known as its substratum, the consideration of the scriptural texts on the falsity of the universe—which would entail the cessation of even that cessation—serves as a restrictive factor; for those texts, by virtue of aiming at the cessation of the entire universe through knowledge, intend the falsity of everything other than the cessation that is their own primary subject matter. If this is argued, we say no: first of all, there is no fault in the initial position, because in the case of an error conditioned by an adjunct (*upādhi*), it is precisely that [cessation] occurring at the time of the removal of the adjunct which possesses such a nature.

Nor is the second [alternative] tenable, because the *Śruti* passage "not this, not this" (*neti neti*) intends precisely the cessation of everything other than the Self according to its natural sense. Nor does it follow that liberation occurs even during the state of one liberated while living (*jīvanmukti*), on the grounds that the Self characterized by the mental mode (*vṛtti*) exists even then; for while the attainment of mere liberation is indeed desired, there is no ground for the attainment of supreme liberation, since that consists in the essential nature of the Self as characterized by the final direct realization (*carama-sākṣātkāra*).

Nor does it follow that the cessation of the direct realization of the *camara* (the yak-tail whisk) would result in its being unattainable (*asādhya*) if it were the Self, for unlike the case where non-engagement would follow if the cessation of ignorance were unattainable, such a consequence does not arise here. Nor should it be argued: "Since there is no difference in the manifestation of bliss between the mental modification (*vṛtti*) that brings about liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*) and the modification that brings about final liberation (*paramamukti*), why could it not be the case that the Self, as characterized by the final moment or the final breath, is itself liberation?
This is because we accept a specific difference in manifestation based on the presence or absence of distraction caused by *prārabdha* karma.

By this, it must be stated that the human goal (puruṣārtha) is to be accomplished through the hearing of the Vedānta and other means; yet that cannot be asserted in your view, because although the Self—consisting of the cognition of bliss permeated by liberation—is indeed the human goal, it is not something to be produced (asādhya). Even if the mental modification (vṛtti) were to be produced, it is not in itself the human goal. Therefore, one must state that the human goal is the manifestation of bliss in the form of the removal of obscuration, which is distinct from the Self and is to be accomplished by the mental modification.

And thus, the objection as to how the Self alone could be the cessation [of ignorance] is refuted; for although the fruit—the manifestation of bliss—is not to be produced in its essential nature (*svarūpataḥ*) because it consists in the attainment of what has already been attained, its status as something to be accomplished is nonetheless established by the mere fact that the mental modification (*vṛtti*) which removes the ignorance veiling it is itself to be accomplished. This is observed in cases such as gold already present in one’s own neck. Therefore, it is established that either the destruction of ignorance is the very nature of the Self, or it is the mental modification taking on the form of that [Self].

As for those positions beginning with the fifth type [of cessation], they are intended for the instruction of those of dull intellect; therefore, we do not seek to justify them. Thus ends the determination of the cessation of ignorance in the Advaitasiddhi. 1.

And although that which removes ignorance is not merely the knowledge consisting of the self-luminous nature of Brahman—since that [knowledge] is the means for establishing it—it is nevertheless that very same [Brahman] as it is mounted upon a non-conceptual mental modification (*aparokṣavṛtti*) produced by hearing (*śravaṇa*) and other means. For this very reason, the following objection is refuted: "Is it self-luminous consciousness that removes ignorance, or is it a non-conceptual modification taking its form? Not the first, because that [consciousness] exists even now."

Not the second [alternative], because it is impossible for truth to be established from what is unreal; and because, given that one experiences a contradiction with consciousness in the form of the cognition "I do not know" when there is ignorance, a contradiction with a modification (vṛtti) in the form of non-cognition is impossible; furthermore, because ignorance is never observed in relation to pleasure and the like when they are being illumined by consciousness. Moreover, just as hatred—which is removable by will—is not subject to the same rule, so too ignorance, which is removed by a modification based on its own nature, would result in the undesirable consequence of its existence without distinction; for either consciousness mounted upon a modification, or the modification bearing the reflection of consciousness, acts as the remover.

Nor is there a contradiction in the unreal producing the real, for this is possible—just as non-existence can produce existence—and because we observe that even the illusory (prātibhāsika) produces empirical (vyāvahārika) pleasure. Nor is there a contradiction with the experience of the cognition "I do not know," which appears to oppose consciousness (cit), because we do not admit that a mental modification (vṛtti) unconnected with consciousness possesses such oppositional power.

As for the claim that [the world] possesses reality like hatred, that is not so; for here too, since the capacity to remove [error] is possible—being based on the direct realization of the reality of the substrate (adhiṣṭhāna), as in the case of the cognition of mother-of-pearl—it does not follow that it possesses reality like the silver to be removed by it. Furthermore, as for the claim that there is no distinction between the final cognitive state and cognitions such as those of a pot insofar as they have consciousness as their object, that is not so; for there is a distinction based on having a delimited or an undelimited object.

As for the objection that if [the knowledge] were its own remover, there would be a contradiction with its continued existence, whereas its removal of its own material cause has never been observed—this is not so; for even that which is not observed elsewhere may be postulated here on the strength of valid evidence (*pramāṇa*). To explain: although it is understood from the statement "Know Māyā to be Prakṛti" that the realization of the true nature of the Self has Māyā as its material cause, its power to remove that very cause is established by such texts as "The knower of the Self crosses over sorrow" and "He shatters the knot of ignorance here, O gentle one. However, if the consciousness reflected in the mental modification (*vṛtti*) is the remover, then there is not even a suspicion of such an objection regarding the aforementioned words. As it has been said:

"Even this solar radiance, though it merely illuminates grass and the like, may burn that very grass by ascending upon a sun-crystal (sūryakānta); one should apply this same logic to consciousness (cit). Nor should it be argued that when there is a direct modification (aparokṣavṛtti), consciousness cannot be the remover [of ignorance] because no delay is observed in the cessation [of ignorance] based on its reflection; for since pure inert matter (jaḍa) cannot remove ignorance due to its inertness, and pure consciousness cannot do so due to its being the illuminator [rather than the agent], it is necessary that the qualified [consciousness] be the remover.

As for the claim that even the liberating knowledge does not have the pure [Brahman] as its object because that is imperceptible, nor does it have the qualified [Brahman] as its object because that would result in it being an error due to the superimposed nature of the latter—that is incorrect; for even though the qualified [Brahman] is the object, there is no error because the limiting adjunct (upādhi) is not itself the object.

As for the question: what is the remover of the final cognition? Is it itself, or something else? Not the first, because if that which is its own counter-positive were to produce its own destruction independently of anything else, it would follow that it is momentary; for even a fire that has consumed its wood is destroyed only by the will of the Lord and so forth. Nor does the powder of *kataka* destroy the mud, nor does it destroy itself, since we observe only their separation. Not the second.

It might be argued that [the pure Self] cannot be the cause of anything because it is not a causal factor for even the slightest thing, and because everything else has ceased to exist; however, this is not so. For we observe that the destruction of the threads is the cause of the destruction of the cloth, and thus it is the destruction of ignorance—which is its own material cause—that brings about the destruction of that [superimposition]. Nor should it be said: "In the case of the destruction of ignorance, is it the Self as characterized by it that is destroyed, or the mental modification (*vṛtti*)? In the first case, the pure [Self] would not be the cause; in the second case, the result would merely be that the counter-positive itself is the destroyer. This objection is invalid in either case, because by taking the *vṛtti* into account, Brahman is conditioned (*upahita*) and thus lacks purity.

For momentariness consists in the fact that, with respect to its status as a counter-positive (*pratiyogitva*), the counter-positive is independent of anything else in its capacity to cause destruction. If it were to depend on a cause under a different limiting condition (*rūpāntarāvacchedena*), then it would not be so; for in that case, the causality of destruction belonging to itself—defined by the state of being the destruction of its own material cause (*upādānanāśatva*)—would fail to entail momentariness. This is because it is logically possible for the counter-positive, which is independent of a second cause, to possess a dual-defined causality of destruction, namely, that which is delimited both by its status as a counter-positive and by its nature as the destruction of its material cause.

In reality, since the cessation of ignorance (*avidyānivṛtti*) is of the nature of a mental modification (*vṛtti*), there is no room for the refutation of that which effects its cessation; and since the cessation of that modification is of the nature of the Self (*ātmarūpa*), there is likewise no room for the refutation of that which produces it. Thus, everything is clear. This concludes the second section, "The Determination of the Remover of Ignorance," in the *Advaitasiddhi*.
Now, in your view, liberation is not merely the cessation of suffering, but also the manifestation of unsurpassed bliss. As it has been said:
"Therefore, the destruction of ignorance is considered the supreme human goal because of the realization of eternal bliss and the total eradication of suffering."

In this regard, the nature of happiness itself is not the human goal (*puruṣārtha*), because we do not observe a desire such as "May I be happy" in the form "May happiness exist," since being a human goal is determined by desire. Otherwise, even the destruction of the self established in the Buddhist school and so forth would be a human goal. For this very reason, the happiness of another person is not a human goal, due to the absence of such a desire and because it would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*).

If it is argued that the status of being a human goal (*puruṣārthatva*) applies to pleasure even when it belongs to another, and the status of not being a human goal applies to something else even when it belongs to oneself—since there is no difference in its being desired—and since one can likewise imagine such a status for pleasure itself; and if it is further argued that because suffering and its causes are seen to be non-human goals precisely by virtue of belonging to oneself, pleasure and the like must also be human goals in that same way—[we reply]: No. For the status of being a human goal in respect to pleasure and the like is caused neither by belonging to another nor by belonging to oneself, as that would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*).

However, because it is being directly realized, and because its presence is unavoidable—just as in the case of the dependence on the means for proving the impermanence of a relationship—it cannot be said that even for God, the happiness of those such as ourselves would constitute a human goal (pumartha). This is because "being unknown as something to be abandoned" is also a necessary factor there; and since the happiness of the self and so forth is known by God and others precisely as something to be abandoned, and because this is accepted as the case regarding intrinsic happiness (svarūpasukha).

Nor is this a point of weight, for even one who maintains that the human goal consists in [bliss] as something related to oneself must necessarily describe it in such a way in order to exclude the status of a human goal from bliss that remains latent.

As for the objection that, even if liberation is a human goal (puruṣārtha) by virtue of being one's own upon direct realization, it would follow that it is not a human goal for the liberated person himself since he consists of the direct realization of bliss; or, if one's own self is a human goal by virtue of its non-connection with anything other than itself, it would follow that a transmigrating soul would have a human goal through the bliss of the liberated state, because that bliss is not connected to anyone other than the transmigrator—that is not so. For it is precisely by virtue of being directly realized that something constitutes a human goal.

Although the direct realization of liberation is a human goal (puruṣārtha) for one who is liberated, it is not so for a transmigrating being (saṃsārin), because [liberation] does not appear to him; or, if it were to appear, it would follow as an undesired consequence that he is no longer a transmigrator. As for the claim that happiness is a human goal by virtue of its appearing to the self (pratyak-prakāśamānatvena), that too is explained away by this very argument, since "appearing to the self" is said to mean nothing other than being directly realized (sākṣātkriyamāṇatā).

As for the claim that pleasure, which manifests as happiness, is the goal of human life (puruṣārtha), and that this does not exist in liberation according to the opponent's view—that is incorrect; for since the over-extension [of the definition] is already avoided by the mere fact of its being directly realized, any further statement would only result in unnecessary complexity.

Now, to whom does this liberation belong as the goal of man? Is it to the "I-sense" (ahamartha), or rather to pure consciousness (cinmātra)? Not the first, because in your own view, the "I-sense" is not connected with liberation. Nor the second, because one never experiences a desire such as "May I be pure consciousness," in the same way that one desires "May I be liberated. This is not so, because it has already been stated that liberation is possible as the goal of man for that aspect of consciousness residing within the "I-sense" which persists until the time of liberation.

Nor should it be argued that if bliss were merely the absence of suffering, it would lack human purpose (apumarthatva) as in the liberation of the Vaiśeṣikas; or that if it were something additional [to the absence of suffering], it would entail duality (sadvitīyatva). For even if it exceeds the mere absence of suffering, it does not exceed the Self. Nor should it be argued that if the Self were solely bliss or solely luminosity, it would lack human purpose due to the absence of either bliss or luminosity; or that if it possessed both natures, its status as an impartite reality (akhaṇḍārthatva) would be lost. This is because bliss and luminosity are of the nature of a single Self, and thus the very state of "bothness" does not exist.

Nor is the simultaneous usage of the terms "bliss" (*sukha*) and "manifestation" (*prakāśa*) untenable due to a lack of difference in meaning; for that usage is justified by the distinction between the objects of exclusion (*vyāvartya*), namely the nature of suffering and insentience (*jaḍa-ātmatva*) as imagined through ignorance (*avidyā*). As for the objection that if bliss—which is the absence of suffering—were truly different from suffering, it would constitute a departure from established doctrine (*apasiddhānta*), whereas if they were non-different, it would fail to serve human ends (*apuruṣārthatā*): that is not so. Since suffering is merely imagined, its difference [from bliss] shares the same status as suffering itself; because that difference lacks ultimate reality, there is no departure from established doctrine.

As for the objection that, although bliss which is self-luminous manifests by itself, it cannot be the goal of man because the absence of suffering does not manifest, that is not so; for since the absence of suffering is not distinct from the Self, it manifests as well when bliss—which is non-different from the Self—manifests. Furthermore, it has already been stated that the failure to manifest in its true nature (as the absence of suffering) is irrelevant. Therefore, bliss non-different from self-luminous consciousness is the goal of man. Thus is established that pure consciousness alone is the possessor of liberation.
Thus, in the Advaitasiddhi, it has been established that liberation is a human goal by virtue of its being of the nature of bliss. || 3 ||

And this is established by the self-experience of those liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*). A person liberated while living is one whose ignorance has been removed by the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), yet for whom the appearance of the body and so forth continues. Nor does it follow that the body must fall immediately upon the destruction of ignorance through the knowledge of reality; for just as fear and trembling may persist due to residual impressions (*saṃskāra*) even after the delusion of a snake has ceased, and just as the spinning of a wheel persists even after the contact with the stick has ceased, the persistence of its effects is possible even when ignorance has been removed, because of the persistence of residual impressions.

Nor should it be said that the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) belongs only to action and knowledge and not to anything else; for we observe the fragrance of flowers in a flower-casket even after the flowers have been removed. Furthermore, there is the following inference: "The destruction under discussion is pervaded by a latent impression, because, while being distinct from the destruction of a latent impression, it is a destruction, like the destruction of knowledge. Thus, although a latent impression is an effect, like cessation (*dhvaṃsa*), it is without a material cause (*nirupādānaka*); and like ignorance (*avidyā*), it rests upon the pure Self (*śuddhātman*) and therefore does not depend on ignorance.

Nor should it be argued that for the persistence of the effects of existence superimposed [upon Brahman]—such as the body of residual impressions (*saṃskāra-deha*) and their causes like *prārabdha*-karma—the persistence of the ignorance that is their material cause would necessarily follow; for we observe the persistence of things in a state of destruction even without an inherent cause (*samavāyi-kāraṇa*). Nor should it be asked how there can be persistence over many moments when there is only persistence for a single moment; for once a sufficient explanation exists, the postulation of a series of moments is not a necessary requirement.

In that case, there is stability for only a moment, because [the cause] at an equal time does not produce [the effect]; however, here, the cause—conjoined with the absence of an obstacle—is absent for that duration. For this very reason, the objection—"How can that which is superimposed and has not been removed by a prior cognition be removed by a [subsequent cognition] whose object is no more than that?"—is refuted, because there is a distinction based on whether the absence of an obstacle acts as a cooperative factor or not.

The production of the manifestation of bliss during the state of liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*) is indeed desirable; for once the reality is known, the persistence of defects is possible through sublation, just as in the case of a double moon and the like. Nor is there a discrepancy here on the grounds that defects cannot be removed by knowledge, as was the case in that [other] instance; for even here, a defect that cannot be removed by knowledge is possible so long as an obstacle remains, since no such defect exists anywhere that cannot be removed by any knowledge whatsoever. As it has been said: "Indeed, there is no defect that exists by its very nature."

Alternatively, the persistence of the body and so forth occurs due to the persistence of a trace (*leśa*) of ignorance (*avidyā*). Now, one might object: "A 'trace' is not a part, because ignorance is partless; for this very reason, the claim that ignorance remains for a time according to the analogy of a burnt cloth is also refuted, since this analogy is impossible in the case of something partless. We reply: No, for the word 'trace' refers simply to a particular form (*ākāra*), since scripture—such as "Indra is perceived in many forms through his powers of illusion" (*indro māyābhiḥ pururūpa īyata*)—reveals that ignorance possesses multiple forms.

Even when the substrate ceases, the form persists, just as the universal persists even when the individual instance ceases. Now, what is this so-called "form" (ākāra)? Is it the universal (jāti), or a property (dharma) consisting of power (śakti) and so forth, or a particular state (avasthāviśeṣa) like that of gold and its earring? It cannot be the first two, because if those two were the material cause (upādāna) for the delusion of the body and so forth, they would necessarily result in being ignorance (avidyā); whereas if they were not the material cause, the delusion of the body and so forth could not arise due to the absence of any other material cause. Furthermore, since it must necessarily be either ignorance or its effect—given that it is distinct from the Self and is removable by knowledge—it follows that it is indeed ignorance.

Nor is the third [alternative] possible, because of the impossibility of persistence without that which persists. If it be argued that this is not so, because it is impossible for a state to persist without that which possesses the state, we reply: no. For even though the power of ignorance—which possesses manifold capacities—namely, the power that causes the delusion of ultimate reality and so forth regarding the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), and the power that produces causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) within the phenomenal world, have both ceased through the direct realization of truth (*tattvasākṣātkāra*) occurring simultaneously with *prārabdha* karma, nevertheless, the power that generates the appearance of objects capable of immediate perception continues to persist; and ignorance, possessing that [power], likewise [persists].

It remains indeed; thus, there is no room for the aforementioned objection. Nor can it be asked how one is designated as "liberated" while ignorance still exists? It is because of the mere destruction of its power (*śakti*). Therefore, at the proper time, there is the destruction of all-powerful ignorance by means of a cognition of the same nature that is unobstructed. Thus says the Śruti: "From meditating upon Him, from union with Him, and from becoming His very essence, there is, moreover, at the end, the cessation of the entire illusion (*māyā*)."

Nor should it be argued that this scripture does not serve as an authority regarding the persistence of even a trace [of ignorance] because of its connection with the word "no more" (*na ca bhūyaḥ*); for the connection of the substantive (*viśeṣya*) is more important than the connection of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), and furthermore, such an inverted construction is untenable due to its separation from the phrase "from the state of reality" (*tattvabhāvāt*) and because of the redundancy of the word "end" (*anta*).

Nor should it be argued that there is a circular dependency—namely, that the persistence of the residual trace (leśa) depends on the continuation of karma, and the persistence of the residual trace depends on the obstruction of knowledge by that [karma]—because, first, with respect to its cognition (*jñapti*), the persistence of the residual trace is already understood from such scriptural passages as, "And again at the end, there is the cessation of all illusion" (*bhūyaścānte viśvamāyānivṛtti*); nor does it apply to its existence (*sthiti*), because there is no fault since they exist simultaneously.

Alternatively, "leśa" (residue) refers to the subtle state of ignorance. Just as it is accepted in the *Vārttika*: "Therefore, for one engaged in the fruit [of action] through sacrifice and the like, there is merely a potency; even at the time of the production of the animal and so forth, the *apūrva* is not distinct from that," whereby—even though the sacrifice has passed away—an *apūrva* in the form of the subtle state of the sacrifice is admitted as that which effects the status of being a means (*sādhanatā*) for the sacrifice; likewise, even though ignorance has passed away, its residue in the form of a subtle state is accepted as being conducive to the perception of the body and so forth, just as in the case of the scripture that apprehends the capacity to produce heaven.

Because the scriptural texts on liberation while living (jīvanmukti) accept such a meaning, liberation while living is therefore more appropriately established through the persistence of a trace of ignorance (avidyā-leśa). Thus ends the "Establishment of Liberation While Living" in the Advaitasiddhi. 4.

As for the claim in the opponent’s view—that even for one possessing direct knowledge (*aparokṣajñāna*), if there is an absence of devotion that has reached its highest limit and is the cause of the supreme bliss appropriate to oneself, then due to the absence of the grace of the Lord (*īśvaraprasāda*) which is accomplished by that devotion, the persistence of *saṃsāra* through *prārabdha*-karma constitutes *jīvanmukti*; whereas if that [devotion] exists, then due to the presence of grace, liberation (*mukti*) occurs in the form of the manifestation of the essential bliss of one's own nature—which is inherently devoid of the states of low or high—characterized by the cessation of all suffering without remainder—that is not correct, because of such scriptural texts as "For him, the delay is only so long" (*tāvadevāsya ciram*).

For it has been established that for one who has realized the truth (*tattva-sākṣātkāra*), only the exhaustion of *prārabdha-karma* remains to be awaited for the attainment of liberation (*kaivalya*); thus, it is impossible to assert a dependence upon the grace of God (*īśvara-prasāda*). Furthermore, the *Smṛtis*, *Purāṇas*, and other such texts are intended as mere praise (*stuti*) when they contradict the *Śruti*.

"Only he whom this [Self] chooses can attain Him; to him this Self reveals its own form. Since it is taught here that even the grace of the Lord, which arises from devotion, is useful only for the purpose of attaining direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of Him, the Smṛtis and other texts must also follow this principle. There is no evidence for the reverse relationship—that grace is the means to liberation—because the exhaustion of *prārabdha* karma is accomplished through experience alone, independent of grace. Grace is not employed for the exhaustion of *prārabdha* karma, as that is established simply by experiencing the fruits of such karma.

Nor is there a state of high or low in liberation, because such a distinction depends upon a second entity and is therefore impossible at that time; furthermore, this is supported by the scriptural text stating, "He attains the highest equality. If liberation were subject to degrees of excellence, it would be non-eternal like heaven and other such states, and one would experience suffering, aversion, and so forth upon seeing something superior.

Is it not the case that the absence of gradation in liberation is due either to the non-existence of difference, or to the equality of difference even when it exists? It cannot be the first, because difference is established by scripture.
