Nor can it be the latter; for as to this equality, does it pertain to the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*), or only among the individual souls themselves? It cannot be the first, because between those two there is a gradation based on their being all-pervading versus atomic, the state of being the subordinate and the superior, independence versus dependence, and so forth. Furthermore, [if they were equal], it would follow that there are multiple lords, which would render the activity of the world impossible.

Furthermore, this is because it would contradict the Smṛtis that establish the gradations of non-duality, the Sūtras such as "excluding the activity of governing the world," and the inferences that apprehend superiority and inferiority. Nor is the latter [position] tenable; for Lakṣmī is the sovereign (śeṣin) with respect to the individual souls (jīvas), and since other souls are inferior to Viṣvaksena and others who are the controllers over them, [as stated in] Taittirīya and other Śrutis beginning with "She is the very essence of bliss":
"O great sage, among even millions of liberated Siddhas, one who is solely devoted to Nārāyaṇa and whose self is perfectly tranquil is extremely rare."

If it is argued that there is a contradiction with the Smṛtis beginning with "Thus," and with the inferences supported by Śruti and reasoning stated in Sūtras such as "The participation in increase and decrease [is possible] because of being included within [the Supreme], due to the consistency of both," we say no; for since there is no difference [between the individual soul and the Supreme], gradation is not established. Furthermore, that we have already explained how the Śruti and other texts do not intend to establish difference. As for the refutation offered after raising the second alternative, that is an untimely display of bravado; for if difference exists, there can be no supreme identity consisting of non-difference, and if that [identity] exists, difference itself is absent.

Furthermore, does this statement regarding gradation refer to supreme liberation (*paramamukti*), or to non-supreme liberation consisting of residence in the world of Brahmā (*brahmaloka*) and so forth? It cannot be the first, because in the final section of the third chapter of the *Brahma-sūtras*—specifically in the sūtra "Thus there is no restriction regarding the fruit of liberation, because that state is determined" (*evaṃ muktiphalāniyamastadavasthāvadhṛteḥ*)—having raised the doubt that there might be gradation even in liberation, as there are distinctions such as being attained in this life or the next pertaining to knowledge (as stated in the preceding sūtra, "Even [the result] may be in this life, provided there is no obstacle to what is intended, for that is seen"), such gradation is explicitly denied. As for the second alternative, it would entail an undesirable consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*).

As for the argument that the enjoyment of a liberated soul is inferior to the enjoyment of the Lord because it is an enjoyment of a soul, like the enjoyment of one in saṃsāra; in this same way, the formal argument (prayoga) should be inferred by taking the knowledge and other attributes of the soul as the subject (pakṣa). The bliss of the Lord is superior to the bliss of the soul because it is the bliss of the controller, whatever is thus is so, just as the bliss of the master is superior to the bliss of the servant.

[The opponent argues: "Īśvara possesses an excellence of essential nature, such as bliss, superior to that of the individual soul (jīva), because while desiring that [excellence], he is capable of attaining it; for whoever, while desiring something, is capable of attaining it, possesses it—just as is commonly accepted. Such arguments are intended to prove gradation [in the nature of bliss]. [Reply: That is not so. Regarding the first [reason], since the liberated soul is of the very nature of Brahman, there is no individual-soul-hood (jīvatva) produced by limiting adjuncts (upādhi); thus, the locus [of the reason] is unestablished (āśrayāsiddhi). Furthermore, because [the liberated soul] lacks the status of Īśvara, the probandum (sādhya) is unestablished (sādhyāprasiddhi), and the reason itself is unestablished in its own nature (svarūpāsiddhi).

In the second inference, if the proof of gradation is intended for the time of the division between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*), it is a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*). If it is intended for a time other than that, the aforementioned defect does not cease. This is because scriptures such as "This is the bliss... state that there is a gradation consisting of each subsequent state being a hundredfold of the preceding, starting from human bliss up to the bliss of Brahman; however, since these refer to gradation through limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), it is impossible to assert such gradation in the unconditioned bliss of the essential nature (*svarūpa-ānanda*).

By this, the following argument is refuted: "The cessation of bondage under discussion is based on a substratum that possesses a gradation relative to its own counter-correlate (the bondage), because it is a cessation of bondage, like the cessation of shackles. This is because gradation belongs to a genus residing in qualities (*guṇa*), and thus it is impossible to predicate it of the Self, which is the substratum of the cessation of bondage.

For this very reason, the attempt to prove a gradation inherent in the cessation itself is also discarded; for since both parties agree that bliss (*ānanda*) is the very nature (*svarūpa*) of the Self, it lacks the status of a quality (*guṇa*), and therefore it is impossible to assert such gradation even with respect to that [cessation].

By this, the following objection is refuted: that although there is no disparity in the number or dimension of the innate blisses (*svarūpa-sukha*) because each is singular and atomic, there is nevertheless a disparity in their essential nature (*svarūpa-kṛta-vaiṣamya*) within liberation—just as there is between the bliss produced by drinking water and the bliss produced by drinking nectar, or like the degrees of sweetness and sweeter-taste; for even though in worldly pleasure there is a gradation caused by the relative excellence of its means, such gradation does not exist in the bliss of the essential nature.

Nor is there a contradiction with established tradition in asserting that liberation as *sālokya* (residing in the same world) and so forth is inferior to liberation as *sāyujya* (union) and so forth; for this is logically consistent insofar as they constitute forms of higher and lower liberation. The designation of superiority regarding liberation as *sāyujya* and so forth is based merely on the absence of inferiority. Now, it may be argued that *sāyujya* does not mean identity.

This is because, despite the existence of difference, the term *sāyujya* (union) is mentioned in such scriptural passages as "He attains union and residence in the same world with the Moon"; because in texts such as "Having entered the Supreme Self, they remain outside while still united," only the entry of those who are *sayuj* (united) is mentioned; because the word *yuja* denotes a relationship, as in the etymology "the state of being *sayuj* is *sāyujya*"; and because the word *yoga*, which signifies relationship, is employed for *sāyujya* in the Smṛti: "Sālokya, Sāmīpya, Sārūpya, and Yoga [are the four types of liberation]."

If it is argued that what is called *sāyujya* (union) is merely a state of close contact—like that of milk and water, or like a deity possessing another body—and not actual identity, we say no; for since such contact with the all-pervading Lord is eternally established, it cannot constitute a human goal (*apuruṣārtha*). Nor can this contact between a living soul residing in this world and a Lord residing in another world, limited by a non-worldly body, be something to be accomplished, according to the Vedic scripture: "In this very place, one attains Brahman."

Just as the attainment of the world of Brahmā (brahmaloka) is a goal to be accomplished through such means as departing from the body and traveling upward, so too is supreme liberation—the non-difference of the individual soul (jīva), which is limited by adjuncts (upādhi), from the unlimited Brahman. This is because [supreme liberation] lacks the nature of a fruit pertaining to the next world; furthermore, in passages such as "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme," the attainment (avāpti) is of the very nature of Brahman, and therefore union (sāyujya) must also be accepted as being of that same nature.

In cases such as "union with the moon" (*candramasaḥ sāyujyam*), there is no inconsistency—unlike the impossibility of identifying that which is delimited by one limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) with that which is delimited by another—and furthermore, since an objection has already been stated against accepting the conventional meaning, the word *sāyujya* here intends the absence of differentiation.

As for the claim that—because the term *akāmahata* (one who is not overcome by desire) is used in every successive statement that reveals a hundredfold increase in bliss—there must be a gradation even within the bliss of one liberated and free from desire, just as there is in human bliss; that is not so. For it is logically consistent with the scriptural statement, "Other beings subsist on a mere fraction of this very bliss," that all worldly forms of bliss are included within the supreme bliss. It does not mean that the bliss of each respective person free from desire is limited to that specific amount, such that a gradation would have to be postulated even therein.

And thus, there is no contradiction with such Vedic texts as "He enjoys all desires" and "Make me immortal there where the desires of desire are attained," nor with the statement in the *Brahmāṇḍa-purāṇa* that "He is indeed liberated when he is not struck by desire."

Now, if a single *śrotriya* is being referred to in every instance, then multiple human pleasures and so forth—each increased a hundredfold with certainty (*sāvadhāraṇa*)—would be contradictory within one person. If they are distinct individuals, then since the quality of "being unassailed by desire" (*akāmahatatva*) and so on is heard to be uniform [in all cases], it would lack the capacity to distinguish between them, making a systematic gradation of bliss impossible. Therefore, for the sake of establishing this gradation, the term "desireless" (*akāma*) must be taken as referring to one who desires that specific state, while the term "desiring" (*kāma*) refers to one who desires something other than it; however, in that case, there would be the fault of assuming what is not stated in the text (*aśrutakalpanā*) and the sublation of the literal meaning (*bādha*).

If it is argued that a desireless mendicant has no experience of the bliss of Indra or other such states—whether in the position of Indra or the position of a king—and therefore, after the previous passage of the Śruti has stated the gradation among those who are not liberated, the subsequent passage beginning with “And of one who is learned in the Vedas” (*śrotriyasya ca*) and “And he who is learned in the Vedas” (*yaśca śrotriyaḥ*) speaks of that [bliss] regarding the liberated one; we say no. For although the liberated one who is untouched by desire is one and the same in all these passages, since all forms of bliss are included within his bliss, it is he alone who must be mentioned in each respective instance of bliss being described.

It is referred to [as such] because its designation as Indra and so forth is appropriate everywhere due to its equality with them, according to the maxim: "That which has entered more does not lose its original nature. For in the case of equality, the relevant factor is the possession of properties belonging to that same class, and not also the non-possession of properties other than those, on account of the resulting complexity (*gaurava*).

As for the argument that liberation is characterized by mutual gradations because its means possess mutual gradations, like [other] accepted cases—that is not so, because it is unproven (*asiddhi*). Now, one might object: "In the view that liberation is accomplished through dying at Prayāga, hatred toward the Lord, and so forth, and in the view that it is accomplished through the combination of knowledge and action (*jñāna-karma-samuccaya*), there is no lack of proof, since the means such as dying at Prayāga and the duties of caste and stage of life (*varṇāśrama-dharma*) are inherently unequal."

Even according to the view that [liberation] is to be accomplished solely through knowledge (*jñāna*), the fact that the knowledge of Brahman—which resides in gods, humans, and others, and which is the cause of liberation—is to be accomplished by hearing many and even more numerous scriptural branches (*śākhā*) and has as its object many and even more numerous attributes, is established by such scriptural passages as: "O God, who other than I is able to know that Lord who is both intoxicated and free from intoxication? and "Indeed, all qualities are to be meditated upon by Brahmā alone, not by other gods, much less by all human beings," as well as by such traditional texts (*smṛti*) as: "Brahmā knows that, but even he does not know it perfectly; how then could other gods, great sages, or mortals [know it]? Thus, even if one holds that [liberation] is achieved through knowledge alone, the knowledge of Brahman—the cause of liberation for those among gods and humans—possesses a vast and increasingly extensive range of attributes, being attainable only through the study of many and even more numerous branches of scripture.

If it is argued that its establishment occurs through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) even without [explicit] scriptural connection (*yoga*), we say no; for on either the view of action alone or the view of their combination, liberation would result in being non-eternal due to being achievable through action, which contradicts such scriptural passages as "There is no other path. Furthermore, regarding the third alternative, the cited scriptures are intent upon demonstrating the rarity of the knowledge of Brahman, and do not establish that it is achievable through the aforementioned means. Nor can its establishment be achieved through presumptive testimony, because the direct realization of Brahman, having the attributeless (*nirguṇa*) as its object, cannot possibly have attributes as its object. As for that which was said—
He for whom one prays for blessings is not a servant; he is indeed a merchant.
He alone is the servant, and he alone is the master; they both are seekers of virtue, not seekers of desire.

[Objection: It has been argued that because the *Smṛti* states, "One who is not desirous of liberation is better than one who is desirous of liberation, provided he possesses exclusive devotion," it follows that a devotee who does not seek liberation (*amumukṣu*) is superior to a devotee who seeks liberation (*mumukṣu*). Furthermore, since this superiority is established by worldly custom, and because the *Smṛti* states, "Devotion is weightier than [even] perfection" (*bhaktiḥ siddher garīyasī*), it follows that devotion—which is the cause of a higher form of liberation—is superior even to the liberation accomplished through slight devotion. [Reply: That is not so. What has been established regarding the weightiness of that devotion which belongs to one who does not desire fruits—such as in the passage beginning with "He who [desires] no blessings"—due to a longing for the [divine] qualities (*guṇa*), refers specifically to [its role] in the direct realization of Reality (*tattva-sākṣātkāra*).

This brings about swiftness, but it does not imply a gradation in liberation. Even the "greater weight" established by such statements as "Devotion to the Perfected One" (Gītā 7.17) exists merely because it generates that [swift attainment], just as a father is greater than a son. As for the verse:
"But others, knowing this not thus, worship having heard from others;
they too, being devoted to what they have heard, surely cross over death."
By the word "also" (api) here, [it is meant]:
"Women, Vaiśyas, and likewise Śūdras—even they attain the supreme goal;
how much more so the meritorious Brāhmaṇas, as well as devoted royal sages!"

Regarding the claim that "in this context, through the principle of *kaimutya* (the 'how much more so' argument) and by means of the gradation of the means (*sādhana*), there arises a cognition of that [gradation] in the end-result (*sādhya*)," that is not correct. For the connection of the phrase "even in crossing" (*taraṇe 'pi*) is not with the means, but rather with the qualified person (*adhikārī*). Thus, since the point culminates merely in the connection with the result in the form of a delayed crossing, and since even the *kaimutya* argument is justified simply by the attainment of the result of speed, the mere gradation of the means does not necessitate a gradation of the result. Indeed, a gradation in the jar is never observed to follow from a gradation in the stick. As for the statement:
"By the excellence of the means, they shall attain an excellent end-result"—[this is also not established].
Brahmā and the others are mentioned in sequence, just as they are heard in the Ānanda-śruti.

As for the claim that [the statement] "Thus in the *Brāhma* [Upaniṣad]: 'Superior is your knowledge, and superior is your goal'"—and likewise in the *Mokṣadharma*, where that statement occurs regarding the goal according to the gradation of the means—that is not correct. For the superiority of the goal based on the excellence of the means pertains to the state of non-supreme liberation (*aparamamukti*). Furthermore, even the mention of superiority in knowledge refers to the cognition concerning the Saguna Brahman which serves as the cause for direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*). Therefore, the gradation of the means held by others—which is based on the fact that meditations such as the *Dahara-vidyā* concern a greater or lesser number of qualities—is also explained in this same way; thus, there is no fault whatsoever.
Therefore, liberation is the attainment of the bliss of one's own nature, which consists of the self-luminous Self; in that regard, there can be no gradation whatsoever. (1)
Thus ends the refutation of gradation in liberation in the Advaitasiddhi.
He who, disregarding all the gods, was chosen by Lakṣmī alone according to her own will;
he who, merely being remembered, constantly protects everyone with his whole being;
and he who, having severed the crocodile with his discus, liberated the great elephant—[to that Viṣṇu, salutations].
Salutations to that Viṣṇu who, even out of anger, bestows his own abode upon [his devotee].
Victorious are the illustrious Mādhava Sarasvatīs, the best among self-controlled ascetics, by whose grace we have become thoroughly proficient in the meaning of the scriptures. (3)
May the virtuous ones like you grant even a single glance of compassionate vision— spontaneous, straightforward, long-reaching through love, and purifying all.
For once made the object of such a gaze, even one who is somehow fallen becomes instantly pure and holy.
May this work of mine, setting aside its faults, be possessed of excellent virtues. 4.
Through the greatness of my gurus, through my acquaintance with various branches of knowledge, and through the Veda,
there has arisen within me a perfect realization of the bliss of the Supreme Brahman, which pacifies all misfortunes.
Therefore, all of this has been placed with the utmost effort within this treatise. || 5 ||
In this world, a wretched man of poor intellect, claiming to speak the truth about what is not the truth,
loudly prattles forth a spurious refutation at an inappropriate time;
what learned person would offer a reply to such a one?
For a lion does not merely imitate the howl of a village dog.
